### DLL Loading Behavior

- **Common DLL preloading effect** — commonly used DLLs are often already loaded in memory. _Why:_ this reduces the likelihood that a duplicate malicious DLL with the same name will be loaded later. _[GCFA p.80]_
- **Windows DLL load check order** — Windows checks whether a DLL is already loaded in memory before searching for it on disk. _Why:_ this behavior affects which DLL names are practical hijack targets. _[GCFA p.80]_
- **Obscure DLL targeting** — hijacked DLLs are often less common DLLs. _Why:_ obscure DLLs are less likely to already be resident in memory, making disk-based hijacking more viable. _[GCFA p.80]_
- **Duplicate-name preemption** — if the intended DLL name is already loaded, an attacker’s duplicate DLL on disk may not be loaded. _Why:_ memory-resident modules can prevent the malicious replacement from taking effect. _[GCFA p.80]_

### Follow-On Tradecraft

- **Code injection pairing** — DLL hijacking is often combined with code injection. _Why:_ injected code can provide another detection path back to the suspicious DLL or process. _[GCFA p.80]_
- **Command-and-control beaconing pairing** — DLL hijacking is often paired with C2 network beaconing. _Why:_ outbound network behavior can expose malware that was initially loaded through a hijack. _[GCFA p.80]_
- **Network activity from hijacked code** — code loaded through hijacking may contact remote systems. _Why:_ network connections are detectable artifacts that can lead investigators back to the loaded DLL. _[GCFA p.80]_
- **Named pipe creation** — hijacked code may create named pipes. _Why:_ named pipes can be anomalous interprocess communication artifacts during endpoint analysis. _[GCFA p.80]_
- **Process injection by hijacked code** — hijacked code may inject into other processes. _Why:_ injection can reveal attacker behavior even when the initial DLL load is subtle. _[GCFA p.80]_
- **Anomalous behavior as pivot** — many abnormal actions can lead investigators back to a DLL in an unusual location. _Why:_ behavioral detections can uncover the original hijack mechanism. _[GCFA p.80]_
- **Ultimate hijack discovery path** — suspicious post-load behavior can help identify the DLL hijack itself. _Why:_ analysts may first detect network, pipe, or injection activity before tracing it to the hijacked DLL. _[GCFA p.80]_

### Forwarded-Function Detection

- **Matt Green detection idea** — Matt Green of the Velociraptor project proposed a detection method for certain DLL hijacks. _Why:_ the method focuses on structural relationships between DLLs rather than only file paths. _[GCFA p.80]_
- **Proxying legitimate DLL functions** — in many hijacks, the malicious DLL must forward legitimate function requests to the original DLL. _Why:_ proxying lets the legitimate program keep working while attacker code also runs. _[GCFA p.80]_
- **Forwarded functions in malicious DLLs** — malicious DLLs can implement forwarded functions to pass calls onward. _Why:_ this is a practical way for attacker DLLs to preserve expected application behavior. _[GCFA p.80]_
- **Legitimate forwarded functions** — forwarded DLL functions can occur in benign software. _Why:_ analysts should treat forwarding as suspicious only in the right context, not as automatically malicious. _[GCFA p.80]_
- **Rare same-name cross-location forwarding** — it is unusual for two DLLs with the same name but different paths to forward functions to each other. _Why:_ this uncommon pattern can indicate hijacking. _[GCFA p.80]_
- **WinSxS exception context** — same-name DLL forwarding is especially suspicious outside locations such as `WinSxS`. _Why:_ `WinSxS` can contain legitimate side-by-side component behavior that may otherwise resemble the pattern. _[GCFA p.80]_
- **Velociraptor VQL detection** — Velociraptor includes VQL intended to search for this same-name, different-location forwarding pattern. _Why:_ a reusable query gives analysts a scalable way to hunt for this class of hijack. _[GCFA p.80]_

### WMI Event Consumer Backdoors

- **WMI event consumer backdoor** — Windows Management Instrumentation can be abused to watch for a defined event and then launch attacker-controlled code when that event occurs. _Why:_ this creates a persistence path that activates automatically from system events. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **WMI trigger model** — WMI supports trigger definitions, called filters, that evaluate whether a chosen condition has occurred. _Why:_ the filter is the activation logic for the backdoor. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **WMI execution action** — When a WMI filter condition is met, WMI can run a script or executable through an event consumer. _Why:_ this turns an event subscription into code execution. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Event Filter** — The event filter represents the trigger condition in a WMI persistence setup. _Why:_ investigators must identify what event causes the malicious action to fire. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Event Consumer** — The event consumer stores or references the script or executable that will be launched. _Why:_ this component contains the attacker’s execution payload or command path. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Binding** — The binding links a specific event filter to a specific event consumer. _Why:_ without the binding, the trigger and payload are not joined into a working persistence mechanism. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Three-part WMI persistence structure** — A complete WMI event consumer backdoor requires a filter, a consumer, and a binding between them. _Why:_ responders should check all three objects when validating or removing persistence. _[GCFA p.~82]_

### WMI Trigger Conditions

- **Time-based filter** — A WMI filter can be configured to trigger on a recurring time interval. _Why:_ periodic triggers can run malware repeatedly without a traditional scheduled task. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Twenty-second interval example** — The page gives an example of a WMI filter firing every 20 seconds. _Why:_ short intervals can support beaconing, watchdog behavior, or repeated execution. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Service-start trigger** — A WMI filter can activate when a service starts. _Why:_ service lifecycle events can hide persistence behind normal operating system activity. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Service-stop trigger** — A WMI filter can activate when a service stops. _Why:_ attackers can tie execution to defensive shutdowns or system state changes. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **User-authentication trigger** — A WMI filter can fire when a particular user authentication event occurs. _Why:_ this lets malware execute only when a chosen user logs on or authenticates. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **File-creation trigger** — A WMI filter can activate when a file is created. _Why:_ file-based conditions can serve as covert triggers or staging signals. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Folder-existence trigger** — A WMI filter can be based on whether a folder exists. _Why:_ attackers can use filesystem state as a control condition for execution. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **File-existence trigger** — A WMI filter can be based on whether a file exists. _Why:_ a file can act as a marker that enables or disables malicious activity. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Immediate-registration trigger** — A WMI event filter can be arranged to fire as soon as it is registered. _Why:_ this allows a MOF or PowerShell setup step to cause immediate code execution. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Windows-event trigger flexibility** — WMI event filters can be tied to many Windows event types. _Why:_ broad trigger coverage makes WMI persistence adaptable and easy to overlook. _[GCFA p.~82]_

### Setup And Tooling

- **PowerShell setup path** — PowerShell can be used to create WMI event consumer persistence. _Why:_ attackers can configure persistence using native administrative tooling. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **`mofcomp.exe` setup path** — `mofcomp.exe` can be used to register WMI persistence components from a MOF file. _Why:_ this native compiler can load attacker-defined WMI classes or subscriptions into the repository. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **`Get-WmiObject` detection role** — The PowerShell cmdlet `Get-WmiObject` can be used to find suspicious WMI entries. _Why:_ responders can query WMI directly for malicious filters, consumers, and bindings. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **`Get-WmiObject` removal support** — `Get-WmiObject` can assist with removing suspicious WMI objects. _Why:_ identifying the objects is part of dismantling the persistence chain. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Managed Object Format file** — The filter, consumer, and binding are often defined in a MOF file. _Why:_ MOF files provide a structured way to install WMI repository objects. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **MOF repository registration** — A MOF file can register new classes or objects into the WMI repository. _Why:_ malicious persistence may be stored in WMI rather than in common Run keys or startup folders. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **PowerShell `Set-WmiInstance`** — `Set-WmiInstance` can be used to create WMI persistence objects. _Why:_ this gives attackers a stealthier setup route than dropping and compiling a MOF file. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **PowerShell `CreateInstance`** — `CreateInstance` can also be used to create WMI event subscription components. _Why:_ investigators should not rely only on MOF artifacts when hunting WMI persistence. _[GCFA p.~82]_

### Privileges And Execution Context

- **Administrative privilege requirement** — Creating this WMI backdoor requires administrative rights. _Why:_ the technique usually appears after privilege escalation or administrative compromise. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **SYSTEM execution context** — WMI consumers execute with SYSTEM privileges. _Why:_ a successful WMI consumer gives the attacker high-privilege code execution. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Detection difficulty** — WMI event consumer backdoors can be hard to detect without suitable tools. _Why:_ persistence stored in WMI is less visible than many file- or registry-based mechanisms. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Security-operations blind spot** — WMI is frequently underexamined by defenders despite its powerful capabilities. _Why:_ overlooked administrative subsystems are attractive places for durable persistence. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Attacker adoption** — Attackers have recognized and used WMI’s capabilities for persistence. _Why:_ WMI should be treated as a normal persistence-hunting surface, not an edge case. _[GCFA p.~82]_

### Attack Workflow

- **Step 1 · Create event filter** — The attacker first defines the event condition that should be monitored. _Why:_ this establishes when the backdoor will activate. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Step 1 example · Twenty-second trigger** — The page’s example filter fires every twenty seconds. _Why:_ frequent time-based triggers can support repeated command execution or beaconing. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Step 2 · Add event consumer** — The attacker then creates an event consumer containing a script or executable to run. _Why:_ this object defines what code executes after the trigger. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Step 2 example · PowerShell beacon** — The page gives an example of a consumer running PowerShell that contacts a command-and-control server. _Why:_ WMI persistence can directly enable outbound attacker communications. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Step 3 · Bind filter to consumer** — The attacker links the event filter and event consumer with a binding. _Why:_ the binding makes the trigger cause the payload to execute. _[GCFA p.~82]_
- **Repository loading** — After the binding is created, the persistence mechanism is loaded into the WMI repository. _Why:_ WMI repository storage lets the backdoor survive beyond the initial setup command. _[GCFA p.~82]_

- **APT29 WMI persistence** — APT29 has used WMI as a persistence mechanism. _Why:_ WMI event subscriptions are associated with advanced intrusion activity. _[GCFA p.~82]_

- **`__EventFilter as $Filter` · Filter instance** — The MOF defines a `__EventFilter` instance and assigns it the alias `$Filter`. _Why:_ the event filter defines which WMI event causes the persistence mechanism to activate. _[GCFA p.~83]_
- **`EventNamespace = "ROOT\\subscription"` · Filter event namespace** — The event filter’s namespace value is `ROOT\subscription`. _Why:_ this identifies the WMI namespace context associated with the event filter. _[GCFA p.~83]_

### PowerShell-Based WMI Persistence Discovery

- **PowerShell as a WMI defense tool** — PowerShell can query WMI artifacts used by attackers and therefore works as a defensive collection method as well as a potential offensive tool. _Why:_ defenders can use built-in Windows capabilities to hunt WMI persistence without deploying specialized software. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **Native WMI support in PowerShell** — PowerShell has built-in WMI access, making it suitable for collecting WMI eventing data. _Why:_ native access lowers collection friction during incident response. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **PowerShell scalability** — PowerShell can be scaled across systems for WMI event-consumer discovery. _Why:_ enterprise hunting requires collecting the same artifacts from many hosts. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **No specialized detection tool required** — Suspicious WMI event consumers can be found with built-in PowerShell commands. _Why:_ responders can investigate WMI persistence even in constrained environments. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **WMI event consumers as an insidious threat** — WMI event consumers are treated as a stealthy persistence mechanism worth targeted detection. _Why:_ persistence hidden in WMI may survive reboots and avoid obvious file-system indicators. _[GCFA p.~84]_

### Core WMI Collection Commands

- **`Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __EventFilter`** — this command queries WMI event filters in the `root\Subscription` namespace. _Why:_ event filters define the trigger condition for WMI event-based persistence. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **`Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __EventConsumer`** — this command queries WMI event consumers in the `root\Subscription` namespace. _Why:_ consumers contain or reference the action executed after a WMI trigger fires. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **`Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __FilterToConsumerBinding`** — this command queries bindings between WMI filters and consumers in the `root\Subscription` namespace. _Why:_ bindings reveal which trigger is connected to which payload. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **Event filter collection** — the slide’s command set gathers WMI event filters from the target system. _Why:_ filters identify the system event or condition that starts the persistence chain. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **Event consumer collection** — the slide’s command set gathers WMI event consumers from the target system. _Why:_ consumers expose the execution behavior or malicious payload. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **Filter-to-consumer binding collection** — the slide’s command set gathers WMI filter-to-consumer bindings from the target system. _Why:_ the binding connects the trigger and action into an executable persistence mechanism. _[GCFA p.~84]_

### Class-Specific Querying

- **`-Class` parameter** — PowerShell’s WMI query can be narrowed with a specific class name. _Why:_ targeted class queries can reduce output volume during investigation. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **`-Class CommandLineEventConsumer` example** — `CommandLineEventConsumer` is given as an example of a narrower class query. _Why:_ command-line consumers are especially relevant because they can directly launch commands or scripts. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **Class narrowing caution** — using a very specific class is recommended only when standard benign entries cannot be allowlisted. _Why:_ over-narrowing may miss malicious consumers implemented through other WMI consumer classes. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **Allowlisting standard false positives** — normal WMI entries should be allowlisted where possible before resorting to narrower queries. _Why:_ allowlisting preserves broader detection coverage while reducing analyst noise. _[GCFA p.~84]_

### Recommended Namespace Coverage

- **Dual-namespace collection strategy** — responders should consider running WMI eventing collection against both `root\Subscription` and `root\Default`. _Why:_ attackers may place persistence outside the most commonly checked namespace. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **`root\Subscription` namespace** — `root\Subscription` is the standard namespace queried on the slide. _Why:_ Microsoft documentation and many observed WMI event consumers use this location. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **`root\Default` namespace** — `root\Default` can also host equivalent malicious WMI persistence. _Why:_ defenders who only check `root\Subscription` may miss non-standard placements. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **Common attacker placement** — most WMI event consumers observed in real intrusions are described as using `root\Subscription`. _Why:_ this makes `root\Subscription` a high-priority hunting location. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **Alternative attacker placement** — the same persistence concept can be embedded in `root\Default`. _Why:_ adversaries can shift to less-monitored namespaces as detection improves. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **Detection adaptation risk** — attackers may move WMI persistence to non-standard locations as organizations improve standard WMI consumer detection. _Why:_ detection logic must account for adversary migration paths. _[GCFA p.~84]_

### Best-Practice Command Set

- **Best-practice `root\Subscription` filter query** — `Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __EventFilter` is part of the recommended collection set. _Why:_ it captures trigger definitions from the standard WMI eventing namespace. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **Best-practice `root\Subscription` consumer query** — `Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __EventConsumer` is part of the recommended collection set. _Why:_ it captures payload-bearing consumer objects from the standard namespace. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **Best-practice `root\Subscription` binding query** — `Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __FilterToConsumerBinding` is part of the recommended collection set. _Why:_ it captures trigger-to-action relationships from the standard namespace. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **Best-practice `root\Default` filter query** — `Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Default -Class __EventFilter` is part of the recommended collection set. _Why:_ it checks for trigger definitions in a less-standard namespace. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **Best-practice `root\Default` consumer query** — `Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Default -Class __EventConsumer` is part of the recommended collection set. _Why:_ it checks for payload-bearing consumers outside the usual namespace. _[GCFA p.~84]_
- **Best-practice `root\Default` binding query** — `Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Default -Class __FilterToConsumerBinding` is part of the recommended collection set. _Why:_ it checks whether non-standard namespace filters and consumers are linked into working persistence. _[GCFA p.~84]_

## Page 86

### WMI Persistence Hunting Scope

- **Enterprise WMI event hunting** — Large-scale review of WMI event data requires allowlists and filtering logic so unusual entries can stand out. _Why:_ enterprise datasets are too large to triage effectively without reducing expected noise. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Anomaly detection requirement** — WMI persistence hunting depends on distinguishing normal WMI consumers from suspicious or rare ones. _Why:_ attacker persistence can hide among legitimate WMI infrastructure. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Primary hunting object** — WMI event consumers should be examined before filters or bindings. _Why:_ consumers usually contain the execution details most useful for detecting malicious activity. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Consumer-first workflow** — The recommended initial focus is on WMI consumers rather than event filters or bindings. _Why:_ consumer fields tend to support higher-confidence searches using suspicious terms. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Blocklist searching** — Event consumers often expose data suitable for searching with known-bad or suspicious keywords. _Why:_ command lines and scripts are more actionable than trigger metadata during first-pass triage. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Post-detection pivot** — After identifying a malicious consumer, the consumer name can be used to locate its binding. _Why:_ the binding connects the suspicious action to the WMI trigger chain. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Event filter pivot** — A malicious consumer’s name can also be used to find the related event filter. _Why:_ the filter explains what condition caused the consumer to execute. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Trigger insight** — The associated event filter may reveal execution conditions such as periodic timing, system startup, or a user logon. _Why:_ trigger context helps reconstruct persistence behavior and attacker intent. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Event filter optionality** — Finding the event filter is useful but not always required once a bad consumer is confirmed. _Why:_ the consumer alone may be enough to identify malicious execution content. _[GCFA p.~86]_

### High-Priority Consumer Types

- **Command-line consumers** — CommandLine-style WMI consumers are called out as a key class to prioritize. _Why:_ they can directly expose executable paths, command arguments, and script interpreters. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Active script consumers** — ActiveScript-style WMI consumers are also called out as a key class to prioritize. _Why:_ they can contain script content or script-hosting behavior used for persistence. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Consumer type reduction** — WMI investigations may encounter multiple consumer classes, but the dataset can be narrowed to CommandLineEventConsumer and ActiveScriptEventConsumer. _Why:_ those two classes cover the attack patterns described as currently observed in the wild. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **CommandLineEventConsumer focus** — CommandLineEventConsumer is one of the two consumer classes recommended for focused hunting. _Why:_ known real-world WMI persistence attacks use this class. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **ActiveScriptEventConsumer focus** — ActiveScriptEventConsumer is one of the two consumer classes recommended for focused hunting. _Why:_ known real-world WMI persistence attacks use this class. _[GCFA p.~86]_

### Allowlisting Cautions

- **Allowlist creation** — Once WMI event data is collected broadly, common normal consumers can usually be identified and allowlisted. _Why:_ environment-specific baselines improve detection quality. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Environment specificity** — Normal WMI consumers vary by organization. _Why:_ an allowlist from one enterprise may miss or misclassify entries in another. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Frequent legitimate consumers** — The page provides examples of commonly seen legitimate WMI consumers and related entries. _Why:_ these examples support initial filtering and triage. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Global allowlist risk** — Broad allowlisting must be handled carefully. _Why:_ attackers can choose names that resemble legitimate entries to avoid detection. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Allowlist auditing** — Existing allowlists should be reviewed periodically for excessive permissiveness. _Why:_ stale or loose rules can become attacker hiding places. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Attacker naming abuse** — Malicious WMI consumers named `SCM Event Consumer` have been observed in real incidents. _Why:_ a name close to a known-good consumer can exploit analyst assumptions or detection allowlists. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **BadRabbit WMI naming** — BadRabbit ransomware used the malicious consumer name `SCM Event Consumer`. _Why:_ this demonstrates attacker attempts to blend malicious WMI persistence into normal-looking data. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Legitimate name distinction** — The legitimate consumer name is `SCM Event Log Consumer`, not `SCM Event Consumer`. _Why:_ the missing word is a meaningful difference during allowlist matching. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Variant naming abuse** — Other ransomware has used the name `SCM Events Log Consumer`. _Why:_ near-miss naming can bypass loose string matching or analyst review. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **KernCap.vbs overwrite reports** — The commonly legitimate `KernCap.vbs` script has reportedly been replaced with malicious content while keeping the same filename. _Why:_ filename-based allowlisting alone can miss tampered legitimate-looking scripts. _[GCFA p.~86]_
- **Attacker use of defender assumptions** — Attackers may deliberately exploit common tools, naming conventions, and hunting methods used by defenders. _Why:_ detections must account for adversarial attempts to blend into expected artifacts. _[GCFA p.~86]_

### WMI Event Consumers

- **CommandLineEventConsumer** — this WMI consumer type can run an executable as the action associated with an event filter trigger. _Why:_ it is a persistence and execution location where investigators may find attacker-launched binaries. _[GCFA p.87]_
- **CommandLineEventConsumer payload field** — the consumer properties may directly reference a suspicious executable name such as `evil.exe`. _Why:_ the executable path or command line can identify the persisted payload. _[GCFA p.87]_
- **CommandLineEventConsumer complex command usage** — the configured action may use a trusted Windows binary such as `rundll32.exe` together with arguments. _Why:_ attackers may hide malicious execution behind legitimate Windows utilities. _[GCFA p.87]_
- **CommandLineEventConsumer PowerShell usage** — the configured action may invoke `powershell.exe` with parameters. _Why:_ PowerShell command lines can contain encoded or scripted payload logic useful for detection and triage. _[GCFA p.87]_
- **ActiveScriptEventConsumer** — this WMI consumer type is another common way to create malicious event-consumer behavior. _Why:_ investigators should inspect it alongside command-line consumers when hunting WMI persistence. _[GCFA p.87]_
- **ActiveScriptEventConsumer flexibility** — the script action can be supplied either by pointing to a script file on disk or by storing the script content directly in the consumer configuration. _Why:_ evidence may exist as a filesystem artifact, an embedded WMI value, or both. _[GCFA p.87]_
- **ActiveScriptEventConsumer supported languages** — this consumer supports Visual Basic script and JScript. _Why:_ expected script language choices constrain what investigators should look for in this WMI class. _[GCFA p.87]_
- **ActiveScriptEventConsumer PowerShell limitation** — PowerShell scripts are not used as the script language inside this consumer type. _Why:_ PowerShell activity in WMI persistence is more likely to appear through another consumer type, such as command-line execution. _[GCFA p.87]_
- **Standard Consumer Classes reference** — the page cites Microsoft documentation for standard WMI consumer classes at `http://for508.com/9oah4`. _Why:_ this identifies the external reference for the class list and expected consumer behavior. _[GCFA p.87]_

### Standard Consumer Classes Table

- **ActiveScriptEventConsumer · Function** — executes a predefined Visual Basic or JScript script. _Why:_ this table cell defines the expected behavior of this consumer class. _[GCFA p.87]_
- **CommandLineEventConsumer · Function** — starts an arbitrary process. _Why:_ this table cell identifies the class most directly associated with process-launch persistence. _[GCFA p.87]_
- **LogFileEventConsumer · Function** — writes content to a plain text log file. _Why:_ this table cell shows that not every consumer launches code; some produce file-based output artifacts. _[GCFA p.87]_

### Persistence Mechanism Coverage

- **autorunsc.exe** — Sysinternals Autoruns command-line tooling is presented as a way to identify malware persistence mechanisms. _Why:_ responders commonly use it early to enumerate autostart execution points. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **AutoStart Locations** — Autostart execution locations are listed as a major persistence category to check. _Why:_ many intrusions rely on startup-triggered execution for re-entry after reboot or user logon. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **Service Creation or Replacement** — Creating a new Windows service or replacing an existing service is listed as a persistence mechanism. _Why:_ services can provide durable execution with elevated or system-level context. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **Service Failure Recovery** — Windows service recovery behavior is identified as a persistence area, with Kansa’s `Get-SvcFail.ps1` named for collection. _Why:_ malicious code can be launched through recovery actions when a service fails. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **Kansa `Get-SvcFail.ps1`** — The page names `Get-SvcFail.ps1` as the Kansa script associated with service failure recovery checks. _Why:_ this gives responders a specific collection script for hunting service-recovery persistence. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **Scheduled Tasks** — Scheduled tasks are listed as a common persistence mechanism. _Why:_ tasks can trigger attacker code on time, event, logon, or other recurring conditions. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **DLL Hijacking** — DLL hijacking is listed as a persistence technique associated with timeline analysis and file system forensics. _Why:_ this technique may not be obvious from registry autorun locations and often requires disk-artifact review. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **DLL Hijacking Detection Method** — The page specifically links DLL hijacking discovery with timelining and file system forensic analysis. _Why:_ responders should not rely only on autorun enumeration for this class of persistence. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **WMI Event Consumers** — WMI event consumers are listed as a persistence mechanism. _Why:_ WMI subscriptions can trigger attacker-controlled commands or scripts based on system events. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **Group Policy Persistence** — Group Policy is listed as a more advanced persistence mechanism. _Why:_ domain or local policy mechanisms can execute scripts or modify settings in ways that persist across normal cleanup. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **MS Office Add-In Persistence** — Microsoft Office add-ins are listed as a more advanced persistence mechanism. _Why:_ add-ins can load attacker code when Office applications start. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **BIOS Flashing Persistence** — BIOS flashing is listed as a more advanced persistence mechanism. _Why:_ firmware-level modification is rare but can survive operating system remediation. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **Advanced Persistence Variability** — Group Policy, Office add-ins, and BIOS flashing are marked as variable advanced cases. _Why:_ responders should expect these mechanisms to differ by environment and attacker implementation. _[GCFA p.~88]_

### Prevalence and Rarity

- **Persistence Discovery Scope** — The page states that new persistence mechanisms will probably continue to appear indefinitely, similar to application vulnerabilities. _Why:_ investigators should avoid assuming that known ASEPs are a complete universe of attacker options. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **Top-Six Persistence Coverage** — The first six persistence categories on the page are described as accounting for roughly 98% of mechanisms responders are likely to encounter. _Why:_ this prioritizes investigation effort toward the highest-yield persistence locations. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **Rare Persistence Remainder** — The remaining approximate 2% of persistence mechanisms are characterized as unusual or obscure. _Why:_ uncommon techniques still matter in advanced or unusual intrusions, but they are less frequently found. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **Firmware Implants** — Firmware implants are given as an example of rare, esoteric persistence. _Why:_ firmware compromise can persist outside normal operating-system artifact locations. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **New DLL Hijacking Forms** — Novel DLL hijacking variants are given as another example of rare persistence. _Why:_ attackers may adapt loader behavior and file-placement tricks beyond common cases. _[GCFA p.~88]_

### Autoruns and ASEPs

- **ASEP Collection** — Sysinternals Autoruns can collect data from most autostart extensibility points. _Why:_ broad ASEP enumeration helps responders quickly identify many common persistence mechanisms. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **Autoruns Investigation Role** — Autoruns is described as a standard incident-response tool. _Why:_ it is commonly among the first persistence-review tools used during an investigation. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **Autoruns Review Priority** — The page notes that Autoruns output is often reviewed early in an investigation. _Why:_ early persistence triage can reveal how malware survives reboots and where containment must focus. _[GCFA p.~88]_
- **Autoruns Limitations by Artifact Type** — Some persistence mechanisms, including DLL hijacking and Group Policy scripts, are more often found through timelines and disk forensics than through Autoruns-style enumeration. _Why:_ tool choice must match the persistence artifact, or important evidence may be missed. _[GCFA p.~88]_

### autorunsc.exe Scope

- **autorunsc.exe live-system use** — `autorunsc.exe` is presented as a tool to run on a live Windows system. _Why:_ live collection can reveal currently configured persistence locations without requiring offline registry parsing. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Autorunsc command-line role** — `autorunsc` is the command-line edition of Sysinternals Autoruns. _Why:_ command-line execution supports scripted collection and redirected forensic output. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Autoruns persistence coverage** — Autoruns is described as having very broad knowledge of Windows autostart locations. _Why:_ broad coverage makes it useful for persistence hunting across many Windows mechanisms. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Boot-time program visibility** — Autoruns identifies programs configured to launch during system startup. _Why:_ boot execution is a common persistence opportunity for malware and administrative tools. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Logon-time program visibility** — Autoruns identifies programs configured to launch when a user logs in. _Why:_ user-logon persistence is a frequent attacker technique. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Built-in application trigger visibility** — Autoruns reports programs that start when built-in Windows applications are launched. _Why:_ application-triggered autostarts can hide persistence outside simple Run-key checks. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Internet Explorer trigger coverage** — Autoruns includes autostarts associated with Internet Explorer. _Why:_ browser-related extensions and helpers can provide persistence or execution opportunities. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Explorer trigger coverage** — Autoruns includes autostarts associated with Windows Explorer. _Why:_ shell-related persistence can execute during normal desktop use. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Media-player trigger coverage** — Autoruns includes autostarts associated with media players. _Why:_ application integration points can be abused to launch unwanted code. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Startup folder coverage** — Autoruns includes entries located in Startup folders. _Why:_ Startup folders are simple persistence locations that should be reviewed during triage. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Run-key coverage** — Autoruns includes entries configured in `Run` registry keys. _Why:_ `Run` keys are common Windows persistence locations. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **RunOnce-key coverage** — Autoruns includes entries configured in `RunOnce` registry keys. _Why:_ `RunOnce` can execute code at the next logon or startup and may be used for staged activity. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Other registry autostart coverage** — Autoruns reviews additional registry keys beyond `Run` and `RunOnce`. _Why:_ persistence hunting requires checking more than the most familiar locations. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Explorer shell-extension reporting** — Autoruns reports Explorer shell extensions. _Why:_ malicious or suspicious shell extensions can load within Explorer processes. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Toolbar reporting** — Autoruns reports toolbar entries. _Why:_ toolbars can represent browser or shell persistence mechanisms. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Browser Helper Object reporting** — Autoruns reports browser helper objects. _Why:_ BHOs can be abused for browser-based persistence and monitoring. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Winlogon notification reporting** — Autoruns reports Winlogon notification entries. _Why:_ Winlogon integration points are high-value persistence and credential-theft locations. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Autostart service reporting** — Autoruns reports automatically started services. _Why:_ services are durable persistence mechanisms and often require close validation. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Autoruns comparative breadth** — The courseware notes that Autoruns exceeds typical autostart utilities in coverage. _Why:_ investigators should prefer broad enumeration when searching for persistence. _[GCFA p.~89]_

### Collection Commands

- **Network-share CSV collection command** — `C:\>autorunsc -accepteula [options] > \\server\share\autoruns.csv` redirects autorunsc output to `\\server\share\autoruns.csv`. _Why:_ writing results to a remote share preserves output away from the examined host. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Generic VirusTotal command form** — `autorunsc -v [options] > output-file.csv` shows VirusTotal-enabled output redirected to `output-file.csv`. _Why:_ hash reputation checks can be captured alongside autorun entries. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Recommended full collection command** — `C:\>autorunsc -accepteula -a * -s -h -c -vr > \\siftworkstation\share\out.csv` runs autorunsc with license acceptance, all-entry enumeration, signature verification, hashing, CSV output, and VirusTotal reporting. _Why:_ this combines broad persistence collection with enrichment and exports it to a forensic workstation share. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Recommended output destination** — The example writes results to `\\siftworkstation\share\out.csv`. _Why:_ the destination implies centralized collection from the target to a SIFT workstation share. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **Example prompt context** — The examples use `C:\>` as the Windows command prompt. _Why:_ this identifies the commands as Windows command-line usage. _[GCFA p.~89]_

### Useful Options

- **`-accepteula` option** — `-accepteula` automatically accepts the Microsoft software license prompt. _Why:_ this prevents interactive license prompts from blocking scripted live response collection. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-a *` option** — `-a *` tells autorunsc to display every autostart entry category. _Why:_ all-category collection reduces the chance of missing persistence outside default locations. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-h` option** — `-h` includes file hashes in the output. _Why:_ hashes support malware lookups, deduplication, and evidence correlation. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-m` option** — `-m` suppresses signed Microsoft entries. _Why:_ hiding trusted Microsoft-signed entries can reduce noise during triage. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-s` option** — `-s` verifies digital signatures. _Why:_ signature status helps distinguish expected software from suspicious or tampered binaries. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-c` option** — `-c` prints results in CSV format. _Why:_ CSV output is easier to ingest, sort, preserve, and analyze at scale. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-v[rs]` option family** — `-v[rs]` queries VirusTotal using file hashes to identify possible malware. _Why:_ reputation enrichment can quickly prioritize suspicious autorun entries. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-vr` usage in example** — The worked command uses `-vr` as the VirusTotal-related option. _Why:_ the example shows the specific VirusTotal mode expected for the collection workflow. _[GCFA p.~89]_

### Autostart Category Selector Cells

- **`-a *` category** — The `*` selector means all autostart entry categories. _Why:_ it is the broadest collection mode. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-a b` category** — The `b` selector targets boot-execute entries. _Why:_ boot-execute entries can run very early during startup. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-a c` category** — The `c` selector targets codec entries. _Why:_ codec registration can be abused to load code through media handling. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-a d` category** — The `d` selector targets AppInit DLL entries. _Why:_ AppInit DLLs can cause DLL loading into user-mode processes and are a known persistence mechanism. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-a e` category** — The `e` selector targets Explorer add-ons. _Why:_ Explorer add-ons can execute within shell activity. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-a g` category** — The `g` selector targets Sidebar gadgets on Windows Vista and later. _Why:_ gadget-based startup locations may exist on supported Windows versions. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-a h` category** — The `h` selector targets image hijack entries. _Why:_ image hijacks can redirect or alter program execution. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-a i` category** — The `i` selector targets Internet Explorer add-ons. _Why:_ IE add-ons can provide browser-based persistence or malicious code loading. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-a k` category** — The `k` selector targets Known DLL entries. _Why:_ Known DLL configuration affects DLL resolution and can be relevant to hijacking investigations. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-a l` category** — The `l` selector targets logon startups and is the default selection. _Why:_ default autorunsc output focuses on common user-logon persistence. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-a m` category** — The `m` selector targets WMI entries. _Why:_ WMI persistence can trigger code execution through event subscriptions. _[GCFA p.~89]_
- **`-a n` category** — The `n` selector targets Winsock protocol and network provider entries. _Why:_ network provider and Winsock modifications can indicate persistence, interception, or malicious networking hooks. _[GCFA p.~89]_

### Autoruns Entry Categories

- **`o` option · Office add-ins** — The `o` category selects Microsoft Office add-in autorun locations. _Why:_ malicious Office add-ins can provide persistence inside Office applications. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`p` option · Printer monitor DLLs** — The `p` category selects printer monitor dynamic-link libraries. _Why:_ printer monitor DLLs are load points that can be abused for persistence or code execution. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`r` option · LSA security providers** — The `r` category selects Local Security Authority security provider entries. _Why:_ LSA providers run in a sensitive authentication-related context and are high-value persistence locations. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`s` option · Autostart services and active drivers** — The `s` category selects automatically starting services and drivers that are not disabled. _Why:_ services and drivers are common long-lived Windows persistence mechanisms. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`t` option · Scheduled tasks** — The `t` category selects scheduled task autorun entries. _Why:_ scheduled tasks are frequently used to trigger recurring or event-based attacker execution. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`w` option · Winlogon entries** — The `w` category selects Winlogon-related autorun entries. _Why:_ Winlogon extensibility points can execute code during user logon and are important persistence locations. _[GCFA p.90]_

### Autoruns Output Formatting Options

- **`-c` option · CSV output** — The `-c` flag prints Autoruns results in comma-separated value format. _Why:_ CSV output supports parsing, filtering, and importing results into analysis tools. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`-ct` option · Tab-delimited output** — The `-ct` flag prints Autoruns results using tab-separated fields. _Why:_ tab-delimited output is useful for spreadsheet import and script-based processing. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`-x` option · XML output** — The `-x` flag prints Autoruns results as XML. _Why:_ XML preserves structured output for automated collection and downstream parsing. _[GCFA p.90]_

### Autoruns Enrichment And Filtering Options

- **`-h` option · File hashes** — The `-h` flag includes cryptographic hash values for files in the output. _Why:_ hashes allow file identification, reputation checks, and correlation across hosts. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`-m` option · Microsoft-entry hiding** — The `-m` flag suppresses Microsoft entries from the displayed results. _Why:_ hiding trusted vendor entries helps analysts focus on less common or suspicious autoruns. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`-m` with `-s` · Signed-entry hiding behavior** — When `-m` is combined with signature verification, it hides signed entries. _Why:_ this changes the filter from Microsoft-specific suppression to signature-based suppression, affecting what remains visible. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`-s` option · Signature verification** — The `-s` flag verifies digital signatures for autorun files. _Why:_ signature status helps distinguish trusted software from unsigned or suspicious binaries. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`-t` option · UTC timestamps** — The `-t` flag displays timestamps normalized to UTC. _Why:_ UTC normalization helps correlate autorun artifacts across systems and time zones. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`-t` timestamp format** — Timestamps shown by `-t` use the `YYYYMMDD-hhmmss` format. _Why:_ the fixed timestamp format supports consistent sorting and timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`-u` with VirusTotal enabled · Unknown or detected files** — When VirusTotal checking is active, `-u` shows files that VirusTotal does not know about or files with at least one detection. _Why:_ this filter highlights files with suspicious or absent reputation signals. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`-u` without VirusTotal enabled · Unsigned files only** — When VirusTotal checking is not active, `-u` limits output to unsigned files. _Why:_ unsigned autorun files are often higher priority for manual review. _[GCFA p.90]_

### VirusTotal Options

- **`-v[rs]` option · VirusTotal hash lookup** — The `-v[rs]` option queries VirusTotal at `www.virustotal.com` using file hashes to check for malware reputation. _Why:_ hash-based reputation checks can quickly identify known malicious autorun files. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`r` modifier for `-v` · Report opening** — Adding `r` to the VirusTotal option opens reports for files that have non-zero detections. _Why:_ direct report access helps analysts inspect detection context for flagged files. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`s` modifier for `-v` · Upload previously unseen files** — If VirusTotal reports that a file has not been scanned before, the file is uploaded when the `s` modifier is supplied. _Why:_ this can obtain reputation results for unknown files but also shares the sample with VirusTotal. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **VirusTotal delay · Scan result availability** — VirusTotal scan results may take five minutes or longer to become available. _Why:_ analysts should not assume immediate results after submitting a previously unseen file. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`-vt` option · Terms-of-service acceptance** — The `-vt` option indicates acceptance of VirusTotal terms before using VirusTotal functionality. _Why:_ VirusTotal integration requires terms acceptance before automated queries or uploads. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **VirusTotal terms URL** — The displayed terms-of-service link is `https://www.virustotal.com/en/about/terms-of-service/`. _Why:_ this is the referenced location for the legal terms tied to VirusTotal use. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **Omitting `-vt` without prior acceptance · Interactive prompt** — If the VirusTotal terms have not already been accepted and `-vt` is omitted, Autoruns prompts interactively. _Why:_ unattended collection can pause or fail if the prompt appears during scripted execution. _[GCFA p.90]_

### Target Selection Options

- **`-z` option · Offline Windows scan target** — The `-z` flag specifies an offline Windows installation to scan. _Why:_ this supports autorun analysis against mounted disk images or offline systems. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`user` argument · Specific account selection** — The `user` argument names the account whose autorun entries should be shown. _Why:_ user-scoped autoruns can differ by profile and may reveal per-user persistence. _[GCFA p.90]_
- **`user` argument wildcard · All profiles** — Supplying `*` for the user argument scans every user profile. _Why:_ scanning all profiles reduces the chance of missing persistence installed under a different account. _[GCFA p.90]_

### Display Control

- **`-nobanner` option · Banner suppression** — The `-nobanner` flag prevents display of the startup banner and copyright text. _Why:_ suppressing banners makes scripted output cleaner and easier to parse. _[GCFA p.90]_

### Documentation Practice

- **Document as you work** — incident responders should record findings continuously during analysis. _Why:_ ongoing documentation prevents important details from being lost as new evidence accumulates. _[GCFA p.91]_
- **Finding organization** — a spreadsheet or similar organized notes system is especially valuable for tracking discovered evidence. _Why:_ incident response produces many related observations that need to remain searchable and correlated. _[GCFA p.91]_
- **Course-provided indicators workbook** — the class includes an indicators spreadsheet that has been refined through prior operational use. _Why:_ students do not need to design a tracking structure from scratch during the course. _[GCFA p.91]_
- **Per-lab documentation** — the course recommends adding information to the workbook after every lab. _Why:_ frequent updates keep the record close to the actual analysis timeline. _[GCFA p.91]_
- **Incident context capture** — students should record as much incident-related information as possible while working. _Why:_ small details can become important when later reconstructing attacker behavior. _[GCFA p.91]_
- **Cognitive load during analysis** — even a short additional analysis period can produce enough information to become difficult to mentally track. _Why:_ relying on memory alone increases the risk of confusing hosts, accounts, artifacts, or indicators. _[GCFA p.91]_
- **Specific IP recording** — analysts should write down specific IP addresses identified during the investigation. _Why:_ IP addresses are key indicators for scoping, pivoting, and correlation. _[GCFA p.91]_
- **Specific host recording** — analysts should write down specific hosts identified during the investigation. _Why:_ hostnames are essential for scoping compromise and mapping affected systems. _[GCFA p.91]_
- **Compromised account recording** — analysts should write down accounts believed to be compromised. _Why:_ account tracking supports containment, credential response, and lateral-movement analysis. _[GCFA p.91]_
- **Beginner requirement status** — maintaining this spreadsheet is not mandatory for students who are just starting to learn analysis. _Why:_ the course frames the practice as strongly helpful rather than an initial hard requirement. _[GCFA p.91]_
- **Final challenge benefit** — documenting important findings during the labs will materially help during the final challenge. _Why:_ prior observations provide leads and reduce rediscovery work. _[GCFA p.91]_
- **Tradecraft list reuse** — an initial list of observed adversary tradecraft makes it easier to find malicious activity on additional systems. _Why:_ known techniques and indicators guide hunting on newly examined hosts. _[GCFA p.91]_

- **Encrypted transfer** — Although HTTP is used, the transmitted remoting data is encrypted. _Why:_ network capture may not expose command content in plaintext. _[GCFA p.~99]_

### Performance Comparison

- **Jason Hofferle comparison** — Jason Hofferle compared looping WMI collection against `Invoke-Command` concurrency. _Why:_ the comparison provides measured evidence for choosing concurrent remoting. _[GCFA p.~99]_
- **Test data source** — The comparison retrieved entries from the Windows Security event log. _Why:_ security log collection is a common DFIR triage task. _[GCFA p.~99]_
- **Events retrieved per host** — The comparison collected the last 20 Security log events. _Why:_ this defines the exact workload used in the timing comparison. _[GCFA p.~99]_
- **Initial test host count** — The first comparison used 100 computers. _Why:_ this establishes the scale for the measured timing difference. _[GCFA p.~99]_
- **Loop method** — One tested method used a loop to run the WMI command across the 100 systems. _Why:_ loop-based remote collection is the slower baseline being contrasted. _[GCFA p.~99]_
- **Invoke-Command method** — The other tested method used `Invoke-Command` concurrent connections. _Why:_ this is the faster remoting approach highlighted by the page. _[GCFA p.~99]_
- **Invoke-Command 100-host result** — `Invoke-Command` completed the 100-system collection in 15 seconds. _Why:_ this demonstrates the speed advantage of concurrent remote execution. _[GCFA p.~99]_
- **Loop 100-host result** — The loop-based approach required more than 6 hours for the same 100-system task. _Why:_ this shows why serial collection can be impractical in enterprise IR. _[GCFA p.~99]_
- **Scaled host count** — The PowerShell job was also scaled to 1,000 systems. _Why:_ this tests whether the approach remains useful beyond a small enterprise sample. _[GCFA p.~99]_
- **Invoke-Command 1,000-host result** — The 1,000-system PowerShell job completed in 131 seconds. _Why:_ this supports the claim that PowerShell remoting can handle large incident-response collection jobs quickly. _[GCFA p.~99]_

### PowerShell Remoting Execution Model

- **Invoke-Command remote processing** — `Invoke-Command` runs the requested processing and filtering on the destination system instead of doing that work locally. _Why:_ remote-side processing reduces data movement during enterprise-scale collection. _[GCFA p.~100]_
- **Invoke-Command filtering location** — filtering performed through `Invoke-Command` occurs on the remote host. _Why:_ filtering at the source limits how much evidence data must traverse the network. _[GCFA p.~100]_
- **WMI loop collection behavior** — the WMI-based loop described here retrieves the full event log back to the analyst or collection host before filtering occurs. _Why:_ pulling entire logs first can be inefficient during large investigations. _[GCFA p.~100]_
- **WMI loop filtering location** — in the WMI loop approach, event-log filtering is completed on the host system after collection. _Why:_ local filtering increases network transfer and collector-side workload. _[GCFA p.~100]_
- **Remote filtering advantage** — shifting processing and filtering to each endpoint is the preferred pattern for broad incident-response collection. _Why:_ distributed filtering scales better when many systems must be queried quickly. _[GCFA p.~100]_
- **Large-scale IR collection requirement** — enterprise incident response benefits from minimizing the amount of raw data sent back to the collection system. _Why:_ network and collector bottlenecks can slow triage across many hosts. _[GCFA p.~100]_

### Background Jobs

- **PowerShell remote background jobs** — PowerShell can run remote executions as background jobs. _Why:_ background execution lets analysts launch work without waiting interactively for each remote command to finish. _[GCFA p.~100]_
- **`-AsJob` parameter** — `-AsJob` is the PowerShell parameter used to manage remote execution as a background job. _Why:_ this flag supports asynchronous collection during long-running or broad remote operations. _[GCFA p.~100]_
- **Long-running script use case** — background jobs are especially useful when a script requires a long time to complete. _Why:_ analysts can continue other response work while collection continues. _[GCFA p.~100]_
- **Many-system execution use case** — background jobs are especially useful when commands or scripts must run across many systems. _Why:_ asynchronous execution improves scalability during enterprise-wide response. _[GCFA p.~100]_
- **`Get-Job` cmdlet** — `Get-Job` is used to check the status of PowerShell background jobs. _Why:_ responders need job-state visibility to track remote collection progress and completion. _[GCFA p.~100]_

## Page 101

### PowerShell Remoting Security Model

- **PowerShell remoting authentication posture** — PowerShell remoting is presented as the preferred security case for remote administration. _Why:_ responders can collect data remotely without broadly exposing privileged credentials. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **PowerShell remoting encryption** — Remote PowerShell sessions are encrypted automatically. _Why:_ network collection and administration traffic is protected in transit. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **PowerShell remoting authentication mechanism** — Remote PowerShell authentication uses Kerberos by default. _Why:_ Kerberos provides strong domain authentication without sending reusable passwords to the target host. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Default token behavior** — PowerShell remoting defaults to nondelegated Kerberos authentication. _Why:_ the remote host receives an authentication context that cannot be reused to access additional systems. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Nondelegated Kerberos security benefit** — Nondelegated Kerberos blocks the theft of delegate tokens from the remote system. _Why:_ attackers cannot steal that remote-session token and pivot with it to other hosts. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Credential non-transfer** — PowerShell remoting does not pass the user’s credentials to the remote machine by default. _Why:_ credential theft tools on the target have less sensitive material available to recover. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Mimikatz exposure reduction** — Because credentials are not placed on the remote host by default, tools such as Mimikatz should not find those credentials there. _Why:_ this lowers the chance that incident-response activity spreads privileged credential material across compromised systems. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Incognito exposure reduction** — Because delegated credentials are not made available on the target by default, tools such as Incognito should not be able to use them from that host. _Why:_ token-theft tooling has fewer useful artifacts to abuse. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Domain Admin credential containment** — Default PowerShell remoting helps prevent high-value credentials, including Domain Admin credentials, from being distributed across many machines. _Why:_ responders often use powerful accounts, so credential containment directly affects enterprise-wide compromise risk. _[GCFA p.~101]_

### Logon Type And Credential Caching

- **PowerShell remoting logon type** — Remote PowerShell sessions are treated as non-interactive logons, specifically Type 3. _Why:_ Type 3 behavior avoids the credential caching associated with more interactive access methods. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Enter-PSSession logon behavior** — Even an interactive-looking `Enter-PSSession` shell is still handled as a non-interactive remote session. _Why:_ analysts may assume an interactive shell caches credentials, but this page states that `Enter-PSSession` does not do so. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Enter-PSSession credential caching** — `Enter-PSSession` does not cache the user’s credentials on the remote system. _Why:_ this makes it safer for responders than remote-access methods that leave reusable credential material behind. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Password hash protection** — PowerShell remoting does not cache password hashes on the remote host under its default model. _Why:_ cached hashes are a common post-exploitation target for credential theft and lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **RDP comparison** — PowerShell remoting is described as safer than RDP for remote administration. _Why:_ RDP-style interactive access can expose credential material in ways that default PowerShell remoting avoids. _[GCFA p.~101]_

### Dual-Hop Authentication And CredSSP

- **Dual-hop authentication definition** — Dual-hop authentication occurs when a script connects to one remote system and then needs that system to access a third system. _Why:_ this pattern changes the credential-risk model because the first remote host must authenticate onward. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **CredSSP role** — CredSSP is the service identified as implementing dual-hop authentication. _Why:_ responders need to recognize the specific mechanism that enables credential delegation. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **CredSSP single sign-on characterization** — CredSSP is described as essentially a single sign-on mechanism. _Why:_ it provides convenience by delegating authentication, but that convenience creates credential exposure. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **CredSSP warning** — CredSSP should be avoided for PowerShell remoting. _Why:_ it places sensitive credential material on the remote system. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **CredSSP credential storage** — CredSSP stores credentials on the remote host. _Why:_ any remote host using CredSSP becomes a place where credential theft may succeed. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **CredSSP hash exposure** — CredSSP can leave the user’s password hash on the remote system. _Why:_ password hashes can be extracted and reused or cracked by attackers. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **CredSSP token exposure** — CredSSP can leave an authentication token on the remote host. _Why:_ stolen tokens can support lateral movement or privilege abuse. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **CredSSP and Mimikatz** — Mimikatz is identified as a tool that can extract credential material exposed by CredSSP. _Why:_ this ties the configuration choice directly to a known credential-dumping capability. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Dual-hop script risk** — Scripts that require access to a third machine may force use of delegated authentication. _Why:_ a script design choice can accidentally convert a safer remote session into a credential-exposure scenario. _[GCFA p.~101]_

### Batch Scripts And Network Shares

- **PowerShell versus batch scripts** — PowerShell remoting is presented as a strong replacement for traditional remote batch-script workflows. _Why:_ common batch-script designs often require delegation that PowerShell remoting can avoid. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Remote batch script binary retrieval** — Batch scripts run on remote hosts often require the target host to authenticate to a network share to fetch binaries. _Why:_ this pattern can require credential delegation to the remote host. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Remote batch script data output** — Batch scripts run remotely often authenticate to a network share to write collected output. _Why:_ pushing data to a share from the remote host may require delegated credentials. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Network share pull pattern** — Scripts that pull binaries from file shares generally require delegation authority. _Why:_ delegated authority makes credentials available on the remote machine. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Network share dump pattern** — Scripts that write collected data to file shares generally require delegation authority. _Why:_ this can leave responder or administrator credentials exposed on the target host. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Delegation authority risk** — Delegation authority leaves credentials accessible on the remote system. _Why:_ compromised endpoints can then become credential-harvesting points during response activity. _[GCFA p.~101]_

### Named Tools, Commands, And Reference

- **`Enter-PSSession`** — `Enter-PSSession` is the PowerShell command named for entering a remote shell session. _Why:_ the page explicitly notes that even this shell does not cache credentials under the default remoting model. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Mimikatz** — Mimikatz is named as a tool relevant to extracting credential material from remote systems. _Why:_ its presence in the lesson highlights why avoiding delegated credentials matters during incident response. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Incognito** — Incognito is named as a tool relevant to token or credential abuse on remote systems. _Why:_ nondelegated PowerShell remoting reduces what this class of tool can use from the target. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **CredSSP** — CredSSP is named as the dual-hop authentication mechanism to avoid. _Why:_ it changes PowerShell remoting from a credential-minimizing model into one that can expose hashes and tokens. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **Kerberos** — Kerberos is named as the authentication protocol used by default for PowerShell remoting. _Why:_ it underpins the secure default authentication behavior described on the page. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **RDP** — RDP is named as a less safe alternative compared with PowerShell remoting. _Why:_ the comparison frames PowerShell remoting as the lower-credential-exposure option for remote administration. _[GCFA p.~101]_
- **External CredSSP reference** — The page cites “Accidental Sabotage: Beware of CredSSP” at `http://for508.com/whnby`. _Why:_ the reference points to additional guidance about the credential risks of CredSSP. _[GCFA p.~101]_

### Kansa Extensibility

- **PowerShell as an extensibility advantage** — PowerShell provides broad access to Windows administration and collection capabilities. _Why:_ Kansa can leverage many native Windows data sources and automation patterns. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Low barrier to Kansa customization** — Because Kansa uses PowerShell, writing or modifying modules is relatively approachable. _Why:_ incident responders can build collection logic without needing a specialized compiled language workflow. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Existing Kansa modules as learning material** — Reviewing Kansa’s built-in modules can teach responders what data types are useful in incident response. _Why:_ the module set acts as a practical checklist for host-based triage data. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Tool-independent value of Kansa modules** — Even responders who do not deploy Kansa can use its module ideas to collect equivalent data with other tools. _Why:_ the investigative value lies in the data categories, not only in the Kansa framework. _[GCFA p.103]_

### Live Response and Rootkit Risk

- **Live response criticism** — A major concern with live response collection is that malware on the endpoint may deceive the collection process. _Why:_ live data can be incomplete or manipulated when the running system is compromised. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Rootkit deception risk** — A malicious rootkit can interfere with what live response tools observe. _Why:_ hidden activity may not appear in normal command, API, or scripting output. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Rootkit purpose** — Rootkits are commonly used by malware to conceal malicious presence or behavior. _Why:_ their goal directly conflicts with forensic visibility. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Rootkit operating level** — Rootkits often operate at low system layers, including the operating system kernel. _Why:_ low-level placement gives them influence over what higher-level tools can see. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Windows API dependency** — Many live response methods depend on the Windows API for data collection. _Why:_ if API results are tampered with, multiple tools may inherit the same false view. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **System commands as API-dependent collectors** — Standard system commands are included among live response tools that commonly rely on Windows API calls. _Why:_ command-line output is not automatically trustworthy on a rootkitted host. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **WMI as API-dependent collection** — WMI-based collection is also subject to Windows API trust assumptions. _Why:_ WMI results may be affected if the underlying system interfaces are subverted. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **.NET as API-dependent collection** — .NET-based live response tools can depend on Windows APIs for host data. _Why:_ managed tooling may still reflect manipulated operating-system responses. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **PowerShell as API-dependent collection** — PowerShell collection can rely on Windows APIs. _Why:_ PowerShell output may be incomplete if a rootkit filters or alters API results. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Rootkit API subversion** — A rootkit can alter API function behavior so collection tools receive incomplete data. _Why:_ missing artifacts can cause responders to underestimate compromise scope. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Rootkit prevalence caveat** — Rootkits are described as uncommon compared with how often they are sometimes claimed to appear. _Why:_ responders should account for rootkit risk without assuming every host requires deep forensic treatment. _[GCFA p.103]_

### Collection Strategy Trade-Offs

- **Rootkit-present collection approach** — If a rootkit is suspected or confirmed, collection should shift to memory forensics or disk forensics. _Why:_ these methods can bypass or expose manipulation occurring inside the live operating system. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Memory forensics rootkit value** — Memory analysis can identify a rootkit and its behavior. _Why:_ rootkit code or altered kernel structures may be visible in volatile memory. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Disk forensics rootkit value** — Disk analysis can identify a rootkit and related activity. _Why:_ persistent files, drivers, configuration, or artifacts may remain available outside live API views. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Deep-dive forensic cost** — Full memory or disk forensic analysis is too time-intensive to perform across hundreds of systems as a default response action. _Why:_ large incidents require scalable triage methods before exhaustive examination. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Live response scalability trade-off** — Large-scale collection commonly favors the speed and efficiency of live response toolkits. _Why:_ responders need timely visibility across many endpoints during enterprise incidents. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Sample-based deep forensics** — Broad live response collection is typically supplemented with deeper forensic analysis on a smaller subset of systems. _Why:_ this balances enterprise-scale coverage with higher-confidence examination where needed. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Rootkit identification dilemma** — Determining whether and where a rootkit exists is difficult because the answer may require the very forensic work being prioritized. _Why:_ responders must decide where to spend deep-analysis effort without perfect initial certainty. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Security alerts as rootkit indicators** — Security alerts may help determine whether a rootkit is involved or where to investigate. _Why:_ alerts can guide targeted deep-dive collection. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Forensic examinations as rootkit indicators** — Prior forensic analysis can help answer whether rootkit activity is present and where it may reside. _Why:_ confirmed artifacts can drive scoping and collection decisions. _[GCFA p.103]_
- **Threat intelligence as rootkit guidance** — Threat intelligence can help assess whether a campaign or actor is likely to use rootkits. _Why:_ intelligence can prioritize hosts or techniques for deeper validation. _[GCFA p.103]_

- **Flat configuration format** — `Modules.conf` is a plain, line-oriented configuration file rather than a nested or database-backed format. _Why:_ responders can quickly edit the collection plan with a text editor. _[GCFA p.104]_

### Order of Volatility

- **Volatility-aware ordering** — `Modules.conf` should be arranged according to the volatility of the data being collected. _Why:_ evidence likely to change or disappear should be captured before less fragile evidence. _[GCFA p.104]_
- **Execution order control** — Moving a module entry nearer the top of `Modules.conf` causes it to run earlier than entries below it. _Why:_ responders can prioritize fragile artifacts by reordering lines. _[GCFA p.104]_
- **Frequently changing artifacts** — Network state, system memory, and Prefetch data are identified as examples of highly changeable artifacts. _Why:_ these evidence sources can be overwritten or altered quickly during system activity. _[GCFA p.104]_
- **Early collection rationale** — Volatile evidence should be collected early to reduce the chance that it is overwritten unnecessarily. _Why:_ delayed acquisition can destroy or distort incident evidence. _[GCFA p.104]_
- **Network data priority** — Network-related modules are placed near the top of the displayed configuration. _Why:_ active connections and cached network state can change rapidly during response. _[GCFA p.104]_
- **Prefetch priority** — Prefetch-related modules are shown near the top, though commented out. _Why:_ Prefetch is treated as volatile enough to be considered early in collection planning. _[GCFA p.104]_
- **DNS cache priority** — `Get-DNSCache.ps1` is placed near the top of the active module list. _Why:_ DNS cache entries can expire or be overwritten, so they are valuable to collect early. _[GCFA p.104]_
- **ARP priority** — `Get-Arp.ps1` is listed near the top, though disabled in the screenshot. _Why:_ ARP information represents volatile local network state. _[GCFA p.104]_

### Target Selection

- **`-TargetList .\hostlist`** — this option tells `kansa.ps1` to run collectors against hosts named in the `.\hostlist` file. _Why:_ defines how responders scope collection to selected machines. _[GCFA p.~106]_
- **Host list format** — the host list file is expected to contain one computer name per line. _Why:_ prevents malformed targeting input during incident-response collection. _[GCFA p.~106]_
- **Omitting `-TargetList`** — when no target list is provided, Kansa queries Active Directory for computer accounts and targets every discovered computer. _Why:_ this can expand collection from a small list to the whole domain. _[GCFA p.~106]_
- **Active Directory dependency** — Kansa’s AD-based target discovery requires the Active Directory module included with Remote Server Administration Tools. _Why:_ explains why AD discovery fails unless RSAT’s AD tooling is installed. _[GCFA p.~106]_

- **`-TargetCount` purpose** — `-TargetCount` limits how many systems Kansa queries or targets when using AD discovery. _Why:_ lets responders avoid unintentionally launching collection across too many hosts. _[GCFA p.~106]_
- **`-TargetCount 250`** — the example command caps the run at 250 targets. _Why:_ captures the exact demonstrated limit value. _[GCFA p.~106]_

- **Remote object conversion** — Kansa collectors commonly take PowerShell objects returned from remote systems and convert them into tab-separated output. _Why:_ makes large-scale results easier to parse with analysis tools. _[GCFA p.~106]_

## Page 108

### Kansa Third-Party Binary Support

- **Kansa execution scope** — Kansa is not restricted to WMI queries or native PowerShell cmdlets. _Why:_ responders can extend Kansa beyond built-in Windows and PowerShell collection methods. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **Third-party collection need** — Some incident-response collection tasks require external tools even though PowerShell is highly capable. _Why:_ analysts should know when Kansa needs helper binaries instead of pure PowerShell. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **External binary execution** — Kansa can deploy and run standalone executables on remote systems. _Why:_ this enables enterprise-scale use of trusted forensic utilities through Kansa. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **Binary staging directory** — Third-party executables intended for Kansa deployment are placed under `.\Modules\bin\`. _Why:_ Kansa expects binary dependencies to be available from this module-support directory. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **Collector-script dependency marker** — A collector that needs a binary must include a special dependency comment on the second line of the script. _Why:_ Kansa uses this marker to identify which executable must be copied to targets. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **Kansa dependency directive** — The special comment used for binary dependencies is called a directive by Kansa’s author. _Why:_ this is the mechanism that connects a script module to its required executable. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **`BINDEP` meaning** — `BINDEP` identifies a binary dependency. _Why:_ Kansa scans comments for this token to decide what binary must be pushed. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **Directive syntax example** — The `Get-Autorunsc.ps1` module declares its dependency with `# BINDEP .\Modules\bin\Autorunsc.exe`. _Why:_ this exact value shows how Kansa maps the Autoruns collector to `Autorunsc.exe`. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **Directive as PowerShell comment** — The binary dependency line is syntactically a comment, not executable PowerShell code. _Why:_ the script remains valid PowerShell while still carrying Kansa-specific metadata. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **Directive behavior** — The `BINDEP` directive tells Kansa to copy `.\Modules\bin\Autorunsc.exe` to remote targets before running the collector. _Why:_ this ensures the remote endpoint has the executable needed by the module. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **`kansa.ps1 -Pushbin` requirement** — Kansa must be run with `-Pushbin` when binaries need to be copied to remote systems. _Why:_ without this flag, declared binary dependencies may not be deployed. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **`-Pushbin` omission case** — If the needed binary already exists on the remote system, `-Pushbin` can be left out. _Why:_ skipping the copy step can reduce collection time on later runs. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **Default remote binary location** — Kansa copies pushed binaries to `%SystemRoot%` by default. _Why:_ responders should know where third-party tools may appear on target systems. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **Typical `%SystemRoot%` value** — `%SystemRoot%` commonly resolves to `C:\Windows`. _Why:_ this gives the usual on-disk location where Kansa-deployed binaries may be staged. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **Binary cleanup choice** — The module author decides whether a pushed executable is removed after execution. _Why:_ cleanup behavior affects target-system residue and future run speed. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **Keeping binaries on targets** — A binary may intentionally be left in place for reuse in later collections. _Why:_ leaving it staged can make repeated executions faster. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **`-Rmbin` cleanup flag** — Running Kansa with `-Rmbin` removes pushed binaries after use. _Why:_ this flag reduces leftover responder tooling on endpoints. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **Binary persistence option** — Kansa-deployed binaries can either be deleted after execution or retained for later use. _Why:_ responders must balance endpoint cleanliness against operational speed. _[GCFA p.~108]_
- **Kansa output handling** — Results from these tool-backed modules are returned and formatted as PowerShell objects. _Why:_ this keeps third-party tool output compatible with Kansa’s PowerShell-based processing pipeline. _[GCFA p.~108]_
