### KAPE Overview

- **KAPE** — KAPE is a no-cost Windows forensic triage collection and processing tool authored by Eric Zimmerman. _Why:_ identifies the tool’s purpose, platform context, and provenance. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **KAPE primary purpose** — KAPE is built to gather selected forensic artifacts into a triage collection and can also run post-collection processing. _Why:_ distinguishes KAPE from tools that only copy files or only analyze data. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **KAPE target files** — KAPE uses community-developed target definitions to specify which artifacts should be collected. _Why:_ target files define the evidence scope of a KAPE acquisition. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **KAPE triage image** — The artifacts selected by KAPE targets are gathered into a triage image. _Why:_ explains the output concept produced during collection. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **KAPE meta-files** — Multiple KAPE targets can be bundled into meta-files for particular investigation categories. _Why:_ enables repeatable collection profiles for different case types. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **!SANS_Triage.tkape** — KAPE includes a meta-file named `!SANS_Triage.tkape`. _Why:_ this is a ready-made SANS-oriented collection profile. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **!SANS_Triage.tkape coverage** — `!SANS_Triage.tkape` includes targets for most artifacts covered in SANS FOR498, FOR500, and FOR508. _Why:_ shows that the profile is broad enough for common SANS DFIR workflows. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **KAPE reliability and speed** — KAPE is presented as a fast and dependable way to collect forensic data from a system. _Why:_ supports its use during time-sensitive incident response. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **KAPE operating system support** — KAPE is currently limited to Windows. _Why:_ responders must account for platform support before deployment. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **KAPE removable-media execution** — KAPE can be run from a USB thumb drive. _Why:_ supports portable live-response collection without installation. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **KAPE remote staging** — KAPE can be pushed or downloaded onto a remote endpoint for execution. _Why:_ enables remote enterprise triage workflows. _[GCFA p.~111]_

### Forensic Soundness Table

- **Forensically sound · Full metadata preservation** — KAPE preserves complete file metadata during collection. _Why:_ metadata retention is critical for timeline reconstruction and evidentiary integrity. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Forensically sound · Detailed audit logs** — KAPE records detailed logs of its collection activity. _Why:_ audit trails help validate what was collected and how the tool behaved. _[GCFA p.~111]_

### Robustness Table

- **Robust · Volume Shadow Copy support** — KAPE can collect from Windows Volume Shadow Copies. _Why:_ shadow copies may contain historical versions of artifacts unavailable in the live file system. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Robust · Alternate data stream extraction** — KAPE can extract NTFS alternate data streams. _Why:_ ADS content may hide downloaded-file metadata or attacker-staged data. _[GCFA p.~111]_

### Flexibility Table

- **Flexible · Locked-file handling** — KAPE can collect files that are locked by the operating system or active processes. _Why:_ important forensic artifacts are often locked while Windows is running. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Flexible · SHA-1 file deduplication** — KAPE can deduplicate collected files using SHA-1 hashing. _Why:_ reduces collection size while preserving unique content. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Flexible · SFTP network transfer** — KAPE can send collection results across a network using SFTP. _Why:_ supports centralized evidence collection from remote systems. _[GCFA p.~111]_

### Extensibility Table

- **Extensible · Investigative customization** — KAPE can be customized to fit specific investigative requirements. _Why:_ teams can tune collection scope instead of relying only on default artifacts. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Extensible · Custom targets and modules** — Users can create their own KAPE targets and modules. _Why:_ custom definitions allow KAPE to support new artifacts, tools, and workflows. _[GCFA p.~111]_

### Output Destinations

- **Attached-drive output** — KAPE results can be written to a locally attached drive. _Why:_ supports direct collection to removable or external storage. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **File-share output** — KAPE can send results to a network file share. _Why:_ enables centralized collection in environments with accessible shares. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **SFTP-server output** — KAPE can send results to an SFTP server. _Why:_ supports secure transfer to a remote evidence repository. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Amazon AWS cloud output** — KAPE results can be sent to cloud storage or infrastructure through Amazon AWS. _Why:_ supports scalable remote collection workflows. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Microsoft Azure cloud output** — KAPE results can be sent to Microsoft Azure. _Why:_ enables cloud-hosted evidence intake for Microsoft-oriented environments. _[GCFA p.~111]_

### Remote Collection Workflows

- **PowerShell Remoting with KAPE** — Mark Hallman and Carlos Cajigas published approaches that use PowerShell Remoting to make endpoints download and run KAPE. _Why:_ provides a method for orchestrating KAPE across many systems. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **KAPE batch mode** — The published remote workflows run KAPE in batch mode. _Why:_ batch execution supports repeatable large-scale collection without manual interaction on each endpoint. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Cloud SFTP collection workflow** — The referenced remote workflows send collected KAPE data to a cloud-hosted SFTP server. _Why:_ allows distributed endpoints to return evidence to a centralized remote destination. _[GCFA p.~111]_

### Feature List

- **Portable execution** — KAPE does not require installation. _Why:_ responders can run it quickly with minimal endpoint changes. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Audit logging feature** — KAPE provides detailed audit logs. _Why:_ logging supports defensibility and troubleshooting of collection activity. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Flexible and customizable collection** — KAPE’s collection behavior can be adjusted by investigators. _Why:_ supports targeted evidence gathering instead of one-size-fits-all acquisition. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Wildcard and recursion handling** — KAPE is described as avoiding wildcard and recursion problems seen in other tools. _Why:_ reduces the risk of missed artifacts or uncontrolled collection expansion. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Team standardization** — KAPE makes it easier for teams to standardize the artifacts they collect. _Why:_ consistent collection improves repeatability and comparison across cases. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Locked system-file collection** — KAPE can collect locked operating-system files. _Why:_ many high-value forensic artifacts are unavailable through ordinary copy operations. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Alternate data stream collection** — KAPE can collect alternate data streams. _Why:_ ADS may contain security-relevant metadata or concealed content. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Volume Shadow Copy collection** — KAPE supports collection from Windows Volume Shadow Copies. _Why:_ historical snapshots can preserve evidence that was modified or deleted from the live file system. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Inline deduplication** — KAPE can deduplicate during collection rather than only afterward. _Why:_ lowers storage and transfer requirements during triage. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **Module-based post-processing** — KAPE can post-process collected data through module capabilities. _Why:_ allows collection and analysis workflows to be chained in one toolset. _[GCFA p.~111]_
- **High-speed operation** — KAPE is characterized as exceptionally fast. _Why:_ speed matters when collecting from live systems or many endpoints. _[GCFA p.~111]_

### KAPE Target Collection Inputs

- **KAPE target collection** — KAPE collection requires specifying where evidence resides, what should be collected, and where copied evidence should be written. _Why:_ these three inputs define the scope and destination of a triage acquisition. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **Evidence source location** — The source data location may be identified by a drive letter. _Why:_ drive-level selection controls which volume KAPE searches for artifacts. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **Evidence source directory** — The source data location may be a directory rather than an entire drive. _Why:_ directory-scoped collection can narrow acquisition to a known evidence location. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **F-Response source** — KAPE can collect from data exposed through F-Response. _Why:_ this supports remote or forensic-access collection workflows where disks are presented through F-Response. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **`--tsource` role** — The `--tsource` option identifies the location KAPE should search for target artifacts. _Why:_ without a valid source, KAPE cannot locate the files or artifacts requested by targets. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **Collection content category** — KAPE targets define what evidence should be collected. _Why:_ targets translate investigative goals into concrete artifact paths and patterns. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **File system collection** — KAPE target selection can include file-system artifacts. _Why:_ file-system data often contains core evidence for timeline, execution, and user-activity analysis. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **Execution evidence collection** — KAPE target selection can include artifacts showing program execution. _Why:_ execution evidence is central for identifying malware launch, attacker tooling, and user activity. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **`--target` role** — The `--target` option specifies the target configuration KAPE should run. _Why:_ this determines the artifact set collected from the source. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **Collection destination** — KAPE requires a destination where copied artifacts will be stored. _Why:_ the destination preserves collected evidence separately from the source. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **Destination directory** — KAPE output can be written to a local directory. _Why:_ local folders are a simple destination for triage collections. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **Destination UNC path** — KAPE output can be written to a UNC network path. _Why:_ network destinations support centralized evidence collection from endpoints. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **Destination VHD/VHDX container** — KAPE output can be placed into a VHD or VHDX virtual disk container. _Why:_ containerized output can simplify transport, mounting, and preservation of collected evidence. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **`--tdest` role** — The `--tdest` option identifies where KAPE should copy collected data. _Why:_ this controls the final evidence storage location. _[GCFA p.~112]_

### KAPE Option Details

- **`tsource` accepted value type** — `tsource` can point to either a drive letter or a directory. _Why:_ analysts can collect from whole volumes or narrower folder paths. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **`tsource` format example `C`** — The page lists `C` as a valid-style source format. _Why:_ this shows that a bare drive letter may be accepted as source input. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **`tsource` format example `D:`** — The page lists `D:` as a valid-style source format. _Why:_ this shows that a drive letter with a colon may be used. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **`tsource` format example `F:\`** — The page lists `F:\` as a valid-style source format. _Why:_ this shows that a rooted drive path may be used. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **`target` value** — The `target` option takes the target configuration name without its file extension. _Why:_ analysts must provide the correct logical target name rather than a full filename. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **`--tlist` switch** — The `--tlist` switch lists available KAPE targets. _Why:_ it helps analysts discover valid target names before running a collection. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **`tdest` value** — The `tdest` option specifies the directory where KAPE copies files. _Why:_ this determines where acquired artifacts are placed. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **Automatic destination creation** — KAPE creates the destination directory if it is missing. _Why:_ this reduces setup friction and prevents failure solely because the output folder does not yet exist. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **`tdest` local path support** — `tdest` can be a normal filesystem directory. _Why:_ this supports straightforward local evidence output. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **`tdest` UNC support** — `tdest` can be a UNC path. _Why:_ this enables output to network shares for centralized collection. _[GCFA p.~112]_

### Additional KAPE Options

- **`tvss` option** — The `tvss` option finds, mounts, and searches available Volume Shadow Copies for the specified `--tsource`. _Why:_ shadow copies may contain historical versions of artifacts that no longer exist in the live filesystem. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **Volume Shadow Copy search scope** — `tvss` operates against the source identified by `--tsource`. _Why:_ analysts must understand that shadow-copy handling is tied to the selected evidence source. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **`vhdx` option** — The `vhdx` option creates a VHDX virtual hard disk from the contents of `--tdest`. _Why:_ VHDX output can package collected evidence into a mountable container. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **`vhd` option** — The `vhd` option creates a VHD virtual hard disk from the contents of `--tdest`. _Why:_ VHD output provides another mountable container format for collected evidence. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **VHD/VHDX source contents** — The virtual disk options use the contents of the destination directory as the material for the container. _Why:_ container creation happens from collected output, not directly from the original source. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **`debug` option** — Setting `debug` to true enables debug-level messages. _Why:_ debug output can assist troubleshooting when a KAPE run does not behave as expected. _[GCFA p.~112]_

- **gKAPE GUI** — KAPE ships with a graphical front end named `gKAPE`. _Why:_ the GUI helps users work with KAPE options without manually composing every command. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **gKAPE option navigation** — gKAPE helps users browse available KAPE options. _Why:_ this reduces the chance of missing or mistyping supported switches. _[GCFA p.~112]_
- **gKAPE command generation** — gKAPE can generate complex KAPE command lines. _Why:_ analysts can build a command interactively and reuse it later in scripted workflows. _[GCFA p.~112]_

### VQL Design And Query Capabilities

- **Flexibility as a design goal** — Velociraptor was designed from the start with flexibility as a central objective. _Why:_ flexibility explains why the tool can support many collection, monitoring, and response workflows. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **VQL** — Velociraptor’s main flexibility mechanism is VQL, the Velociraptor Query Language. _Why:_ VQL is the core interface analysts use to express collection and analysis logic. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Purpose-built query language** — VQL is a custom query language created specifically for Velociraptor. _Why:_ analysts should treat it as a specialized DFIR query system rather than a generic shell or SQL clone. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Simple query construction** — VQL lets analysts write comparatively simple queries that can still be used for powerful operations. _Why:_ this lowers the barrier for building useful endpoint collection and hunting logic. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Operating-system analysis coverage** — VQL queries can inspect many different areas of an operating system. _Why:_ this makes VQL useful beyond a single artifact type or narrow telemetry source. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **One-time collection mode** — VQL queries can be run once for immediate data acquisition. _Why:_ this supports targeted incident-response collection from endpoints. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Continuous streaming mode** — VQL queries can also be configured to continuously send results from clients to the frontend server. _Why:_ streaming enables ongoing telemetry rather than only point-in-time triage. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Client-to-frontend data flow** — Continuous VQL output streams from the Velociraptor client back to the frontend server. _Why:_ understanding this direction matters for network design, monitoring, and data-ingest expectations. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Continuous monitoring** — Streaming VQL results gives Velociraptor continuous monitoring capability. _Why:_ analysts can use Velociraptor as a persistent detection platform, not just a collection tool. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Automated response** — VQL-driven monitoring can support automated response actions. _Why:_ Velociraptor can move from passive observation into active containment or collection workflows. _[GCFA p.114]_

### VQL Monitoring And Response Examples

- **Windows failed-logon monitoring** — Velociraptor can continuously watch selected Windows Event Logs, including failed authentication events in the Security log. _Why:_ failed-logon telemetry is useful for detecting brute force, password spraying, and unauthorized access attempts. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Security log EID 4625** — Failed Windows logons are specifically tied to Security event ID 4625. _Why:_ EID 4625 is the concrete event identifier analysts can query or monitor. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Sysmon process-creation monitoring** — Velociraptor can monitor all process creation events through the Sysmon event log. _Why:_ process creation data is central to endpoint detection and timeline reconstruction. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Sysmon EID 1** — Sysmon process creation is identified as event ID 1. _Why:_ EID 1 is the specific event number analysts can use when building process-monitoring logic. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Endpoint DNS monitoring** — Velociraptor can monitor DNS queries made by endpoints. _Why:_ DNS telemetry can reveal command-and-control lookups, suspicious domains, and lateral movement infrastructure. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **New service creation monitoring** — Velociraptor can watch for newly created Windows services. _Why:_ malicious services are a common persistence and execution mechanism. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Automatic service executable acquisition** — When a new service is observed, Velociraptor can automatically collect the executable behind that service. _Why:_ immediate acquisition preserves a suspicious binary for forensic analysis before it is removed or changed. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Executable-name matching** — Velociraptor can watch for new executables based on filename. _Why:_ name-based matching can catch known suspicious tools or malware naming patterns. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Executable-hash matching** — Velociraptor can watch for new executables based on hash value. _Why:_ hash matching enables detection of known malware or known-good/known-bad binaries. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Executable-parent matching** — Velociraptor can watch for new executables based on parent process characteristics. _Why:_ parent-child process relationships help identify suspicious execution chains. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Executable characteristic matching** — Velociraptor can watch for new executables using additional properties beyond name, hash, or parent. _Why:_ flexible matching allows analysts to encode broader detection criteria. _[GCFA p.114]_
- **Executable termination response** — Velociraptor can kill newly observed executables that match selected criteria. _Why:_ this gives the tool an active response capability against suspicious or malicious processes. _[GCFA p.114]_

## Page 119

### Velociraptor Scaling

- **Single-server workload pressure** — a Velociraptor server may become overloaded when it must simultaneously manage endpoint/client communication and run analyst-facing data queries. _Why:_ this identifies a scaling limit in centralized DFIR collection and analysis infrastructure. _[GCFA p.~119]_

- **Client communication load** — endpoint/client communication is one of the workload categories that can consume Velociraptor server resources. _Why:_ client handling competes with analysis activity for the same server capacity. _[GCFA p.~119]_

- **Analyst query load** — analyst data searches and investigative queries are another workload category that can tax the Velociraptor server. _Why:_ intensive querying can degrade the same system responsible for client coordination. _[GCFA p.~119]_

- **Dedicated analysis server** — when combined client and analyst workloads become too heavy, analysis should be moved to a separate system. _Why:_ separating collection/control from analysis improves scalability and reduces operational contention. _[GCFA p.~119]_

### External Analysis Platforms

- **Elasticsearch** — Elasticsearch is identified as a strong platform for offloading Velociraptor analysis workloads. _Why:_ it provides a dedicated backend for searching and analyzing collected forensic data. _[GCFA p.~119]_

- **Splunk** — Splunk is identified as another strong option for handling offloaded analysis workloads. _Why:_ it can absorb analyst search activity outside the primary Velociraptor server. _[GCFA p.~119]_

### VQL Transformation Table

- **View specific columns · Data operation** — the operation is selecting only particular output fields. _Why:_ limiting columns reduces noise and keeps visible data focused. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **View specific columns · VQL operator** — the operator pattern shown is `SELECT <column> FROM`. _Why:_ `SELECT` controls which fields appear in the result set. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **View specific columns · Example VQL** — the example query is `SELECT Exe,Hash FROM source()`. _Why:_ it shows how to display executable and hash fields from the current source data. _[GCFA p.~120]_

- **Expose nested JSON field · Data operation** — the operation is accessing a field nested inside a JSON-like structure. _Why:_ Velociraptor results may contain nested objects that require explicit field traversal. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **Expose nested JSON field · VQL operator** — the operator pattern shown is `<column>.<nested field name>`. _Why:_ dot notation lets an analyst address a nested value directly. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **Expose nested JSON field · Example VQL** — the example query is `SELECT Exe,Hash.MD5 FROM source()`. _Why:_ it extracts the executable name and the MD5 value nested under `Hash`. _[GCFA p.~120]_

- **Filter for keyword · Data operation** — the operation is keeping rows that match a keyword. _Why:_ keyword filters isolate suspicious or relevant records. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **Filter for keyword · VQL operator** — the operator pattern shown is `WHERE <column> =~ 'keyword'`. _Why:_ this pattern applies a match condition against a selected column. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **Filter for keyword · Example VQL** — the example condition is `WHERE Exe =~ 'mimikatz'`. _Why:_ it demonstrates filtering process executable data for a known credential-theft tool name. _[GCFA p.~120]_

- **Negate filter for keyword · Data operation** — the operation is excluding rows that match a keyword. _Why:_ negative filtering removes common or unwanted records from review. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **Negate filter for keyword · VQL operator** — the operator pattern shown is `WHERE NOT <column> =~ 'keyword'`. _Why:_ `NOT` inverts the match so matching rows are removed instead of retained. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **Negate filter for keyword · Example VQL** — the example condition is `WHERE NOT Exe =~ 'svchost'`. _Why:_ it demonstrates excluding rows whose executable field matches `svchost`. _[GCFA p.~120]_

- **Join multiple filters · Data operation** — the operation is combining more than one filter condition. _Why:_ multi-condition filtering narrows results more precisely than a single condition. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **Join multiple filters · VQL operator** — the table specifies Boolean `AND|OR` for combining filters. _Why:_ Boolean logic controls whether conditions must all match or whether any one condition is enough. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **Join multiple filters · Example VQL** — the example condition is `WHERE NOT Exe =~ 'svchost' AND NOT Exe =~ 'edge'`. _Why:_ it shows how to exclude multiple executable-name patterns in one filter. _[GCFA p.~120]_

- **Group like values · Data operation** — the operation is grouping rows that share the same value. _Why:_ grouping collapses repeated values into analyzable clusters. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **Group like values · VQL operator** — the operator pattern shown is `GROUP BY <column>`. _Why:_ `GROUP BY` organizes records around distinct values in a selected field. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **Group like values · Example VQL** — the example grouping is `GROUP BY Hash.MD5`. _Why:_ it groups records by MD5 hash value, which can expose repeated binaries. _[GCFA p.~120]_

- **Count occurrences · Data operation** — the operation is counting how many records occur in each result context. _Why:_ counts help identify common, rare, or repeated artifacts. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **Count occurrences · VQL operator** — the function pattern shown is `count() AS <new column name>`. _Why:_ `count()` produces an aggregate value and `AS` labels the output column. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **Count occurrences · Example VQL** — the example query is `SELECT Exe,Hash.MD5,count() AS Count FROM source()`. _Why:_ it outputs executable names, MD5 values, and a calculated count column named `Count`. _[GCFA p.~120]_

- **Sort alphanumerically · Data operation** — the operation is ordering results by alphanumeric sort. _Why:_ sorting helps surface high, low, first, or last values depending on the chosen order. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **Sort alphanumerically · VQL operator** — the operator pattern shown is `ORDER BY <column> <DESC>`. _Why:_ `ORDER BY` sorts a chosen field, and `DESC` can request descending order. _[GCFA p.~120]_
- **Sort alphanumerically · Example VQL** — the example sort is `ORDER BY Count`, with the page noting that ascending order is the default. _Why:_ analysts must specify descending order when they do not want the default ascending sort. _[GCFA p.~120]_

## Page 125

### Credential Harvesting Priority

- **Credential harvesting · Post-exploitation priority** — Attackers commonly treat credential collection as the top operational task immediately after gaining post-exploitation access. _Why:_ credential access often determines whether the intrusion can expand beyond the initially compromised host. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Credential harvesting · Domain administrator objective** — The attacker’s desired credential target is often a domain administrator account. _Why:_ domain administrator access can enable broad enterprise control and rapid lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Initial compromise · Limited access** — Attackers usually do not begin with enough privileges to move freely across an enterprise. _Why:_ defenders should expect privilege escalation or credential theft attempts shortly after the first foothold. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Privilege escalation · Network compromise requirement** — Full network compromise usually requires either privilege escalation or acquisition of more privileged credentials. _Why:_ escalation and credential acquisition are key phases to monitor after intrusion discovery. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Lateral movement · Credential dependency** — Many lateral movement methods require valid credentials or reusable credential material. _Why:_ account telemetry can reveal movement that would not appear as exploit activity. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Windows activity · Account linkage** — Most Windows actions are associated with an account identity. _Why:_ account-based logging gives investigators a strong basis for reconstructing attacker behavior. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Privileged accounts · Movement enabler** — Lateral movement in Windows is difficult without privileged account access. _Why:_ privileged account use is a high-value detection point. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Vulnerability exploitation · Credential exception** — Exploiting vulnerabilities is one of the few ways to move laterally without relying on a privileged account. _Why:_ defenders should distinguish credential-driven movement from exploit-driven propagation. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Credential harvesting · Stealth and ease** — Using credentials can be a comparatively easy and quiet way for attackers to move through a network. _Why:_ legitimate authentication may blend into normal administrative activity unless monitored carefully. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Sleeper accounts · Persistence role** — Newly created or retained accounts can give attackers access again after remediation. _Why:_ overlooked accounts can undermine incident cleanup and enable re-entry. _[GCFA p.~125]_

- **Event logs · Detection source** — Windows event logs are listed as a primary source for credential and account activity detection. _Why:_ event IDs provide structured evidence of logons, account creation, authentication, and privileged use. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Event ID 4624 · Logons** — Windows event ID 4624 is associated with successful logon activity. _Why:_ successful logons are core evidence for tracking account use and possible lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Event ID 4720 · Account creation** — Windows event ID 4720 is associated with account creation. _Why:_ new accounts may indicate attacker persistence or evasion. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Event ID 4776 · Local account authentication** — Windows event ID 4776 is listed for local account authentication activity. _Why:_ local account use can expose abuse of shared or compromised local credentials. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Event ID 4672 · Privileged account usage** — Windows event ID 4672 is associated with privileged account use. _Why:_ privileged logon events help identify high-impact account activity during an intrusion. _[GCFA p.~125]_

- **Unix secure logs · Detection source** — Unix “secure” logs are listed as a source for account activity monitoring. _Why:_ cross-platform account telemetry matters in mixed Windows and Unix environments. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Windows account logging · Detection value** — Windows provides strong logging for account activity. _Why:_ Windows authentication events can support account-centric investigation and threat hunting. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Unix account logging · Detection value** — Unix systems also provide useful account activity logging. _Why:_ Unix authentication records can reveal attacker access outside Windows-only telemetry. _[GCFA p.~125]_

### Account Monitoring

- **Account activity · Trackability** — Account activity is described as relatively easy to monitor and follow. _Why:_ defenders can use account behavior as a dependable investigative axis. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Domain administrator accounts · Monitoring priority** — Extremely privileged accounts, including domain administrators, are especially practical and important to track. _Why:_ misuse of these accounts can indicate severe compromise. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Compromised accounts · Monitoring requirement** — Known compromised accounts should be tracked as part of detection and response. _Why:_ attackers may continue using credentials after the initial compromise is known. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Privileged accounts · Monitoring requirement** — Privileged account usage should be monitored in addition to known compromised accounts. _Why:_ unexpected privileged activity may indicate escalation or unauthorized administration. _[GCFA p.~125]_

- **New account creation · Low-frequency event** — New account creation is described as an infrequent event in many environments. _Why:_ low baseline frequency makes these events suitable for alerting and review. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **New account creation · Threat actor use** — Some attackers create accounts to avoid existing monitoring. _Why:_ defenders who only track known accounts may miss attacker-controlled identities. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Sleeper accounts · Remediation bypass** — Attacker-created accounts may survive cleanup and allow quick access after the breach response. _Why:_ account inventory review is necessary before declaring remediation complete. _[GCFA p.~125]_

### Anomalous Login Detection

- **Anomalous logins · Detection category** — Unusual login behavior is listed as a detection focus. _Why:_ deviations from normal account behavior can reveal lateral movement or unauthorized access. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Device-to-device anomaly · Workstation-to-workstation logins** — Logins from one workstation to another are specifically listed as anomalous activity. _Why:_ this pattern is uncommon in many enterprise client-server models and often aligns with attacker lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Network anomaly · Sensitive networks** — Logins involving sensitive network segments are listed as a monitoring focus. _Why:_ access into protected areas may indicate privilege misuse or intrusion expansion. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Time anomaly · After-hours logins** — Logins outside normal working hours are listed as suspicious account activity. _Why:_ unusual timing can reveal unauthorized access that avoids business-hour scrutiny. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Anomalous login maturity · Device dimension** — Mature account monitoring can identify abnormal logins between devices. _Why:_ source and destination host relationships help expose lateral movement paths. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Anomalous login maturity · Network segment dimension** — Mature monitoring can detect abnormal authentication between network segments. _Why:_ segment-aware detection helps identify movement into unusual or sensitive areas. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Anomalous login maturity · Time-of-day dimension** — Mature account management can detect unusual login times. _Why:_ time-based baselines help surface attacker activity outside expected user behavior. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Workstation lateral movement · Common attacker behavior** — Moving laterally between workstations is described as a common attacker behavior. _Why:_ workstation-to-workstation authentication can be a strong hunting signal. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Server-client models · Workstation movement rarity** — Workstation-to-workstation movement is rare in most server-client enterprise models. _Why:_ rarity makes this behavior easier to prioritize during triage. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Lateral movement capability · Limiting control** — The ability to move laterally between workstations can be restricted. _Why:_ reducing this capability decreases attacker mobility after compromise. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Lateral movement capability · Audit control** — Workstation lateral movement can be audited. _Why:_ auditing creates evidence for detecting and reconstructing unauthorized movement. _[GCFA p.~125]_

### Shared Local Administrator Risk

- **Shared local administrator account · Enterprise vulnerability** — Many enterprises have a local administrator account that uses the same password on multiple systems. _Why:_ password reuse turns one host compromise into a broader lateral movement opportunity. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Shared local administrator password · Lateral movement effect** — If one system with a reused local admin password is compromised, attackers may access many other systems. _Why:_ reused local credentials can expand the breach rapidly. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Shared local administrator password · Credential expansion** — Each additional system reached with shared local admin credentials may expose more credentials. _Why:_ lateral movement can compound credential theft across the environment. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Local account usage · Enterprise rarity** — Local account use is described as uncommon in enterprise environments. _Why:_ uncommon local authentication is a useful signal for detection. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Local account usage · Event log visibility** — Local account usage can be monitored through event logs. _Why:_ event logs can expose abuse of local credentials during lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Local account usage plus privileged monitoring · Abuse detection** — Local account monitoring combined with privileged account monitoring can often reveal misuse. _Why:_ correlating local and privileged activity strengthens detection of credential abuse. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Microsoft operating systems · Local admin restrictions** — Recent Microsoft operating systems have significantly reduced what local administrator accounts can do remotely. _Why:_ built-in platform restrictions can reduce risk from reused local administrator credentials. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Local administrator account · C$ share limitation** — A local administrator account cannot remotely write to the `C$` administrative share in the described newer Windows behavior. _Why:_ this limits one common remote file-copy method used for lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Local administrator account · Admin$ share limitation** — A local administrator account cannot remotely write to the `Admin$` administrative share in the described newer Windows behavior. _Why:_ this restricts another common administrative path used for remote execution setup. _[GCFA p.~125]_
- **Local administrator account · Remote management limitation** — A local administrator account cannot use some remote management capabilities in the described newer Windows behavior. _Why:_ reduced remote management rights limit the practical usefulness of stolen local admin credentials. _[GCFA p.~125]_

### Local Administrator Protections

- **Remote execution tools** — Tools such as `schtasks`, `at`, and WMI can be used for remote tasking or execution in Windows environments. _Why:_ these mechanisms are relevant because attackers and responders both use them for remote administration and lateral movement. _[GCFA p.126]_

- **WinRM exception for WMI/PowerShell** — When Windows Remote Management is enabled, WMI and PowerShell remoting can still operate with a local administrator account. _Why:_ this limits the effectiveness of local-account restrictions because remote management paths may remain usable. _[GCFA p.126]_

- **Local administrator account usage** — A local administrator account can still authenticate through WMI or PowerShell if Windows Remote Management is active. _Why:_ defenders must account for service configuration, not only account type, when reducing remote-access risk. _[GCFA p.126]_

- **Built-in Administrator exemption** — The protections discussed do not apply to the built-in Windows Administrator account. _Why:_ RID-500 accounts can remain a privileged bypass path even when other local administrator controls are deployed. _[GCFA p.126]_

- **RID 500** — The built-in Windows Administrator account is identified by RID `500`. _Why:_ RID value is a stable way to recognize the built-in Administrator even if the account has been renamed. _[GCFA p.126]_

- **Enterprise exposure from RID 500** — Many organizations still leave the built-in Administrator account enabled and in use. _Why:_ continued use of RID 500 increases lateral-movement and credential-reuse risk. _[GCFA p.126]_

### Local Admin Attack-Surface Reduction

- **Unique local admin passwords** — Enterprises can reduce risk by assigning a different password to each local administrator account. _Why:_ unique passwords prevent compromise of one local admin credential from automatically enabling access across many systems. _[GCFA p.126]_

- **Network-logon denial for local admins** — Enterprises can reduce exposure by denying network logons for local administrator accounts. _Why:_ blocking network logons limits the usefulness of local admin credentials for remote lateral movement. _[GCFA p.126]_

### Authentication Credentials

- **Authentication credentials** — authentication credentials are used to demonstrate that a user or entity is who they claim to be. _Why:_ identity proof is the starting point for determining whether later access is legitimate or credential-based abuse. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Username and password** — a username paired with a password is one example of an authentication credential. _Why:_ this is the most familiar credential form and is commonly targeted during credential theft. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Password-derived hash** — a hash generated from a plaintext password can function as an authentication-related secret. _Why:_ stolen hashes may allow authentication attacks even when the plaintext password is unavailable. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Long-term key derived from a password** — systems may store or use a durable cryptographic key derived from the user’s password instead of the password itself. _Why:_ long-lived derived secrets can become high-value artifacts during incident response. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Certificate and private key** — a certificate/private-key pair can serve as an authentication credential. _Why:_ compromise of private keys can let an attacker impersonate a user or system without knowing a password. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Credentials beyond passwords** — credentials are not limited to usernames and passwords; they also include keys, certificates, and other identity-proving secrets. _Why:_ investigations must look for multiple credential types, not only password exposure. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Authentication process** — authentication is the procedure by which a user proves their identity to a system. _Why:_ distinguishing identity proof from access permission helps classify credential artifacts correctly. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Private keys as identity proof** — a private key can prove identity when it is a secret available only to the legitimate user or entity. _Why:_ possession-based secrets can be abused for impersonation if copied or stolen. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **User-held secrets** — authentication may rely on secrets that only the intended user is expected to possess. _Why:_ forensic review should consider whether such secrets were exposed, exported, or reused. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Multifactor authentication expansion** — authentication requirements can be strengthened by adding more than one proof factor. _Why:_ MFA changes both attacker tradecraft and the artifacts analysts should expect to find. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **“Something you have” factor** — MFA may include a possession-based component, such as a device, token, key, or other item controlled by the user. _Why:_ compromise may involve theft, registration, or misuse of a possession factor. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **“Something you are” factor** — MFA may include an inherent-user component, such as a biometric characteristic. _Why:_ this shows authentication can depend on biometric or identity-bound evidence rather than only memorized secrets. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Plaintext password avoidance** — computer systems generally avoid storing passwords in readable plaintext form. _Why:_ plaintext password storage would create direct credential exposure if the system were compromised. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Password storage as hashes or derived keys** — systems reduce password-theft risk by storing hashes or long-term keys derived from the original password. _Why:_ these stored values remain sensitive because they may support cracking, pass-the-hash-style abuse, or other credential attacks. _[GCFA p.125]_

### Authorization Credentials

- **Authorization credentials** — authorization credentials are used to obtain access to a resource after identity has been established. _Why:_ these artifacts can grant access even when the original authentication secret is not known. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Kerberos service tickets** — Kerberos service tickets are an example of authorization credentials used to access resources. _Why:_ stolen or misused tickets can enable access to services under the associated account’s privileges. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Session cookies** — session cookies are an example of authorization credentials. _Why:_ cookie theft can allow session hijacking without the attacker knowing the password. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Authorization tokens** — authorization tokens are an example of credentials used to access resources. _Why:_ token theft can provide cloud, web, API, or application access tied to the victim’s permissions. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Authorization follows authentication** — after a user successfully proves identity, the system issues authorization credentials for that session. _Why:_ analysts can separate the initial login event from later session or token-based resource access. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Session-bound authorization material** — authorization credentials are issued for the authenticated session. _Why:_ session artifacts can reveal access scope, duration, and possible hijacking opportunities. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Authorization credentials as digital identity proof** — once authentication is complete, issued authorization credentials act as digital evidence that the user has been authenticated. _Why:_ possession of these artifacts may be treated by systems as sufficient proof to permit access. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Protocol-dependent authorization forms** — the exact authorization credential type depends on the protocol in use. _Why:_ responders must know the protocol context to identify the correct artifacts, such as tickets, cookies, or tokens. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Possession grants access** — whoever possesses valid authorization credentials can access resources according to the linked account’s allowed rights. _Why:_ attackers may bypass password collection by stealing reusable session or authorization artifacts. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Privileges tied to the account** — authorization credentials confer the rights and privileges assigned to the associated user account. _Why:_ the impact of credential theft depends on the account’s effective permissions. _[GCFA p.125]_

### Authentication Versus Authorization

- **Two related access-control processes** — secure resource access depends on both authentication and authorization. _Why:_ incidents often involve abuse of either identity proof, resource-access proof, or both. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Identity requirement** — systems must know who the user is before access can be evaluated. _Why:_ attribution and access decisions depend on a verified identity claim. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Rights and privileges requirement** — systems must also determine what permissions the identified user has for specific resources. _Why:_ identity alone is insufficient; access depends on assigned privileges. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Authentication versus authorization distinction** — authentication establishes identity, while authorization determines or enables resource access based on rights. _Why:_ separating the two helps analysts interpret logs, tickets, tokens, sessions, and privilege use accurately. _[GCFA p.125]_

### Single Sign-On

- **Single sign-on concept** — networks may use SSO so a user authenticates once near the start of a session. _Why:_ one successful authentication can lead to many later accesses without repeated password prompts. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **SSO across on-premises systems** — single sign-on can let users interact with multiple internal network systems after initial authentication. _Why:_ a single compromised session may expose many internal resources. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **SSO across cloud systems** — single sign-on can also support access to cloud-hosted resources. _Why:_ credential investigations must include both local enterprise and cloud access paths. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Reduced repeated authentication prompts** — SSO allows users to access systems without proving identity again for every request. _Why:_ this convenience increases the importance of protecting issued tickets, cookies, and tokens. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **Initial identity proof in SSO** — in an SSO flow, the user proves identity at the beginning of the session. _Why:_ the first authentication event may be the key event that enables subsequent activity. _[GCFA p.125]_
- **SSO and downstream access** — after initial authentication, later resource interactions may rely on issued authorization credentials rather than fresh password entry. _Why:_ forensic timelines should connect initial login evidence with later token- or ticket-backed activity. _[GCFA p.125]_

### Group-Based Rights and Privileges

- **Microsoft account rights assignment** — Microsoft systems can grant rights and privileges directly to specific user accounts. _Why:_ direct user-level grants are part of the effective permission set investigators must consider. _[GCFA p.~128]_

- **Direct user privilege management risk** — Assigning rights one user at a time becomes hard to administer and increases the chance of mistakes. _Why:_ mismanaged direct grants can leave unexpected privileged accounts in an environment. _[GCFA p.~128]_

- **Microsoft-recommended privilege model** — Microsoft recommends assigning rights and privileges to groups rather than primarily to individual users. _Why:_ group-based administration is the expected baseline when assessing whether permissions are configured normally. _[GCFA p.~128]_

- **Group membership as privilege delivery** — A user receives the rights and privileges assigned to a group when that user account is added to the group. _Why:_ group membership changes can immediately expand an account’s authority. _[GCFA p.~128]_

- **Effective user privilege calculation** — A user account’s resulting rights and privileges come from both its group memberships and any rights assigned directly to that account. _Why:_ incident responders must review both group-derived and individually assigned privileges to determine true account capability. _[GCFA p.~128]_

### Attacker Targeting of Privileged Groups

- **Privileged group targeting** — Attackers prioritize accounts belonging to highly privileged groups. _Why:_ compromising one such account can provide broad administrative control. _[GCFA p.~128]_

- **Domain Admins as high-value targets** — Domain Admins are specifically identified as an example of a highly privileged group. _Why:_ membership in this group often gives attackers powerful domain-level control. _[GCFA p.~128]_

- **Enterprise Admins as high-value targets** — Enterprise Admins are specifically identified as another highly privileged group. _Why:_ this group can provide even broader enterprise-level authority in Active Directory environments. _[GCFA p.~128]_

- **Compromised privileged account impact** — Control of an account in a privileged group gives the attacker the rights and privileges assigned to that group. _Why:_ account compromise must be evaluated based on inherited group authority, not only the account name. _[GCFA p.~128]_

- **Malicious group membership modification** — Attackers may change an account’s group membership to grant added rights and privileges to accounts they control. _Why:_ unauthorized group changes are a key evidence point for privilege escalation and persistence. _[GCFA p.~128]_

### NT Hash Generation

- **Local account password example** — the depicted user password is `P4ssw0rd!`. _Why:_ this is the sample plaintext input used to illustrate Windows password hashing. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **NT one-way hash function input** — the example password `P4ssw0rd!` is passed into `MD4(P4ssw0rd!)`. _Why:_ this shows the page’s concrete password-to-hash transformation. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Example NT hash value** — the shown output hash is `6ced6cb821b81327d4b8b096947e0615`. _Why:_ this is the exact sample NT hash value visible in the diagram. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **NT one-way hash function** — Windows uses the NTOWF algorithm to derive a password hash from each account’s plaintext password. _Why:_ responders often recover hashes rather than passwords, so knowing how Windows derives them is foundational. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Plaintext password storage** — Windows does not normally save user passwords in plaintext form. _Why:_ forensic acquisition of Windows account data usually yields hashes or protected credential material, not cleartext passwords. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Per-user hash generation** — NTOWF produces a hash value for the plaintext password associated with a user account. _Why:_ each account’s stored authentication material is tied to that account’s password. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **NT hash name** — the output of the NTOWF process is called the NT hash. _Why:_ this is the credential artifact commonly targeted in Windows incident response. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **NT acronym meaning** — `NT` expands to `New Technology`. _Why:_ the label explains the historical origin of the NT hash terminology. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **NT naming era** — Microsoft adopted the `New Technology` naming convention in the early 1990s. _Why:_ this places the NT hash design in its historical Windows lineage. _[GCFA p.~129]_

### Hash Algorithm Properties

- **One-way hash property** — a hash value cannot be directly converted back into the original plaintext password through mathematical reversal. _Why:_ attackers and responders must crack, guess, or otherwise obtain the password rather than simply decrypting the hash. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Deterministic hashing** — the same plaintext password always produces the same hash output when processed by the same hash function. _Why:_ this enables password guessing and hash comparison workflows. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Input sensitivity** — even a very small change in the plaintext input creates a completely different hash result. _Why:_ this explains why near-miss password guesses do not produce partially similar hashes. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Incorrect character effect** — a password typed with only one wrong character yields a hash with no meaningful resemblance to the correct password’s hash. _Why:_ this property affects authentication failure behavior and cracking strategy. _[GCFA p.~129]_

### NTOWF Implementation Details

- **Case-sensitive input** — NTOWF processes the password with character case preserved. _Why:_ `Password` and `password` are different inputs and therefore hash differently. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Unicode password input** — the NTOWF input is the Unicode-encoded version of the plaintext password. _Why:_ encoding affects the exact byte sequence submitted to MD4. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Single MD4 round** — NTOWF applies one round of the MD4 hash function to the encoded password. _Why:_ this precise construction defines how NT hashes are generated. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **MD4 age** — MD4 is more than three decades old. _Why:_ the age of the primitive helps explain why NT hash security is considered weak by modern standards. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **MD4 weakness** — MD4 is regarded as mathematically weak. _Why:_ this weakness contributes to the risk of offline cracking against recovered NT hashes. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Modern Microsoft use** — Microsoft systems still use this NT hash approach through Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025. _Why:_ responders should expect NT hashes on current Windows platforms, not only legacy systems. _[GCFA p.~129]_

### LM Hash Compatibility

- **LM hash predecessor** — the NT hash replaced the older LANMAN hash, also called the LM hash. _Why:_ LM hashes are historically important because they were weaker and influenced backward-compatibility behavior. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **LANMAN expansion** — `LANMAN` refers to `Local Area Network Manager`. _Why:_ this identifies the full name behind the legacy Windows hash term. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **LM hash weakness** — the LM hash is described as even weaker than the NT hash. _Why:_ LM material is especially risky if present in old systems or legacy configurations. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Earlier Windows usage** — older Windows operating systems used LM hashes. _Why:_ legacy hosts may expose different credential artifacts than modern supported systems. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Historical dual storage** — Windows previously stored both LM and NT hashes for compatibility. _Why:_ forensic review of older systems may encounter both hash types. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Current LM placeholder behavior** — supported Windows versions now store a blank-password hash placeholder in the LM hash field instead of generating a real LM hash. _Why:_ the LM storage location may still exist, but its value should not be interpreted as a real user password hash on modern supported systems. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Reason LM generation stopped** — modern Windows avoids creating and storing real LM hashes because the algorithm is too weak. _Why:_ this reduces exposure of easily cracked credential material. _[GCFA p.~129]_

### Local Accounts And SAM Storage

- **Microsoft account categories** — Microsoft environments distinguish between local accounts and domain accounts. _Why:_ credential storage, scope, and compromise impact differ between these account types. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Local account scope** — a local account exists on a single individual computer. _Why:_ compromise or modification of a local account is normally scoped to that host. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Same-name local accounts** — two separate computers can each have a local account with the same username, such as `Bob`. _Why:_ matching names across machines do not prove the accounts are the same identity. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Local account independence** — same-named local accounts on different computers have no direct relationship to each other. _Why:_ responders must treat them as separate security principals unless other evidence links them. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Local account discreteness** — local accounts with matching names on separate systems are independent accounts that merely share a label. _Why:_ username reuse can mislead timeline and lateral movement analysis. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Password reset isolation** — changing the password for a local account on one computer does not change the password for a same-named local account on another computer. _Why:_ remediation must address each affected host or account store separately. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **Local account hash location** — a local account’s password hash is stored on the local machine. _Why:_ investigators must acquire the relevant host data to recover local account hashes. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **SAM hive** — local account password hashes reside in the Security Account Manager registry hive. _Why:_ the SAM is a core forensic artifact for local Windows account credential analysis. _[GCFA p.~129]_
- **SAM acronym** — `SAM` stands for `Security Account Manager`. _Why:_ this identifies the registry hive referenced in Windows local account credential storage. _[GCFA p.~129]_

### Diagram Labels And Values

- **Diagram account context** — the diagram is specifically labeled as a local account whose user sets a password. _Why:_ the illustrated hashing flow applies to local account password storage. _[GCFA p.~129]_

### Windows Domain Accounts

- **Domain-account usage in Windows domains** — Windows domain users commonly sign in with domain accounts rather than purely local machine accounts. _Why:_ domain credentials are central to enterprise authentication and are frequent DFIR targets. _[GCFA p.~130]_

- **Domain-account storage location** — Domain account records are maintained on domain controllers in the network. _Why:_ responders need to know that domain credential and account state is controlled by domain infrastructure, not only by endpoints. _[GCFA p.~130]_

- **Domain-controller replication of accounts** — Domain accounts are present across all domain controllers in the domain. _Why:_ compromise or changes to domain account data can have domain-wide impact. _[GCFA p.~130]_

- **Domain-wide account usability** — A domain account can be used throughout the domain rather than being limited to a single host. _Why:_ this enables normal enterprise access but also supports attacker lateral movement when credentials are stolen. _[GCFA p.~130]_

- **Rights and privileges on domain accounts** — Domain accounts have rights and privileges associated with them. _Why:_ the value of a compromised account depends heavily on what access its assigned privileges permit. _[GCFA p.~130]_

- **Per-system authorization decision** — Individual systems evaluate a domain account’s assigned rights and privileges when deciding whether to permit access. _Why:_ authentication alone does not guarantee access; host-level authorization still determines what actions are allowed. _[GCFA p.~130]_

- **Domain password update propagation** — When a user changes a domain-account password, that change is replicated to every domain controller. _Why:_ responders investigating credential changes must account for directory replication across controllers. _[GCFA p.~130]_

- **Domain-wide password-change effect** — A changed domain password becomes effective across the entire domain. _Why:_ a password reset can invalidate attacker access broadly, assuming replication completes and no alternate credential material remains usable. _[GCFA p.~130]_

### Local Account Password Hashing

- **Local-account password input** — When a user sets a password for a local account, the plaintext password is the initial input to the Windows password-hashing process. _Why:_ this identifies the source material from which stored credential verifiers are derived. _[GCFA p.~130]_

- **NTOWF role** — The plaintext local-account password is processed by the NTOWF to derive the account’s NT Hash. _Why:_ NTOWF explains how Windows converts a password into the hash material commonly targeted by credential theft tools. _[GCFA p.~130]_

- **NT Hash generation** — The NTOWF output is the NT Hash for the local account password. _Why:_ NT Hashes can be abused directly in some attacks even when the plaintext password is unknown. _[GCFA p.~130]_

- **SAM hive storage of local hash** — The resulting NT Hash for the local account is stored in the system’s SAM hive. _Why:_ the SAM hive is a key forensic artifact for local account credential analysis and offline password-hash extraction. _[GCFA p.~130]_

## Page 132

### Local Account Authorization

- **Post-authentication authorization** — after a user’s identity has been verified, the operating system decides what that user may do on the system. _Why:_ separates identity proof from permission enforcement during incident analysis. _[GCFA p.~132]_

- **Authorization basis** — the system grants or denies access according to rights and privileges tied to the user account. _Why:_ account capability depends on assigned privileges, not merely successful login. _[GCFA p.~132]_

- **Group membership as privilege source** — a local account receives its effective rights and privileges through the groups to which the account belongs. _Why:_ group membership is a key place to inspect when determining how an account obtained local capabilities. _[GCFA p.~132]_

- **Local account access control** — local account authorization governs actions on the system where that account exists. _Why:_ local accounts can have machine-specific permissions that differ from domain-wide permissions. _[GCFA p.~132]_

### Example Authorized Actions

- **Allow log on locally** — an account may be granted the right to sign in interactively at the local computer. _Why:_ this right affects whether a user can obtain direct console access. _[GCFA p.~132]_

- **Allow log on through RDP** — an account may be granted permission to authenticate through Remote Desktop Protocol. _Why:_ RDP logon rights are important when investigating remote interactive access. _[GCFA p.~132]_

- **Log on as a service** — an account may be authorized to run as the security context for a Windows service. _Why:_ service logon rights can enable persistent execution under a chosen account. _[GCFA p.~132]_

- **Shut down the system** — an account may be granted the privilege to power off or shut down the host. _Why:_ shutdown rights can affect availability and may matter during privilege review or abuse analysis. _[GCFA p.~132]_

### Workgroup Local Accounts

- **Workgroup authentication scope** — in a workgroup, users authenticate with accounts that exist separately on each individual computer. _Why:_ investigators must not assume one account database controls every host. _[GCFA p.133]_

- **Per-computer user accounts** — the same person may need a distinct account on every computer they use in a workgroup. _Why:_ account identity and credential evidence must be evaluated host by host. _[GCFA p.133]_

- **Independent account creation** — local accounts are created independently on each machine rather than centrally provisioned. _Why:_ account presence, naming, and password history may differ across systems. _[GCFA p.133]_

- **Separate SAM per computer** — each computer maintains its own Security Account Manager registry hive. _Why:_ local credential artifacts are distributed across endpoints instead of stored in one central location. _[GCFA p.133]_

- **Client SAM** — the illustrated client computer has its own SAM. _Why:_ the client’s local account database is an independent forensic evidence source. _[GCFA p.133]_

- **Server SAM** — the illustrated server computer has its own SAM. _Why:_ the server’s local account database must be examined separately from the client’s. _[GCFA p.133]_

- **Diagram label: “Each has a separate SAM”** — the page emphasizes that both shown machines maintain separate SAM databases. _Why:_ this reinforces that local authentication data is not shared automatically between workgroup hosts. _[GCFA p.133]_

- **SAM username storage** — each computer’s SAM hive stores the valid local usernames for that machine. _Why:_ user enumeration for local accounts depends on the SAM from the specific host under investigation. _[GCFA p.133]_

- **SAM NT hash storage** — each computer’s SAM hive stores NT hashes for its local users. _Why:_ password-derived authentication material is recoverable and attributable at the individual-host level. _[GCFA p.133]_

- **SAM as local validation source** — a machine uses its own SAM data to know which local usernames and NT hashes are valid. _Why:_ compromised local credentials may work only where matching account data exists. _[GCFA p.133]_

## Page 134

### NTLMv2 Remote Local-Account Authentication

- **NTLM purpose** — New Technology Local Area Network Manager is a Windows authentication protocol used when a user signs in to a remote system with a local account. _Why:_ this explains why NTLM artifacts can matter in lateral movement and remote logon investigations. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Remote target context** — The authentication scenario shown is client-to-server access where the account being used exists on the remote server. _Why:_ local-account remote authentication differs from domain authentication and affects where credential material is validated. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Current NTLM version** — NTLM version 2 is the current form of the protocol described on the page. _Why:_ investigators should expect NTLMv2 rather than NTLMv1 in properly configured modern Windows environments. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **NTLMv1 security status** — NTLM version 1 is described as having serious security weaknesses. _Why:_ the presence of NTLMv1 can indicate insecure configuration and elevated credential-theft risk. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **NTLMv1 hardening guidance** — NTLMv1 should be turned off across Windows environments. _Why:_ disabling it reduces exposure to known weaknesses in the older protocol. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Common protocol expectation** — Because NTLMv1 is insecure, NTLMv2 is normally the NTLM variant in use. _Why:_ this sets the baseline expectation when interpreting authentication behavior. _[GCFA p.~134]_

### Exchange Diagram

- **Diagram participants** — The diagram shows a client on one side and a server on the other. _Why:_ these roles define who sends the request, who issues the challenge, and who validates the response. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Step 1 label** — The first diagrammed message is an authentication request. _Why:_ this is the start of the NTLMv2 negotiation sequence. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Step 2 label** — The second diagrammed message is a challenge. _Why:_ the server-generated challenge is the unpredictable value that drives response calculation. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Step 3 label** — The third diagrammed message is a response. _Why:_ this response is the value the server checks to decide whether authentication succeeds. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Client-side calculation input shown** — The diagram represents a function using the challenge and an NT hash as inputs. _Why:_ the client proves knowledge of the password-derived hash without sending the password itself. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Client-side calculation output shown** — The diagram shows the function producing a response. _Why:_ that response is the proof value transmitted back to the server. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Server-side calculation input shown** — The server side also shows a function using the challenge and an NT hash. _Why:_ the server independently recreates the expected response for comparison. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Server-side calculation output shown** — The server-side function also produces a response value. _Why:_ matching this computed value against the client’s response determines the authentication result. _[GCFA p.~134]_

### Step 1 Authentication Request

- **Initial NTLMv2 action** — The client begins the NTLMv2 exchange by sending an authentication request to the server. _Why:_ this identifies the first network action in the authentication flow. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Account name in request** — The authentication request contains the server-local account name being used for the attempted authentication. _Why:_ account identity is supplied before the challenge-response proof is computed. _[GCFA p.~134]_

### Step 2 Server Challenge

- **Challenge issuer** — The server sends the NTLM challenge to the client. _Why:_ the server controls the challenge value that prevents simple replay of a static password hash. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Challenge content** — The NTLM challenge is a pseudorandom number generated by the server. _Why:_ randomness makes each authentication attempt distinct. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Client response calculation trigger** — After receiving the challenge, the client computes an NTLM response. _Why:_ this is the client’s proof that it possesses the correct password-derived secret. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Client calculation input: challenge** — The server’s challenge is one input to the client’s response function. _Why:_ binding the response to the challenge helps prevent reuse of an old response. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Client calculation input: NT hash** — The NT hash of the authenticating account’s password is another input to the client’s response function. _Why:_ this password-derived value is the secret used to prove account knowledge. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Client calculation input: session metadata** — Metadata about the session is included in the client-side response calculation. _Why:_ session context contributes to the computed NTLMv2 response. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Client-side function result** — The client’s function produces the NTLM response. _Why:_ this computed response is what the client later transmits for validation. _[GCFA p.~134]_

### Step 3 Client Response

- **Password-derived hash use** — The client calculates the NTLM response using the hash derived from the password entered during logon. _Why:_ this ties the remote authentication attempt to the credential supplied by the user or process. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Response transmission** — In the third exchange step, the client sends the computed NTLM response to the server. _Why:_ this message gives the server the value it must verify. _[GCFA p.~134]_

### Server Validation

- **Server-side recomputation** — After receiving the client’s NTLM response, the server computes what the response should be on its own. _Why:_ independent recomputation allows validation without receiving the plaintext password. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Server validation input: original challenge** — The server uses the same challenge value it previously sent to the client. _Why:_ both sides must calculate against the same challenge for comparison to be meaningful. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Server validation input: SAM-stored NT hash** — The server uses the NT hash for the user account password stored in its SAM hive. _Why:_ for local-account authentication, the remote server’s SAM contains the credential verifier. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Server validation input: session metadata** — The server includes the session metadata in its own response calculation. _Why:_ matching the client’s calculation requires the same contextual inputs. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Same-function validation** — The server applies the same function used by the client to generate an expected NTLM response. _Why:_ identical algorithms and inputs should produce identical output only when the credential secret matches. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Response comparison** — The server compares its locally generated response with the response received from the client. _Why:_ this comparison is the core pass/fail decision point. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Successful authentication condition** — Authentication succeeds when the server-computed response and the client-supplied response match. _Why:_ a match demonstrates that the client had the correct password-derived NT hash. _[GCFA p.~134]_
- **Failed authentication condition** — Authentication fails when the server-computed response and the client-supplied response differ. _Why:_ a mismatch indicates the supplied credential proof is invalid for that account. _[GCFA p.~134]_

### Domain Account Storage
- **Domain account scale rationale** — local Windows accounts are not practical for large enterprise identity management. _Why:_ explains why organizations centralize user identity in domains. _[GCFA p.135]_
- **Enterprise identity model** — most organizations use domain accounts for user authentication rather than relying only on per-host accounts. _Why:_ domain accounts are the normal enterprise account source investigators must understand. _[GCFA p.135]_
- **Domain account database** — domain account data is kept in `NTDS.dit`. _Why:_ `NTDS.dit` is a key forensic and credential-protection artifact. _[GCFA p.135]_
- **Domain controller storage location** — each domain controller stores domain account information in its own copy of `NTDS.dit`. _Why:_ every domain controller may contain sensitive domain credential material. _[GCFA p.135]_
- **Domain account content** — `NTDS.dit` contains account records that include NT hashes. _Why:_ possession of this file can expose reusable authentication secrets. _[GCFA p.135]_
- **Domain replication behavior** — changes to domain account data are copied across domain controllers. _Why:_ investigators must account for synchronization when analyzing account or password changes. _[GCFA p.135]_
- **Domain controller consistency** — replication keeps domain controllers aligned with one another. _Why:_ consistent domain state affects where account changes may be observed. _[GCFA p.135]_

- **NT hash generation for domains** — domain account passwords have NT hashes computed and stored. _Why:_ those hashes support NTLM-family authentication and are valuable to attackers. _[GCFA p.135]_
- **NTLMv2 with local accounts** — NTLMv2 can authenticate local Windows accounts. _Why:_ the same protocol family applies outside domain authentication. _[GCFA p.135]_
- **NTLMv2 with domain accounts** — NTLMv2 can also authenticate domain accounts. _Why:_ domain accounts may still expose NTLM-based attack and detection surfaces. _[GCFA p.135]_
- **Kerberos adoption point** — Microsoft has preferred Kerberos for domain authentication since Windows Server 2000. _Why:_ Kerberos is the expected default protocol in modern Windows domains. _[GCFA p.135]_
- **Kerberos credential dependency** — Kerberos authentication does not use the NT hash directly. _Why:_ Kerberos analysis requires different credential artifacts than NTLM analysis. _[GCFA p.135]_
- **Kerberos long-term keys** — Kerberos uses long-term keys derived from the plaintext password. _Why:_ password-derived Kerberos keys are sensitive authentication secrets. _[GCFA p.135]_

- **Domain-wide credential exposure** — the file contains password hashes for all users in the domain. _Why:_ this makes `NTDS.dit` a major target during credential theft and post-exploitation. _[GCFA p.135]_
- **Username exposure** — the file contains usernames in addition to hashes. _Why:_ user identifiers paired with hashes enable targeted cracking and account abuse. _[GCFA p.135]_
