### SMB Session Hijacking

- **Authenticated Session State** — by this stage, the compromised client has successfully established an authenticated connection with `Server2`. _Why:_ this marks the point where the attacker-controlled system can act within a valid SMB session. _[GCFA p.~151]_

- **Compromised Client Behavior** — after authentication succeeds, the compromised client stops relaying or maintaining communication with `User1`'s system. _Why:_ dropping the original user connection is part of taking over the session after authentication has been completed. _[GCFA p.~151]_

- **Session Hijack Outcome** — the compromised client takes control of the authenticated session and continues communicating with `Server2` as `User1`. _Why:_ this explains the impact of the attack: the attacker-controlled client can access resources with the victim account’s identity. _[GCFA p.~151]_

- **Victim Account Context** — the ongoing interaction with `Server2` occurs under `User1`'s account. _Why:_ attribution and authorization decisions on the server side may reflect the victim user rather than the attacker-controlled host. _[GCFA p.~151]_

### SMB Signing Mitigation

- **SMB Digital Signatures** — requiring digital signatures on every SMB connection can reduce exposure to this session-hijacking attack type. _Why:_ SMB signing helps prevent tampering or relay-style manipulation of SMB traffic. _[GCFA p.~151]_

- **Windows 11 Version 24H2 Default** — Windows 11 `24H2` was the first Windows release to require SMB signing by default. _Why:_ this identifies the operating-system baseline where the mitigation became enabled without separate administrator action. _[GCFA p.~151]_

- **Legacy Application Compatibility Risk** — enforcing SMB signing can cause older applications to stop working correctly. _Why:_ compatibility concerns are a practical reason organizations may avoid deploying the mitigation broadly. _[GCFA p.~151]_

- **Organizational Adoption Reality** — relatively few organizations have enabled mandatory SMB signing everywhere. _Why:_ investigators and defenders should not assume this protection is present in real environments. _[GCFA p.~151]_

- **SMB Signing Reference URL** — the courseware points readers to `https://for508.com/wl2kz` for additional information about SMB signing in Windows. _Why:_ this is the referenced external source for deeper technical background on the mitigation. _[GCFA p.~151]_

## Page 152

### Coercion / Forced Authentication Attacks

- **Coercion attack concept** — an attacker abuses normal service behavior to make one Windows system initiate authentication to another system. _Why:_ this turns legitimate service features into a way to expose authentication material. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Forced authentication concept** — forced authentication is a coercion technique where a service is induced to authenticate outbound to a host chosen by the attacker. _Why:_ the attacker does not need the target account’s password first; they only need to trigger an authentication attempt. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **NTLMv2 manipulation** — coercion attacks are another way to interfere with the NTLMv2 authentication process. _Why:_ this expands NTLM attack surface beyond direct hash theft or relay. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Service-feature abuse** — attackers can use built-in service capabilities to require a computer to authenticate to another computer. _Why:_ the attack may appear as normal Windows service activity rather than a standalone credential-dumping action. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Privileged service-account exposure** — coerced authentication can cause privileged service accounts to authenticate. _Why:_ captured authentication from high-value service identities can provide significant escalation opportunities. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Outbound authentication requirement** — some Windows services can be asked to perform actions that require them to make an outbound authentication request. _Why:_ any feature with this property can become an authentication-coercion primitive. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Attacker-selected destination** — the remote system receiving the authentication can be chosen arbitrarily by the attacker when the abused service allows it. _Why:_ control of the destination lets the attacker capture or influence the authentication exchange. _[GCFA p.152]_

### Print Spooler Example

- **Print spooler coercion** — the print spooler service can be asked to send an RPC notification when a print job finishes. _Why:_ this is a concrete service behavior that can be weaponized to trigger authentication. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Arbitrary RPC notification target** — the print spooler notification can be directed to an arbitrary system. _Why:_ this lets an attacker point the authentication flow at infrastructure they control. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Print-job completion trigger** — the example notification condition is completion of a print job. _Why:_ this identifies the specific event used to justify the outbound RPC notification. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Notification request text** — the diagram shows the coerced request as “Notify me when a print job completes.” _Why:_ this captures the user-visible service action being abused in the example. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Print spooler service-account authentication** — to deliver the RPC notification, the print spooler’s service account must authenticate to the remote system. _Why:_ the authentication requirement is what creates the credential-exposure opportunity. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Forced service-account authentication** — attackers can use the print spooler behavior to make the service account authenticate to a host they choose. _Why:_ the service’s legitimate workflow becomes a method for producing attacker-observable authentication traffic. _[GCFA p.152]_

### Accounts and Identity

- **Computer service account** — the account commonly forced to authenticate is often the computer’s own service account. _Why:_ machine accounts can be valuable because they participate in domain authentication and may hold useful privileges. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Machine-account naming convention** — the computer service account is represented by the computer name followed by a dollar sign. _Why:_ recognizing the trailing `$` helps identify machine accounts in captured authentication data and logs. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Frequent authenticating principal** — in these attacks, the computer service account is frequently the identity that performs the outbound authentication. _Why:_ investigators should expect coerced traffic to involve machine-account names, not only human user accounts. _[GCFA p.152]_

### Captured Authentication Material

- **Attacker-controlled receiver** — when authentication is directed to an attacker-controlled system, software on that system can observe the exchange. _Why:_ destination control enables credential-capture tooling to collect protocol artifacts. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Malware capture role** — malware on the attacker-controlled system can capture authentication data from the exchange. _Why:_ endpoint or network detections may need to look for capture tooling on the receiving host. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **NTLM challenge capture** — the attacker can capture the NTLM challenge. _Why:_ the challenge is required for later cracking attempts against the captured response. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **NTLM response capture** — the attacker can capture the NTLM response. _Why:_ the response is the crackable proof material derived from the account’s secret. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Challenge-and-response pair** — both the NTLM challenge and NTLM response can be taken from the authentication exchange. _Why:_ the pair enables offline password-guessing workflows. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Offline cracking workflow** — captured NTLM challenge-response material can be moved offline for brute-force cracking. _Why:_ offline cracking avoids repeated live authentication attempts and can proceed without further interaction with the victim. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Plaintext password objective** — brute-force cracking is used to try to recover the account’s original plaintext password. _Why:_ obtaining the plaintext password can enable broader reuse than a single captured exchange. _[GCFA p.152]_

### Protocol Downgrade

- **Authentication downgrade opportunity** — attackers can capture the exchange and downgrade the authentication protocol to make cracking easier. _Why:_ weaker protocol choices can materially reduce cracking difficulty. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Attacker control of accessed system** — because the attacker controls the system being accessed, they can influence which NTLM version is accepted. _Why:_ the server-side position lets the attacker shape the authentication negotiation. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **NTLMv2 refusal** — the attacker-controlled system can refuse NTLMv2. _Why:_ rejecting the stronger protocol can push the victim toward a weaker authentication method. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **NTLMv1 request** — the attacker-controlled system can request use of NTLMv1 instead of NTLMv2. _Why:_ NTLMv1 is weaker and therefore more favorable for password cracking. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Cracking advantage of NTLMv1** — NTLMv1 is identified as easier to crack than NTLMv2. _Why:_ protocol downgrade attempts are important indicators of credential-harvesting intent. _[GCFA p.152]_

### Targeted Services and Features

- **Print servers as targets** — print servers are listed as services that can be targeted for forced authentication. _Why:_ print infrastructure is a known coercion surface in Windows environments. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Encrypting File System as target** — Encrypting File System is listed as a Windows feature that can be abused for coercion. _Why:_ defenders should not restrict coercion hunting only to printing services. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Windows Lock Screen configuration as target** — Windows Lock Screen configuration is listed as another coercion target. _Why:_ configuration-related features can also create outbound authentication paths. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **WebDAV as target** — WebDAV is listed as a service or feature that can be manipulated for forced authentication. _Why:_ WebDAV traffic and authentication attempts can be relevant during coercion investigations. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Other Windows features** — additional Windows features beyond the named examples may have similar coercible behavior. _Why:_ the technique is a class of abuse, not a single-service vulnerability. _[GCFA p.152]_
- **Print servers are not unique** — the page explicitly notes that print servers are only one example of systems that can be forced to authenticate. _Why:_ mitigation and detection strategies must cover multiple coercion vectors. _[GCFA p.152]_

### Coercion Plus Relay Attack Flow

- **Coercion and relay combination** — coercion attacks can be chained with relay attacks so that a forced authentication is immediately reused against another target. _Why:_ this turns an induced login event into unauthorized access on a separate system. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Step 1 · Print-notification coercion trigger** — the diagram’s first action is a request equivalent to “tell me when a print job finishes.” _Why:_ print-related notification behavior can be abused as the initial coercion mechanism. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Step 2 · Server1$ authentication to compromised client** — Server1$ sends an authentication request toward the compromised client. _Why:_ the coerced machine account begins authenticating to attacker-controlled infrastructure. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Step 3 · Relayed Server1$ authentication to Server2** — the compromised client forwards Server1$’s authentication request to Server2. _Why:_ the attacker redirects the victim’s authentication attempt to the real target. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Step 4 · Server2 challenge to relay malware** — Server2 sends an authentication challenge back toward the relay malware on the compromised client. _Why:_ this challenge is needed to continue the relayed authentication exchange. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Step 5 · Server2 challenge relayed to Server1$** — the challenge from Server2 is passed back to Server1$. _Why:_ Server1$ is tricked into computing a valid response for Server2’s challenge. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Step 6 · Server1$ response to compromised client** — Server1$ sends its authentication response back toward the compromised client. _Why:_ the attacker receives the victim account’s valid response material without knowing the account secret. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Step 7 · Server1$ response relayed to Server2** — the compromised client forwards Server1$’s response to Server2. _Why:_ Server2 accepts the authentication as if Server1$ directly completed it. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Relay malware role** — malware on the compromised client performs the relay between Server1$ and Server2. _Why:_ the relay component is what converts coerced authentication into target access. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Compromised client role** — the attacker-controlled or compromised client sits between Server1 and Server2 in the authentication path. _Why:_ this position lets the attacker relay messages while impersonating the coerced account to the target. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Server1 role** — Server1 is the system whose privileged machine or service account is coerced into authenticating. _Why:_ the attacker’s effective privileges depend on the account being coerced. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Server1$ account identity** — the diagram identifies the coerced account as Server1$. _Why:_ the trailing dollar sign indicates a computer account, which may hold meaningful network privileges. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Server2 role** — Server2 is the attacker’s intended access target in the relay scenario. _Why:_ the relayed authentication is aimed at gaining a session on this server. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Privileged account coercion** — an attacker can force a privileged account to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system. _Why:_ coerced authentication provides the input needed for a relay attack. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Example coercion path** — the page’s example shows authentication moving from Server1 to the compromised client before being relayed onward. _Why:_ this illustrates the attacker-controlled interception point. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Relay redirection target** — the attacker-controlled system can redirect the authentication request to a server the attacker wants to access. _Why:_ relay attacks let the attacker choose the target that receives the victim’s authentication. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Privileged service account completion** — the privileged service account completes authentication to Server2 in the example. _Why:_ Server2 sees a valid authentication from the coerced identity. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Hijacked session identity** — the resulting session is shown as a hijacked session as Server1$. _Why:_ the attacker gains a session under the coerced account’s identity. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Hijacked session privilege level** — after the relay succeeds, the attacker receives the rights and privileges associated with the service account. _Why:_ impact is determined by the coerced account’s authorization on Server2. _[GCFA p.~153]_

- **Target access outcome** — the attack gives the adversary access to Server2 through the relayed Server1$ authentication. _Why:_ this is the practical objective of combining coercion with relay. _[GCFA p.~153]_

## Page 154

### Process Tokens

- **Process token assignment** — every running process is associated with a security token. _Why:_ the token is the operating-system object used to evaluate what the process is allowed to do. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **User context for processes** — a process executes in the security context of a user account. _Why:_ investigators can tie process authority back to the account whose rights the process inherited. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Process capability control** — the process token governs which operations code inside the process may perform. _Why:_ malicious code running in a process is constrained or empowered by that process token. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **User-account rights analogy** — processes need rights and privileges defined for them just as user accounts do. _Why:_ authorization applies not only to interactive users but also to code executing on their behalf. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Inherited account authority** — a process receives the rights and privileges of the user account linked to its token. _Why:_ compromise of a user context gives attacker-controlled processes that account’s effective permissions. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Authorization use** — Windows uses the process token to decide whether actions attempted by the process should be permitted. _Why:_ access decisions can be understood by examining the token’s identity, groups, privileges, and integrity level. _[GCFA p.~154]_

### Primary Tokens

- **Primary token creation** — Windows creates a primary token when a user successfully logs on. _Why:_ logon establishes the security identity later used by that user’s processes. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Session primary token** — after logon, the user session is assigned the primary token. _Why:_ the session token becomes the default security basis for new processes in that session. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Default process token inheritance** — processes created inside the user’s session normally use that session’s primary token. _Why:_ this explains why processes launched by a logged-on user usually share the same account context. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Primary token attachment** — the primary token is attached to processes belonging to the logged-on user. _Why:_ the attachment is what gives those processes the user’s identity and permissions. _[GCFA p.~154]_

### Token Contents

- **User SID in token** — the primary token contains the user account’s security identifier. _Why:_ the SID is the durable identifier Windows uses for the user, independent of display names. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **User SID meaning** — a security identifier is a unique numeric identifier for a user on the system. _Why:_ SID-based identity is central to Windows authorization and forensic attribution. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Group SIDs in token** — the token stores the SIDs for all groups of which the account is a member. _Why:_ group membership can grant or deny access even when the user SID alone would not. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Group 1 SID diagram field** — the illustrated primary token includes a first group SID entry. _Why:_ the diagram shows that group memberships are explicit token components. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Group 2 SID diagram field** — the illustrated primary token includes a second group SID entry. _Why:_ multiple group memberships may contribute to the process’s authorization context. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Group 3 SID diagram field** — the illustrated primary token includes a third group SID entry. _Why:_ the token can contain more than one group SID rather than a single group value. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Additional group SID entries** — the diagram indicates the group SID list can continue beyond the three shown entries. _Why:_ accounts may belong to many groups, and each can affect process access. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Privileges in token** — the primary token records privileges granted to the account. _Why:_ privileges control special system capabilities that may matter more than ordinary file or registry permissions. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Integrity level in token** — the primary token includes the process integrity level. _Why:_ integrity levels influence whether a process can modify or interact with objects at different trust levels. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Logon ID in token** — the primary token includes the logon ID. _Why:_ the logon ID can help correlate processes and activity to a specific authenticated session. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Other token details** — the primary token contains additional security-related details beyond SID, group SID, privilege, integrity level, and logon ID fields. _Why:_ a full token inspection may reveal authorization-relevant metadata not visible in a simplified diagram. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Account details in token** — the token contains information describing the user account. _Why:_ account metadata helps determine the identity under which a process is executing. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Group membership details in token** — the token contains the account’s group membership information. _Why:_ group-derived rights are often the reason a process can access protected resources. _[GCFA p.~154]_
- **Granted privilege details in token** — the token identifies privileges assigned to the account. _Why:_ high-impact privileges can explain administrative or forensic-significant behavior by a process. _[GCFA p.~154]_

## Page 155

### Impersonation Tokens

- **Impersonation token purpose** — an impersonation token lets an execution thread run as a user other than the process account. _Why:_ this is the core Windows mechanism that allows services to perform work using a client’s identity. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Thread-level identity switching** — impersonation applies at the thread level rather than requiring the whole process to change its security context. _Why:_ investigators must understand that different threads in one process may operate with different user privileges. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Different-user execution context** — a thread using an impersonation token executes code under the security context of another account. _Why:_ this explains how activity from a service process may still represent actions authorized by a specific user. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Primary process token default** — threads usually run under the security context supplied by the process’s primary token. _Why:_ this is the baseline behavior from which impersonation is the exception. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Primary token is not mandatory for every thread** — a thread does not have to use the process primary token and may instead use a separate impersonation token. _Why:_ this distinction matters when attributing file, database, or network access to a user versus a service account. _[GCFA p.155]_

### Processes and Threads

- **Process thread count** — a process contains one or more execution threads. _Why:_ impersonation is implemented through threads, so the process/thread relationship is foundational. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Shared process memory** — threads inside the same process share that process’s memory space. _Why:_ a service may host multiple threads with shared memory while each thread performs work under different security contexts. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **CPU scheduling unit** — a thread receives CPU time to execute instructions. _Why:_ the thread, not merely the process container, is the active unit performing operations. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Thread as work executor** — the thread is the component that actually carries out process work. _Why:_ forensic attribution must consider thread-level security context when available. _[GCFA p.155]_

### Server-Side Impersonation

- **Typical impersonation scenario** — server processes commonly use impersonation when acting for client users. _Why:_ this is a normal administrative and application behavior that can affect evidence interpretation. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Client request handling** — when a client asks a server to perform an action, the server may create a thread that uses a token representing the client. _Why:_ this explains how client privileges flow into server-side work. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **File access example** — a server may impersonate a user to access files using that user’s rights. _Why:_ file system activity by a server process may be constrained by, and attributable to, the requesting user’s permissions. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Database access example** — a server may impersonate a client when handling database access requests. _Why:_ database operations may occur through a service process while still reflecting a client user’s authorization. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Privilege constraint model** — impersonation lets a server limit its actions to what the requesting client is authorized to do. _Why:_ this is both a security control and an attribution clue during incident analysis. _[GCFA p.155]_

### Security Impersonation Levels

- **Impersonation privilege levels** — impersonation tokens can be issued with different security impersonation levels. _Why:_ the level determines how far the impersonated identity can be used. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Key impersonation levels named on page** — the two emphasized levels are `SecurityImpersonation` and `SecurityDelegation`. _Why:_ these are the specific levels the courseware calls out as most important for investigations. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **`SecurityImpersonation` level** — a `SecurityImpersonation` token lets the thread act for the client only on the local machine. _Why:_ this limits the blast radius of the impersonated identity to local resources. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **`SecurityImpersonation` locality** — the page states that `SecurityImpersonation` is valid only on the local system. _Why:_ this distinguishes local-only impersonation from delegation that can cross machine boundaries. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **`SecurityDelegation` level** — a `SecurityDelegation` token lets the thread act for the client on the local host and on remote hosts. _Why:_ delegation enables broader lateral or remote resource access under the user’s identity. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **`SecurityDelegation` credential dependency** — `SecurityDelegation` is associated with the user’s credentials in LSASS. _Why:_ LSASS-backed credentials make delegation powerful and forensically significant. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **`SecurityDelegation` remote validity** — delegation-level impersonation remains valid when accessing remote systems. _Why:_ this capability is important when evaluating remote access performed by services. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Impersonation level reference URL** — the page points readers to `https://for508.com/8l9mu` for additional information about impersonation levels. _Why:_ this identifies the external reference supplied by the courseware. _[GCFA p.155]_

### Diagram Facts

- **Diagram process container** — the diagram shows a `Process` containing multiple threads. _Why:_ it visually reinforces that impersonation can vary inside one process. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Diagram Thread 1** — `Thread 1` is shown using a primary process token. _Why:_ this represents the normal thread identity inherited from the process. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Diagram Thread 1 token account** — `Thread 1` is labeled with `Primary Process Token - Service Account`. _Why:_ it shows the service account as the baseline process identity. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Diagram Thread 2** — `Thread 2` is shown with a `SecurityImpersonation` level token. _Why:_ it illustrates a thread impersonating a user for local-only activity. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Diagram Thread 2 user** — `Thread 2` is labeled `Impersonation Token - User 1`. _Why:_ it shows that a thread can operate as a specific client user distinct from the service account. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Diagram Thread 3** — `Thread 3` is shown with a `SecurityDelegation` level token. _Why:_ it illustrates the stronger impersonation form that can extend to remote systems. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Diagram Thread 3 user** — `Thread 3` is labeled `Impersonation Token - User 2`. _Why:_ it shows that separate threads in the same process may impersonate different users. _[GCFA p.155]_
- **Same-process mixed tokens** — the diagram presents one process with a service-account primary token, one `SecurityImpersonation` token, and one `SecurityDelegation` token at the same time. _Why:_ this is the key forensic takeaway: process identity alone may not fully explain actions performed by its threads. _[GCFA p.155]_

## Page 156

### Process Token Theft

- **Access token purpose** — a Windows access token encodes the permissions and privileges available to a specific user account. _Why:_ token contents define what actions code can perform under that identity. _[GCFA p.~156]_

- **Token-to-execution relationship** — processes and threads that run for a user account have an associated token. _Why:_ investigators can reason about process authority by examining the token attached to that execution context. _[GCFA p.~156]_

- **Primary token theft** — an attacker may steal a primary token from a process. _Why:_ a primary token can be reused to start execution under another user’s security context. _[GCFA p.~156]_

- **Impersonation token theft** — an attacker may steal an impersonation token. _Why:_ impersonation tokens let malicious code act as another identity within a thread context. _[GCFA p.~156]_

- **Stolen-token process creation** — an attacker can start a new process using a stolen token. _Why:_ the new process inherits the victim account’s effective authority. _[GCFA p.~156]_

- **Stolen-token thread execution** — an attacker can run a thread with a stolen token. _Why:_ this allows malicious code inside an existing process to operate as the token’s user. _[GCFA p.~156]_

- **Privilege consequence of token theft** — a process or thread running with the stolen token can perform actions available to the original user. _Why:_ token theft converts the victim’s privileges into attacker-controlled execution capability. _[GCFA p.~156]_

- **Token application to malicious code** — an attacker can take the token linked to one process and assign that security context to malicious execution. _Why:_ this is the core mechanism by which token theft enables privilege misuse. _[GCFA p.~156]_

- **New-process attack path** — one implementation path is launching a separate process under the stolen token. _Why:_ this can create a distinct malicious process whose authority comes from the compromised account. _[GCFA p.~156]_

- **Existing-process thread attack path** — another implementation path is applying an impersonation token to a new thread inside an already running process. _Why:_ this can hide malicious activity within an existing process while still using the stolen identity. _[GCFA p.~156]_

- **Primary-to-impersonation conversion** — an impersonation token can be derived from a primary token. _Why:_ attackers are not limited to the original token form and can adapt the token type to their chosen execution method. _[GCFA p.~156]_

- **Attacker choice of token strategy** — because primary tokens and impersonation tokens can support different execution approaches, the attacker can select the method that best fits the operation. _Why:_ defenders should consider both new-process and thread-level token misuse during investigation. _[GCFA p.~156]_

- **Post-theft execution authority** — once malicious code runs in a process or thread using the stolen token, it operates with that token’s rights and privileges. _Why:_ the security impact is determined by the stolen account’s effective access, not by the attacker’s original account. _[GCFA p.~156]_

- **Labeled benign user figure** — the page includes a figure labeled “Good Guy.” _Why:_ the visual reinforces that the stolen token originates from a legitimate user context. _[GCFA p.~156]_

### Attack Mechanics

- **Primary token source** — The privileged token found in the example is a primary token. _Why:_ primary tokens can exist when a privileged user leaves an interactive or service-related session active. _[GCFA p.157]_

- **Chosen attacker method** — Instead of starting a new process, the attacker creates an impersonation token at delegation level from the primary token. _Why:_ this keeps execution inside the existing Mimikatz process while changing the thread’s identity. _[GCFA p.157]_
- **New execution thread** — The attack starts a new thread under the existing Mimikatz process using the domain administrator’s impersonation token. _Why:_ responders must inspect thread-level token context, not only process-level ownership. _[GCFA p.157]_
- **SecurityDelegation-level token** — The impersonation token is created at the `SecurityDelegation` level. _Why:_ delegation-level impersonation is especially powerful because it can allow the impersonated identity to be used for remote access scenarios. _[GCFA p.157]_

## Page 158

### Kerberos Delegation

- **Kerberos delegation** — a Kerberos capability that lets a service authenticate onward to another system while acting for a client. _Why:_ it explains how multi-tier applications access back-end resources under the user's identity. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Delegation-level token** — a token that allows a server-side thread to operate as the client when accessing other systems. _Why:_ this token can extend a user's effective access beyond the initial server. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Delegation-level token risk** — delegation tokens are hazardous because they place trust in a server to authenticate to additional systems for the client. _Why:_ if that server is compromised or overtrusted, an attacker may be able to reach other services as the user. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Delegation business need** — delegation is sometimes required for legitimate application designs. _Why:_ some services must retrieve remote resources for users rather than only serve local content. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Web-to-database delegation example** — the slide's example shows a web server needing to access a remote database as the client. _Why:_ it demonstrates why delegation exists in real enterprise applications. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Client data retrieval flow** — the web server retrieves database records for the client and then returns the resulting data through the web application. _Why:_ this shows the intended end-to-end use of delegated authentication. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Delegation enablement requirement** — delegation must be intentionally enabled for services that need it. _Why:_ delegation should not be assumed or broadly available by default. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Microsoft delegation models** — Microsoft supports multiple delegation configurations intended to align with least privilege. _Why:_ defenders can reduce delegation exposure by choosing narrower models. _[GCFA p.~158]_

### Diagrammed Authentication Flow

- **User 1** — the diagram labels the client-side user identity as “User 1.” _Why:_ this is the identity being delegated through the application chain. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Client** — the diagram includes a client system that initiates the request. _Why:_ the client is the origin of the authenticated interaction. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Authenticated request** — the client sends an authenticated request toward the web server. _Why:_ delegation begins from an already authenticated client-to-service session. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Web server** — the diagram places the web server between the client and the database server. _Why:_ this service is the delegated middle tier. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Database server** — the diagram includes a separate database server as the downstream resource. _Why:_ this is the remote system the web server accesses for the user. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Request as User 1** — the web server sends a request to the database server using User 1's identity. _Why:_ this is the practical effect of Kerberos delegation. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Process** — the diagram represents execution on the web server as a process. _Why:_ it anchors the token discussion to process and thread security context. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Thread 1** — one thread in the web server process is shown using the service account's primary process token. _Why:_ it distinguishes the service's own identity from delegated user identity. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Primary process token** — the web server process has a primary token associated with the service account. _Why:_ this is the service's baseline identity before impersonation or delegation. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Service account** — the primary process token in the diagram belongs to a service account. _Why:_ service accounts commonly own server processes in Windows environments. _[GCFA p.~158]_

### Delegation Types

- **Server delegation options** — the slide lists three server delegation categories. _Why:_ each category carries a different administrative model and risk profile. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Unconstrained delegation** — one listed delegation type is unconstrained delegation. _Why:_ it is the broadest and riskiest delegation model shown on the page. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Constrained delegation** — one listed delegation type is constrained delegation. _Why:_ it narrows where a service may act for clients. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Resource-based constrained delegation** — one listed delegation type is resource-based constrained delegation. _Why:_ it shifts trust decisions toward the target resource owner. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **RBCD abbreviation** — the slide abbreviates resource-based constrained delegation as RBCD. _Why:_ this acronym is commonly used in Windows delegation discussions and attack paths. _[GCFA p.~158]_

### Unconstrained Delegation

- **Unconstrained delegation desirability** — unconstrained delegation is described as the least preferred option. _Why:_ it creates the largest blast radius if abused. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Unconstrained delegation behavior** — unconstrained delegation permits a service to act for its clients on any other system. _Why:_ this broad authority can expose many downstream systems to delegated access abuse. _[GCFA p.~158]_

### Constrained Delegation

- **Constrained delegation improvement** — constrained delegation is described as a better option than unconstrained delegation. _Why:_ it limits the destinations where delegated authentication is allowed. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Constrained delegation policy** — constrained delegation uses policy settings to define where a service may act for clients. _Why:_ explicit allow lists are a least-privilege control. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Constrained delegation target scope** — constrained delegation allows delegation only to specifically named systems. _Why:_ this reduces unintended lateral access through a delegated service. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Web server constrained delegation example** — in the slide scenario, the web server could be permitted to delegate only to the database server. _Why:_ it shows how constrained delegation can match a specific application dependency. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Constrained delegation suitability** — constrained delegation may fit the web-server-to-database-server design shown in the diagram. _Why:_ the needed downstream resource is known and limited. _[GCFA p.~158]_

### Administrative Control

- **Unconstrained delegation administration** — unconstrained delegation is configured by domain administrators. _Why:_ control is centralized and requires domain-level authority. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Constrained delegation administration** — constrained delegation is also configured by domain administrators. _Why:_ traditional delegation settings are managed at the domain level. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **Domain controller configuration location** — unconstrained and constrained delegation settings are configured on domain controllers. _Why:_ delegation trust is enforced through Active Directory domain infrastructure. _[GCFA p.~158]_

### Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

- **RBCD decision owner** — resource-based constrained delegation lets server administrators choose which services they trust for client delegation. _Why:_ the resource owner controls who may delegate to that resource. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **RBCD trust direction** — RBCD moves the delegation trust decision to the individual resource. _Why:_ this changes delegation governance from centralized domain-admin configuration to resource-side authorization. _[GCFA p.~158]_
- **RBCD least-privilege relevance** — RBCD is presented as a Microsoft mechanism for applying least privilege to delegation. _Why:_ it can restrict delegated access based on the target service's explicit trust choices. _[GCFA p.~158]_

### Kerberos Delegation Abuse

- **Delegation-enabled server compromise** — Any server configured for Kerberos delegation can become a delegation-abuse point if an attacker compromises it. _Why:_ delegation trust expands the attacker’s ability to act through the server. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **Trusted server as attack pivot** — A compromised trusted server can use its delegation position to make requests as another user. _Why:_ the attacker can inherit delegated access instead of authenticating only as the compromised server. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **Web server delegation risk** — If a web server is configured for unconstrained delegation, compromising that web server can expose clients who authenticate to it. _Why:_ the server may receive delegation material usable beyond the original web application context. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **Client credential theft through unconstrained delegation** — With unconstrained delegation on the compromised web server, any client that uses the server may have credentials stolen. _Why:_ the attacker can collect delegated authentication material from normal client use. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **Arbitrary system access through stolen delegation material** — Stolen delegated credentials from an unconstrained delegation server may be usable to authenticate to other systems in the environment. _Why:_ unconstrained delegation can let the attacker move beyond the originally accessed service. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **Delegation token theft** — The page identifies theft of delegation tokens as the mechanism enabling abuse after server compromise. _Why:_ these tokens allow the attacker to authenticate remotely as the client. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **Remote authentication on behalf of a client** — Delegation tokens permit authentication to remote services using the client’s identity. _Why:_ this is the core capability attackers exploit when abusing Kerberos delegation. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **Unconstrained delegation blast radius** — Unconstrained delegation can allow access to arbitrary systems after the trusted server is compromised. _Why:_ it creates broad lateral-movement potential from one server compromise. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **Constrained delegation mitigation** — Constrained delegation reduces impact by limiting which systems the delegated identity can access. _Why:_ narrowing allowed targets restricts attacker movement after compromise. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **Resource-based constrained delegation mitigation** — Resource-based constrained delegation also reduces impact by restricting the systems reachable through delegation. _Why:_ target-side delegation control limits abuse paths. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **Delegation server monitoring requirement** — Servers authorized for delegation should be watched for unusual activity. _Why:_ abnormal behavior on these trusted systems may indicate delegation abuse or credential theft. _[GCFA p.159]_

### Diagram Facts

- **Diagram subject** — The diagram illustrates abuse of Kerberos delegation after a trusted server is compromised. _Why:_ it visually models the attack path from client authentication to delegated access. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **User 1 entity** — The diagram includes a user labeled `User 1`. _Why:_ this is the client identity whose authentication can be delegated. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **Client entity** — The diagram includes a system labeled `Client`. _Why:_ the client initiates the authenticated request that creates delegation risk. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **Authenticated request flow** — The diagram shows an `Authenticated Request` from the client side toward the compromised web server. _Why:_ client authentication to the trusted server is the event that can expose delegated credentials. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **Compromised web server entity** — The diagram labels the web server with skull icons as `Web Server`, indicating compromise or attacker control. _Why:_ this server is the abused delegation trust point. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **Request as User 1 to web server** — The diagram shows the web server receiving or handling a request as `User 1`. _Why:_ it demonstrates that the server can operate using the client’s identity. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **Request as User 1 to downstream systems** — The diagram shows a delegated `Request as User 1` from the web server toward other services. _Why:_ it demonstrates lateral use of the client identity after delegation abuse. _[GCFA p.159]_

- **File Server target** — The diagram includes a `File Server` as another downstream service reachable from the web server. _Why:_ file server access is another example of lateral movement enabled by delegation. _[GCFA p.159]_

### Credential-Theft Technique Set

- **Password spraying** — one listed credential-theft/reuse method is spraying passwords across accounts. _Why:_ this pattern is designed to reduce lockout risk while testing many users. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Password cracking** — one listed credential-theft/reuse method is recovering plaintext from stolen password hashes. _Why:_ stolen hashes can become usable credentials if cracked. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **LSA Secrets** — one listed credential-theft source is Windows Local Security Authority Secrets. _Why:_ this store can contain recoverable plaintext credentials. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Kerberoasting** — one listed credential attack targets Kerberos service tickets for offline cracking. _Why:_ it can expose service account passwords without requiring domain admin rights. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Golden Tickets** — Golden Tickets are listed as an additional credential theft or reuse technique. _Why:_ investigators should consider forged Kerberos ticket abuse during credential-compromise analysis. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Silver Tickets** — Silver Tickets are listed as an additional credential theft or reuse technique. _Why:_ forged service-ticket activity is part of the credential-reuse threat model. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **DCSync** — DCSync is listed as an additional credential theft or reuse technique. _Why:_ domain replication abuse can expose credential material. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Skeleton Keys** — Skeleton Keys are listed as an additional credential theft or reuse technique. _Why:_ this technique can enable unauthorized authentication using modified domain authentication behavior. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Cloud credential theft** — cloud credential theft is listed as an additional credential theft or reuse technique. _Why:_ credential investigations must include cloud identities and tokens, not only on-premises Windows credentials. _[GCFA p.160]_

### Password Guessing And Spraying

- **Password guessing target pattern** — password guessing repeatedly tests possible passwords for a single user account. _Why:_ repeated failures for one user are a key detection pattern. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Password spraying target pattern** — password spraying tests a limited set of passwords against many user accounts. _Why:_ a small number of attempts per account can make the attack less obvious in per-user lockout logic. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Password spraying lockout advantage** — spraying can avoid triggering account-lockout thresholds. _Why:_ defenders should look for distributed failures across many users, not only locked accounts. _[GCFA p.160]_

### Password Cracking

- **Password cracking input** — cracking begins after an attacker has obtained a hashed password representation. _Why:_ hash theft can still lead to plaintext credential compromise. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Password cracking objective** — the goal of password cracking is to discover the original plaintext password. _Why:_ once plaintext is known, the credential can be reused directly. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Password cracking candidate loop** — cracking tests a sequence of possible passwords. _Why:_ candidate generation strategy affects cracking success and speed. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Password cracking hash step** — each candidate password is hashed during the cracking process. _Why:_ cracking compares hash outputs rather than comparing plaintext to the stolen value. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Password cracking comparison step** — the computed hash for each candidate is compared to the stolen hash. _Why:_ a hash match identifies the likely original password. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Password cracking success condition** — when a candidate produces the same hash as the stolen hash, the plaintext password has been recovered. _Why:_ this converts a stolen hash into a usable password. _[GCFA p.160]_

### LSA Secrets

- **LSA Secrets credential content** — LSA Secrets can hold plaintext passwords for certain accounts. _Why:_ this registry-backed store is a credential-extraction target. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **LSA Secrets protection state** — passwords in LSA Secrets are stored in encrypted form. _Why:_ attackers need the ability to decrypt or otherwise access protected secret material. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **LSA Secrets registry location** — LSA Secrets reside under the Security hive path `SECURITY/Policy/Secrets`. _Why:_ this path is a concrete forensic location for credential-artifact review. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Manual service-account exposure** — manually created service accounts can have their plaintext passwords exposed through LSA Secrets. _Why:_ persistent service credentials may be recoverable from local systems. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Service-account logon requirement** — service accounts need to authenticate without an interactive user present. _Why:_ this operational need explains why service-account secrets may be stored locally. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Auto-logon exposure** — systems configured for automatic user logon store the user’s password in LSA Secrets. _Why:_ kiosk-style or convenience logon configurations create credential-recovery risk. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Public kiosk example** — a public kiosk is given as an example of a system that may use automatic logon. _Why:_ kiosk systems can unintentionally preserve reusable account passwords. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Auto-start utility exposure** — utilities that launch automatically, such as VPN clients, may store passwords in LSA Secrets. _Why:_ third-party or support software can add unexpected credential artifacts. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **LSA Secrets privilege requirement** — local administrator privileges are required to decrypt and view LSA Secrets. _Why:_ local admin compromise can expose locally stored plaintext credentials. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Credential-attack privilege pattern** — LSA Secrets access follows the broader pattern that many credential attacks require local administrator rights. _Why:_ local privilege escalation materially increases credential-theft impact. _[GCFA p.160]_

### Kerberoasting

- **Kerberoasting target** — Kerberoasting abuses Kerberos service tickets. _Why:_ service tickets can be obtained and attacked offline. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Service-ticket encryption basis** — Kerberos service tickets are encrypted with a key derived from the relevant service account’s plaintext password. _Why:_ weak service-account passwords make ticket ciphertext crackable. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Manual service-account risk** — manually created service accounts are vulnerable when their creator selected a weak password. _Why:_ human-chosen service passwords can be guessed through offline cracking. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Kerberoasting cracking result** — cracking a vulnerable service ticket can reveal the plaintext password of the service account. _Why:_ this grants direct reusable access as that service account. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Built-in service-account mitigation** — Windows built-in service accounts receive randomized passwords. _Why:_ random high-entropy passwords make practical cracking infeasible. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **gMSA mitigation** — Group Managed Service Accounts are assigned randomized passwords. _Why:_ gMSAs reduce Kerberoasting risk compared with manually managed weak passwords. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Domain-controller password assignment** — the domain controller assigns randomized passwords to built-in service accounts and gMSAs. _Why:_ centralized automated password generation avoids weak human-selected service credentials. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Randomized-password cracking resistance** — the randomized passwords for built-in service accounts and gMSAs are computationally impractical to crack. _Why:_ this sharply lowers the value of captured service tickets. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **LSA Secrets mitigation overlap** — using these randomized service-account password mechanisms also avoids placing service-account passwords in LSA Secrets. _Why:_ the same design reduces both Kerberoasting and local secret-extraction exposure. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Kerberoasting privilege requirement** — Kerberoasting does not require elevated domain privileges. _Why:_ any ordinary domain user may be able to request service tickets for attack. _[GCFA p.160]_
- **Domain-controller ticket issuance behavior** — domain controllers issue requested service tickets. _Why:_ normal Kerberos functionality enables ticket acquisition without privileged access. _[GCFA p.160]_

### Kerberos Ticket Forgery

- **Kerberos TGT encryption basis** — Ticket-granting tickets are protected using a long-term key derived from the cleartext password of the `krbtgt` service account. _Why:_ compromise of this key undermines the trust anchor used to validate TGTs. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Stolen `krbtgt` long-term key impact** — If an attacker obtains the `krbtgt` long-term key, they can create forged ticket-granting tickets. _Why:_ forged TGTs can grant domain access without needing normal authentication. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Golden ticket definition** — A forged ticket-granting ticket created using the stolen `krbtgt` long-term key is commonly called a Golden ticket. _Why:_ this identifies a high-impact Kerberos persistence and privilege abuse technique. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Golden ticket account-name control** — A Golden ticket can specify whatever account name the attacker chooses. _Why:_ investigators cannot assume the named account in the ticket reflects a legitimate authentication event. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Golden ticket group-membership control** — A Golden ticket can contain attacker-selected group memberships. _Why:_ this allows fabricated authorization claims, including privileged group access. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Golden ticket lifetime control** — A Golden ticket can be assigned an attacker-chosen expiration time. _Why:_ unusually long-lived tickets can support durable persistence. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Golden ticket long-term usability** — Golden tickets may remain usable for years if created with a long expiration period and not invalidated by remediation. _Why:_ incident response must address ticket-signing keys, not only reset ordinary user credentials. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Service-account long-term key risk** — If an attacker steals the long-term key tied to a service account, they can forge tickets for that specific service. _Why:_ service-ticket forgery can bypass normal Kerberos service authentication. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Silver ticket definition** — A forged service ticket created from a compromised service-account key is known as a Silver ticket. _Why:_ this distinguishes service-specific ticket forgery from domain-wide Golden ticket abuse. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Silver ticket scope** — Silver tickets apply to the service whose account key was compromised. _Why:_ the affected service account determines the attacker’s usable target surface. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Service-account remediation gap** — Compromised service accounts are often missed during cleanup. _Why:_ overlooked service credentials can leave a post-incident path back into the environment. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Silver ticket persistence value** — A compromised service account can provide a continuing foothold after other access is removed. _Why:_ service accounts may survive password resets focused only on users or administrators. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Silver ticket privilege-escalation value** — A compromised service account can give attackers an easier privilege-escalation path when they regain access later. _Why:_ residual service-account compromise can convert limited access into higher-impact access. _[GCFA p.~161]_

### DCSync

- **DCSync prerequisite** — Domain administrator credentials can enable an attacker to perform a DCSync attack. _Why:_ possession of high-privilege domain credentials can expose credential material at domain scale. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **DCSync replication behavior** — DCSync works by requesting replicated information from `NTDS.dit` from a domain controller. _Why:_ the attack abuses domain replication mechanisms rather than requiring direct file access to the domain controller database. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **DCSync target data source** — The replicated information comes from the `NTDS.dit` database. _Why:_ `NTDS.dit` contains domain account credential material relevant to enterprise compromise. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **DCSync domain-controller role** — A domain controller provides the replicated `NTDS.dit` information during the attack. _Why:_ defenders should monitor replication-like requests involving domain controllers. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **DCSync credential exposure** — DCSync can reveal long-term keys for any account. _Why:_ this can enable additional attacks such as Kerberos ticket forgery against many identities. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **DCSync execution location** — DCSync can be launched from any computer joined to the domain. _Why:_ attackers do not need to execute tooling directly on a domain controller to extract replicated credential material. _[GCFA p.~161]_

### Skeleton Key

- **Mimikatz skeleton key capability** — Mimikatz includes an attack technique called skeleton key. _Why:_ Mimikatz artifacts or commands may indicate attempts to alter domain authentication behavior. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Skeleton key domain-controller patching** — The skeleton key technique modifies a domain controller. _Why:_ the attack changes authentication handling at a critical infrastructure point. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Skeleton key authentication bypass** — After skeleton key patching, any account can authenticate when a special attacker-defined password is supplied. _Why:_ this creates broad unauthorized access without changing each account’s legitimate password. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Skeleton key attacker-controlled password** — The password accepted by the patched domain controller is chosen by the attacker. _Why:_ responders must treat the domain controller itself as compromised, not merely individual user passwords. _[GCFA p.~161]_

### Cloud Access Keys

- **Cloud credential targeting** — Attackers also target cloud credentials. _Why:_ investigations limited to on-premises credentials may miss cloud persistence and access paths. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Cloud access-key creation** — Cloud user accounts can have access keys created for them. _Why:_ access keys may provide a separate authentication mechanism from an interactive password. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Cloud access-key function** — Access keys can act like an alternate username and password for the cloud account. _Why:_ stolen keys can allow account use without knowing the user’s primary password. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Cloud access-key local storage** — Access keys are stored on a user’s system in a hidden folder that remains accessible. _Why:_ local endpoint collection can uncover cloud credentials even when the folder is not normally visible. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Cloud access-key typical host** — The system containing cloud access keys is often an administrator’s workstation. _Why:_ administrator endpoints may hold high-value credentials for cloud environments. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Cloud CLI configuration condition** — These locally stored access keys appear when the cloud service’s command-line interface has been installed and configured. _Why:_ cloud CLI usage creates endpoint artifacts that can become credential-theft targets. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Cloud access-key theft impact** — Theft of access keys can let attackers enter the cloud environment with the same rights as the associated user. _Why:_ access-key compromise can become full cloud account compromise within that user’s permission scope. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Cloud access-key permission inheritance** — Stolen access keys carry the user’s rights and permissions. _Why:_ authorization impact depends on the compromised cloud user’s assigned privileges. _[GCFA p.~161]_

### Cloud Authorization Tokens

- **Cloud authorization-token issuance** — Cloud providers issue different kinds of authorization tokens after an account successfully authenticates. _Why:_ post-authentication tokens can become credential artifacts separate from passwords. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Microsoft Entra ID example** — Microsoft Entra ID is given as an example of a cloud identity provider that issues such tokens. _Why:_ Entra ID tokens are relevant to Microsoft cloud identity investigations. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Primary Refresh Token definition** — Microsoft Entra ID issues a Primary Refresh Token, abbreviated `PRT`, after successful authentication. _Why:_ the PRT is a key post-authentication artifact for cloud access. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **PRT authentication-claim content** — A PRT contains claims describing how the authentication occurred. _Why:_ these claims influence downstream access decisions. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **PRT MFA claim relevance** — PRT claims can indicate that multifactor authentication requirements were satisfied. _Why:_ stolen tokens may carry evidence of MFA completion into attacker sessions. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **PRT conditional-access claim relevance** — PRT claims can include conditional-access-related signals. _Why:_ token theft may preserve access context that would otherwise need to be re-established. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **PRT Kerberos analogy** — A PRT functions similarly to a Kerberos TGT. _Why:_ both are primary tokens used to obtain further access credentials after initial authentication. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **PRT access-token role** — A PRT is used to obtain access tokens for cloud services. _Why:_ stealing the PRT can enable access to downstream services. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **PRT session-cookie role** — A PRT can also be used to obtain session cookies for cloud-based services. _Why:_ derived cookies may provide browser or application access without repeating login steps. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **PRT-derived credential examples** — PRT-derived credentials include PRT cookies. _Why:_ responders must look beyond the PRT itself and consider credentials derived from it. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **PRT theft identity impact** — Theft of a PRT can allow an attacker to act as the authenticated user. _Why:_ the attacker can assume the user’s cloud identity without knowing or replaying the original password. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **PRT-derived credential theft impact** — Theft of PRT-derived credentials, such as PRT cookies, can also allow impersonation of the authenticated user. _Why:_ derived artifacts may be enough for cloud session takeover. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **PRT replay authentication bypass** — A stolen PRT or derived credential lets the attacker avoid repeating the authentication steps. _Why:_ MFA or conditional access may not be re-prompted during token-based session use. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **PRT claim persistence** — Claims inside the PRT persist into later use of the token. _Why:_ authentication context can survive beyond the original login event. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Derived-token claim persistence** — Claims from the PRT are also carried through derived cookies or access tokens. _Why:_ downstream credentials may inherit trusted authentication context. _[GCFA p.~161]_
- **Cross-computer token use** — PRT claims and derived-token claims can be presented in an attacker session even when that session starts on a different computer. _Why:_ token theft can move authenticated cloud context away from the original endpoint. _[GCFA p.~161]_

### BloodHound Purpose And Model

- **BloodHound** — BloodHound maps Active Directory relationships as a graph. _Why:_ graphing AD relationships exposes privilege paths that are hard to see from lists. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **BloodHound node types · Users** — User accounts can appear as graph nodes in BloodHound. _Why:_ users often provide the starting or intermediate identity in an escalation path. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **BloodHound node types · Computers** — Computer objects can appear as graph nodes in BloodHound. _Why:_ compromised systems can become stepping stones for credential collection and lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **BloodHound node types · Groups** — AD groups can appear as graph nodes in BloodHound. _Why:_ group membership often controls administrative reach and privilege escalation. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **BloodHound node types · Domains** — Domains can appear as graph nodes in BloodHound. _Why:_ domain-level trust and privilege relationships shape attack paths. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **BloodHound node types · OUs** — Organizational Units can appear as graph nodes in BloodHound. _Why:_ OU-linked policy and delegation can influence effective permissions. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **BloodHound node types · GPOs** — Group Policy Objects can appear as graph nodes in BloodHound. _Why:_ GPO relationships can grant or imply control paths within AD. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **BloodHound edges** — BloodHound represents relationships between objects as edges. _Why:_ edges are the links that turn isolated AD objects into navigable attack paths. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **MemberOf edge** — BloodHound can represent group membership with a MemberOf relationship. _Why:_ membership relationships often explain how a lower-privileged identity inherits higher privilege. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **HasSession edge** — BloodHound can show that a user currently has a session on a system. _Why:_ active sessions indicate where credentials or tokens may be available to steal. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **AdminTo edge** — BloodHound can show that an identity or group has administrative rights over a system. _Why:_ local admin rights define practical lateral movement targets. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **TrustedBy edge** — BloodHound can model trust relationships using TrustedBy edges. _Why:_ trust relationships can create cross-boundary escalation opportunities. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **BloodHound path** — A BloodHound path is a chain of graph nodes connected by relationship edges. _Why:_ a path converts scattered AD relationships into an actionable route to a target. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Path to Domain Admin** — BloodHound can identify a sequence of relationships that leads to Domain Admin privileges. _Why:_ Domain Admin is a high-value objective for attackers and a critical exposure for defenders. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **BloodHound as an audit tool** — BloodHound is useful for defensive auditing, not only offensive operations. _Why:_ defenders can use the same graph visibility to remove dangerous paths before attackers exploit them. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **BloodHound as an attack tool** — BloodHound also supports offensive planning. _Why:_ attackers can use its output to reduce trial-and-error during privilege escalation. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Dangerous trust visualization** — BloodHound helps reveal risky trust relationships. _Why:_ trust paths can grant unintended access across users, systems, and groups. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Misconfiguration visualization** — BloodHound helps expose AD misconfigurations. _Why:_ configuration mistakes often create practical escalation paths. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Reduced brute force** — BloodHound greatly lowers the amount of guessing needed to reach Domain Admin. _Why:_ attackers can follow known graph paths instead of probing blindly. _[GCFA p.~162]_

### BloodHound Graph Example

### Active Directory Complexity

- **Graph-based attacker mindset** — The page contrasts list-oriented defensive thinking with graph-oriented attacker thinking. _Why:_ attackers benefit when defenders fail to reason about chained relationships. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **BloodHound graph theory use** — BloodHound applies graph theory to uncover hidden or unintended AD relationships. _Why:_ graph analysis can reveal privilege paths not obvious from individual settings. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **AD complexity** — Active Directory environments are highly complex. _Why:_ complexity makes unintended privilege paths more likely. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **AD complexity growth** — AD environments commonly become more complicated as networks evolve. _Why:_ accumulated changes can create legacy trust and permission exposures. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Group changes affect trust** — Changes to groups can alter the AD trust and privilege model. _Why:_ group membership is a core mechanism for inherited access. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Domain changes affect trust** — Changes involving domains can alter the AD trust model. _Why:_ domain relationships define broad authentication and authorization boundaries. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **OU changes affect trust** — Changes to Organizational Units can affect effective AD trust and control. _Why:_ OU structure can influence delegation and policy application. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **GPO changes affect trust** — Changes to Group Policy Objects can affect the trust model. _Why:_ GPOs can assign rights, configure systems, and create control relationships. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Visualizing cumulative AD changes** — The combined effect of many AD object and policy changes is difficult to understand manually. _Why:_ defenders may miss escalation paths unless relationships are modeled together. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Proactive BloodHound use** — Defenders or penetration testers should ideally run BloodHound before an adversary does. _Why:_ early discovery allows remediation before compromise. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Sensitive group discovery** — BloodHound can quickly find paths to highly sensitive groups. _Why:_ those paths identify concrete privilege escalation risk. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Sensitive account discovery** — BloodHound can quickly find paths to highly sensitive accounts. _Why:_ exposed privileged accounts become practical attacker objectives. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Realism of simplified graph** — The slide states that the simplified example resembles patterns found in many real networks. _Why:_ the risk is not theoretical; common enterprise AD structures can contain similar chains. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **User identification** — BloodHound can identify users in the environment. _Why:_ users are key nodes for credential theft and privilege chaining. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Group identification** — BloodHound can identify groups in the environment. _Why:_ groups explain inherited access and privilege concentration. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Session location identification** — BloodHound can identify where users currently have sessions. _Why:_ session location helps attackers choose where to dump credentials. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Credential dumping guidance** — BloodHound can indicate where an attacker should attempt credential dumping next. _Why:_ targeted dumping is more efficient and less noisy than random collection. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Lateral movement guidance** — BloodHound can indicate where an attacker should move laterally next. _Why:_ it turns AD relationship data into an operational movement plan. _[GCFA p.~162]_

### Detection And Collection Behavior

- **BloodHound stealth** — BloodHound activity is difficult to detect in many environments. _Why:_ its data collection resembles normal enterprise directory activity. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **BloodHound LDAP collection** — BloodHound gathers data using LDAP requests. _Why:_ LDAP is common in AD environments, making collection blend into routine traffic. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **LDAP normality** — LDAP requests are common in enterprise networks. _Why:_ common protocol use reduces the distinctiveness of BloodHound collection. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Older BloodHound detection pattern** — Older BloodHound activity could sometimes be spotted through many nearly simultaneous LDAP sessions in AD logs. _Why:_ bursty LDAP session behavior can stand out from normal directory usage. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **SharpHound role** — SharpHound is the data collector for BloodHound. _Why:_ detecting or constraining collection often means focusing on SharpHound behavior. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Newer SharpHound LDAP caching** — Current SharpHound versions use cached LDAP connections. _Why:_ cached connections reduce the collection footprint that older detection methods relied on. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **NetFlow detection attempt** — Analysts have attempted to detect BloodHound by using NetFlow logs to track LDAP sessions. _Why:_ flow data may expose unusual directory-collection patterns even when host logs are limited. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Directory Service Access auditing** — Analysts have attempted detection through AD Directory Service Access audit logs. _Why:_ object access auditing can reveal suspicious directory enumeration. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Honey token detection** — Honey tokens have been used as a possible BloodHound detection strategy. _Why:_ interaction with decoy AD objects can reveal enumeration or misuse. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **EDR behavioral detection** — EDR tools may detect BloodHound-related activity through behavioral clues. _Why:_ process and object interaction patterns can supplement weak LDAP-only detection. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Named pipe clue** — EDR tools may watch for connections to particular named-pipe objects. _Why:_ named-pipe interaction can provide a behavioral indicator associated with tooling. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **Post-theft misuse detection** — The page states that inappropriate activity after credential theft is often the most reliable detection point. _Why:_ successful credential abuse can be more visible than the earlier graph collection step. _[GCFA p.~162]_

- **GoFetch** — GoFetch is an automation tool that attempts to perform steps needed to obtain Domain Admin rights. _Why:_ automation can operationalize BloodHound findings into real compromise actions. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **DeathStar** — DeathStar is another automation tool that attempts to automate the path to Domain Admin. _Why:_ it represents a noisy but effective way to chain enumeration, credential theft, and movement. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **GoFetch noisiness** — GoFetch is described as very noisy compared with BloodHound collection itself. _Why:_ noisy automation creates more detection opportunities than passive graph collection. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **DeathStar noisiness** — DeathStar is grouped with noisy Domain Admin automation tools. _Why:_ automation artifacts may be easier to detect than manual or stealthier enumeration. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **GoFetch BloodHound input** — GoFetch consumes the BloodHound graph. _Why:_ it turns graph relationships into an automated attack workflow. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **GoFetch Invoke-Mimikatz use** — GoFetch uses Invoke-Mimikatz. _Why:_ Invoke-Mimikatz supports automated credential theft in the GoFetch workflow. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **GoFetch Invoke-Psexec use** — GoFetch uses Invoke-Psexec. _Why:_ Invoke-Psexec supports automated lateral movement in the GoFetch workflow. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **GoFetch credential theft automation** — GoFetch automates credential theft. _Why:_ automated theft accelerates privilege escalation once a graph path is known. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **GoFetch lateral movement automation** — GoFetch automates lateral movement. _Why:_ it can move through systems along graph-derived opportunities. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **DeathStar PowerShell Empire use** — DeathStar uses PowerShell Empire. _Why:_ PowerShell Empire provides the automation framework for its enumeration and movement actions. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **DeathStar account enumeration** — DeathStar enumerates accounts. _Why:_ account discovery helps approximate the relationship data BloodHound would provide. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **DeathStar BloodHound approximation** — DeathStar approximates BloodHound-like enumeration. _Why:_ it can derive attack-relevant account information even when not directly using BloodHound output. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **DeathStar credential theft** — DeathStar performs credential theft. _Why:_ stolen credentials enable escalation and movement toward Domain Admin. _[GCFA p.~162]_
- **DeathStar lateral movement** — DeathStar automates lateral movement. _Why:_ automated movement allows rapid chaining of compromised access across systems. _[GCFA p.~162]_
