## Page 164

### Technical Mitigation Table

- **Technology · Least Privilege** — the listed mitigation technology is least privilege. _Why:_ this identifies privilege reduction as a defensive control against credential theft and lateral movement. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Least Privilege · Benefit and notes** — ordinary users should not receive local administrator privileges, and access should be limited to what is required. _Why:_ reducing local admin rights limits the value of stolen user credentials. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Technology · Protocol Signing** — the listed mitigation technology is protocol signing. _Why:_ protocol-level integrity checks are a direct defense against relay-style attacks. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Protocol Signing · Benefit and notes** — services such as SMB and LDAP can be configured to require digital signatures, which blocks relay attacks against those protocols. _Why:_ unsigned protocol traffic is easier for attackers to relay or tamper with. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Technology · Credential Guard** — the listed mitigation technology is Credential Guard. _Why:_ it protects high-value authentication material on Windows systems. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Credential Guard · Benefit and notes** — Credential Guard uses hypervisor-based isolation to protect password hashes and Kerberos tickets. _Why:_ isolating credential material makes LSASS-focused dumping attacks harder. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Technology · Restricted Admin Mode / Remote Credential Guard** — the listed mitigation technology combines Restricted Admin Mode and Remote Credential Guard. _Why:_ these controls reduce credential exposure during remote administration. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Restricted Admin Mode / Remote Credential Guard · Benefit and notes** — these features reduce credential exposure on systems reached through Remote Desktop Protocol. _Why:_ RDP logons are common places where reusable credentials can otherwise land on remote hosts. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Technology · Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA)** — the listed mitigation technology is Group Managed Service Accounts. _Why:_ managed service identities reduce weaknesses caused by manually maintained service passwords. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **gMSA · Benefit and notes** — gMSA secures and randomizes service-account passwords that would otherwise be manually created, stores management in the domain-controller context, and rotates those passwords frequently. _Why:_ rotating strong service credentials reduces cracking and reuse risk. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **dMSA · Server 2025 availability** — delegated Managed Service Accounts are noted as available in Windows Server 2025. _Why:_ this identifies a newer service-account management option. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Technology · Deny interactive logon** — the listed mitigation technology is denying interactive logon. _Why:_ restricting logon rights limits how stolen service credentials can be abused. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Deny interactive logon · Benefit and notes** — service accounts should be assigned rights that prevent interactive logon if their credentials are stolen. _Why:_ a stolen service account is less useful if it cannot be used for hands-on access. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Technology · Protected Users** — the listed mitigation technology is the Protected Users security group. _Why:_ this group changes authentication behavior for sensitive accounts. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Protected Users · Benefit and notes** — membership in Protected Users prevents credential delegation and credential caching for those accounts. _Why:_ blocking cached and delegated credentials reduces credential theft opportunities. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Technology · Reduce NTLM usage** — the listed mitigation technology is reducing NTLM usage. _Why:_ limiting NTLM reduces exposure to attacks that rely on NTLM authentication. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Reduce NTLM usage · Benefit and notes** — Windows 11 includes capabilities to restrict which hosts use NTLM or accept NTLM. _Why:_ controlling NTLM availability narrows where NTLM-based attacks can succeed. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Technology · Disable weaker protocols** — the listed mitigation technology is disabling weaker protocols. _Why:_ removing legacy cryptographic and authentication mechanisms lowers attack surface. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Disable weaker protocols · Benefit and notes** — organizations should disable NTLMv1 and, where feasible, disable Kerberos RC4-HMAC-MD5. _Why:_ these weaker protocols are more attractive targets for credential attacks. _[GCFA p.164]_

### Mitigation Coverage

- **SEC599 mitigation coverage** — SEC599 is identified as the course that discusses these mitigations in greater detail. _Why:_ this points learners to a deeper source for defensive implementation guidance. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Earlier Windows pass-the-hash mitigations** — older Windows releases added several defenses against pass-the-hash activity. _Why:_ pass-the-hash resistance has existed across multiple Windows generations, not only in recent releases. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Restricted Administrator accounts** — Restricted Administrator accounts are named as one earlier pass-the-hash mitigation. _Why:_ account restrictions can reduce the ability to reuse local administrator credentials remotely. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Protected User security group** — the Protected User security group is named as one earlier pass-the-hash mitigation. _Why:_ Protected Users changes credential handling in ways that interfere with common credential-theft paths. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Protected Processes** — Protected Processes are named as one earlier pass-the-hash mitigation. _Why:_ process protection can interfere with credential dumping from sensitive Windows processes. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Windows 10 · Credential Guard introduction** — Windows 10 introduced Credential Guard. _Why:_ this establishes when Microsoft added hypervisor-assisted credential isolation to Windows client systems. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Windows 10 · Remote Credential Guard introduction** — Windows 10 introduced Remote Credential Guard. _Why:_ this identifies the Windows generation that added improved RDP credential protection. _[GCFA p.164]_

### Remote Logon Credential Exposure

- **Restricted Admin RDP access · Hash exposure** — Restricted Admin RDP access does not place password hashes on the remote system. _Why:_ this reduces the chance that a compromised remote host yields reusable credential material. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Remote Credential Guard · Hash exposure** — systems using Remote Credential Guard do not expose hashes on the destination system. _Why:_ protecting hashes during remote administration weakens credential-harvesting opportunities. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Remote interactive RDP logon · Credential protection** — even during an interactive RDP session, Restricted Admin or Remote Credential Guard prevents hashes from becoming available on the remote host. _Why:_ interactive remote logons are otherwise high-risk credential exposure events. _[GCFA p.164]_

### Protected Users

- **Protected Users · NTLM restriction** — accounts in Protected Users cannot authenticate using NTLM. _Why:_ NTLM is commonly abused in relay and pass-the-hash workflows. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Protected Users · WDigest restriction** — accounts in Protected Users cannot authenticate using WDigest. _Why:_ WDigest has historically exposed reusable credential material. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Protected Users · SSP restriction** — accounts in Protected Users cannot authenticate using SSP. _Why:_ blocking SSP authentication reduces exposure through additional credential-handling paths. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Protected Users · Credential caching restriction** — Protected Users accounts cannot have their credentials cached. _Why:_ cached credentials can be recovered and reused by attackers. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Protected Users · Delegation restriction** — Protected Users accounts cannot have their credentials delegated. _Why:_ blocking delegation limits credential forwarding and impersonation risk. _[GCFA p.164]_

### LSASS Protection

- **Protected Processes · Signed-code requirement** — Protected Processes only run signed code. _Why:_ requiring signed code blocks many code-injection approaches used against protected processes. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Protected Processes · LSASS dumping impact** — when LSASS is enabled as a protected process, many credential-dumping techniques that rely on code injection stop working. _Why:_ LSASS is a primary source of credential material during post-compromise activity. _[GCFA p.164]_

### Local Administrator Accounts

- **Local administrator network authentication restriction** — local administrator accounts can generally be blocked from authenticating over the network. _Why:_ this limits pass-the-hash movement using local admin credentials. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Pass-the-hash network restriction** — network authentication restrictions can include blocking pass-the-hash use by local administrator accounts. _Why:_ stolen local admin hashes lose value when they cannot authenticate to other hosts. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **RID 500 built-in administrator exception** — the RID 500 built-in Administrator account is called out as an exception to easy network-authentication restriction. _Why:_ this account may remain usable where other local administrator accounts are restricted. _[GCFA p.164]_

### Credential Guard

- **Credential Guard · Hypervisor use** — Credential Guard uses a hypervisor to isolate credential material. _Why:_ hypervisor isolation places sensitive data outside normal LSASS memory access paths. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Credential Guard · Domain credential relocation** — Credential Guard moves domain credentials out of LSASS. _Why:_ removing domain credentials from LSASS reduces the payoff of LSASS dumping. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Credential Guard · Ticket relocation** — Credential Guard moves Kerberos tickets out of LSASS. _Why:_ attackers often seek tickets for pass-the-ticket and related attacks. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Credential Guard · Hash relocation** — Credential Guard moves hashes out of LSASS. _Why:_ hashes are reusable in pass-the-hash attacks if obtained. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Credential Guard · LSAIso process** — Credential Guard places protected credential material into an isolated process named LSAIso. _Why:_ LSAIso provides a stronger protection boundary than ordinary LSASS storage. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Credential Guard · Defensive limitation** — the page states that all listed mitigations can be bypassed. _Why:_ responders should treat these controls as risk reduction, not absolute prevention. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Credential Guard and related controls · Practical effect** — enabling these defenses makes credential-theft attacks substantially harder. _Why:_ layered controls increase attacker effort and reduce common credential-dumping success. _[GCFA p.164]_

### Local Administrator Password Solution

- **Unique local administrator passwords** — local administrator passwords should be unique rather than shared across workstation groups. _Why:_ shared local admin passwords allow one stolen hash or password to compromise many machines. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Workstation segment password reuse risk** — reusing the same local administrator password across a workstation segment is identified as a risk. _Why:_ workstation-wide reuse enables broad lateral movement. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Microsoft LAPS** — Microsoft released Local Administrator Password Solution to manage local administrator account security centrally. _Why:_ centralized management makes unique local administrator passwords operationally practical. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **LAPS · Active Directory integration** — LAPS centralizes local administrator account management within Active Directory. _Why:_ AD-backed storage and management supports enterprise-scale local admin password control. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Hash reuse reduction** — password hashes are much less useful when the same credential cannot be reused on other systems. _Why:_ pass-the-hash depends heavily on credential reuse across machines. _[GCFA p.164]_

### Protocol Signing And Weaker Protocols

- **SMB signing** — SMB can be configured to require digital signatures. _Why:_ signing reduces the feasibility of relay attacks against SMB. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **LDAP signing** — LDAP can be configured to require digital signatures. _Why:_ signing reduces the feasibility of relay attacks against LDAP. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Protocol signing · Relay risk reduction** — requiring signatures on protocols such as SMB and LDAP greatly lowers relay-attack risk. _Why:_ relay attacks depend on forwarding authentication without sufficient integrity protection. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Organization-wide NTLMv1 disablement** — NTLMv1 should be disabled throughout the organization. _Why:_ NTLMv1 is a weaker authentication protocol and increases credential-attack risk. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Kerberos RC4-HMAC-MD5 disablement** — Kerberos RC4-HMAC-MD5 should be disabled wherever possible. _Why:_ removing weaker Kerberos encryption reduces attack options against Kerberos credentials. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Weaker protocol reduction** — disabling NTLMv1 and Kerberos RC4-HMAC-MD5 reduces attacks against weaker authentication mechanisms. _Why:_ attackers prefer legacy protocols and weaker cryptography when available. _[GCFA p.164]_

### Service Accounts

- **Service installation credential prompt** — some service installers ask administrators to provide service-account credentials during installation. _Why:_ installation workflows often lead to manually created long-lived service credentials. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Manual service account creation** — administrators often create a dedicated standard user account for a service. _Why:_ manually created service accounts can become weak, persistent credential targets. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Service account password weakness** — manually created service-account passwords are often not hard to crack. _Why:_ weak service passwords can be recovered and reused by attackers. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Service account non-expiring password practice** — manually created service-account passwords are often configured never to expire. _Why:_ non-expiring credentials remain useful to attackers for long periods if compromised. _[GCFA p.164]_
- **Built-in Windows service accounts** — Windows includes built-in service accounts, with Network Service shown as an example on the page. _Why:_ built-in service identities are contrasted with manually created service accounts. _[GCFA p.164]_

## Page 165

### Managed Service Accounts

- **Built-in service-type account passwords** — Windows automatically changes very long, complex passwords for built-in service-related accounts such as service accounts and Local System. _Why:_ automatic high-entropy rotation reduces credential reuse and manual password-management risk. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **Manual service account choice** — When a custom service identity is required, the preferred option is a Group Managed Service Account rather than a normal user account assigned to run a service. _Why:_ ordinary user accounts used as services create weaker lifecycle and credential-management exposure. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **Group Managed Service Account (gMSA)** — A gMSA is a managed domain service identity designed for services that need controlled password creation, rotation, and distribution. _Why:_ it gives service identities built-in credential handling closer to Windows-managed accounts. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **gMSA multi-host use** — A gMSA can be assigned across more than one computer, including clustered server deployments. _Why:_ this supports services that fail over or run on multiple hosts without sharing a manually maintained user password. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **gMSA password creation control** — gMSA use gives Windows control over how the service account password is generated. _Why:_ centrally generated credentials are less likely to be weak, reused, or mishandled. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **gMSA password rotation control** — gMSA use gives Windows control over service-account password changes. _Why:_ automatic rotation limits the useful lifetime of a stolen service credential. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **gMSA password delivery control** — gMSA credentials are securely delivered to the domain controller as part of the managed-account process. _Why:_ secure delivery prevents administrators or scripts from needing to expose service passwords. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **gMSA domain-controller handling** — The domain controller treats gMSA credentials similarly to built-in service-account credentials. _Why:_ this places custom service identities under the same kind of managed credential model as native Windows service accounts. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **gMSA interactive-logon restriction** — gMSA accounts include extra constraints that make direct interactive sign-in harder. _Why:_ reducing interactive use limits the value of the account for hands-on attacker access. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **gMSA Active Directory location** — gMSA objects appear under the Managed Service Accounts area in Active Directory Users and Computers. _Why:_ their separate location distinguishes managed service identities from ordinary user accounts during administration and review. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **gMSA account separation** — gMSA storage under Managed Service Accounts differentiates them from standard user accounts. _Why:_ clear separation helps defenders identify whether services are using purpose-built managed identities or risky ordinary users. _[GCFA p.165]_

### Delegated Managed Service Accounts

- **Delegated Managed Service Accounts (dMSA)** — Windows Server 2025 introduces dMSA as another managed service-account option with results similar to gMSA. _Why:_ dMSA gives defenders an additional managed-identity mechanism for service accounts. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **dMSA computer binding** — dMSA provides added binding between the managed service account and particular computers. _Why:_ tighter host association can reduce misuse of the service identity outside intended systems. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **dMSA migration support** — dMSA includes capabilities intended to help move legacy user-account-based services into dMSA-managed identities. _Why:_ migration support helps replace weaker historical service-account patterns without requiring a full redesign. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **dMSA availability baseline** — The page identifies Server 2025 as the starting point for dMSA availability. _Why:_ investigators and administrators need OS-version context when evaluating whether dMSA should be present or usable. _[GCFA p.165]_

### NTLM and SMB Hardening

- **Windows 11 NTLM restriction features** — Windows 11 added features that limit NTLM usage. _Why:_ reducing NTLM availability shrinks exposure to NTLM-based credential abuse. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **Server 2025 NTLM restriction features** — Server 2025 added features that limit NTLM usage. _Why:_ server-side NTLM controls matter because servers often host high-value authentication paths. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **Failed NTLM logon thresholds** — Windows 11 and Server 2025 introduced thresholds for failed NTLM authentication attempts. _Why:_ thresholds help slow or block password spraying and password guessing against NTLM. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **Password spray defense** — Failed-NTLM thresholds are specifically described as a countermeasure against password spraying. _Why:_ password spray attacks rely on repeated low-volume guesses across accounts. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **Password guessing defense** — Failed-NTLM thresholds are also described as a countermeasure against password guessing attacks. _Why:_ limiting repeated NTLM failures reduces brute-force-style discovery of valid passwords. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **Outbound SMB NTLM disablement** — Outbound SMB connections can be configured so they do not use NTLM. _Why:_ blocking NTLM over outbound SMB reduces opportunities for NTLM capture, relay, and pass-the-hash workflows. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **Outbound SMB NTLM allow-listing** — Outbound SMB NTLM can be permitted only for selected legacy systems. _Why:_ exception-based enablement preserves compatibility while reducing NTLM exposure elsewhere. _[GCFA p.165]_
- **Pass-the-hash risk reduction** — Restricting NTLM for outbound SMB is presented as a way to lower pass-the-hash risk. _Why:_ pass-the-hash depends on reusable NTLM-derived credentials being accepted by remote services. _[GCFA p.165]_

- **RunAs · Credentials on Target** — `RunAs` normally results in credentials being present on the target host. _Why:_ this creates a credential-theft opportunity on the system where the command is run. _[GCFA p.166]_

## Page 167

### Hash Exposure and Interactive Logons

- **Privileged interactive logon avoidance** — The strongest protection for password hashes is to avoid signing in interactively with highly privileged accounts. _Why:_ interactive privileged sessions create opportunities for attackers to capture reusable credential material. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Local administrator rights as credential-theft enabler** — Preventing attackers from obtaining local administrator privileges is a core hash-protection measure. _Why:_ local admin control can allow access to credential-stealing techniques and tools. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Hash presence condition** — Password hashes are present only during interactive logon sessions. _Why:_ defenders can reduce hash exposure by controlling where and how interactive sessions occur. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Console logon risk** — Console logons with privileged accounts should be avoided. _Why:_ console sessions can place privileged hashes on the endpoint where the session occurs. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Default RDP risk** — Standard Remote Desktop Protocol logons with privileged accounts should be avoided. _Why:_ RDP interactive sessions can leave privileged hashes available on the target system. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **runas risk** — Use of `runas` with highly privileged credentials should be avoided. _Why:_ it can create an interactive authentication context that exposes credential material. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Server logon sensitivity** — Avoiding privileged interactive logons is especially important on servers. _Why:_ many users may access servers, and attackers already present on the host can wait for valuable accounts to log in. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **High-value account waiting tactic** — Attackers may remain hidden on a server until a privileged or otherwise valuable account authenticates. _Why:_ the later logon can provide the credential material needed for escalation or lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~167]_

### RDP Session Persistence

- **Improper RDP termination risk** — Credential hashes are commonly stolen when RDP sessions are disconnected instead of fully ended. _Why:_ leaving sessions alive can leave hashes available after the user stops actively working. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Open interactive session persistence** — Hashes remain on a system while the associated interactive session is still open. _Why:_ session lifetime directly affects how long credential material remains exposed. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Disconnected-but-not-closed RDP session behavior** — If an RDP session is disconnected without being closed, the hash can remain on the host as long as that session exists. _Why:_ a user may believe they have left the system, while their credential material is still present. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Group Policy disconnected-session limit** — Group Policy can enforce a timeout for disconnected sessions. _Why:_ automatically ending stale RDP sessions reduces the time hashes remain exposed. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Old RDP session termination** — A disconnected-session time limit can effectively close abandoned RDP sessions. _Why:_ terminating old sessions removes credential material that would otherwise remain available. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Disconnected-session timeout tradeoff** — Setting the disconnected-session timeout too aggressively can cause users to lose work during routine network interruptions. _Why:_ the defensive control must balance credential protection against operational reliability. _[GCFA p.~167]_

### Enterprise Tiered Access Model

- **Microsoft enterprise access model** — Microsoft recommends an enterprise access model for credential security. _Why:_ structured administrative boundaries reduce credential exposure and limit escalation paths. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Trust tiers in Active Directory** — The access model uses multiple trust tiers inside an Active Directory domain. _Why:_ separating administrative scopes prevents credentials from higher-trust areas being exposed to lower-trust systems. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Tiered access model age** — Microsoft has advocated the tiered access model for roughly ten years. _Why:_ the model is a long-standing enterprise defense pattern rather than a new or experimental recommendation. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Least privilege principle** — Administrative accounts should be used only where their privileges are required. _Why:_ limiting account use reduces unnecessary credential exposure across the environment. _[GCFA p.~167]_

### Tier 0

- **Tier 0 scope** — Tier 0 contains domain controllers and Domain Admin accounts. _Why:_ these assets and identities control the highest-trust layer of the domain. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Domain Admin privilege purpose** — Domain Admin rights are needed only for configuring domain controllers. _Why:_ using these accounts elsewhere exposes excessive privilege beyond the actual administrative need. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Domain Admin usage boundary** — Domain Admin accounts should not be used anywhere except on domain controllers. _Why:_ this prevents Tier 0 credentials from being exposed on lower-trust machines. _[GCFA p.~167]_

### Tier 1

- **Tier 1 scope** — Tier 1 consists of servers and accounts used to administer servers. _Why:_ server administration is separated from both domain-control functions and workstation administration. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Server admin workstation denial** — Server administrator accounts should be denied access to workstations. _Why:_ compromise of a workstation should not expose credentials that can administer servers. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Server admin domain-controller denial** — Server administrator accounts should be denied access to domain controllers. _Why:_ server admin credentials should not become a path into Tier 0 systems. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Server admin usage boundary** — Server administrator accounts should be used only on servers. _Why:_ restricting their logon locations limits where their hashes can appear. _[GCFA p.~167]_

### Tier 2

- **Tier 2 scope** — Tier 2 covers workstations and other end-user devices. _Why:_ these systems form the lowest-trust administrative tier in the model. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Workstations as highest-risk devices** — Workstations and user devices are the highest-risk systems in the environment. _Why:_ they are the devices most exposed to user activity and Internet-originated threats. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Internet interaction risk** — Users most often interact with the untrusted Internet from workstations and similar devices. _Why:_ this makes workstation compromise more likely than compromise of more isolated infrastructure. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Workstation admin privilege limit** — An administrator account used for workstation access should have rights only on workstations. _Why:_ a stolen workstation admin credential should not grant access beyond the workstation tier. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Workstation admin server denial** — Workstation administrator accounts should be explicitly blocked from connecting to servers. _Why:_ this prevents a compromised workstation credential from becoming a server compromise path. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Workstation admin domain-controller denial** — Workstation administrator accounts should be explicitly blocked from connecting to domain controllers. _Why:_ this prevents low-tier credential theft from directly reaching Tier 0 assets. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Workstation compromise containment** — If a workstation is compromised and an administrative credential is stolen, the intended blast radius is limited to other workstations. _Why:_ tier boundaries constrain lateral movement after credential theft. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Server escalation prevention** — A stolen workstation admin credential should not be usable to escalate into sensitive servers. _Why:_ this protects Tier 1 assets from Tier 2 compromise. _[GCFA p.~167]_

- **Domain-controller escalation prevention** — A stolen workstation admin credential should not be usable to escalate into domain controllers. _Why:_ this protects Tier 0 domain control from lower-tier credential theft. _[GCFA p.~167]_

## Page 168

### Secure Administrative Workstations

- **Secure Administrative Workstation (SAW)** — administrators should use a hardened administrative workstation whenever they type or submit an administrative credential. _Why:_ limiting where privileged credentials are entered reduces where those credentials can be exposed. _[GCFA p.~168]_

- **Privileged Access Workstation (PAW)** — PAW is another name for a secure administrative workstation. _Why:_ both terms refer to the same defensive control, so analysts should recognize either label in documentation or environment reviews. _[GCFA p.~168]_

- **Administrative Credential Entry** — privileged credentials should be entered only from designated secure administrative systems. _Why:_ credential-entry locations define where high-value authentication material may become exposed. _[GCFA p.~168]_

- **Interactive Logon Credential Exposure** — an interactive logon that receives a credential creates the session type with the highest credential exposure risk described on this page. _Why:_ incident responders should treat interactive administrative sessions as especially sensitive credential-exposure events. _[GCFA p.~168]_

- **Restricted Interactive Administrative Logons** — interactive logons using administrative credentials should be limited to hardened administrative workstations. _Why:_ this reduces the chance that privileged credentials are placed on ordinary or compromised endpoints. _[GCFA p.~168]_

- **Designated Administrative Workstations** — administrative logons should occur only on systems specifically assigned for privileged work. _Why:_ designated systems make privileged access easier to control, monitor, and harden. _[GCFA p.~168]_

- **Per-Tier SAWs** — each administrative tier should ideally have its own separate secure administrative workstations. _Why:_ separating workstations by tier helps prevent one compromised system from exposing credentials across multiple privilege tiers. _[GCFA p.~168]_

- **Single-System Compromise Risk** — using the same administrative workstation across tiers can allow one host compromise to endanger credentials for more than one tier. _Why:_ this creates a broader credential-theft blast radius from a single endpoint incident. _[GCFA p.~168]_

### Segmentation And Zero Trust

- **Network Segmentation Within Tiers** — segmentation should be applied inside administrative tiers, not only between them. _Why:_ limiting network reachability reduces attacker movement after credential compromise. _[GCFA p.~168]_

- **Zero-Trust Principles Within Tiers** — zero-trust controls should be used inside tiers to avoid unnecessary implicit connectivity. _Why:_ compromised credentials become less useful when systems cannot freely connect without business justification. _[GCFA p.~168]_

- **Business-Need Connectivity** — IP connectivity between systems should be reduced when no business requirement exists. _Why:_ unnecessary network paths increase post-compromise options for an attacker. _[GCFA p.~168]_

- **Credential Compromise Damage Reduction** — segmentation and zero-trust controls reduce the impact of a stolen administrative credential. _Why:_ credential theft is less damaging when the credential cannot be used broadly across reachable systems. _[GCFA p.~168]_

### References

- **Microsoft Enterprise Access Model Reference** — the page points readers to `https://for508.com/ezdtb` for Microsoft’s enterprise access model. _Why:_ this reference supports the administrative tiering and access-control model discussed on the page. _[GCFA p.~168]_

- **Kerberos And AD Tiering Reference** — the page points readers to `https://for508.com/z5sbe` for securing Kerberos and implementing the Active Directory tiered model. _Why:_ this reference expands on Kerberos hardening and tiered administration defenses. _[GCFA p.~168]_

## Page 177

### Windows Prefetch Availability

- **Windows Prefetch scope** — Prefetch is present on Windows workstation editions. _Why:_ the artifact should be expected on client Windows systems during execution analysis. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Windows workstation default behavior** — Windows workstation operating systems enable prefetching by default. _Why:_ investigators can normally assume the artifact may exist unless disabled or cleaned. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Windows Server distinction** — The page distinguishes workstation operating systems from server operating systems for default Prefetch behavior. _Why:_ artifact expectations differ between client and server investigations. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Prefetch disabling possibility** — Prefetching can be disabled. _Why:_ absence of Prefetch data is not by itself proof that an application never ran. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Windows 7 SSD observation** — Some observed Windows 7 systems with solid-state drives had Prefetch disabled. _Why:_ older SSD-equipped systems may lack expected Prefetch evidence. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Newer Windows SSD behavior** — The SSD-related disabling pattern was not observed as applying to newer Windows versions. _Why:_ analysts should not automatically extend Windows 7 SSD assumptions to later systems. _[GCFA p.~177]_

### Prefetch Function

- **Prefetching definition** — Prefetching loads important data and code from storage into memory before the operating system actually needs them. _Why:_ explains why execution-related cache files exist as a performance side effect. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Performance purpose** — Prefetch improves system performance by preloading code pages. _Why:_ the forensic artifact is created for optimization, not for auditing. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **First-run creation** — A `.pf` file is created in the Prefetch folder after an application is executed for the first time. _Why:_ Prefetch file creation can indicate an initial execution event. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Cache manager role** — The cache manager observes files and directories used by an application. _Why:_ Prefetch can reveal supporting resources touched during program execution. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Helper-file tracking** — Files that assist an application’s execution are recorded into that application’s Prefetch file. _Why:_ referenced helper files can provide context about program behavior. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Directory-reference tracking** — Directories referenced by an application are also tracked in the related Prefetch file. _Why:_ folder references can help reconstruct where an executed program interacted with the file system. _[GCFA p.~177]_

### Prefetch Location And Naming

- **Prefetch directory path** — Prefetch files are stored under `C:\Windows\Prefetch`. _Why:_ this is the primary collection location for Prefetch artifacts. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Prefetch file extension** — Prefetch artifacts use the `.pf` extension. _Why:_ the extension identifies the files to parse or triage. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Filename pattern** — A Prefetch filename uses an executable name, a dash, a hash value, and the `.pf` extension. _Why:_ the name itself encodes execution-related identity information. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Filename example** — `CHROME.EXE-46AA1511.pf` is shown as an example Prefetch filename. _Why:_ demonstrates the executable-plus-hash naming convention. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Executable-name component** — The first part of a Prefetch filename is the executable’s name. _Why:_ analysts can quickly associate the artifact with a program. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Dash separator** — A dash separates the executable name from the hash in the Prefetch filename. _Why:_ parsing the filename requires recognizing the delimiter. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Hash representation** — The hash portion of the Prefetch filename is displayed in hexadecimal. _Why:_ duplicate names with different hashes can indicate different execution paths or contexts. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Hash input basis** — The Prefetch hash is based on the executable’s directory path. _Why:_ the hash can help distinguish same-named executables launched from different locations. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Command-line influence** — For certain programs, command-line options also affect the Prefetch hash. _Why:_ multiple Prefetch files may result from different invocation contexts, not only different executable paths. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Command-line hash example** — `svchost.exe` is given as an example of a program whose Prefetch hash can depend on command-line options. _Why:_ service-hosting binaries require cautious interpretation of multiple Prefetch hashes. _[GCFA p.~177]_

### Version Limits And Compression

- **Windows 7 Prefetch limit** — Windows 7 and earlier systems limit the Prefetch directory to 128 files. _Why:_ older systems may evict older execution artifacts sooner. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Pre-Windows 8 Prefetch limit** — The 128-file cap applies to Windows versions before Windows 8. _Why:_ evidence availability is constrained on legacy systems. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Windows 8+ Prefetch limit** — Windows 8 and later systems can maintain up to 1,024 Prefetch files. _Why:_ newer systems may preserve a larger execution-history set. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Windows 10 compression** — Prefetch files on Windows 10 are compressed. _Why:_ parsing tools must support the compressed Prefetch format. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Windows 11 compression** — Prefetch files on Windows 11 are compressed. _Why:_ investigators need compatible tooling for modern Prefetch analysis. _[GCFA p.~177]_

### Forensic Value

- **Execution indication** — A Prefetch file is evidence that an application executed. _Why:_ Prefetch is a core application-execution artifact. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Execution count storage** — Prefetch stores the total number of times the application has executed. _Why:_ run count helps estimate repeated use rather than a single launch. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Original execution path** — Prefetch stores the original path from which the program executed. _Why:_ path evidence can distinguish legitimate binaries from lookalikes in unusual locations. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Last execution time** — Prefetch stores the most recent execution time. _Why:_ last-run timing supports timeline reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Windows 8 execution-time expansion** — Starting with Windows 8, Prefetch can contain as many as eight execution timestamps. _Why:_ multiple run times provide more detailed execution history. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Windows 11 execution-time continuity** — The availability of up to eight embedded execution times continues through Windows 11. _Why:_ modern systems can provide several historical launch times from a single artifact. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Prefetch creation time as run time** — The file system creation time of the Prefetch file can add another execution-related timestamp. _Why:_ the Prefetch file’s creation time often corresponds to the first observed execution. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Nine possible run times** — Combining eight embedded run times with the Prefetch file creation time can yield nine run times for one application. _Why:_ this gives analysts a richer execution timeline than the embedded timestamps alone. _[GCFA p.~177]_

### Duplicate Executable Names

- **Multiple same-name Prefetch files** — Analysts should watch for several Prefetch files sharing the same executable name. _Why:_ duplicate executable names can signal execution from more than one location. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Different-location implication** — For most applications, same executable name with different Prefetch hashes suggests same-named binaries ran from different paths. _Why:_ this can expose renamed malware or copied administrative tools. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **`cmd.exe` duplicate example** — Multiple Prefetch files for `cmd.exe` may indicate a file named `cmd.exe` ran from a nonstandard directory. _Why:_ a command shell outside its expected location can be an important investigative lead. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Standard `cmd.exe` location** — The normal path referenced for `cmd.exe` is `C:\Windows\System32`. _Why:_ deviations from this path can help identify suspicious binaries. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Nonstandard `cmd.exe` significance** — A `cmd.exe` outside `C:\Windows\System32` may become a valuable finding. _Why:_ attackers sometimes use trusted names in unusual locations to blend in. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **Duplicate-name exceptions** — Some Windows hosting applications are exceptions to the simple duplicate-name interpretation rule. _Why:_ these binaries can legitimately produce multiple Prefetch hashes. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **`svchost` exception** — `svchost` is listed as a hosting application where duplicate Prefetch hashes need special interpretation. _Why:_ service-host behavior can create multiple Prefetch variants without implying separate malicious copies. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **`dllhost` exception** — `dllhost` is listed as another hosting application exception. _Why:_ COM hosting behavior can affect Prefetch interpretation. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **`backgroundtaskhost` exception** — `backgroundtaskhost` is identified as a hosting application exception. _Why:_ background task hosting can produce Prefetch patterns that differ from ordinary applications. _[GCFA p.~177]_
- **`rundll32` exception** — `rundll32` is identified as a hosting application exception. _Why:_ DLL execution through a host binary can create multiple Prefetch entries tied to invocation context. _[GCFA p.~177]_

## Page 178

### Prefetch File Naming and Hashing

- **Prefetch hash input** — the Prefetch filename hash is derived from the executable’s complete path plus any command-line parameters used at launch. _Why:_ different launch contexts for the same binary can produce separate Prefetch artifacts. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **Multiple Prefetch files per executable** — one executable can legitimately have more than one Prefetch file. _Why:_ analysts should not treat duplicate-looking Prefetch entries for the same program name as inherently suspicious. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **svchost.exe Prefetch multiplicity** — `svchost.exe` commonly appears with multiple Prefetch files because Windows normally starts it with varied command-line arguments. _Why:_ this is expected operating-system behavior and helps avoid false positives during execution analysis. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **Prefetch hash calculator reference** — the page cites a Prefetch hash calculator at `https://for508.com/rlhjb`. _Why:_ such tooling can help validate or reproduce Prefetch filename hash behavior during analysis. _[GCFA p.~178]_

### Live Response Evidence Risk

- **Live response tool execution artifact** — running response utilities directly on a target host can create new Prefetch files for those utilities. _Why:_ examiner activity can alter execution artifacts on the system being investigated. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **Prefetch directory capacity limit** — Windows systems retain only a finite number of Prefetch files. _Why:_ new Prefetch creation can force older Prefetch evidence out of the directory. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **Oldest Prefetch deletion risk** — executing live response tools may cause the oldest Prefetch files to be removed. _Why:_ this can destroy older program-execution evidence relevant to intrusion reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **Collection priority recommendation** — investigators should often collect the Prefetch directory early in live response. _Why:_ prioritizing this directory reduces the chance that volatile execution-history artifacts are overwritten by response activity. _[GCFA p.~178]_

### Prefetch Enablement Registry Locations

- **Two-key Prefetch configuration model** — Prefetch enablement is controlled by two separate Windows registry locations. _Why:_ absence of Prefetch artifacts should be checked against configuration before concluding that execution did not occur. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **Missing Prefetch audit trigger** — if a workstation lacks Prefetch data, the relevant registry settings should be reviewed. _Why:_ Prefetch may have been disabled or configured in a way that explains missing artifacts. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **PrefetchParameters registry path** — one Prefetch configuration location is `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management\PrefetchParameters`. _Why:_ this key contains the `EnablePrefetcher` value that controls Prefetch behavior. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **EnablePrefetcher value** — the `EnablePrefetcher` registry value should be audited when evaluating Prefetch availability. _Why:_ its numeric setting identifies whether application-launch and/or boot Prefetching is active. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **EnablePrefetcher = 0** — value `0` means Prefetch is disabled. _Why:_ this setting can explain absent Prefetch execution artifacts. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **EnablePrefetcher = 1** — value `1` enables application-launch Prefetching. _Why:_ this setting supports collection of program-execution traces but not boot Prefetching. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **EnablePrefetcher = 2** — value `2` enables boot Prefetching. _Why:_ this setting supports boot optimization artifacts but not application-launch Prefetch artifacts. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **EnablePrefetcher = 3** — value `3` enables both application-launch and boot Prefetching. _Why:_ this is the broadest setting and should allow normal Prefetch artifact generation for executions and boot activity. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **SysMain registry path** — the second Prefetch-related configuration location is `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\SysMain`. _Why:_ the SysMain service state can affect Prefetch-related functionality. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **SysMain Start value** — the `Start` registry value under `SysMain` should be audited. _Why:_ it indicates how the SysMain service is configured to start or whether it is disabled. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **SysMain Start = 0-2** — values from `0` through `2` indicate automatic start behavior. _Why:_ automatic service startup supports normal Prefetch/SysMain operation. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **SysMain Start = 3** — value `3` indicates manual start behavior. _Why:_ manual startup may affect whether Prefetch-related service behavior is active in a given system state. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **SysMain Start = 4** — value `4` indicates the service is disabled. _Why:_ a disabled SysMain service can help explain missing or reduced Prefetch-related artifacts. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **Microsoft Prefetch disabling reference** — the page cites Microsoft documentation on disabling Prefetch at `https://for508.com/dv689`. _Why:_ vendor documentation can support interpretation of Prefetch configuration values. _[GCFA p.~178]_

### SuperFetch Artifacts

- **SuperFetch storage location** — some Windows versions store SuperFetch artifacts inside the Prefetch folder. _Why:_ investigators may encounter non-`.pf` Prefetch-directory artifacts that still relate to application execution behavior. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **SuperFetch file naming pattern** — SuperFetch database files use names matching `Ag*.db`. _Why:_ this pattern helps identify SuperFetch artifacts during directory review. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **AgAppLaunch.db example** — `AgAppLaunch.db` is listed as an example SuperFetch database filename. _Why:_ recognizing this file helps distinguish SuperFetch data from standard Prefetch files. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **AgRobust.db example** — `AgRobust.db` is listed as another example SuperFetch database filename. _Why:_ this provides another concrete filename analysts may see in the Prefetch directory. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **Limited SuperFetch parser support** — few forensic tools parse SuperFetch data. _Why:_ analysts may need specialized research or manual methods if SuperFetch artifacts become important. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **SuperFetch evidentiary overlap** — SuperFetch information is often redundant with Prefetch data. _Why:_ standard Prefetch analysis may already answer many execution-history questions without requiring SuperFetch parsing. _[GCFA p.~178]_

- **SuperFetch deeper-analysis reference** — the page cites `https://for508.com/wu15h` for additional information on parsing or understanding SuperFetch-related execution artifacts. _Why:_ this reference supports deeper analysis when standard Prefetch artifacts are insufficient. _[GCFA p.~178]_

## Page 179

### Prefetch Execution Timing

- **Prefetch first-execution inference** — an executable’s first known run time can be inferred from the creation time of its corresponding `.pf` file, adjusted backward by about 10 seconds. _Why:_ this gives investigators an approximate earliest observed execution time from filesystem metadata. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Prefetch last-execution inference** — an executable’s most recent run time can be inferred from the modification time of its corresponding `.pf` file, adjusted backward by about 10 seconds. _Why:_ this provides a quick way to estimate recent program execution without parsing the file internals first. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Embedded last-run timestamp** — a prefetch file also stores the last execution time inside the `.pf` content itself. _Why:_ embedded metadata can corroborate or refine filesystem timestamp interpretation. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Windows 8+ execution-history depth** — Windows 8 and later prefetch files can contain the eight most recent execution times. _Why:_ multiple embedded timestamps help reconstruct repeated program usage rather than only the latest run. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Filesystem timestamps as execution evidence** — prefetch file creation and modification timestamps can be used alongside embedded prefetch timestamps to estimate program first and last execution. _Why:_ this expands the available evidence when analyzing application execution. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **First execution wording caveat** — the safer interpretation is “first execution known from available prefetch evidence,” not necessarily the program’s true first execution ever. _Why:_ prefetch evidence is bounded and may not preserve older activity. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Windows 7 prefetch capacity** — Windows 7 is limited to 128 prefetch files. _Why:_ older execution evidence may disappear once the prefetch directory reaches its limit. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Windows 8+ prefetch capacity** — Windows 8 and newer systems can retain up to 1024 prefetch files. _Why:_ the larger limit improves retention but still does not guarantee complete execution history. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Prefetch aging behavior** — if an application has not run recently, its prefetch file can age out and be removed from the Prefetch folder. _Why:_ absence or recent creation of a `.pf` file may reflect retention behavior rather than true first use. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Recreated prefetch file behavior** — if a program runs again after its earlier prefetch file was deleted, Windows creates a new `.pf` file with a new creation timestamp. _Why:_ the new creation time can mislead analysts into thinking the program first ran later than it actually did. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Cross-artifact validation** — other application-execution artifacts should be used to corroborate prefetch-derived timing. _Why:_ multiple evidence sources help narrow the earliest known execution time despite incomplete prefetch retention. _[GCFA p.179]_

### Prefetch Timestamp Delay

- **Filesystem timestamp delay** — prefetch filesystem creation and modification times are typically written about 10 seconds after program execution begins. _Why:_ investigators must account for this delay when converting `.pf` filesystem timestamps into execution estimates. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Reason for the delay** — during the first roughly 10 seconds of execution, the prefetcher monitors what the program accesses and records that activity into the `.pf` file. _Why:_ this explains why the `.pf` file may not be created or updated immediately at process start. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Creation/update timing consequence** — the `.pf` file is created or modified after the monitoring interval rather than exactly at launch. _Why:_ raw filesystem times may be slightly later than the actual execution start. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Approximation warning** — the 10-second adjustment is approximate, not an exact rule. _Why:_ rigid timestamp math can introduce error when the observed delay differs from the typical value. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Shorter embedded-timestamp gap** — embedded prefetch timestamps may differ from filesystem timestamps by less than 10 seconds. _Why:_ smaller or faster-loading applications may complete relevant startup activity before the full approximate interval. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Adjustment scope** — subtracting about 10 seconds applies to prefetch filesystem timestamps, not to embedded execution timestamps parsed from inside the `.pf` file. _Why:_ embedded timestamps already represent execution timing and should not receive the same filesystem correction. _[GCFA p.179]_

### Execution Evidence Limits

- **Prefetch creation is not proof of successful execution** — the existence of a `.pf` file does not guarantee that the program completed or ran successfully. _Why:_ analysts should avoid overstating what prefetch proves. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Failed or broken program attempts can create prefetch files** — programs that attempt to execute but fail can still receive a `.pf` artifact. _Why:_ a prefetch hit may indicate an attempted launch rather than a functioning execution. _[GCFA p.179]_
- **Need for supporting execution artifacts** — other evidence of execution should be checked to validate the prefetch interpretation. _Why:_ corroboration helps distinguish successful execution from failed launch attempts or ambiguous prefetch activity. _[GCFA p.179]_

## Page 186

### Application Compatibility And ShimCache

- **Application Compatibility subsystem** — Windows evaluates launched programs to decide whether compatibility properties should be applied so the program can run on the current OS or under settings that mimic an older OS. _Why:_ this explains why the artifact exists and why application launches can create AppCompatCache evidence. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Shim definition** — A shim is a compatibility setting or property applied to a program so it can run as if it were on a different Windows version or environment. _Why:_ “ShimCache” is named from this compatibility mechanism. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **ShimCache common name** — AppCompatCache is often called ShimCache because it is tied to Windows compatibility shims. _Why:_ investigators and tools commonly refer to this artifact by either name. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Compatibility wizard user path** — Normal users can trigger compatibility behavior by running a program through the Windows compatibility wizard. _Why:_ ShimCache entries are not necessarily malicious; legitimate user activity can create them. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Built-in shim volume** — A default Windows installation includes hundreds of predefined compatibility shims. _Why:_ Windows has a broad compatibility database available before any investigation begins. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Compatibility database purpose** — Windows consults its compatibility data to determine whether a program should receive shim behavior. _Why:_ this decision process is what causes executables to be evaluated and recorded. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Programs checked even without shimming** — Executables are evaluated and added to AppCompatCache even when no compatibility shim is ultimately required. _Why:_ AppCompatCache can record program presence or launch-related evaluation without proving that a shim was applied. _[GCFA p.186]_

### Forensic Value

- **Tracked executable path** — AppCompatCache records the executable file path. _Why:_ full paths help identify where a program resided when Windows evaluated it. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Tracked executable modification time** — AppCompatCache records the executable’s last modification timestamp. _Why:_ comparing this stored value to the current filesystem timestamp can reveal later changes or manipulation. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Execution-oriented artifact use** — Investigators use AppCompatCache to support analysis of application execution. _Why:_ the artifact can connect program names, paths, and timestamps to activity on a host. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Executable name value** — AppCompatCache information can help identify the executable name. _Why:_ the name is a primary clue for determining what program may have run or been evaluated. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Full path value** — AppCompatCache information can include the full path to the executable. _Why:_ location context can distinguish benign copies, renamed tools, temporary directories, or attacker staging paths. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Last modification value** — AppCompatCache information can include the executable’s last modification time. _Why:_ this timestamp can be compared against filesystem metadata and other execution artifacts. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Reshim on content update** — Windows may create another AppCompatCache entry when an executable’s contents change. _Why:_ this can show that a file was updated after a prior compatibility evaluation. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Reshim on rename** — Windows may create another AppCompatCache entry when an executable is renamed. _Why:_ duplicate or changed entries can help prove renaming activity. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Moved executable indicator** — A mismatch between the current file metadata and the ShimCache stored modification time can support a conclusion that the executable was moved. _Why:_ moved files may carry metadata relationships inconsistent with the cached record. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Renamed executable indicator** — A mismatch between the current file’s modified time and the ShimCache modified time can support a conclusion that the executable was renamed. _Why:_ ShimCache may preserve a prior evaluation record after the filename changes. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Timestamp manipulation indicator** — If the file’s present Modified timestamp differs from the ShimCache Modified timestamp, timestamp tampering is a possible explanation. _Why:_ attackers may alter filesystem times, while ShimCache can retain an earlier observed value. _[GCFA p.186]_

### Registry Locations

- **Windows 7+ registry location** — On Windows 7 and later, AppCompatCache is stored at `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SessionManager\AppCompatCache\AppCompatCache`. _Why:_ this is the registry value investigators parse for modern Windows ShimCache data. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Windows 7+ registry key path** — The modern AppCompatCache key is `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SessionManager\AppCompatCache\`. _Why:_ this key contains the AppCompatCache value in the SYSTEM hive. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Windows XP registry location** — On Windows XP, AppCompatCache is stored under `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SessionManager\AppCompatibility\AppCompatCache`. _Why:_ XP uses a different registry path than later Windows versions. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **SYSTEM hive storage** — AppCompatCache resides in the Windows SYSTEM registry hive. _Why:_ investigators need the SYSTEM hive to extract this artifact offline. _[GCFA p.186]_

### Version-Specific Behavior

- **Windows XP entry count** — Windows XP stores 96 AppCompatCache entries. _Why:_ the smaller limit affects how much historical program activity may remain available. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Windows XP execution timestamp** — On Windows XP, the Last Execution Time is equivalent to the Last Update Time. _Why:_ XP provides stronger execution-time evidence than later versions. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Windows XP 32-bit extra fields** — Windows XP 32-bit AppCompatCache also tracked file size and last execution time. _Why:_ these fields can provide details unavailable in later AppCompatCache formats. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Windows 7+ entry count** — Windows 7 and later store 1,024 AppCompatCache entries. _Why:_ modern systems retain a larger cache than XP, but still have a finite history. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Windows 7 through Windows 11 entry count** — Windows 7, Windows 8, Windows 8.1, Windows 10, and Windows 11 use a 1,024-entry AppCompatCache limit. _Why:_ this identifies the expected cache capacity across client versions. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **Server version entry count** — Windows Server 2008, 2012, 2016, 2019, and 2022 use a 1,024-entry AppCompatCache limit. _Why:_ server investigations should expect the same stated modern cache size. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **InsertFlag meaning** — On Windows 7 and later, InsertFlag can suggest execution. _Why:_ this field may help triage execution likelihood. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **InsertFlag limitation** — InsertFlag is not conclusive proof of execution. _Why:_ investigators should not treat this field as definitive by itself. _[GCFA p.186]_

- **OS matrix · Win10/11 → Last Modified Date** — Windows 10 and 11 record the executable’s last modified date. _Why:_ this timestamp can expose movement, renaming, updating, or timestamp manipulation when compared to the current file. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **OS matrix · Win10/11 → File Size** — Windows 10 and 11 have no File Size field marked in the table. _Why:_ investigators should not rely on ShimCache for file size on these versions. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **OS matrix · Win10/11 → Last Execution Time** — Windows 10 and 11 have no Last Execution Time field marked in the table. _Why:_ modern ShimCache does not directly supply last execution time in the shown matrix. _[GCFA p.186]_
- **OS matrix · Win10/11 → Insert Flag** — Windows 10 and 11 include Insert Flag. _Why:_ this field may help assess execution likelihood but remains non-definitive. _[GCFA p.186]_

## Page 187

### AppCompatCache Entry Limits

- **AppCompatCache capacity · 96-entry limit** — the artifact can be capped at 96 stored entries on some Windows versions. _Why:_ investigators should understand that older activity may be absent because the cache has finite capacity, not necessarily because the program was never seen. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **AppCompatCache capacity · Windows Server 2003** — Windows Server 2003 can store as many as 512 AppCompatCache entries. _Why:_ expected artifact depth differs by operating system, affecting how much historical program evidence may remain. _[GCFA p.~187]_

### AppCompatCache Review Order And Write Timing

- **AppCompatCache ordering** — parsed AppCompatCache output places the newest observed items first. _Why:_ this ordering helps triage recent activity, especially on Windows versions where execution timestamps are not available. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Modern AppCompatCache timestamp limitation** — newer Windows versions do not include an execution time in AppCompatCache records. _Why:_ analysts must avoid treating cache order as an exact execution timeline. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **AppCompatCache write behavior · shutdown** — new cache entries are committed to the registry only when the system shuts down. _Why:_ offline registry analysis may miss applications observed since the last shutdown. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **AppCompatCache write behavior · reboot** — on Windows 10 and later, rebooting also causes AppCompatCache data to be written into the registry. _Why:_ reboot history affects whether recent application evidence is present in the SYSTEM hive. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Pre-shutdown AppCompatCache storage** — before shutdown or reboot, shimmed application information exists only in memory. _Why:_ live memory can contain AppCompatCache evidence that has not yet reached the registry. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Current SYSTEM hive limitation** — programs executed or identified after the most recent reboot may not appear in the current SYSTEM hive. _Why:_ absence from the hive is not reliable proof that an application was not run or observed. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Buffered AppCompatCache data** — pending AppCompatCache information is buffered in system memory before it is committed. _Why:_ memory acquisition may preserve artifact data that disk-only collection misses. _[GCFA p.~187]_

### Deleted Tools And Missing Prefetch

- **AppCompatCache as deleted-tool evidence** — AppCompatCache may preserve evidence of a program after an attacker deletes the tool itself. _Why:_ the cache can reveal tooling that no longer exists on disk. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **AppCompatCache after Prefetch deletion** — AppCompatCache can still provide evidence when matching Prefetch `.pf` files have also been removed. _Why:_ it may be one of the few remaining clues that a deleted executable existed. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Prefetch file extension** — Prefetch artifacts are identified with the `.pf` extension on this page. _Why:_ the page contrasts AppCompatCache with deleted Prefetch evidence. _[GCFA p.~187]_

### Re-Shimming And File Changes

- **Rewritten executable behavior** — if an application is written back to disk, it may be shimmed again. _Why:_ repeated AppCompatCache entries can reflect changes to the same tool rather than separate unrelated programs. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **PsExec example** — `psexec` is given as an example of software that may be rewritten to disk. _Why:_ this helps analysts interpret multiple AppCompatCache entries involving common remote-execution tooling. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Modified executable behavior** — when an executable is changed, Windows may create another AppCompatCache entry for it. _Why:_ multiple entries can indicate alteration of a tool after initial presence. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Renamed executable behavior** — renaming an application can cause it to be shimmed again and produce another AppCompatCache record. _Why:_ this can expose attempts to disguise a downloaded or staged tool. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Downloaded-file rename detection** — extra AppCompatCache entries can help determine whether a downloaded file was renamed on the host. _Why:_ rename evidence is useful for reconstructing attacker staging and evasion behavior. _[GCFA p.~187]_

### Modification Time Comparison

- **Stored AppCompatCache modification time** — AppCompatCache records include a last-modified time value for the application. _Why:_ this timestamp can be compared against the file system copy of the executable. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Timestamp manipulation check** — the AppCompatCache modification time can serve as a comparison point when assessing whether an executable’s timestamps were altered. _Why:_ mismatched values may reveal timestomping or other time-manipulation activity. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Modification-time mismatch implication** — if the AppCompatCache last-modified time differs from the executable’s current last-modified time, the executable’s timestamp was likely changed. _Why:_ this discrepancy is a practical indicator of possible anti-forensic activity. _[GCFA p.~187]_

### Execution Interpretation

- **Windows Vista execution limitation** — beginning with Windows Vista, simply finding an executable in AppCompatCache no longer proves that it ran. _Why:_ analysts must avoid overclaiming execution based solely on cache presence. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Pre-execution recording** — Windows can record executables in AppCompatCache before they are executed. _Why:_ the artifact may show exposure or discovery of a file rather than program launch. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **GUI folder browsing trigger** — testing indicated that viewing folders containing executables through Windows graphical tools can cause executables to be recorded. _Why:_ AppCompatCache entries may result from browsing activity rather than execution. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **File Explorer trigger example** — File Explorer is named as a Windows GUI application that may contribute to pre-execution AppCompatCache recording. _Why:_ analysts should consider ordinary folder viewing as a possible source of entries. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Downloaded executable visibility** — AppCompatCache can be useful when a user downloads an executable but does not run it. _Why:_ the cache may reveal potentially malicious files that Prefetch would not record. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Unzipped tool-folder visibility** — AppCompatCache can capture executables inside an extracted tool folder even if not every program is launched. _Why:_ this may expose the full contents of attacker tooling staged on disk. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Prefetch comparison** — Prefetch records only items that are explicitly executed. _Why:_ Prefetch is narrower than AppCompatCache for identifying unexecuted tools. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **AppCompatCache broader snapshot** — AppCompatCache may record every executable item in a viewed or staged location. _Why:_ it can provide a wider investigative picture than execution-only artifacts. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Attacker information leakage** — AppCompatCache can reveal files that an attacker may not expect investigators to see. _Why:_ the artifact may expose staged tools or renamed binaries even without direct execution evidence. _[GCFA p.~187]_

### InsertFlag

- **InsertFlag field** — AppCompatCache contains a data-structure value named `InsertFlag`. _Why:_ many tools expose this value, so analysts need to understand its limitations. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **InsertFlag introduction** — `InsertFlag` first appeared in Windows Vista. _Why:_ the field is not available across all Windows versions and must be interpreted by OS generation. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Original InsertFlag research finding** — earlier research found that when `InsertFlag` was not set, the application had not executed. _Why:_ this historical interpretation explains why tools may associate the field with execution. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Windows 10 AppCompatCache format change** — the AppCompatCache data structure changed in Windows 10. _Why:_ parsers must account for structural differences across versions. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Windows 11 AppCompatCache format change** — the AppCompatCache data structure also changed in Windows 11. _Why:_ Windows 11 cache parsing requires support for the newer format. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Eric Zimmerman parser support** — Eric Zimmerman rediscovered the newer AppCompatCache structure and added support for it to his parsing tool. _Why:_ this identifies a tool lineage capable of interpreting newer Windows cache formats. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Modern InsertFlag unreliability** — recent testing indicates that `InsertFlag` is not reliable for determining execution. _Why:_ investigators should not use the flag as a definitive execution indicator. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Prefetch contradiction case** — modern systems can show Prefetch evidence proving execution while AppCompatCache still has `InsertFlag` set to false. _Why:_ this directly demonstrates that a false flag does not rule out execution. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Tool labeling issue** — many tools label `InsertFlag` as `Execution`. _Why:_ parser labels can encourage overinterpretation unless the analyst understands the underlying artifact. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Recommended InsertFlag interpretation** — `InsertFlag` should be treated as a noteworthy data point, not conclusive proof for or against execution. _Why:_ this prevents false conclusions from an unreliable field. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Execution-method variability** — some application types or launch methods may update `InsertFlag` more consistently than others. _Why:_ execution context may affect artifact behavior, but the page says more research is required. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **InsertFlag research gap** — additional research is needed to determine when `InsertFlag` behaves reliably. _Why:_ current knowledge is insufficient for strong execution claims based on the field alone. _[GCFA p.~187]_

### SYSTEM Hive And Control Sets

- **Multiple AppCompatCache databases** — an examiner may need to review more than one AppCompatCache database. _Why:_ limiting analysis to one control set can miss historical data. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Control-set location** — each control set in the SYSTEM hive can contain its own AppCompatCache database. _Why:_ AppCompatCache review should account for all relevant SYSTEM control sets. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Historical control-set value** — different control sets may preserve additional historical AppCompatCache data depending on how Windows used them. _Why:_ inactive control sets can sometimes extend the investigator’s view of past application presence. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Running-system active key** — on a live system, the active and most current AppCompatCache data is under `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet`. _Why:_ this path identifies the live control set to examine for the newest cache state. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **CurrentControlSet volatility** — `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet` is a volatile key. _Why:_ offline hive analysis cannot assume this key exists or maps directly without resolving the active control set. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Offline current-control-set resolution** — when examining an offline SYSTEM hive, the current control set must be identified using the `Current` value. _Why:_ this determines which numbered control set corresponds to the live `CurrentControlSet`. _[GCFA p.~187]_
- **Select key path** — the `Current` value used to resolve the active control set is located in `SYSTEM\Select`. _Why:_ this registry path is required to map offline control sets correctly. _[GCFA p.~187]_
