## Page 190

### Amcache.hve Purpose

- **Amcache.hve** — a Windows Application Compatibility registry hive used as a broad execution-related artifact store. _Why:_ it can help reconstruct activity involving programs, drivers, and application inventory. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Amcache.hve Windows coverage** — the artifact exists on Windows 8 and later and was also backported to patched Windows 7 systems. _Why:_ analysts may encounter it on both newer systems and updated Windows 7 hosts. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Amcache.hve database scope** — the hive contains a large amount of system-related metadata, not only simple execution records. _Why:_ it supports broader forensic interpretation than a single-purpose run log. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **RecentFileCache.bcf replacement** — Amcache.hve superseded the older `RecentFileCache.bcf` execution artifact. _Why:_ analysts should look for Amcache rather than the older artifact on supported or patched systems. _[GCFA p.190]_

### Location

- **Amcache.hve path** — the hive is stored at `C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve`. _Why:_ this is the acquisition and parsing target for the artifact. _[GCFA p.190]_

### Tracked Entities

- **Installed applications** — Amcache records information about software installed on the system. _Why:_ installed-program inventory can provide context for legitimate and suspicious activity. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Executed programs** — Amcache can include records associated with programs that ran. _Why:_ it is commonly used during execution analysis. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Loaded drivers** — Amcache tracks driver-related information. _Why:_ driver records can expose kernel-level components, persistence, or malicious driver use. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Unassociated executables** — Amcache can track executables that are not tied to an installed application entry. _Why:_ standalone tools, attacker utilities, and dropped binaries may appear outside normal installation records. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Additional tracked activity** — Amcache covers more than installed applications, executed programs, and drivers. _Why:_ investigators should not treat the artifact as a narrow execution-only source. _[GCFA p.190]_

### Captured Metadata

- **Full path** — Amcache can store the complete filesystem path for executables and drivers. _Why:_ paths help identify where a binary lived and whether it ran from suspicious locations. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **File size** — Amcache records file size. _Why:_ size helps correlate records to files and matters because hashing has a size limit. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **File modification time** — Amcache can include the file’s modification timestamp. _Why:_ modification time helps compare filesystem state, compilation history, and potential timestomping. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Compilation time** — Amcache can include compile-time metadata. _Why:_ compile times can support malware clustering, tool attribution, or timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Publisher metadata** — Amcache stores publisher information for executables. _Why:_ publisher data helps separate signed vendor binaries from suspicious or masquerading files. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Driver publisher metadata** — Amcache can store publisher information for loaded drivers. _Why:_ driver publisher data is useful when validating kernel components and detecting rogue drivers. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Multiple timestamps** — Amcache contains several timestamp fields. _Why:_ timestamp variety can support timeline construction, but analysts must know which field means what in the relevant format version. _[GCFA p.190]_

### SHA1 Hashing

- **Executable SHA1 hashes** — Amcache can store SHA1 hashes for executable files. _Why:_ hashes allow reliable identification even when filenames are changed. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Driver SHA1 hashes** — Amcache can store SHA1 hashes for driver files. _Why:_ driver hashes help identify known legitimate or malicious kernel components. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Hash rarity** — built-in forensic artifacts rarely include executable or driver hashes. _Why:_ Amcache is unusually valuable because it provides a direct content identifier. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Known-good identification** — Amcache SHA1 values can help recognize legitimate files such as Microsoft binaries. _Why:_ known-good matching reduces investigative noise. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Known-bad identification** — Amcache SHA1 values can help identify malicious tools even after renaming, such as a renamed `mimikatz.exe`. _Why:_ hash-based identification defeats simple filename masquerading. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **SHA1 size threshold** — Amcache SHA1 values are valid only for files smaller than `31,457,280` bytes. _Why:_ files at or above this size may lack a usable Amcache hash. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Approximate SHA1 threshold** — the hash limit is about `31.4 MB`. _Why:_ analysts can quickly estimate whether a missing or invalid hash may be size-related. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Likely hashing rationale** — Microsoft likely imposed the hash limit to avoid spending resources hashing very large files. _Why:_ this explains why large binaries may be treated differently. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Most executables under limit** — the page notes that most executables are expected to fall below roughly 31 MB. _Why:_ Amcache hashes should be available for many ordinary program files. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Installer package exception** — software installers may exceed the Amcache hashing size limit. _Why:_ large installers may not yield valid SHA1 values in the artifact. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Malware size exception** — some malware can exceed the Amcache hashing threshold. _Why:_ lack of an Amcache hash does not rule out maliciousness. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Malware size inflation trend** — some malware has grown larger to exploit security-product file-size analysis limits. _Why:_ unusually large malicious binaries may be designed to evade automated inspection. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Large-file tradeoff** — oversized executables may evade some automated limits but can also attract analyst attention. _Why:_ abnormal size can itself become an investigative clue. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **File size captured with hash context** — Amcache records file size in addition to any available SHA1. _Why:_ analysts can evaluate whether the SHA1 limit may apply to a specific record. _[GCFA p.190]_

### Versioning And Format Behavior

- **Frequent schema changes** — Microsoft has substantially changed the Amcache database format at least four times since its introduction. _Why:_ parsers and field interpretations may differ by system patch level. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Windows 8 first-execution field** — earlier Windows 8-era Amcache data included first-execution time information. _Why:_ older Amcache formats may contain evidence no longer present in newer formats. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **First-execution removal** — the first-execution time field is no longer available in the current format described by the page. _Why:_ analysts should not expect that field on modern systems. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Blanche Lagny finding** — Blanche Lagny determined that Amcache format depends on DLL version rather than the nominal Windows version. _Why:_ OS name alone is insufficient for choosing the correct parser or schema interpretation. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **DLL-version dependency** — the Amcache structure is governed by the relevant DLL version. _Why:_ patch state can change artifact structure independently of the Windows release label. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Patch-level dependency** — the format encountered during analysis is largely determined by the system’s patch level. _Why:_ investigators must account for updates when interpreting Amcache fields. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Version examples** — Windows 7 and Windows 10 are examples where OS version alone does not determine the Amcache structure. _Why:_ two systems with recognizable OS labels may still use different artifact formats. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Course coverage scope** — the course page states it covers the most current Amcache database version. _Why:_ older systems may not match the structure being taught on this page. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Older-patch warning** — systems on older patch levels may show data structures that differ greatly from the current version. _Why:_ analysts should verify format before relying on field meanings. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Blanche Lagny research value** — Lagny’s research document is identified as the key reference for both older and newer Amcache versions. _Why:_ it is the recommended source when working with non-current Amcache formats. _[GCFA p.190]_

### Interpretation Limits

- **Program-execution grouping** — Amcache is traditionally categorized as a program-execution artifact. _Why:_ this explains why it is commonly consulted during execution timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Not execution-only evidence** — Amcache records do not always prove a program executed. _Why:_ analysts must avoid overstating execution based solely on presence in the hive. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Automated discovery entries** — Amcache entries may be created through automated file discovery. _Why:_ passive discovery can create records without user or attacker execution. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Installation-created entries** — software installation activity can also create Amcache entries. _Why:_ an entry may reflect installation inventory rather than a run event. _[GCFA p.190]_
- **Execution caveat** — Amcache entries can be caused by mechanisms other than execution. _Why:_ corroboration with other artifacts is required before making a firm execution claim. _[GCFA p.190]_

## Page 191

### Amcache Interpretation

- **Amcache inclusion** — a file appearing in Amcache should not be treated by itself as proof that the file ran. _Why:_ investigators need to avoid overstating execution evidence from this artifact. _[GCFA p.191]_

- **Amcache tracked-file categories** — Blanche Lagny identified three broad groups of files recorded by the newer Amcache format. _Why:_ the category a file belongs to changes how strongly the entry can be interpreted. _[GCFA p.191]_

### Amcache Tracked File Categories

- **Tracked category 1 · Executed GUI applications** — Amcache may record GUI programs that were run and received application-compatibility shims. _Why:_ this is the only listed category that directly relates to execution. _[GCFA p.191]_

- **Tracked category 1 · Shim requirement** — the execution-related category is limited to GUI applications that required compatibility shimming. _Why:_ Amcache execution-related coverage is narrower than “all executed programs.” _[GCFA p.191]_

- **Tracked category 2 · Copied executables** — Amcache may record executable files copied during application execution. _Why:_ a recorded executable may have been copied as a side effect rather than launched. _[GCFA p.191]_

- **Tracked category 2 · Copied drivers** — Amcache may record driver files copied during application execution. _Why:_ driver presence in Amcache can reflect installation or copy activity rather than driver execution. _[GCFA p.191]_

- **Tracked category 3 · Compatibility Appraiser scan hits** — Amcache may record executables located in directories scanned by the Microsoft Compatibility Appraiser scheduled task. _Why:_ scheduled inventory activity can create Amcache entries unrelated to program launch. _[GCFA p.191]_

- **Compatibility Appraiser scanned directory · Program Files** — one directory named for Compatibility Appraiser scanning is `Program Files`. _Why:_ executables in this location may be inventoried without being executed. _[GCFA p.191]_

- **Compatibility Appraiser scanned directory · Program Files x86** — one directory named for Compatibility Appraiser scanning is `Program Files x86`. _Why:_ executables in this location may appear in Amcache because of scanning. _[GCFA p.191]_

- **Compatibility Appraiser scanned directory · Desktop** — one directory named for Compatibility Appraiser scanning is `Desktop`. _Why:_ executables on a user desktop may be recorded due to scheduled scanning rather than launch. _[GCFA p.191]_

### Execution-Evidence Limits

- **Execution relevance limited to first category** — among the three listed categories, only shimmed GUI applications are tied to execution. _Why:_ the other two categories describe copy or inventory activity, not program launch. _[GCFA p.191]_

- **Small execution-related subset** — shimmed GUI executions represent only a small portion of the files Amcache can track. _Why:_ most Amcache entries may need interpretation as presence or metadata evidence instead of execution evidence. _[GCFA p.191]_

- **Category separation by elimination** — distinguishing the execution-related entries can require ruling out the copy-related and Compatibility Appraiser inventory categories. _Why:_ Amcache does not make execution interpretation straightforward for every entry. _[GCFA p.191]_

- **Recommended Amcache use** — the artifact is recommended primarily as evidence that executables or drivers existed on the system. _Why:_ presence evidence is more defensible than claiming execution from Amcache alone. _[GCFA p.191]_

- **Amcache metadata value** — Amcache is useful because it records metadata about each tracked file. _Why:_ file metadata can support identification, correlation, and timeline analysis even without proving execution. _[GCFA p.191]_

- **Prefetch as execution corroboration** — Prefetch is named as an artifact that can be used to demonstrate program execution and execution timing. _Why:_ stronger execution proof should come from artifacts designed to record launches. _[GCFA p.191]_

## Page 192

### Amcache.hve Purpose

- **Amcache.hve review focus** — this page uses Amcache.hve to evaluate whether executables existed on a Windows system. _Why:_ Amcache is useful for presence-based executable inventory during forensic triage. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **Executable presence, not guaranteed execution** — entries in the shown Amcache areas should be interpreted as evidence that an executable was on the system, not as definitive proof that it ran. _Why:_ overclaiming execution from Amcache can produce incorrect forensic conclusions. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **Modern Amcache last-write limitation** — on newer Amcache formats, registry key last-write timestamps usually do not represent program execution time. _Why:_ investigators should avoid treating these timestamps as run times. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **Windows 8-era contrast** — older Windows 8-era Amcache behavior differed from the modern behavior discussed here. _Why:_ Amcache interpretation depends on database generation and Windows version era. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **Compatibility Appraiser timing source** — modern Amcache key last-write times are generally tied to when the Microsoft Compatibility Appraiser scheduled task inserted data into the database. _Why:_ this explains why last-write timestamps often cluster around inventory/update activity rather than user execution. _[GCFA p.192]_

### InventoryApplicationFile Key

- **InventoryApplicationFile as starting point** — the InventoryApplicationFile key is recommended as an initial review location when analyzing Amcache. _Why:_ it gives a direct path into executable-oriented records. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **InventoryApplicationFile subkey naming** — InventoryApplicationFile contains subkeys named for applications or executables. _Why:_ these names let an examiner quickly spot binaries worth investigating. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **Executable-name duplicates** — the same executable filename may appear in more than one InventoryApplicationFile subkey. _Why:_ duplicate names can represent separate copies in different directories. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **Path-related suffix hash** — the hash-like string appended after each executable name has not been reverse engineered. _Why:_ analysts should not assume they can decode that suffix into a path or other field. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **Suffix likely path-derived** — the unknown suffix appears to relate to the executable’s full path. _Why:_ this helps explain why identical filenames can have different subkey names. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **Per-key values as enrichment** — once an interesting InventoryApplicationFile entry is found, its registry values provide supporting metadata. _Why:_ these fields can supply hash, path, size, version, publisher, and compile-time context. _[GCFA p.192]_

### InventoryApplication Key

- **InventoryApplication purpose** — InventoryApplication records installed applications within the Amcache hive. _Why:_ it can provide application-level context beyond a single executable file record. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **InventoryApplication subset limitation** — InventoryApplication only covers part of what InventoryApplicationFile tracks. _Why:_ a missing InventoryApplication match does not mean the executable was absent from InventoryApplicationFile. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **InventoryApplication enrichment** — matching InventoryApplication entries can include installation date and more detailed publisher information. _Why:_ these fields help establish application provenance and installation context. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **Installation-date granularity** — InventoryApplication installation dates have one-day precision. _Why:_ analysts should not infer a more exact install time from that field. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **ProgramId linkage** — InventoryApplicationFile and InventoryApplication records are associated through the ProgramId value. _Why:_ ProgramId is the join field for correlating executable-file metadata to application metadata. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **InventoryApplication entry names** — entries under InventoryApplication are named using ProgramId values. _Why:_ this makes the cross-reference from an InventoryApplicationFile record straightforward. _[GCFA p.192]_

### Field Interpretation

- **FileId meaning** — the FileId value contains the SHA1 hash associated with the executable, except that the leading four zero characters are not part of the actual SHA1. _Why:_ analysts must remove the Amcache prefix before treating the value as the SHA1 indicator. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **Displayed FileId hash material** — the shown FileId is `0000fa68db2187b6987910942bb0dd3778d5ede0f9db`. _Why:_ this is the page’s concrete example of the Amcache SHA1-bearing field. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **Derived SHA1 from FileId** — removing the leading `0000` from the displayed FileId yields `fa68db2187b6987910942bb0dd3778d5ede0f9db`. _Why:_ this is the hash value an analyst would use for indicator matching. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **LowerCaseLongPath meaning** — LowerCaseLongPath stores the executable’s full path in lowercase form. _Why:_ full path context distinguishes same-name executables in different locations. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **Size meaning** — the Size value stores the file size. _Why:_ file size helps identify, compare, and validate a binary. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **LinkDate meaning** — LinkDate stores the PE header compilation or link timestamp. _Why:_ compile time is commonly used in malware indicators and clustering. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **ProgramId meaning** — ProgramId is the value used to cross-reference InventoryApplicationFile with InventoryApplication. _Why:_ it connects file-level evidence to installed-application metadata. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **Full-path callout** — the page explicitly labels LowerCaseLongPath-style data as the full path. _Why:_ path evidence is central to determining where an executable resided. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **SHA1 callout** — the page explicitly identifies the FileId-derived data as the executable’s SHA1 hash. _Why:_ SHA1 enables reputation checks, IOC matching, and cross-case comparison. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **PE-header callout** — the page explicitly identifies LinkDate as PE-header compilation time. _Why:_ this timestamp can support malware family analysis or build-time assessment. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **Application cross-reference callout** — the page instructs analysts to cross-reference InventoryApplication for additional information. _Why:_ InventoryApplication can add context that is absent from the file-level record. _[GCFA p.192]_
- **File-size callout** — the page explicitly identifies Size as file size. _Why:_ size is a simple but useful binary-identification attribute. _[GCFA p.192]_

## Page 194

### Amcache Driver-Auditing Context

- **Amcache.hve driver auditing** — this page focuses on using Amcache.hve to review driver-related evidence. _Why:_ driver artifacts can expose kernel-level components relevant to incident response. _[GCFA p.194]_
- **Loaded drivers in advanced-malware cases** — drivers are high-value evidence when a host may contain sophisticated malware. _Why:_ kernel drivers can enable deep persistence, concealment, and defensive bypass. _[GCFA p.194]_
- **Driver abuse by rootkits** — rootkits commonly make use of drivers. _Why:_ driver-level code can hide files, processes, or activity from normal user-mode visibility. _[GCFA p.194]_
- **Driver abuse by bootkits** — bootkits may rely on driver-style components. _Why:_ boot-level or kernel-level components can survive early in the startup chain and complicate remediation. _[GCFA p.194]_
- **Driver abuse for security-tool evasion** — real-world evasion capabilities may use drivers. _Why:_ kernel-mode control can interfere with monitoring, collection, or protection tools. _[GCFA p.194]_
- **InventoryDriverBinary key** — Amcache.hve’s `InventoryDriverBinary` area records useful information about drivers observed on the system. _Why:_ it gives investigators a structured source for driver inventory and triage. _[GCFA p.194]_
- **One driver per subkey** — driver information is organized so that each driver has its own subkey. _Why:_ per-driver records support item-by-item review and anomaly hunting. _[GCFA p.194]_
- **Known-good and known-bad hash comparison** — driver records can be checked against trusted or malicious hash sets. _Why:_ hash reputation can quickly separate routine drivers from suspicious ones. _[GCFA p.194]_
- **Driver modification time comparison** — a driver’s modification time can be compared with suspicious activity windows. _Why:_ temporal overlap can strengthen or weaken a hypothesis about compromise timing. _[GCFA p.194]_
- **Driver signing as an analytic field** — whether a driver is signed is a useful anomaly-hunting attribute. _Why:_ unsigned or unexpectedly signed drivers can warrant deeper inspection. _[GCFA p.194]_
- **64-bit Windows driver signing expectation** — on 64-bit systems, drivers are expected to be signed. _Why:_ a missing signature on such systems is a strong triage signal. _[GCFA p.194]_
- **PE-header metadata review** — metadata stored in the driver’s PE header can be used during review. _Why:_ missing or inconsistent publisher, product, or version data can indicate suspicious or unusual binaries. _[GCFA p.194]_

### Command-Line Options

- **`b` option** — option `b` accepts a file containing SHA-1 hashes to include in results. _Why:_ this supports hash-based allowlisting when an investigation needs to focus on known files. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`b` option precedence note** — the output states that blocklisting takes priority over allowlisting. _Why:_ if a hash appears in both include and exclude inputs, exclusion controls the final result set. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`f` option** — option `f` supplies the `Amcache.hve` file to parse. _Why:_ this is the required input that tells the parser which Amcache hive to process. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`f` option requirement** — the tool help marks `f` as required. _Why:_ parsing cannot proceed unless the target Amcache hive is provided. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`i` option** — option `i` includes file entries belonging to program entries. _Why:_ this changes output scope so program-associated files are included instead of omitted. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`w` option** — option `w` accepts a file containing SHA-1 hashes to exclude from results. _Why:_ this supports filtering known-benign or otherwise unwanted hashes from parser output. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`w` option precedence note** — the help text states that blocklisting overrides allowlisting. _Why:_ exclusion filters remain authoritative even when an item is also selected for inclusion. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`csv` option** — option `csv` specifies the directory where CSV results will be written. _Why:_ analysts need a defined output directory for downstream review and evidence handling. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`csv` option requirement** — the tool help marks `csv` as required. _Why:_ the parser requires an output destination for generated CSV files. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`csvf` option** — option `csvf` sets the CSV output filename. _Why:_ this allows a specific report filename instead of the default naming behavior. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`csvf` override behavior** — when `csvf` is present, it replaces the default CSV filename. _Why:_ this affects artifact naming and prevents confusion when scripting or batching output. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`dt` option** — option `dt` sets a custom timestamp display format. _Why:_ timestamp formatting affects consistency when correlating Amcache output with other forensic timelines. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`dt` documentation pointer** — the help text points to `https://goo.gl/CNVq0k` for date/time formatting options. _Why:_ analysts can use that reference to construct supported timestamp formats. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **Default `dt` format** — the default timestamp format is `yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss`. _Why:_ knowing the default prevents misreading parser output timestamps. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`mp` option** — option `mp`, when true, displays timestamps at higher precision. _Why:_ greater timestamp precision can matter during close event-ordering analysis. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **Default `mp` value** — `mp` defaults to `FALSE`. _Why:_ high-precision timestamps are not shown unless the analyst explicitly enables them. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`nl` option** — option `nl`, when true, ignores transaction log files for dirty hives. _Why:_ transaction logs can affect hive recovery and parsed completeness when a hive was not cleanly closed. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **Default `nl` value** — `nl` defaults to `FALSE`. _Why:_ by default, the parser does not ignore transaction logs for dirty hives. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`debug` option** — option `debug` displays debug-level processing information. _Why:_ debug output can help troubleshoot parser behavior or input problems. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **`trace` option** — option `trace` displays trace-level processing information. _Why:_ trace output provides more granular execution detail for troubleshooting. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **Short option syntax** — single-letter options use one leading dash. _Why:_ correct syntax is required for command-line parsing. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **Long option syntax** — long-form commands use two leading dashes. _Why:_ correct long-option syntax prevents command failures or ignored parameters. _[GCFA p.~196]_

### Default Extraction Behavior

- **Default file-entry scope** — by default, AmcacheParser does not extract file details for files tied to Program entries. _Why:_ default output may omit relevant file records unless the analyst changes the option set. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **Default unassociated output** — the default behavior provides only file entries that are not associated with Program entries. _Why:_ analysts may otherwise mistake default output for a complete Amcache file inventory. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **Program-associated inclusion method** — using the `-i` switch includes full information for Programs and their related files. _Why:_ this switch is required when an investigation needs the broader Program-linked file dataset. _[GCFA p.~196]_

- **Last modified date field** — AmcacheParser can extract last-modified timestamps. _Why:_ modification time contributes to timeline construction and file-history analysis. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **Compilation time field** — AmcacheParser can extract compilation timestamps. _Why:_ compile time can help cluster binaries, identify build periods, and spot anomalous timestamp patterns. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **Language ID field** — AmcacheParser can extract language ID values. _Why:_ language metadata can support software identification and anomaly detection. _[GCFA p.~196]_

### Hash Filtering Across Systems

- **SHA-1 allowlisting support** — AmcacheParser can use SHA-1 values to include selected files. _Why:_ this is useful when searching many systems for specific known hashes. _[GCFA p.~196]_
- **SHA-1 blocklisting support** — AmcacheParser can use SHA-1 values to exclude selected files. _Why:_ this helps remove known-benign or irrelevant files from large Amcache datasets. _[GCFA p.~196]_

### Output Naming and Key Mapping

- **Multiple CSV outputs** — AmcacheParser produces several `.csv` files from one Amcache hive. _Why:_ separating parsed data by artifact type makes review and filtering more practical. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **Microsoft Amcache schema growth** — newer Windows versions continue adding more information into `Amcache.hve`. _Why:_ parser coverage and analyst expectations must account for schema changes across operating-system versions. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **Parser key selection** — AmcacheParser focuses on extracting data from the Amcache keys considered most analytically useful. _Why:_ the tool prioritizes high-value forensic locations rather than treating every hive component equally. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **Output filename convention** — AmcacheParser output names usually resemble the original `Amcache.hve` key names. _Why:_ filename-to-key similarity helps analysts trace CSV records back to their registry source. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **Output filename exceptions** — some AmcacheParser output filenames do not exactly match the corresponding Amcache key name. _Why:_ analysts should not assume every CSV name maps literally to a same-named hive key. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **ProgramEntries source key** — `Amcache_ProgramEntries` is populated from the `InventoryApplication` key. _Why:_ knowing this mapping prevents misattribution of installed-application data during analysis. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **ProgramEntries naming mismatch cause** — the `Amcache_ProgramEntries` name differs because older Amcache versions used a different name for the relevant application-inventory key. _Why:_ backward compatibility in parser naming can obscure the modern source key. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **ProgramEntries content** — `Amcache_ProgramEntries` contains metadata about installed applications. _Why:_ installed-application metadata supports software inventory, legitimacy checks, and timeline context. _[GCFA p.197]_

### InventoryApplicationFile Handling

- **InventoryApplicationFile split output** — data from `InventoryApplicationFile` is divided into two AmcacheParser CSV outputs. _Why:_ separating associated and unassociated executable records improves triage. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **InventoryApplicationFile importance** — `InventoryApplicationFile` is presented as arguably the most important Amcache key. _Why:_ it contains high-value executable presence information for forensic investigation. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **Associated file category** — one `InventoryApplicationFile` output category contains items associated with installed software. _Why:_ association with installed software can help explain why an executable exists on the system. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **Unassociated file category** — the other `InventoryApplicationFile` output category contains items not tied to known installed software. _Why:_ lack of association can make a file more suspicious during anomaly hunting. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **Both file categories are useful** — both associated and unassociated `InventoryApplicationFile` outputs can contain valuable investigative information. _Why:_ legitimate and suspicious leads may exist in either category. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **Unassociated category priority** — unassociated file entries receive special attention when hunting unusual executables. _Why:_ suspicious tools often appear as standalone files rather than normal installed-program components. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **UnassociatedFileEntries content** — `UnassociatedFileEntries` records executables present on the system that may not belong to an installation package. _Why:_ executable presence outside installer context can indicate manual staging or attacker tooling. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **Unassociated-file investigative question** — if an executable is not associated with installed software, the analyst should determine how it arrived on the host. _Why:_ origin analysis helps distinguish legitimate portable utilities from attacker-dropped binaries. _[GCFA p.197]_

### Suspicious Standalone Executable Examples

- **Dropped wiping tools** — standalone wiping utilities are an example of binaries to look for in unassociated Amcache file entries. _Why:_ data-destruction tools may indicate anti-forensics or destructive activity. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **Dropped credential dumpers** — credential dumping utilities are an example of suspicious standalone binaries discoverable through unassociated entries. _Why:_ such tools indicate attempts to harvest authentication material. _[GCFA p.197]_

- **Dropped network scanners** — network scanning utilities are an example of standalone binaries to investigate in unassociated Amcache output. _Why:_ scanning tools can indicate reconnaissance or lateral-movement preparation. _[GCFA p.197]_

### Application Execution Analysis at Scale

- **Application-execution artifacts** — records showing which programs ran on a host are strong candidates for enterprise-wide comparison and frequency analysis. _Why:_ unusual execution patterns can expose attacker tooling across many systems. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Stacking application-execution data** — execution artifacts can be aggregated across hosts to identify rare, suspicious, or repeated program activity. _Why:_ stacking turns per-host forensic artifacts into scalable intrusion-triage evidence. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Small execution-artifact databases** — the data stores used for many execution artifacts are generally compact. _Why:_ small artifact sources are practical to collect from many endpoints during incident response. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Ease of collection** — application-execution databases are described as straightforward to acquire. _Why:_ low collection friction makes broad enterprise triage feasible during an active investigation. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Normalization suitability** — execution-artifact databases can be converted into consistent analytical formats without major difficulty. _Why:_ normalized data supports searching, stacking, and comparison across many systems. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Enterprise-wide searching** — investigators should query application-execution artifacts across the environment rather than only on one host. _Why:_ attacker tools and staging patterns often repeat across compromised systems. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Running software as usage evidence** — programs observed as executed on a system help explain how that system was being used. _Why:_ execution evidence links host activity to user behavior, administrative activity, or intrusion activity. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Execution artifacts in intrusion cases** — application-execution evidence is especially valuable when investigating compromises. _Why:_ tool execution can reveal attacker objectives and operational phases. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Reconnaissance inference** — specific executed tools can indicate discovery or enumeration activity. _Why:_ recognizing reconnaissance tooling helps reconstruct attacker progression. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Credential-dumping inference** — some executed programs can point to credential theft activity. _Why:_ credential access changes incident scope and containment priorities. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Lateral-movement inference** — execution of certain utilities can indicate movement between systems. _Why:_ lateral-movement evidence helps identify additional compromised hosts. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Scale requirement during intrusions** — execution artifacts must be gathered and reviewed broadly to be effective in intrusion response. _Why:_ single-system analysis can miss repeated attacker behavior elsewhere in the enterprise. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **ShimCache as triage data** — ShimCache has historically been used effectively for quick investigative screening. _Why:_ it can help rapidly surface executed or present programs relevant to compromise analysis. _[GCFA p.200]_

### Collection Methods

- **Initial collection challenge** — the first practical obstacle in execution-artifact analysis is obtaining the data. _Why:_ analysis cannot begin until artifact sources are collected from target systems. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Agent-based collection** — endpoint agents can be used to acquire application-execution artifacts. _Why:_ agents can support broad, repeatable collection across managed systems. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Script-based collection** — collection scripts are another method for gathering execution-artifact data. _Why:_ scripts provide a practical alternative where agent-based collection is unavailable or unsuitable. _[GCFA p.200]_

### Malware 101 Search Patterns

- **Short executable names** — one-character executable filenames are recommended as suspicious search targets. _Why:_ attackers often use abbreviated names that stand out from normal software naming patterns. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Two-character executable names** — two-letter executable filenames are also recommended for hunting. _Why:_ very short executable names can indicate hastily staged or intentionally obscure tooling. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Executions from temp locations** — programs launched from temporary directories are highlighted as suspicious. _Why:_ malware and attacker tools are commonly staged in writable temporary paths. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Executions from `$Recycle.Bin`** — executed files located under `$Recycle.Bin` are called out as a hunt target. _Why:_ adversaries may hide tools in recycle-bin paths to avoid casual inspection. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Executions from System Volume Information** — launches from `System Volume Information` are identified as unusual. _Why:_ execution from this protected-looking system folder can indicate attacker staging or concealment. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Known malware-name searching** — investigators should search execution artifacts for common malware names. _Why:_ simple name-based searches can quickly reveal known attacker tools. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **`pwdump` search term** — `pwdump` is given as an example malware or attacker-tool name to search for. _Why:_ finding this name can indicate password-hash dumping activity. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **`mimikatz` search term** — `mimikatz` is given as another known tool name to search for. _Why:_ execution evidence for this tool can indicate credential theft or credential abuse activity. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Rare built-in tools** — built-in utilities may still be suspicious when they are uncommon in a particular network segment or host population. _Why:_ rarity within the environment can make otherwise legitimate binaries useful detection leads. _[GCFA p.200]_

### Indicators of Compromise

- **Known-malware IOCs** — known malicious filenames or identifiers should be searched across collected execution artifacts. _Why:_ matching known malware indicators can quickly identify affected systems. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Known-tool IOCs** — known attacker-tool names should be searched across the enterprise. _Why:_ repeated tool execution can map the spread of attacker operations. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Staging-directory IOCs** — known attacker staging folders should be used as search indicators. _Why:_ repeated staging paths can reveal systems touched by the same intrusion workflow. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Attacker file knowledge** — once a specific attacker-used file is known, it becomes a high-value search indicator. _Why:_ the same file may appear on other compromised systems. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Attacker folder knowledge** — once a specific attacker-used directory is known, it can be searched across execution artifacts. _Why:_ shared folder patterns can expose additional hosts with similar compromise characteristics. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **IOC-driven system identification** — known malicious files, tools, and folders can identify systems showing the same attack traits. _Why:_ IOC searches help expand incident scope beyond the originally discovered machine. _[GCFA p.200]_

- **Execution-analysis scaling** — the page frames appcompatprocessor.py as a way to scale execution artifact analysis beyond manual review. _Why:_ large incident-response datasets often make manual ShimCache and Amcache review impractical. _[GCFA p.~201]_
- **Automated incident-response workflow** — appcompatprocessor.py is described as automating work that would otherwise consume significant analyst time. _Why:_ automation reduces triage time during active investigations. _[GCFA p.~201]_
- **Advanced analytics** — appcompatprocessor.py’s value comes from analytic capabilities applied after ingestion, not only from parsing artifacts. _Why:_ analytics help surface suspicious execution patterns in large collections of records. _[GCFA p.~201]_

- **SQL enrichment** — the tool supports easy stacking and enrichment through the SQL database. _Why:_ enrichment lets analysts add context and compare execution artifacts across hosts or files. _[GCFA p.~201]_

## Page 210

### Windows Event Log Locations

- **NT-family event logs through Windows Server 2003** — Windows NT, Windows 2000, Windows XP, and Windows Server 2003 use the older `.evt` event log file format. _Why:_ the file extension quickly identifies the legacy event log format expected on these systems. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Legacy event log directory** — On NT, Windows 2000, Windows XP, and Windows Server 2003, the default event log storage path is `%systemroot%\System32\config`. _Why:_ this is the primary default directory to collect pre-Vista event logs from. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Legacy Security log filename** — On the listed pre-Vista systems, the Security event log is shown as `SecEvent.evt`. _Why:_ filename-level knowledge helps locate security audit records during triage or collection. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Legacy Application log filename** — On the listed pre-Vista systems, the Application event log is shown as `AppEvent.evt`. _Why:_ this identifies the default application event log file to collect on older Windows systems. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Legacy System log filename** — On the listed pre-Vista systems, the System event log is shown as `SysEvent.evt`. _Why:_ system-level operational events may be recovered from this legacy log file. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Pre-Vista event log default path repeated in text** — Event logs from Windows versions before Vista are located by default at `%systemroot%\System32\config`. _Why:_ the repeated path reinforces the key acquisition location for older Windows hosts. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Vista-and-newer event logs** — Windows Vista, Windows 7, Windows 8, Windows 10, and Windows 11 use the newer `.evtx` event log format. _Why:_ the extension distinguishes modern event logs from legacy `.evt` files. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Modern event log directory** — On Vista, Windows 7, Windows 8, Windows 10, and Windows 11, the default event log storage path is `%systemroot%\System32\winevt\Logs`. _Why:_ this is the default collection location for modern Windows event logs. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Modern Security log filename** — Modern Windows systems use `Security.evtx` as a shown example of a Security event log filename. _Why:_ this is a key audit log commonly needed for authentication and authorization analysis. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Modern Application log filename** — Modern Windows systems use `Application.evtx` as a shown example of an Application event log filename. _Why:_ application-level execution and service events may appear in this file. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Modern System log filename** — Modern Windows systems use `System.evtx` as a shown example of a System event log filename. _Why:_ system service, driver, boot, and operational events may be found there. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Additional modern log filenames** — The page indicates that `Security.evtx`, `Application.evtx`, and `System.evtx` are examples among other `.evtx` logs. _Why:_ analysts should not limit collection to only the three classic logs on modern Windows. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Remote event log server support** — Vista-and-newer event logging can use a remote log server. _Why:_ relevant evidence may exist outside the endpoint being examined. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **External log collectors** — The newer event log format supports sending logs to a remote collector. _Why:_ remote log aggregation can preserve events that are absent, overwritten, or tampered with on the source host. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **External-server evidence possibility** — Analysts should remember that additional event logs may be available on external servers. _Why:_ endpoint-only collection may miss centrally stored evidence. _[GCFA p.210]_

### Event Log History and Format Behavior

- **Windows event log origin** — Windows event logs in their current lineage began with Windows NT 3.1 in 1993. _Why:_ this explains why older Windows log behavior follows long-standing NT design patterns. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Windows NT evolution** — Event logging received only modest updates across the Windows NT generation. _Why:_ artifact expectations remain relatively stable across older NT-line systems. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Stable legacy names and paths** — Event log names and storage locations mostly stayed the same through Windows Server 2003. _Why:_ this supports consistent collection procedures across pre-Vista systems. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Original event log extension** — The original Windows event log format used the `.evt` extension. _Why:_ `.evt` files indicate the older binary event log structure. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Binary event log storage** — Legacy event logs are stored in binary form. _Why:_ simple byte-string searching is harder against these logs than against plain text records. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Byte-level search limitation** — Because logs are binary, raw byte-level string searches are complicated. _Why:_ analysts generally need event log parsers rather than relying only on basic string extraction. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Circular buffer implementation** — Event logs use a circular buffer model. _Why:_ log capacity and retention behavior directly affect whether older events remain available. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Circular overwrite behavior** — The circular buffer eventually wraps and replaces the oldest events with newer ones. _Why:_ absence of old events may reflect normal log rollover rather than deliberate deletion. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Vista and Server 2008 transition** — Starting with Windows Vista and Windows Server 2008, Microsoft changed event log structures, log categories, and storage locations substantially. _Why:_ collection and parsing expectations differ sharply between pre-Vista and modern Windows logs. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Historic performance cost** — Event logging historically imposed significant performance overhead on Windows systems. _Why:_ performance concerns help explain the redesign of the event log format. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **EVTX design motivation** — The `.evtx` format was introduced to address performance problems and other limitations of older event logging. _Why:_ the newer format affects both availability and parser requirements for forensic analysis. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Modern log usage likelihood** — Because the newer event log format is optimized, modern systems are more likely to have event logs enabled and in use. _Why:_ investigators can often expect richer event log evidence on newer Windows versions. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Modern structure changes** — Vista-and-newer systems introduced major structural changes to event logs. _Why:_ tools and procedures designed for `.evt` logs may not apply to `.evtx` logs. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Modern log type expansion** — Vista-and-newer systems use many more event log types than older Windows systems. _Why:_ important evidence may reside in specialized logs beyond Security, Application, and System. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Modern log count** — Vista-and-newer systems can have more than 300 event logs. _Why:_ broad log collection may be necessary to avoid missing artifact-specific records. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **New folder for expanded logs** — Microsoft created a new event log directory to store the 300-plus logs on Vista-and-newer systems. _Why:_ the path change is tied to the expanded modern logging model. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Modern event log default path repeated in text** — Vista-and-newer logs are found by default at `%systemroot%\System32\winevt\logs`. _Why:_ this is the principal filesystem location for modern event log acquisition. _[GCFA p.210]_

### Registry-Configurable Log Locations

- **Default locations are not guaranteed** — The listed event log folders are default locations only. _Why:_ collection should account for administrator-configured log paths. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Registry controls custom log paths** — Administrators can configure individual event log locations through registry keys. _Why:_ investigators may need registry review to find nonstandard log storage locations. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Application log registry key** — The Application event log configuration key is `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\EventLog\Application`. _Why:_ this key may identify a customized Application log location. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **System log registry key** — The System event log configuration key is `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\EventLog\System`. _Why:_ this key may reveal where the System log is actually stored. _[GCFA p.210]_
- **Security log registry key** — The Security event log configuration key is `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\EventLog\Security`. _Why:_ this key may reveal a nondefault Security log path, which is critical for audit evidence collection. _[GCFA p.210]_

## Page 211

### Event Log Maximum-Size Handling

- **Log size limit behavior options** — Windows Event Viewer provides three configured behaviors for what happens after an event log reaches its maximum allowed size. _Why:_ the setting determines whether evidence is retained, overwritten, archived, or blocked until manual action. _[GCFA p.~211]_

- **Overwrite events as needed** — the default configuration allows older events in the log to be replaced once the log reaches its configured maximum size. _Why:_ default rollover can destroy older forensic evidence without requiring administrator action. _[GCFA p.~211]_

- **Overwrite events as needed · Default status** — the overwrite-as-needed option is identified as the default event log behavior. _Why:_ investigators should expect many systems to be configured for automatic event replacement unless changed. _[GCFA p.~211]_

- **Archive the log when full** — this option creates an archived copy when the active log reaches capacity and prevents overwriting of existing events. _Why:_ archived logs may preserve older evidence that would otherwise be overwritten. _[GCFA p.~211]_

- **Archive naming pattern** — archived Security logs are indicated by filenames using the pattern `Archive-Security-<Date>`. _Why:_ this filename pattern gives investigators a concrete artifact name to search for when looking for retained event history. _[GCFA p.~211]_

- **Archive storage risk** — if archived logs are not monitored, the archive process can consume all available drive space. _Why:_ log retention settings can create operational risk and may affect system behavior or availability. _[GCFA p.~211]_

- **Do not overwrite events** — this option stops event replacement when the log reaches its maximum size. _Why:_ it preserves existing events but can prevent newer activity from being recorded once the log is full. _[GCFA p.~211]_

- **Full-log error behavior** — under the no-overwrite setting, reaching the maximum log size causes error messages indicating that the event log is full. _Why:_ such errors can explain missing newer events and show that logging capacity was exhausted. _[GCFA p.~211]_

- **Manual clearing requirement** — with the no-overwrite setting, an administrator must manually clear the logs after they fill. _Why:_ manual clearing becomes a notable administrative action and may itself affect evidence preservation. _[GCFA p.~211]_

### Source Reference

- **Event Viewer reference** — the page cites an Event Viewer Wikipedia reference at `http://for508.com/1kf3q`. _Why:_ the citation identifies the external reference associated with the described event log behavior options. _[GCFA p.~211]_

- **Continued importance of primary logs** — Security, System, and Application logs remain important despite later expansion of Windows logging. _Why:_ newer logs supplement rather than replace the core investigative sources. _[GCFA p.212]_
- **Specialized log expansion** — Windows added additional logs over time for more focused logging needs. _Why:_ specialized logs can contain evidence absent from broad legacy logs. _[GCFA p.212]_

- **Server 2008 custom-log expansion** — Windows Server 2008 is identified as part of the expanded custom-log era. _Why:_ server investigations may include many specialized event channels. _[GCFA p.212]_

- **PowerShell specialized logging** — PowerShell is named as a process or subsystem with specialized logs. _Why:_ PowerShell activity is highly relevant to intrusion response and threat hunting. _[GCFA p.212]_
- **Task Scheduler specialized logging** — Task Scheduler is named as a process or subsystem with specialized logs. _Why:_ scheduled-task logs help detect persistence and automated execution. _[GCFA p.212]_

- **Windows 10 log count** — modern Windows 10 systems commonly contain more than 300 event logs. _Why:_ investigators must account for a large event-log surface rather than only the classic logs. _[GCFA p.212]_
- **Windows 11 log count** — modern Windows 11 systems commonly contain more than 300 event logs. _Why:_ triage methods must scale to hundreds of event channels. _[GCFA p.212]_
- **Windows 7 comparison** — the number of logs on modern Windows 10 and 11 systems is described as more than double the number found on Windows 7. _Why:_ expectations from older Windows versions understate the evidence available on current systems. _[GCFA p.212]_
- **Large log count challenge** — the page notes that reviewing the number of available logs can be intimidating. _Why:_ investigators need prioritization and filtering strategies for modern Windows event log review. _[GCFA p.212]_
- **Large log count benefit** — the page frames the expansion of logs as beneficial for forensic work. _Why:_ more event channels increase the chance that relevant activity survives somewhere on disk. _[GCFA p.212]_
- **Segmented data benefit** — specialized logs provide more segmented data. _Why:_ segmentation can make relevant events easier to isolate and interpret. _[GCFA p.212]_
- **Longer evidence retention benefit** — specialized logs can keep important information longer than a high-turnover general log. _Why:_ lower-volume channels may retain older events after busy logs have overwritten them. _[GCFA p.212]_
- **Security log turnover risk** — the Security log is specifically called out as vulnerable to rapid event turnover. _Why:_ heavy Security log volume can erase older evidence before collection. _[GCFA p.212]_
- **Unused log caveat** — many event logs on a typical system may contain little or no data. _Why:_ log existence alone does not prove the channel contains useful evidence. _[GCFA p.212]_
- **File-size triage technique** — sorting the event log folder by file size can quickly reveal which logs are unused or minimally used. _Why:_ file size helps prioritize event channels during triage. _[GCFA p.212]_

## Page 213

### Security Log Investigative Scope

- **Security log prominence** — The Windows Security log is commonly the primary event log examined in Windows forensic investigations. _Why:_ many core incident-response questions are answered from security-audit activity rather than troubleshooting logs. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Security log vs. System/Application logs** — The System and Application logs are characterized as more useful for administrator troubleshooting than for many forensic questions. _Why:_ this helps prioritize which Windows logs to review first during an investigation. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Audit-policy dependency** — The Security log records an event when a system or user action matches the active audit policy. _Why:_ absence of an event may reflect policy configuration rather than absence of activity. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **User authentication coverage** — The Security log can contain authentication-related activity. _Why:_ authentication records help reconstruct account access and possible compromise. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Logon coverage** — Logon activity is specifically listed as Security log content. _Why:_ logon records support timeline reconstruction and account-use analysis. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Runas coverage** — Use of the `runas` command is included among authentication-related activity that may be reflected in the Security log. _Why:_ `runas` can show alternate-credential use or privilege changes during an intrusion. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Remote access coverage** — Remote access activity is listed as an example of authentication-related Security log content. _Why:_ remote logons are often central to lateral-movement investigations. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Post-authentication behavior** — The Security log can help show what a user account did after authentication. _Why:_ this links account access to actions performed on the system. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **User actions** — User behavior and actions are explicitly identified as Security log review targets. _Why:_ these records help attribute system activity to accounts. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **File access auditing** — The Security log can include file-access audit events. _Why:_ file-access records can reveal interaction with sensitive or targeted data. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Folder access auditing** — Folder access is listed as Security log audit content. _Why:_ folder-level auditing can show access to protected directories even when individual file activity is incomplete. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Share access auditing** — Access to network or local shares is listed as Security log content. _Why:_ share-access records can identify data staging, lateral access, or unauthorized browsing. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Privilege-use auditing** — Privilege-use auditing can generate events tied to protected-resource activity. _Why:_ use of sensitive privileges may expose administrator-level actions during compromise. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Object auditing** — Object auditing can trigger Security log records when protected files or folders are accessed. _Why:_ object access events can provide evidence of interaction with specific protected resources. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Protected file/folder access evidence** — Security events may show that a protected file or folder was accessed. _Why:_ this can support findings about data exposure or unauthorized access. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Accessing account identification** — Object-access events may identify the user account that accessed a protected object. _Why:_ account attribution is critical for scoping and timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Access timestamp evidence** — Object-access events may include the date and time of protected-object access. _Why:_ timestamps allow investigators to align access with other host and network activity. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Security-setting auditing** — Security settings themselves can be audited. _Why:_ changes to audit or security policy can indicate attacker tampering or administrative changes affecting evidence quality. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Security-policy modification records** — The Security log can preserve records of changes to existing system security policies. _Why:_ policy-change events help identify weakened controls or attempts to reduce visibility. _[GCFA p.~213]_

### Success and Failure Auditing

- **Successful-attempt auditing** — Audit policy can be configured to log successful actions. _Why:_ successful activity can show real account use after compromise. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Failed-attempt auditing** — Audit policy can be configured to log failed actions. _Why:_ failed activity can expose guessing, probing, or denied access attempts. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Granular audit selection** — Success and failure auditing allow more precise control over what events are recorded. _Why:_ focused logging reduces noise while preserving events considered important by administrators. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Tailored data reduction** — Audit policy can limit recorded events to actions the organization considers useful. _Why:_ this explains why environments may intentionally lack broad audit coverage. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Comprehensive logging tradeoff** — Logging everything is desirable for forensics but can create performance and storage costs. _Why:_ investigators must account for operational constraints when judging missing logs. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Audit-policy review need** — Audit policy should be reviewed and validated. _Why:_ weak or misunderstood audit settings can leave important investigative gaps. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Successful logon value** — Successful logon auditing can help track use of a compromised account across an environment. _Why:_ this supports lateral-movement and account-abuse scoping. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Failed logon value** — Failed logon auditing can indicate password-guessing activity. _Why:_ repeated failures may reveal brute-force or credential-stuffing behavior. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Success-and-failure logon rationale** — Logging both successful and failed logon attempts may be necessary even if the reason is not obvious to non-security staff. _Why:_ the two outcomes answer different investigative questions. _[GCFA p.~213]_

### Per-Account Auditing

- **Account-specific audit tuning** — Auditing can be customized for an individual user account. _Why:_ investigators and administrators can increase visibility around accounts of special concern. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Group Policy audit control** — Group Policy can enable detailed auditing for specific accounts. _Why:_ this provides a managed way to focus audit collection without increasing logging for every user. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Suspected compromised account monitoring** — If a particular account is suspected of compromise, Group Policy can apply more detailed auditing to that account. _Why:_ targeted logging helps collect higher-value evidence during an active investigation. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Critical account monitoring** — Administrator and other critical accounts can receive more detailed auditing through Group Policy. _Why:_ privileged accounts have high investigative value and high attacker interest. _[GCFA p.~213]_

### Security Log Protections

- **Higher protection level** — The Security log has stronger protections than the System and Application logs. _Why:_ its contents are more sensitive and more directly tied to security enforcement and auditing. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **XP SP2 API change** — Beginning with Windows XP Service Pack 2, the ability for non-security applications to generate Security log events through the relevant API was deprecated. _Why:_ this reduced the ability of ordinary third-party software to write into the Security log. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Windows Security Service restriction** — After the XP SP2 change, Security log event generation was limited to the Windows security component rather than general applications. _Why:_ this strengthens trust in the provenance of Security log entries. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **LSASS write authority** — The Local Security Authority Subsystem Service, `LSASS`, is the only process identified as able to update the Security log. _Why:_ investigators can treat Security log insertion as controlled by the core Windows security subsystem. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Third-party insertion limitation** — Third-party applications cannot insert events into the Security log. _Why:_ this reduces the likelihood that arbitrary applications fabricated normal Security log entries through supported APIs. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **LSASS security-policy role** — `LSASS` has this Security log role because it enforces the system security policy. _Why:_ the log’s authority is tied to the subsystem responsible for security decisions. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Administrator review requirement** — Only accounts with administrator privileges can review the Security log. _Why:_ access to security-audit evidence is restricted to privileged users. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Administrator export requirement** — Only administrator-privileged accounts can export the Security log. _Why:_ exporting audit evidence requires elevated rights and may itself be relevant during investigation. _[GCFA p.~213]_
- **Administrator clear requirement** — Only administrator-privileged accounts can clear the Security log. _Why:_ log clearing is a high-value anti-forensic action and requires privileged access. _[GCFA p.~213]_

- **Account Logon category scope** — this category records account authentication activity. _Why:_ authentication records help identify credential use and failed or successful sign-in attempts. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Account Logon for domain accounts** — domain-account authentication events are recorded on the domain controller. _Why:_ investigators must check domain controllers for domain credential authentication evidence. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Account Logon for non-domain accounts** — local or non-domain account authentication is recorded on the local system. _Why:_ host-local account activity may not appear on a domain controller. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Account Mgmt category name** — the table lists “Account Mgmt” as a Windows Security event category. _Why:_ this category points investigators toward account-change activity. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Account Mgmt category scope** — this category records account upkeep and account-related changes. _Why:_ account creation, modification, or maintenance can reveal persistence or privilege changes. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Directory Service category name** — the table lists “Directory Service” as a Windows Security event category. _Why:_ this category isolates Active Directory object-access auditing. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Directory Service category scope** — this category records attempted access to Active Directory objects. _Why:_ AD object access can expose reconnaissance, privilege abuse, or directory tampering. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Logon Events category name** — the table lists “Logon Events” as a Windows Security event category. _Why:_ this category tracks interactive and other system access sessions. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Logon Events category scope** — this category records each logon and logoff instance on a system. _Why:_ session timing is central to reconstructing user or attacker activity. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Logon Events storage location** — logon/logoff events are stored on the system that made the authorization decision. _Why:_ investigators need to know which host should contain the relevant access record. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Object Access category name** — the table lists “Object Access” as a Windows Security event category. _Why:_ this category directs attention to audited resource access. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Object Access category scope** — this category records access to objects configured in a system access control list. _Why:_ it can show use of sensitive files, folders, registry keys, printers, or other protected resources. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Policy Change category name** — the table lists “Policy Change” as a Windows Security event category. _Why:_ policy modifications can indicate defense evasion or administrative misuse. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Policy Change category scope** — this category records changes to user rights, audit policy, or trust policy. _Why:_ these changes can alter privilege, visibility, or domain trust behavior. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Privilege Use category name** — the table lists “Privilege Use” as a Windows Security event category. _Why:_ this category highlights use of assigned user rights. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Privilege Use category scope** — this category records each instance where an account exercises a user right. _Why:_ privilege usage can reveal escalation, lateral movement, or sensitive administrative action. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Process Tracking category name** — the table lists “Process Tracking” as a Windows Security event category. _Why:_ this category supports process-level activity reconstruction. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Process Tracking category scope** — this category includes process starts, process exits, handle activity, object access, and related process details. _Why:_ process telemetry helps connect execution activity to users and timelines. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **System Events category name** — the table lists “System Events” as a Windows Security event category. _Why:_ this category identifies host-level security-relevant system activity. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **System Events category scope** — this category records system startup, system shutdown, and actions that affect the Security log. _Why:_ these events can show reboots, log disruption, or security-impacting state changes. _[GCFA p.215]_

### Audit Policy Behavior

- **Security event categories as triage aids** — Security event categories provide a fast way to locate event log records that may matter to an investigation. _Why:_ category filtering reduces noise during event log review. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Category source** — Security event categories are driven by the audit policies enabled on the Windows system. _Why:_ missing events may reflect configuration, not necessarily absence of activity. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **No Auditing setting** — each category can be configured with no auditing. _Why:_ disabled auditing means events from that category should not be expected in the logs. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Success auditing setting** — each category can be configured to record successful activity. _Why:_ success events show actions that completed and may confirm access or execution. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Failure auditing setting** — each category can be configured to record failed activity. _Why:_ failure events can reveal attempted access, probing, or blocked attacker actions. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Success and Failure auditing setting** — each category can be configured to record both successful and failed activity. _Why:_ collecting both outcomes gives a fuller picture of attempted and completed behavior. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Recorded event category marking** — when a Security event is generated and written to the log, the event is tagged with its matching category. _Why:_ the category tag enables targeted filtering and interpretation. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Disabled category expectation** — when auditing is turned off for a category, events of that category should not appear in the log. _Why:_ this prevents analysts from treating absent records as proof the activity did not occur. _[GCFA p.215]_

### Microsoft Audit Category Definitions

- **Audit account logon events** — this audit category records each attempt to authenticate an account. _Why:_ it captures authentication attempts that may indicate valid use, password guessing, or compromise. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Audit account logon events for domain accounts** — domain accounts are authenticated by a domain controller. _Why:_ domain authentication evidence must be sought on domain controllers. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Audit account logon events for local accounts** — local accounts are authenticated on local systems. _Why:_ local authentication evidence is host-specific. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Audit account management** — this audit category records account-management events on a computer. _Why:_ account administration events can reveal persistence or unauthorized account manipulation. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Account management example: password changes** — password changes are an example of account maintenance covered by account management auditing. _Why:_ password changes may show takeover, recovery, or attacker-controlled credential rotation. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Account management example: user accounts** — user-account maintenance is included in account management auditing. _Why:_ user-account changes can expose creation, deletion, or modification of identities. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Account management example: group modifications** — group changes are included in account management auditing. _Why:_ group membership changes can grant or remove privileges. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Audit directory service access** — this audit category records access to an Active Directory object when that object has its own SACL configured. _Why:_ it can expose access to specifically audited directory objects. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Directory service SACL requirement** — directory service access auditing depends on the Active Directory object having a system access control list specified. _Why:_ without the SACL, object access may not be logged. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Audit logon events** — this audit category records each time a user logs on to or logs off from a computer. _Why:_ it supports reconstruction of system access sessions. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Logon Events vs. Account Logon distinction** — logon events are separate from account logon events. _Why:_ confusing the two can send investigators to the wrong system or event type. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Logon Events authorization focus** — logon events track the decision to authorize access to a specific system. _Why:_ they identify access to a host, not merely credential validation. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Account Logon authentication focus** — account logon events track authentication activity. _Why:_ they identify credential verification activity, especially for domain accounts. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Audit object access** — this audit category records access to an object when that object has its own SACL configured. _Why:_ object access records can show interaction with sensitive resources. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Object access SACL requirement** — object access auditing requires the target object to have a system access control list specified. _Why:_ audit policy alone may not generate object-access records unless the object is configured for auditing. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Object access example: files** — files are examples of objects that can be audited through object access. _Why:_ file access may show data theft, staging, or tampering. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Object access example: folders** — folders are examples of objects that can be audited through object access. _Why:_ folder access can show browsing or interaction with sensitive directories. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Object access example: registry keys** — registry keys are examples of objects that can be audited through object access. _Why:_ registry access can reveal configuration changes, persistence, or reconnaissance. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Object access example: printers** — printers are examples of objects that can be audited through object access. _Why:_ printer access may matter in investigations involving lateral movement, data handling, or device misuse. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Audit policy change** — this audit category records changes to user-rights assignment policies, audit policies, or trust policies. _Why:_ attackers may modify these policies to gain access, reduce logging, or alter trust relationships. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Policy change target: user rights assignment** — changes to user-rights assignment policies are included in policy change auditing. _Why:_ these changes affect what privileged actions accounts can perform. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Policy change target: audit policies** — changes to audit policies are included in policy change auditing. _Why:_ audit-policy changes can increase or suppress forensic visibility. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Policy change target: trust policies** — changes to trust policies are included in policy change auditing. _Why:_ trust-policy changes can affect cross-domain or inter-system access. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Audit privilege use** — this audit category records each time a user exercises a user right. _Why:_ it can identify use of sensitive privileges during attacker or administrator activity. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Audit process tracking** — this audit category records detailed tracking information for process-related activity. _Why:_ process tracking helps reconstruct execution and process behavior. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Process tracking example: program activation** — program activation is included in process tracking auditing. _Why:_ it can identify when a program was launched. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Process tracking example: process exit** — process termination is included in process tracking auditing. _Why:_ exit events help bound execution duration. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Process tracking example: handle duplication** — handle duplication is included in process tracking auditing. _Why:_ handle activity can matter for process interaction and access analysis. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Process tracking example: indirect object access** — indirect object access is included in process tracking auditing. _Why:_ it can reveal object interactions mediated through process behavior. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **Audit system events** — this audit category records computer restarts and shutdowns by users. _Why:_ restart and shutdown events affect timelines and may indicate attacker cleanup or operational changes. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **System events affecting security** — system events also include events that affect system security. _Why:_ these records can indicate changes with security impact. _[GCFA p.215]_
- **System events affecting the Security log** — system events include events that affect the Security log itself. _Why:_ Security log impact can signal tampering, clearing, or logging disruption. _[GCFA p.215]_
