### Tracking Account Usage Scenario

- **Account logon attempts** — Investigators can use logon-event review to identify which accounts were used in attempted authentications. _Why:_ attempted account use can reveal credential attacks, misuse, or attacker movement. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Compromised-account tracking** — Logon events can be reviewed to follow usage of accounts already suspected or known to be compromised. _Why:_ successful authentication activity can show where an intruder used stolen credentials. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Account usage as a common event-log use case** — Reviewing event logs to determine account usage is a frequent investigative task. _Why:_ account activity is central to reconstructing user and attacker behavior. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Logon and logoff timing** — Knowing when an account logged on and later logged off can help reconstruct the duration of a user session. _Why:_ session timing provides corroboration with other forensic artifacts. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Logon data as corroboration** — Account logon and logoff records can support conclusions drawn from other forensic evidence. _Why:_ independent artifacts strengthen timelines and attribution hypotheses. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Network-wide successful-logon review** — When credentials may be compromised, successful logons across the network can be examined to identify systems the attacker accessed. _Why:_ stolen credentials often leave authentication traces during lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Remote-logon visibility** — Remote logons are recorded and can reveal useful information about how a user or attacker moves through the environment. _Why:_ remote authentication patterns help profile traversal and access attempts. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Authentication-to-resource profiling** — Remote logon records can show attempts to authenticate against network resources. _Why:_ these attempts help map the actor’s access path and target selection. _[GCFA p.~219]_

### Relevant Event IDs

- **Event ID 4624** — This event indicates a successful logon. _Why:_ it is a primary artifact for identifying successful account access. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Event ID 4625** — This event indicates a failed logon. _Why:_ failed authentication records can expose guessing, spraying, or misused credentials. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Event ID 4634** — This event indicates a successful logoff. _Why:_ it can help bound the end of a user session when recorded. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Event ID 4647** — This event indicates a user-initiated logoff. _Why:_ it is useful when standard logoff event recording is incomplete or unreliable. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Event IDs 4634/4647** — The slide groups these IDs as successful-logoff indicators. _Why:_ both can contribute to session-end analysis. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Event ID 4648** — This event records a logon performed with explicit credentials, such as RunAs. _Why:_ explicit credential use may reveal privilege changes or use of alternate accounts. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Event ID 4672** — This event records special privileges assigned to a new logon. _Why:_ it highlights administrator-equivalent or privileged account activity. _[GCFA p.~219]_

### Windows Version Context

- **Windows 2008 logon-event simplification** — Beginning with Windows 2008, account-usage event IDs were reduced to a smaller set of possibilities. _Why:_ analysts should expect newer Windows systems to use fewer logon-action IDs than older systems. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Windows XP logon-event volume** — Windows XP used 24 event IDs for logon-related actions. _Why:_ event ID expectations differ by operating-system generation. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Common successful-session pair** — Event IDs 4624 and 4634 commonly pair successful logon and successful logoff activity. _Why:_ the pair can define the beginning and end of a session. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Session-period inference** — The 4624/4634 event pair can indicate the elapsed period of a complete user session. _Why:_ session duration is useful in timeline analysis and activity correlation. _[GCFA p.~219]_

### Investigative Notes

- **Security log** — The relevant source for these logon-account investigations is the Windows Security log. _Why:_ these authentication and privilege events are recorded there when auditing is configured. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Unreliable 4634 logging** — Windows does not consistently record Event ID 4634 logoff events. _Why:_ absence of 4634 should not be treated as proof that no logoff occurred. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Use 4647 as a companion logoff signal** — Analysts should also search for Event ID 4647 when looking for logoff activity. _Why:_ it can fill gaps left by inconsistent 4634 recording. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **4647 interactive-logoff scope** — Event ID 4647 represents user-initiated logoff for interactive logons. _Why:_ it can help confirm a user-driven end to an interactive session. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **4647 remote-interactive relevance** — Event ID 4647 can also apply to remote interactive sessions. _Why:_ it helps analyze logoff behavior for remote desktop-style access. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Failed-logon review** — Event ID 4625 failures are commonly reviewed for password-guessing evidence. _Why:_ repeated failures can indicate brute force, spraying, or other credential attacks. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Explicit alternate credentials** — Event ID 4648 is generated when different explicit credentials are supplied. _Why:_ it can reveal use of alternate accounts during activity. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **RunAs example** — The RunAs command is an example of activity that can generate Event ID 4648. _Why:_ RunAs usage may show deliberate execution under another account context. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Administrator credential prompt example** — Running an application as administrator and entering administrator credentials can produce Event ID 4648. _Why:_ this records privilege-shifting behavior through explicit credential entry. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **4672 with standard logon event** — Event ID 4672 is recorded for administrator-equivalent logons in addition to the normal Event ID 4624. _Why:_ privileged sessions may have both a standard logon record and a privilege-assignment record. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Mixed audit dependency** — The event IDs listed on the page are generated by a combination of Success and Failure audit settings. _Why:_ missing either audit type can reduce visibility into account usage. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Audit-policy justification** — These event IDs support enabling both Success and Failure auditing in the Logon Events Audit Policy. _Why:_ both successful access and failed attempts are needed for complete account-usage analysis. _[GCFA p.~219]_

### Exploits And Logon Visibility

- **Backdoor access limitation** — Logon events are not recorded when access occurs through backdoors or similar unauthorized mechanisms. _Why:_ attackers may enter through channels that bypass normal authentication logging. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Remote exploit limitation** — Remote exploit access may leave no standard logon record in the event logs. _Why:_ exploit-driven access can avoid normal logon APIs. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Unauthorized access caveat** — Similar unauthorized access methods can result in no event-log logon entry. _Why:_ lack of logon events does not exclude compromise. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Remote code execution example** — Remote code execution is listed as an exploit class that may produce no normal logon event. _Why:_ code execution through exploitation may bypass standard access workflows. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Service exploitation example** — Service exploitation is another access path that may not create a logon record. _Why:_ compromising a service can provide execution without ordinary account logon telemetry. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Client-side attack with backdoor example** — Client-side compromise that results in a backdoor may not create a normal logon event. _Why:_ post-exploitation backchannels can operate outside standard authentication logging. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Backchannel explanation** — These missing logon records occur because the attacker is using a backchannel rather than normal access mechanisms. _Why:_ this explains why Security log authentication evidence may be absent even during compromise. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Standard API bypass** — Exploit and backdoor access can circumvent the standard APIs used for normal access. _Why:_ event-log coverage depends on the access path reaching audited Windows authentication mechanisms. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **True remote exploit rarity** — The page states that true remote exploits are uncommon. _Why:_ analysts should still expect many intrusions to involve credentialed access somewhere in the chain. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Administrative account use for lateral movement** — In many cases, attackers still need administrative account usage to move laterally to a system. _Why:_ lateral movement often produces authentication evidence even if initial access did not. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Administrative account use for code installation** — Installing code on another system commonly requires administrative account activity. _Why:_ this can create at least initial logging tied to the attack. _[GCFA p.~219]_
- **Initial attack logging from credentialed actions** — Even when exploitation is involved, administrative credential use may provide some early event-log evidence of the attack. _Why:_ investigators should look for credentialed activity around lateral movement and installation steps. _[GCFA p.~219]_

## Page 221

### Windows Event Record Structure

- **Recorded event metadata** — each Windows event includes fields beyond the core event identifiers that describe what happened and why the event was generated. _Why:_ these fields provide investigative context needed to interpret event cause, source, and relevance. _[GCFA p.221]_
- **Event Viewer detailed Event Properties view** — the slide’s listed fields are shown through Event Viewer’s detailed Event Properties interface. _Why:_ investigators commonly use this view to inspect the structured contents of individual events. _[GCFA p.221]_
- **Event XML storage format** — Windows event elements are stored as XML, even when displayed through Event Viewer. _Why:_ XML storage allows many tools, not only Event Viewer, to parse and render the same event data. _[GCFA p.221]_
- **Tool-independent event parsing** — Windows event XML can be parsed and displayed by multiple tools. _Why:_ responders can process event logs at scale or with specialized forensic tooling instead of relying only on the GUI. _[GCFA p.221]_

### Event Property Fields

- **Logged** — records the time at which the event was generated, shown in the local time of the system. _Why:_ this is the primary timeline anchor for the event, but analysts must account for local system time settings. _[GCFA p.221]_
- **Level** — records the reason the event was produced and may also express the event’s severity. _Why:_ this helps distinguish routine informational records from warnings, errors, or higher-priority activity. _[GCFA p.221]_
- **User** — identifies the account associated with triggering the event. _Why:_ this can tie activity to a specific account during account-usage or intrusion analysis. _[GCFA p.221]_
- **Computer** — identifies the host on which the event occurred. _Why:_ this is especially important when reviewing event logs collected from multiple systems at the same time. _[GCFA p.221]_
- **Source** — identifies the application, service, or Microsoft component that wrote the event. _Why:_ source attribution helps determine which subsystem observed or reported the activity. _[GCFA p.221]_
- **Task Category** — classifies the event into a category; in Security logs, this corresponds to the Security Event Category controlled by audit policy. _Why:_ category mapping helps analysts connect logged events to the system’s configured auditing behavior. _[GCFA p.221]_
- **Event ID** — assigns a distinct numeric code to a system function or event type. _Why:_ Event IDs are often one of the strongest indicators of what action caused the record, provided the analyst has a reliable Event ID reference. _[GCFA p.221]_
- **General Description** — provides a predefined textual explanation of the event and may include extra contextual values. _Why:_ although descriptions may be vague, they can sometimes expose useful data such as remote IP addresses or hostnames. _[GCFA p.221]_
- **Details** — optionally stores additional raw event data or error-code information. _Why:_ raw details can preserve machine-readable values that are not obvious in the human-readable description. _[GCFA p.221]_

### Reference

- **Event Logging and Viewing URL** — the page cites `http://for508.com/-g1h6` as a reference for event logging and viewing. _Why:_ this gives analysts an external reference point for understanding Windows event logging concepts and tools. _[GCFA p.221]_

### Logon Event Interpretation

- **Logon events · Authorization context** — Windows logon events can provide detailed information about how account authorization occurred on a system when the analyst knows where to inspect and how to interpret the fields. _Why:_ correct interpretation turns generic login records into actionable forensic evidence. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **Logon events · Date field** — logon records can show the date associated with an authentication attempt. _Why:_ dates support timeline reconstruction for account activity. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **Logon events · Time field** — logon records can show the time associated with an authentication attempt. _Why:_ precise timing supports correlation with process execution, lateral movement, and other host artifacts. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **Logon events · Username field** — logon records can identify the account name involved in the authentication event. _Why:_ account attribution is central to determining whose credentials were used. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **Logon events · Hostname field** — logon records can include the host involved in the authentication event. _Why:_ host context helps map where account activity occurred. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **Logon events · Success or failure status** — logon records can indicate whether the authentication attempt succeeded or failed. _Why:_ failed and successful activity together can reveal guessing, misuse, or confirmed access. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **Logon events · Access method** — logon records can reveal the mechanism used for the attempted logon. _Why:_ the method often matters as much as the account name because it separates local use, remote access, services, and automation. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **Logon type events · Description location** — logon type information appears inside the Description data of logon events. _Why:_ analysts must inspect the descriptive event content to recover the logon method. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **Logon type events · Attempt characterization** — logon type values provide additional detail about how authentication was attempted. _Why:_ this supports classification of the activity beyond simple success or failure. _[GCFA p.~223]_

### Investigative Uses

- **Hands-on-keyboard determination** — logon type data can help determine whether a login was performed through direct interactive input. _Why:_ this helps distinguish likely physical or console use from remote access paths. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **SMB-created session identification** — logon type data can help identify sessions created remotely through Server Message Block connections. _Why:_ SMB logons are common in file access, administrative activity, and lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **Remote Desktop identification** — logon type data can help identify sessions created through Remote Desktop. _Why:_ RDP use is a major investigative signal for interactive remote access. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **System-based versus user-based logons** — logon type values can help separate system-driven logons, such as Scheduled Task activity, from interactive user logons. _Why:_ this reduces false assumptions about whether a person was actively using the machine. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **Scheduled Task logon classification** — Scheduled Task activity is an example of system-based logon behavior. _Why:_ task-driven authentication can explain account activity that does not reflect a live user session. _[GCFA p.~223]_

### Version-Specific RDP Behavior

- **Windows Server 2012 R2 · Restricted Admin Mode RDP** — on Windows Server 2012 R2, RDP connections made with Restricted Admin Mode are logged as type `3`. _Why:_ analysts could otherwise misclassify this RDP activity as ordinary network logon behavior. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **Windows 10 and later · Restricted Admin Mode RDP type** — starting with Windows 10, Restricted Admin Mode RDP connections are logged as type `10`. _Why:_ the same access pattern is represented differently across Windows versions. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **Windows 10 and later · RestrictedAdminMode field** — from Windows 10 onward, Restricted Admin Mode RDP records mark the `RestrictedAdminMode` field as `Yes`. _Why:_ this field confirms Restricted Admin Mode use instead of relying only on the logon type value. _[GCFA p.~223]_

### Enterprise Auditing

- **Logon types · Security filtering** — logon type knowledge can be used to filter security event data across an enterprise. _Why:_ filtering by type helps analysts focus on specific access patterns such as RDP, services, or network logons. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **Logon types · Security auditing** — logon type values can support enterprise security auditing. _Why:_ recurring or unexpected logon types can reveal policy gaps or abnormal administrative behavior. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **Type 10 · RDP indicator** — seeing logon type `10` in event logs indicates Remote Desktop activity. _Why:_ this is a direct way to identify remote interactive access. _[GCFA p.~223]_
- **Type 10 · Terminal server context** — logon type `10` may be expected on a terminal server. _Why:_ environment role affects whether RDP activity is normal or suspicious. _[GCFA p.~223]_

## Page 224

### Logon Session Correlation

- **Logon ID for session matching** — Windows assigns a Logon ID to an account session when the logon occurs. _Why:_ this identifier lets an examiner connect related activity to the same authenticated session. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Logon ID as a logon-to-logoff bridge** — The same Logon ID can be used to associate a successful logon event with a later logoff event. _Why:_ matching these events allows session duration analysis. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Session-duration calculation** — A user session length can be derived by subtracting the logon timestamp from the logoff timestamp for events sharing the same Logon ID. _Why:_ duration helps establish how long an account was active on a system. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Example session duration** — The page’s example calculates the account session as roughly 19 hours. _Why:_ this demonstrates the practical use of Logon ID correlation. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Example logon time** — The example successful logon occurred on 11/10/2020 at 1:11:38 PM. _Why:_ this is the starting timestamp used in the session-length calculation. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Example logoff time** — The example user-initiated logoff occurred on 11/11/2020 at 8:12:10 AM. _Why:_ this is the ending timestamp used in the session-length calculation. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Session-length use case: account profiling** — Session duration can support analysis of how an account was used. _Why:_ account-use patterns can help distinguish normal activity from suspicious behavior. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Session-length use case: intrusion impact** — Session duration can support damage assessment during an intrusion investigation. _Why:_ knowing how long an account was active helps bound attacker opportunity. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Session-length use case: timekeeping disputes** — Session duration may be relevant to timecard or work-hours investigations. _Why:_ logon/logoff records can provide evidence about system presence. _[GCFA p.224]_

### Event IDs

- **Event ID 4624** — Windows Security Event ID 4624 records a successful logon. _Why:_ it provides the beginning point for a correlated account session. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Event ID 4647** — Windows Security Event ID 4647 records a user-initiated logoff. _Why:_ it can provide the ending point for a session tied to a Logon ID. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Event ID 4634 as an alternative logoff marker** — A successful logoff event with ID 4634 can be used instead of 4647 when that event is available. _Why:_ investigators should not depend on only one logoff event type when calculating session duration. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Event IDs 4624 and 4634 for lock/unlock Type 7 sessions** — Screen locking and unlocking activity can appear as Type 7 instances of 4624 and 4634. _Why:_ these records provide finer-grained visibility into interactive user presence. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Event ID 4800** — Windows Event ID 4800 can record workstation locking. _Why:_ lock events help reconstruct when a user stopped actively using the session. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Event ID 4801** — Windows Event ID 4801 can record workstation unlocking. _Why:_ unlock events help identify resumed interactive activity. _[GCFA p.224]_

### Logon Types

- **Interactive logon usefulness** — Session-length analysis is most valuable for interactive logons. _Why:_ these sessions usually represent meaningful user presence on the system. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Logon Type 2** — Type 2 is an interactive logon type highlighted as useful for session-duration analysis. _Why:_ it commonly reflects direct local user interaction. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Logon Type 10** — Type 10 is an interactive logon type highlighted as useful for session-duration analysis. _Why:_ it commonly reflects remote interactive access. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Logon Type 11** — Type 11 is included among interactive-style logons where session-length analysis is useful. _Why:_ it can represent cached interactive logon activity relevant to user presence. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Logon Type 12** — Type 12 is included among interactive-style logons where session-length analysis is useful. _Why:_ it is part of the set of logon types the page treats as useful for session-duration work. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Logon Type 3** — Type 3 network logons often last only briefly. _Why:_ short-lived network sessions can mislead analysts if interpreted like an interactive desktop session. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Logon Type 5** — Type 5 batch/service-style logons are grouped with non-interactive logons that tend to connect briefly. _Why:_ these events are usually less useful for measuring human session duration. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Remote-share document example** — Opening a document from a remote share can create a Type 3 logon and logoff even while the document remains open. _Why:_ the logoff does not necessarily mean the user stopped using the file. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Remote-share save example** — Saving later changes to the same remote document can trigger another Type 3 session. _Why:_ repeated network logons may reflect file access operations rather than continuous user presence. _[GCFA p.224]_

### Related Activity Linking

- **Logon ID for user activity tracking** — The Logon ID can help connect actions performed during the same authenticated session. _Why:_ it gives analysts a way to group evidence around one account session. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Special privileges linked by Logon ID** — Special user privilege events can be tied to a session through the Logon ID. _Why:_ this helps identify when elevated rights were associated with a specific logon. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Process tracking linked by Logon ID** — Process-tracking events can be associated with the session Logon ID. _Why:_ this can connect process execution to the account session that launched it. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Object access linked by Logon ID** — Object access events can be tied back to a session using the Logon ID. _Why:_ this helps attribute file, registry, or other object interactions to a session. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Screen lock/unlock linked by Logon ID** — Locking and unlocking activity can be correlated with the session. _Why:_ this refines the timeline of when the session was actively available to the user. _[GCFA p.224]_

### Linked Logon ID

- **Linked Logon ID introduction** — The Linked Logon ID field was added in Windows 10. _Why:_ this field expands session correlation beyond the primary Logon ID. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Linked Logon ID purpose** — Linked Logon ID connects a session to the Logon ID of related authentication activity. _Why:_ it helps show relationships between multiple authentication contexts. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Administrator dual-session behavior** — Administrator logons can create two sessions: one with elevated privileges and one with lower privileges. _Why:_ investigators may need to correlate both sessions to understand all activity from one admin login. _[GCFA p.224]_
- **Non-admin Linked Logon ID behavior** — Non-administrator sessions commonly have the Linked Logon ID set to zero. _Why:_ a zeroed value can indicate there is no linked elevated/lower-privilege pair to correlate. _[GCFA p.224]_

## Page 227

### Built-In Windows Accounts

- **Special Windows accounts in logs** — Windows event logs commonly include built-in or service-style accounts in addition to ordinary human user accounts. _Why:_ investigators should not assume every account name in a log represents an interactive user. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **Unexpected account names** — Seeing account names that differ from normal user accounts in Windows logs can be confusing during review. _Why:_ analysts need to distinguish expected service identities from suspicious account usage. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **Process account requirement** — Every Windows process and service runs under an account that carries some security privileges. _Why:_ account context explains what access a process or service could exercise. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **Boot-time process context** — Some Windows processes run before any user signs in. _Why:_ log entries before user logon can still be legitimate system activity. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **Background maintenance context** — Some Windows processes run without the user explicitly initiating or noticing them. _Why:_ background service activity can create logons unrelated to direct user action. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **Service account purpose** — Windows includes service accounts so processes can execute under different security contexts. _Why:_ security context helps determine whether an event reflects system, service, network, or user activity. _[GCFA p.~227]_

### Built-In Account Reference Table

- **SYSTEM · Description** — Identified as the strongest local account, with unrestricted system access. _Why:_ compromise of activity running as SYSTEM implies full local control. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **LOCAL SERVICE · Description** — Identified as a restricted account with privileges comparable to an authenticated user and network access limited to null-session communication. _Why:_ this account’s limited network capability affects how analysts interpret outbound authentication. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **NETWORK SERVICE · Description** — Identified as having somewhat more authority than LOCAL SERVICE and as able to reach network resources similarly to an authenticated account. _Why:_ services using this identity may legitimately authenticate across the network. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **`<Hostname>$` · Description** — Identified as the computer account present on every domain-joined Windows host. _Why:_ machine-account logons can represent host authentication rather than human account use. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **DWM · Description** — Identified as associated with the Desktop Window Manager or Window Manager group. _Why:_ DWM-style account names in logon events may be normal Windows graphical subsystem activity. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **UMFD · Description** — Identified as a font driver host account. _Why:_ UMFD-style account names may reflect Windows driver or display-related activity rather than user behavior. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **ANONYMOUS LOGON · Description** — Identified as a credential-free null session used to authenticate to a resource. _Why:_ anonymous logon events can indicate null-session access and require careful interpretation. _[GCFA p.~227]_

### SYSTEM Account

- **SYSTEM · Historical role** — Before Windows 2003, SYSTEM was the main account used for actions not tied to a specific user. _Why:_ older Windows activity may show broad use of SYSTEM for non-user operations. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **SYSTEM · Privilege level** — SYSTEM is the highest-privileged account on the local machine. _Why:_ actions under SYSTEM can have complete control over the host. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **SYSTEM · Compromise impact** — If an attacker subverts a process running as SYSTEM, the attacker can gain absolute access on that system. _Why:_ SYSTEM-context process compromise is a high-severity finding. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **SYSTEM · Least privilege shift** — Microsoft introduced more restricted service accounts as part of its Trustworthy Computing Initiative. _Why:_ this explains why later Windows versions show service identities other than SYSTEM. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **SYSTEM · Security design rationale** — The newer restricted accounts better align with least-privilege principles than running most non-user work as SYSTEM. _Why:_ expected account choice can indicate whether a service is using an overly powerful context. _[GCFA p.~227]_

### LOCAL SERVICE Account

- **LOCAL SERVICE · Privilege model** — LOCAL SERVICE is intended to operate with restricted privileges similar to a standard user account. _Why:_ this account should not be treated as equivalent to SYSTEM in access analysis. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **LOCAL SERVICE · Intended service use** — LOCAL SERVICE is used for services that do not need network access. _Why:_ network-facing activity under this account may deserve closer review. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **LOCAL SERVICE · Network authentication limit** — LOCAL SERVICE cannot authenticate to network resources. _Why:_ this constrains what remote access should be possible from services using this identity. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **LOCAL SERVICE · Null-session network behavior** — LOCAL SERVICE is limited to null-session style communication for network interactions. _Why:_ null-session artifacts can be expected when this identity communicates over the network. _[GCFA p.~227]_

### NETWORK SERVICE Account

- **NETWORK SERVICE · Relationship to LOCAL SERVICE** — NETWORK SERVICE is similar to LOCAL SERVICE but has somewhat greater privileges. _Why:_ the two accounts should not be treated as identical during privilege analysis. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **NETWORK SERVICE · Computer-account impersonation** — NETWORK SERVICE can act as a normal computer account. _Why:_ network logons from this account may appear as machine-authenticated activity. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **NETWORK SERVICE · Network authentication** — NETWORK SERVICE can authenticate over the network. _Why:_ this account is expected for services that need remote resource access. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **NETWORK SERVICE · Intended service use** — NETWORK SERVICE is assigned to processes or services requiring network access. _Why:_ service design intent helps separate normal network service behavior from anomalous activity. _[GCFA p.~227]_

### Computer Accounts

- **`<Hostname>$` · Domain-joined host identity** — Every Windows computer joined to a domain has a machine account. _Why:_ machine accounts are normal Active Directory principals and can appear in logs. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **`<Hostname>$` · Active Directory authentication** — The computer account allows the host itself to authenticate when communicating with Active Directory. _Why:_ domain communication may be recorded under the machine identity instead of a person. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **`<Hostname>$` · Network and domain resource access** — The computer account supports host access to network and domain resources. _Why:_ resource access by a machine account can be legitimate system behavior. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **`<Hostname>$` · Naming convention** — The account name is based on the system name. _Why:_ analysts can map the account back to a specific host. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **`<Hostname>$` · Dollar-sign suffix** — The computer account name must end with `$`. _Why:_ the trailing dollar sign is a key indicator that the principal is a machine account. _[GCFA p.~227]_

### DWM and UMFD Accounts

- **DWM and UMFD · Documentation gap** — Microsoft has published very little information about these built-in accounts. _Why:_ analysts may need to rely on observed behavior and context rather than official documentation. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **DWM and UMFD · Increased prevalence** — These accounts have become more commonly observed in recent Windows environments. _Why:_ their presence in logs may be normal on modern systems. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **DWM · Apparent role** — DWM appears to be associated with Windows Manager or Desktop Window Manager activity. _Why:_ DWM account logons may relate to desktop/session management rather than attacker-created accounts. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **UMFD · Apparent role** — UMFD appears to be associated with driver activity. _Why:_ UMFD account logons may reflect system or driver-related operations. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **DWM and UMFD · Remaining uncertainty** — The page states that more information is needed about these accounts. _Why:_ analysts should avoid overclaiming their meaning without supporting evidence. _[GCFA p.~227]_

### ANONYMOUS LOGON

- **ANONYMOUS LOGON · Common misunderstanding** — ANONYMOUS LOGON is described as the built-in account that is most frequently misinterpreted. _Why:_ investigators may incorrectly treat anonymous events as automatically malicious or as normal without context. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **ANONYMOUS LOGON · Original purpose** — The account was created to let Windows systems communicate without explicit credentials. _Why:_ anonymous logons can be part of legacy or compatibility behavior. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **ANONYMOUS LOGON · Null Session equivalence** — Anonymous logons are also referred to as Null Sessions. _Why:_ recognizing both terms helps correlate documentation, tools, and event-log interpretation. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **ANONYMOUS LOGON · Older or insecure system behavior** — On older or poorly secured systems, anonymous logons/null sessions can be used to enumerate account information. _Why:_ anonymous activity may expose reconnaissance opportunities on weakly configured systems. _[GCFA p.~227]_
- **ANONYMOUS LOGON · Security-enumeration context** — The page indicates anonymous logons/null sessions can be used for security-related enumeration, though the visible text cuts off after the word `security`. _Why:_ the truncated source still signals that null sessions have investigative relevance beyond simple connectivity. _[GCFA p.~227]_

## Page 228

### Anonymous Logon Context

- **Anonymous Logon legacy access** — older Windows environments allowed Anonymous Logon activity to reach items such as policy information, registry content, and network shares. _Why:_ this explains why Anonymous Logon events can appear for benign legacy-compatible Windows behavior rather than intrusion activity. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Anonymous Logon restrictions in newer Windows** — Windows versions beginning with XP and Server 2003 gradually disabled many Anonymous Logon capabilities by default. _Why:_ investigators should account for OS version when deciding whether Anonymous Logon behavior is expected. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Anonymous Logon remaining network role** — despite reduced default privileges, Anonymous Logon is still commonly used in Windows networks. _Why:_ its presence in logs is not automatically suspicious. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Anonymous Logon and file sharing** — Windows file-sharing services can legitimately generate Anonymous Logon activity. _Why:_ file server roles can create expected background authentication noise. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Anonymous Logon and print sharing** — Windows print-sharing services can legitimately involve Anonymous Logon usage. _Why:_ print services may explain events that otherwise look like unexplained account access. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Anonymous Logon and browse list maintenance** — Windows networks may use Anonymous Logon while maintaining the network browse list. _Why:_ browse-list maintenance is a benign explanation for recurring Anonymous Logon events. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Anonymous Logon likelihood with sharing services** — environments that provide file sharing, print sharing, or browse-list-related services are likely to show Anonymous Logon entries. _Why:_ service inventory helps determine whether these events are normal for the host or network. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Anonymous Logon interpretation caution** — an Anonymous Logon event should not be treated as automatic proof of enumeration or attack. _Why:_ premature conclusions can misclassify normal Windows network behavior as compromise. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Anonymous Logon requires context** — additional environmental and event context is normally needed before assigning meaning to Anonymous Logon activity. _Why:_ surrounding evidence is required to distinguish benign service behavior from suspicious reconnaissance. _[GCFA p.~228]_

### Built-In Account Logon Noise

- **Slide example account pattern** — the example shows successful logons from many built-in accounts occurring near a normal user logon. _Why:_ built-in account events can cluster around human activity and complicate timeline review. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Example user account** — `rsydow` is identified as a user account on the system in the example. _Why:_ it provides the human-account reference point among noisier built-in account events. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Built-in accounts can dominate logs** — successful logons by built-in accounts usually appear in much larger numbers than logons by ordinary user accounts. _Why:_ analysts should expect high event volume from system identities and avoid treating every logon equally. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Built-in account event noise** — built-in account logons can make Windows Security logs noisy. _Why:_ filtering and triage are needed to focus on events most likely tied to human actions. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Built-in account logon type 2** — the example includes built-in account logons using logon type `2`. _Why:_ system or built-in identities may appear with interactive-style logon types, adding ambiguity during review. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Built-in account logon type 3** — the example includes built-in account logons using logon type `3`. _Why:_ network-style logons from built-in accounts may be routine and numerous. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Built-in account logon type 5** — the example includes built-in account logons using logon type `5`. _Why:_ service logon activity from built-in accounts can inflate log volume. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Human activity focus** — forensic review often prioritizes actions performed by human users over background activity from built-in system accounts. _Why:_ user-driven activity is usually more relevant for account usage, intrusion reconstruction, and scope analysis. _[GCFA p.~228]_
- **Filtering system accounts** — many system or built-in accounts can be filtered out to make actual user accounts easier to analyze. _Why:_ reducing routine system identity noise improves analyst focus and event-log signal. _[GCFA p.~228]_

## Page 229

### Privileged Logon Tracking

- **Privileged-account monitoring** — watching activity from administrator-level accounts is a strong method for finding unusual or hostile behavior. _Why:_ intruders commonly need elevated rights to steal credentials and move laterally. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Administrative privilege as attacker milestone** — during an intrusion, an adversary generally must obtain at least administrator-level access to collect credentials and operate effectively across the environment. _Why:_ this makes privileged-account use a useful detection choke point. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Privileged-account auditing** — auditing and controlling administrator-equivalent accounts can expose even advanced adversary activity. _Why:_ elevated account use is difficult for an attacker to avoid once they need broad access. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Event ID 4672 trigger condition** — Windows records Event ID 4672 when an account receives privileges associated with administrator-level access during logon. _Why:_ this event marks the assignment of sensitive rights, not merely a normal authentication. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Full administrator membership not required** — an account does not need to be a complete local administrator to generate Event ID 4672. _Why:_ admin-equivalent rights can be enough to make an account forensically important. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Admin-equivalent privilege examples** — privileges such as `SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege`, `SeDebugPrivilege`, and `SeImpersonatePrivilege` can cause Event ID 4672 because they provide administrator-equivalent capability. _Why:_ analysts should not filter only on formal Administrators-group membership. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Event ID 4624 plus 4672 interpretation** — a successful logon event immediately followed by a special-logon event indicates that the account logged on and was assigned elevated privileges. _Why:_ the pair supports the conclusion that privileged access occurred on the host. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Administrative logon proof requirement** — the combination of Event ID 4624 and Event ID 4672 is needed to prove that an administrator-level account logged on to the system. _Why:_ Event ID 4672 alone shows privilege assignment, while Event ID 4624 establishes the logon. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Privilege verification alternative** — if the account still exists, its privileges can also be checked in the SAM database or Active Directory. _Why:_ account stores can corroborate whether the account was privileged. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Rare-admin-login hosts** — Event ID 4672 is especially valuable on systems where administrator logons do not usually occur. _Why:_ rare elevated access has a higher signal-to-noise ratio. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Service-account discovery** — Event ID 4672 can help identify highly privileged service accounts. _Why:_ those accounts often need special auditing and protection. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Password-reset planning use** — privileged-logon events can support planning for password resets of high-value accounts. _Why:_ analysts can identify which privileged accounts are active and where they are used. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Compromised-service-account detection** — Event ID 4672 can help locate suspicious use of service accounts with elevated privileges. _Why:_ abused service accounts are common persistence and lateral-movement assets. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Scheduled-task behavior** — scheduled tasks configured to run administratively or with highest privileges also produce Event ID 4672. _Why:_ scheduled-task activity can create privileged-logon evidence that is not an interactive admin session. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Event ID 4672 noise** — focusing on Event ID 4672 produces many non-malicious events. _Why:_ analysts must separate routine privileged activity from suspicious use. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Local SYSTEM noise** — the local `SYSTEM` account commonly generates Event ID 4672 records. _Why:_ routine operating-system activity can inflate special-logon results. _[GCFA p.229]_
- **Machine-account noise** — computer-account activity commonly seen in Active Directory environments can also appear in Event ID 4672 data. _Why:_ domain-joined systems may create privileged-logon noise unrelated to human administrator activity. _[GCFA p.229]_

- **Event 4672 · Subject Security ID** — the subject SID is `S-1-5-21-3446421715-2530590580-3149308974-1103`. _Why:_ the SID is the durable account identifier for correlating the account even if the displayed name changes. _[GCFA p.~230]_

- **SeSecurityPrivilege** — the logon received `SeSecurityPrivilege`. _Why:_ this privilege can allow security auditing and log access operations that are highly relevant during forensic review. _[GCFA p.~230]_

- **SeSystemEnvironmentPrivilege** — the logon received `SeSystemEnvironmentPrivilege`. _Why:_ this privilege can affect system environment settings and is a marker of elevated authority. _[GCFA p.~230]_
- **SeImpersonatePrivilege** — the logon received `SeImpersonatePrivilege`. _Why:_ impersonation rights are important because they can enable a process to act under another security context. _[GCFA p.~230]_

## Page 231

### Event ID 4648 Meaning

- **Event ID 4648** — Windows records this Security log event when a logon attempt uses credentials explicitly supplied for that action. _Why:_ it identifies activity where a user changes authentication context rather than relying only on the current session. _[GCFA p.~231]_
- **Explicit credential use** — A user may deliberately supply a different account to perform a specific local or remote action. _Why:_ this can reveal privilege switching, lateral movement, or administrative activity tied to a different account than the logged-on user. _[GCFA p.~231]_
- **Run As example** — Launching an executable with the Windows “Run As” option is one way to perform an action with alternate credentials. _Why:_ this creates evidence that the action was not necessarily performed under the desktop user’s normal account context. _[GCFA p.~231]_
- **Command-line credential example** — Supplying a username argument to tools is another way to execute an action under a different user context. _Why:_ command-line driven credential use is common in administration and attacker tradecraft. _[GCFA p.~231]_
- **PsExec credential use** — PsExec is listed as a tool that can accept an explicit username for changing user context. _Why:_ PsExec is commonly used for remote administration and lateral movement, so Event ID 4648 can help attribute the supplied credential. _[GCFA p.~231]_
- **Enter-PSSession credential use** — Enter-PSSession is listed as a tool that can use an explicitly specified username. _Why:_ PowerShell remoting activity may generate evidence of alternate credential use. _[GCFA p.~231]_
- **net use credential use** — `net use` is listed as a command that can take a supplied username to access resources under another account. _Why:_ mapped share and SMB access may be traceable through explicit credential events. _[GCFA p.~231]_
- **Remote Desktop credential prompt** — Microsoft Remote Desktop Connection asks the user for a username and password when starting an RDP connection to a remote host. _Why:_ RDP sessions commonly produce Event ID 4648 evidence showing which account was typed for the remote authentication. _[GCFA p.~231]_
- **Original and alternate accounts in one event** — Event ID 4648 records both the current session’s user and the explicitly supplied credential. _Why:_ investigators can distinguish the operator’s local context from the account used against the target. _[GCFA p.~231]_
- **Subject section role** — The event’s Subject section identifies the account tied to the original logon session. _Why:_ this field helps attribute who was already logged on when alternate credentials were used. _[GCFA p.~231]_
- **Account Whose Credentials Were Used section role** — The event’s Account Whose Credentials Were Used section identifies the alternate account supplied for the action. _Why:_ this is the key field for determining which credential was explicitly used. _[GCFA p.~231]_
- **Target Server section role** — The event can include a Target Server section showing where the supplied credential was used. _Why:_ this links the explicit credential to the destination system or service. _[GCFA p.~231]_
- **Process Information section role** — The event can include local process details associated with the credential-use activity. _Why:_ process metadata helps identify which application or subsystem initiated the authentication. _[GCFA p.~231]_
- **Network Information section role** — The event can include network connection details related to the explicit credential action. _Why:_ network address and port fields can help separate remote service access from purely local credential use. _[GCFA p.~231]_
- **SPN in Additional Information** — The Target Server Additional Information field can contain the service principal name for the service accessed on the target. _Why:_ the SPN identifies the exact service identity involved in Active Directory authentication. _[GCFA p.~231]_
- **Service Principal Name uniqueness** — SPNs uniquely identify services within an Active Directory forest. _Why:_ SPNs help investigators distinguish which service on a server was accessed with the alternate credential. _[GCFA p.~231]_

### Service Principal Names

- **SPN structure** — a service principal name is formed from a service class plus the host name where that service instance runs. _Why:_ this lets analysts identify which network service an authenticated connection targeted. _[GCFA p.232]_
- **Service class** — the service class is a standardized label assigned to a particular category of service. _Why:_ it reveals the type of service represented by an SPN. _[GCFA p.232]_
- **SPN learning reference** — the page points to `https://for508.com/k1vny` for additional information about SPNs. _Why:_ this gives analysts a supporting reference for interpreting SPN syntax and meaning. _[GCFA p.232]_
- **TERMSRV/server1 SPN** — `TERMSRV/server1` is shown as an example SPN. _Why:_ it demonstrates how the service class and host name appear together in an event. _[GCFA p.232]_
- **TERMSRV service class** — `TERMSRV` is the service class associated with Terminal Services. _Why:_ seeing `TERMSRV` in an SPN points to Terminal Services activity. _[GCFA p.232]_
- **Terminal Services and RDP** — Terminal Services is the service used for Remote Desktop Protocol connections. _Why:_ a `TERMSRV` SPN can indicate RDP-related authentication or access. _[GCFA p.232]_

### Explicit Credential Use Over SMB

- **Explicit credentials to SMB** — the page describes explicit credential use to start an SMB connection from `Client11` to `Server1`. _Why:_ this identifies a logon pattern where one account initiates access using another account’s credentials. _[GCFA p.232]_
- **Example SMB mapping command** — `net use S: \\server1\share /user:fictivecorp\administrator` is shown as a command that maps an SMB share using alternate credentials. _Why:_ this command pattern can explain Event ID 4648-style explicit credential activity. _[GCFA p.232]_
- **`net use` command purpose** — `net use` is used in the example to connect a local drive letter to a remote network share. _Why:_ analysts can map command-line evidence to the resulting authentication events. _[GCFA p.232]_
- **Mapped drive letter** — the example maps the remote share to local drive letter `S:`. _Why:_ the drive letter can help correlate shell activity, user behavior, and later file access. _[GCFA p.232]_
- **Remote share path** — the network share in the example is `\\server1\share`. _Why:_ the UNC path identifies the target host and share name involved in the access. _[GCFA p.232]_
- **Alternate credential flag** — `/user:fictivecorp\administrator` supplies the alternate account in the `net use` example. _Why:_ this flag is a direct indicator that credentials other than the current logon context were used. _[GCFA p.232]_
- **Alternate account domain** — the alternate credential specifies domain `fictivecorp`. _Why:_ the domain component helps distinguish local, domain, and cross-domain credential use. _[GCFA p.232]_
- **Alternate account name** — the alternate credential specifies account `administrator`. _Why:_ use of an administrative account can elevate the significance of the connection. _[GCFA p.232]_
- **Network Information section** — the Network Information section contains the target IP address and port number for the connection. _Why:_ these fields help identify the remote endpoint and protocol. _[GCFA p.232]_
- **SMB port value** — port `445` is shown as the relevant network port for the SMB example. _Why:_ TCP 445 strongly supports interpretation of the activity as SMB access. _[GCFA p.232]_

### Target Server and CIFS

### RDP Session Scope

- **Remote Desktop Protocol session tracking** — the page focuses on using Windows artifacts to follow RDP session activity. _Why:_ RDP is a common remote-access path that often needs reconstruction during intrusion analysis. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **RDP in enterprise environments** — RDP is widely used in many corporate networks. _Why:_ common legitimate use makes RDP evidence both important and noisy. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **RDP by attackers** — attackers frequently use RDP during intrusions. _Why:_ RDP can provide direct interactive access without deploying custom malware. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Sophos 2023 incident sample size** — Sophos reviewed 150 incidents in 2023 for the statistic cited on the page. _Why:_ the statistic is based on a defined investigation set, not a generic claim. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Sophos 2023 RDP frequency** — Sophos found RDP usage in 90% of the 2023 incidents they analyzed. _Why:_ this highlights RDP as a high-priority artifact family in modern investigations. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Sophos reference URL** — the page cites `https://for508.com/5gh9e` for the Sophos RDP statistic. _Why:_ the shortened link identifies the external source behind the percentage claim. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Domain Administrator RDP impact** — a Domain Administrator account can permit remote access to systems across an Active Directory forest. _Why:_ stolen privileged credentials can make ordinary RDP a powerful intrusion mechanism. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Backdoor tradeoff** — attackers may not need complex backdoors if they already control credentials that permit RDP access. _Why:_ investigators should treat credentialed RDP access as potentially sufficient for persistence and movement. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Group Policy limitation** — Group Policy can restrict broad RDP access by privileged accounts. _Why:_ the presence or absence of such controls changes how much reach a compromised admin account provides. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Group Policy rarity note** — the page states that such RDP-limiting Group Policy controls are uncommon in practice. _Why:_ investigators should not assume RDP reach is tightly constrained unless policy evidence proves it. _[GCFA p.234]_

### Relevant Event IDs

- **Event ID 4778** — Windows Security Event ID 4778 records that a session was reconnected. _Why:_ it can identify RDP reconnection activity that may not appear as a fresh RDP logon. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Event ID 4779** — Windows Security Event ID 4779 records that a session was disconnected. _Why:_ it helps identify the end or interruption point of a remote or switched session. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **4778 and 4779 pairing** — Event IDs 4778 and 4779 can be used together to frame the bounds of RDP session activity. _Why:_ paired reconnect/disconnect records help reconstruct session timelines. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Specialized RDP event IDs** — 4778 and 4779 are specialized event IDs tied to RDP behavior in addition to normal logon event codes. _Why:_ relying only on generic logon events can miss useful RDP-specific evidence. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Security log location** — the relevant 4778 and 4779 records are found in the Windows Security log. _Why:_ analysts need to know which log source to collect and search. _[GCFA p.234]_

### 4778 And 4779 Evidence Value

- **No complete RDP history** — Event IDs 4778 and 4779 do not provide a full historical listing of every RDP connection. _Why:_ absence of these events does not prove absence of RDP activity. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Reconnect design purpose** — 4778 and 4779 are primarily intended to record session reconnect and disconnect behavior rather than all new RDP sessions. _Why:_ this explains why they capture only a subset of total RDP use. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Subset visibility** — 4778 and 4779 show only some RDP activity. _Why:_ analysts must combine them with other logon and RDP-related artifacts. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Gap-filling value** — the reconnect focus of 4778 and 4779 can be useful because reconnects may be missed by workflows that look only for standard RDP logons. _Why:_ these events can reveal activity hidden from narrower searches. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **RDP reconnect logon type** — RDP session reconnects are often recorded as Event ID 4624 with Logon Type 7. _Why:_ Type 7 may be mistaken for only lock or unlock behavior, causing RDP reconnects to be overlooked. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Typical Type 7 interpretation** — Event ID 4624 Logon Type 7 is commonly interpreted as a screen lock or unlock event. _Why:_ this common assumption can hide RDP reconnect evidence. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Standard RDP logon type** — Event ID 4624 Logon Type 10 is the usual logon type associated with standard RDP logons. _Why:_ Type 10 searches alone do not cover all RDP session activity. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Type 10-only blind spot** — an analyst who searches only for Event ID 4624 Logon Type 10 may miss RDP reconnects. _Why:_ reconnects may instead appear through Type 7 and the 4778/4779 event pair. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **4778 and 4779 recovery path** — missed reconnects from a Type 10-only search may still be found by reviewing Event IDs 4778 and 4779. _Why:_ these events broaden RDP timeline coverage. _[GCFA p.234]_

### Client Identity Fields

- **Remote client IP in 4778/4779** — Event IDs 4778 and 4779 include the IP address of the system that established the session. _Why:_ the IP can identify the apparent source of the remote connection. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Remote client hostname in 4778/4779** — Event IDs 4778 and 4779 include the hostname of the connecting client system. _Why:_ the hostname can help attribute the session to a particular endpoint. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Client identity source** — the client name and IP address are supplied through the RDP client application. _Why:_ these values are useful but should be understood as client-provided connection metadata. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **4624 hostname limitation** — the hostname in Event ID 4624 may often represent an intermediary system rather than the original RDP client. _Why:_ 4778 and 4779 can provide better source context than 4624 alone. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **4778/4779 source advantage** — 4778 and 4779 are valuable because they can record both the IP address and hostname of the actual system that made the connection. _Why:_ this can improve source attribution during RDP investigations. _[GCFA p.234]_

### Correlated Events

- **4778 with nearby 4624** — a 4778 session reconnection should often have a nearly simultaneous Event ID 4624 successful logon. _Why:_ 4778 shows the remote session reconnect, while 4624 shows that supplied credentials were accepted. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **4778 meaning boundary** — Event ID 4778 by itself indicates that a remote session was successfully reconnected. _Why:_ it does not, on its own, prove the credential validation details captured by 4624. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **4624 meaning boundary** — Event ID 4624 indicates successful authentication because the provided credentials were accepted. _Why:_ it complements 4778 when reconstructing a reconnect. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **4779 with nearby 4647** — a 4779 session disconnection can correspond with an Event ID 4647 successful logoff. _Why:_ the pair can help confirm session termination activity. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **4647 meaning** — Event ID 4647 records a successful logout/logoff. _Why:_ it can help anchor the end of a user session near a 4779 disconnect. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Nearby-event context** — events occurring close together in time can add meaning to 4778 and 4779 records. _Why:_ RDP session interpretation is stronger when reconnect, logon, disconnect, and logoff evidence aligns. _[GCFA p.234]_

### Workstation Session Behavior

- **4779 before 4778 pattern** — on workstations, Event ID 4779 may appear immediately before Event ID 4778. _Why:_ this sequence can reflect local console disconnection before an RDP session connects. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Single interactive logon constraint** — Windows workstations allow only one interactive logon at a time. _Why:_ this behavior explains why an existing console session may be disconnected when RDP begins. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Console user displacement** — if a user is already logged on at the console, an incoming RDP connection requires that console session to be disconnected first. _Why:_ this creates a characteristic disconnect-then-connect event sequence. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Immediate workstation sequence meaning** — a workstation 4779 followed immediately by 4778 can be normal RDP takeover behavior rather than two unrelated sessions. _Why:_ understanding the sequence prevents misreading the timeline. _[GCFA p.234]_

### Fast User Switching

- **Non-RDP 4778/4779 events** — not every 4778 or 4779 event is caused by RDP use. _Why:_ analysts must avoid treating these event IDs as exclusively remote-access evidence. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Fast User Switching reuse** — Windows also uses these events to record station changes caused by Fast User Switching. _Why:_ this creates legitimate non-RDP records with the same event IDs. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Fast User Switching session name** — when 4778 or 4779 reflects Fast User Switching, the session name is `Console`. _Why:_ the session name can help separate local console switching from RDP activity. _[GCFA p.234]_

### Auxiliary RDP Logs

- **RDPCoreTS auxiliary log** — `Remote Desktop Services-RDPCoreTS` can contain additional RDP-related information. _Why:_ this log can corroborate or enrich Security log findings. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **TerminalServices-RdpClient auxiliary log** — `TerminalServices-RdpClient` can record complementary RDP client-side information. _Why:_ it provides another evidence source when reconstructing RDP activity. _[GCFA p.234]_
- **Auxiliary log role** — `Remote Desktop Services-RDPCoreTS` and `TerminalServices-RdpClient` are complementary rather than replacements for Security log review. _Why:_ complete RDP analysis benefits from multiple event sources. _[GCFA p.234]_

- **RDP client closure behavior** — closing the RDP client instead of performing a complete logout can affect whether session reconnect or disconnect events are generated. _Why:_ investigators must account for user/client behavior when interpreting gaps in RDP event trails. _[GCFA p.~235]_
- **RDP full logout behavior** — a full logout differs from simply closing the RDP client and may produce different session accounting artifacts. _Why:_ the logout method can explain why expected RDP session lifecycle events are present or absent. _[GCFA p.~235]_
- **Event ID 4624 for RDP review** — Windows Security Event ID 4624 is usually the broadest event source for reviewing RDP access. _Why:_ it is the primary logon event to check when reconstructing RDP use. _[GCFA p.~235]_
- **Event ID 4624 · Logon Type 3** — Logon Type 3 within Event ID 4624 is relevant when reviewing possible RDP-related access. _Why:_ RDP investigations should include this logon type rather than focusing only on interactive RDP logons. _[GCFA p.~235]_
- **Event ID 4624 · Logon Type 7** — Logon Type 7 within Event ID 4624 is part of the recommended RDP access review set. _Why:_ unlock or reconnect-style activity can be relevant to RDP session reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~235]_
- **Event ID 4624 · Logon Type 10** — Logon Type 10 within Event ID 4624 is relevant to Remote Interactive logon activity. _Why:_ it is a key indicator for direct RDP logon analysis. _[GCFA p.~235]_
- **Auxiliary RDP logs** — RDP analysis should cross-check Security log findings with Remote Desktop Services-RDPCoreTS and TerminalServices-RdpClient logs. _Why:_ auxiliary logs can show RDP activity that complements or clarifies Security Event ID 4624 evidence. _[GCFA p.~235]_
- **Auxiliary RDP log location** — the Remote Desktop Services-RDPCoreTS and TerminalServices-RdpClient logs reside in the same general event log directory as other Windows event logs. _Why:_ investigators can locate them alongside the standard event log set during collection or triage. _[GCFA p.~235]_

- **RDPCoreTS Event ID 131** — Event ID 131 in the RDPCoreTS log records outbound RDP connection activity. _Why:_ it can identify systems a host attempted to reach over RDP. _[GCFA p.~235]_
- **RDPCoreTS Event ID 131 · Destination hostname** — RDPCoreTS Event ID 131 can include the remote destination hostname. _Why:_ hostnames help tie outbound RDP activity to specific remote systems. _[GCFA p.~235]_

- **TerminalServices-RdpClient Event ID 1024 · Destination hostname** — TerminalServices-RdpClient Event ID 1024 can record the destination hostname for an outbound RDP session. _Why:_ it helps identify the remote endpoint contacted by the user or process. _[GCFA p.~235]_
- **TerminalServices-RdpClient Event ID 1024 · Destination IP address** — TerminalServices-RdpClient Event ID 1024 can record the destination IP address for an outbound RDP session. _Why:_ it enables correlation with firewall, proxy, EDR, and network telemetry. _[GCFA p.~235]_
- **TerminalServices-RdpClient Event ID 1102** — Event ID 1102 in the TerminalServices-RdpClient log records outbound RDP connections. _Why:_ it is another client-side event source for identifying RDP destinations. _[GCFA p.~235]_
- **TerminalServices-RdpClient Event ID 1102 · Destination hostname** — TerminalServices-RdpClient Event ID 1102 can include the hostname of the RDP destination. _Why:_ this value helps attribute outbound RDP activity to a specific remote host. _[GCFA p.~235]_
- **TerminalServices-RdpClient Event ID 1102 · Destination IP address** — TerminalServices-RdpClient Event ID 1102 can include the IP address of the RDP destination. _Why:_ this value supports network-level correlation and scoping. _[GCFA p.~235]_

- **RogueRDP social engineering** — RogueRDP depends on deceiving users into starting outbound RDP sessions. _Why:_ user action can create attacker access without an inbound RDP login attempt against the victim. _[GCFA p.~235]_

- **RogueRDP resource abuse** — if the victim connects to an attacker-controlled RDP endpoint and shares resources, the attacker can use those shared resources to reach into the victim computer. _Why:_ the attacker may gain access through normal RDP redirection features rather than exploiting a software vulnerability. _[GCFA p.~235]_

### RDP Session Hijacking

- **RDP hijacking detection challenge** — hijacking earlier RDP sessions can help attackers reduce their forensic footprint and avoid detection. _Why:_ analysts may need indirect evidence rather than relying only on obvious fresh logon records. _[GCFA p.~235]_

- **Event ID 4778 as a pivot point** — Event ID 4778 should be used to guide examination of other system artifacts around the same time. _Why:_ the event alone may not prove malicious activity, but it helps focus timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.~235]_
- **Cross-artifact review after Event ID 4778** — when Event ID 4778 appears, investigators should inspect other artifacts on the host near that timestamp. _Why:_ surrounding evidence may reveal whether the session activity was malicious. _[GCFA p.~235]_

### Timeline Interpretation

- **Event burst** — multiple Security log entries occur within only a few seconds of each other. _Why:_ dense timing requires event correlation rather than isolated event review. _[GCFA p.236]_
- **Reconnect before logon** — the `4778` reconnect at `11:53:53 AM` precedes the `4624` logon at `11:53:56 AM`. _Why:_ sequence order shows that the session was reattached before the successful logon record appeared. _[GCFA p.236]_
- **Unlock confirmation** — the `4801` event at `11:53:56 AM` supports the view that Windows treated the action as an unlock. _Why:_ this explains why the associated 4624 logon type is `7`. _[GCFA p.236]_
- **Same-account correlation** — the `4778` reconnect and `4624` logon both involve `rsydow`. _Why:_ matching the account connects the events into the same activity chain. _[GCFA p.236]_
- **Existing session condition** — an earlier RDP session for the user remained active rather than fully ended. _Why:_ an existing session causes later access to be logged as a reconnect instead of a clean new RDP logon. _[GCFA p.236]_
- **RDP re-entry behavior** — when the user connected again over RDP, Windows reattached the existing session. _Why:_ this behavior changes the logon evidence investigators should expect. _[GCFA p.236]_
- **Unexpected logon type** — the RDP reconnect was recorded as Type `7`, not Type `10`. _Why:_ RDP activity can be missed if searches require 4624 Logon Type 10. _[GCFA p.236]_
- **Standard RDP logon type** — Logon Type `10` is described as the usual logon type for RDP. _Why:_ it is the expected value many investigators search for when hunting RDP activity. _[GCFA p.236]_
- **NLA-related variation** — RDP activity often appears as Logon Type `3` instead of Type `10` when Network Level Authentication is in use. _Why:_ NLA changes the observable logon pattern and broadens the event types investigators must consider. _[GCFA p.236]_
- **Network Level Authentication definition** — NLA authenticates the account at the network layer before the RDP server connection is established. _Why:_ this explains why RDP may create network-style logon evidence. _[GCFA p.236]_
- **NLA prevalence** — NLA is enabled by default in many environments. _Why:_ Type 3 RDP-adjacent evidence is common enough to account for during investigations. _[GCFA p.236]_
- **Type 10 filtering limitation** — filtering only for Event ID `4624` with Logon Type `10` will not find all RDP activity. _Why:_ reconnects and NLA behavior can produce Type 7 or Type 3 evidence instead. _[GCFA p.236]_
- **Multi-event reconstruction** — the page presents the case as an example of combining several event records to understand one machine action. _Why:_ single-event interpretation would miss the full RDP reconnect story. _[GCFA p.236]_

### Receiving Versus Initiating System

- **Receiving-system logging** — the Security log events shown are recorded on the system receiving the RDP connection. _Why:_ investigators should look on the target host for these 4624, 4778, and 4801 records. _[GCFA p.236]_
- **Initiating-system absence** — the RDP client system will not contain these same receiving-side Security log records. _Why:_ absence of these events on the source machine is expected and should not disprove RDP use. _[GCFA p.236]_
- **Initiator-side evidence source** — the page points to TerminalServices-RDPClient log entries for activity on the initiating system. _Why:_ client-side RDP investigations require a different log source than the receiving system’s Security log. _[GCFA p.236]_

- **4624 Workstation Name limitation** — in this example, the 4624 Workstation Name field only gives the log-originating machine name. _Why:_ this value does not reliably identify the remote RDP client. _[GCFA p.236]_
- **4624 IP limitation** — the page notes that the 4624 IP information may point to a different system such as a VPN concentrator. _Why:_ network infrastructure can obscure the true endpoint behind the RDP connection. _[GCFA p.236]_

## Page 237

### RDP Session Correlation

- **Generated Windows hostnames** — Automatically generated Windows computer names can be unusual in many enterprise environments and may serve as useful compromise indicators when seen in RDP-related evidence. _Why:_ rare hostnames can help distinguish attacker-controlled or nonstandard systems from normal assets. _[GCFA p.~237]_

- **Event 4624 and Event 4778 correlation** — A Logon ID in a 4624 logon event may differ from the Logon ID in the related 4778 RDP reconnect event. _Why:_ investigators should not assume these two events always share the same Logon ID when reconstructing an RDP session. _[GCFA p.~237]_

- **Event ID 4778 meaning** — Event 4778 represents an RDP session reconnect event. _Why:_ it helps identify when an existing Remote Desktop session was resumed rather than newly created. _[GCFA p.~237]_

- **Event ID 4779 meaning** — Event 4779 represents an RDP session disconnect event. _Why:_ it helps distinguish session interruption from account logoff or fresh authentication. _[GCFA p.~237]_

- **4778/4779 Logon ID behavior** — RDP reconnect and disconnect events use the Logon ID associated with the earliest still-active interactive session for the same user. _Why:_ this explains why their Logon IDs may not align with nearby 4624 events. _[GCFA p.~237]_

- **Earliest non-terminated session** — For 4778 and 4779 events, the relevant session is the oldest interactive session for that user that has not yet ended. _Why:_ this session-selection rule affects timeline correlation and prevents incorrect linkage to the wrong logon event. _[GCFA p.~237]_

- **Event ID 4647 meaning** — Event 4647 records a user-initiated logoff. _Why:_ it provides a boundary for determining which later interactive session may be treated as the earliest active session. _[GCFA p.~237]_

- **Interactive session after last 4647** — The Logon ID used by 4778/4779 often belongs to the interactive session created after that user’s most recent 4647 logoff event. _Why:_ this gives analysts a practical method for locating the session context behind reconnect and disconnect activity. _[GCFA p.~237]_

- **Prior session causing ID mismatch** — In the shown example, an older active session existed, so the 4624 and matching 4778 events did not share the same Logon ID. _Why:_ this demonstrates that a mismatch can be expected behavior rather than evidence that the events are unrelated. _[GCFA p.~237]_

### Additional RDP Logging

- **RDP logging breadth** — Remote Desktop Protocol activity is recorded in several Windows log locations rather than a single event source. _Why:_ investigators should not rely on one log when reconstructing RDP use. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **RDP directionality** — Correctly separating the system that initiated RDP from the system that received RDP is essential. _Why:_ source-versus-target confusion can invert attacker movement paths. _[GCFA p.239]_

### Security Log Limits

- **Security log value** — Windows Security logon events can reveal substantial detail about both local and remote logons. _Why:_ they are a primary source for account-usage reconstruction. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Security log rollover risk** — if the Security log overwrites itself every `24-48` hours, relevant RDP evidence may be lost quickly. _Why:_ short retention can erase the incident window before collection begins. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Centralization requirement** — without archived or centralized logs, investigators may lack the time span needed to locate evidence. _Why:_ endpoint-only retention may be insufficient during delayed investigations. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Post-Vista custom logs** — Windows versions after Vista and Windows Server 2008 include many additional specialized logs. _Why:_ these logs can preserve forensic traces outside the main Security, System, and Application logs. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Custom log scope** — specialized Windows logs usually record a narrower activity set than broad system logs. _Why:_ lower event volume can allow them to retain older data. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Custom log retention advantage** — narrow-purpose logs can extend farther back in time than Security, System, or Application logs. _Why:_ they can fill investigative gaps after high-volume logs roll over. _[GCFA p.239]_

### RDP Service Logs

- **Multiple RDP logs** — the Remote Desktop service maintains several separate logs. _Why:_ investigators have multiple possible sources for RDP evidence. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Duplicate RDP information** — several RDP logs may contain overlapping data. _Why:_ duplicate records can corroborate events when one log is incomplete. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Unclear design rationale** — the course notes that the reason for the many RDP logs is not obvious. _Why:_ responders should expect redundancy without assuming every channel has unique purpose. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Potential missing logs** — one or more relevant logs may be absent. _Why:_ investigators should check multiple channels rather than treating a missing log as proof of no RDP activity. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Limited log retention** — some RDP logs may exist but hold only a small time range. _Why:_ retention differences affect how far back session reconstruction can go. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **RDP custom logs as gap-fillers** — Remote Desktop custom logs can often compensate when the Security log does not cover the needed period. _Why:_ they may preserve connection evidence that the Security log has already overwritten. _[GCFA p.239]_

### TerminalServices-RDPClient Operational Log

- **RDPClient Operational uniqueness** — `Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-RDPClient/Operational` is singled out as different from many other RDP logs. _Why:_ it records client-side movement rather than only destination-side activity. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Source-side recording** — the `Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-RDPClient/Operational` log is written on the system that initiated the RDP connection. _Why:_ it can identify systems reached from a compromised host. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Attacker movement mapping** — this client-side log can show the places an attacker connected to from the examined machine. _Why:_ it supports lateral-movement reconstruction from the attacker’s launch point. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Windows logging asymmetry** — Windows more commonly records activity on the destination system than on the source system. _Why:_ source-side RDPClient evidence is unusually valuable. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Incident-response value** — the RDPClient Operational log has become favored in incident response because of its unusual source-side data. _Why:_ it can expose outbound RDP paths that target logs alone may not show. _[GCFA p.239]_

### RDPClient Event IDs

- **Event ID 1024** — RDPClient Operational event `1024` records the name of a system accessed over RDP. _Why:_ destination hostnames help build a lateral-movement timeline. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Event ID 1102** — RDPClient Operational event `1102` records the IP address of a system accessed over RDP. _Why:_ destination IPs can identify targets even when hostnames are missing or ambiguous. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Event ID 1029** — RDPClient Operational event `1029` stores a Base64 form of a SHA-256 hash of the username used for the RDP connection. _Why:_ it preserves account-related evidence without storing the username directly. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Event ID 1029 irreversibility** — the username hash in event `1029` cannot be directly reversed to recover the original username. _Why:_ investigators need candidate-based comparison rather than decoding. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Event ID 1029 brute-force approach** — if investigators have likely usernames, including all valid domain usernames, they can test candidates against the stored hash. _Why:_ this can identify which account was used despite the hash being one-way. _[GCFA p.239]_
- **Username candidate list** — a domain-wide list of valid usernames can be used as the candidate set for event `1029` hash testing. _Why:_ enterprise directories often provide a practical search space. _[GCFA p.239]_
