### Event ID 1029 Username Hashing

- **Event ID 1029 hash input** — the base64-encoded hash value is calculated from the username being tested. _Why:_ reproducing the value can help identify which username was supplied during an RDP-related event. _[GCFA p.240]_
- **Username placeholder** — `USERNAME` must be replaced with the specific account name whose associated base64-encoded hash is being calculated. _Why:_ using the wrong username string produces the wrong comparison value. _[GCFA p.240]_
- **CyberChef option** — CyberChef can be used as an alternative way to calculate the Event ID 1029-related value. _Why:_ it gives analysts a repeatable tool-based method instead of manually building the calculation. _[GCFA p.240]_
- **CyberChef recipe URL** — a prepared recipe is identified at `https://for508.com/1029`. _Why:_ the recipe provides a known workflow for reproducing the hash value. _[GCFA p.240]_
- **Domain exclusion** — Event ID 1029 derives its value from the username only, not from the domain portion. _Why:_ analysts should not include domain names when recreating the hash. _[GCFA p.240]_
- **UPN example handling** — for `administrator@fictivecorp.com`, the hash input would be only `administrator`. _Why:_ this shows that the suffix after `@` is excluded from the calculation. _[GCFA p.240]_
- **Case sensitivity** — the Event ID 1029 value changes when the username’s capitalization changes. _Why:_ capitalization can explain why expected username hashes fail to match. _[GCFA p.240]_
- **Capitalization variant: `Administrator`** — `Administrator` would produce a different Event ID 1029 value than differently cased forms of the same name. _Why:_ user-entered case is part of the forensic signal. _[GCFA p.240]_
- **Capitalization variant: `administrator`** — `administrator` would produce a distinct Event ID 1029 value from `Administrator` or other mixed-case variants. _Why:_ exact casing must be tested during analysis. _[GCFA p.240]_
- **Capitalization variant: `ADMINistTRator`** — `ADMINistTRator` would generate its own unique Event ID 1029 value. _Why:_ odd attacker-entered capitalization may be recoverable indirectly through hash reproduction. _[GCFA p.240]_

## Page 242

### Account Logon Events

- **Account Logon Events** — this Windows audit category is separate from the Logon Events category. _Why:_ analysts must not treat authentication logging and logon/session logging as the same evidence source. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Account Logon Events · Recording Location** — these events are written on the system that checks whether the supplied credentials are valid. _Why:_ the relevant evidence may be on a different host than the one where the user session appears. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Local Account or Workgroup Authentication** — when credentials belong to a local account or workgroup context, the workstation records the Account Logon event. _Why:_ local-account authentication evidence should be sought on the endpoint itself. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Domain or Active Directory Authentication** — when credentials belong to a domain account, the domain controller records the Account Logon event. _Why:_ domain-account authentication evidence often lives on DCs, not on the workstation under investigation. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Logon Events vs. Account Logon Events** — a major audit-policy challenge is distinguishing session/authorization events from credential-authentication events. _Why:_ confusing these categories can cause missed or misattributed login evidence. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Logon Events** — Logon Events are generated where Windows makes the authorization decision for the access attempt. _Why:_ these events identify where a logon/session was accepted for local or resource access. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Logon Events · Client Example** — a workstation used directly by a user can record Logon Events because authorization is decided there. _Why:_ endpoint Security logs can show local interactive session activity. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Logon Events · Server Example** — a server providing a file share can record Logon Events because it authorizes access to that resource. _Why:_ resource servers may hold evidence of access even when credentials were authenticated elsewhere. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Account Logon Events · Authentication Decision** — Account Logon Events are generated where Windows verifies the credential material itself. _Why:_ this identifies the system that accepted or rejected the username/password or ticket workflow. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Account Logon Events · Local Account Host** — for a local account, the validating system can be the client or member server that owns that account. _Why:_ local account investigations require checking the machine where the account database exists. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Account Logon Events · Domain Account Host** — for a domain account, the validating system is a domain controller. _Why:_ domain controller logs are essential for reconstructing domain-account authentication. _[GCFA p.242]_

### Domain Authentication Flow

- **Windows Domain Accounts** — in a domain environment, most user accounts are domain accounts. _Why:_ analysts should assume authentication records commonly reside on domain infrastructure. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Domain Credential Storage** — domain-account credentials are stored on the domain controller rather than the local workstation. _Why:_ endpoint-only review may miss the authentication record for a domain user. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **User Transparency** — users may not notice the domain authentication process because they repeatedly use the same workstation. _Why:_ normal user experience does not reveal where forensic evidence is produced. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Domain Workstation Logon Requirement** — before a domain user can log on to a workstation, the username and password must be checked by a domain controller. _Why:_ a workstation logon can require DC-side evidence even when the session is local to the endpoint. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Domain Authentication Protocols** — domain credential validation can use either NTLM or Kerberos. _Why:_ the protocol determines which event IDs should be searched. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Account Logon Events · Domain Validation Record** — Account Logon Events document the credential-validation process on the domain controller that performed the check. _Why:_ the authenticating DC becomes the authoritative log source for that authentication attempt. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Single Domain Logon · Multi-System Evidence** — one domain-account logon can create events on both the workstation and the domain controller. _Why:_ complete reconstruction requires correlating endpoint and DC logs. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Single Domain Logon · Workstation Events** — the workstation may record Logon Events such as Event ID 4624 and Event ID 4634. _Why:_ these events help show session start and end activity on the endpoint. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Single Domain Logon · Domain Controller Events** — the domain controller may record Account Logon Events such as Event ID 4776, 4768, or 4769. _Why:_ these events show the authentication protocol activity behind the workstation session. _[GCFA p.242]_

### Local Account Authentication

- **Local Account Definition** — a local account is created only on the workstation and is not part of a domain. _Why:_ this account type changes where authentication evidence is logged. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Local SAM Database** — local-account authentication is performed by the workstation using its local SAM database. _Why:_ the endpoint itself is the credential-validation authority for local accounts. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Local Account Logging Pattern** — when a local account is used, both Logon Events and Account Logon Events can appear in the workstation event logs. _Why:_ the same endpoint may contain both session evidence and authentication evidence. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Enterprise Local Account Rarity** — local-account logons are described as uncommon in enterprise environments. _Why:_ unusual local-account use can deserve extra investigative attention. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Local Account Forensic Value** — local-account authentication can be an important artifact to hunt for in enterprise investigations. _Why:_ it may indicate unauthorized or rogue local accounts were created on the system. _[GCFA p.242]_

### NTLM Event IDs

- **Authentication Protocol Split** — Account Logon event IDs are grouped according to the authentication protocol in use. _Why:_ analysts must query NTLM and Kerberos event IDs separately to avoid gaps. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **NTLM Account Authentication · Event ID 4776** — Event ID 4776 records account authentication using NTLM. _Why:_ this is the key Account Logon event ID for NTLM validation activity. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **NTLM Success and Failure · Event ID 4776** — both successful and failed NTLM authentication attempts use Event ID 4776. _Why:_ filtering only by event ID does not distinguish accepted credentials from rejected ones. _[GCFA p.242]_

### Kerberos Event IDs

- **Kerberos TGT Request · Event ID 4768** — Event ID 4768 records a Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket request. _Why:_ TGT activity is an early indicator of Kerberos authentication flow. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Kerberos TGT Result · Event ID 4768** — Event ID 4768 can represent either a successful or failed TGT request. _Why:_ analysts must inspect event details to determine outcome. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Kerberos Service Ticket Request · Event ID 4769** — Event ID 4769 records a Kerberos service ticket request. _Why:_ this indicates an attempt to access a server-side resource. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Kerberos Resource Access Intent · Event ID 4769** — a service ticket request corresponds to requested access to a server resource. _Why:_ this event can help link authentication activity to resource access. _[GCFA p.242]_
- **Kerberos Pre-Authentication Failure · Event ID 4771** — Event ID 4771 records failed Kerberos pre-authentication. _Why:_ this event is a key failed-logon signal in Kerberos environments. _[GCFA p.242]_

## Page 243

### Kerberos Domain Authentication

- **Windows domain default authentication** — Starting with Windows 2000 Server, Windows domains use Kerberos as the default authentication protocol. _Why:_ establishes which authentication events should normally be expected in domain log analysis. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **Kerberos versus NTLM workflow** — Kerberos requires more protocol exchanges than NTLM. _Why:_ more authentication steps generally means more event-log artifacts for investigators. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **Kerberos logging volume** — Kerberos produces more log entries than NTLM. _Why:_ investigators should expect Kerberos activity to leave a broader event trail. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **Initial Kerberos credential submission** — A user begins Kerberos authentication by presenting credentials to an authentication server. _Why:_ identifies the first authentication stage that can generate domain-controller evidence. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **Typical Kerberos authentication server** — The Kerberos authentication server is usually a domain controller. _Why:_ directs investigators toward domain-controller logs when reconstructing domain authentication. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **Credential verification step** — The authentication server validates the submitted credentials before issuing Kerberos material. _Why:_ failed validation can produce different event evidence than successful authentication. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **Ticket-granting ticket issuance** — When credentials are valid, the user receives a ticket-granting ticket, or TGT. _Why:_ TGT issuance marks successful Kerberos authentication. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **TGT lifetime** — A TGT is issued for a limited period rather than indefinitely. _Why:_ ticket validity windows help bound authenticated activity in timelines. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **TGT identity function** — A TGT serves as proof that the account has already authenticated. _Why:_ explains why later resource access can occur without resubmitting the original password. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **TGT as reusable authentication proof** — The TGT can be reused as a form of digital identity evidence during Kerberos operations. _Why:_ helps explain why possession of a ticket can enable access workflows. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **Service access requirement** — Accessing another system or resource, such as a server, requires a separate service ticket. _Why:_ service-ticket requests can reveal target-resource access after initial authentication. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **Service Ticket concept** — A Kerberos service ticket is the ticket requested for access to a specific service or remote resource. _Why:_ service-ticket events help identify what systems or services an account attempted to use. _[GCFA p.243]_

### Kerberos Event IDs

- **Event ID 4768** — Windows commonly records Kerberos TGT requests with Event ID `4768`. _Why:_ this event is central for identifying initial Kerberos authentication attempts. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **Event ID 4771** — Windows commonly records Kerberos pre-authentication logon failures with Event ID `4771`. _Why:_ this event can indicate bad passwords, password spraying, or other failed Kerberos authentication activity. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **Event ID 4769** — Windows commonly records Kerberos service-ticket requests with Event ID `4769`. _Why:_ this event helps map authenticated access attempts to services. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **Common Kerberos event set** — The page highlights `4768`, `4771`, and `4769` as the most common Kerberos-related event IDs. _Why:_ these IDs provide a focused starting point for Kerberos log review. _[GCFA p.243]_

- **Patch KB5049614** — Microsoft released update `KB5049614` in January 2025. _Why:_ patch level affects which Kerberos event fields may appear in logs. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **Patch-added Kerberos fields** — `KB5049614` added more fields to Event ID `4768` and Event ID `4769`. _Why:_ investigators comparing logs across systems must account for schema differences caused by patching. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **Affected operating systems** — The added Kerberos fields apply to Windows Server 2016 and later systems. _Why:_ older servers may lack the same event detail even for similar authentication activity. _[GCFA p.243]_
- **Bold-field note** — The courseware states that bolded fields in the example represent fields added by the January 2025 patch. _Why:_ those fields identify newly available forensic detail on patched systems. _[GCFA p.243]_

- **Misconfiguration Detection** — the added encryption details can help identify Kerberos configuration problems. _Why:_ unexpected encryption support or selection may indicate domain or endpoint misconfiguration. _[GCFA p.244]_

- **Weak Encryption Abuse Detection** — the added encryption details can help detect malicious use of weaker Kerberos encryption types. _Why:_ attackers may attempt to force or exploit weaker encryption during Kerberos activity. _[GCFA p.244]_

- **Domain controller separation** — the machine that records the logon event is often not the same system as the domain controller that issued the service ticket. _Why:_ Kerberos authentication evidence is distributed across systems. _[GCFA p.~245]_

- **Event ID 4768 error context** — Kerberos Event ID 4768 can contain logon failure reason information. _Why:_ failed Kerberos ticket-granting-ticket activity may reveal username guessing, policy issues, or time synchronization problems. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Event ID 4771 error context** — Kerberos Event ID 4771 can contain logon failure reason information. _Why:_ this event is central for analyzing Kerberos pre-authentication failures. _[GCFA p.~247]_

- **Event ID 4625 error context** — Failed Logon Event ID 4625 can contain logon failure reason information. _Why:_ this event records unsuccessful logon attempts on the system making the authorization decision. _[GCFA p.~247]_

- **NTLM/failed-logon code 0xC0000070 · EID 4776/4625** — NTLM or failed-logon code `0xC0000070` maps to logon from an unauthorized workstation. _Why:_ this code can identify attempts from systems the account is not permitted to use. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Reason · unauthorized workstation logon** — The table labels the `0xC` / `0xC0000070` condition as logon from an unauthorized workstation. _Why:_ workstation restrictions can explain failed access even when the account and password are valid. _[GCFA p.~247]_

- **Kerberos code 0x12 · EID 4768/4771** — Kerberos failure code `0x12` maps to an account that is locked, disabled, or expired. _Why:_ this helps identify account-state problems and possible lockout activity. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **NTLM/failed-logon code 0xC0000234 · EID 4776/4625** — NTLM or failed-logon code `0xC0000234` maps to an account locked, disabled, or expired condition. _Why:_ this can support lockout investigations and brute-force timelines. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Reason · account locked, disabled, or expired** — The table labels the `0x12` / `0xC0000234` condition as an account locked, disabled, or expired. _Why:_ account state is a separate analytic category from password correctness. _[GCFA p.~247]_

- **NTLM/failed-logon code 0xC0000071 · EID 4776/4625** — NTLM or failed-logon code `0xC0000071` maps to an expired-password condition. _Why:_ this helps analysts distinguish credential age policy failures from attack behavior. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Reason · password expired** — The table labels the `0x17` / `0xC0000071` condition as password expired. _Why:_ expired credentials can generate failures that resemble unauthorized access attempts unless decoded. _[GCFA p.~247]_

- **Kerberos code 0x18 · EID 4768/4771** — Kerberos failure code `0x18` maps to an invalid-password condition. _Why:_ repeated occurrences can indicate password guessing or stale stored credentials. _[GCFA p.~247]_

- **Reason · password invalid** — The table labels the `0x18` / `0xC000006A` condition as password invalid. _Why:_ invalid-password failures are a primary signal for brute-force, password spraying, and stale credential use. _[GCFA p.~247]_

- **Kerberos code 0x25 · EID 4768/4771** — Kerberos failure code `0x25` maps to excessive clock skew between systems. _Why:_ Kerberos is time-sensitive, so clock drift can block authentication without credential compromise. _[GCFA p.~247]_

### Kerberos Failure Behavior

- **Kerberos pre-authentication failure logging** — When Kerberos pre-authentication fails, Event ID 4771 is recorded on the authentication server. _Why:_ the domain controller or authentication server log is the authoritative place to find these pre-authentication failures. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Event ID 4771 timestamp data** — Event ID 4771 provides date and time information for the failed Kerberos pre-authentication attempt. _Why:_ timing supports attack reconstruction and correlation with endpoint activity. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Event ID 4771 hostname data** — Event ID 4771 includes the hostname associated with the failed Kerberos pre-authentication attempt. _Why:_ host context helps identify the source or involved system in an authentication failure. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Event ID 4771 client IP data** — Event ID 4771 includes the client IP address associated with the failed Kerberos pre-authentication attempt. _Why:_ source IP addresses help group attempts, identify attack infrastructure, and pivot to network logs. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Event ID 4771 supplied username data** — Event ID 4771 records the username submitted during the failed Kerberos pre-authentication attempt. _Why:_ the attempted username is necessary for account enumeration and password attack analysis. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Event ID 4771 error code meaning** — Event ID 4771 includes an error code that identifies the cause of the Kerberos authentication failure. _Why:_ decoding the code turns a generic failure into a specific investigative explanation. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Kerberos failure event selection** — Kerberos authentication failures may produce either Event ID 4771 or Event ID 4768 with a failure keyword, depending on the failure reason. _Why:_ analysts must search both event IDs to avoid missing Kerberos failures. _[GCFA p.~247]_

### Common Kerberos Error Meanings

- **Kerberos 0x6 meaning** — Kerberos error `0x6` indicates that the referenced user account is invalid or does not exist. _Why:_ this can signal username enumeration or attempts against nonexistent accounts. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Kerberos 0x6 replication caveat** — Kerberos error `0x6` can also occur because Active Directory servers have not replicated consistent account information. _Why:_ replication lag can produce false leads if treated only as hostile username guessing. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Kerberos 0x7 meaning** — Kerberos error `0x7` indicates that the requested server could not be found. _Why:_ this shifts investigation toward service identity, directory state, or replication rather than password correctness. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Kerberos 0x7 replication caveat** — Kerberos error `0x7` can also result from replication issues between Active Directory servers. _Why:_ inconsistent directory data can explain server lookup failures. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Kerberos 0xC policy restriction** — Kerberos error `0xC` indicates that policy blocked the logon. _Why:_ policy denial can create failed authentication records even when submitted credentials are otherwise valid. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Kerberos 0xC workstation restriction** — Kerberos error `0xC` can mean the client computer is not permitted to access the target resource. _Why:_ workstation-based access restrictions are important when validating whether a failure is expected administrative policy behavior. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Kerberos 0xC time/date restriction** — Kerberos error `0xC` can also reflect restrictions based on allowed logon times or dates. _Why:_ time-window policy failures can explain patterned authentication failures. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Kerberos 0x12 meaning** — Kerberos error `0x12` indicates an account that is locked, disabled, or expired. _Why:_ this supports account-state analysis and can explain why valid credentials no longer authenticate. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Kerberos 0x17 meaning** — Kerberos error `0x17` indicates that the account password has expired. _Why:_ this distinguishes password lifecycle failure from incorrect password entry. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Kerberos 0x18 meaning** — Kerberos error `0x18` indicates that the submitted password is wrong. _Why:_ this is a high-value indicator for password guessing, spraying, and stale credential use. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Kerberos 0x25 meaning** — Kerberos error `0x25` indicates that the client and server clocks differ beyond the acceptable Kerberos tolerance. _Why:_ time skew can break authentication and also complicate timeline correlation. _[GCFA p.~247]_
- **Kerberos timing dependency** — Kerberos depends on synchronized time to help expire old ticket-granting tickets. _Why:_ time synchronization is both an operational requirement and an investigative consideration for Kerberos failures. _[GCFA p.~247]_

### NTLM Account Logon Monitoring

- **NTLM in enterprise Windows environments** — NTLM authentication is less common than other Windows domain authentication activity, but it can still appear in enterprise networks. _Why:_ investigators should not ignore NTLM simply because Kerberos is the normal domain default. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **Remote local-account authentication** — when a local account is used remotely, the system being accessed records the activity as an NTLM Account Logon. _Why:_ this helps distinguish local-account use against a host from normal domain-authentication patterns. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **Event ID 4776** — NTLM Account Logon activity is logged with Windows Security Event ID 4776. _Why:_ this event ID is the key log target for NTLM credential-authentication review. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **Event ID 4776 host location** — remote authentication with a local account is recorded on the host that was accessed. _Why:_ analysts need to query the destination system, not only domain controllers or the source endpoint. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **Pass-the-hash dependency on NTLM** — pass-the-hash attacks use NTLM authentication. _Why:_ Event ID 4776 monitoring can expose activity patterns relevant to pass-the-hash investigations. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **NTLM Account Logon monitoring value** — tracking NTLM Account Logon events can provide useful investigative signal. _Why:_ NTLM activity may identify local-account access, legacy authentication, or credential-abuse techniques. _[GCFA p.248]_

### Event ID 4776 Failure Codes

- **Event ID 4776 failure code creation** — when Event ID 4776 records a failed authentication, Windows generates an associated error code. _Why:_ the code provides more detail than the event ID alone. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **Event ID 4776 Event Description storage** — the failure error code is stored in the event description. _Why:_ investigators must inspect the description fields, not just the event header. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **Event ID 4776 error-code purpose** — the error code explains why credential authentication was rejected. _Why:_ denial reason helps separate typo, policy restriction, disabled account, expired account, and attack-like behavior. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **Error codes as user-action evidence** — authentication error codes can provide clues about what a user or attacker attempted. _Why:_ failure reasons can support behavioral interpretation during timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **Locked account interpretation** — an account-lockout error may indicate password guessing, though it may also result from strict lockout policies. _Why:_ the code is a lead, not proof of attack by itself. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **Restricted-workstation authentication attempts** — error code `0xC0000070` indicates the account is not permitted to log on from the computer used. _Why:_ such attempts may suggest a user or attacker tried to reach unauthorized resources. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **Restricted-workstation attempts and enumeration** — `0xC0000070` activity may also indicate broad network enumeration. _Why:_ repeated access attempts across systems can reveal reconnaissance or lateral-movement behavior. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **Event ID 4625 relationship** — Windows Logon Event ID 4625, Failed Logon, uses the same error-code set as Event ID 4776. _Why:_ analysts can interpret failure codes consistently across NTLM Account Logon and failed logon events. _[GCFA p.248]_

### Error Code Values

- **`0xC0000064`** — the submitted username does not correspond to an existing account. _Why:_ this can indicate username guessing, bad input, stale scripts, or enumeration attempts. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **`0xC000006A`** — the username exists, but the supplied password is wrong. _Why:_ this is useful for identifying password guessing against valid accounts. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **`0xC000006F`** — the account is not permitted to log on at the attempted time. _Why:_ this points to time-based logon restrictions rather than a simple credential mismatch. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **`0xC0000070`** — the account is not permitted to log on from the attempted computer. _Why:_ this can reveal policy-restricted access attempts, unauthorized resource targeting, or network enumeration. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **`0xC0000071`** — the account password has expired. _Why:_ this distinguishes expired-password failures from bad-password attempts. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **`0xC0000072`** — the account is disabled. _Why:_ authentication attempts against disabled accounts can indicate stale services, old credentials, or attacker testing. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **`0xC0000193`** — the account itself has expired. _Why:_ this identifies failures caused by account lifecycle status rather than password validity. _[GCFA p.248]_
- **`0xC0000234`** — the account is locked. _Why:_ this may support investigation of password-guessing activity or lockout-policy side effects. _[GCFA p.248]_

- **Event ID 4798** — Windows records this event when the local group membership of a user account is queried. _Why:_ this can reveal attempts to discover what privileges or local access a specific user has. _[GCFA p.252]_
- **Event ID 4799** — Windows records this event when membership of a security-enabled local group is queried. _Why:_ this can expose reconnaissance against groups that grant access or administrative capability. _[GCFA p.252]_

### Platform Support

- **Windows Server 2016 support** — Windows Server 2016 introduced the same class of account and group enumeration events. _Why:_ server-side visibility can help detect enterprise reconnaissance against users and groups. _[GCFA p.252]_
- **New event category** — The page describes these events as a newer logging capability for tracking enumeration of sensitive enterprise accounts and groups. _Why:_ this fills a prior visibility gap in Windows event logs. _[GCFA p.252]_

### Attack Context

- **Enumeration as attack-cycle behavior** — Querying accounts and groups has long been a common attacker activity. _Why:_ adversaries need identity and privilege information to choose escalation and movement paths. _[GCFA p.252]_
- **Early-stage reconnaissance** — Account and group enumeration usually occurs early in an intrusion. _Why:_ detecting it early can shorten attacker dwell time and improve mitigation options. _[GCFA p.252]_
- **Early identification value** — Recognizing enumeration activity quickly supports faster defensive response. _Why:_ mitigation is generally easier and cheaper before attackers complete credential theft or broad lateral movement. _[GCFA p.252]_
- **Reduced attacker progress** — If malicious enumeration is detected through these events, the attacker likely has not yet completed later objectives. _Why:_ this gives responders a better chance to contain the incident before major damage occurs. _[GCFA p.252]_

- **Tuning requirement** — These events must be filtered and tuned before they become operationally useful. _Why:_ tuning separates ordinary system behavior from suspicious reconnaissance. _[GCFA p.252]_
- **Sensitive-group focus** — Investigators should prioritize enumeration involving sensitive groups. _Why:_ privileged group discovery is more likely to support escalation or lateral movement. _[GCFA p.252]_
- **Unusual-account focus** — Analysts should focus on accounts that should not normally perform enumeration. _Why:_ unexpected querying accounts can indicate compromised credentials or attacker-run commands. _[GCFA p.252]_
- **Unusual-process focus** — Analysts should prioritize uncommon processes used to perform enumeration. _Why:_ suspicious process context can distinguish attacker tooling from normal Windows management activity. _[GCFA p.252]_

## Page 255

### Log Entry Locations

- **Windows log storage model** — Windows environments record event activity on individual systems rather than in one inherent central location. _Why:_ responders must know which endpoint or server holds the relevant evidence. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Host-specific evidence location** — Each Windows computer writes activity into its own event logs. _Why:_ authentication evidence may exist only on the machine that generated it. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Incident response log targeting** — Knowing which system records a given activity is necessary for efficient collection and analysis. _Why:_ collecting from the wrong host can miss the only available evidence. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Distributed logging implication** — Because Windows logs are spread across hosts, organizations benefit from forwarding them to a centralized store. _Why:_ centralization reduces evidence loss and speeds correlation. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **SIEM relevance** — A SIEM is identified as an example of a centralized repository for Windows event data. _Why:_ SIEM ingestion can preserve and correlate authentication artifacts across systems. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Big data analytics platform relevance** — A large-scale analytics platform is also identified as a suitable centralized log repository. _Why:_ high-volume authentication and authorization events often require scalable search and correlation. _[GCFA p.~255]_

### Authentication Scenario Scope

- **Scenario focus** — The page focuses on common authentication and authorization cases and where their logs are created. _Why:_ mapping actions to log locations is central to forensic reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Generating system rule** — The system that creates a log event stores that event locally. _Why:_ evidence location follows the system that generated the event, not necessarily the investigator’s point of interest. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Security log storage** — The generating system stores relevant entries in its local Security event log. _Why:_ Security.evtx is the primary source for Account Logon and Logon events in this scenario. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Other applicable logs** — Activity may also create entries in additional logs besides the Security log. _Why:_ Security log review may not capture every artifact for the same activity. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **No forwarding condition** — If log forwarding or central aggregation is absent, locally stored logs may be the sole evidence source. _Why:_ responders must preserve local logs before they roll over or are cleared. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Limited review scope** — The page limits its discussion to Account Logon and Logon events in each system’s Security log. _Why:_ the stated scope prevents overgeneralizing the page to all possible Windows artifacts. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Additional logs caveat** — The page notes that other logs can be created for the same activity, as discussed elsewhere in the course section. _Why:_ authentication investigations should not stop at the two Security event categories when more context is needed. _[GCFA p.~255]_

### Local Account Usage

- **Local account manageability** — Most organizations do not heavily depend on local accounts because they are difficult to administer at scale. _Why:_ local account use can be unusual enough to deserve scrutiny in enterprise investigations. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Local account scalability** — Local accounts do not scale well across organizations. _Why:_ widespread or unexpected local account activity may indicate administrative shortcuts or attacker persistence. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Legitimate local account use** — Some organizations still use local accounts despite management drawbacks. _Why:_ investigators must distinguish suspicious use from accepted operational practice. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Attacker local account creation** — Attackers may create local accounts to maintain backdoor access. _Why:_ local account authentication can be a persistence or lateral movement indicator. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Local account log placement** — When a local account is used, the relevant authentication and authorization events are generated on the computer where that local account exists. _Why:_ investigators should collect logs from the target system hosting the account. _[GCFA p.~255]_

- **Account Logon meaning** — Account Logon events represent authentication activity. _Why:_ they show credential validation rather than merely session creation. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Logon meaning** — Logon events represent authorization of a logon session. _Why:_ they show that access was granted to a system or service. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Event ID 4776** — Windows Event ID 4776 represents NTLM authentication in this local-account scenario. _Why:_ it records credential validation for NTLM-based access. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **Event ID 4624** — Windows Event ID 4624 represents successful logon authorization in this scenario. _Why:_ it confirms that a logon session was created after authentication. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **4776 storage location** — Event ID 4776 is created on the system where the local account exists. _Why:_ responders should look on the server hosting the local account, not just the client. _[GCFA p.~255]_
- **4624 storage location** — Event ID 4624 is created on the system where the local account exists. _Why:_ successful access evidence resides on the machine containing the local account. _[GCFA p.~255]_

### Account Logon Versus Logon Events

- **Account Logon event creation** — NTLMv2 domain-account authentication to a file share creates an Account Logon event. _Why:_ Account Logon records identify where credential validation occurred. _[GCFA p.~256]_
- **Logon event creation** — the same access also creates a Logon event on the accessed server. _Why:_ Logon records identify where the authenticated account obtained access to a resource. _[GCFA p.~256]_
- **Domain account authentication location** — domain account authentication occurs on a domain controller. _Why:_ credential-validation evidence may be absent from the file server and present on DCs instead. _[GCFA p.~256]_
- **Resource authorization location** — authorization occurs on the server that hosts the requested resource. _Why:_ access decisions depend on local resource permissions and server security configuration. _[GCFA p.~256]_
- **Authentication versus authorization split** — the DC validates credentials, while the server decides whether the authenticated account is allowed to use the share. _Why:_ investigators must separate credential success from actual resource access. _[GCFA p.~256]_

- **Kerberos SPN requirement** — Kerberos needs a service principal name to identify the target service. _Why:_ without a usable SPN, the client cannot request the proper Kerberos service ticket. _[GCFA p.~256]_
- **SPN naming basis** — the page states that SPNs are based on a system hostname or fully qualified domain name. _Why:_ hostname/FQDN targeting supports Kerberos resolution more naturally than raw IP targeting. _[GCFA p.~256]_
- **IP-address access behavior** — accessing a resource by IP address, as shown in the `net use` example, usually causes NTLMv2 to be used. _Why:_ this explains why modern domain environments can still produce NTLMv2 artifacts. _[GCFA p.~256]_
- **Modern AD NTLMv2 fallback** — even current Windows Active Directory domains commonly use NTLMv2 when the resource is addressed by IP. _Why:_ responders should not assume NTLMv2 is limited to legacy environments. _[GCFA p.~256]_
- **Microsoft IP-address SPN option** — Microsoft provides a way to support IP addresses in SPNs so Kerberos can be used for such access. _Why:_ this is an exception that can change expected log locations and protocol artifacts. _[GCFA p.~256]_
- **IP-address SPN default state** — the IP-address SPN option is not enabled by default. _Why:_ the default expectation for IP-based share access remains NTLMv2. _[GCFA p.~256]_
- **Low adoption of IP-address SPNs** — few organizations deploy IP-address SPNs. _Why:_ most investigations should treat IP-based SMB access as likely NTLMv2 unless environment evidence shows otherwise. _[GCFA p.~256]_
- **IP-to-hostname management burden** — IP-address SPNs are uncommon because manually maintaining IP-to-hostname relationships is complex. _Why:_ operational complexity explains why the Kerberos exception is rarely configured. _[GCFA p.~256]_
- **Reference URL** — the page provides `https://for508.com/g0knz` for more information about IP-address SPN support. _Why:_ this is the cited courseware reference for the Kerberos-over-IP exception. _[GCFA p.~256]_

- **Required DC Access** — the domain controller must be accessed during the logon process for the logon to finish. _Why:_ analysts should expect DC access artifacts even for a user logging on at a client workstation. _[GCFA p.~257]_
- **Service Ticket Requirement for DC Access** — access to the domain controller requires a service ticket. _Why:_ this explains why a second TGS request appears in the sequence. _[GCFA p.~257]_
- **DC TGS Request Setup** — the page states that a TGS request is made for the domain controller, but the provided page text ends before the sentence completes. _Why:_ this marks the visible start of the DC service-ticket stage without inventing missing continuation text. _[GCFA p.~257]_

## Page 258

### Kerberos Service Ticket Events

- **Domain controller service ticket request** — requesting access to a domain controller causes the domain controller to log Kerberos service-ticket activity as Event ID 4769. _Why:_ this identifies the TGS stage of domain-account network logon activity. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Event ID 4769 location** — the Event ID 4769 entry for the domain controller service ticket is recorded on the domain controller. _Why:_ investigators must collect Account Logon evidence from the DC, not only from the endpoint. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Event ID 4769 Service Name field** — in this scenario, the Service Name field contains the domain controller computer account name. _Why:_ the service name helps distinguish which Kerberos service ticket was requested. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **TGS Reply service ticket** — after the client receives the domain controller service ticket in the TGS Reply, that ticket is used for the next access step. _Why:_ this links the ticket-granting stage to the later resource-access event. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Application request to domain controller** — the client uses the received service ticket to submit an AP request to the domain controller. _Why:_ the AP request is the point where the service ticket is presented for access. _[GCFA p.~258]_

### Logon Events

- **Domain controller authorization decision** — because the domain controller controls access to its resources, it makes an authorization decision when the service ticket is presented. _Why:_ this explains why a Logon event is generated in addition to Account Logon events. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Event ID 4624 on domain controller** — the domain controller records Event ID 4624 when it grants the account network access. _Why:_ this event confirms successful logon authorization at the resource side. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3** — the domain controller’s Event ID 4624 uses Logon Type 3 for this activity. _Why:_ Logon Type 3 identifies the access as a network logon rather than an interactive logon. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Network logon to domain controller** — Event ID 4624 with Logon Type 3 represents the account logging on to the domain controller over the network. _Why:_ this helps differentiate domain-controller resource access from local console use. _[GCFA p.~258]_

### Account Logon vs. Logon Event Placement

- **Typical domain-account pattern** — a domain account logging on to the network commonly produces both Account Logon events and Logon events. _Why:_ investigators should expect multiple event categories for one user logon workflow. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Account Logon event storage** — the Account Logon events in this pattern are recorded on the domain controller. _Why:_ authentication evidence for domain accounts is centralized at the DC. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Logon event storage on client** — the client computer records Logon events because it makes its own authorization decision for the account. _Why:_ endpoint logs may contain evidence of the same domain-account session. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Logon event storage on domain controller** — the domain controller also records Logon events because it separately decides whether to permit the account’s access. _Why:_ the same authentication sequence can leave successful-logon artifacts on multiple systems. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Service ticket presentation as trigger** — Logon events are tied to systems deciding whether to allow access after service tickets are presented. _Why:_ this connects Kerberos ticket use to Windows Logon event generation. _[GCFA p.~258]_

### Additional Kerberos and Session Artifacts

- **Additional service tickets** — logs may show other service tickets beyond the domain controller service ticket. _Why:_ a single domain logon can produce several Kerberos events that should not be mistaken for unrelated activity. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **krbtgt service ticket visibility** — service tickets for the krbtgt service on the domain controller may also appear. _Why:_ krbtgt-related entries are expected Kerberos artifacts during normal domain authentication. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Logoff Event ID 4634** — Event ID 4634 may appear as part of the observed sequence. _Why:_ short-lived network sessions can create logoff evidence even during routine authentication. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Rapid network-session teardown** — network logon sessions on the domain controller may be created and ended quickly. _Why:_ brief session lifetimes explain why logon and logoff events may appear close together. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Computer account participation** — the computer account for the requesting client also logs on to the domain controller during the authentication process. _Why:_ machine-account events may accompany user-account activity and should not be ignored. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Computer account logs on domain controller** — the client computer account’s authentication activity generates related log entries on the domain controller. _Why:_ DC logs can include both user and workstation account evidence from the same workflow. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Slide simplification caveat** — some expected entries are omitted from the teaching slide for clarity. _Why:_ real investigations should anticipate more events than a simplified diagram shows. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Real-log completeness caveat** — entries omitted from the slide will still be present in actual event logs. _Why:_ analysts should not treat the slide’s reduced event set as the full forensic footprint. _[GCFA p.~258]_

### Event Volume

- **Domain logon event volume** — when a user signs in at a client using a domain account, the process commonly generates twelve or more event log entries. _Why:_ multiple artifacts are normal for one domain logon and should be correlated rather than counted as separate incidents. _[GCFA p.~258]_

- **Multi-stage recording** — the generated events document different stages of the domain logon process. _Why:_ reconstructing the sequence requires correlating authentication, ticket, logon, and logoff artifacts. _[GCFA p.~258]_

## Page 259

### Kerberos Remote Logon Flow

- **Kerberos Remote Logon with Domain Account** — the page describes where authentication and logon records appear when a domain account accesses a remote server using Kerberos. _Why:_ investigators need to know which host records each part of the transaction. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Client Role** — the client initiates the Kerberos service-access sequence. _Why:_ the client is the source of the ticket request and later presents the service ticket to the destination server. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Domain Controller Role** — the domain controller handles the ticket-granting service exchange for the requested service. _Why:_ the domain controller is where the Kerberos service-ticket request event is recorded. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Server Role** — the destination server receives the service ticket and decides whether the user may access the requested network service. _Why:_ successful or failed network logon authorization is recorded on the server being accessed. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Step 1 · TGS Request** — the client sends a ticket-granting service request to the domain controller. _Why:_ this is the Kerberos step that asks for access to a specific service. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Step 2 · TGS Reply** — the domain controller returns a ticket-granting service reply to the client. _Why:_ this response carries the service ticket the client will later present to the server. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Step 2 · Service Ticket** — the TGS reply includes the service ticket for the requested service. _Why:_ the service ticket is the credential used to request access from the target server. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Step 3 · AP Request** — the client sends an application protocol request to the server. _Why:_ this is the point where the client presents the service ticket to the actual service host. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Step 4 · AP Reply** — the server returns an application protocol reply to the client. _Why:_ this completes the client-server service-authentication exchange shown in the Kerberos flow. _[GCFA p.259]_

### Service Ticket Request

- **Service Access Prerequisite** — before using a Kerberos-protected service, the client must obtain a service ticket from the domain controller. _Why:_ the absence or presence of this request helps reconstruct Kerberos-based access attempts. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Previously Issued TGT** — the client uses an already issued ticket-granting ticket when requesting a service ticket. _Why:_ this links service access back to the earlier Kerberos authentication phase. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **TGS Request Purpose** — the ticket-granting service request asks the domain controller for a ticket to a specific desired service. _Why:_ the requested service identifies what resource the user was trying to access. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Event ID 4769 Location** — the service-ticket request creates Windows Security Event ID 4769 on the domain controller. _Why:_ analysts should search the domain controller, not the target server, for this Kerberos service-ticket request record. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Diagram Value · 4769 (Server)** — the slide labels Event ID 4769 with “Server” in the Kerberos remote-logon diagram. _Why:_ the event records the Kerberos service-ticket request associated with the server/service being requested. _[GCFA p.259]_

### Service Ticket Use

- **TGS Reply Delivery** — the domain controller sends the service ticket back to the client in the TGS reply. _Why:_ the client receives the artifact it must present during service access. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **AP Request Ticket Presentation** — the client provides the service ticket to the destination server inside the application protocol request. _Why:_ this is the server-side point where the user’s Kerberos authorization context becomes available. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Server Long-Term Key** — the server uses its copy of the long-term key for the relevant service account to decrypt the service ticket. _Why:_ this explains why the server can read and validate ticket contents without asking the client for the user’s password. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Service Account Key Association** — the long-term key used by the server corresponds to the service account tied to the requested service. _Why:_ service-account configuration determines whether the server can decrypt the presented ticket. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Service Ticket Contents · User SID** — the service ticket contains the user’s security identifier. _Why:_ the SID supplies the server with the user identity needed for authorization decisions. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Service Ticket Contents · Group Memberships** — the service ticket includes the user’s group membership data. _Why:_ group memberships influence whether the user is allowed to access the server or service. _[GCFA p.259]_

### Server Authorization Events

- **Authorization Decision Point** — after reading the service ticket, the server decides access based on the user’s rights and privileges. _Why:_ Kerberos authentication alone is not the same as successful authorization to the network resource. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Successful Network Logon Event** — if the account has the required access rights and privileges, the server records Event ID 4624 with Logon Type 3. _Why:_ this event confirms successful network logon authorization on the destination system. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Diagram Value · 4624 (type 3)** — the server side of the diagram shows Event ID 4624 with Logon Type 3. _Why:_ this is the event/logon-type combination expected for successful Kerberos remote network access. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Logon Type 3** — Logon Type 3 represents a network logon in this Kerberos remote-access scenario. _Why:_ it distinguishes remote network access from interactive and other logon categories. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Failed Network Authorization Event** — if the requesting account lacks the rights and privileges required for network access to the system, Event ID 4625 is recorded. _Why:_ this identifies failed server-side authorization for the attempted remote access. _[GCFA p.259]_

- **Event ID 4625 Condition** — Event ID 4625 appears when the account is not granted permission to access the target system over the network. _Why:_ the failure indicates an access-control problem or denied access attempt rather than a successful logon. _[GCFA p.259]_

## Page 260

### Account Logon vs. Logon Event Placement

- **Authentication event location rule** — Account Logon events are recorded on the system that stores the account being authenticated. _Why:_ this tells an investigator where to search for authentication evidence. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **Local account authentication location** — When a local account is used, Account Logon events are generated on the client or member server where that local account exists. _Why:_ local-account authentication evidence may not appear on a domain controller. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **Domain account authentication location** — When a domain account is used, Account Logon events are generated on a domain controller. _Why:_ domain-account authentication evidence must be sought from DC Security logs rather than only endpoint logs. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **Authorization event location rule** — Logon events are recorded on the system being accessed. _Why:_ this separates proof of credential validation from proof that access to a target system was granted or attempted. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **Event-location logic** — The slide’s summary is derived by applying the distinction between where authentication happens and where authorization happens. _Why:_ this prevents searching the wrong host class for the wrong event category. _[GCFA p.260]_

### Clients Table

- **Clients · Logon events** — Client systems record Logon events that show access to the client. _Why:_ these events identify accounts attempting to use or reach the client endpoint. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **Clients · Account Logon events** — Client systems record Account Logon events only when authenticating accounts that are local to that client. _Why:_ a client’s Account Logon evidence is limited to its own local-account authentications. _[GCFA p.260]_

### Domain Controllers Table

- **DCs · Domain account Account Logon events** — Domain controllers contain Account Logon events for domain accounts. _Why:_ domain-account authentication evidence is centralized on DCs. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **DCs · Kerberos Account Logon events** — Domain controllers record Account Logon events for domain accounts authenticated with Kerberos. _Why:_ Kerberos authentication activity for domain users must be investigated on DCs. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **DCs · NTLM Account Logon events** — Domain controllers record Account Logon events for domain accounts authenticated with NTLM. _Why:_ NTLM authentication involving domain accounts is also visible on DCs. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **DCs · Logon events** — Domain controllers record Logon events showing access to the domain controller itself. _Why:_ DC logs include not only authentication activity, but also authorization events for sessions accessing the DC. _[GCFA p.260]_

### Member Servers Table

- **Member Servers · Logon events** — Member servers record Logon events that show access to the server. _Why:_ these events identify accounts attempting to access the member server. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **Member Servers · Account Logon events** — Member servers record Account Logon events when authenticating accounts that are local to that server. _Why:_ local administrator or other server-local account use can leave authentication evidence on the server itself. _[GCFA p.260]_

### Client Behavior

- **Client access logging** — A client generates Logon events whenever an account attempts to access that client. _Why:_ endpoint access attempts should be traced in the client’s Logon event records. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **Client Account Logon limitation** — A client has Account Logon events only when the account used is a local account stored on that client. _Why:_ absence of Account Logon events on a client does not rule out domain-account access. _[GCFA p.260]_

### Domain Controller Behavior

- **DC domain-authentication coverage** — Domain controllers hold Account Logon events for all domain accounts. _Why:_ DCs are the authoritative source for domain-account authentication evidence. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **Equal DC role in Active Directory** — Domain controllers operate as peer systems within an Active Directory domain. _Why:_ authentication evidence is not necessarily confined to one preferred DC. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **Typical DC count** — An Active Directory domain commonly has at least two domain controllers. _Why:_ investigators may need to collect or query multiple DCs to find a specific authentication event. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **Authentication event distribution across DCs** — The Account Logon event for a particular authentication may reside on any domain controller in the domain. _Why:_ checking only one DC can miss the relevant event. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **Organization-wide DC access** — Systems across an organization commonly need repeated access to domain controllers. _Why:_ DC logs can contain large volumes of activity from many hosts. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **Authenticated session dependency** — Establishing authenticated sessions commonly requires access to a domain controller. _Why:_ normal domain authentication creates frequent DC interaction that must be distinguished from suspicious access. _[GCFA p.260]_
- **High DC Logon event volume** — Domain controllers accumulate many Logon events because access to them is frequently granted. _Why:_ analysts should expect noisy DC Logon logs and filter carefully. _[GCFA p.260]_

### Member Server Behavior

- **Member server rule equivalence** — Member servers follow the same event-location rules as client systems. _Why:_ the same authentication-versus-authorization logic applies when investigating server access. _[GCFA p.260]_

## Page 261

### Modern Authentication Scope

- **Modern authentication alternatives** — Microsoft provides cloud-based authentication methods in addition to traditional Active Directory domain controller authentication. _Why:_ investigators must know that authentication evidence may exist outside on-premises AD infrastructure. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Cloud-first identity model** — An organization can choose an architecture that does not rely on Active Directory at all. _Why:_ absence of domain controller logs does not mean authentication did not occur. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Direct Entra join** — New Windows computers can be joined directly to an Entra ID tenant. _Why:_ endpoint identity context may be Entra-based rather than AD-domain-based. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Entra ID naming** — Entra ID is the current name for what was formerly Azure AD. _Why:_ analysts may encounter either term in documentation, tooling, or older artifacts. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Entra ID authority role** — In an Entra-joined environment without AD, Entra ID acts as the central authentication authority. _Why:_ primary authentication records should be sought in cloud Entra logs. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Cloud authentication logs** — Authentication activity for Entra-based authentication is recorded in cloud-hosted Entra ID logs. _Why:_ endpoint-only or DC-only collection can miss key authentication evidence. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Active Directory not required** — When systems are directly joined to Entra ID, on-premises Active Directory is no longer required for authentication. _Why:_ investigation workflows must adapt when no AD domain controllers exist. _[GCFA p.~261]_

### Windows Hello Authentication

- **Windows Hello purpose** — Windows Hello supports passwordless authentication. _Why:_ account access may not involve reusable password entry. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Windows Hello for Business purpose** — Windows Hello for Business also enables passwordless sign-in. _Why:_ enterprise authentication artifacts may reflect key-based authentication rather than password use. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Certificate-backed authentication** — Windows Hello and Hello for Business can rely on certificates. _Why:_ certificate artifacts and cloud identity logs may be relevant to authentication reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Public/private key authentication** — Windows Hello and Hello for Business can use asymmetric key pairs. _Why:_ compromise analysis should account for key material and device-bound authentication mechanisms. _[GCFA p.~261]_

### Endpoint Logon Events

- **Endpoint logon persistence** — Even with Entra ID authentication, Windows Logon events are still created on the accessed endpoint. _Why:_ local event logs remain useful for proving where an Entra account was used. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Client log recording** — Clients continue to record Logon events in the same general way as previously described for other authentication models. _Why:_ endpoint Security logs remain part of the timeline. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Member server log recording** — Member servers also continue to record Logon events in the same general way. _Why:_ server-side event collection can still identify account usage. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Other logs unchanged** — Logs outside the authentication-authority distinction generally remain the same. _Why:_ analysts should not discard normal Windows artifact expectations solely because the device is Entra joined. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Endpoint analysis takeaway** — From an endpoint-forensics perspective, Logon events remain available to show Entra account usage locations. _Why:_ endpoint logs can corroborate cloud identity records. _[GCFA p.~261]_

### Event ID 4624 Behavior

- **Network logon event ID** — Network-based logons still generate Windows Security Event ID 4624. _Why:_ standard successful-logon detection logic remains applicable. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Network logon type** — Network-based logons still use Logon Type 3. _Why:_ Type 3 remains the key indicator for remote network access such as share access. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **RDP logon event ID** — Remote Desktop Protocol logons still generate Windows Security Event ID 4624. _Why:_ RDP activity remains visible through standard successful-logon events. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **RDP logon type** — Remote Desktop Protocol logons still use Logon Type 10. _Why:_ analysts can continue using Type 10 to identify RDP sessions in Entra-joined environments. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Local interactive event ID** — Local interactive sign-ins still generate Windows Security Event ID 4624. _Why:_ physical or console-style access remains visible in endpoint Security logs. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Local logon Type 2** — A local logon on an Entra-joined device may appear as Logon Type 2. _Why:_ Type 2 remains one possible indicator of local interactive use. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Local logon Type 7** — A local logon on an Entra-joined device may appear as Logon Type 7. _Why:_ unlock-style logon records may be part of Entra authentication behavior. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Local logon Type 11** — A local logon on an Entra-joined device may appear as Logon Type 11. _Why:_ cached or related local authentication modes may appear during Entra account use. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Variable local logon type cause** — Entra ID authentication differences can cause local interactive Event ID 4624 records to use Type 2, Type 7, or Type 11. _Why:_ investigators should avoid treating only one local logon type as valid for Entra devices. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **AD comparison for RDP and network logons** — RDP and network logons remain the same as in an Active Directory environment. _Why:_ existing event-ID and logon-type interpretation still applies for those access paths. _[GCFA p.~261]_

### Account Naming Artifacts

- **Reported domain value** — The domain field commonly appears as `AzureAD` for Entra accounts. _Why:_ the logged domain may not match the actual tenant name. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Tenant-name mismatch** — The `AzureAD` domain value is typically used regardless of the Entra tenant’s real name. _Why:_ analysts should not infer the tenant name from the domain field alone. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **Email address recording** — The full email address tied to the Entra account is also recorded. _Why:_ the email address can identify the actual user and tenant context more precisely than the domain field. _[GCFA p.~261]_

### Course Scope

- **Entra ID depth limitation** — Detailed Entra ID internals are outside the scope of this course page. _Why:_ this page is focused on endpoint-analysis implications rather than full cloud-forensics methodology. _[GCFA p.~261]_
- **FOR509 reference** — Entra ID details are covered in FOR509: Enterprise Cloud Forensics and Incident Response. _Why:_ deeper cloud identity investigation requires material beyond this FOR508 discussion. _[GCFA p.~261]_

- **Private key secrecy** — the authentication design depends on the private key remaining secret and available only to the authorized user. _Why:_ compromise or misuse analysis must focus on access to the protected key material and the user’s unlock factor. _[GCFA p.262]_
- **Entra ID default authentication** — this passwordless key-based technology is the default authentication approach for Entra ID. _Why:_ Entra ID environments may commonly produce authentication artifacts tied to this model rather than classic domain password flows. _[GCFA p.262]_

### Account Management Event Hunting

- **Unauthorized account creation** — investigators should search for newly created user accounts that were not approved. _Why:_ adversaries may create backdoor accounts to preserve access after initial compromise. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Unauthorized group membership modification** — investigators should look for changes that add or alter account membership in groups without authorization. _Why:_ group membership changes can grant persistence or privilege escalation. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Account modification as persistence** — attackers may create new accounts or alter existing accounts to maintain access to systems. _Why:_ account-level persistence can survive many host-level cleanup actions. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Account modification as privilege escalation** — attackers may change accounts or group membership to raise permissions. _Why:_ elevated rights expand attacker control and investigative scope. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Account and group changes generate Security events** — modifications to user accounts or their group memberships are logged as Windows Security event IDs. _Why:_ the Security log is the primary evidence source for this activity. _[GCFA p.265]_

### Relevant Event IDs

- **Event ID 4720** — Windows records this event when a user account is created. _Why:_ it can reveal attacker-created backdoor accounts. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Event ID 4726** — Windows records this event when a user account is deleted. _Why:_ account deletion can indicate cleanup, concealment, or unauthorized account lifecycle activity. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Event ID 4722** — Windows records this event when a user account is enabled. _Why:_ enabling an account may restore access through a dormant or disabled identity. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Event ID 4725** — Windows records this event when a user account is disabled. _Why:_ disabling accounts can be part of attacker disruption, cleanup, or administrative response timelines. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Event ID 4728** — Windows records this event when a member is added to a security-enabled global group. _Why:_ global group additions can grant domain-wide privileges. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Event ID 4732** — Windows records this event when a member is added to a security-enabled local group. _Why:_ local group additions can grant elevated rights on a specific computer. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Event ID 4738** — Windows records this event when a user account is changed. _Why:_ it supports auditing of detailed account alterations such as password updates or account renames. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Event ID 4756** — Windows records this event when a member is added to a security-enabled universal group. _Why:_ universal group membership may affect access across the forest. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Event ID 4723** — Windows records this event when a user changes their own password. _Why:_ it distinguishes user-initiated password changes from administrator resets. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Event ID 4724** — Windows records this event when an administrator resets a user password. _Why:_ administrator-driven resets can indicate account takeover, remediation, or malicious control. _[GCFA p.265]_

### Security Log Location

- **Security event log** — the account management events discussed on this page are recorded in the Windows Security event log. _Why:_ responders should query this log when investigating account creation, deletion, enablement, disablement, or group membership changes. _[GCFA p.265]_

### Active Directory Group Scope

- **Local group scope** — local groups apply only to the individual local system where they exist. _Why:_ a local group change affects privileges on that specific host rather than the whole domain. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Local group example** — the Administrators group is given as an example of a local group. _Why:_ membership in this group can grant administrative control over a local computer. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Global group scope** — global groups are valid throughout an Active Directory domain. _Why:_ membership changes may affect access across domain resources. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Global group example** — Domain Admins is given as an example of a global group. _Why:_ additions to this group can indicate major domain-level privilege escalation. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Universal group scope** — universal groups are valid across the entire Active Directory forest. _Why:_ membership changes can have forest-wide access implications. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Group event selection depends on scope and type** — Windows uses different event IDs for membership changes depending on the group’s scope and whether it is security-enabled. _Why:_ analysts must map the event ID to the group type to understand privilege impact. _[GCFA p.265]_

### Privileged Group Abuse

- **Rogue account privilege escalation** — attackers can increase a maliciously created account’s permissions by adding it to privileged groups. _Why:_ this can convert persistence into administrative control. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Compromised account privilege escalation** — attackers can raise the access level of an already compromised account by modifying its group membership. _Why:_ this may avoid creating a new account while still expanding attacker privileges. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Security-enabled global group addition** — adding a user to a security-enabled global group generates Event ID 4728. _Why:_ this is a key signal for domain-scope privilege changes. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Security-enabled local group addition** — adding a user to a security-enabled local group generates Event ID 4732. _Why:_ this is a key signal for host-specific privilege changes. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Security-enabled universal group addition** — adding a user to a security-enabled universal group generates Event ID 4756. _Why:_ this can indicate access expansion across the forest. _[GCFA p.265]_

### Fine-Grained Account Changes

- **User account changed event** — Event ID 4738 is generated for changes to a user account. _Why:_ it provides a broad audit point for account attribute changes. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Password update auditing** — Event ID 4738 can help identify account changes that include password updates. _Why:_ password changes may indicate attacker control, user activity, or administrative remediation. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Account rename auditing** — Event ID 4738 can help identify account name changes. _Why:_ renaming can be used to disguise unauthorized accounts or alter identity evidence. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **User-initiated password change distinction** — password changes by the account user generate Event ID 4723. _Why:_ it separates voluntary password changes from administrative resets during timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.265]_
- **Administrator password reset distinction** — password resets performed by an administrator generate Event ID 4724. _Why:_ it identifies privileged intervention and may reveal attacker or responder actions. _[GCFA p.265]_

### Event Log Explorer Capabilities

- **Event Log Explorer · Tool role** — Event Log Explorer is a third-party Windows event-log review and management application. _Why:_ it gives forensic analysts an alternative when Microsoft’s native viewer is too limited. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · Course context** — The page presents Event Log Explorer in the FOR508 Advanced Incident Response, Threat Hunting, and Digital Forensics material. _Why:_ it frames the tool as part of a DFIR log-analysis workflow. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · `.evt` support** — Event Log Explorer can read legacy Windows `.evt` event-log files. _Why:_ older systems and archived evidence may still use the pre-Vista log format. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · `.evtx` support** — Event Log Explorer can read modern Windows `.evtx` event-log files. _Why:_ this is the standard format for current Windows event-log evidence. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · Modern Windows coverage** — The tool supports logs from modern Windows operating systems. _Why:_ analysts can use one interface across many current Windows evidence sources. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · Multiple-log loading** — The tool can open more than one log file at the same time. _Why:_ simultaneous access reduces switching and supports cross-log investigation. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · Parallel searching** — Multiple opened logs can be searched together. _Why:_ this helps find related activity across systems or log sources quickly. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · Parallel filtering** — Multiple opened logs can be filtered together. _Why:_ analysts can apply the same investigative criteria across many logs at once. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · Correlation support** — Opening many logs at once supports correlation work. _Why:_ timelines and repeated attacker activity are easier to identify across machines. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · Log merging** — Event Log Explorer can merge logs together. _Why:_ merged views help analysts compare events from different logs in one review stream. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · Remote log access** — The tool can access event logs from remote systems. _Why:_ this supports live review without first collecting every log into a local file. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · Multiple remote systems** — Event Log Explorer can open logs from several remote systems at the same time. _Why:_ this enables live multi-host review during incident response. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · Corruption tolerance** — Event Log Explorer is highly tolerant of damaged event logs. _Why:_ forensic collections from live systems may produce logs that native tools cannot open. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · Corrupted-log handling** — Working with corrupted log files is described as one of the tool’s major advantages. _Why:_ damaged logs may still contain recoverable forensic evidence. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · Standard Mode** — Standard Mode opens a log through API-style methods. _Why:_ this provides a conventional parsing path when the log is readable through normal interfaces. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · Direct Mode** — Direct Mode reads the event log by parsing the raw file content. _Why:_ raw parsing can recover or review data when normal API-style access fails. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · Offline-parser benefit** — Direct raw parsing gives the tool some benefits of an offline parser. _Why:_ offline-style parsing is useful for evidence files rather than live-only viewing. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Event Log Explorer · GUI review benefit** — The tool combines parser-style access with a graphical review interface. _Why:_ analysts can inspect difficult logs without abandoning an interactive review workflow. _[GCFA p.268]_

### Windows Event Viewer Limitations

- **Windows Event Viewer · Large-log review weakness** — The built-in Windows Event Viewer can be awkward for reviewing many events. _Why:_ cumbersome interfaces slow investigations and increase the chance of missed evidence. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Windows Event Viewer · Multi-security-log limitation** — Windows Event Viewer cannot load multiple Security logs from different systems for parallel filtering or searching. _Why:_ cross-host comparison is common in incident response, especially for lateral movement. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Windows Event Viewer · Corruption intolerance** — Windows Event Viewer is poor at handling corrupted logs. _Why:_ a native viewer failure does not mean the evidence has no usable records. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Forensic collection · Live-system corruption risk** — Event logs can become corrupted when they are collected from running systems. _Why:_ live acquisition creates evidence-handling conditions where tool tolerance matters. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Responder behavior · Viewer failure risk** — Less experienced responders may stop investigating when Event Viewer cannot open a collected log. _Why:_ analysts should try more capable tools before treating the log as unusable. _[GCFA p.268]_
- **Tool-selection lesson** — The page emphasizes that better alternatives exist when Event Viewer fails. _Why:_ tool limitations should not prematurely end log analysis. _[GCFA p.268]_
