## Page 272

### Unexpected Network Logons

- **Lateral movement network logons** — many lateral movement methods create Windows Security Event ID 4624 with Logon Type 3 on the destination host. _Why:_ this event pattern is a common starting point for identifying remote access to a target system. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Event ID 4624** — this Windows Security log event records a successful logon. _Why:_ successful authentication records can show which account accessed a system during suspected lateral movement. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Logon Type 3** — Logon Type 3 represents a network logon. _Why:_ most non-RDP remote access activity appears under this logon type, so it is central to lateral movement triage. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Target-system recording** — Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 is generated on the system being accessed remotely. _Why:_ responders should look on the destination host, not only the originating host, when investigating network-based lateral movement. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Authenticated remote access requirement** — most lateral movement techniques require valid authentication to the remote system. _Why:_ the account used in the logon can connect the activity to a compromised credential or authorized user context. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **RDP exception** — RDP is called out as an exception to the general pattern where most remote-system logons are recorded as Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3. _Why:_ investigators should not assume all lateral movement, especially RDP, will fit the Network Logon pattern. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **High-volume Event ID 4624 Type 3 activity** — many legitimate and suspicious actions can produce Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3. _Why:_ the event alone is not enough to determine whether activity was benign or malicious. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Need for follow-on analysis** — additional investigation is required to determine what activity followed or caused a network logon. _Why:_ Logon Type 3 is a broad signal that must be interpreted with surrounding evidence. _[GCFA p.272]_

### Lateral Movement Techniques

- **Network share access** — accessing a remote network share can generate Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 on the target system. _Why:_ remote share use is a common lateral movement path and can leave successful network logon evidence. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Named pipes** — use of named pipes can generate Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 on the target system. _Why:_ named pipes are used by several remote administration and attack techniques, so their logon context can help explain lateral movement. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Remote scheduled tasks** — remotely using scheduled tasks can generate Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 on the target system. _Why:_ attackers often create or run tasks remotely for execution, persistence, or movement between hosts. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Remote service execution** — executing services remotely can generate Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 on the target system. _Why:_ remote service creation or execution is a common administrative and adversary technique that needs contextual review. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **PsExec** — PsExec is specifically included as an example of remote service execution that can generate Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3. _Why:_ PsExec-style activity is widely associated with lateral movement and remote command execution. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **DCOM abuse** — abusing DCOM for remote activity can generate Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 on the target system. _Why:_ DCOM can enable remote execution paths that may blend with legitimate administrative behavior. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **PowerShell remoting** — PowerShell remoting can generate Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 on the target system. _Why:_ PowerShell remoting is a frequent administrative channel and attacker tradecraft path. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **wmic /node** — using `wmic /node` can generate Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 on the target system. _Why:_ remote WMI execution is a common lateral movement technique and may be visible through network logon records. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **winrs** — using `winrs` can generate Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 on the target system. _Why:_ WinRS supports remote command execution and can leave network logon evidence on the destination host. _[GCFA p.272]_

### Detection Starting Points

- **Unexpected source computer** — detection may begin when an unusual computer is seen making a network logon to a system. _Why:_ an unexpected source host can indicate compromised credentials or unauthorized lateral movement. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Unexpected account** — detection may begin when an unusual account is used for a network logon. _Why:_ abnormal account use can reveal credential misuse or attacker-controlled access. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Unexpected network logon** — Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 can be used to identify unexpected connections to a system. _Why:_ these records can provide the first observable sign of remote access requiring investigation. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Technique-specific artifacts** — detection can also begin with artifacts produced by one of the lateral movement techniques rather than with the logon event itself. _Why:_ responders may first notice execution, service, task, PowerShell, or other evidence and only later connect it to a network logon. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Anomaly-first investigation** — an investigation may start when a suspicious artifact from a lateral movement method is detected. _Why:_ correlating that artifact back to logon records can identify the account and source system involved. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Logon-first investigation** — an investigation may start from suspicious Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 activity and then branch into other logs or forensic artifacts. _Why:_ the logon gives a timestamp, account, and origin point for deeper analysis. _[GCFA p.272]_

### Correlation Sources

- **Security log events** — Security log records around the network logon time should be reviewed for context. _Why:_ related authentication, authorization, and account activity can clarify what happened after access was established. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Process creation events** — process creation records around the network logon time should be examined. _Why:_ remote execution often results in new processes that explain the purpose of the connection. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **PowerShell logs** — PowerShell logging around the network logon time can provide additional context. _Why:_ PowerShell remoting or script execution may reveal commands run during lateral movement. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Sysmon network connection events** — Sysmon network connection telemetry around the network logon time can be used for correlation. _Why:_ network telemetry can help connect the source, destination, and activity surrounding the logon. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Other forensic artifacts** — forensic evidence outside event logs may be needed to interpret the network logon. _Why:_ artifacts left by tools or techniques can identify the specific lateral movement method used. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Multi-source analysis** — understanding the activity usually requires combining several data sources. _Why:_ no single log source is likely to provide the full account of the remote activity. _[GCFA p.272]_

### Event Context

- **Account detail in logon event** — the Logon event includes information about the account used for the connection. _Why:_ the account field helps determine whether access came from an expected user, service account, or compromised credential. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Originating system detail in logon event** — the Logon event includes information about the system from which the connection originated. _Why:_ the source system can identify the lateral movement pivot point. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Context for suspiciousness** — the account and source system details provide clues for distinguishing routine activity from suspicious activity. _Why:_ the same technique may be benign or malicious depending on who used it and from where. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Technique indicators may be legitimate** — indicators associated with lateral movement methods often also appear during normal operations. _Why:_ responders must avoid treating every occurrence as malicious without surrounding context. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Normal-versus-malicious judgment** — surrounding context is required to separate ordinary administrative behavior from attacker activity. _Why:_ many lateral movement artifacts overlap with legitimate enterprise administration. _[GCFA p.272]_
- **Correlation with logon events** — when another artifact is detected first, corresponding Logon events should be correlated to enrich the investigation. _Why:_ logon records can add the user account and source host behind the suspicious artifact. _[GCFA p.272]_

## Page 273

### Network Connection Logging

- **Successful TCP/UDP connections** — Windows hosts generally do not record every successful TCP or UDP connection because the event volume would be very large. _Why:_ absence of connection logs is normal and should not be mistaken for proof that no connection occurred. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Windows successful connection auditing** — Windows is capable of recording details about successful network connections when the relevant logging is enabled. _Why:_ investigators should know the artifact can exist even though it is often disabled. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **High-volume logging constraint** — Successful network connection logging is uncommon primarily because it can create excessive log volume. _Why:_ explains why investigators often need alternate telemetry sources. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Windows Defender Firewall log** — Host firewall logging can record connection activity, with `pfirewall.log` identified as the Windows Defender Firewall log file. _Why:_ this file can provide host-side network evidence when firewall logging is enabled. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Windows Firewall successful connection logging** — Windows Firewall logs can be configured to capture successful network connections. _Why:_ enabled firewall logging may reveal network sessions otherwise missing from standard event logs. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Windows Firewall logging rarity** — Windows Firewall successful-connection logging is rarely enabled in typical environments. _Why:_ investigators should not assume `pfirewall.log` contains successful connection history. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Windows Filtering Platform logging** — Windows Filtering Platform can record connection events in the Security log. _Why:_ WFP events may provide host-based evidence of network activity. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Security Event ID 5156** — Windows Filtering Platform connection activity is associated with Security log Event ID `5156`. _Why:_ this event ID is a specific pivot for finding permitted network connections. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Windows Filtering Platform successful connection logging** — WFP logging can be enabled to capture successful network connections. _Why:_ when available, it can help reconstruct authenticated network activity. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Windows Filtering Platform logging rarity** — WFP successful-connection logging is also rarely enabled. _Why:_ lack of Event ID `5156` records may reflect configuration rather than absence of traffic. _[GCFA p.273]_

### Sysmon

- **Sysmon** — Sysmon is a no-cost Microsoft Sysinternals extension that increases Windows auditing capability. _Why:_ it is a common optional telemetry source in incident response investigations. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Sysmon source team** — Sysmon is produced by Microsoft’s Sysinternals team. _Why:_ establishes the tool’s provenance and expected operational context. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Sysmon reference URL** — The page gives `https://for508.com/am6zl` as the Sysmon reference link. _Why:_ identifies the specific course-provided pointer for the tool. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Sysmon Event ID 3** — Sysmon uses Event ID `3` for network connection events. _Why:_ this is the key event ID to search when Sysmon network logging is configured. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Sysmon successful connection default** — Sysmon does not log successful network connections by default. _Why:_ investigators must verify the deployed Sysmon configuration before relying on Event ID `3`. _[GCFA p.273]_

### Network Monitoring Sources

- **External network monitoring** — Investigators should use network monitoring telemetry when it exists. _Why:_ network-side sources can compensate for missing host successful-connection logs. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Zeek** — Zeek is listed as an example of a dedicated network monitoring tool. _Why:_ Zeek logs can help identify protocols, ports, hosts, and session activity. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Zeek domain** — The page identifies `zeek.org` as the Zeek website. _Why:_ provides the named source location for the monitoring platform. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **NetFlow/IPFIX** — NetFlow/IPFIX data is listed as a useful network telemetry source. _Why:_ flow records can reveal communication pairs and ports even without packet contents. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Network appliance telemetry** — NetFlow/IPFIX may be gathered from network appliances. _Why:_ routers, switches, or similar infrastructure may hold relevant lateral movement evidence. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **XDR** — XDR is listed as an example of a telemetry source that may include network monitoring data. _Why:_ some endpoint/security platforms aggregate network evidence useful for lateral movement analysis. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **EDR network expansion** — Some EDR products add network security monitoring capabilities. _Why:_ endpoint tools may provide more than process and host telemetry. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **XDR marketing label** — EDR products with expanded network monitoring are often branded as XDR. _Why:_ investigators may need to search XDR consoles for network evidence. _[GCFA p.273]_

### Authenticated Remote Access

- **Post-authentication access** — After authentication to a remote Windows system, the session may access multiple services, protocols, and Windows components. _Why:_ a single authenticated logon can represent several possible lateral movement mechanisms. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Nature of remote access** — Determining what kind of access occurred helps identify likely lateral movement paths. _Why:_ knowing the accessed service narrows the investigation from generic logon evidence to a specific technique. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Protocol and port analysis** — Network protocols and their associated ports can help classify the type of communication. _Why:_ port/protocol mapping is a practical way to infer the accessed Windows service. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Connection-port correlation** — Correlating observed connection activity with port numbers can identify the protocol used during an authenticated session. _Why:_ this converts raw network events into meaningful lateral movement hypotheses. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Suspicious source-and-account pairing** — Suspicious connections should be evaluated using both the source system and the account involved. _Why:_ source host plus credential context helps distinguish expected administration from possible compromise. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Network data for lateral movement** — Network telemetry can help determine which lateral movement vector may have been used. _Why:_ it directs the investigator toward the most relevant follow-on artifacts. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Target artifact narrowing** — Understanding the likely network vector helps focus searches for additional evidence on the target system. _Why:_ different lateral movement methods leave different Windows artifacts. _[GCFA p.273]_

### Port Indicators

- **TCP port 445** — Communication over TCP `445` suggests SMB activity. _Why:_ SMB is a major Windows lateral movement and remote file/service access pathway. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **TCP port 135** — Communication over TCP `135` suggests direct RPC activity. _Why:_ RPC activity can indicate remote Windows management or lateral movement behavior. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **TCP port 5985** — Communication over TCP `5985` indicates PowerShell remoting or related Windows Remote Management activity. _Why:_ this port is a strong pivot for WinRM-based lateral movement. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **WinRM** — Windows Remote Management activity is associated with TCP `5985` on this page. _Why:_ WinRM artifacts should be considered when this port appears in authenticated-session telemetry. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **winrs** — `winrs` is listed as an example of Windows Remote Management activity tied to TCP `5985`. _Why:_ command execution through WinRM may explain remote activity on that port. _[GCFA p.273]_

### Correlation With System Activity

- **Process launch review** — Investigators should inspect process execution around the time of the network connection. _Why:_ nearby process starts may identify the tool or command that initiated lateral movement. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **System activity review** — Other host activity around the connection time should also be examined. _Why:_ related artifacts can corroborate the network event and clarify attacker actions. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Attack-specific artifacts** — Investigators should search for logs and artifacts associated with particular attack types. _Why:_ technique-specific evidence can confirm the suspected lateral movement mechanism. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Subsequent lateral movement coverage** — Later course material discusses techniques that create Event ID `4624` Logon Type `3` on the target host. _Why:_ this page frames those later artifacts as follow-on evidence after network-protocol analysis. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Target-side Logon Type 3** — The lateral movement techniques referenced produce Windows Security Event ID `4624` with Logon Type `3` on the target system. _Why:_ this event is a central target-host artifact for authenticated network logons. _[GCFA p.273]_
- **Additional target artifacts** — The referenced lateral movement techniques also create artifacts beyond Event ID `4624` Logon Type `3`. _Why:_ investigators should not stop at the logon event and should seek technique-specific traces. _[GCFA p.273]_

## Page 275

### Network Share Lateral Movement

- **Network share auditing scenario** — The page’s investigation scenario is to review activity involving network shares. _Why:_ share access can reveal lateral movement, data staging, malware distribution, or unauthorized internal access. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Network shares as investigation evidence** — Reviewing which shares were accessed can support many investigation types, including employee activity reviews and external intrusion cases. _Why:_ touched shares help reconstruct where data moved or where an actor interacted with shared resources. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Touched shares as data-flow evidence** — Identifying accessed file shares helps analysts understand movement of data through an environment. _Why:_ share access can show collection paths, staging locations, or operational reach during an intrusion. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **File share mounting as lateral movement technique** — Adversaries commonly mount file shares while moving across systems in an enterprise. _Why:_ mounted shares are a routine mechanism for reaching other hosts and shared repositories. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **File shares for malware distribution** — Attackers may use mounted network shares to place or spread malicious files. _Why:_ share access can indicate propagation infrastructure or malware deployment paths. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **File shares for data collection** — Attackers may use mounted shares to gather data for theft. _Why:_ share activity can expose collection behavior before exfiltration. _[GCFA p.275]_

### Relevant Event IDs

- **Event ID 5140** — Windows records that a network share was accessed. _Why:_ this is a primary event for identifying share-level access on a host. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Event ID 5145** — Windows records access to a shared object when Detailed File Share auditing is enabled. _Why:_ this event can identify item-level access inside a share. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Event IDs 5142–5144** — Windows uses this event range for share creation, share modification, and share deletion activity. _Why:_ changes to shares can reveal attacker-created access paths or altered sharing configuration. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Event ID 5142** — This event is part of the share lifecycle tracking range for share creation, modification, and deletion. _Why:_ share lifecycle events can expose new or manipulated shares during an investigation. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Event ID 5143** — This event is part of the share lifecycle tracking range for share creation, modification, and deletion. _Why:_ share lifecycle events can expose new or manipulated shares during an investigation. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Event ID 5144** — This event is part of the share lifecycle tracking range for share creation, modification, and deletion. _Why:_ share lifecycle events can expose new or manipulated shares during an investigation. _[GCFA p.275]_

### Audit Policy Requirements

- **Object access auditing requirement** — Network share auditing requires object access auditing to be enabled. _Why:_ without the correct audit policy, the expected share-access events may not exist. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Audit File Share policy path** — The Advanced Audit Policy Configuration setting named `Object Access -> Audit File Share` must be configured to audit network shares. _Why:_ this setting enables collection of share-access telemetry. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Event ID 5140 enablement behavior** — After `Object Access -> Audit File Share` is enabled, Windows records Event ID 5140 for network share access on the system. _Why:_ this links the audit setting directly to the share-access event analysts expect to query. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Audit Detailed File Share policy path** — The Advanced Audit Policy Configuration setting named `Object Access -> Audit Detailed File Share` can be enabled to collect item-level shared-object access. _Why:_ this setting is needed when share-level events are not detailed enough. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Event ID 5145 enablement behavior** — Enabling `Object Access -> Audit Detailed File Share` produces Event ID 5145 events for individual item access. _Why:_ this provides file-level visibility inside shares. _[GCFA p.275]_

### Event ID 5140 Fields And Limits

- **Event ID 5140 share name** — Event ID 5140 includes the accessed share name. _Why:_ the share name identifies which shared resource was touched. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Event ID 5140 folder path** — Event ID 5140 records the folder path associated with the share. _Why:_ the backing path helps map a share name to the local filesystem location. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Event ID 5140 logon account** — Event ID 5140 records the account used for the share access. _Why:_ the account links the share access to a user or security principal. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Event ID 5140 remote IP address** — Event ID 5140 records the remote IP address making the connection. _Why:_ the source IP helps identify the system initiating access. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Security log share name** — The Security event log provides the share name for a network share connection. _Why:_ this field helps analysts identify the targeted shared resource. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Security log remote machine IP** — The Security event log provides the IP address of the remote system connecting to the share. _Why:_ this gives source attribution for the share access. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Account Name correlation** — The `Account Name` field can be used to track the account involved in the share-access activity. _Why:_ correlating by account helps connect share access with other actions performed by the same principal. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Logon ID correlation** — The `Logon ID` field can be used to track other activity from the same logon session. _Why:_ the logon session identifier helps join related events across the Security log. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Event ID 5140 file-detail limitation** — Event ID 5140 does not identify the specific files accessed within a share. _Why:_ analysts cannot rely on 5140 alone for file-level access reconstruction. _[GCFA p.275]_

### Detailed File Share Auditing

- **Detailed File Share auditing purpose** — Detailed File Share auditing provides visibility into individual files or items accessed through a share. _Why:_ item-level access can show exactly what was touched rather than only which share was used. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Event ID 5145 item-level detail** — Event ID 5145 records individual item access. _Why:_ this can reveal specific accessed files during a share-based investigation. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Event ID 5145 noise risk** — Detailed File Share auditing can generate a very large number of events. _Why:_ high event volume can create storage, performance, and analysis burdens. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Tactical use of Detailed File Share auditing** — Detailed File Share auditing should be used selectively rather than broadly. _Why:_ selective deployment limits noise while preserving visibility where it matters. _[GCFA p.275]_
- **Sensitive-system use case** — Detailed File Share auditing is likely best enabled only for highly sensitive systems. _Why:_ sensitive systems justify the higher event volume because file-level access has greater investigative value. _[GCFA p.275]_

## Page 276

### Event ID 5140 Purpose

- **Event ID 5140** — records that a Windows network share object was accessed. _Why:_ it is a core Security log artifact for identifying SMB/file-share access during lateral movement investigations. _[GCFA p.~276]_
- **File share access tracking** — Event ID 5140 can identify the share that was reached over the network. _Why:_ share names help scope what remote resource an account interacted with. _[GCFA p.~276]_
- **Share disk location tracking** — Event ID 5140 can report the local filesystem path backing the accessed share. _Why:_ the on-disk path connects a network share name to the actual server directory that may need forensic review. _[GCFA p.~276]_
- **Source IP tracking** — Event ID 5140 can show the IP address of the system that initiated share access. _Why:_ the source address helps identify the remote host involved in possible lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~276]_
- **Account tracking** — Event ID 5140 can show which user account was used for the share access. _Why:_ the account field ties the network-share activity to credential use. _[GCFA p.~276]_

### Event Generation Behavior

- **One event per share session** — Event ID 5140 is created when access to a shared object is granted for a session, not for every individual file request inside the share. _Why:_ investigators must not assume one 5140 event equals one file access. _[GCFA p.~276]_
- **Shared-folder example** — if a user accesses one shared folder and then opens 100 files inside it within a short interval, only one Event ID 5140 may be produced. _Why:_ file-level activity can be much larger than the 5140 count suggests. _[GCFA p.~276]_
- **Initial-access timestamp** — the event time represents the first access to the shared folder for that session. _Why:_ later activity may occur after the logged time without additional 5140 entries. _[GCFA p.~276]_
- **Unlogged follow-on access** — later access within the same share session may not create more Event ID 5140 records. _Why:_ timeline analysis must account for silent activity after the initial share-access event. _[GCFA p.~276]_

### Access Field Semantics

- **Accesses field behavior** — Event ID 5140 always displays `ReadData (or ListDirectory)` as the requested access. _Why:_ this field does not prove the actor only read or listed content. _[GCFA p.~276]_
- **Modification blind spot** — Event ID 5140 can still show `ReadData (or ListDirectory)` even when files were changed. _Why:_ responders should not rule out writes based solely on the 5140 access string. _[GCFA p.~276]_
- **File-addition blind spot** — Event ID 5140 can still show `ReadData (or ListDirectory)` even when files were added. _Why:_ new-file creation may be hidden behind the same generic access value. _[GCFA p.~276]_
- **Deletion blind spot** — Event ID 5140 can still show `ReadData (or ListDirectory)` even when files were deleted. _Why:_ destructive activity may not be visible in this event’s access summary. _[GCFA p.~276]_
- **Reason for generic access value** — the `ReadData (or ListDirectory)` value reflects the initial access granted to each object. _Why:_ the field captures session-opening access rather than all later permission use. _[GCFA p.~276]_
- **Write/modify omission** — later requests for permissions such as writing or modifying data are not captured by Event ID 5140. _Why:_ determining actual file changes requires other evidence. _[GCFA p.~276]_

### Event ID 5145 Relationship

## Page 277

### Named Pipe Fundamentals

- **Named pipes** — Windows named pipes function like temporary memory-backed objects that processes can use to exchange data. _Why:_ they are an interprocess communication mechanism that can also support lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Named pipes · data handling** — A named pipe can hold data temporarily in a first-in, first-out sequence. _Why:_ FIFO behavior explains how one process can enqueue data and another can retrieve it in order. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Named pipes · naming** — A named pipe has an assigned name that processes can use as a reference, similar to how files are referenced by name. _Why:_ named access lets separate processes locate and use the same communication object. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Named pipes · local process communication** — Named pipes can be used by processes running on the same computer. _Why:_ local named-pipe activity can represent normal IPC or malware component coordination. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Named pipes · remote process communication** — Named pipes can also be reached from another system over an SMB connection. _Why:_ remote named-pipe access is a common lateral-movement and remote-control communication path. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Interprocess communication need** — Processes commonly need mechanisms to pass information to other processes. _Why:_ named pipes are one Windows mechanism that satisfies this requirement. _[GCFA p.~277]_

### IPC$ And SMB

- **IPC$ share** — The IPC$ administrative share exposes named pipes for network access. _Why:_ remote named-pipe communication typically depends on IPC$ access. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **IPC$ · purpose** — IPC$ supports interprocess communication between processes on different computers. _Why:_ it provides the network-facing path for cross-host named-pipe use. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **SMB protocol** — SMB can be used to connect to the IPC$ share. _Why:_ SMB-backed IPC$ access means named-pipe traffic may appear within ordinary Windows file-sharing traffic. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **IPC$ compared with file shares** — A normal shared folder exposes files, while IPC$ exposes named pipes on the system. _Why:_ this distinction helps analysts interpret IPC$ connections as IPC access rather than ordinary file browsing. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **SMB port** — SMB named-pipe communication can use TCP port 445. _Why:_ traffic over TCP/445 may carry remote named-pipe communication, including malicious C2 traffic. _[GCFA p.~277]_

- **Diagram · Pipe_123** — The example named pipe is labeled `Pipe_123`. _Why:_ this is the specific pipe name shown for the communication example. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Diagram · Computer1** — `Computer1` is the system hosting the named pipe `Pipe_123`. _Why:_ host location matters when determining where the pipe object resides. _[GCFA p.~277]_

- **Diagram · Process 1** — `Process 1` is shown on `Computer1` interacting with `Pipe_123`. _Why:_ it represents the local process using the pipe. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Diagram · Process 2** — `Process 2` is shown on `Computer2` communicating remotely with the pipe. _Why:_ it represents the remote process using IPC$ and SMB to exchange data. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Diagram · IPC$** — `IPC$` is shown between the two computers as the share used for pipe access. _Why:_ it identifies the network share involved in remote named-pipe communication. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Diagram · SMB** — `SMB` is shown as the protocol carrying the connection between `Computer1` and `Computer2`. _Why:_ SMB provides the transport path analysts should consider when reviewing network and log evidence. _[GCFA p.~277]_

- **Pipe_123 · local write/read pattern** — One process on `Computer1` could write data into `Pipe_123`, and another process on `Computer1` could read that data. _Why:_ this demonstrates the local IPC model. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Pipe_123 · remote read pattern** — `Process 2` on `Computer2` could request access through `IPC$` to read a message from `Pipe_123` on `Computer1`. _Why:_ this is the remote named-pipe behavior relevant to lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Pipe_123 · remote write pattern** — `Process 2` on `Computer2` could write a new message into `Pipe_123`. _Why:_ remote processes can send data back through the same pipe mechanism. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Pipe_123 · Process 1 retrieval** — `Process 1` could retrieve the message placed into the pipe by `Process 2`. _Why:_ this completes the cross-host exchange shown in the example. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Named pipes · bidirectional channel** — The example establishes two-way communication between processes across the network. _Why:_ bidirectional communication supports remote control and malware coordination. _[GCFA p.~277]_

### Attacker Use

- **Named pipes · malware communication** — Attackers commonly use named pipes to let malware on separate systems communicate. _Why:_ this technique can support command, control, and coordination inside a compromised environment. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Named pipes · stealth advantage** — Named pipes can avoid the need to open a new unusual listening port on a compromised host. _Why:_ avoiding abnormal ports can make attacker communication less obvious. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Named pipes · traffic blending** — Remote named-pipe traffic can blend into existing SMB communications. _Why:_ defenders may overlook malicious communication if it is hidden inside common Windows network activity. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Named pipes · SMB channel reuse** — Because SMB already commonly uses TCP/445, named-pipe communication over SMB can ride on an expected enterprise network channel. _Why:_ normal-looking TCP/445 traffic may still carry malicious IPC activity. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Cobalt Strike** — Cobalt Strike is named as a C2 platform that uses named pipes for communication inside compromised networks. _Why:_ Cobalt Strike named-pipe use is a concrete detection and hunting target. _[GCFA p.~277]_
- **Other C2 platforms** — C2 frameworks beyond Cobalt Strike also use named pipes for internal compromised-network communication. _Why:_ detections should focus on the technique, not only one named tool. _[GCFA p.~277]_

### Named Pipes and IPC$

- **Named pipes · Legitimate Windows use** — named pipes are used by normal Windows features, including network logon activity. _Why:_ named pipe activity can be benign and should not be treated as suspicious by default. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **IPC$ access · Not automatically malicious** — a connection to the `IPC$` share does not, by itself, prove malicious activity. _Why:_ investigators need context before labeling `IPC$` activity as lateral movement or abuse. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **IPC$ access · Context requirement** — `IPC$` access should be evaluated using the source and destination computers involved in the connection. _Why:_ unusual host pairings can turn otherwise normal activity into a useful lead. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **IPC$ access · Account context** — the account used for an `IPC$` connection is a key part of determining whether the activity is expected or suspicious. _Why:_ privileged, rare, or unexpected account use can indicate attacker activity. _[GCFA p.~278]_

### Sysmon Named Pipe Evidence

- **Sysmon · Named pipe visibility** — Sysmon can provide detail about which named pipe was accessed. _Why:_ Windows share access logs may show `IPC$` access without identifying the specific pipe involved. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Sysmon Event ID 18 · Pipe connection** — Sysmon records Event ID `18` when a process connects to a named pipe. _Why:_ this event can identify pipe usage associated with suspicious `IPC$` activity. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Sysmon Event ID 18 · Timestamp correlation** — Event ID `18` timestamps can be compared with suspicious `IPC$` access times. _Why:_ time alignment helps determine which named pipe was likely accessed during the suspicious share connection. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Sysmon Event ID 18 · Suspicious IPC$ triage** — Event ID `18` can help determine the pipe name used at the time of suspicious `IPC$` access. _Why:_ the pipe name is often needed to distinguish normal Windows behavior from tool or malware behavior. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Sysmon Event ID 17 · Pipe creation** — Sysmon records Event ID `17` when a named pipe is created. _Why:_ creation telemetry can identify the process responsible for making the pipe available. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Sysmon Event ID 17 · Process attribution** — after a pipe name is identified, Event ID `17` can be used to find the process on the target host that created or used that pipe. _Why:_ process attribution links network-facing pipe activity to executable behavior on the destination system. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Sysmon Event ID 17 · Creator process data** — Event ID `17` includes information about the process that created the named pipe. _Why:_ this supports attribution to legitimate services, administration tools, malware, or attacker tooling. _[GCFA p.~278]_

### EDR and Threat Intelligence

- **EDR tools · Named pipe telemetry** — endpoint detection and response products may also expose named pipe usage data. _Why:_ EDR data can supplement or replace Sysmon coverage when investigating pipe access. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Suspicious named pipe · External lookup** — when a pipe name appears suspicious, searching the web can help identify prior reporting about that pipe. _Why:_ known pipe names may appear in malware writeups, attack reports, or tooling documentation. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Suspicious named pipe · Threat intelligence query** — querying a cyber threat intelligence platform can help determine whether the same pipe has been observed in malware or campaigns. _Why:_ external sightings can strengthen or weaken the hypothesis that the pipe is attacker-related. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Named pipe names · Malware association** — some malware families or attack campaigns reuse recognizable named pipe names. _Why:_ a pipe name can become an indicator that guides scoping and attribution. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Named pipe names · Legitimate reuse caution** — many normal Windows components use well-known named pipes. _Why:_ matching a known pipe name does not automatically prove malicious activity. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Suspicious origin · Service identification** — if the source host or account makes a pipe connection suspicious, searching the pipe name may reveal what service was accessed. _Why:_ identifying the service can explain the activity even when it is unrelated to malware. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Named pipe research · Non-malware value** — pipe-name research can be useful even when no malware association exists. _Why:_ it can still identify legitimate Windows functionality or application behavior behind the connection. _[GCFA p.~278]_

### Windows Named Pipe Implementation

- **Named pipes · File-like treatment** — Windows handles named pipes as a special category of file. _Why:_ this explains why pipe objects can be referenced through filesystem-like paths. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Named pipes · Virtual filesystem** — named pipes are exposed through a virtual filesystem. _Why:_ investigators can enumerate and reference pipe objects using filesystem-style syntax. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Named Pipe File System · Implementation** — the virtual filesystem for named pipes is the Named Pipe File System. _Why:_ this identifies the Windows subsystem responsible for exposing named pipe objects. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **`npfs.sys` · Named pipe driver** — the Named Pipe File System is implemented by the `npfs.sys` driver. _Why:_ the driver name is useful when reasoning about Windows internals and pipe object handling. _[GCFA p.~278]_

### PowerShell Pipe Enumeration

- **PowerShell pipe listing · Command prompt** — the page shows a PowerShell prompt of `PS C:\>`. _Why:_ the command is intended to be run from PowerShell on a Windows system. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **PowerShell pipe listing · Command** — `(get-childitem \\.\pipe\).FullName` lists named pipe full names. _Why:_ this provides a direct way to enumerate pipes present on a host. _[GCFA p.~278]_

- **PowerShell pipe listing · `\\.\pipe\` path** — the command targets the local named pipe namespace at `\\.\pipe\`. _Why:_ this is the Windows path used to access named pipe objects on the local system. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **PowerShell pipe listing · `.FullName` property** — the command outputs the `FullName` property of each pipe object. _Why:_ this returns complete pipe paths rather than abbreviated object listings. _[GCFA p.~278]_

### Investigation Workflow and Noise

- **Named pipes · Interprocess communication** — named pipes are commonly used for communication between processes. _Why:_ high legitimate usage makes pipe telemetry common and potentially noisy. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Named pipe access events · Noise risk** — events that record named pipe access can produce large volumes of normal activity. _Why:_ investigators need filtering and correlation to avoid chasing routine system behavior. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Event ID 5140 · Suspicious IPC$ reference** — suspicious `IPC$` connections can be observed through Windows Event ID `5140`. _Why:_ this event can provide the share-access anchor for a named pipe investigation. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Event ID 5140 plus Sysmon timing · Search narrowing** — correlating suspicious `IPC$` access from Event ID `5140` with named pipe connection timestamps can reduce the investigation window. _Why:_ timestamp alignment helps isolate the relevant pipe activity from background noise. _[GCFA p.~278]_
- **Named pipe investigation · Timestamp-driven approach** — the recommended workflow is to align suspicious share access times with named pipe connection events. _Why:_ time correlation connects network share evidence to the specific pipe and process involved. _[GCFA p.~278]_

- **Cobalt Strike artifact hypothesis** — the missing ADMIN$ context may be caused by the tool used in the attack, with Cobalt Strike named as the example. _Why:_ event-field anomalies can point to tool behavior, but should not be treated as definitive attribution by themselves. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **Cobalt Strike lateral movement** — the slide’s events represent lateral movement performed with Cobalt Strike. _Why:_ this gives the scenario context for interpreting the anomalous event pattern. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **Insufficient attribution from shown events alone** — the slide states that identifying Cobalt Strike would be difficult using only the displayed event information. _Why:_ share and logon events can show what happened without proving the exact tool. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **Need for host follow-up** — each involved system should be examined for unusual processes and other suspicious activity. _Why:_ process and host artifacts are needed to fully understand the attack mechanism. _[GCFA p.279]_

### IPC$ Meaning

- **IPC$ share definition** — `IPC$` is the default Interprocess Communication share. _Why:_ it is a standard SMB/RPC artifact often involved in remote operations. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **IPC$ authentication requirement** — access to underlying named pipes through IPC$ requires authentication. _Why:_ IPC$ events can expose network-based credential use even when file movement is not occurring. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **IPC$ named-pipe access** — an IPC$ connection provides access to named pipes on the system. _Why:_ named pipes are used by SMB/RPC remote-management workflows and many attack tools. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **IPC$ file-transfer limitation** — IPC$ access by itself cannot be used to move files. _Why:_ analysts should not mistake IPC$ alone for file-copy capability. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **IPC$ as context filler** — the related IPC$ Event ID 5140 record can supply the account and source details missing from the ADMIN$ event. _Why:_ both records are needed in the example to reconstruct the activity. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **IPC$ identity fields** — the IPC$ event includes account name, SID, domain, and logon ID. _Why:_ these fields allow attribution to the authenticated principal. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **IPC$ network fields** — the IPC$ event includes source IP address and source port. _Why:_ these fields identify the remote origin of the SMB/RPC authentication. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **Typical 5140 completeness** — although the example ADMIN$ record is missing key context, similar identifying information is commonly present in both related events. _Why:_ analysts should expect richer correlation data in many normal cases. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **IPC$ beyond mapped shares** — IPC$ authentication is used for more than mapping file shares. _Why:_ standalone IPC$ activity can still reflect remote administration or attack tooling. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **IPC$ as network-authentication tell** — many attacks leave IPC$ authentication as a sign of network-based credential use. _Why:_ IPC$ events can be detection leads even without file-share mapping. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **Standalone IPC$ with credentials** — an IPC$ share mapped by itself with user credentials may indicate a tool or process enumerating information. _Why:_ this can reveal reconnaissance or remote-management behavior. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **IPC$ source-address triage** — the source address in a standalone IPC$ event may warrant investigation when the activity is not known legitimate administration. _Why:_ source host review can distinguish expected admin activity from suspicious tooling. _[GCFA p.279]_

### SMB/RPC Behavior

- **SMB/RPC explanation** — the relationship between IPC$ and ADMIN$ events is tied to how SMB/RPC networking works. _Why:_ understanding protocol behavior prevents analysts from treating related events as unrelated noise. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **Named-pipe dependency** — IPC$ supports access to named pipes used beneath SMB/RPC workflows. _Why:_ remote actions can leave IPC$ artifacts before or alongside administrative-share access. _[GCFA p.279]_
- **Two-event reconstruction** — in the example, both the IPC$ and ADMIN$ records are required to understand the full activity. _Why:_ one event supplies identity and source context, while the other shows the lateral-movement-enabling share access. _[GCFA p.279]_

### Scenario

- **Scheduled task investigation goal** — the page’s investigative objective is to find and review scheduled tasks. _Why:_ scheduled tasks are a common Windows mechanism for persistence and lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~281]_

### Relevant Event IDs

- **Task Scheduler Event ID 106** — records creation of a scheduled task in the Task Scheduler operational log. _Why:_ it can show when a task-based persistence or execution mechanism was first placed. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Security Event ID 4698** — records creation of a scheduled task in the Windows Security log. _Why:_ it provides Security-log visibility into new scheduled task creation. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Task Scheduler Event ID 140** — records modification of an existing scheduled task in the Task Scheduler operational log. _Why:_ attackers may alter a task instead of creating a new one. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Security Event ID 4702** — records modification of a scheduled task in the Windows Security log. _Why:_ it can preserve detailed evidence that a task’s configuration changed. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Task Scheduler Event ID 141** — records deletion of a scheduled task in the Task Scheduler operational log. _Why:_ deletion shortly after execution can indicate attacker cleanup. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Security Event ID 4699** — records deletion of a scheduled task in the Windows Security log. _Why:_ it can reveal attempts to remove task-based evidence. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Task Scheduler Event ID 200** — records execution/start of a scheduled task in the Task Scheduler operational log. _Why:_ it helps establish when task-driven code ran. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Task Scheduler Event ID 201** — records completion of a scheduled task in the Task Scheduler operational log. _Why:_ it helps determine that a scheduled task finished and supports execution timeline reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Security Event ID 4700** — records that a scheduled task was enabled in the Security log. _Why:_ enabling an existing task may activate persistence without creating a new task. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Security Event ID 4701** — records that a scheduled task was disabled in the Security log. _Why:_ disabling can be part of attacker cleanup or operational control. _[GCFA p.~281]_

### Investigative Notes

- **Local scheduled task execution** — scheduled tasks can run on the same host where they are configured. _Why:_ local task activity may indicate host-level persistence or execution. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Remote scheduled task execution** — scheduled tasks can also be created or run against another system. _Why:_ this makes scheduled tasks useful for lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Remote task logon side effect** — remotely scheduled tasks generate Windows Logon Event ID 4624 with Logon Type 3. _Why:_ the network logon event is a key clue when task logs do not identify remote scheduling directly. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Post-execution task deletion** — attackers often remove scheduled tasks after the task has run. _Why:_ deleted-task events can be as important as created-task events when reconstructing attacker behavior. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Task Scheduler operational logging default state** — the Task Scheduler operational log is no longer enabled by default on modern systems. _Why:_ investigators may miss scheduled-task evidence unless logging was enabled beforehand. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Group Policy enablement** — the page recommends enabling Task Scheduler logging through Group Policy. _Why:_ centralized enablement improves the chance of preserving scheduled-task evidence across many endpoints. _[GCFA p.~281]_

### Task Scheduler Operational Log

- **Granular scheduled-task logging** — Windows can record detailed scheduled-task activity, including creation and execution. _Why:_ these records support precise task timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Operational log name** — the dedicated scheduled-task log is `Microsoft-Windows-Task Scheduler/Operational`. _Why:_ investigators need the exact log name to query the correct event source. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Windows 7 introduction** — the Task Scheduler operational log first appeared with Windows 7. _Why:_ this defines the minimum Windows generation where this artifact is expected. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Dedicated log purpose** — the operational log is specifically focused on scheduled-task activity. _Why:_ it can reduce noise compared with broader logs. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Longer retention than Security log** — scheduled-task operational events tend to remain available longer than equivalent Security-log events. _Why:_ it may preserve older attacker activity after Security events have rolled over. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Historical attacker evidence** — the Task Scheduler operational log is useful for finding older adversary actions and tradecraft. _Why:_ persistence and lateral movement artifacts may remain visible there after other logs age out. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Former default logging** — Task Scheduler history was originally logged by default. _Why:_ default behavior differs across Windows generations and affects evidence expectations. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Modern default logging** — Windows 10 and Windows 11 appear to have task history disabled by default. _Why:_ absence of events may reflect default configuration rather than absence of attacker activity. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Task history relationship** — disabling task history effectively disables the related Task Scheduler operational evidence. _Why:_ task-history configuration directly controls whether these events are available. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Group Policy enablement option** — Task Scheduler operational logging can be enabled by Group Policy. _Why:_ enterprise policy can ensure consistent collection across systems. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **`wevtutil` enablement option** — Task Scheduler operational logging can be enabled with the `wevtutil` command-line tool. _Why:_ responders and administrators can enable the log from the command line. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Task Scheduler GUI enablement option** — Task Scheduler operational logging can be enabled from the graphical Task Scheduler application. _Why:_ administrators can turn on task history without using command-line tooling. _[GCFA p.~281]_

### Task Scheduler Operational Event IDs

- **Event ID 106 meaning** — in the Task Scheduler operational log, Event ID 106 indicates scheduled-task creation. _Why:_ it marks the introduction of a task. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Event ID 140 meaning** — in the Task Scheduler operational log, Event ID 140 indicates scheduled-task update. _Why:_ it identifies configuration changes to an existing task. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Event ID 141 meaning** — in the Task Scheduler operational log, Event ID 141 indicates scheduled-task deletion. _Why:_ it can reveal cleanup after malicious execution. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Event ID 200 meaning** — in the Task Scheduler operational log, Event ID 200 indicates scheduled-task execution. _Why:_ it records when a task started running. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Event ID 201 meaning** — in the Task Scheduler operational log, Event ID 201 indicates scheduled-task completion. _Why:_ it records when a task finished running. _[GCFA p.~281]_

### Security Log Scheduled Task Auditing

- **Security-log prerequisite** — scheduled-task events in the Security log require Object Access auditing to be enabled. _Why:_ without this audit policy, expected Security events may not exist. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Security-log detail level** — Security-log scheduled-task events provide more detailed information than the Task Scheduler operational events. _Why:_ Security events can add context useful for attribution and timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Security-log scheduled-task event count** — five Security events are used to represent scheduled-task activity. _Why:_ investigators should query the full set rather than only creation events. _[GCFA p.~281]_

### Security Log Event IDs

- **Event ID 4698 meaning** — in the Security log, Event ID 4698 indicates scheduled-task creation. _Why:_ it is a primary Security-log artifact for newly created tasks. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Event ID 4699 meaning** — in the Security log, Event ID 4699 indicates scheduled-task deletion. _Why:_ it can expose attacker cleanup or removal of persistence. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Event ID 4700 meaning** — in the Security log, Event ID 4700 indicates a scheduled task was enabled. _Why:_ enabled-task activity may activate an existing execution path. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Event ID 4701 meaning** — in the Security log, Event ID 4701 indicates a scheduled task was disabled. _Why:_ disabled-task activity may reflect cleanup, staging, or operational changes. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Event ID 4702 meaning** — in the Security log, Event ID 4702 indicates scheduled-task update. _Why:_ task modification can be an attacker technique even when no new task is created. _[GCFA p.~281]_

### Remote Task Detection

- **Remote scheduling capability** — Windows tasks may be scheduled remotely. _Why:_ this expands scheduled tasks from a local persistence artifact into a lateral movement artifact. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Persistence use case** — attackers can use scheduled tasks to maintain access. _Why:_ recurring or trigger-based tasks can relaunch attacker tools. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Lateral movement use case** — attackers can use scheduled tasks to execute code on another host. _Why:_ remote task creation can move execution from one system to another. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Local-versus-remote limitation** — Task Scheduler logs do not distinguish locally scheduled tasks from remotely scheduled tasks. _Why:_ investigators cannot rely on task events alone to prove remote origin. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Remote-task correlation method** — to identify remotely created or executed tasks, look for Logon Event ID 4624 with Logon Type 3 near the task activity time. _Why:_ close timing between a network logon and task events can indicate remote scheduling. _[GCFA p.~281]_
- **Logon Type 3 meaning in this context** — Logon Type 3 represents a network logon associated with remote access. _Why:_ it is the authentication pattern expected when a task is scheduled remotely. _[GCFA p.~281]_

### Scheduled Task Detection

- **Task creation event combinations** — Correlating the specific set of events associated with scheduled task creation can produce useful detections. _Why:_ automated correlation helps analysts and threat hunters find task-based persistence or execution activity. _[GCFA p.282]_

- **Automated task-creation triggers** — Detection logic can be built to alert when the relevant task-creation events appear together. _Why:_ attackers often use scheduled tasks, and event combinations are stronger signals than isolated records. _[GCFA p.282]_

- **Analyst value of task-creation correlation** — Monitoring for task-creation event patterns is described as worthwhile for both analysts and hunt teams. _Why:_ this gives defenders a repeatable way to surface suspicious scheduled task activity across hosts. _[GCFA p.282]_

### Deleted Scheduled Tasks

- **Deleted tasks as a hunt target** — Removed scheduled tasks are identified as a high-confidence behavior to search for. _Why:_ deletion after execution can indicate attacker cleanup. _[GCFA p.282]_

- **Attacker scheduled task cleanup** — Attackers commonly create scheduled tasks on multiple systems and then remove those tasks after they run. _Why:_ cleanup reduces obvious persistence artifacts but leaves deletion evidence that can be hunted. _[GCFA p.282]_

- **Deleted tasks across many systems** — Scheduled task deletion may occur after attackers deploy tasks to a range of hosts. _Why:_ the same behavior appearing across endpoints can indicate lateral movement or coordinated execution. _[GCFA p.282]_

- **Rarity of deleted tasks** — Deleted scheduled tasks are uncommon in many environments. _Why:_ low baseline frequency makes deleted-task alerts more likely to be actionable. _[GCFA p.282]_

- **Filtering legitimate deleted tasks** — Legitimate applications that delete tasks are often identifiable and can be filtered out. _Why:_ filtering known-good sources leaves fewer suspicious deletions for analysts to investigate. _[GCFA p.282]_

- **Deleted malicious tasks** — After benign task deletions are excluded, remaining deleted tasks may represent attacker-created tasks. _Why:_ this narrows investigation scope to artifacts more likely tied to malicious activity. _[GCFA p.282]_

- **TaskScheduler/Operational retention value** — TaskScheduler/Operational entries may remain available longer than comparable Security log entries because the Security log is typically written to more frequently. _Why:_ investigators should check TaskScheduler/Operational even when Security evidence has aged out. _[GCFA p.~283]_
- **TaskScheduler correlation requirement** — identifying a malicious scheduled task from TaskScheduler/Operational data may require combining several event records. _Why:_ no single TaskScheduler event necessarily exposes the full task behavior. _[GCFA p.~283]_
- **Event ID 106 meaning** — TaskScheduler Event ID 106 records registration or creation of a scheduled task. _Why:_ it is a primary indicator that a task was newly added. _[GCFA p.~283]_
- **Event ID 106 limitation** — Event ID 106 exposes only the account responsible for registration and the task name. _Why:_ those fields alone may not reveal what executable will run. _[GCFA p.~283]_
- **Attacker-controlled task name** — the scheduled-task name is supplied by whoever creates the task and may be chosen to appear normal. _Why:_ benign-looking task names should not be trusted without execution-path correlation. _[GCFA p.~283]_
- **Event IDs 200 and 201 investigative use** — TaskScheduler Event IDs 200 and 201 should be reviewed to learn when a task executed or completed and what path was run. _Why:_ these events can connect a task name to the executable path. _[GCFA p.~283]_
- **Event ID 200 role** — TaskScheduler Event ID 200 represents task execution. _Why:_ it helps show that the scheduled task actually launched. _[GCFA p.~283]_
- **Event ID 201 role** — TaskScheduler Event ID 201 represents task completion. _Why:_ it can show both the task name and the action that finished, including the executable path. _[GCFA p.~283]_
- **Security Event ID 4698 meaning** — Windows Security Event ID 4698 records creation of a scheduled task. _Why:_ it can provide a detailed record of the task’s properties. _[GCFA p.~283]_
- **Event ID 4698 detail level** — when scheduled-task auditing is enabled, Event ID 4698 can include trigger data, the creating account, and the command path configured for execution. _Why:_ this information directly supports malicious-task triage. _[GCFA p.~283]_
- **Object access auditing prerequisite** — object access auditing must be enabled to collect the Security log task-creation evidence described on the page. _Why:_ many environments will miss Event ID 4698 task detail if this audit policy is absent. _[GCFA p.~283]_
- **Enterprise audit gap** — not every organization enables the required auditing for detailed scheduled-task Security events. _Why:_ investigators must account for missing 4698 evidence as a configuration issue, not necessarily absence of activity. _[GCFA p.~283]_
- **Description-field time basis** — times shown in the Event 4698 description field are local to the system. _Why:_ timeline analysis must interpret those task times in the host’s local time context. _[GCFA p.~283]_

### Scheduled Task v1.2 Artifacts

- **Task Scheduler v1.2 format** — Windows Vista introduced a newer scheduled-task format identified as version 1.2. _Why:_ the task format determines where artifacts are stored and what fields investigators can parse. _[GCFA p.285]_
- **Server 2008 task format support** — Windows Server 2008 also uses the newer scheduled-task format. _Why:_ analysts should expect the same XML artifact style on Server 2008 systems. _[GCFA p.285]_
- **Task file format** — Version 1.2 scheduled tasks are stored as straightforward XML files. _Why:_ investigators can review them directly without a specialized parser. _[GCFA p.285]_
- **Task file extension behavior** — Version 1.2 task files do not use a filename extension. _Why:_ extensionless files in the task directory may still be readable XML task definitions. _[GCFA p.285]_
- **Primary task storage path** — Version 1.2 task files are saved under `\Windows\System32\Tasks`. _Why:_ this is the main filesystem location to inspect for scheduled-task definitions. _[GCFA p.285]_
- **Environment-variable task path** — The same primary location is represented as `%SystemRoot%\System32\Tasks`. _Why:_ this form is useful when interpreting documentation, scripts, or triage commands across different Windows installations. _[GCFA p.285]_
- **Previous v1.0 task path** — Earlier version 1.0 tasks used `%SystemRoot%\Tasks`. _Why:_ older systems or legacy task artifacts may appear outside the newer `System32\Tasks` location. _[GCFA p.285]_
- **32-bit task storage path** — Tasks created by 32-bit code can be stored in `%SystemRoot%\SysWOW64\Tasks`. _Why:_ this location is uncommon and therefore worth checking for unusual or attacker-created tasks. _[GCFA p.285]_
- **Alternate SysWOW64 path form** — The slide also names `\Windows\SysWOW64\Tasks` as a location to review. _Why:_ analysts should not limit collection to only `System32\Tasks`. _[GCFA p.285]_
- **Task filename behavior** — When a scheduled task is created, Windows creates a file whose name matches the task name. _Why:_ the file name itself can identify the scheduled task being investigated. _[GCFA p.285]_
- **v1.2 information richness** — Version 1.2 XML task files contain more useful detail than older `.job` task files. _Why:_ XML tasks can expose registration, execution, trigger, and account information relevant to lateral movement. _[GCFA p.285]_
- **Task files as event-log supplement** — Scheduled-task XML files complement the Task Scheduler Operational event log. _Why:_ filesystem artifacts may preserve task configuration details that improve or corroborate event-log analysis. _[GCFA p.285]_

## Page 286

### Task Scheduler File Artifacts

- **Deleted task files** — scheduled task files can be removed by an intruder yet still recovered through forensic methods. _Why:_ recovered task files may preserve evidence after attempted cleanup. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **Enterprise-wide task tracking** — matching task files across multiple hosts can reveal the same scheduled task deployed on many systems. _Why:_ identical filenames on separate machines can connect related adversary activity across an environment. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **Repeated task filename indicator** — if one task is scheduled on ten systems, each affected system would contain a task file using the same filename. _Why:_ filename repetition can help cluster compromised hosts or repeated execution mechanisms. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **Task files as event-log enrichment** — scheduled task files add context beyond what is found in Security logs and Task Scheduler/Operational logs. _Why:_ combining file artifacts with event records improves reconstruction of task creation, execution, and cleanup. _[GCFA p.~286]_

### Previous Task Scheduler Format

- **Task Scheduler version 1.0** — the older scheduled task format is version `1.0`. _Why:_ version identification determines which parser and artifact expectations apply. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **XP/Windows Server 2003 usage** — Task Scheduler format `1.0` is used on Windows XP, Windows Server 2003, and earlier systems. _Why:_ operating system age affects task storage format and available fields. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **Older format storage folder** — the older format also uses a `Tasks` folder for storing task files. _Why:_ investigators should check this location on legacy systems and for compatibility artifacts. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **`.job` files** — Task Scheduler version `1.0` stores scheduled tasks as `.job` files. _Why:_ the extension distinguishes legacy binary task artifacts from newer XML task files. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **Legacy Tasks folder path basis** — the legacy `Tasks` folder resides under `%SystemRoot%`, typically the Windows directory. _Why:_ this identifies where legacy `.job` artifacts should be collected. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **Binary `.job` format** — data inside version `1.0` `.job` files is stored in binary form. _Why:_ binary storage requires specialized parsers rather than direct XML/text review. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **Reduced field richness** — version `1.0` `.job` files contain less information than newer version `1.2` scheduled task files. _Why:_ analysts should expect fewer investigative details from legacy task artifacts. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **Registration timestamp** — legacy `.job` files preserve the scheduled task registration date and time. _Why:_ registration time helps establish when the task was created or enrolled. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **User account field** — legacy `.job` files include the user account associated with the task. _Why:_ the account value helps attribute task creation or execution context. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **Full command path field** — legacy `.job` files include the complete path to the command configured for the task. _Why:_ the command path identifies the executable or script used for persistence or execution. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **Execution timestamp** — legacy `.job` files include task execution date and time information. _Why:_ execution timing supports activity timeline reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **At.exe output on XP/Win2003** — `At.exe` creates `.job` files in the legacy format on XP and Windows Server 2003. _Why:_ use of this command can produce recoverable legacy task artifacts. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **Schtasks.exe output on XP/Win2003** — `Schtasks.exe` also creates legacy-format `.job` files on XP and Windows Server 2003. _Why:_ both common task-creation utilities can leave the same class of artifact on those systems. _[GCFA p.~286]_

### Backward Compatibility Artifacts

- **`.job` files on newer Windows** — newer Windows versions may still contain `.job` files in the legacy task folder. _Why:_ investigators should not ignore the old location solely because the OS is newer. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **Duplicate task information** — `.job` files on newer Windows may duplicate information stored in newer version `1.2` task files. _Why:_ duplicate artifacts can preserve evidence if only one location is cleaned. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **Backward compatibility reason** — newer systems may keep legacy `.job` artifacts for compatibility with older task mechanisms. _Why:_ compatibility behavior explains why old-format artifacts can appear on modern hosts. _[GCFA p.~286]_
- **Cleanup oversight opportunity** — if an attacker deletes task artifacts from only one task location, duplicate artifacts in the other location may remain. _Why:_ missed cleanup can expose scheduled task evidence after attacker anti-forensics. _[GCFA p.~286]_
