### Suspicious Service Investigation

- **Suspicious services at boot** — Investigators should examine logs for services that appear suspicious and run during system startup. _Why:_ boot-start services can indicate persistence mechanisms. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Service activity during compromise window** — Investigators should review services that started or stopped during the suspected intrusion period. _Why:_ service lifecycle events can align malware execution or attacker operations to a timeline. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Windows services as operating-system control points** — Windows services influence or manage many operating-system functions. _Why:_ compromise or abuse of services can affect broad system behavior. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Service definition** — A service is a process that can run without interactive user action and does not require any user to be logged on. _Why:_ attackers can use services to execute code outside normal user sessions. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Services as malware targets** — Malware commonly targets or abuses Windows services. _Why:_ service artifacts can reveal malicious behavior on the examined host. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Services as forensic clues** — Service-related artifacts can provide strong evidence of malicious activity on an investigated system. _Why:_ service creation, crashes, start changes, and start/stop events are useful for incident reconstruction. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Malware and worms using services** — Many real-world malware families and worms use Windows services. _Why:_ service-related anomalies should be treated as a common malware tradecraft indicator. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Boot-start services as persistence** — Services configured to start at boot demonstrate persistence capability. _Why:_ malware often wants to survive reboot and resume execution automatically. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Service crashes from attacks** — Services may crash as a result of attacks such as process injection. _Why:_ unexpected crashes can be indirect evidence of exploitation or code injection. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Process/DLL injection crash risk** — Advanced attacks involving process or DLL injection have been observed causing service crashes. _Why:_ crash events can expose otherwise hidden injection activity. _[GCFA p.288]_

### Service Logs

- **Primary service log location** — Service-related events discussed on this page are generally found in the Windows System log. _Why:_ analysts must query the correct event log when hunting service activity. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 4697 exception** — Event ID 4697 is the exception among the listed service events because it is recorded in the Security log. _Why:_ analysts may miss service-install evidence if they search only the System log. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **System-log event set** — Event IDs 7034, 7035, 7036, 7040, and 7045 refer to System log service events. _Why:_ these IDs form the main System-log hunt set for suspicious services. _[GCFA p.288]_

### Service Control Manager

- **Service Control Manager role** — The Service Control Manager governs Windows services. _Why:_ SCM activity explains why service lifecycle changes appear in Windows logs. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **SCM control requests** — The SCM sends control requests to running services and drivers. _Why:_ start and stop actions may reflect SCM-issued commands rather than direct process execution. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **SCM status tracking** — The SCM keeps status information for services. _Why:_ logged service state changes depend on this status tracking. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **SCM System-log updates** — The SCM is responsible for writing service-related events into the System log. _Why:_ SCM-generated entries are central evidence for service timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.288]_

### Event IDs

- **Event ID 7034** — Event 7034 records that a service terminated unexpectedly. _Why:_ service crashes are uncommon enough to merit investigation. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7034 crash rarity** — Services should crash only infrequently under normal conditions. _Why:_ an unexpected service crash can be an anomaly worth triaging. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7034 crash count** — Event 7034 includes how many previous times the service has crashed. _Why:_ repeated failures may distinguish persistent exploitation or unstable injected code from an isolated fault. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7034 injection relevance** — Process or DLL injection can cause service crashes that appear as 7034 events. _Why:_ the event can point to malicious code running inside a service process. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7035** — Event 7035 records that a service received a start or stop control. _Why:_ it shows that SCM was instructed to launch or shut down a service. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7035 start control** — A 7035 event can indicate SCM ordered a service to start. _Why:_ this can mark the beginning of attacker-triggered service execution. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7035 stop control** — A 7035 event can indicate SCM ordered a service to stop. _Why:_ this can show attacker cleanup, service tampering, or defensive disruption. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7035 and 7036 relationship** — A 7036 event shows when the service actually reaches the started or stopped state after the 7035 control. _Why:_ pairing both events separates the control request from the resulting state change. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7036** — Event 7036 records that a service started or stopped. _Why:_ it confirms the service reached an operational or shut-down state. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7036 started state** — A 7036 event can indicate the service is fully operational. _Why:_ this helps determine when service-backed code became active. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7036 stopped state** — A 7036 event can indicate the service is fully stopped. _Why:_ this helps determine when service-backed activity ended. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7040** — Event 7040 records a change to a service start type. _Why:_ start-type changes can convert a service into a persistence mechanism or disable functionality. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7040 Boot value** — A Boot start type means the service starts when the system boots. _Why:_ boot-start configuration is important because it can support malware persistence after reboot. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7040 On Request value** — An On Request start type means another process must ask the SCM to start the service. _Why:_ this distinguishes demand-start services from automatic startup persistence. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7040 Disabled value** — A Disabled start type means the service will not start even if SCM receives a control request for it. _Why:_ attackers may disable services, including security-related services, to weaken defenses. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7040 Windows-service coverage** — 7040 events are mostly logged for Windows services. _Why:_ analysts should understand the event may not cover every installed service equally. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7040 third-party coverage limitation** — Many 7040 events do not include services belonging to third-party security tools or similar products. _Why:_ absence of a 7040 event does not prove that non-Microsoft service start types were unchanged. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7045** — Event 7045 records that a new service was installed on the system. _Why:_ new service installation is a strong starting point for identifying attacker-created services. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7045 operating-system availability** — Event 7045 is available beginning with Windows Server 2008 R2-era systems. _Why:_ analysts must account for OS version when expecting this artifact. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7045 first-install tracking** — 7045 tracks the first time a particular service was installed on the host. _Why:_ it can identify the original appearance time of a suspicious service. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 7045 triage value** — 7045 is especially useful as an initial event to review when hunting suspicious services. _Why:_ attacker service creation is often more distinctive than normal start/stop noise. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **Event ID 4697** — Event 4697 records that a new service was installed on the system in the Security log. _Why:_ it provides a Security-log source for service-install evidence. _[GCFA p.288]_

### Event ID Matrix Facts

- **7034 · Meaning** — Service crashed unexpectedly. _Why:_ abnormal service termination can expose exploitation, injection, or unstable malicious code. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **7034 · Log source** — This event belongs to the System log. _Why:_ correct log selection is required to find the artifact. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **7035 · Meaning** — Service received a Start or Stop control. _Why:_ it records the control action sent to the service. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **7035 · Log source** — This event belongs to the System log. _Why:_ correct log selection is required to reconstruct service control activity. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **7036 · Meaning** — Service entered a started or stopped state. _Why:_ it confirms the actual service state transition. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **7036 · Log source** — This event belongs to the System log. _Why:_ correct log selection is required to validate service execution timing. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **7040 · Meaning** — Service start type changed to Boot, On Request, or Disabled. _Why:_ start-type changes can indicate persistence setup or service suppression. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **7040 · Log source** — This event belongs to the System log. _Why:_ correct log selection is required to find service configuration changes. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **7045 · Meaning** — A new service was installed on the system. _Why:_ newly installed services are high-value artifacts for lateral movement and persistence investigations. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **7045 · Version note** — 7045 is associated with Windows Server 2008 R2 and later. _Why:_ version awareness prevents false expectations on older systems. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **7045 · Log source** — This event belongs to the System log. _Why:_ correct log selection is required to find new-service installation evidence. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **4697 · Meaning** — A new service was installed on the system. _Why:_ it provides another event ID for service-install detection. _[GCFA p.288]_
- **4697 · Log source** — This event belongs to the Security log. _Why:_ it is the listed exception to the System-log service events. _[GCFA p.288]_

## Page 289

### Windows Service Installation Events

- **Service-installation logging signal quality** — New-service installation events are described as having strong investigative value because normal service start/stop noise does not drown out the less common records tied to malicious service creation. _Why:_ service installation is rarer and therefore more useful for alerting than routine service lifecycle activity. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **Legitimate service churn vs. malicious service records** — Frequent starts and stops by normal services can obscure malicious activity in some event categories, but this problem is less severe for service-installation events. _Why:_ analysts can prioritize service-installation telemetry as higher signal than ordinary service state-change telemetry. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **Self-deleting service behavior** — Tools or services that remove themselves after use still generate a service-installation record whenever they are installed. _Why:_ cleanup behavior does not eliminate the historical evidence of the service creation. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **PsExec cleanup behavior** — PsExec is given as an example of a tool that can delete its service when the session ends. _Why:_ this explains why repeated PsExec use may leave multiple service-installation events even if the service is no longer present. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **Event ID 7045 recurrence** — A service that is installed and then removed will produce Event ID 7045 each time it is installed again. _Why:_ repeated 7045 events can expose tools that create temporary services for execution or lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **Event ID 7045 rarity** — Event ID 7045 is characterized as unusual enough to help identify abnormal service creation. _Why:_ unusual event frequency makes it suitable for detection logic and triage. _[GCFA p.~289]_

### Security Event ID 4697

- **Event ID 4697 log location** — Event ID 4697 is recorded in the Windows Security log. _Why:_ analysts must query the Security log, not only the System log, when hunting for service installation evidence. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **Event ID 4697 audit dependency** — Event ID 4697 is available only when the “Audit Security System Extension” policy setting is enabled through local policy or Group Policy. _Why:_ absence of 4697 does not prove service installation did not occur if the required audit setting was disabled. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **Audit Security System Extension source** — The audit setting needed for Event ID 4697 can be configured locally or through domain Group Policy. _Why:_ investigators should account for host-level and domain-level audit configuration when assessing log coverage. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **Event ID 4697 similarity to 7045** — Event ID 4697 records new-service activity similar to System log Event ID 7045. _Why:_ the two events can describe overlapping service-installation activity from different logs. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **Event ID 4697 correlation advantage** — Because 4697 is in the Security log, it can be correlated more directly with other Security log events. _Why:_ same-log correlation can simplify timeline building around authentication, privilege use, and service creation. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **Event ID 4697 initiator-account limitation** — Unlike System Event ID 7045, Event ID 4697 often does not capture the real user account that initiated the service installation. _Why:_ relying only on 4697 can misattribute who caused the service creation. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **Event ID 4697 bootstrap-account behavior** — Event ID 4697 may show the account used to bootstrap the service rather than the original initiating user. _Why:_ analysts must distinguish execution context from the actor account behind the action. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **SYSTEM shown in 4697** — SYSTEM is provided as an example of the account that may appear in Event ID 4697 as the service bootstrap context. _Why:_ a SYSTEM value in 4697 may reflect service startup mechanics rather than the human or remote account responsible. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **System-log correlation requirement** — Event ID 4697 should be correlated with System log entries to avoid losing details that 4697 may omit. _Why:_ combining Security and System logs improves attribution and service-installation reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~289]_

### Service Start Type Values

- **Event ID 4697 start-type field** — Event ID 4697 records service start-type information in a form comparable to Windows Registry service configuration values. _Why:_ the event can reveal how and when the installed service is intended to start. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **Start type 0x00** — The value `0x00` means boot device. _Why:_ this identifies services or drivers intended to load at the earliest boot stage. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **Start type 0x01** — The value `0x01` means I/O subsystem. _Why:_ this indicates a service or driver tied to low-level system initialization. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **Start type 0x02** — The value `0x02` means auto start. _Why:_ automatically starting services are important persistence indicators because they run without manual launch. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **Start type 0x03** — The value `0x03` means manual start. _Why:_ manually started services may reflect on-demand execution rather than automatic persistence. _[GCFA p.~289]_

- **Start type 0x04** — The value `0x04` means disabled. _Why:_ disabled services may still be relevant as remnants, staged artifacts, or changed configurations. _[GCFA p.~289]_

### PsExec Service-Installation Detection

- **PsExec lateral-movement pattern** — PsExec activity can be detected by looking for newly created Windows services. _Why:_ remote execution through service creation leaves durable Windows event artifacts. _[GCFA p. 290]_
- **Sysinternals PsExec behavior** — Microsoft Sysinternals PsExec creates a fresh service instance whenever it runs. _Why:_ repeated service creation is unusual enough to make PsExec executions easy to spot. _[GCFA p. 290]_
- **Windows service-install event** — Event ID `7045` records that a service was installed. _Why:_ this event is logged by default in the System log and is a primary PsExec detection artifact. _[GCFA p. 290]_
- **Security service-install event** — Event ID `4697` may also appear for service installation in the Security log. _Why:_ it can corroborate System log evidence when Security auditing captures the event. _[GCFA p. 290]_
- **Normal service account context** — Legitimate services usually run under built-in service accounts such as `SYSTEM` or `LOCAL SERVICE`. _Why:_ services running as ordinary user accounts are more suspicious. _[GCFA p. 290]_
- **User-context service creation** — PsExec in the example created services associated with a user SID rather than only a built-in account. _Why:_ services tied to user accounts are uncommon and deserve investigation. _[GCFA p. 290]_
- **Domain-user SID indicator** — SID `S-1-5-21-572887454-1858499753-1978773125-1003` is presented as indicating a domain user account. _Why:_ this can identify the user context behind suspicious service execution. _[GCFA p. 290]_
- **High-value account risk** — Services configured with privileged user accounts can indicate either compromise or dangerous administrative misconfiguration. _Why:_ both cases create high-impact lateral-movement risk. _[GCFA p. 290]_
- **Two PsExec executions** — The page describes two PsExec executions on one system separated by roughly five hours. _Why:_ repeated service-install events close in time can show continued remote activity. _[GCFA p. 290]_
- **PSEXESVC service name** — A service named `PSEXESVC` is a strong indicator of Sysinternals PsExec use. _Why:_ it directly suggests remote code execution through PsExec. _[GCFA p. 290]_
- **Attribution method via SID** — The associated SID can be resolved to a username by searching the Security log. _Why:_ resolving the SID helps identify who initiated the activity. _[GCFA p. 290]_
- **Attribution method via logon event** — A corresponding Event ID `4624` logon event can help identify the account behind the PsExec session. _Why:_ logon records tie service creation to authentication activity. _[GCFA p. 290]_

## Page 291

### Services as Attack Artifacts

- **New service discovery** — identifying recently created services can reveal many attack types, including PsExec-style activity and less common malware families. _Why:_ service creation is a high-value pivot for finding execution, lateral movement, and persistence. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **Services in malware workflows** — malware commonly abuses Windows services across multiple phases of an intrusion. _Why:_ service artifacts should not be treated as only persistence evidence; they can also indicate execution and movement. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **Persistent backdoors via services** — backdoors such as Cobalt Strike Beacon may use services to run code. _Why:_ a suspicious service can represent long-term attacker access. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **Meterpreter service usage** — Meterpreter is an example of a backdoor payload that can execute through a service mechanism. _Why:_ service artifacts can expose post-exploitation payload execution. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **Credential dumper service usage** — credential theft tools such as fgdump may use services for execution. _Why:_ service installation or execution can be evidence of credential-access activity. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **Lateral movement service usage** — lateral movement tools can create or use services to execute code on remote systems. _Why:_ service evidence may identify both the target host and the method used for remote execution. _[GCFA p.~291]_

### PsExec 2.30 Key File Artifact

- **Sysinternals PsExec version 2.30 artifact** — PsExec 2.30 introduced an additional file artifact. _Why:_ investigators can use this version-specific behavior to identify newer PsExec activity. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **PsExec key-file directory** — PsExec creates the additional artifact under `C:\Windows`. _Why:_ this location gives investigators a specific filesystem area to inspect for direct or residual evidence. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **PsExec key-file naming pattern** — the file name follows a pattern like `PSEXEC-ORIGINATING_SYSTEM-VALUE000.key`. _Why:_ the structured name can encode attribution-relevant host information. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **`ORIGINATING_SYSTEM` component** — the `ORIGINATING_SYSTEM` portion represents the hostname of the computer that initiated the PsExec session. _Why:_ this can identify the source host used for remote execution. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **`VALUE000` component** — the `VALUE000` portion is an 8-character value. _Why:_ the changing value helps distinguish separate PsExec connections. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **Per-connection PsExec value** — the 8-character value changes for each PsExec connection. _Why:_ multiple key-file references may map to multiple sessions rather than one repeated static artifact. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **CVE-2021-1733 mitigation artifact** — the key file exists as part of a mitigation for a privilege-escalation vulnerability in an earlier PsExec version. _Why:_ the artifact is expected behavior for patched PsExec behavior, not necessarily a separate malware-created file. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **PsExec vulnerability identifier** — the earlier PsExec privilege-escalation issue is identified as `CVE-2021-1733`. _Why:_ the CVE explains why the artifact exists in newer PsExec behavior. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **PsExec key-file deletion** — PsExec deletes the key file after the session is created. _Why:_ the absence of the file on disk does not rule out PsExec use. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **Prefetch residual evidence** — references to the deleted key-file name can remain in Prefetch for `PSEXESVC.exe`. _Why:_ Prefetch may preserve evidence after the original key file has been removed. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **Origin hostname in Prefetch** — Prefetch references may include the key-file name and therefore the originating system name. _Why:_ this can reveal the host from which the PsExec session was launched. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **Remote-side Prefetch target** — the relevant Prefetch evidence is associated with `PSEXESVC.exe`, which PsExec starts on the remote system. _Why:_ the artifact is found on the destination host where PsExec executed. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **USN Journal residual evidence** — references to the PsExec key-file name can also appear in the USN Journal. _Why:_ NTFS change-journal records may preserve traces of a deleted PsExec artifact. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **USN Journal course placement** — the USN Journal artifact is noted as being covered later in Section 5. _Why:_ investigators should correlate this page’s PsExec artifact with later filesystem-journal analysis. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **PsExec `-r` switch behavior** — changing the `PSEXESVC` service name with PsExec’s `-r` option does not change the key-file naming behavior. _Why:_ attackers renaming the service may still leave the same style of key-file reference. _[GCFA p.~291]_
- **Service rename limitation** — even if `PSEXESVC` is renamed, the key-file name still retains its normal PsExec-style format. _Why:_ this artifact can survive a common attempt to make PsExec service names less obvious. _[GCFA p.~291]_

### PsExec Named Pipes

- **PsExec stdin pipe** — the example includes `\\.\pipe\PSEXESVC-SERVER1-3476-stdin`. _Why:_ the pipe records the source host string `SERVER1`, process/session value `3476`, and standard-input channel. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **PsExec stdout pipe** — the example includes `\\.\pipe\PSEXESVC-SERVER1-3476-stdout`. _Why:_ the pipe records the source host string `SERVER1`, process/session value `3476`, and standard-output channel. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **PsExec stderr pipe** — the example includes `\\.\pipe\PSEXESVC-SERVER1-3476-stderr`. _Why:_ the pipe records the source host string `SERVER1`, process/session value `3476`, and standard-error channel. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **Named pipe source host component** — the example pipe names contain `SERVER1`. _Why:_ this component can identify the originating computer involved in PsExec activity. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **Named pipe numeric component** — the example pipe names contain `3476`. _Why:_ this value helps distinguish one PsExec pipe set or session from another. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **Named pipe stream suffixes** — the example uses `stdin`, `stdout`, and `stderr` suffixes. _Why:_ these suffixes show PsExec’s remote command I/O channels. _[GCFA p.~292]_

### Event Log Correlation

- **System Event ID 7045** — Event ID 7045 in the System log can be used to look for timestamps tied to installation of the `PSEXESVC` service. _Why:_ service-install time can anchor the PsExec activity timeline. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **`PSEXESVC` installation timing** — timestamps from the `PSEXESVC` service installation can help determine when the PsExec activity occurred. _Why:_ precise timing supports timeline construction and incident scoping. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **Security Event ID 4624 correlation** — related Event ID 4624 records should be cross-referenced with the service-install event. _Why:_ logon records can connect the service creation to authentication activity. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **Logon Type 3 correlation** — Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 events are specifically relevant to the PsExec investigation. _Why:_ Logon Type 3 represents network logon activity, which matches remote service execution over the network. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **Originating IP confirmation** — correlated 4624 Type 3 records can confirm the source system’s IP address. _Why:_ the IP address helps identify the machine used to initiate lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **User account confirmation** — correlated 4624 Type 3 records can confirm which user account authenticated. _Why:_ the account value identifies the credentials used for the remote execution. _[GCFA p.~292]_

### Threat Reporting Context

- **Palo Alto reporting** — Palo Alto documented Sysinternals PsExec use for lateral movement in 2024. _Why:_ public reporting confirms the technique’s use in real intrusions. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **ShadowPad actor label** — Palo Alto associated the reported activity with a China-attributed APT they call `ShadowPad`. _Why:_ the actor label provides threat-intelligence context for PsExec-based lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **Campaign geography** — the cited ShadowPad activity involved espionage operations across Southeast Asia. _Why:_ regional campaign context can help analysts connect host artifacts to broader intrusion reporting. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **Campaign reference URL** — the page gives `https://for508.com/ofe0y` for additional information about the ShadowPad campaign. _Why:_ the URL provides a supporting source for the threat-reporting example. _[GCFA p.~292]_

### Living-Off-the-Land Alternatives

- **Living-off-the-land equivalence** — built-in Windows tools can produce results similar to PsExec. _Why:_ analysts should not limit detection to the PsExec binary or default service name. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **`net use` share mapping** — the `net use` command can map a network share on the target. _Why:_ mapped shares can provide the file-transfer path needed for remote execution staging. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **Default `C$` share** — `net use` can map the default `C$` administrative share. _Why:_ access to `C$` can allow an attacker to place files on the target filesystem. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **Default `ADMIN$` share** — `net use` can map the default `ADMIN$` administrative share. _Why:_ access to `ADMIN$` can support copying tools or malware into Windows administrative paths. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **Malware copy step** — a mapped share can be used to copy malware onto the target host. _Why:_ file placement is one of the required steps before launching a malicious service remotely. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **`sc` service launch** — the `sc` command can start malware as a service on the remote target. _Why:_ service execution is a common lateral-movement mechanism and mirrors PsExec’s core behavior. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **PsExec-equivalent workflow** — mapping a share, copying a payload, and launching it as a service are essentially the same operational steps PsExec performs. _Why:_ the behavior can remain present even when attackers avoid a standalone PsExec tool. _[GCFA p.~292]_
- **Standalone-tool avoidance** — attackers can replicate PsExec-like behavior without bringing a separate PsExec executable. _Why:_ detection should focus on remote copy and service-creation behaviors, not only on known PsExec files. _[GCFA p.~292]_

## Page 294

### Per-User Services

- **Per-user service instances** — Windows can create services scoped to an individual user logon session. _Why:_ these session-scoped services add noise to service-installation hunting. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **Per-user services · OS introduction** — This behavior was added in Windows 10 and Windows Server releases. _Why:_ analysts should expect this noise primarily on modern Windows hosts, not older Windows versions. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **Per-user services · Session uniqueness** — Each user session can produce a distinct service instance with its own identifier. _Why:_ the same base service can appear as many different service names across logons. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **Per-user services · Detection impact** — These services make “new service” detections harder to use, especially detections based on Security log Event ID 4697. _Why:_ normal user logons can generate many apparently new services. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **Per-user services · Efficiency purpose** — Windows starts and stops these user-specific service instances as an operating-system efficiency mechanism. _Why:_ the activity may be normal OS behavior rather than attacker persistence or execution. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **Per-user services · Name construction** — Windows appends a Locally Unique Identifier to the base service name when naming these service instances. _Why:_ the suffix explains why many service names share a base name but differ at the end. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **LUID reuse within session** — The same Locally Unique Identifier is often used across multiple per-user services created for one session. _Why:_ shared suffixes can help group noisy service events back to the same logon session. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **Security log interpretation** — The Security log treats each per-user service name as a new service. _Why:_ this causes benign session activity to appear similar to newly installed services. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **Event ID 4697 logon noise** — A single user logon can generate multiple Security log Event ID 4697 records because of per-user services. _Why:_ volume alone is not enough to declare service-installation activity malicious on Windows 10+ systems. _[GCFA p.~294]_

### Service Installation Events

- **Windows service abuse** — Attackers commonly misuse Windows services. _Why:_ service-installation telemetry remains a high-value source for lateral movement and execution detection. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **Security log Event ID 4697** — Event ID 4697 records new-service installation activity in the Security log. _Why:_ it can reveal malicious service creation, including lateral movement techniques. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **System log Event ID 7045** — Event ID 7045 records service installation activity in the System log. _Why:_ it is another major source for identifying suspicious service creation. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **Pre-Windows 10 signal quality** — Before Windows 10, new-service events usually had a stronger signal because normal systems did not create many brand-new services. _Why:_ older baselines make service-installation events easier to triage. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **Windows 10 signal degradation** — Windows 10 per-user services reduced the signal-to-noise ratio of new-service detections. _Why:_ benign OS activity can flood the same event stream defenders use for threat hunting. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **System log advantage** — Event ID 7045 in the System log does not currently appear to record these per-user service instances. _Why:_ focusing on 7045 can reduce per-user-service noise compared with 4697. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **System log retention advantage** — The System log commonly covers a longer historical period than the Security log. _Why:_ Event ID 7045 may provide a wider lookback window for service-installation investigations. _[GCFA p.~294]_

### Filtering And Evasion

- **Underscore-based filtering** — Filtering out service names containing `_` can remove many per-user service records. _Why:_ per-user service names commonly include an underscore before the session-specific suffix. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **Underscore-filter weakness** — Excluding every service name with `_` creates an evasion opportunity. _Why:_ an attacker can choose a malicious service name that resembles normal per-user service naming. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **Malicious mimicry example** — A malicious service named `OneSyncSvc_32d44dec` could blend into normal-looking per-user service noise. _Why:_ name-only filtering can hide attacker-created services. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **ServiceFileName filtering** — Filtering by service executable command line can be more reliable than filtering only by service name. _Why:_ benign per-user services may share known executable paths and arguments. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **ServiceFileName ignore-list example** — `C:\Windows\system32\svchost.exe -k UnistackSvcGroup` is an example command line that may be placed on an ignore list after validation. _Why:_ suppressing known benign service host patterns can preserve Event ID 4697 usefulness. _[GCFA p.~294]_
- **Filtered Event ID 4697 value** — Event ID 4697 remains useful when per-user-service noise is handled with appropriate filtering. _Why:_ defenders should tune the event source rather than discard it entirely. _[GCFA p.~294]_

## Page 295

### Remote Registry Modification

- **Remote Registry modification via `reg`** — Windows `reg` can alter registry hives on another host, not only the local machine. _Why:_ remote registry writes can support both lateral movement and persistence. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **Remote registry changes as lateral movement** — Registry run keys can be abused to make code execute on a remote system after the attacker writes the needed value remotely. _Why:_ a persistence mechanism can also become an execution path across systems. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **Remote registry changes as persistence** — A remote registry write can add an autorun value so malware launches later on the target. _Why:_ the registry write may be the persistence action, even if the executable is placed separately. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **File share staging pairing** — Remote registry modification is commonly paired with remote file share access to copy malware onto the destination host. _Why:_ the registry value often points to a payload that must already exist on the remote system. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **Remote Registry service dependency** — The remote registry change is performed through the Windows Remote Registry service. _Why:_ service activity and related named-pipe activity provide corroborating artifacts. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **Modified key timestamp** — The registry key that is changed receives an updated last-written timestamp. _Why:_ registry last-write time can help place the persistence or lateral-movement action on a timeline. _[GCFA p.295]_

### Example Command

- **Command prompt context** — The example is run from `C:\>`. _Why:_ it shows the action is initiated from a Windows command shell. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **Tool name** — The command uses `reg`. _Why:_ `reg.exe` is a native Windows registry-management utility that can be used for remote modification. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **Command action** — The command uses `reg add`. _Why:_ this indicates a registry value is being created or overwritten. _[GCFA p.295]_

- **Remote host name** — The destination computer in the example is `Server1`. _Why:_ host identification is necessary for correlating remote logon and service activity. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **Registry hive** — The example writes under `HKLM`. _Why:_ machine-wide autorun values can affect execution for the system broadly. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **Registry key path** — The key modified is `HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run`. _Why:_ this is a common Windows autorun location used for persistence. _[GCFA p.295]_

- **Suspicious executable name** — The filename `svchosl.exe` is a suspicious misspelling resembling a legitimate Windows process name. _Why:_ lookalike names are common malware masquerading clues. _[GCFA p.295]_

### Protocol And Authentication

- **UNC registry addressing** — Remote registry access is performed by specifying a UNC path to the remote computer and target key. _Why:_ UNC syntax distinguishes remote registry modification from local registry editing. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **Windows Remote Registry Protocol** — `reg` can use the Windows Remote Registry Protocol to operate on remote systems. _Why:_ this identifies the underlying mechanism behind the remote registry write. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **RPC basis** — The Windows Remote Registry Protocol is based on RPC. _Why:_ RPC behavior explains the associated ports, named pipes, and service artifacts. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **Windows single sign-on use** — When the command runs, Windows single sign-on uses the currently logged-on user's credentials to connect to `Server1`. _Why:_ the remote activity may authenticate as the interactive user rather than prompting for new credentials. _[GCFA p.295]_

### RPC And Named Pipes

- **RPC endpoint mapper option** — RPC can use the endpoint mapper on TCP port `135`. _Why:_ port 135 activity may be part of RPC-based remote administration. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **RPC dynamic service port option** — RPC can also use a high-numbered port assigned per service. _Why:_ dynamic RPC ports can complicate network-based detection and correlation. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **RPC over SMB named pipes option** — RPC can use SMB named pipes as its transport channel. _Why:_ this explains why IPC$ share access appears in logs during remote registry modification. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **Remote Registry transport choice** — The Windows Remote Registry Protocol uses SMB named pipes rather than only endpoint-mapper plus dynamic-port RPC. _Why:_ defenders should expect SMB named-pipe artifacts for this technique. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **Primary Remote Registry pipe** — The protocol connects to `\PIPE\winreg`. _Why:_ this named pipe is a direct indicator of Remote Registry communication. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **Additional RPC-related pipes** — The activity can involve other named pipes related to the RPC call. _Why:_ more than one pipe may appear during the same remote registry operation. _[GCFA p.295]_
- **Named pipe creation by service** — The Remote Registry service creates the relevant named pipe when it starts. _Why:_ pipe availability is tied to service execution and can align with service start events. _[GCFA p.295]_

- **Remote Registry service role** — The Remote Registry service is the Windows service that accepts and handles the RPC request sent by the source machine. _Why:_ it identifies the Windows component responsible for registry changes initiated remotely. _[GCFA p.~297]_

- **RPC initiating system** — The remote registry operation originates from another system that sends an RPC message to the target. _Why:_ this ties registry modification activity to lateral administrative access patterns. _[GCFA p.~297]_

- **Event ID 7036 log location** — The Remote Registry service state-change event is recorded in the System log. _Why:_ investigators should check the System log, not only Security, for this service transition. _[GCFA p.~297]_

### Registry Write Timing

- **Deferred registry writes** — Remote Registry does not have to commit changes to the registry immediately after receiving a request. _Why:_ the modification time of a registry key may lag behind the network or service-start activity. _[GCFA p.~297]_

- **Request batching behavior** — Remote Registry can collect multiple received requests and write them later in batches. _Why:_ this batching affects timeline reconstruction and can group multiple operations near the same commit time. _[GCFA p.~297]_

- **Registry key timestamp** — Each registry key stores a timestamp showing the most recent time data was written to that key. _Why:_ key last-write times can identify registry locations modified during suspicious activity. _[GCFA p.~297]_

- **Last-write forensic value** — Registry key last-write timestamps can be used to search for keys modified around the suspected remote connection window. _Why:_ this narrows analysis to keys likely touched during the incident. _[GCFA p.~297]_

### COM And DCOM Concepts

- **COM** — Microsoft Component Object Model is a Windows technology for building binary software components that can be invoked by other software. _Why:_ COM is the underlying object model abused in this lateral movement technique. _[GCFA p.299]_
- **COM design model** — COM supports distributed, object-based component interaction rather than only local monolithic application logic. _Why:_ this explains why COM objects can expose reusable functions to other programs. _[GCFA p.299]_
- **COM longevity** — COM is an older Microsoft technology that remains present in current Windows environments. _Why:_ defenders should still expect COM-related abuse on modern systems. _[GCFA p.299]_
- **COM object implementation** — COM objects are compiled code components. _Why:_ forensic analysis should treat them as executable functionality, not just configuration metadata. _[GCFA p.299]_
- **COM object hosting** — COM objects may reside inside existing executable files. _Why:_ benign applications can unintentionally provide attacker-usable execution surfaces. _[GCFA p.299]_
- **External COM references** — Programs can invoke COM objects from outside the executable that contains them. _Why:_ attackers can drive functionality exposed by another application without directly launching the application in the usual user-facing way. _[GCFA p.299]_
- **COM code reuse purpose** — COM enables multiple applications on the same system to reuse shared component functionality. _Why:_ this legitimate reuse model creates a broad surface for abuse. _[GCFA p.299]_
- **DCOM** — Distributed COM extends COM so remote systems can reference and execute COM objects over the network. _Why:_ DCOM turns local component functionality into a lateral movement mechanism. _[GCFA p.299]_
- **DCOM transport** — DCOM relies on Remote Procedure Calls for remote object interaction. _Why:_ RPC activity is part of the expected communication pattern for this technique. _[GCFA p.299]_
- **Remote COM invocation** — DCOM allows a COM object on one computer to be called from another computer. _Why:_ this is the core remote execution behavior defenders must recognize. _[GCFA p.299]_
- **DCOM permission requirement** — DCOM abuse usually needs local administrator privileges on the destination host. _Why:_ local admin access on the target is a precondition that helps scope investigations and containment. _[GCFA p.299]_

- **COM object instantiation requirement** — a COM object needs the executable that contains it to be running before the object can be used. _Why:_ DCOM abuse leaves process evidence because object activation causes host execution. _[GCFA p.301]_
- **DcomLauncher responsibility** — the DcomLauncher service starts the executable associated with the requested COM object. _Why:_ this makes DcomLauncher a key parent-process pivot for DCOM lateral movement analysis. _[GCFA p.301]_
- **Example associated executable** — the page references `MMC.exe` as the prior example of an executable launched to host a COM object. _Why:_ `mmc.exe` is a concrete process name to check when validating the described DCOM pattern. _[GCFA p.301]_
- **DCOM lateral movement child process pattern** — during DCOM-based lateral movement, the executable containing the COM object, such as `mmc.exe`, is commonly started beneath DcomLauncher. _Why:_ this parent-child relationship helps distinguish DCOM execution from ordinary interactive process starts. _[GCFA p.301]_
- **DcomLauncher service image** — DcomLauncher runs inside `svchost.exe`. _Why:_ investigators must identify the correct `svchost.exe` instance rather than treating all svchost processes as equivalent. _[GCFA p.301]_

- **Network logon meaning** — Logon Type `3` is described as a network logon. _Why:_ this distinguishes remote access from console or interactive logons. _[GCFA p.301]_

## Page 305

### Scenario

- **Explicit-credential lateral movement scenario** — this page focuses on tracking credential switching that commonly occurs when an actor moves between Windows systems. _Why:_ credential changes can expose movement paths during an intrusion. _[GCFA p.305]_

### Relevant Event IDs

- **Event ID 4624** — Windows records successful logons under Event ID 4624. _Why:_ successful logon records are core evidence for tracing access during lateral movement. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Event ID 4624 · Logon Type 9** — Logon Type 9 is the 4624 subtype highlighted for explicit-credential investigations. _Why:_ this logon type can indicate a new credential set being used from an existing session. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Event ID 4648** — Windows records use of explicitly supplied credentials under Event ID 4648. _Why:_ this event can reveal when a tool was given alternate credentials. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Event ID 4648 · Explicit credentials** — EID 4648 is specifically associated with logon activity where credentials are provided directly rather than simply inherited from the current logon. _Why:_ explicit credential use is a strong lead for administrator activity or attacker movement. _[GCFA p.305]_

### Credential Switching

- **Credential changes during lateral movement** — moving from one host to another often requires changing credentials. _Why:_ attackers may need different accounts to access different systems. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Administrators as common credential switchers** — administrators commonly use more than one credential set. _Why:_ legitimate admin behavior forms the baseline that must be separated from attacker behavior. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Attackers as common credential switchers** — attackers also commonly use multiple credentials while trying to move through an environment. _Why:_ this makes explicit-credential events valuable for identifying suspicious movement. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Computer accounts as frequent credential switchers** — system accounts, including machine accounts, may also change credential context frequently. _Why:_ these can create noisy background activity that investigators must filter. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Enterprise credential swapping** — many routine Windows enterprise workflows require a process or user to authenticate with a different credential set. _Why:_ investigators need to distinguish expected credential use from lateral movement. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Computer account impersonation** — a computer account may impersonate a user when authenticating to a resource. _Why:_ this can produce credential-change evidence that is legitimate rather than malicious. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Outlook credential switching** — Outlook may move from the signed-in domain account to a user’s Microsoft cloud identity when connecting to Microsoft 365. _Why:_ Microsoft 365 authentication can generate background explicit-credential noise. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Administrator privilege elevation** — an administrator may switch to a more privileged account for maintenance work. _Why:_ this behavior can resemble attacker credential switching and must be interpreted in context. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Attacker alternate-credential use** — an attacker may switch accounts to reach a host that requires credentials different from those already held. _Why:_ this is the adversary behavior the page is teaching investigators to detect. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Segmented-network credential constraints** — well-segmented environments may require different credentials for different network areas. _Why:_ segmentation can force attackers to expose themselves through repeated credential changes. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Limited-scope credentials** — some credentials may work only in specific parts of the network. _Why:_ constrained credentials can create a traceable sequence of account changes during movement. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Credential-switching as an investigative advantage** — investigators can search for credential-change events because credential swapping is often necessary for movement. _Why:_ the need to change accounts creates useful telemetry. _[GCFA p.305]_

### Event Sources And Filtering

- **Two primary recording patterns** — credential-switching activity is commonly visible through 4624 Logon Type 9 and 4648 explicit-credential events. _Why:_ these two event types are the page’s main investigative pivots. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Background system activity filtering** — investigators should remove common background activity before interpreting these events. _Why:_ filtering reduces false leads from normal system behavior. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Computer-account noise** — computer account activity is specifically named as a common source of background events. _Why:_ machine account events may otherwise obscure meaningful human activity. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Microsoft 365 noise** — Microsoft 365 authentication activity is specifically named as background activity to filter. _Why:_ cloud-service authentication can mimic explicit credential use without indicating lateral movement. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Post-filter residue** — after common background events are removed, remaining activity often consists mainly of administrator activity and attacker activity. _Why:_ the reduced dataset is more useful for hunting suspicious credential use. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Attacker as false administrator** — the page frames attackers using multiple credentials as behaving like unauthorized administrators. _Why:_ attackers may blend into administrative credential-use patterns. _[GCFA p.305]_

### Event ID 4648 Investigative Value

- **4648 origin-system value** — 4648 events are notable because they are often recorded on the system where the activity originated. _Why:_ origin-side logging helps identify where lateral movement began. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Contrast with target-side evidence** — many other lateral-movement artifacts are usually found on the destination system rather than the source. _Why:_ target-only evidence can leave the origin of movement unclear. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **4648 movement direction** — EID 4648 can show where a user was attempting to go from the system under investigation. _Why:_ this helps reconstruct outbound movement from a compromised host. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Incident scoping with 4648** — 4648 events can help quickly identify additional connected systems. _Why:_ connected-system discovery is essential for determining incident scope. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Runas-related 4648 behavior** — the page specifically highlights “runas” 4648 events as unusually useful because of origin-system logging. _Why:_ runas-style credential use can expose the source side of an attempted access path. _[GCFA p.305]_

### Origin Versus Target Interpretation

- **Dual-system 4648 logging** — in some cases, a 4648 event may appear on both the originating host and the destination host. _Why:_ investigators must avoid assuming every 4648 represents only source-side activity. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **RDP with different credentials** — Remote Desktop connections made with alternate credentials can log 4648 events on both systems. _Why:_ RDP can complicate source-versus-target interpretation. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Target Server field** — the event’s Target Server information is the field used to infer whether the 4648 is source-side or target-side. _Why:_ this field helps determine movement direction. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Target Server equals localhost** — when the Target Server value is localhost, the 4648 is recording inbound activity. _Why:_ this indicates the local system is acting as the destination. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Target Server contains remote IP address** — when the Target Server information includes a remote IP address, the 4648 is recording outbound activity. _Why:_ this indicates the local system is the origin of activity toward another host. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **4648 analysis complexity** — interpreting these events can become complicated. _Why:_ source/target ambiguity and dual logging require careful event-field analysis. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **4648 analysis payoff** — despite the complexity, analyzing these events is worthwhile. _Why:_ they can materially improve lateral-movement reconstruction and incident scoping. _[GCFA p.305]_

### Explicit Credentials Without Account Switching

- **4648 without account change** — explicit-credential events can be logged even when the account does not actually change. _Why:_ investigators should not assume every 4648 means a different user account was used. _[GCFA p.305]_
- **Tool-supplied credentials** — 4648 can be recorded when credentials are supplied to a tool, even if the supplied credentials do not result in a different account context. _Why:_ the event can indicate credential handling by a tool rather than a confirmed account switch. _[GCFA p.305]_

## Page 306

### Explicit Credential Use

- **Explicit credentials wording** — the relevant Windows event types use “explicit credentials” language to indicate that authentication was performed with credentials supplied by a tool or process rather than credentials already available in the current logon session. _Why:_ this wording separates normal reuse of in-memory credentials from deliberate credential specification. _[GCFA p.306]_

- **Explicit credentials definition** — explicit credentials are newly provided authentication material used by a program, as opposed to credentials already cached or present in memory. _Why:_ this distinction helps identify tools that intentionally supplied account credentials during activity. _[GCFA p.306]_

- **Memory-resident credentials contrast** — if a tool relies only on credentials already present in memory, that is not the behavior being described as explicit credential use on this page. _Why:_ investigators need to distinguish credential reuse from credential submission. _[GCFA p.306]_

- **Cobalt Strike credential selection** — malware frameworks such as Cobalt Strike commonly require the operator to specify which credentials should be used when executing commands on remote systems. _Why:_ explicit credential prompts in attacker tooling can create Windows log artifacts useful for hunting. _[GCFA p.306]_

- **Remote command execution with chosen credentials** — attacker tools may run remote commands under credentials selected by the operator rather than under the already-authenticated user context. _Why:_ this behavior can reveal lateral movement or remote execution activity in authentication logs. _[GCFA p.306]_

- **PsExec `-u` option** — PsExec supports the `-u` command-line parameter to specify the username used for execution. _Why:_ this flag is a concrete indicator that PsExec may be using explicit credentials. _[GCFA p.306]_

- **PsExec `-p` option** — PsExec supports the `-p` command-line parameter to specify the password used for execution. _Why:_ this flag pairs with `-u` and can explain why Windows records explicit credential use. _[GCFA p.306]_

- **PsExec command-line credential entry** — PsExec can receive credentials directly through command-line parameters. _Why:_ command-line artifacts and authentication logs can corroborate each other during investigation. _[GCFA p.306]_

- **Scripts using explicit credentials** — scripts can be written to provide credentials explicitly during authentication or remote activity. _Why:_ explicit credential artifacts are not limited to commercial tools or malware frameworks; custom automation can produce them too. _[GCFA p.306]_

- **Logging even when credentials match memory** — Windows records explicit credential use even if the supplied credentials are identical to credentials already present in memory. _Why:_ investigators should not dismiss an explicit-credential event merely because the account matches the current user context. _[GCFA p.306]_

- **Malware frequency** — explicit credential use occurs often in malware-driven activity. _Why:_ frequent appearance in malicious workflows makes this behavior a valuable hunting lead. _[GCFA p.306]_

- **Log-hunting value** — explicit credential events provide an additional artifact that analysts can search for in Windows logs. _Why:_ these events can expose credentialed execution patterns that may otherwise blend into normal authentication activity. _[GCFA p.306]_

### Lateral Movement Interpretation

- **Common attacker behavior** — attackers often compromise multiple accounts with different privilege levels. _Why:_ lateral movement investigations should expect more than one account to appear in the evidence. _[GCFA p.~307]_
- **Privilege-driven account switching** — attackers may need several accounts to move laterally and run programs across an enterprise. _Why:_ credential changes can be operationally necessary for the attacker and therefore detectable. _[GCFA p.~307]_
- **Event 4648 detection value** — Event 4648 provides a useful detection point because it records use of explicit or different credentials. _Why:_ defenders can hunt for account switching rather than only successful remote access. _[GCFA p.~307]_
- **Network share mapping trigger** — explicit-credential events may appear during network share mapping. _Why:_ the page’s example shows share mapping as a concrete Event 4648 use case. _[GCFA p.~307]_
- **Lateral movement script trigger** — explicit-credential events may appear when lateral movement scripts execute. _Why:_ scripted remote activity often requires supplied credentials. _[GCFA p.~307]_
- **WinRM trigger** — explicit-credential events may appear during WinRM activity. _Why:_ WinRM is a common remote administration and lateral movement channel. _[GCFA p.~307]_
- **PowerShell Remoting trigger** — explicit-credential events may appear during PowerShell Remoting. _Why:_ PowerShell Remoting commonly involves remote authentication that may use alternate credentials. _[GCFA p.~307]_
- **Local privilege elevation trigger** — explicit-credential events may appear when a user elevates locally to administrator through UAC or another method. _Why:_ Event 4648 is relevant to both remote movement and local credential changes. _[GCFA p.~307]_
- **Target-only limitation** — normally the target-side Event 5140 would provide only the share access details on wkstn01. _Why:_ that view can be insufficient to reveal the originating user context. _[GCFA p.~307]_
- **Originating-system evidence** — when different credentials are used, the originating system can also show evidence of lateral movement through Event 4648. _Why:_ this gives investigators visibility that does not exist in most target-only artifacts. _[GCFA p.~307]_
- **Event 4648 viewpoint** — Event 4648 gives a source-side view of lateral movement. _Why:_ it helps analysts track where remote authentication attempts began. _[GCFA p.~307]_
- **Multi-target usefulness** — source-side Event 4648 tracking is especially useful when an attacker connects from one host to multiple remote systems. _Why:_ it can reveal the fan-out pattern from the originating machine. _[GCFA p.~307]_
- **Need for both event types** — reconstructing the full sequence requires both the originating Event 4648 and the target Event 5140 in this example. _Why:_ together they show the original account, substituted account, source host, target host, and accessed share. _[GCFA p.~307]_

### Event ID 4648 Lateral Movement Clues

- **Event ID 4648 · Movement type hints** — Windows Event ID 4648 can expose clues about the kind of lateral movement being attempted, even when the investigator lacks the matching Event ID 5140 from the destination host. _Why:_ the source-side explicit-credential event may still reveal what service or protocol was targeted. _[GCFA p.308]_

- **Event ID 4648 · Network Information section** — the Network Information portion of Event ID 4648 includes the destination IP address and destination port. _Why:_ these fields help infer what remote service the credential use was aimed at. _[GCFA p.308]_

- **Target port 445** — a destination port value of `445` indicates traffic aimed at SMB. _Why:_ port 445 is a strong protocol clue when reconstructing lateral movement from logs. _[GCFA p.308]_

- **Port 445 · SMB association** — TCP port `445` is used by Server Message Block. _Why:_ identifying SMB narrows the likely remote activity to Windows file sharing or related IPC mechanisms. _[GCFA p.308]_

- **SMB access implication** — when Event ID 4648 shows a target port of `445`, the likely activity is access to a shared folder or a named pipe. _Why:_ both file shares and named pipes are common SMB-backed lateral movement paths. _[GCFA p.308]_

### Event ID 4648 Target Server Fields

- **Target Server section** — Event ID 4648 includes a Target Server section that can show both a Target Server Name field and an Additional Information field. _Why:_ these fields add destination-service context beyond the account and network fields. _[GCFA p.308]_

- **Target Server Name field** — the Target Server Name field records the named remote system involved in the explicit-credential authentication attempt. _Why:_ it helps identify which host the source system attempted to access. _[GCFA p.308]_

- **Additional Information field** — the Additional Information field can contain the service principal name for the service being accessed on the destination host. _Why:_ the SPN can reveal the intended service even when other target-side evidence is unavailable. _[GCFA p.308]_

- **SPN meaning** — an SPN, or service principal name, identifies a specific service instance on a target server. _Why:_ SPNs provide service-level attribution for authenticated network activity. _[GCFA p.308]_

### CIFS And SMB Service Identification

- **CIFS service class** — an SPN service class of `CIFS` refers to the SMB protocol. _Why:_ CIFS in an SPN is a clear indicator that SMB service access was involved. _[GCFA p.308]_

- **CIFS case handling** — `CIFS` service-class matching is case-insensitive. _Why:_ investigators should treat differently capitalized CIFS values as equivalent SMB indicators. _[GCFA p.308]_

- **CIFS SPN access meaning** — a connection to an SPN whose service class is CIFS represents access to the SMB service on that destination system. _Why:_ this links explicit credential use to SMB-based lateral movement or share access. _[GCFA p.308]_

- **SMB service context from SPN** — when Event ID 4648 Additional Information contains a CIFS SPN, it supplies service context that may substitute for missing target-side share-access logs. _Why:_ it can preserve evidence of SMB access intent even without Event ID 5140. _[GCFA p.308]_

### Limits Of Service Identification

- **Service identification limitation** — Event ID 4648 does not always identify the exact service accessed. _Why:_ analysts should avoid overclaiming protocol or tool attribution from 4648 alone. _[GCFA p.308]_

- **PowerShell remoting SPN behavior** — PowerShell remoting may record only the generic `HOST` service class in Event ID 4648. _Why:_ a generic HOST SPN can obscure the specific remote-management mechanism. _[GCFA p.308]_

- **Additional Information review** — investigators should still inspect the Additional Information field for added context. _Why:_ even when imperfect, this field may provide the best available clue about the target service. _[GCFA p.308]_

### Corresponding Target Logon Event

- **Remote access follow-on event** — remote access to the destination system generates a corresponding Event ID 4624 entry on the target. _Why:_ pairing source-side 4648 with target-side 4624 helps confirm successful remote logon activity. _[GCFA p.308]_

- **Event ID 4624 · Logon type 3** — in this scenario, the corresponding Event ID 4624 shows Logon Type `3`. _Why:_ Logon Type 3 identifies a network logon, consistent with remote access over SMB or similar network services. _[GCFA p.308]_

- **Network Logon label** — Logon Type `3` is the Windows “Network Logon” category. _Why:_ this classification distinguishes remote network authentication from local, interactive, or other logon types. _[GCFA p.308]_

## Page 310

### Cobalt Strike Explicit Credential Behavior

- **Explicit credentials** — explicit credential use means a program authenticates with supplied credentials instead of reusing credentials already available in the current logon session. _Why:_ this distinguishes deliberate credential use from normal single sign-on behavior during lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~310]_
- **Tool-driven explicit credential use** — many offensive and administrative tools are designed so that the operator must provide credentials explicitly. _Why:_ these tools can leave Windows log evidence even when the same account is reused. _[GCFA p.~310]_
- **Cobalt Strike explicit credential requirement** — Cobalt Strike is an example of a tool that can require or generate explicit credential logon behavior. _Why:_ Cobalt Strike activity can be detected through Windows authentication artifacts. _[GCFA p.~310]_
- **Cobalt Strike make_token** — `make_token` creates a new logon session associated with explicitly supplied credentials. _Why:_ the resulting logon session can reveal token-manipulation activity. _[GCFA p.~310]_
- **Cobalt Strike pth** — `pth`, meaning pass-the-hash, creates log artifacts that appear the same as `make_token` in the shown Windows logs. _Why:_ analysts should not assume the command was `make_token` solely from the event pattern. _[GCFA p.~310]_
- **Payload credential passing** — Cobalt Strike can pass the newly created explicit-credential logon session to a selected payload. _Why:_ this enables follow-on execution under the chosen identity. _[GCFA p.~310]_
- **Same-account explicit credential use** — explicit credential events can occur even when the supplied account is the same as the account already in use. _Why:_ identical source and destination account names do not rule out attacker-specified credentials. _[GCFA p.~310]_
- **Token manipulation dependency** — Cobalt Strike uses token manipulation heavily when interacting with remote systems and moving laterally. _Why:_ token-focused behavior creates authentication artifacts useful for incident reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~310]_
- **Alternate-identity lateral movement** — Cobalt Strike token commands allow manual or automated remote actions under a different identity. _Why:_ this is a common mechanism for attacker pivoting across hosts. _[GCFA p.~310]_
- **Detection opportunity** — Cobalt Strike token commands generate Windows logs that can be searched by defenders. _Why:_ these events provide evidence of credential use and target selection. _[GCFA p.~310]_

## Page 314

### Initiating-System Evidence

- **Initiating host perspective** — The page focuses on artifacts found on the system used to launch the password-guessing activity, not only on the target system receiving the attempts. _Why:_ the attacker-controlled internal host can contain evidence that identifies where the brute-force or spray activity originated. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Compromised internal launcher** — A breached internal machine may be used to run password-spray attempts against other internal systems. _Why:_ lateral movement investigations should examine both victims and the host that generated the authentication attempts. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Additional evidence on the launcher** — The initiating system can retain logs beyond those seen on the attacked destination. _Why:_ these local artifacts can corroborate that the host actively initiated the spray rather than merely receiving failed logons. _[GCFA p.~314]_

### Target-System Context From Prior Slide

- **Prior target-side artifact** — The preceding slide described logs from a system that was the target of a password spray. _Why:_ target-side evidence provides context for comparing destination failures with source-side initiating artifacts. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Event ID 4625 on attacked system** — Many Windows failed-logon events with Event ID 4625 were shown as evidence of repeated authentication attempts. _Why:_ numerous failed authentications are a common target-side indicator of password guessing. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Many usernames in 4625 events** — A long sequence of different usernames in failed-logon records indicates many accounts were tried. _Why:_ password spraying often tests one or a few passwords across many accounts rather than many passwords against one account. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Short time window for 4625 events** — Numerous authentication attempts in a brief period support the interpretation of password-spray activity. _Why:_ timing density helps distinguish automated or coordinated attacks from ordinary user mistakes. _[GCFA p.~314]_

### Event ID 4648

- **Event ID 4648** — Windows creates Event ID 4648 when a user supplies explicit alternate credentials to start a process or make a network connection. _Why:_ password spraying from a host commonly involves repeated attempts using credentials other than the currently logged-on account. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Alternate credential use** — Supplying credentials different from the current user context can cause Event ID 4648 to be logged. _Why:_ this records a key behavior used when testing many usernames and passwords. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Process launch with explicit credentials** — Starting a process with separately provided credentials is one condition that can generate Event ID 4648. _Why:_ attackers may use tools or commands that attempt actions under alternate account contexts. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Network connection with explicit credentials** — Initiating a network connection with alternate credentials is another condition that can generate Event ID 4648. _Why:_ lateral movement commonly involves testing access to remote systems over network protocols. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Original credential in 4648** — Event ID 4648 records the credential context from which the action began. _Why:_ this can identify the account or session used to launch the password-spray activity. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Provided credential in 4648** — Event ID 4648 also records the credential explicitly supplied for the attempted action. _Why:_ this exposes the account being tested during the spray attempt. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **High volume of 4648 events** — Many Event ID 4648 records appearing close together in time can indicate password spraying. _Why:_ repeated alternate-credential attempts are consistent with automated credential testing. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Changing user context in 4648 events** — Each Event ID 4648 entry may show a different user context being attempted. _Why:_ variation across attempted accounts is a defining clue for password spray activity. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Same starting credential across many attempts** — A pattern where one original credential is used to attempt actions with many other credentials is a strong source-side password-spray indicator. _Why:_ it ties multiple attempted identities back to a single initiating account or session. _[GCFA p.~314]_

### Event ID 4624 Logon Type 9

- **Event ID 4624 with Logon Type 9** — Windows also creates successful-logon Event ID 4624 records with Logon Type 9 when explicit alternate credentials are used. _Why:_ this event can corroborate Event ID 4648 evidence from the initiating system. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Similar details in 4624 Type 9** — Event ID 4624 Logon Type 9 records information similar to the explicit-credential details found in Event ID 4648. _Why:_ investigators can use both records together to validate alternate-credential activity. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Password spray indicator on launcher** — A cluster of Event ID 4648 records over a short interval is an indicator that the local system may be initiating a password spray. _Why:_ the source host repeatedly supplies alternate credentials in rapid succession. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Brute-force and spray overlap in SMB artifacts** — SMB Client Event ID 31001 can appear during password spraying as well as other brute-force password-guessing methods. _Why:_ the same log source is useful for multiple forms of credential-guessing investigation. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Temporal concentration matters** — The page repeatedly emphasizes many events occurring in a short period. _Why:_ event frequency and timing are central to separating attack behavior from isolated failed logons. _[GCFA p.~314]_

- **Credential diversity matters** — The page emphasizes attempts involving many different credentials or user contexts. _Why:_ multiple attempted identities are a key analytical feature of password spray activity. _[GCFA p.~314]_

## Page 315

### NTLM Relay Log Pattern

- **NTLM relay attack** — an attacker can forward an authentication attempt through another host instead of letting the target receive it directly from the true client. _Why:_ this can leave inconsistent origin data in Windows logon telemetry. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **Machine-in-the-middle relay position** — the attacker uses an intermediary system to pass authentication material from one computer to another. _Why:_ the target may log the intermediary’s network address while still recording the relayed client identity. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **Event ID 4624 network-logon relevance** — Windows Security Event ID 4624 can record details for a successful network logon. _Why:_ this event is a key artifact for spotting relayed authentication. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **Normal Event ID 4624 Network Information behavior** — for ordinary network logons, the Network Information section should identify the originating workstation name and its IP address. _Why:_ matching hostname-to-IP data establishes the expected baseline. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **Relayed Event ID 4624 Workstation Name behavior** — during a relay, the Workstation Name can contain the hostname of the system whose authentication was relayed. _Why:_ the client name may appear legitimate even though the connection arrived from another host. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **Relayed Event ID 4624 Source Network Address behavior** — during a relay, the Source Network Address can show the IP address of the attacker-controlled relay system. _Why:_ this field can reveal the actual network source that contacted the target. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **Workstation/IP mismatch anomaly** — an NTLM relay can create a mismatch between the Workstation Name and the Source Network Address in Event ID 4624. _Why:_ this mismatch is the core detection clue shown on the page. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **Host-name relay behavior** — the requesting host’s name can be carried along inside the relayed authentication exchange. _Why:_ this explains why the target logs the victim client’s name even when the packet source is the relay host. _[GCFA p.~315]_

### Example Relay Scenario

- **Client11 role** — Client11 is the system whose authentication attempt is relayed. _Why:_ it is the apparent workstation name in the target’s logon event. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **Client11 IP address** — Client11 is shown with IP address `10.0.2.77`. _Why:_ this is the IP that should align with Client11 in a non-relayed scenario. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **Server2 role** — Server2 is the attacker-controlled relay system in the example. _Why:_ it is the host whose IP appears as the network source on Server1. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **Server2 IP address** — Server2 is shown with IP address `10.0.2.112`. _Why:_ this value appears in the target log as the source address, exposing the relay path. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **Server1 role** — Server1 is the target system receiving the relayed authentication attempt. _Why:_ its Security log contains the Event ID 4624 artifact shown on the page. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **Relay direction** — the example shows authentication being relayed from Client11 through Server2 to Server1. _Why:_ the sequence explains why Server1 logs Client11 as the workstation but Server2’s IP as the source. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **Example anomaly** — Server1 records Workstation Name `CLIENT11` while Source Network Address is `10.0.2.112`. _Why:_ Client11’s displayed IP is `10.0.2.77`, so the logged source address belongs to Server2 instead. _[GCFA p.~315]_
