### Detection and Correlation

- **Required asset knowledge** — detecting the mismatch requires knowing which IP address belongs to which computer. _Why:_ without hostname-to-IP context, the anomaly may not be obvious. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **DHCP complication** — DHCP-assigned addresses can make relay mismatch detection harder. _Why:_ dynamic address assignments require time-aware correlation rather than static lookup. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **DHCP lease log correlation** — investigators may need DHCP lease records to confirm which host held an IP address at the event time. _Why:_ lease logs can validate whether the Event ID 4624 workstation name and source IP should match. _[GCFA p.~315]_
- **Static IP advantage** — relay detection is easier when involved systems use static addresses. _Why:_ stable mappings make a workstation-name/source-address mismatch faster to confirm. _[GCFA p.~315]_

## Page 316

### Weak Kerberos Encryption Abuse

- **Credential attack detection signal** — Some credential-theft and credential-reuse activity can be identified by spotting unusual use of weak Kerberos encryption. _Why:_ abnormal downgrade or legacy crypto use can expose attacker behavior during lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **RC4-HMAC-MD5 support in Windows** — Many Windows environments still allow RC4-HMAC-MD5 Kerberos encryption. _Why:_ continued support creates an opportunity for attackers when the weak option remains enabled. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **RC4-HMAC-MD5 normal-use expectation** — RC4-HMAC-MD5 should generally appear only when stronger Kerberos encryption is unavailable. _Why:_ RC4 use in a modern domain can be suspicious because AES-capable clients should normally avoid it. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **AES support in modern Windows clients** — Current Windows clients can use stronger AES Kerberos encryption variants. _Why:_ AES availability makes RC4-HMAC-MD5 use less expected and more useful as a hunt condition. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Backward-compatibility role of RC4-HMAC-MD5** — RC4-HMAC-MD5 remains primarily for compatibility with older systems. _Why:_ distinguishing legacy compatibility from malicious coercion is important during investigation. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Attack benefit from weak encryption** — Certain credential attacks gain an advantage when Kerberos tickets use RC4-HMAC-MD5. _Why:_ attackers may intentionally cause or request weaker crypto to improve cracking feasibility. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Weakest encryption type abuse** — Attackers can exploit RC4-HMAC-MD5 when it is enabled as the weakest available Kerberos encryption option. _Why:_ enabled weak crypto expands the practical attack surface for credential compromise. _[GCFA p.~316]_

### Kerberoasting Detection

- **Kerberoasting target artifact** — Kerberoasting involves obtaining Kerberos service tickets. _Why:_ service ticket requests are the observable event source for detecting this technique. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Kerberoasting cracking objective** — The attacker attempts to recover the plaintext password for the service account tied to the requested service ticket. _Why:_ successful cracking converts a ticket request into reusable account credentials. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Service ticket encryption relationship** — The service ticket is encrypted using material associated with the service account. _Why:_ that encryption design is what allows offline password guessing against the service account. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Manual service account password risk** — Kerberoasting is practical mainly when the service account uses a human-created password. _Why:_ manually chosen passwords are more likely to be weak enough for offline cracking. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Automatically generated service account password resistance** — Automatically generated service account passwords are typically long and complex enough to make cracking impractical. _Why:_ password generation method materially changes Kerberoasting success likelihood. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Password complexity dependency** — Even for manually assigned service account passwords, cracking duration depends on password strength. _Why:_ complexity affects whether a captured service ticket is realistically exploitable. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Kerberoasting crypto downgrade preference** — Attackers may specifically ask for service tickets encrypted with RC4-HMAC-MD5. _Why:_ RC4-HMAC-MD5 makes offline cracking faster than stronger Kerberos encryption. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Kerberoasting hunt condition** — Service tickets issued with RC4-HMAC-MD5 are a detection lead for Kerberoasting. _Why:_ weak encryption on service tickets can indicate deliberate attacker optimization for cracking. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Kerberoasting event ID** — Windows Event ID 4769 records service ticket requests. _Why:_ this event is the primary log source for detecting suspicious service ticket encryption choices. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Event ID 4769 encryption field** — Event ID 4769 includes the encryption type used when the service ticket was issued. _Why:_ the field allows defenders to identify tickets issued with weaker RC4-based encryption. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Kerberoasting RC4 value 0x17** — For Event ID 4769, Encryption Type `0x17` indicates a weak RC4-based ticket encryption type relevant to Kerberoasting detection. _Why:_ this exact value can be used in SIEM searches and detection rules. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Kerberoasting RC4 value 0x18** — For Event ID 4769, Encryption Type `0x18` may also indicate a weak RC4-based ticket encryption type relevant to Kerberoasting detection. _Why:_ including this value reduces missed detections for RC4-related service ticket issuance. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Kerberoasting with AES** — Kerberoasting can still be attempted when service tickets use AES encryption. _Why:_ absence of RC4 does not fully eliminate Kerberoasting risk. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **AES Kerberoasting impact** — AES-based Kerberoasting is much slower and has a lower chance of success than RC4-based Kerberoasting. _Why:_ encryption type affects attacker economics and prioritization of detections. _[GCFA p.~316]_

### Overpass-the-Hash Detection

- **Overpass-the-Hash credential material** — Overpass-the-Hash can use an NT hash to obtain Kerberos authentication material. _Why:_ this links NTLM credential theft to Kerberos-based lateral movement. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **TGT detection focus** — Defenders should look for Ticket Granting Tickets issued from an NTLM hash rather than normal AES long-term keys. _Why:_ TGT issuance based on weaker key material can reveal Overpass-the-Hash activity. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **NTLM hash Kerberos key equivalence** — The NTLM hash corresponds to an RC4-HMAC-MD5 long-term Kerberos key. _Why:_ this explains why RC4-related Kerberos fields are relevant to NT-hash abuse. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Expected stronger TGT keying** — AES long-term keys are the stronger expected basis for TGT issuance in modern environments. _Why:_ deviation from AES toward RC4 can indicate credential misuse or legacy limitations. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Overpass-the-Hash event ID** — Windows Event ID 4768 records TGT-related activity relevant to Overpass-the-Hash detection. _Why:_ this event is the key log source for identifying suspicious TGT issuance. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Pre-January-2025 / older-than-Server-2016 field** — For earlier logging formats, Event ID 4768 uses the Encryption Type field to expose the relevant RC4 value. _Why:_ detection logic must account for older event schemas. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Server 2016+ after January 2025 field** — For Server 2016 and later systems after the January 2025 update, Event ID 4768 uses Session Type for the relevant value. _Why:_ post-update detection rules need to query the correct field. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Overpass-the-Hash value 0x17** — Event ID 4768 showing `0x17` in the applicable Encryption Type or Session Type field is a weak RC4-related indicator. _Why:_ this value can identify TGT issuance consistent with NT-hash-based Kerberos activity. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Overpass-the-Hash value 0x18** — Event ID 4768 showing `0x18` in the applicable Encryption Type or Session Type field is another weak RC4-related indicator. _Why:_ detections should include both values to avoid incomplete coverage. _[GCFA p.~316]_

### January 2025 Kerberos Event Changes

- **Microsoft January 2025 security update** — Microsoft released a January 2025 security patch that added fields to Kerberos-related Windows events. _Why:_ event schema changes affect how defenders interpret encryption and key availability. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Event ID 4768 update** — The January 2025 patch added new fields to Event ID 4768. _Why:_ TGT analysis after the update has richer context than earlier logs. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Event ID 4769 update** — The January 2025 patch added new fields to Event ID 4769. _Why:_ service ticket analysis after the update can show more than just the issued encryption type. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Client-supported encryption detail** — The added fields provide more information about encryption types supported by the client. _Why:_ defenders can distinguish a client that only supports weak crypto from one that had stronger options available. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Domain-controller-supported encryption detail** — The added fields provide more information about encryption types supported by the domain controller. _Why:_ DC capability context helps explain or challenge why weak encryption was selected. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Client long-term key detail** — The new fields can show long-term keys available on the client side. _Why:_ key availability helps determine whether weak-key use was necessary or suspicious. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Domain controller long-term key detail** — The new fields can show long-term keys available on the domain controller side. _Why:_ this helps validate whether stronger Kerberos key material could have been used. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Protocol availability visibility** — The added event data lets defenders see which Kerberos encryption protocols were available. _Why:_ availability context makes malicious weak-encryption selection easier to detect. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Protocol-use visibility** — The added event data lets defenders see which protocol was actually used to issue TGTs and service tickets. _Why:_ comparing available versus used encryption can reveal downgrade-like behavior. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **TGT issuance context** — The new fields improve visibility into encryption decisions for Ticket Granting Tickets. _Why:_ this supports detection of Overpass-the-Hash and other TGT-related abuse. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Service ticket issuance context** — The new fields improve visibility into encryption decisions for service tickets. _Why:_ this supports detection of Kerberoasting and weak service ticket issuance. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Legacy system identification** — The updated events can help identify systems limited to older encryption protocols such as RC4-HMAC-MD5. _Why:_ defenders must separate legacy operational dependencies from adversary-driven weak encryption use. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Pre-update event limitation** — Before the January 2025 update, Event IDs 4768 and 4769 exposed only one encryption-type field. _Why:_ older logs provide less context and require more cautious interpretation. _[GCFA p.~316]_
- **Pre-update encryption coding** — Before the update, the encryption type appeared as a coded value in the event. _Why:_ analysts need to map values such as `0x17` and `0x18` to weak RC4-related encryption when hunting. _[GCFA p.~316]_

### Kerberos Encryption Type Codes

- **Encryption type 0x1** — The numeric Kerberos encryption identifier `0x1` maps to `DES-CBC-CRC`. _Why:_ DES-based Kerberos encryption is legacy and weak, so seeing it can indicate outdated configuration or suspicious downgrade behavior. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **DES-CBC-CRC default state** — `DES-CBC-CRC` is disabled by default on Windows 7 and Windows Server 2008 R2 and later. _Why:_ use of this value on modern systems is unusual and may indicate insecure legacy compatibility or tampering. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Encryption type 0x3** — The numeric Kerberos encryption identifier `0x3` maps to `DES-CBC-MD5`. _Why:_ this identifies another weak DES-based Kerberos option relevant to downgrade and legacy-authentication investigations. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **DES-CBC-MD5 default state** — `DES-CBC-MD5` is disabled by default beginning with Windows 7 and Windows Server 2008 R2. _Why:_ its appearance on later Windows versions can stand out as a security-relevant anomaly. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Encryption type 0x11** — The numeric Kerberos encryption identifier `0x11` maps to `AES128-CTS-HMAC-SHA1-96`. _Why:_ this value helps distinguish AES-backed Kerberos activity from weaker RC4 or DES activity. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **AES128-CTS-HMAC-SHA1-96 platform support** — `AES128-CTS-HMAC-SHA1-96` is supported starting with Windows Server 2008 and Windows Vista. _Why:_ platform support boundaries help analysts decide whether an observed encryption type is expected for a given environment. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Encryption type 0x12** — The numeric Kerberos encryption identifier `0x12` maps to `AES256-CTS-HMAC-SHA1-96`. _Why:_ this value is important when comparing ticket encryption and session-key encryption in Kerberos event logs. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **AES256-CTS-HMAC-SHA1-96 platform support** — `AES256-CTS-HMAC-SHA1-96` is supported starting with Windows Server 2008 and Windows Vista. _Why:_ AES256 use can indicate stronger Kerberos cryptography when compared with RC4-based values. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Encryption type 0x17** — The numeric Kerberos encryption identifier `0x17` maps to `RC4-HMAC`. _Why:_ `0x17` is a key hunting value for RC4-based Kerberos tickets and possible Kerberoasting or overpass-the-hash activity. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **RC4-HMAC legacy default** — `RC4-HMAC` was the default Kerberos encryption suite for operating systems earlier than Windows Server 2008 and Windows Vista. _Why:_ use of RC4 in newer environments may be suspicious or indicate legacy dependency. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Encryption type 0x18** — The numeric Kerberos encryption identifier `0x18` maps to `RC4-HMAC-EXP`. _Why:_ `0x18` is another RC4-based Kerberos value relevant to weak-encryption detection. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **RC4-HMAC-EXP legacy default** — `RC4-HMAC-EXP` was a default suite before Windows Server 2008 and Windows Vista. _Why:_ its presence can identify legacy or intentionally weakened Kerberos behavior. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Encryption type 0xFFFFFFFF** — The value `0xFFFFFFFF` is associated with Audit Failure events rather than a normal named encryption suite. _Why:_ analysts should not misclassify this value as a successful negotiated Kerberos encryption algorithm. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Encryption type 0xffffffff** — The lowercase representation `0xffffffff` is also shown for the Audit Failure encryption-type value. _Why:_ case variation in logs or tools should not cause analysts to miss the same failure indicator. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Audit Failure encryption type name** — The table gives no encryption-suite name for `0xFFFFFFFF` or `0xffffffff`, showing it as `-`. _Why:_ the dash distinguishes this failure marker from actual cryptographic algorithms. _[GCFA p.317]_

### Rubeus Service Ticket Example

- **Rubeus attack tool** — The page uses Rubeus as the example tool for requesting a Kerberos service ticket with weaker RC4 encryption. _Why:_ Rubeus-generated Kerberos activity is commonly relevant in Windows domain attack investigations. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Weaker RC4 request goal** — The example describes requesting a service ticket that uses weaker RC4 encryption. _Why:_ weaker service-ticket encryption can make offline password attacks more practical. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Kerberoasting relevance** — Obtaining a service ticket encrypted with weaker RC4 can support Kerberoasting by enabling offline brute-force attempts. _Why:_ this links the logged encryption type directly to a common Active Directory credential attack. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Event ID 4769 context** — The shown examples come from the Additional Information section of Windows Security Event ID `4769`. _Why:_ Event ID 4769 is a primary log source for Kerberos service-ticket issuance analysis. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Pre-January 2025 patch comparison point** — One Event ID 4769 example represents output generated before the January 2025 patch. _Why:_ this establishes the baseline field set before Microsoft added or exposed the newer comparison field. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Post-January 2025 patch comparison point** — The second Event ID 4769 example represents output after the January 2025 patch. _Why:_ post-patch events include additional information useful for distinguishing ticket encryption from session encryption. _[GCFA p.317]_

### Ticket Encryption Versus Session Encryption

- **Ticket Encryption Type meaning** — In Event ID 4769, `Ticket Encryption Type` describes the encryption used for the service ticket. _Why:_ analysts must avoid confusing service-ticket encryption with session-key encryption. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Service ticket RC4 value** — In both shown 4769 examples, `Ticket Encryption Type` is `0x17`, meaning the service ticket used RC4-HMAC. _Why:_ this is the weak-encryption indicator relevant to Kerberoasting analysis. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Client session key issuance** — Along with a service ticket, the client receives a session key for communication with the target service. _Why:_ the session key is a separate Kerberos component that may have a different encryption type. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Separate session-key encryption** — The session key is encrypted independently from the service ticket. _Why:_ separate encryption explains why a ticket can use RC4 while the session key uses AES. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Different encryption types in one event** — The post-patch example shows the ticket using `0x17` while the session key uses `0x12`. _Why:_ this difference prevents analysts from assuming all encryption fields in the event describe the same object. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Session Encryption Type 0x12 interpretation** — In the post-patch example, `Session Encryption Type` value `0x12` corresponds to AES256-CTS-HMAC-SHA1-96. _Why:_ the session encryption is stronger than the RC4 service-ticket encryption in the same event. _[GCFA p.317]_

### Overpass-the-Hash and Event ID 4768

- **NT hash theft prerequisite** — If an attacker obtains an NT hash, they can use it to request Kerberos authentication material from a domain controller. _Why:_ NT hash possession enables attacks beyond simple NTLM replay. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Overpass-the-hash objective** — In an overpass-the-hash attack, the attacker can obtain a TGT from the domain controller. _Why:_ a TGT gives the attacker Kerberos-based access paths after hash theft. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **RC4-HMAC-MD5 request behavior** — The described overpass-the-hash method requests the TGT using older RC4-HMAC-MD5 encryption. _Why:_ this ties the attack to legacy RC4 Kerberos encryption choices. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **NT hash as long-term key** — RC4-HMAC-MD5 uses the NT hash as the long-term key. _Why:_ this is why a stolen NT hash can directly support this Kerberos attack path. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Event ID 4768 role** — Windows Security Event ID `4768` records the encryption type used when issuing a TGT. _Why:_ this event is the relevant log source for detecting suspicious TGT encryption choices. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Event ID 4768 value 0x17** — In Event ID 4768, encryption type `0x17` indicates a weaker RC4-based encryption type. _Why:_ this value can flag possible overpass-the-hash or legacy Kerberos behavior. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Event ID 4768 value 0x18** — In Event ID 4768, encryption type `0x18` also indicates weaker RC4-based encryption. _Why:_ analysts should hunt for both RC4-related values, not only `0x17`. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Pass-the-key synonym** — Overpass-the-hash is sometimes referred to as pass-the-key. _Why:_ recognizing both names helps correlate tool output, reports, and detection logic. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **AES long-term key variant** — The same general attack concept can be performed with stolen AES-based long-term keys. _Why:_ RC4 is not the only possible key material for pass-the-key-style Kerberos abuse. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Common NT hash usage** — The page notes that this attack is often carried out with an NT hash. _Why:_ that practical tendency makes RC4-related Event ID 4768 values especially useful hunting leads. _[GCFA p.317]_
- **Hunting unusual Event ID 4768 encryption types** — Analysts should look for uncommon Event ID 4768 encryption types such as `0x17` and `0x18`. _Why:_ these values may reveal RC4-based TGT issuance associated with overpass-the-hash activity. _[GCFA p.317]_

### Event ID 4768 Field Changes

- **January 2025 Microsoft update · Event ID 4768** — Microsoft’s January 2025 patch altered which Kerberos encryption-related fields are recorded in Windows Security Event ID 4768. _Why:_ analysts must know whether a 4768 record was generated before or after the patch to interpret its encryption fields correctly. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Event ID 4768 · Historical encryption ambiguity** — Before the January 2025 update, Event ID 4768 exposed only one encryption-type field. _Why:_ a single field could hide the difference between TGT encryption and session-key or pre-authentication encryption. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Event ID 4768 · Post-patch detail expansion** — After the January 2025 update, Event ID 4768 includes more detailed encryption information. _Why:_ this makes overpass-the-hash and weak-encryption behavior easier to distinguish in logs. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Event ID 4768 · Relationship to Event ID 4769** — The encryption-type numeric values in Event ID 4768 use the same code table referenced for Event ID 4769. _Why:_ investigators can decode 4768 encryption values using the same Kerberos encryption mapping already used for service-ticket analysis. _[GCFA p.~318]_

### Kerberos TGT Encryption Behavior

- **TGT decryption requirement** — Ticket-granting tickets only need to be decrypted by domain controllers. _Why:_ client-side encryption capability does not determine the encryption used to protect the TGT itself. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Domain controller default encryption · Server 2008 and later** — Domain controllers from Windows Server 2008 onward use AES-based Kerberos encryption types by default. _Why:_ AES-protected TGTs are expected in modern Active Directory environments. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Domain functional level · Server 2008 or newer** — If the domain functional level is at least Server 2008, TGTs are encrypted with an AES-based encryption type. _Why:_ RC4 appearing elsewhere in the exchange does not necessarily mean the TGT itself used RC4. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Typical TGT encryption · AES256-HMAC-SHA1** — In Server 2008-or-newer functional-level domains, the common TGT encryption type is AES256-HMAC-SHA1. _Why:_ AES256-HMAC-SHA1 is the expected strong TGT encryption baseline in the described environment. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **TGT encryption in the shown attack** — Even when the attacker requested RC4-HMAC-MD5 for authentication-related material, the TGT still used AES256-HMAC-SHA1 in the shown environment. _Why:_ analysts must separate weak pre-authentication or session encryption from the encryption protecting the TGT. _[GCFA p.~318]_

### AS Reply and Session Key

- **AS Reply contents** — A Kerberos authentication service reply contains the requested TGT and a session key. _Why:_ both objects are relevant when interpreting which encryption type a log field refers to. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Session key purpose** — The AS Reply session key supports later communication between the client and the domain controller during that logon session. _Why:_ compromise or weak encryption of this key affects the Kerberos session beyond the initial request. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Session key encryption key source** — The session key sent to the client is encrypted with the user account’s long-term key. _Why:_ the user’s credential material influences how the client can decrypt and use the session key. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Session key encryption selection** — The encryption type used for the session key depends on what encryption types the client system supports. _Why:_ older or attacker-controlled clients can influence which encryption type appears in the exchange. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Legacy client encryption limitation** — Older systems may support only RC4-HMAC-MD5 for Kerberos encryption. _Why:_ RC4 in Event ID 4768 may indicate legacy compatibility or attacker-forced downgrade behavior. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Stolen NT hash capability** — An attacker who has only a stolen NT hash can request RC4-HMAC-MD5 for the authenticator and later session key. _Why:_ this is a core mechanism behind overpass-the-hash detection in Kerberos logs. _[GCFA p.~318]_

- **Pre-patch Ticket Encryption Type interpretation** — In the older 4768 format, the single Ticket Encryption Type field historically represented the encryption type of the session key sent to the client. _Why:_ treating that value as the TGT encryption type can lead to incorrect conclusions. _[GCFA p.~318]_

- **Post-patch Additional Information · Ticket Encryption Type** — The shown post-patch Event ID 4768 record lists Ticket Encryption Type as `0x12`. _Why:_ this separates the TGT encryption value from the weaker session and pre-authentication encryption values. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Post-patch Additional Information · Session Encryption Type** — The shown post-patch Event ID 4768 record lists Session Encryption Type as `0x17`. _Why:_ this explicitly shows the session key used RC4-HMAC-MD5 in the attack example. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Post-patch Additional Information · Pre-Authentication Type** — The shown post-patch Event ID 4768 record lists Pre-Authentication Type as `2`. _Why:_ this preserves the pre-authentication method indicator while adding more encryption detail. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Post-patch Additional Information · Pre-Authentication EncryptionType** — The shown post-patch Event ID 4768 record lists Pre-Authentication EncryptionType as `0x17`. _Why:_ this directly exposes RC4-HMAC-MD5 use during pre-authentication. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Post-patch client and domain-controller key detail** — The updated 4768 event explicitly records available encryption types and long-term keys for both the client and the domain controller, similar to Event ID 4769. _Why:_ this gives investigators better evidence for whether weak encryption was client-driven, domain-controller-supported, or attacker-requested. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Post-patch AS Request and AS Reply detail** — The updated Additional Information section gives more precise encryption data for both the authentication service request and the AS Reply. _Why:_ analysts can now distinguish pre-authentication encryption, session encryption, and ticket encryption. _[GCFA p.~318]_

### Overpass-the-Hash Indicators

- **Attack scenario in both examples** — Both shown Event ID 4768 examples depict an attacker using a stolen NT hash in an overpass-the-hash attack. _Why:_ the page ties the displayed encryption values to a concrete attack technique. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Attacker encryption request** — In both examples, the attacker explicitly requested RC4-HMAC-MD5 during authentication. _Why:_ requested weak encryption is a key signal of NT-hash-based Kerberos abuse. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Weak encryption value · RC4-HMAC-MD5** — The page identifies `0x17` as the value associated with RC4-HMAC-MD5 in the shown examples. _Why:_ `0x17` is the suspicious weak-encryption value investigators should recognize in these 4768 fields. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Strong TGT encryption value · AES256-HMAC-SHA1** — The page identifies the post-patch Ticket Encryption Type value `0x12` as AES256-HMAC-SHA1 in the shown environment. _Why:_ the same event can show strong TGT protection while still revealing weak client-side authentication or session encryption. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Authenticator composition** — The authenticator used in the authentication service request contains the client’s current timestamp encrypted with the user account’s long-term key. _Why:_ the encryption type protecting this timestamp can reveal whether weak credential-derived material was used. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Pre-authentication weakness in the example** — The shown post-patch event demonstrates that pre-authentication used RC4-HMAC-MD5, represented by `0x17`. _Why:_ this directly supports identifying overpass-the-hash behavior after the January 2025 logging change. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Session encryption weakness in the example** — The shown post-patch event demonstrates that the session encryption type was `0x17`, matching RC4-HMAC-MD5. _Why:_ the client-facing session material used the weak encryption requested by the attacker. _[GCFA p.~318]_
- **Detection improvement after January 2025** — The post-patch 4768 format makes the encryption types used in the exchange more explicit than the older format. _Why:_ investigators can more confidently separate normal AES TGT issuance from suspicious RC4-based authentication behavior. _[GCFA p.~318]_

## Page 319

### Kerberos Encryption Indicators

- **RC4-HMAC-MD5 session-key delivery** — Kerberos may use the older RC4-HMAC-MD5 encryption method so a client can securely receive and use the related session key. _Why:_ this encryption choice can appear in Kerberos activity tied to password-cracking or hash-based attacks. _[GCFA p.319]_

- **Weak Kerberos encryption hunt target** — Responders can search Kerberos logs for weaker encryption types as a detection lead. _Why:_ weak encryption choices can indicate Kerberoasting or overpass-the-hash activity. _[GCFA p.319]_

- **Encryption type 0x17** — Kerberos encryption type `0x17` is identified as the common weak encryption value responders should look for. _Why:_ this specific value is a practical log indicator for RC4-HMAC-MD5 use. _[GCFA p.319]_

- **Kerberoasting with AES** — Kerberoasting is not limited to RC4-HMAC-MD5 and can also be performed using newer AES encryption types. _Why:_ relying only on weak-encryption detections will miss some Kerberoasting activity. _[GCFA p.319]_

- **Overpass-the-hash with AES** — Overpass-the-hash can also operate with newer AES-based Kerberos encryption types. _Why:_ AES use does not rule out credential-abuse activity. _[GCFA p.319]_

- **Kerberoasting RC4 preference** — Kerberoasting commonly uses RC4-HMAC-MD5 because it makes offline password cracking faster than stronger encryption choices. _Why:_ attackers often favor the algorithm that reduces cracking time. _[GCFA p.319]_

- **Plaintext password cracking impact** — The RC4-HMAC-MD5 Kerberos encryption type reduces the effort needed to recover the underlying plaintext password during Kerberoasting. _Why:_ the cryptographic choice directly affects attacker success speed. _[GCFA p.319]_

### Overpass-The-Hash Conditions

- **Domain-controller encryption support** — In overpass-the-hash, an attacker can use any Kerberos encryption type the domain controller supports if they possess the matching long-term key. _Why:_ available attacker material determines which encryption types are possible. _[GCFA p.319]_

- **Long-term key requirement** — Use of a chosen Kerberos encryption type in overpass-the-hash requires the attacker to have stolen the associated long-term key. _Why:_ this distinguishes broader key theft from possession of only an NT hash. _[GCFA p.319]_

- **NT-hash-only limitation** — If the attacker has only the NT hash, they must use RC4-HMAC-MD5 when requesting a Ticket Granting Ticket. _Why:_ NT-hash-only overpass-the-hash creates a more detectable weak-encryption pattern. _[GCFA p.319]_

- **TGT request constraint** — An NT-hash-only attacker must request the TGT using the RC4-HMAC-MD5 encryption type. _Why:_ the AS Request encryption type can expose this form of credential abuse. _[GCFA p.319]_

- **AES long-term key capability** — If an attacker has stolen AES-based long-term Kerberos keys, they can use AES in the authentication exchange. _Why:_ stronger encryption in logs may still represent malicious activity. _[GCFA p.319]_

- **AS Request evasion** — An attacker with AES-based long-term keys can avoid suspicious RC4-HMAC-MD5 log entries by using AES during the AS Request. _Why:_ absence of weak encryption does not prove the authentication was legitimate. _[GCFA p.319]_

### Detection Limits

- **RC4-HMAC-MD5 hunting value** — Searching for RC4-HMAC-MD5 usage can identify many Kerberoasting and overpass-the-hash cases. _Why:_ it is a useful high-signal hunt method for common attack implementations. _[GCFA p.319]_

- **Incomplete RC4 coverage** — Not every Kerberoasting or overpass-the-hash attack will generate RC4-HMAC-MD5 indicators. _Why:_ attackers using AES-compatible key material can avoid this detection pattern. _[GCFA p.319]_

- **Weak-encryption indicator scope** — Weak Kerberos encryption is an indicator, not a comprehensive detector, for Kerberos credential attacks. _Why:_ defenders must account for attacks that use modern AES encryption types. _[GCFA p.319]_

## Page 320

### Credential Theft And Reuse Detection

- **Credential-theft lateral movement** — investigators should hunt for account activity or access paths that do not match normal behavior. _Why:_ stolen credentials often authenticate successfully, so abnormal usage may be the main observable signal. _[GCFA p.320]_
- **Pass-the-hash detection focus** — pass-the-hash hunting should include unusual appearances of Event ID `4624` with Logon Type `9`, Event ID `4648`, and Event ID `4776`. _Why:_ these events can expose credential reuse patterns even when the authentication itself succeeds. _[GCFA p.320]_
- **Pass-the-ticket detection focus** — pass-the-ticket hunting should include unusual appearances of Event ID `4624` with Logon Type `9` and Event ID `4648`. _Why:_ ticket misuse may be visible through atypical logon or explicit-credential activity. _[GCFA p.320]_
- **Delegation abuse detection focus** — delegation abuse may show an unusual request origin or Event ID `4769` involving an unexpected target server. _Why:_ abnormal Kerberos service-ticket requests can indicate misuse of delegation paths. _[GCFA p.320]_
- **Coercion or forced authentication detection focus** — coercion and forced-authentication cases should be checked for unusual service-account logons. _Why:_ attackers may force systems or accounts to authenticate in ways that differ from normal service behavior. _[GCFA p.320]_

### Pass-The-Hash And NTLMv2

- **Credential attacks resemble valid authentication** — many credential-theft techniques produce log activity that looks like ordinary credential use. _Why:_ responders cannot rely on a simple “malicious authentication” label in event logs. _[GCFA p.320]_
- **Pass-the-hash from the target system’s view** — a system receiving an NTLMv2 request cannot distinguish pass-the-hash from a normal NTLMv2 login based only on the request. _Why:_ the protocol exchange still validates correctly even when the secret was stolen. _[GCFA p.320]_
- **Stolen-hash invisibility** — the accessed host does not know whether the hash used to compute the NTLMv2 response came from the legitimate user or from theft. _Why:_ successful pass-the-hash activity can lack a direct host-side indicator of compromise. _[GCFA p.320]_

- **Credential switching indicator** — attackers may maliciously alternate between stolen credential sets. _Why:_ recognizing credential switching helps identify pass-the-hash and other stolen-credential operations. _[GCFA p.~321]_

- **Deployment test systems** — defenders should create test systems to receive and observe package deployments. _Why:_ controlled endpoints can capture what deployment tools are pushing. _[GCFA p.~322]_

- **Patch deployment accounts require restriction** — Accounts used for patch deployment should be tightly limited. _Why:_ reducing account scope lowers the attacker’s ability to abuse deployment infrastructure broadly. _[GCFA p.323]_

- **Patch deployment systems require heavy monitoring** — Systems that perform patch deployment should be heavily observed. _Why:_ unusual activity from deployment servers may reveal unauthorized package pushes or attacker-controlled changes. _[GCFA p.323]_

- **Unique deployment accounts improve alerting** — Creating dedicated accounts for patch deployment, rather than using generic Domain Admin access, can make alerts easier to generate and interpret. _Why:_ distinct account purpose makes anomalous use more visible. _[GCFA p.323]_

- **Avoid relying only on Domain Admin for deployment** — Using only broad Domain Admin accounts for patch deployment weakens detection specificity. _Why:_ generic privileged accounts make it harder to distinguish normal administration from malicious deployment activity. _[GCFA p.323]_

- **Patch cycles are normally controlled** — Patch management schedules are generally governed by strict operational windows. _Why:_ deviations from expected patch timing can become a detection opportunity. _[GCFA p.323]_

- **Restrict patch activity to specific days** — Limiting patch deployment to defined days can help expose unauthorized use of deployment tooling. _Why:_ activity outside approved dates becomes easier to flag. _[GCFA p.323]_

- **Restrict patch activity to specific times** — Limiting patch deployment to defined time windows can help identify abnormal use. _Why:_ out-of-window deployment activity may indicate attacker abuse or unauthorized administrative action. _[GCFA p.323]_

- **Out-of-band tool use as a signal** — Use of patch or endpoint management tools outside approved maintenance windows can be more readily detected when schedules are tightly defined. _Why:_ timing anomalies are useful when the tool itself is legitimate. _[GCFA p.323]_

- **Test systems can collect package deployment evidence** — Purpose-built test systems can be created and monitored to collect logs of package deployments. _Why:_ controlled endpoints can act as sensors for detecting suspicious or unexpected deployment activity. _[GCFA p.323]_

- **Test systems can log deployment activity** — Monitoring test systems for package deployment logs can provide evidence of what the management system is pushing. _Why:_ logs from instrumented endpoints help confirm deployment behavior and timing. _[GCFA p.323]_

- **Malicious deployments may be targeted** — Attacker-controlled deployments may affect only selected systems rather than the whole enterprise. _Why:_ absence of enterprise-wide deployment does not rule out malicious use of management tooling. _[GCFA p.323]_

- **Multiple monitored systems may be necessary** — More than one test or monitoring system may be required to cover important network segments. _Why:_ targeted deployments may only reach particular segments, so a single sensor can miss activity. _[GCFA p.323]_

- **Important network segments need coverage** — Test or monitoring systems should be placed to represent critical network areas. _Why:_ visibility must align with where targeted malicious deployments are likely to occur. _[GCFA p.323]_

- **Host intrusion prevention systems (HIPS)** — HIPS telemetry is useful for detecting or investigating malware-related lateral movement. _Why:_ behavior-blocking or exploit-prevention alerts may expose malicious activity that does not appear clearly in standard logs. _[GCFA p.325]_

- **Microsoft Exploit Guard reporting** — Microsoft Exploit Guard telemetry can contribute useful evidence for malware-based lateral movement investigations. _Why:_ exploit mitigation alerts can point to abuse of vulnerabilities or suspicious process behavior. _[GCFA p.325]_

### Memory and Process Analysis

- **Memory analysis** — examining system memory can help identify systems that have been compromised. _Why:_ malware, injected code, and volatile execution artifacts may be visible in memory even when disk artifacts are limited. _[GCFA p.325]_

- **Running process analysis** — reviewing active processes can help locate compromised machines. _Why:_ malicious execution often appears as abnormal processes, injected processes, or suspicious process relationships. _[GCFA p.325]_

## Page 327

### Event Log Storage

- **Windows event log file format** — Windows event logs are kept in `.evtx` files using a binary XML representation. _Why:_ parsers must understand the stored format, not just the Event Viewer display. _[GCFA p.327]_
- **Event Viewer display mismatch** — The names shown in Event Viewer can differ from the underlying XML element names stored in the `.evtx` record. _Why:_ field-name assumptions can break when using third-party or scripted log analysis tools. _[GCFA p.327]_
- **Event Viewer abstraction** — Microsoft Event Viewer shows a simplified rendering of the event data rather than a literal view of the stored binary XML. _Why:_ investigators must distinguish presentation-layer labels from stored artifact structure. _[GCFA p.327]_
- **Event Viewer scalability limitation** — Event Viewer is not well suited for large-scale log analysis. _Why:_ forensic workflows often require external tooling for searching, normalization, and correlation. _[GCFA p.327]_
- **Tool output awareness** — Analysts need to know how their chosen log-analysis tool maps `.evtx` data into displayed fields. _Why:_ the same stored event may appear with different labels or structures across tools. _[GCFA p.327]_

### Event Type Context

- **Example event** — The page uses Windows Security Event ID `4624` as the example record. _Why:_ Event ID `4624` is central to logon analysis. _[GCFA p.327]_
- **Example logon meaning** — The shown `4624` event represents an interactive sign-in. _Why:_ interactive logons help identify direct local or console-style user activity. _[GCFA p.327]_
- **Example account** — The example logon involves user `tanderson`. _Why:_ account attribution depends on preserving the exact account value shown in the event. _[GCFA p.327]_
- **Example domain** — The example account belongs to domain `FICTIVECORP`. _Why:_ domain context distinguishes local accounts from domain identities. _[GCFA p.327]_
- **Displayed Logon Type label** — Event Viewer presents the logon type value under a field labeled `Logon Type`. _Why:_ this label is a presentation name and may not exist in the same form in the stored XML. _[GCFA p.327]_
- **Displayed Account Name label** — Event Viewer presents the username under a field labeled `Account Name`. _Why:_ analysts should not assume the Event Viewer label is the native `.evtx` element name. _[GCFA p.327]_
- **Displayed Account Domain label** — Event Viewer presents the domain under a field labeled `Account Domain`. _Why:_ parser field naming may differ from the Event Viewer view. _[GCFA p.327]_
- **Underlying field-name warning** — The labels `Logon Type`, `Account Name`, and `Account Domain` are not stored in that exact displayed format inside the binary XML `.evtx` file. _Why:_ reliable analysis requires mapping display labels back to stored event elements. _[GCFA p.327]_

### EvtxECmd Map Purpose

- **EvtxECmd CSV generation** — EvtxECmd can turn Windows event log XML data into CSV output by applying XPath-based map definitions. _Why:_ this explains how raw EVTX event content becomes analyst-friendly tabular data. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **XPath role** — XPath expressions are used to select particular XML elements or values from an event record. _Why:_ precise XML selection is what lets the parser extract the intended fields instead of the whole event. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **Map file concept** — Each event type that EvtxECmd parses can be represented by its own map file. _Why:_ event-specific maps let the tool handle different event schemas consistently. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **Map extraction logic** — A map defines which values should be pulled from an event and identifies those values with XPath notation. _Why:_ this is the rule set that controls what appears in the CSV. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **Map output formatting** — Extracted event values can be formatted and combined into designated CSV columns. _Why:_ derived columns can present multiple XML fields as one analyst-readable output value. _[GCFA p.~329]_

### Map Metadata

- **EventId map value** — The shown EvtxECmd map targets Windows Event ID `4624`. _Why:_ Event ID 4624 is the logon event type being parsed in the example. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **Channel map value** — The shown map applies to the `Security` event log channel. _Why:_ the channel scopes where the mapped event records are expected to come from. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **Maps collection** — The map contains a `Maps` section with individual output property definitions. _Why:_ each map entry controls one output field or grouped output value. _[GCFA p.~329]_

### PayloadData1 Mapping

- **PayloadData1 property** — The first shown map entry writes extracted data into `PayloadData1`. _Why:_ this generic output column is reused to store event-specific data of interest. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **PayloadData1 formatted value** — `PayloadData1` is constructed as `Target: %TargetDomainName%\%TargetUserName%`. _Why:_ the output combines domain and user into a single target-account display value. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **PayloadData1 first variable name** — The map defines a variable named `TargetDomainName`. _Why:_ this variable supplies the domain component of the formatted target account field. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **TargetDomainName XPath** — `TargetDomainName` is extracted with `/Event/EventData/Data[@Name="TargetDomainName"]`. _Why:_ this XPath points to the XML data element containing the target account domain. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **PayloadData1 second variable name** — The map defines a variable named `TargetUserName`. _Why:_ this variable supplies the username component of the formatted target account field. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **TargetUserName XPath** — `TargetUserName` is extracted with `/Event/EventData/Data[@Name="TargetUserName"]`. _Why:_ this XPath points to the XML data element containing the target account name. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **PayloadData1 combined semantics** — The final `PayloadData1` output contains both `TargetDomainName` and `TargetUserName`. _Why:_ analysts must understand that one CSV cell may represent multiple original XML fields. _[GCFA p.~329]_

### Standard Map Fields

- **UserName standardized field** — `UserName` can hold user and domain information from supported event IDs. _Why:_ it provides a consistent place for identity-related values across event types. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **RemoteHost standardized field** — `RemoteHost` can hold an IP address, hostname, or both from event records. _Why:_ it standardizes remote endpoint information for analysis. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **ExecutableInfo standardized field** — `ExecutableInfo` is intended for executable-related details such as process command lines, scheduled task information, or service-installation data. _Why:_ executable context is often central to incident reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **PayloadData1-6 standardized fields** — `PayloadData1` through `PayloadData6` are six flexible columns for event-specific values chosen by the map author. _Why:_ these fields let EvtxECmd preserve useful data without requiring a unique column for every event variation. _[GCFA p.~329]_

### PayloadData Design Tradeoff

- **Generic PayloadData design** — `PayloadData1-6` are intentionally non-specific fields. _Why:_ Windows events vary widely, and fixed unique columns for every possible extracted value would make the CSV unwieldy. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **Column-count rationale** — Creating separate columns for every event-specific value would produce hundreds of CSV columns. _Why:_ excessive column counts reduce usability for timeline and spreadsheet analysis. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **Column reuse behavior** — Different event types can reuse the same `PayloadData1-6` columns for different meanings. _Why:_ analysts cannot assume a PayloadData column has one universal meaning across all event IDs. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **Mixed-event CSV implication** — A CSV containing multiple event IDs may contain unrelated kinds of data in the same `PayloadData1-6` columns. _Why:_ interpretation requires event-aware context rather than column name alone. _[GCFA p.~329]_
- **Analyst interpretation requirement** — Analysts may need to consult the event ID and the relevant map file to understand a `PayloadData1-6` value. _Why:_ correct interpretation depends on how that specific event’s map populated the generic field. _[GCFA p.~329]_

- **Keyword filtering** — Free-text searches can locate executable names, account names, or any distinctive string in the dataset. _Why:_ keyword searches help pivot from known indicators to matching event records. _[GCFA p.~331]_

## Page 336

### Event Log Clearing Scope

- **Investigation objective** — determine whether Windows event logs were changed through clearing activity. _Why:_ cleared logs can indicate attempted evidence destruction or trace removal. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Event log clearing** — log clearing is a recurring issue to evaluate during event log review. _Why:_ attackers or administrators with sufficient rights may remove prior activity records. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Track-covering capability** — a user with administrator-level access, whether authorized or obtained through compromise, may be able to clear logs to hide actions. _Why:_ admin privilege changes the forensic risk profile of a suspect account. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Observed frequency** — despite the capability, event log clearing is described as not occurring very often. _Why:_ absence of clearing does not rule out compromise, but clearing is still notable when present. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Traceability of clearing** — Windows log clearing is difficult to perform without leaving an artifact. _Why:_ defenders can often detect that logs were cleared even if prior events are gone. _[GCFA p.336]_

### Privileges Required

- **Administrator requirement** — clearing event logs requires administrator rights. _Why:_ log clearing implicates accounts or processes with elevated permissions. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Local Administrators** — members of the local Administrators group can clear event logs. _Why:_ local admin membership is sufficient authority for this evidence-impacting action. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Domain Administrators** — Domain Admin accounts have the ability to clear event logs. _Why:_ domain-level compromise can enable log clearing across systems where those rights apply. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Local SYSTEM** — the local SYSTEM account has privileges to clear event logs. _Why:_ activity under SYSTEM may reflect service, malware, or tool execution with maximum local authority. _[GCFA p.336]_

### Relevant Event IDs

- **Event ID 1102** — Windows records Security log clearing with event ID 1102. _Why:_ this is the primary artifact for identifying Security log clearing. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Event ID 1102 log location** — when the Security log is cleared, the 1102 record is written into the Security log. _Why:_ the cleared log still receives a marker that the clearing occurred. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Event ID 104** — Windows records clearing of non-Security logs with event ID 104. _Why:_ this event identifies clearing activity outside the Security log. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Event ID 104 log location** — clearing any log other than Security generates the 104 record in the System log. _Why:_ investigators must check System for evidence of other logs being cleared. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Security log clear artifact** — after the Security log is cleared, Windows adds an 1102 event showing that the clear occurred. _Why:_ the action leaves a direct evidentiary marker. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Non-Security log clear artifact** — clearing any event log except Security creates a 104 event in System. _Why:_ clearing Application, System-adjacent, or other logs may be detected through System log review. _[GCFA p.336]_

### Clearing Behavior

- **All-or-nothing clearing** — standard log clearing removes the log as a whole rather than deleting individual records. _Why:_ a wholesale gap can indicate deliberate log removal. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Selective deletion caveat** — selective event deletion attacks exist even though normal clearing is all-or-nothing. _Why:_ investigators should not assume every tampering method produces only full-log clearing artifacts. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Previous events may be unavailable** — after clearing, earlier entries from the affected log may no longer be accessible. _Why:_ investigators may need to rely on the clear event itself and other corroborating sources. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Clearing account visibility** — even when prior events are gone, the clearing record can identify the account that performed the clear. _Why:_ attribution of the clearing action may be evidentiary. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Last-cleared timing** — reviewing 1102 and 104 events can show when logs were most recently cleared. _Why:_ timing helps correlate the action with suspected compromise, administration, or incident windows. _[GCFA p.336]_

### Clearing Methods

- **GUI clearing** — clearing logs through the graphical interface is recorded. _Why:_ investigators should not limit detection to command-line activity. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Command-line clearing** — clearing logs from the command line is recorded. _Why:_ attacker and administrator tooling can still leave clear-event artifacts. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **wevtutil** — `wevtutil` is given as an example command-line utility for clearing logs. _Why:_ use of this Windows tool may explain or correlate with 1102 or 104 clear events. _[GCFA p.336]_

### Investigative Value

- **Evidentiary significance** — the fact that a specific user account cleared logs can itself be important evidence. _Why:_ the clearing action may demonstrate consciousness of wrongdoing or improper data handling. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Hacking investigations** — log-clearing evidence is especially relevant in intrusion cases. _Why:_ attackers may clear logs to hide compromise activity. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Data spoliation investigations** — log-clearing evidence is relevant when destruction or alteration of evidence is at issue. _Why:_ clearing logs may support a spoliation finding or investigative theory. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Legitimacy check** — 1102 and 104 events should be compared against known legitimate administrator work. _Why:_ this separates expected maintenance from suspicious activity. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Retention policy check** — log-clearing timing should be evaluated against data retention requirements. _Why:_ unexpected clearing may violate policy or reduce forensic visibility. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Security policy check** — log-clearing activity should be assessed against security policies. _Why:_ unauthorized clearing may indicate misuse or compromise of privileged access. _[GCFA p.336]_

### Detection And Alerting

- **Alert recommendation** — organizations should configure alerts for event IDs 1102 and 104. _Why:_ these events provide direct notification that logs were cleared. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **High-fidelity signal** — event log clearing is characterized as a high-confidence alert condition. _Why:_ log clearing is uncommon and closely tied to evidence removal or disruptive activity. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Ransomware tradecraft** — ransomware incidents commonly involve many cleared event logs. _Why:_ widespread log clearing can be a strong behavioral indicator during ransomware response. _[GCFA p.336]_
- **Monitoring priority** — cleared-log events should be closely monitored in enterprise environments. _Why:_ rapid detection can preserve investigative context and accelerate incident response. _[GCFA p.336]_

## Page 339

### Event Log Attack Overview

- **Event logging as an attack target** — Windows event logging is described as an increasingly targeted forensic evidence source. _Why:_ investigators should not assume event logs are complete or untouched. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Selective event deletion** — Recent attack techniques have demonstrated that individual event records can be removed instead of clearing an entire log. _Why:_ missing evidence may be targeted and subtle rather than caused by obvious log clearing. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Arbitrary event removal** — The page states that attackers can remove chosen events from logs. _Why:_ any single event’s absence may not prove the activity did not occur. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Event ID 1102 removal** — Selective deletion can remove Event ID 1102, the Security log clearing indicator. _Why:_ the normal alert for log clearing can itself be hidden. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Administrative privilege requirement** — The described event log manipulation methods require administrator-level rights. _Why:_ evidence of admin compromise increases the plausibility of log tampering. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Caution in event log analysis** — Analysts are advised to treat event log evidence carefully because manipulation is possible. _Why:_ event logs remain valuable, but completeness and integrity require validation. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Most attackers still leave logs alone** — The page notes that many attackers do not attempt to clean or manipulate event logs. _Why:_ investigators should not discard event logs as unreliable by default. _[GCFA p.339]_

### Windows Event Log Protections

- **Log file locking** — Windows event logs are characterized as locked and protected files. _Why:_ their protected design historically made direct tampering difficult. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Corruption sensitivity** — Event log files are described as highly resistant to tolerating corruption. _Why:_ crude edits may break the log or the service, creating forensic artifacts. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Security log writer** — The Security event log is writable only by LSASS. _Why:_ write access to Security logs is tightly controlled by Windows architecture. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **LSASS role** — LSASS is identified as the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service. _Why:_ LSASS control over Security logging ties log integrity to a sensitive authentication subsystem. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **No event-level Windows API** — The page states that Windows does not provide API functions for directly interacting with individual events. _Why:_ normal programmatic interfaces do not support selective editing of records. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **All-or-nothing clearing model** — Windows log clearing was designed to clear whole logs rather than selected records. _Why:_ selective deletion is outside the intended Windows event log model. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Individual record immutability expectation** — Individual event records are described as not meant to be selectively removable. _Why:_ selective record disappearance is suspicious and may indicate specialized tooling. _[GCFA p.339]_

### Historical Event Editing Tools

- **WinNT/2000-era selective deletion proof of concept** — Tools capable of deleting chosen records from live logs existed as far back as Windows NT/2000. _Why:_ selective event tampering is not a new theoretical risk. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **WinZapper** — WinZapper is identified as an early event log editing tool. _Why:_ it provides historical context for event log anti-forensics. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **WinZapper reliability limitation** — WinZapper is described as unreliable. _Why:_ failed tampering may leave crashed services or corrupted logs as evidence. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **WinZapper service crash risk** — WinZapper could crash the Event Log Service. _Why:_ service failure can become an artifact of attempted log manipulation. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **WinZapper corruption risk** — WinZapper could corrupt event logs. _Why:_ malformed or unreadable logs may point to tampering attempts. _[GCFA p.339]_

### DanderSpritz eventlogedit

- **Shadow Brokers disclosure** — The Shadow Brokers leak exposed DanderSpritz to the public. _Why:_ leaked offensive tooling expanded awareness and availability of event log manipulation capabilities. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **DanderSpritz implant** — DanderSpritz is described as a capable implant. _Why:_ event log editing can be part of a broader post-compromise toolkit. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **eventlogedit tool name** — DanderSpritz includes a tool named `eventlogedit`. _Why:_ this name is a direct indicator to recognize in tool discussions or evidence. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **eventlogedit header manipulation** — `eventlogedit` removes visible entries by modifying event headers so parsing skips targeted events. _Why:_ the record may be hidden from normal viewing without being physically erased. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **eventlogedit residual data** — Events targeted by `eventlogedit` remain present inside the log file. _Why:_ forensic tools may recover records hidden from normal parsing. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **eventlogedit recoverability** — The page states that forensic analysis can recover events hidden by `eventlogedit`. _Why:_ analysts should parse logs with forensic tooling rather than relying only on Event Viewer. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **EvtxECmd detection** — Eric Zimmerman’s EvtxECmd automatically detects the `eventlogedit` attack during event parsing. _Why:_ tool-assisted parsing can reveal manipulation that normal review may miss. _[GCFA p.339]_

### Mimikatz event::drop

- **Mimikatz event log functionality** — Benjamin Delpy added event log manipulation capability to Mimikatz. _Why:_ a common credential-theft tool can also interfere with logging. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Mimikatz `event::drop`** — The page lists Mimikatz `event::drop` as a selective event log attack technique. _Why:_ this command is a known anti-logging capability. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Event Log Service patching** — Mimikatz can patch the Event Log Service. _Why:_ patching the service can prevent future Security events from being recorded. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Security log recording stop** — The Mimikatz capability can stop new entries from being written to the Security log. _Why:_ later activity may be absent because logging was disabled, not because activity did not happen. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Clearing without Event ID 1102** — The Mimikatz capability can clear the whole log without creating Event ID 1102. _Why:_ absence of Event ID 1102 does not exclude log clearing. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **No re-enable capability** — The page states that this Mimikatz capability does not yet turn event logging back on. _Why:_ persistent logging gaps can reveal use of the technique. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Log gap artifact** — Mimikatz-based logging stoppage can produce obvious gaps in event records. _Why:_ timeline discontinuities become a key detection clue. _[GCFA p.339]_

### Service Suspension and Memory Attacks

- **Event Log Service suspension** — The page lists suspending the Event Log Service as an event log attack method. _Why:_ stopping the service temporarily can create opportunities to alter logs. _[GCFA p.339]_

- **Memory-based attacks** — The page lists memory-based event log attacks. _Why:_ manipulation may occur in RAM rather than through direct file editing. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Memory-mapped log targeting** — Researchers have examined modifying memory-mapped event log segments. _Why:_ RAM-level alteration may affect log contents before or during persistence. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Direct RAM modification** — The page describes attacks that alter event log data directly in memory. _Why:_ live memory acquisition and timeline validation may be important when tampering is suspected. _[GCFA p.339]_

### Log Noise and Anti-Forensics

- **Noise-filling tactic** — The page notes an observed adversary who tried to fill logs with noise instead of clearing them. _Why:_ log flooding can bury useful evidence without triggering classic clearing indicators. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Alternative to clearing** — Filling logs with excessive events is presented as another anti-forensic approach. _Why:_ investigators should watch for abnormal event volume as well as missing records. _[GCFA p.339]_

### Mitigations and Detection

- **Event log forwarding** — Forwarding event logs is listed as a mitigation. _Why:_ off-host copies can preserve evidence even if local logs are manipulated. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Logging heartbeat** — A recurring log “heartbeat” is listed as a mitigation. _Why:_ missing expected heartbeat events can reveal logging interruption. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Log gap analysis** — Analyzing gaps in log timelines is listed as a mitigation. _Why:_ discontinuities can expose logging stoppage or tampering. _[GCFA p.339]_
- **Enterprise logging implication** — The page begins to state that event log manipulation should push organizations toward stronger log handling. _Why:_ centralized or resilient logging becomes more important when endpoint logs can be altered. _[GCFA p.339]_

## Page 340

### Centralized Event Logging

- **Central log forwarding** — Sending event records to a central repository reduces the chance that endpoint-only log tampering will erase all evidence. _Why:_ off-host storage can preserve records even if the compromised system is later altered. _[GCFA p.340]_
- **Centralized storage limitation** — Central collection helps against tools that alter or remove local event records, but it does not solve attacks that prevent logs from being generated or forwarded at all. _Why:_ defenders must distinguish deleted local history from a host that stopped producing telemetry. _[GCFA p.340]_
- **DanderSpritz mitigation scope** — A forwarding-and-central-storage model is presented as a mitigation for DanderSpritz-style event log attacks. _Why:_ this identifies a specific adversary tool class where retained remote logs may remain useful. _[GCFA p.340]_
- **Logging shutdown gap** — Attacks that stop logging entirely require detection beyond simple central storage. _Why:_ no forwarded event exists if the source system stops emitting records. _[GCFA p.340]_
- **Missing-forwarder analytics** — Defenders may need analytics that detect systems that have not sent logs for a defined interval. _Why:_ lack of expected telemetry can itself be an incident indicator. _[GCFA p.340]_
- **Logging-gap analytics** — Defenders may need analytics that flag abnormal gaps in a system’s event stream. _Why:_ suspicious silence can indicate tampering, service failure, or deliberate evasion. _[GCFA p.340]_

## Page 341

### Evidence of Malware Execution

- **Malware execution investigation goal** — The page frames the task as finding software that may be malicious and determining whether it actually ran. _Why:_ execution status separates mere presence from compromise activity. _[GCFA p. 341]_

### Relevant Event Logs

- **System Event Log · Review target** — The System log should be checked for Critical, Warning, and Error severity records tied to system failures or process crashes. _Why:_ malware can destabilize hosts, and crashes may expose failed or partial execution. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Application Event Log · Review target** — The Application log is relevant for Windows Error Reporting, application crashes, and application hangs. _Why:_ malfunctioning malware or affected applications may leave execution evidence outside the Security log. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Application Event IDs 1000-1002** — Event IDs in the 1000 through 1002 range are called out as relevant to WER, application crash, and application hang analysis. _Why:_ these IDs can point investigators toward programs that faulted or generated diagnostic reporting. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Application Event ID 1000** — Application log Event ID 1000 records application error events. _Why:_ an application error may identify a suspicious executable that attempted to run and crashed. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Application Event ID 1002** — Application log Event ID 1002 records application hang events. _Why:_ hangs can reveal unstable or failed execution of malicious or compromised programs. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Application Event ID 1001** — Application log Event ID 1001 records Windows Error Reporting activity. _Why:_ it can show that Windows generated extra diagnostic data for a failing application, including potentially malfunctioning malware. _[GCFA p. 341]_

### Investigative Notes

- **Crashed applications** — Investigators should record applications that crashed during the time window under review. _Why:_ a crash may identify a suspicious executable or a victim process affected by malware. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Crashed processes** — Investigators should note process crashes, not only full application failures. _Why:_ process-level failures can expose attempted execution or malware side effects. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **System reboots** — Reboots should be tracked as part of the malware execution review. _Why:_ unexpected restarts can indicate instability caused by malware, exploitation, or attacker activity. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Report.wer review** — Windows Error Reporting files named `Report.wer` should be examined when they were created during relevant time periods. _Why:_ WER reports can contain diagnostic evidence about a failing program and its execution context. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Windows Defender logs** — Windows Defender logs should be reviewed during the investigation. _Why:_ Defender may have recorded detections, warnings, or other activity tied to suspicious software. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Anti-virus logs** — Logs from installed anti-virus products should also be examined. _Why:_ endpoint security tools may identify malware that standard Windows logs only show indirectly. _[GCFA p. 341]_

### Log Source Strategy

- **Event log review for malware** — Reviewing Windows event logs is a logical step when trying to identify malicious software. _Why:_ execution, failures, detections, and system instability can all produce event artifacts. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **System and Application logs vs. Security log** — Depending on audit configuration, the System and Application logs may contain more useful malware-execution evidence than the Security log. _Why:_ investigators should not assume the Security log is the richest source for this question. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Audit policy dependency** — The usefulness of the Security log depends heavily on what auditing was enabled. _Why:_ missing audit settings can prevent expected execution evidence from being recorded. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Security log process tracking capability** — The Security event log can record every executed process when Process Tracking is enabled. _Why:_ this capability can provide direct execution evidence when configured. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Process Tracking logging volume** — Process Tracking commonly produces a large amount of log data. _Why:_ the volume explains why many environments disable it despite its forensic value. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Process Tracking deployment reality** — In many enterprise environments, Process Tracking is disabled except on especially important systems. _Why:_ investigators often cannot rely on comprehensive Security log process execution records across all hosts. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **PowerShell log centralization gap** — PowerShell logs may not be centrally collected. _Why:_ the absence of centralized PowerShell telemetry can force host-by-host or alternate-log analysis. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **WMI log centralization gap** — WMI logs may not be centrally collected. _Why:_ WMI-based malicious activity may be missed unless local logs or other sources are reviewed. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **System and Application logs as fallback sources** — Investigators may need to rely on System and Application logs to find unusual activity. _Why:_ these logs can preserve useful signals when stronger execution telemetry is absent. _[GCFA p. 341]_

### Event ID Interpretation

- **Security log Event IDs** — Event IDs are well documented and useful when analyzing the Security event log. _Why:_ Security log IDs often provide more predictable investigative meaning. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **System log Event IDs** — Event IDs are less useful for many System log reviews. _Why:_ their meanings are less consistently documented and may vary by context. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Application log Event IDs** — Event IDs are less reliable as standalone indicators for many Application log reviews. _Why:_ a single Application event ID can correspond to many different conditions. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **System and Application Event ID documentation** — Event IDs in System and Application logs are described as poorly documented compared with Security log IDs. _Why:_ analysts must inspect context and content rather than depending only on the numeric ID. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **One Event ID, multiple meanings** — A single System or Application event ID can have many different interpretations. _Why:_ treating the ID alone as definitive can lead to incorrect conclusions. _[GCFA p. 341]_

### Review Priorities

- **Critical events** — Critical-severity events should be prioritized in System and Application log review. _Why:_ these records can identify severe failures that may coincide with malware execution or impact. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Error events** — Error-severity events should be prioritized in System and Application log review. _Why:_ application or system errors may reveal crashed malware or affected components. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Warning events** — Warning-severity events should be prioritized in System and Application log review. _Why:_ warnings can include security-product alerts or instability signals that do not rise to full errors. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Large event volume** — System and Application logs can contain many Critical, Error, and Warning records. _Why:_ analysts need filtering and triage rather than assuming every such event is equally important. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Duplicate recurring events** — Many high-severity-looking events may be repeated entries generated hourly, at each boot, or on other recurring schedules. _Why:_ recurring noise must be distinguished from unusual activity. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Outlier-focused review** — Investigators should look for unusual events rather than only counting common repeated records. _Why:_ rare or time-correlated anomalies are more likely to point to meaningful malware activity. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Security product warnings** — Antivirus or other security-product warnings are especially important during malware tracking. _Why:_ these warnings may directly identify suspicious behavior or malicious files on the host. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Suspicious activity detections** — Security-product events may show that suspicious activity was identified on the system. _Why:_ this can provide an investigative lead even when execution telemetry is incomplete. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Unexplained reboots** — Reboots without a clear benign cause should be investigated. _Why:_ malware or exploitation can trigger instability that forces a restart. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Crashed system processes** — Crashes of system processes should be treated as notable malware-investigation artifacts. _Why:_ malware can interfere with or destabilize core operating system processes. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Malware instability** — The page emphasizes that malware activity often causes crashes as well as successful compromises. _Why:_ failed or unstable execution can still leave valuable forensic evidence. _[GCFA p. 341]_
- **Common malware-triggered events** — Some System and Application event IDs are commonly generated by malware-related activity. _Why:_ these IDs can help direct analysis when reviewing broad event log data. _[GCFA p. 341]_
