## Page 367

### PowerShell Logging Scope

- **PowerShell activity logging objective** — investigators should collect records of PowerShell execution, including pipeline results, complete user-run script content, and remoting activity. _Why:_ these records can reconstruct attacker or administrator actions performed through PowerShell. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Pipeline output as evidence** — PowerShell logging can include output produced as commands pass objects through the pipeline. _Why:_ output may reveal command results, enumerated systems, discovered credentials, or other attacker-visible data. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Full script content as evidence** — PowerShell-specific logging can capture the complete script text executed by a user. _Why:_ script contents expose intent and behavior beyond merely knowing that PowerShell ran. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **PowerShell remoting instances** — PowerShell remoting activity is part of the logging scope for investigation. _Why:_ remoting records help identify lateral movement and remote administration paths. _[GCFA p.367]_

### Relevant Event IDs

- **Event ID 4103** — this event records PowerShell module logging data and pipeline output. _Why:_ it can show command activity and command-produced data useful for reconstructing execution. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Event ID 4104** — this event records PowerShell script block logging. _Why:_ it can preserve the code that was executed, which is often the most direct evidence of PowerShell abuse. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Event ID 400** — this older Windows PowerShell log event remains worth reviewing during deeper analysis. _Why:_ legacy PowerShell logs may contain useful execution context even when newer logging is absent or incomplete. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Event ID 800** — this older Windows PowerShell log event remains useful for investigative review. _Why:_ it can provide additional historical PowerShell activity evidence outside the newer operational channel. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Event IDs 4105 and 4106** — these PowerShell execution events are often considered too verbose for practical threat hunting. _Why:_ excessive event volume can bury higher-value signals and reduce hunting efficiency. _[GCFA p.367]_

### Event Log Files

- **Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell%4Operational.evtx** — this EVTX file is associated with Windows PowerShell version 5 logging. _Why:_ it is a primary location for modern Windows PowerShell operational evidence. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Microsoft-Windows-PowerShellCore%4Operational.evtx** — this EVTX file is associated with PowerShell Core versions 6 and 7. _Why:_ systems using newer cross-platform PowerShell versions may store evidence in this separate channel. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational log** — PowerShell audit records are written to this operational channel. _Why:_ analysts should review this channel for script block and module logging evidence. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Windows PowerShell.evtx** — this is the older PowerShell event log. _Why:_ although historically less informative, it can still provide useful Event ID 400 and 800 records. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **WinRM/Operational log** — this log records both inbound and outbound PowerShell remoting. _Why:_ WinRM evidence can identify remote PowerShell use, including lateral movement or remote administration. _[GCFA p.367]_

### Version Behavior

- **PowerShell version 5 logging improvement** — practical, high-value PowerShell logging became available starting with PowerShell v5. _Why:_ systems below this version may lack the richer evidence needed for detailed reconstruction. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **PowerShell v5 robust logging** — version 5 introduced substantially stronger logging capabilities than earlier PowerShell releases. _Why:_ v5-era logging can expose attacker commands and scripts that older logging may miss. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **PowerShell Core versions 6 and 7** — PowerShell Core activity for these versions is associated with the PowerShellCore operational EVTX file. _Why:_ analysts must check the correct log channel for Core-based PowerShell activity. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Downgrade attack command** — `powershell -Version 2` is shown as a way attackers may attempt to run an older PowerShell engine. _Why:_ forcing version 2 can evade newer logging features and reduce available forensic evidence. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **PowerShell downgrade risk** — analysts should watch for attempts to run older PowerShell versions to bypass logging. _Why:_ downgrade behavior can be both an evasion technique and an indicator of suspicious activity. _[GCFA p.367]_

### Script Block Logging

- **Script block concept** — a script block is a unit of PowerShell code intended to perform a task. _Why:_ understanding this unit explains what Event ID 4104 is designed to capture. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Simple script blocks** — a script block may be as small as a single function. _Why:_ even compact PowerShell logic can be logged and reviewed as executable evidence. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Complex script blocks** — a script block may also be a larger script that invokes several cmdlets. _Why:_ attackers can perform multi-step operations inside one logged code unit. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Script block logging content** — script block auditing can capture the full command or script body. _Why:_ this can reveal the exact logic used for discovery, execution, persistence, theft, or destruction. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Script block executor identity** — script block auditing can identify the user who ran the code. _Why:_ user attribution helps tie PowerShell activity to an account and timeline. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Script block timing** — script block auditing can record when the code ran. _Why:_ timestamps allow correlation with process execution, network activity, file changes, and other artifacts. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Script block deobfuscation** — script block logging includes scripts and can provide some deobfuscation. _Why:_ deobfuscated content can expose attacker intent that would otherwise be hidden by encoding or obfuscation. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Event ID 4104 script contents** — Event ID 4104 records script block content. _Why:_ it is one of the strongest PowerShell artifacts for determining what code executed. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Event ID 4104 first-run behavior** — Event ID 4104 logs a script block only the first time it executes. _Why:_ repeated execution may not generate repeated full-content records, affecting timeline completeness. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Event ID 4104 volume-control purpose** — the first-execution behavior is intended to limit log volume. _Why:_ analysts should understand why repeated activity may be underrepresented in the log. _[GCFA p.367]_

### Execution Sources

- **Command shell-launched PowerShell** — PowerShell activity can be audited even when invoked from a command shell. _Why:_ attackers frequently launch PowerShell from `cmd.exe` or similar command-line contexts. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **PowerShell ISE-launched code** — activity can be audited when PowerShell runs through the Integrated Scripting Environment. _Why:_ interactive script development or execution may still leave operational log evidence. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Custom-hosted PowerShell components** — activity can be audited when PowerShell components are hosted by custom applications. _Why:_ adversaries may embed PowerShell in nonstandard hosts to avoid obvious `powershell.exe` process evidence. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Host-independent operational logging** — PowerShell audit events are recorded in the operational log regardless of the execution host described on the page. _Why:_ investigators should check the PowerShell operational channel even when PowerShell was not launched in the usual console. _[GCFA p.367]_

### Investigative Value

- **PowerShell ubiquity** — PowerShell is widespread across Microsoft environments. _Why:_ its normal administrative presence makes it common in both legitimate operations and intrusions. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Administrative usefulness** — PowerShell simplifies many administrative tasks. _Why:_ its legitimate utility makes outright blocking difficult in many organizations. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Attacker capability surface** — PowerShell gives attackers a broad set of offensive capabilities. _Why:_ a single built-in tool can support many phases of an intrusion. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Privilege escalation via PowerShell** — privilege escalation is identified as a malicious activity that can be performed with PowerShell. _Why:_ PowerShell logs may reveal attempts to gain higher privileges. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Credential theft via PowerShell** — credential stealing is identified as possible through PowerShell. _Why:_ captured commands or scripts may show credential access behavior. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Data destruction via PowerShell** — destructive activity can be carried out with PowerShell. _Why:_ PowerShell evidence may help explain deletion, wiping, or sabotage events. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Data exfiltration via PowerShell** — data theft and outbound transfer can be performed using PowerShell. _Why:_ logged scripts may identify collection and exfiltration mechanisms. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Kerberos ticket dumping in pure PowerShell** — the page notes that Kerberos ticket dumping can be implemented entirely in PowerShell. _Why:_ credential theft may occur without a separate obvious binary tool. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Common adversary use** — PowerShell is widely used by real-world adversaries. _Why:_ PowerShell artifacts deserve routine review during incident response and threat hunting. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Access restriction difficulty** — PowerShell is hard to restrict in many environments. _Why:_ defenders often need monitoring and detection rather than relying only on prevention. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Historical audit difficulty** — PowerShell was historically difficult to audit well. _Why:_ older systems or weaker configurations may have limited evidence. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Possible sole evidence source** — PowerShell logging may be the only meaningful artifact for reconstructing PowerShell activity. _Why:_ other artifacts may show only that PowerShell ran, not what it did. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Prefetch correlation example** — seeing `PowerShell.exe` in Prefetch is an example trigger to examine PowerShell logs more deeply. _Why:_ Prefetch can prove execution, while PowerShell logs may reveal executed content. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Memory process correlation example** — finding a PowerShell process in memory is another reason to review PowerShell-specific logs. _Why:_ memory evidence can identify execution, while event logs can provide historical command detail. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Module logging investigative value** — module logging can provide strong visibility into PowerShell activity. _Why:_ it can expose command behavior and pipeline data useful for incident reconstruction. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Script block logging investigative value** — script block logging can provide detailed visibility into PowerShell code execution. _Why:_ it may reveal full attacker scripts rather than only process names or command-line fragments. _[GCFA p.367]_

### Default Logging Limitations

- **Most logging disabled by default** — many PowerShell logging features are not enabled automatically. _Why:_ analysts cannot assume rich PowerShell evidence exists on a system. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Potential evidence absence** — needed PowerShell log data may be unavailable because logging was not enabled. _Why:_ missing logs may reflect configuration limitations rather than lack of activity. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Automatic suspicious-script logging** — Microsoft includes a built-in feature that logs suspicious scripts automatically. _Why:_ some high-risk script content may be captured even without full script block logging. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Suspicious-script logging without script block logging** — suspicious script capture can occur even when script block logging is disabled. _Why:_ organizations without full auditing may still retain selected high-value PowerShell evidence. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **Operational log review in unaudited environments** — investigators should still review the Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational log when full auditing was not enabled. _Why:_ automatic suspicious-script logging may have generated useful records anyway. _[GCFA p.367]_

### Remoting Evidence

- **WinRM inbound remoting records** — WinRM/Operational records incoming PowerShell remoting activity. _Why:_ inbound records can show remote access to the investigated host. _[GCFA p.367]_
- **WinRM outbound remoting records** — WinRM/Operational records outgoing PowerShell remoting activity. _Why:_ outbound records can show the investigated host being used to administer or attack other systems. _[GCFA p.367]_

## Page 368

### PowerShell Core Logging

- **PowerShell logging after PSv5** — PowerShell logs began capturing more valuable investigative content after PowerShell version 5 was released. _Why:_ later PowerShell telemetry can expose attacker activity that older logging may miss. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **PowerShell Core versions** — PowerShell 6 and PowerShell 7 are “Core” editions rebuilt on .NET Core. _Why:_ their architecture affects deployment, logging, and forensic collection scope. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **PowerShell Core platform support** — PowerShell Core can run on Windows, macOS, and Linux. _Why:_ investigators may need to account for PowerShell activity outside traditional Windows-only environments. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **PowerShell Core coexistence** — PowerShell 6 and 7 are designed to run alongside PowerShell 5 rather than replace it. _Why:_ a host can contain multiple PowerShell engines with separate telemetry. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **PowerShell Core installation locations** — PowerShell Core versions use installation paths separate from PowerShell 5. _Why:_ responders must know that binaries and artifacts may not reside with legacy Windows PowerShell files. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **PowerShell Core group policy separation** — PowerShell Core uses different Group Policy settings from PowerShell 5. _Why:_ enabling logging for Windows PowerShell does not automatically configure Core logging. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **PowerShell Core log separation** — PowerShell Core maintains logs separate from PowerShell 5 logs. _Why:_ reviewing only the legacy PowerShell log can miss activity executed through PowerShell 6 or 7. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **Dual script-block logging requirement** — If both PowerShell 5 and PowerShell Core are installed, script-block logging must be enabled for both. _Why:_ attackers can choose the less-monitored engine if only one version is configured. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **PowerShell Core administrative templates** — Enabling script-block logging for PowerShell Core currently requires adding administrative templates to the domain controller. _Why:_ defenders may incorrectly assume the standard templates already cover Core editions. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **PowerShell Core policy location** — After the required templates are installed, logging configuration is similar but lives under PowerShell Core policies. _Why:_ the policy path distinction matters when auditing enterprise logging configuration. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **PowerShell Core script-block log file** — Script-block logging for PowerShell Core appears in `Microsoft-Windows-PowerShellCore%4Operational.evtx`. _Why:_ this is the event log file responders must collect and review for PowerShell 6/7 script content. _[GCFA p.368]_

### Attacker Adaptation

- **PowerShell Core deployment lag** — PowerShell Core versions may take time to become common across environments. _Why:_ defenders may under-prioritize logs for newer engines during early adoption. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **Auditing at first deployment** — New PowerShell versions should have auditing enabled when they are initially rolled out. _Why:_ delayed logging creates a visibility gap that attackers can exploit. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **Attacker awareness of PowerShell logging** — Adversaries understand that PowerShell logs can expose their actions. _Why:_ this motivates evasion techniques and engine selection during intrusions. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **Logging evasion behavior** — Attackers actively attempt to avoid PowerShell logging. _Why:_ absence of expected logs may itself be relevant when reconstructing activity. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **Likely migration to PSv7** — Attackers are expected to use PowerShell 7 when available because it may be less consistently logged. _Why:_ newer engine usage can indicate an attempt to exploit weak logging coverage. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **Dual-log review requirement** — Systems with both PowerShell 5 and PowerShell Core require review of both logging locations. _Why:_ a complete response cannot rely on only one PowerShell event source. _[GCFA p.368]_

### WinRM Operational Log

- **WinRM Operational log purpose** — `Microsoft-Windows-WinRM/Operational` records WinRM connection activity. _Why:_ WinRM telemetry helps trace remote PowerShell access. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **WinRM and PowerShell remoting** — WinRM is the main protocol used by PowerShell remoting. _Why:_ WinRM events can identify remote PowerShell sessions even when command content is incomplete. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **WinRM source-system availability** — The WinRM Operational log is present on the system initiating the connection. _Why:_ source-side logs can corroborate outbound remoting activity. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **WinRM destination-system availability** — The WinRM Operational log is also present on the system receiving the connection. _Why:_ destination-side logs can confirm inbound remote administration or attacker access. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **WinRM Event ID 6 destination hostname** — Event ID 6 records the remote destination hostname. _Why:_ this helps map which host a remoting connection targeted. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **WinRM Event ID 6 destination IP** — Event ID 6 records the destination IP address. _Why:_ IP data supports timeline correlation and network pivot analysis. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **WinRM Event ID 6 logged-on user** — Event ID 6 records the currently logged-on user. _Why:_ this associates remoting activity with an interactive user context. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **WinRM Event ID 91 session source** — Event ID 91 records where session creation originated. _Why:_ this helps identify the source of a PowerShell remoting session. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **WinRM Event ID 168 authentication account** — Event ID 168 records the user account used for authentication. _Why:_ this identifies credentials involved in the remote session. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **Combined PowerShell and WinRM logs** — The combined set of PowerShell and WinRM logs can be critical for investigating malicious PowerShell use. _Why:_ no single log source gives the full picture of execution, remoting, and authentication. _[GCFA p.368]_

### PowerShell Version 2 Downgrade Attacks

- **PowerShell v2 downgrade attack effect** — Running PowerShell through the version 2 engine can bypass modern logging coverage. _Why:_ attackers can reduce visibility by forcing an older engine. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **Downgrade impact on PowerShell logging** — PowerShell logging techniques become less effective during v2 downgrade attacks. _Why:_ responders may find fewer event records despite substantial command execution. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **Downgrade impact on event logs** — Most commands and scripts executed through PowerShell v2 may not appear in event logs. _Why:_ missing command telemetry can obstruct reconstruction of attacker actions. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **Downgrade impact on ConsoleHost history** — PowerShell v2 downgrade activity may not appear in `ConsoleHost_history`. _Why:_ shell history cannot be assumed complete when v2 is used. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **Downgrade impact on transcripts** — PowerShell v2 downgrade activity may not appear in Transcript logs. _Why:_ transcript-based collection can miss commands executed under the older engine. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **PowerShell v2 detection log** — Invocation of the PowerShell 2.0 engine can be detected in the older `Windows PowerShell.evtx` log. _Why:_ the legacy log remains useful for spotting downgrade attempts. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **PowerShell v2 detection event ID** — Event ID 400 can indicate use of the PowerShell 2.0 engine. _Why:_ this event provides a specific artifact to hunt for downgrade execution. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **PowerShell v2 EngineVersion search term** — Searching for `EngineVersion=2.0` can identify PowerShell v2 engine use. _Why:_ this string is a direct indicator of downgrade execution. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **PowerShell v2 HostVersion search term** — Searching for `HostVersion=2.0` can identify PowerShell v2 host use. _Why:_ this provides another query term for detecting downgrade activity. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **Command-line auditing for downgrade detection** — Command-line auditing can help detect PowerShell v2 downgrade attempts. _Why:_ process command lines may reveal the downgrade even when PowerShell logs are sparse. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **Downgrade command pattern** — Variations of `powershell -Version 2` are useful search targets for downgrade detection. _Why:_ this command-line pattern shows an attempt to force the older engine. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **PowerShell v2 removal recommendation** — PowerShell v2 should be disabled and removed from as many systems as possible. _Why:_ removing the engine eliminates this downgrade path. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **PowerShell v2 attack surface** — PowerShell v2 increases attack surface because it lacks modern logging capabilities. _Why:_ weak telemetry makes it attractive for stealthy execution. _[GCFA p.368]_
- **Downgrade prevention by removal** — PowerShell downgrade attacks cannot occur on systems where PowerShell v2 is not installed. _Why:_ absence of the old engine prevents attackers from invoking it. _[GCFA p.368]_

### PowerShell Logging Enablement

- **Administrative Template configuration** — PowerShell logging can be activated through Administrative Templates in Group Policy. _Why:_ tells defenders the enterprise-scale control plane for enabling these artifacts. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Group Policy dependency** — organizations must take explicit configuration action before most PowerShell logging data will exist. _Why:_ absence of logs may reflect missing policy rather than absence of activity. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Default logging limitation** — most PowerShell logging options are not enabled by default. _Why:_ investigators cannot assume useful PowerShell telemetry exists unless logging was previously configured. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Enterprise enablement requirement** — useful PowerShell forensic data generally requires proactive deployment across the environment. _Why:_ incident response value depends on pre-incident logging posture. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Robust logging needs setup** — comprehensive PowerShell auditing requires advance configuration beyond Microsoft’s limited defaults. _Why:_ default telemetry is insufficient for full reconstruction of PowerShell abuse. _[GCFA p.370]_

### Script Block Logging

- **Script block scope** — a PowerShell script block can include cmdlets, functions, or entire scripts. _Why:_ defines the execution units that script block auditing can record. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Execution source coverage** — script block logging applies to PowerShell use from a command shell. _Why:_ captures common attacker and administrator invocation paths. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **ISE coverage** — script block logging also applies when PowerShell runs through the Integrated Scripting Environment. _Why:_ investigators should consider ISE-launched activity within the same audit surface. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Custom host coverage** — script block logging can capture activity executed through custom PowerShell hosts or embedded PowerShell components. _Why:_ attackers cannot avoid this logging merely by avoiding `powershell.exe`. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **PowerShell v5 capability** — PowerShell version 5 introduced script block logging as a major auditing feature. _Why:_ version level materially affects forensic visibility. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Full content capture** — script block auditing can record the complete command or script content. _Why:_ provides high-value evidence of attacker intent and exact executed logic. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Executor attribution** — script block auditing can include the user who ran the PowerShell content. _Why:_ supports attribution to accounts involved in suspicious execution. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Execution timing** — script block auditing can record when the PowerShell activity occurred. _Why:_ supports timeline reconstruction during incident response. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **First-run recording behavior** — PowerShell v5 records script block contents only on the first execution of that content. _Why:_ repeated execution may not generate duplicate content logs, which affects evidence expectations. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Log-volume rationale** — the first-run-only behavior is intended to reduce event log volume. _Why:_ explains why repeated malicious commands may not appear repeatedly as full script block entries. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Event ID 4104** — PowerShell script block contents are recorded under Event ID `4104`. _Why:_ gives investigators the specific event identifier to search for script content. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Script block event destination** — script block audit entries are written to `Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational`. _Why:_ identifies the event log where investigators should look. _[GCFA p.370]_

### Suspicious Script Logging

- **Automatic suspicious-script logging** — PowerShell v5 includes automatic logging for scripts Microsoft considers suspicious. _Why:_ some malicious PowerShell may be recorded even without full logging enabled. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Blocklisted component trigger** — Microsoft’s limited default suspicious-script logging is based on scripts containing blocklisted elements. _Why:_ explains why only some suspicious activity may appear by default. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Warning event marker** — suspicious-script events should be searched for with the event level or label `Warning`. _Why:_ gives analysts a concrete filter for finding automatically flagged PowerShell activity. _[GCFA p.370]_

### Module Logging

- **PowerShell v3 module logging** — module logging has existed since PowerShell version 3. _Why:_ older systems may support module-level telemetry even without PowerShell v5. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Historical deployment difficulty** — module logging was traditionally difficult to configure effectively. _Why:_ explains why many organizations may lack these records. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Low historical adoption** — module logging was unlikely to have been widely used in many environments. _Why:_ helps set realistic expectations during evidence collection. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Improved value in PowerShell v5** — module logging becomes more useful in PowerShell version 5. _Why:_ PowerShell version affects the value of enabled telemetry. _[GCFA p.370]_

### Recommended PowerShell Audit Policy

- **Module Logging recommendation** — a strong PowerShell audit policy should enable Module Logging. _Why:_ module telemetry contributes one perspective on PowerShell use. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Script Block Logging recommendation** — a strong PowerShell audit policy should enable PowerShell Script Block Logging. _Why:_ script block logs can expose executed commands and script contents. _[GCFA p.370]_
- **Transcription recommendation** — a strong PowerShell audit policy should enable PowerShell Transcription. _Why:_ transcription adds another view of PowerShell activity that can complement event logs. _[GCFA p.370]_

### Automatic PowerShell Script Block Logging

- **PowerShell v5+ feature** — newer PowerShell versions, beginning with v5, can log complete script blocks. _Why:_ full script content gives investigators far more detail than only process command lines. _[GCFA p.372]_
- **Script block logging value** — complete script block logging is useful for tracking attackers using PowerShell. _Why:_ attackers commonly use PowerShell for execution, staging, and living-off-the-land activity. _[GCFA p.372]_
- **Rogue administrator relevance** — script block logging can also expose misuse by administrators. _Why:_ insider or administrative abuse may otherwise resemble authorized activity. _[GCFA p.372]_
- **Dependency on prior enablement** — ordinary script block logging is most useful when enabled before the malicious activity occurs. _Why:_ investigators cannot recover non-collected script block logs after the fact. _[GCFA p.372]_
- **Microsoft security design concern** — Microsoft anticipated that organizations might ignore script block logging until after an incident. _Why:_ automatic logging helps preserve evidence even when proactive auditing is weak. _[GCFA p.372]_
- **Automatic suspicious script detection** — PowerShell can identify potentially malicious script blocks without full script block logging being configured. _Why:_ this creates a fallback source of forensic evidence. _[GCFA p.372]_
- **Automatic log destination** — suspicious script blocks are automatically written to the PowerShell Operational log. _Why:_ analysts should query that log even when script block logging was not explicitly enabled. _[GCFA p.372]_
- **Dangerous command alert list** — Microsoft implemented a list of risky PowerShell commands or terms that trigger automatic logging. _Why:_ matching these indicators can surface high-value events for investigation. _[GCFA p.372]_
- **Nasreddine Bencherchali research** — researcher Nasreddine Bencherchali extracted the alert list from the related DLL. _Why:_ the extracted list helps analysts understand why certain scripts are automatically logged. _[GCFA p.372]_
- **Audit policy independence** — automatic suspicious script logging can produce useful PowerShell evidence regardless of the configured audit policy. _Why:_ this improves forensic visibility on systems without ideal logging settings. _[GCFA p.372]_

### Warning-Level EID 4104 Filtering

- **Suspicious event labeling** — Windows marks script block events it considers suspicious as Event ID 4104 with level `Warning`. _Why:_ warning-level 4104 records are a strong first-pass triage target. _[GCFA p.372]_
- **Distinguishing suspicious 4104 events** — the warning level helps separate suspicious 4104 records from other 4104 script block entries. _Why:_ analysts can reduce noise by prioritizing records Windows already flagged. _[GCFA p.372]_
- **First-pass filtering** — warning-level 4104 events can be used as an initial filter during review. _Why:_ this narrows the dataset before deeper script content analysis. _[GCFA p.372]_
- **Centralization pre-filter** — warning-level 4104 events can be forwarded or centralized preferentially when collecting all 4104 events is too large. _Why:_ this preserves high-signal PowerShell evidence while managing log volume. _[GCFA p.372]_
- **Data-volume concern** — collecting every EID 4104 event may generate too much data in some environments. _Why:_ filtering strategy affects both storage costs and analytic practicality. _[GCFA p.372]_

- **Obfuscation goal · Security-tool avoidance** — Attackers use PowerShell obfuscation to reduce the chance that defensive products will recognize malicious script content. _Why:_ detection logic based only on obvious strings or keywords can miss transformed scripts. _[GCFA p.~378]_
- **Obfuscation goal · Analyst slowdown** — PowerShell obfuscation is also intended to make human review more difficult. _Why:_ difficult-to-read scripts increase triage time during incident response. _[GCFA p.~378]_
- **Analysis visibility** — Highly obfuscated PowerShell is often visually obvious to an analyst once seen. _Why:_ strange syntax can be a strong suspiciousness indicator during manual review. _[GCFA p.~378]_
- **Scale limitation** — Although obfuscation can be easy to spot manually, identifying it reliably across large log volumes is difficult. _Why:_ enterprise hunting requires scalable analytics, not only analyst intuition. _[GCFA p.~378]_
- **Detection pressure** — Improvements in antivirus, enterprise detection and response tooling, and logging have pushed attackers toward more complex PowerShell evasion. _Why:_ defensive maturity changes attacker tradecraft. _[GCFA p.~378]_
- **Keyword-detection weakness** — Attackers design obfuscated PowerShell to defeat simple keyword-matching approaches. _Why:_ detections that only search for obvious command names or strings are fragile. _[GCFA p.~378]_
- **PowerShell flexibility** — PowerShell allows the same behavior to be expressed in many syntactically different ways. _Why:_ flexible language features create a large obfuscation surface. _[GCFA p.~378]_
- **Script-equivalence problem** — Many different-looking PowerShell scripts can perform the same underlying action. _Why:_ defenders must look beyond exact text matches to behavior and normalized content. _[GCFA p.~378]_

- **Encoding-resilient inspection concept** — AMSI is positioned as useful even when scripts have been repeatedly encoded or obfuscated. _Why:_ defenders need controls that observe the executable form, not only the original text. _[GCFA p.~378]_

### CyberChef Purpose and Scope

- **CyberChef** — browser-based analysis tool used for transforming encrypted, encoded, compressed, and otherwise represented data. _Why:_ DFIR analysts commonly need to normalize suspicious strings before they can interpret payload behavior. _[GCFA p.379]_

- **CyberChef · Obfuscation Analysis** — the tool is useful for recognizing and reversing many forms of script or data obfuscation. _Why:_ malicious PowerShell, VBScript, and droppers often hide intent behind layered encodings. _[GCFA p.379]_

- **CyberChef · Encoding Detection** — the tool includes a “Magic” capability that attempts to infer likely decoding operations automatically. _Why:_ automated recipe guessing can speed up first-pass triage of heavily transformed attacker content. _[GCFA p.379]_

- **CyberChef · Public Release** — CyberChef was released as open-source software by the United Kingdom’s GCHQ. _Why:_ investigators can inspect, host, and use the tool without relying only on a closed commercial service. _[GCFA p.379]_

- **CyberChef · Data Format Coverage** — CyberChef supports many data-format operations rather than only one encoding family. _Why:_ attacker payloads frequently combine different transformations, so broad coverage reduces tool-switching. _[GCFA p.379]_

- **CyberChef · Browser Execution Model** — CyberChef performs its operations through a web-browser interface. _Why:_ analysts can manipulate data interactively without building one-off command-line pipelines for every transformation. _[GCFA p.379]_

## Page 381

### PowerShell Transcript Logging Scope

- **Transcript logging command capture** — PowerShell transcript logs record commands entered during an interactive terminal session. _Why:_ command input can reveal exactly what an operator or attacker attempted. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Transcript logging output capture** — PowerShell transcript logs also record the output produced after those commands run. _Why:_ command results can show whether activity succeeded and what data was exposed. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Terminal-only visibility** — Transcript logging is limited to input and output shown through the PowerShell terminal interface. _Why:_ analysts must understand that transcript logs do not provide the same internal execution detail as other PowerShell telemetry. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Difference from Script Block Logging** — Transcript logs contain a different kind of evidence than Script Block Logging. _Why:_ the two sources answer different forensic questions and should not be treated as substitutes. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Lower storage footprint** — Transcript logs generally consume less storage than other PowerShell log types. _Why:_ smaller log volume makes centralized collection more practical at enterprise scale. _[GCFA p.381]_

### Version Support And Enablement

- **PowerShell v4+ native support** — Native PowerShell transcription logging is available starting with PowerShell version 4. _Why:_ responders need version context when determining whether the feature could have been configured on a host. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Disabled default state** — PowerShell transcription logging is not enabled by default. _Why:_ absence of transcript files does not prove PowerShell was unused. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Historical availability in PowerShell v2** — Transcript capability existed as early as PowerShell version 2. _Why:_ older systems may still have transcript evidence if administrators explicitly configured it. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Legacy Start-Transcript requirement** — Older transcript collection commonly depended on running `Start-Transcript` before the relevant activity occurred. _Why:_ this limits the reliability of transcript evidence on systems without native policy-based transcription. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Legacy profile.ps1 placement** — Another older approach was placing transcript startup logic in each user’s `profile.ps1`. _Why:_ per-user profile dependence creates coverage gaps and potential tampering points. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Modern native transcription** — Current PowerShell includes built-in transcription logging capability. _Why:_ modern enterprise deployments can enable transcript capture more consistently. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Enterprise recommendation** — The course recommends transcription logging for modern enterprise environments. _Why:_ transcript output can provide evidence unavailable from other PowerShell logs. _[GCFA p.381]_

### Group Policy Configuration

- **Global enablement by Group Policy** — PowerShell transcription can be enabled broadly using Windows Group Policy. _Why:_ centralized policy improves consistency across many endpoints. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Group Policy path** — The policy location is `Computer Configuration/Administrative Templates/Windows Components/Windows PowerShell/Turn on PowerShell Transcription`. _Why:_ this exact path lets administrators and investigators verify whether transcription was configured. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Output folder determined at enablement** — The transcript destination is configured when transcription logging is enabled. _Why:_ knowing the configured destination guides evidence collection. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Group Policy output control** — Group Policy can define where PowerShell transcript logs are written. _Why:_ defenders can forward transcripts away from attacker-controlled user profiles. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Output Directory option** — The configuration includes an output directory setting for transcript storage. _Why:_ this setting controls whether logs remain local or are redirected elsewhere. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Forwarding use case** — The output directory can point to a protected destination such as a write-only share. _Why:_ forwarding reduces the chance that an attacker can erase or alter local transcript evidence. _[GCFA p.381]_

### Default Storage Behavior

- **Default user Documents location** — If no destination is configured, transcripts are written under `\Users\<account>\Documents`. _Why:_ responders should check user profile Documents folders when no centralized path is known. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Per-user default placement** — The default path is inside each user’s profile. _Why:_ transcript collection may require examining multiple user profiles on the same system. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Daily folder organization** — Transcript sessions are placed into folders organized by date. _Why:_ date-based folders help correlate transcripts with incident timelines. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Timestamped session files** — Individual transcript files include timestamps in their names. _Why:_ filename timestamps help identify session timing even before reviewing file contents. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Text-file format** — Transcript sessions are stored as text files. _Why:_ they are easy for analysts to read but also easy for attackers to edit. _[GCFA p.381]_

### Forensic Value Compared With Other Logs

- **Unique displayed-content evidence** — Transcript logs preserve what appeared in the PowerShell terminal. _Why:_ this can reveal user-visible or session-visible results that other logs may omit. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Input evidence** — Transcript logs include commands entered by the user or operator. _Why:_ typed commands can expose attacker tradecraft and intent. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Output evidence** — Transcript logs include command responses shown after execution. _Why:_ output can expose collected credentials, queried data, or error messages. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **PowerShell remoting relevance** — Transcript logs may capture output even when the person running the command did not directly see it because of remoting behavior. _Why:_ this widens the evidentiary value of transcripts in remote administration or attacker sessions. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Script Block Logging comparison** — Script Block Logging would capture script content used to run PowerShell code. _Why:_ it is better suited to reconstructing executed script logic. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Download cradle comparison** — Script Block Logging may capture a download cradle used to retrieve and run code. _Why:_ this helps identify in-memory execution mechanisms. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Transcript logging comparison** — Transcript logging would show the script name or typed download cradle along with resulting terminal output. _Why:_ this connects execution with observed results. _[GCFA p.381]_

### Mimikatz Example

- **Mimikatz as example tool** — The page uses Mimikatz as the example credential-dumping tool run through PowerShell. _Why:_ credential theft cases often require knowing not only execution but also results. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Mimikatz execution via PowerShell** — The scenario involves launching Mimikatz through PowerShell. _Why:_ PowerShell can act as the execution vehicle for credential-dumping activity. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Script Block Logging Mimikatz evidence** — In the example, Script Block Logging would show the code or retrieval method used to execute Mimikatz. _Why:_ this helps prove how the tool was launched. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Transcript Mimikatz evidence** — In the example, transcript logging would show the invoked script name or typed download cradle and Mimikatz output. _Why:_ this can expose what the tool returned to the operator. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Mimikatz success determination** — Transcript logs may be the only source that clearly shows whether the Mimikatz run succeeded. _Why:_ success or failure changes incident scope and response priorities. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Collected-data determination** — Transcript logs may reveal what information the attackers obtained from Mimikatz output. _Why:_ knowing exposed material is critical for credential reset and impact assessment. _[GCFA p.381]_

### Storage And Protection Guidance

- **Smaller collection burden** — Because transcript logs capture terminal input and output rather than full event telemetry, their size is often much smaller than corresponding event logs. _Why:_ this supports broader retention and central collection. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Large-scale collection feasibility** — The lower transcript volume makes enterprise-wide collection more achievable. _Why:_ organizations can preserve useful PowerShell evidence without the same storage pressure as verbose event logging. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **User-profile storage risk** — Keeping transcript logs under user profiles is discouraged. _Why:_ attackers with access to the account may be able to interfere with those files. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Plain-text tampering risk** — Transcript logs are text files and can be easily removed or changed by an attacker with sufficient access. _Why:_ integrity of local transcript evidence may be questionable. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Write-only storage recommendation** — A stronger design is to send transcripts to a location where ordinary users can write new logs but cannot read, alter, or delete existing ones. _Why:_ this protects transcript evidence from casual attacker cleanup. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Security-team exception** — The page notes that security-team accounts may need broader access to the protected transcript folder. _Why:_ analysts require access for monitoring, triage, and investigations. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Network-share recommendation** — The preferred protected transcript destination is a network share. _Why:_ remote storage reduces dependence on compromised endpoints. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Cross-user privacy control** — Microsoft guidance referenced by the page says access should be restricted so users cannot view transcripts from other users or systems. _Why:_ transcripts may contain sensitive commands, output, and credentials. _[GCFA p.381]_
- **Microsoft documentation reference** — The cited reference is Microsoft’s PowerShell Group Policy settings documentation at `https://for508.com/05zvl`. _Why:_ it provides the vendor source for configuring transcription policy. _[GCFA p.381]_

## Page 385

### PSReadLine History Artifact

- **PSReadLine history file** — PowerShell console command history is stored in a file named `ConsoleHost_history.txt`. _Why:_ this file can reveal commands an interactive user or attacker typed. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **History file directory** — The shown storage directory is `%UserProfile%\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadline`. _Why:_ investigators need the exact per-user location to collect the artifact. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Per-user storage** — PowerShell console history is written inside each user profile rather than to a single system-wide file. _Why:_ responders must inspect every relevant user profile, not only the administrator account. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Flat text format** — `ConsoleHost_history.txt` is a plain text command list. _Why:_ it can be reviewed quickly with ordinary text tools and is easy to parse. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Command count limit** — PSReadLine records the most recent 4,096 commands entered in the PowerShell console. _Why:_ older commands can roll off, so absence of a command does not prove it was never run. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Console-only scope** — The artifact records commands typed in the PowerShell console. _Why:_ it identifies interactive console activity specifically. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **PowerShell ISE exclusion** — Commands typed in PowerShell ISE are not captured by this console history file. _Why:_ investigators should not expect ISE activity to appear in this artifact. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Default availability** — PSReadLine command history is enabled by default on Windows 10 and later with PowerShell v5. _Why:_ responders can often rely on this artifact existing without prior logging configuration. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **PowerShell v5 logging context** — PowerShell version 5 introduced stronger event logging and also included PSReadLine history capability. _Why:_ host PowerShell version affects available forensic telemetry. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **PowerShell 5.1 integration** — PSReadLine became a default PowerShell component in PowerShell 5.1. _Why:_ version 5.1 systems commonly produce this history artifact by default. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Original project source** — PSReadLine began as a GitHub-hosted PowerShell add-on. _Why:_ knowing its origin helps explain why it resembles shell history features from other environments. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Bash History analogy** — PSReadLine history is comparable in purpose to Linux Bash history. _Why:_ analysts familiar with Unix shell artifacts can apply similar investigative thinking on Windows. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Reference link** — The page cites `http://for508.com/1uige` for “PSReadLine: A bash-inspired readline implementation for PowerShell.” _Why:_ the link points to supporting material about the PSReadLine implementation. _[GCFA p.385]_

### Collection and Evidentiary Behavior

- **Administrator console behavior** — Commands typed in an elevated Administrator PowerShell console still write to the currently logged-on user’s `ConsoleHost_history.txt`. _Why:_ privileged command evidence may reside in the non-admin user profile that launched the elevated shell. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **No Windows protection** — Windows does not protect `ConsoleHost_history.txt` against user modification or deletion. _Why:_ the artifact is useful but should be treated as tamperable evidence. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Attacker modification risk** — A knowledgeable attacker can edit the history file. _Why:_ responders should corroborate its contents with event logs, transcripts, prefetch, and other artifacts. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Attacker deletion risk** — A knowledgeable attacker can remove the history file. _Why:_ missing history may itself be suspicious but is not conclusive without supporting evidence. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Temporary logging suppression** — Command history recording can be temporarily disabled. _Why:_ a gap in PSReadLine history can result from attacker action during an interactive session. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Disable actions are self-recording** — The commands used to disable PSReadLine history are themselves written to the history file. _Why:_ investigators may find direct evidence of attempted history suppression. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Disable settings are not persistent** — The page states the shown suppression methods are temporary rather than permanent. _Why:_ later sessions may resume history capture unless additional persistence is used. _[GCFA p.385]_

### Anti-Forensic Commands

- **History suppression command** — `Set-PSReadLineOption -HistorySaveStyle SaveNothing` disables saving PSReadLine command history for the session. _Why:_ this command is a direct indicator of attempted command-history suppression. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Module removal command** — `Remove-Module -Name PsReadline` unloads the PSReadLine module. _Why:_ removing the module can stop the history feature from recording subsequent commands. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **PSReadLine module target** — The module name shown for removal is `PsReadline`. _Why:_ module removal events or history entries using this name can indicate anti-forensic behavior. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **HistorySaveStyle value** — The disabling option uses the value `SaveNothing`. _Why:_ this exact value identifies the setting that prevents history persistence. _[GCFA p.385]_

### Comparison to Transcript Logging

- **Command-only capture** — PSReadLine history records typed commands but does not record command output. _Why:_ the artifact can show intent or execution attempts but not resulting data. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **No timestamp metadata** — PSReadLine history does not include timestamps. _Why:_ command ordering may be visible, but precise timing must be reconstructed from other sources. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **No extra session metadata** — PSReadLine history lacks richer metadata beyond the command text. _Why:_ user, host, time, and execution context must be validated elsewhere. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Interactive-session limitation** — PSReadLine history is recorded only for explicitly interactive PowerShell console sessions. _Why:_ scripted, noninteractive, or alternate-host activity may not appear. _[GCFA p.385]_
- **Default-on advantage** — Compared with transcript logging, PSReadLine’s benefit is default availability for all users. _Why:_ it may exist even where administrators never configured transcript logging. _[GCFA p.385]_

- **Displayed application** — The screenshot shows `ConsoleHost_history.txt` opened in Notepad. _Why:_ it demonstrates that the artifact is directly readable as text. _[GCFA p.385]_

- **Event log analysis dependency** — Windows event-log analysis requires acquiring the relevant logs before examination can begin. _Why:_ without collection, the analyst has no event records to query, preserve, or correlate. _[GCFA p.388]_
- **Preferred collection state** — In the best case, relevant Windows logs have already been sent to a centralized collection server before the investigation starts. _Why:_ forwarded logs reduce reliance on the potentially compromised endpoint and speed analysis. _[GCFA p.388]_
- **Fallback collection requirement** — If logs were not already centralized, the investigator should be ready to collect them from multiple sources. _Why:_ incident response often requires gathering evidence across several hosts or storage locations. _[GCFA p.388]_
- **Collection categories shown** — The page separates event-log acquisition into live-system collection and log forwarding. _Why:_ these are different operational models: direct host extraction versus prior centralized ingestion. _[GCFA p.388]_

### Sysmon Overview

- **Sysmon** — Microsoft provides Sysmon as a no-cost logging add-on for Windows systems. _Why:_ it expands host telemetry available to investigators beyond default Windows logging. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Sysmon origin** — Sysmon was created by Mark Russinovich of Microsoft Sysinternals. _Why:_ its Sysinternals origin helps explain why it is widely trusted and commonly deployed in Windows DFIR work. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Sysmon purpose** — Sysmon was made to close visibility gaps left by native Windows event logging. _Why:_ default Windows logs often miss or underrepresent activity that matters during intrusion analysis. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Sysmon DFIR design goal** — Sysmon was specifically designed for digital forensics and incident response work inside Microsoft’s corporate environment. _Why:_ the tool’s event coverage reflects practical investigation needs rather than only operating-system auditing needs. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Sysmon as preferred log source** — The page presents Sysmon as potentially the single most valuable Windows log source, despite not being included with Windows by default. _Why:_ this frames Sysmon as a high-priority telemetry source for endpoint investigations. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Sysmon as examiner wish list** — Sysmon records many artifact types that forensic analysts commonly want represented in event logs. _Why:_ it provides direct visibility into actions that otherwise require multiple artifacts or manual reconstruction. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Sysmon as lightweight endpoint detection** — Sysmon can be treated as a free, lightweight endpoint detection capability. _Why:_ it gives defenders useful detection telemetry without requiring a commercial EDR platform. _[GCFA p.393]_

### Deployment And Configuration

- **Sysmon installation** — Installing Sysmon is described as straightforward. _Why:_ low deployment complexity makes it realistic to add to incident response and enterprise monitoring programs. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Sysmon configuration** — Sysmon is described as easy to configure. _Why:_ practical configuration matters because Sysmon’s value depends heavily on event selection and filtering. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Sysmon pre-filtering** — Sysmon supports preconfigured filtering before logs are generated or retained. _Why:_ pre-filtering reduces noise and improves signal quality during investigations. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Sysmon allowlisting** — Sysmon configurations can include allowlists to suppress known-benign activity. _Why:_ allowlisting helps control event volume and makes high-frequency telemetry usable. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Sysmon log-size reduction** — Filtering and allowlisting can reduce the amount of Sysmon data produced. _Why:_ smaller logs are easier to collect, retain, search, and forward at scale. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Sysmon scalability** — Sysmon is designed to scale across environments. _Why:_ scalability determines whether detailed endpoint telemetry can be collected across many hosts rather than only during isolated response actions. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Sysmon SIEM integration** — Sysmon was designed to work with SIEM-style collection and analysis systems. _Why:_ centralized ingestion makes endpoint activity searchable across an enterprise. _[GCFA p.393]_

### Sysmon Event Log Location

- **Sysmon operational log** — Sysmon creates a Windows event log named `Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational`. _Why:_ investigators need this exact log name to collect and query Sysmon events. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Sysmon log readability** — Sysmon event records are described as more descriptive than much native Windows logging. _Why:_ clearer event contents reduce interpretation errors during forensic review. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Sysmon versus Security 4688** — Sysmon can make process-execution collection more practical than relying on traditional Security log Event ID `4688`. _Why:_ Security `4688` process auditing can be noisy or less manageable at scale. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Security log Event ID 4688** — Windows Security Event ID `4688` is identified as a traditional source for process-execution events. _Why:_ it provides a native comparison point for why Sysmon process telemetry is often preferred. _[GCFA p.393]_

### Activity Types Captured

- **Network activity** — Sysmon can record network-related activity. _Why:_ network telemetry helps identify command-and-control, reconnaissance, lateral movement, and suspicious outbound behavior. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Process execution** — Sysmon can log process starts. _Why:_ process creation is central to reconstructing attacker execution chains. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Command lines** — Sysmon can capture command-line details. _Why:_ command-line arguments often reveal attacker intent, encoded payloads, tools, and target paths. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **File hashes** — Sysmon can record hashes for files involved in activity. _Why:_ hashes support malware identification, correlation, reputation checks, and cross-host scoping. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **File creation** — Sysmon can log newly created files. _Why:_ file creation events help identify dropped payloads, staging files, tools, and persistence artifacts. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Creation-time changes** — Sysmon can record changes to file creation times. _Why:_ timestamp modification can indicate timestomping or other anti-forensic behavior. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Registry changes** — Sysmon can capture registry modification activity. _Why:_ registry changes are common in persistence, configuration changes, malware staging, and system manipulation. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **DLL loading** — Sysmon can log DLL load activity. _Why:_ DLL load visibility helps detect suspicious library loading, search-order hijacking, and injected or malicious modules. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Driver loading** — Sysmon can log driver load activity. _Why:_ driver telemetry helps identify kernel-level components, rootkits, and privileged malware behavior. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Remote thread creation** — Sysmon can capture remote thread creation. _Why:_ remote thread creation is a common process-injection technique. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Process injection indicator** — The page explicitly associates remote thread creation with injection. _Why:_ this links a specific Sysmon-observable behavior to a known attacker technique. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Named pipe creation** — Sysmon can record named pipe creation. _Why:_ named pipes are often used for interprocess communication, malware coordination, and lateral movement tooling. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Alternate data streams** — Sysmon can capture alternate data stream activity. _Why:_ ADS artifacts may hide payloads or metadata in NTFS file streams that are easy to overlook. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **WMI event consumers** — Sysmon can record WMI Event Consumer activity. _Why:_ WMI event consumers can be used for stealthy persistence and automated execution. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **Raw disk access** — Sysmon can detect raw disk access. _Why:_ direct disk access may indicate forensic tools, credential theft, malware, or attempts to bypass normal file-system access controls. _[GCFA p.393]_

- **SHA2 hash support** — Sysmon can provide SHA2-family hashes for files. _Why:_ stronger hash values improve reliable file identification and modern threat-intelligence matching. _[GCFA p.393]_
- **IMPHash support** — Sysmon can provide import hashes. _Why:_ IMPHash values can help cluster related Windows PE files by imported API structure. _[GCFA p.393]_

## Page 397

### Lateral Movement Overview

- **Lateral movement** — attackers move from one host to another inside a network to progress toward objectives. _Why:_ this behavior is central to scoping and threat hunting during intrusions. _[GCFA p.397]_
- **Attacker dependency on lateral movement** — intruders generally need at least one lateral movement method during a compromise, regardless of sophistication. _Why:_ responders should expect and hunt for these behaviors in real incidents. _[GCFA p.397]_
- **Responder value of lateral movement knowledge** — knowing common movement methods helps analysts hunt faster, scope incidents sooner, and anticipate likely next actions. _Why:_ it converts attacker tradecraft into concrete forensic leads. _[GCFA p.397]_
- **FOR508 reference** — the page points to SANS FOR508 as the course source for tools and techniques used to hunt the listed artifacts. _Why:_ it identifies the course context for the artifact checklist. _[GCFA p.397]_

### PowerShell Remoting Overview
- **PowerShell Remoting · Process pair** — `powershell.exe` is the local PowerShell process associated with remoting activity, while `wsmprovhost.exe` is the remote-side host process commonly involved in receiving and executing remoting commands. _Why:_ process pairing helps reconstruct source and destination activity. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Enter-PSSession command** — `Enter-PSSession -ComputerName host` opens an interactive PowerShell remoting session to the named host. _Why:_ this command is direct evidence of interactive remote administration or lateral movement. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Invoke-Command command** — `Invoke-Command -ComputerName host -ScriptBlock {Start-Process c:\temp\evil.exe}` remotely runs a script block on the target host and starts `c:\temp\evil.exe`. _Why:_ this shows remote command execution and a specific launched payload path. _[GCFA p.399]_

### PowerShell Remoting · Source-Side Event Logs
- **Source security.evtx · 4648** — Event ID `4648` records a logon attempt using explicit alternate credentials. _Why:_ alternate credentials can identify lateral movement using a different account than the current session. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source security.evtx · 4648 current user** — Event `4648` can expose the currently logged-on user name. _Why:_ this ties the remoting attempt to the initiating local account. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source security.evtx · 4648 alternate user** — Event `4648` can expose the alternate user name supplied for authentication. _Why:_ this identifies the credential set used for the remote connection. _[GCFA p.399]_

- **Source security.evtx · 4648 process** — Event `4648` can include the process name that initiated the credentialed logon. _Why:_ this helps attribute the authentication attempt to PowerShell or another tool. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source WinRM Operational · 161** — `Microsoft-Windows-WinRM%4Operational.evtx` Event ID `161` records a remote authentication error. _Why:_ failed remoting authentication can reveal attempted access even when execution did not succeed. _[GCFA p.399]_

- **Source WinRM Operational · 6 destination** — Event `6` can include the destination host name or IP address. _Why:_ this maps the source system to the remote target. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source WinRM Operational · 6 current user** — Event `6` can include the current logged-on user name. _Why:_ this links the WSMan session to the initiating account. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source WinRM Operational · 8** — WinRM Operational Event ID `8` is associated with WSMan session initialization activity. _Why:_ it contributes to a timeline of remoting session setup and teardown. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source WinRM Operational · 15** — WinRM Operational Event ID `15` is associated with WSMan session initialization activity. _Why:_ it can corroborate remoting session lifecycle evidence. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source WinRM Operational · 16** — WinRM Operational Event ID `16` is associated with WSMan session initialization activity. _Why:_ it helps identify WSMan remoting sequence details. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source WinRM Operational · 33** — WinRM Operational Event ID `33` is associated with WSMan session initialization activity. _Why:_ it can support session reconstruction. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source WinRM Operational · 8/15/16/33 session close** — Events `8`, `15`, `16`, and `33` may record WSMan session closure. _Why:_ session closure helps bound the duration of remote activity. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source WinRM Operational · 8/15/16/33 current user** — Events `8`, `15`, `16`, and `33` may include the currently logged-on user name. _Why:_ account context helps attribute the remoting session. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source PowerShell Operational · 40961** — `Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell%4Operational.evtx` Event ID `40961` records local startup of `powershell.exe` and the related user account. _Why:_ it links local PowerShell launch to a user. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source PowerShell Operational · 40962** — `Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell%4Operational.evtx` Event ID `40962` records local startup of `powershell.exe` and the related user account. _Why:_ it corroborates PowerShell launch activity. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source PowerShell Operational · 8193** — PowerShell Operational Event ID `8193` indicates session creation. _Why:_ it helps prove that a PowerShell remoting session was established. _[GCFA p.399]_
