- **Source PowerShell Operational · 8197 session close** — Event `8197` can record session closure. _Why:_ it helps identify when the remoting session ended. _[GCFA p.399]_

### PowerShell Remoting · Source-Side Registry
- **Source ShimCache · SYSTEM hive** — ShimCache in the `SYSTEM` hive may contain `powershell.exe`. _Why:_ this can show that PowerShell was present in application compatibility execution-related artifacts. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source BAM/DAM · SYSTEM hive** — BAM/DAM in the `SYSTEM` hive can record last execution time for `powershell.exe`. _Why:_ this helps establish recent PowerShell execution on the source. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source AmCache.hve · first execution** — `AmCache.hve` may record first execution information for `powershell.exe`. _Why:_ first-run evidence helps establish whether PowerShell activity is newly observed on the system. _[GCFA p.399]_

### PowerShell Remoting · Source-Side File System
- **Source Prefetch directory** — PowerShell remoting source artifacts may appear under `C:\Windows\Prefetch\`. _Why:_ Prefetch can provide execution timing and file-use context. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source Prefetch · powershell.exe file** — The source host may contain a `powershell.exe-(hash).pf` Prefetch file. _Why:_ this supports execution of PowerShell from a specific path. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source Prefetch · scripts within 10 seconds** — PowerShell scripts with `.ps1` extensions launched within 10 seconds of `powershell.exe` startup can be tracked inside the `powershell.exe` Prefetch file. _Why:_ script paths embedded in Prefetch can reveal executed script content indirectly. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source command history path** — PowerShell command history may reside at `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadline\ConsoleHost_history.txt`. _Why:_ this file can contain typed commands used to initiate remoting. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Source PSReadLine history size** — With PowerShell version 5, each user can have a history file retaining the previous `4096` commands. _Why:_ a large per-user command history can preserve attacker tradecraft. _[GCFA p.399]_

### PowerShell Remoting · Destination-Side Event Logs
- **Destination security.evtx · 4624** — Event ID `4624` with Logon Type `3` records a network logon on the destination. _Why:_ PowerShell remoting commonly produces network logon evidence on the target. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination security.evtx · 4624 source and user** — Event `4624` can include the source IP address and logon user name. _Why:_ these fields tie the destination logon to its originating host and account. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination security.evtx · 4672** — Event ID `4672` records assignment of special privileges to a logon. _Why:_ this can identify administrative-level access during remoting. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination security.evtx · 4672 user** — Event `4672` can include the logon user name. _Why:_ this identifies the account receiving elevated privileges. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination security.evtx · 4672 admin rights** — Event `4672` indicates logon by a user with administrative rights. _Why:_ administrative privilege is a key lateral movement indicator. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination PowerShell Operational · 4103** — PowerShell Operational Event ID `4103` records module or script-related logging activity. _Why:_ it can reveal executed PowerShell content on the target. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination PowerShell Operational · 4104** — PowerShell Operational Event ID `4104` records script block logging. _Why:_ script block logs can expose malicious code executed through remoting. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination PowerShell Operational · 4103/4104 suspicious defaults** — In PowerShell version 5, suspicious scripts are logged by default through these script logging mechanisms. _Why:_ default logging can capture high-risk content even without full logging configuration. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination PowerShell Operational · 4103/4104 full logging** — If configured, these events can log all script content rather than only suspicious content. _Why:_ full script logging gives broader visibility into remote execution. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination PowerShell Operational · 53504** — Event ID `53504` records the authenticating user. _Why:_ it identifies the user account that authenticated for the remoting activity. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination Windows PowerShell.evtx · 400** — Event ID `400` with `ServerRemoteHost` indicates the start of a remoting session. _Why:_ it marks the beginning of remote PowerShell activity. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination Windows PowerShell.evtx · 403** — Event ID `403` with `ServerRemoteHost` indicates the end of a remoting session. _Why:_ it helps define session duration. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination Windows PowerShell.evtx · 800** — Event ID `800` can contain partial script code. _Why:_ partial code fragments may still reveal attacker commands or payload paths. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination WinRM Operational · 91** — WinRM Operational Event ID `91` records session creation. _Why:_ it corroborates remote session establishment on the destination. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination WinRM Operational · 142** — WinRM Operational Event ID `142` records WSMan operation failure. _Why:_ failed WSMan operations may reveal attempted remoting actions. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination WinRM Operational · 169** — WinRM Operational Event ID `169` records the authenticating user. _Why:_ it links the WinRM activity to the account used. _[GCFA p.399]_

### PowerShell Remoting · Destination-Side Registry
- **Destination ShimCache · wsmprovhost.exe** — ShimCache in the `SYSTEM` hive may contain `wsmprovhost.exe`. _Why:_ this supports execution of the remoting host process on the destination. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination ShimCache · evil.exe** — ShimCache in the `SYSTEM` hive may contain `evil.exe`. _Why:_ this can preserve evidence of the remotely launched payload. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination SOFTWARE execution policy path** — The PowerShell execution policy value is located at `Microsoft\PowerShell\1\ShellIds\Microsoft.PowerShell\ExecutionPolicy` in the `SOFTWARE` hive. _Why:_ this registry value can show whether script execution controls were weakened. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination execution policy abuse** — An attacker may alter the PowerShell execution policy to a less restrictive value such as `bypass`. _Why:_ reducing execution restrictions can enable malicious scripts to run. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination AmCache.hve · wsmprovhost.exe** — `AmCache.hve` may record first execution information for `wsmprovhost.exe`. _Why:_ first-run evidence supports remote PowerShell host execution on the target. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination AmCache.hve · evil.exe** — `AmCache.hve` may record first execution information for `evil.exe`. _Why:_ this can identify initial execution of the payload. _[GCFA p.399]_

### PowerShell Remoting · Destination-Side File System
- **Destination file creation · evil.exe** — The destination file system may contain a created `evil.exe`. _Why:_ payload creation is direct evidence of staging or remote execution. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination Enter-PSSession profile directory** — Use of `Enter-PSSession` may create a user profile directory on the destination. _Why:_ profile creation can reveal that an interactive remote session occurred. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination Prefetch directory** — Destination Prefetch artifacts may reside under `C:\Windows\Prefetch\`. _Why:_ this directory can preserve target-side execution evidence. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination Prefetch · evil.exe** — The destination may contain `evil.exe-(hash).pf`. _Why:_ this supports execution of the payload on the target. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Destination Prefetch · wsmprovhost.exe** — The destination may contain `wsmprovhost.exe-(hash).pf`. _Why:_ this supports execution of the WinRM PowerShell provider host. _[GCFA p.399]_

### Evidence Of Program Execution · UserAssist
- **UserAssist description** — UserAssist stores execution metadata for programs launched through graphical user interface activity. _Why:_ it can link user-driven GUI execution to a specific profile. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **UserAssist hive** — UserAssist data is stored in the user’s `NTUSER.DAT` hive. _Why:_ the artifact is user-specific rather than only system-wide. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **UserAssist registry path** — UserAssist counts are located at `Current User\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\UserAssist\{GUID}\Count`. _Why:_ this path tells an examiner where to recover the artifact. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **UserAssist GUID purpose** — UserAssist GUIDs identify the category of execution represented by the entries. _Why:_ GUID interpretation determines whether the artifact refers to an executable or shortcut. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **UserAssist GUID CEBFF5CD** — `CEBFF5CD` identifies executable file execution. _Why:_ this GUID helps isolate direct program launches. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **UserAssist GUID F4E57C4B** — `F4E57C4B` identifies shortcut file execution. _Why:_ shortcut launches may show user activity even when the target executable path is indirect. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **UserAssist encoding** — UserAssist values are encoded with ROT-13. _Why:_ examiners must decode values before interpreting paths or names. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **UserAssist application path** — UserAssist can record the application path. _Why:_ paths identify which program was launched. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **UserAssist last run time** — UserAssist can record the last run timestamp. _Why:_ this helps place GUI execution on a timeline. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **UserAssist run count** — UserAssist can record how many times an application was run. _Why:_ frequency can distinguish one-off execution from repeated use. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **UserAssist focus time** — UserAssist can record application focus duration. _Why:_ focus duration can suggest how long a user interacted with an application. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **UserAssist focus count** — UserAssist can record how many times the application received focus. _Why:_ focus count adds context about user interaction. _[GCFA p.399]_

### Evidence Of Program Execution · BAM/DAM
- **BAM definition** — BAM stands for Background Activity Moderator. _Why:_ knowing the component clarifies the source of the execution artifact. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **DAM definition** — DAM stands for Desktop Activity Moderator. _Why:_ it is a related execution-tracking artifact. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **BAM/DAM scope** — BAM and DAM track execution of Windows Store applications and desktop applications. _Why:_ this expands coverage beyond traditional desktop programs. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **BAM location** — BAM user settings are located at `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\bam\UserSettings\{SID}`. _Why:_ the SID key maps execution evidence to a user account. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **DAM location** — DAM user settings are located at `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\dam\UserSettings\{SID}`. _Why:_ this provides the parallel DAM path for user-scoped execution data. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **BAM/DAM executed path** — BAM/DAM can provide the full path of an executed file. _Why:_ full paths identify exact program locations. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **BAM/DAM last execution time** — BAM/DAM can provide the last execution date and time. _Why:_ this supports recent execution timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **BAM/DAM retention** — BAM/DAM commonly retains up to about one week of data. _Why:_ this limits how far back investigators can rely on the artifact. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Windows 10 BAM key** — On Windows 10, the `bam` key is the relevant key identified for this artifact. _Why:_ platform-specific paths prevent looking in the wrong location. _[GCFA p.399]_

### Evidence Of Program Execution · SRUM
- **SRUM definition** — System Resource Usage Monitor tracks system performance data over time. _Why:_ it provides execution and resource-use evidence beyond simple process start artifacts. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **SRUM retention** — SRUM tracks approximately 30 to 60 days of system performance information. _Why:_ it can provide longer historical coverage than some execution artifacts. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **SRUM applications run** — SRUM can record applications that ran. _Why:_ this helps identify program execution. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **SRUM responsible users** — SRUM can record user accounts associated with activity. _Why:_ user attribution is central to forensic reconstruction. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **SRUM network connections** — SRUM can track network connection activity. _Why:_ this links applications to network behavior. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **SRUM bytes sent and received** — SRUM can record bytes sent and received per application per hour. _Why:_ transfer volume can identify data movement or beaconing behavior. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **SRUM supported systems** — SRUM is identified for Windows 8 and later. _Why:_ OS version determines whether the artifact should exist. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **SRUM file path** — SRUM data is stored at `C:\Windows\System32\sru\SRUDB.dat`. _Why:_ this is the database file examiners need to collect. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **SRUM database format** — `SRUDB.dat` is stored as an Extensible Storage Engine database. _Why:_ parsing requires ESE-aware tooling. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **SRUM Network Data Usage table** — Table `{973F5D5C-1D90-4944-BE8E-24B94231A1746}` stores Network Data Usage. _Why:_ this table helps analyze application network volume. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **SRUM Application Resource Usage table** — Table `{D10CA2FE-6FCF-4F6D0-848E-B2E99266FA89}` stores Application Resource Usage. _Why:_ this table helps analyze process resource activity. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **SRUM Network Connectivity Usage table** — Table `{DD6636C4-8929-4683-974E-22C046A43763}` stores Network Connectivity Usage. _Why:_ this table helps analyze connectivity history. _[GCFA p.399]_

### Evidence Of Program Execution · ShimCache
- **ShimCache description** — The Windows Application Compatibility Database helps Windows detect potential compatibility issues for executable files. _Why:_ its compatibility function leaves useful executable presence artifacts. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **ShimCache cached path** — ShimCache caches executable file paths. _Why:_ paths can reveal programs that existed on the system. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **ShimCache cached modified time** — ShimCache caches the binary’s last modified timestamp. _Why:_ this timestamp can support temporal analysis of executable presence. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **ShimCache Windows XP path** — On Windows XP, ShimCache is located at `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatibility`. _Why:_ OS-specific paths guide collection and parsing. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **ShimCache Windows 7+ path** — On Windows 7 and later, ShimCache is located at `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatCache`. _Why:_ the artifact moved for later Windows versions. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **ShimCache executable presence** — Any executable present in the file system may appear in ShimCache. _Why:_ the artifact is not limited to confirmed user execution. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **ShimCache malware discovery** — ShimCache can be useful for identifying malware presence. _Why:_ it can preserve traces of suspicious binaries. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **ShimCache peripheral evidence** — ShimCache can show executables from drives and peripheral media. _Why:_ it may expose programs introduced from removable or external sources. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **ShimCache deleted-file evidence** — ShimCache may retain evidence for files that no longer exist on the Windows system. _Why:_ it can reveal historical executable presence after cleanup. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **ShimCache full executable path** — ShimCache can include the full path of an executable. _Why:_ full paths aid scoping and source identification. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **ShimCache Windows 7 entry limit** — Windows 7 ShimCache contains up to `128` entries. _Why:_ the limit affects expected coverage and artifact completeness. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **ShimCache Windows XP entry limit** — Windows XP ShimCache contains up to `96` entries. _Why:_ limited capacity affects historical retention. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **ShimCache last modification time** — ShimCache records last modification time. _Why:_ this can help place executable creation or modification in context. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **ShimCache temporal sorting** — Executables can be sorted by modified time to infer when an executable was created in the file system. _Why:_ sorting can help build an executable introduction timeline. _[GCFA p.399]_

### Evidence Of Program Execution · Jump Lists
- **Jump Lists purpose** — Windows Jump Lists let users quickly access frequently used or recently used items from the taskbar. _Why:_ they capture user interaction with files and applications. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Jump Lists pinned application behavior** — When an application is pinned and the user right-clicks it, Windows displays Jump Lists. _Why:_ this explains how the artifact is generated through normal UI behavior. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Jump Lists location** — Automatic Jump Lists are stored at `%USERPROFILE%\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Recent\AutomaticDestinations`. _Why:_ this is the collection path for user-specific Jump List artifacts. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Jump List filename basis** — Each Jump List file is named using the application identifier, or AppID, for that application. _Why:_ AppID mapping identifies the application responsible for a Jump List. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Jump List embedded OLE files** — Jump List files contain embedded OLE files. _Why:_ embedded objects may hold target and usage details. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Automatic Jump List creation time** — The Automatic Jump List creation time corresponds to the first time an item was added to the Jump List. _Why:_ it can identify when the artifact first became populated. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Jump List first entry** — The first entry represents the first time the application added data to the AutomaticDestinations file. _Why:_ it can establish the earliest recorded application interaction. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Jump List last modification time** — The last modification time corresponds to the last time an item was added to the Jump List. _Why:_ it helps identify the most recent update to the artifact. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Jump List MRU ordering** — Jump List entries are maintained in most-recently-used order. _Why:_ ordering helps interpret user recency when timestamps are limited. _[GCFA p.399]_

### Evidence Of Program Execution · Prefetch
- **Prefetch purpose** — Prefetch improves system performance by preloading code pages used by executable processes. _Why:_ the optimization mechanism creates forensic records of execution. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Prefetch mapped file behavior** — Prefetch maps preloaded code pages into files in predictable locations accessible to applications. _Why:_ predictable storage makes artifacts collectible and parsable. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Prefetch XP limit** — Windows XP limits Prefetch to `128` files. _Why:_ older entries may be overwritten once the limit is reached. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Prefetch Windows 7 limit** — Windows 7 limits Prefetch to `128` files. _Why:_ retention depends on the file cap. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Prefetch Windows 8+ limit** — Windows 8 and later support up to `1024` Prefetch files. _Why:_ later systems can retain broader execution history. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Prefetch location** — Prefetch files are stored in `C:\Windows\Prefetch`. _Why:_ this is the collection location for Prefetch artifacts. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Prefetch filename format** — Prefetch files use the pattern `(exename)-(hash).pf`. _Why:_ the executable name and hash help associate the artifact with a specific path. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Prefetch hash basis** — The Prefetch hash is calculated from the file path. _Why:_ the hash distinguishes same-named executables in different locations. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Prefetch first execution timestamp** — Prefetch can show the date and time when a file with a given name and path was first executed. _Why:_ this establishes first-known run time. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Prefetch creation time meaning** — The creation time of a `.pf` file represents the first time the file was executed. _Why:_ filesystem metadata on the Prefetch file itself can indicate first run. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Prefetch last run time** — Prefetch records the last run time for the executable name and path. _Why:_ this identifies most recent execution. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Prefetch modification time meaning** — The last modification date of the `.pf` file represents the last execution. _Why:_ this gives a quick filesystem timestamp proxy for most recent run. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Prefetch embedded volume data** — Each `.pf` file contains embedded volume information. _Why:_ volume data helps tie execution to a storage device. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Prefetch embedded file data** — Each `.pf` file contains embedded file references used by the program. _Why:_ referenced files can reveal program behavior and dependencies. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Prefetch embedded directory data** — Each `.pf` file contains embedded directory references used by the program. _Why:_ directory references can expose working paths and accessed locations. _[GCFA p.399]_

### Evidence Of Program Execution · Amcache.hve
- **Amcache application tracking** — `Amcache.hve` tracks installed applications. _Why:_ installed program records can support software inventory and timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Amcache executed-or-present programs** — `Amcache.hve` tracks programs that were executed or present. _Why:_ the artifact may show both execution and presence, requiring careful interpretation. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Amcache driver tracking** — `Amcache.hve` tracks loaded drivers. _Why:_ driver artifacts can reveal kernel-level components or persistence. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Amcache first execution basis** — Amcache tracks first execution of an executable based on the file’s `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` created timestamp. _Why:_ this ties first-run interpretation to NTFS metadata. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Amcache location** — Amcache is located at `C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve`. _Why:_ this is the file examiners must collect for Amcache analysis. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Amcache insertion key caution** — An executable insertion key may not prove execution. _Why:_ presence in Amcache must not be overinterpreted without corroboration. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Amcache last write interpretation** — A last write timestamp may indicate first execution. _Why:_ registry timing can support first-run analysis when interpreted correctly. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Amcache SHA1 hashes** — Amcache can store SHA1 hashes for executables and drivers. _Why:_ hashes support malware identification and file correlation. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Amcache path metadata** — Amcache can provide file path metadata for program execution. _Why:_ paths identify where the executable resided. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Amcache size metadata** — Amcache can provide executable size metadata. _Why:_ size helps identify and compare files. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Amcache creation metadata** — Amcache can provide file creation metadata. _Why:_ creation times support file timeline reconstruction. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Amcache compile-time metadata** — Amcache can provide compile time information. _Why:_ compile timestamps can help assess file provenance and suspicious aging. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Amcache publisher metadata** — Amcache can provide publisher information. _Why:_ publisher data can help distinguish known software from suspicious binaries. _[GCFA p.399]_
- **Amcache PE header metadata** — Amcache can provide Portable Executable header metadata. _Why:_ PE metadata supports executable triage and malware analysis. _[GCFA p.399]_

## Page 409

### Memory Forensics Rationale

- **RAM as operating-system transit point** — Operating-system activity passes through physical memory during normal execution. _Why:_ memory can expose evidence that may not remain available in files or logs. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **CPU–memory–disk hierarchy** — The page depicts a computing hierarchy involving CPU, cache, RAM, virtual memory, and disk. _Why:_ it frames RAM as a central evidence source between processor activity and longer-term storage. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **RAM between CPU and operations** — Memory functions as an intermediary between processor execution, the operating system, and user or system activity. _Why:_ this makes RAM a high-value source for reconstructing what the machine was doing. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Broad historical coverage in RAM** — Many events of investigative interest on modern computers leave data in memory at some point. _Why:_ memory acquisition can preserve traces from diverse system activity. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Files in memory** — File-related data can appear in RAM. _Why:_ investigators may recover evidence about accessed or active files even when disk artifacts are incomplete. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Network connections in memory** — Network-connection data can be present in RAM. _Why:_ this helps reconstruct communication activity during incident response. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Registry hives in memory** — Windows registry hive data can be found in memory. _Why:_ registry-backed configuration and execution evidence may be available from a memory image. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Running malware in memory** — Active malicious code can reside in RAM. _Why:_ memory analysis can reveal malware that is executing, hidden, unpacked, or not easily visible on disk. _[GCFA p.409]_

### Memory-Resident Evidence Types

- **Processes** — Information about running processes can be present in memory. _Why:_ process artifacts support execution analysis and malware triage. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Threads** — Thread-related execution state can reside in memory. _Why:_ thread evidence helps analysts understand what code was executing inside processes. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Malware** — Malicious programs may be captured in RAM. _Why:_ memory can expose malware even when disk files are deleted, packed, or hidden. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Rootkit technologies** — Rootkit-related components may appear in memory. _Why:_ rootkits often manipulate live OS state, making memory analysis important for detection. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Network sockets** — Socket information can be recovered from memory. _Why:_ sockets can identify active or recent communication endpoints. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **URLs** — Web addresses may be present in RAM. _Why:_ URLs can identify visited resources, command-and-control locations, or malicious infrastructure. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **IP addresses** — IP address values may be found in memory. _Why:_ IP artifacts can support timeline building, scoping, and network attribution. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Open files** — Metadata or content related to currently opened files can exist in RAM. _Why:_ open-file evidence can reveal active user or process activity. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **User-created content** — Data generated by the user may remain in memory. _Why:_ volatile memory can contain user activity that is not yet written to disk. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Passwords** — Password material can be present in RAM. _Why:_ memory may expose credentials useful for understanding compromise impact and attacker access. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Encryption keys** — Cryptographic keys may be stored in memory while in use. _Why:_ recovered keys can enable decryption or prove that encrypted resources were accessible. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Hardware configuration** — Hardware-related configuration details can appear in RAM. _Why:_ this can help establish system context during forensic reconstruction. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Software configuration** — Software settings and configuration data can reside in memory. _Why:_ configuration artifacts may explain system behavior or attacker changes. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Windows registry keys** — Registry key data may be available in memory. _Why:_ registry artifacts can show persistence, configuration, execution history, and system state. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Windows event logs** — Event-log data can be present in memory. _Why:_ memory may retain log-related evidence useful when on-disk logs are altered or unavailable. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Directories** — Directory-related data can be found in memory. _Why:_ directory residue can help identify filesystem locations involved in user or attacker activity. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Drivers** — Driver information can be present in RAM. _Why:_ driver artifacts are important for kernel-level malware and rootkit investigations. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Memory-mapped residue** — Data mapped into process or system memory may remain as residual evidence. _Why:_ this residue can preserve traces of previous activity beyond currently visible files and processes. _[GCFA p.409]_

### Memory Analysis Evolution

- **Older memory-analysis approach** — Earlier memory examination often relied on searching raw memory for strings and byte patterns. _Why:_ this explains why older analysis was less structured and less precise. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Unstructured memory challenge** — Raw memory can appear disordered when viewed without knowledge of internal structures. _Why:_ analysts need structure-aware methods to interpret volatile data reliably. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Improved memory-structure knowledge** — Modern analysts have better understanding of memory-resident data structures. _Why:_ this enables more targeted and meaningful extraction from memory images. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Modern memory-forensics tooling** — Newer tools support detailed examination of memory contents. _Why:_ tooling allows analysts to move beyond simple keyword searching into structured artifact recovery. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Granular memory examination** — Current memory forensics can inspect memory at a finer level than broad raw searches. _Why:_ granular analysis improves artifact identification and reconstruction of system state. _[GCFA p.409]_

### Investigative Uses

- **Command-history reconstruction** — Memory contents may help infer commands typed by a previous user. _Why:_ recovered command activity can reveal attacker actions or administrator response steps. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Prior-user activity reconstruction** — Memory can support reconstruction of what an earlier person did on the system. _Why:_ volatile artifacts can connect activity to interactive use. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Old email discovery** — Email content or remnants may be recoverable from memory. _Why:_ communications can provide context, phishing evidence, or data-exposure indicators. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Malicious website discovery** — Memory may contain evidence of harmful sites visited by the user. _Why:_ web artifacts can identify infection vectors or attacker infrastructure. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Exited-application residue** — Data from applications that are no longer running may remain in memory. _Why:_ this can preserve evidence after process termination. _[GCFA p.409]_
- **Clear-text password recovery** — Plaintext credentials may still be present in RAM. _Why:_ this is critical for credential exposure assessment and post-compromise containment. _[GCFA p.409]_

## Page 410

### Memory Analysis Advantages

- **RAM as a malware-discovery source** — System memory is presented as the strongest location for finding malicious code activity. _Why:_ active malware must appear in memory to run, even when it avoids disk-based detection. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Running configuration visibility** — Memory analysis can reveal the live configuration of the system being examined. _Why:_ runtime configuration helps investigators understand the actual operating state rather than relying only on static disk artifacts. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **System inconsistency detection** — Memory analysis can expose contradictions or mismatches inside the running system. _Why:_ inconsistencies may indicate tampering, stealth mechanisms, rootkits, or other malicious manipulation. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Packer bypass value** — Examining memory can bypass executable packers. _Why:_ packed malware often has to unpack or reveal executable content in RAM before it can operate. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Binary-obfuscation bypass value** — Memory can help analysts get past binary obfuscation techniques. _Why:_ runtime state may expose behavior or code/data forms that are harder to understand from the obfuscated file alone. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Rootkit bypass value** — Memory analysis can help bypass rootkits. _Why:_ rootkits may hide files, processes, or other artifacts from normal operating-system views, while memory can still contain evidence of their presence. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Kernel-mode rootkit relevance** — Kernel-level hiding tools are specifically included among the techniques memory analysis can help overcome. _Why:_ kernel-mode malware can manipulate privileged system views, making independent memory inspection especially important. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Hiding-tool bypass value** — Memory analysis can help defeat tools designed to conceal malware or activity. _Why:_ hidden components still need runtime structures or execution context that may remain observable in RAM. _[GCFA p.410]_

### Recent Activity Analysis

- **Recent activity tracking** — Memory can be used to analyze and follow recent actions on the system. _Why:_ volatile runtime evidence can preserve activity that may not yet exist, or may never exist, in durable logs or files. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Contextual activity reconstruction** — Memory analysis can identify recent actions together with their surrounding context. _Why:_ context helps distinguish benign user behavior from attacker behavior and connects related artifacts. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **User activity profiling** — RAM can support profiling of legitimate user actions. _Why:_ understanding normal or recent user behavior helps establish timelines and identify deviations. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Attacker activity profiling** — RAM can support profiling of adversary behavior. _Why:_ attacker tools, commands, handles, sessions, and process relationships may be visible during or shortly after execution. _[GCFA p.410]_

### Memory-Only Evidence

- **Unique evidence source** — Memory can contain evidence unavailable from any other location. _Why:_ some artifacts are volatile by design and disappear when power is lost or memory is overwritten. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Memory-resident malware** — Malware may exist only in memory. _Why:_ malware that never writes to disk can evade disk imaging and file-based scanning. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Chat thread recovery** — Chat conversations may be recoverable from memory. _Why:_ many chat applications do not save conversation logs to disk by default. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Internet activity recovery** — Internet-use artifacts may exist in memory. _Why:_ browsing activity, especially privacy-mode activity, may leave volatile traces even when disk artifacts are reduced. _[GCFA p.410]_

### Malware Runtime Behavior

- **Malware hiding-versus-execution tradeoff** — Malware faces a conflict between remaining concealed and executing successfully. _Why:_ code that runs must interact with memory and system resources, creating opportunities for detection. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Execution requirement** — Malware must execute to achieve its purpose. _Why:_ execution creates live artifacts such as process state, threads, loaded modules, handles, and runtime data. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Hiding limitation** — Malware may be able to hide well or execute well, but doing both at the same time is described as extremely difficult. _Why:_ this makes RAM a high-value source for defeating stealth. _[GCFA p.410]_

### RAM as a Secondary Evidence Store

- **Increasing memory capacity** — System RAM is growing larger over time. _Why:_ larger memory can retain more runtime artifacts for forensic analysis. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Reduced practical volatility** — As RAM sizes increase, memory is characterized as behaving less like a fleeting source and more like a secondary storage area. _Why:_ more retained data improves the chance of recovering useful evidence from memory captures. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Process identification** — Memory analysis can identify running processes. _Why:_ process enumeration is central to finding malicious execution and understanding system activity. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Thread identification** — Memory analysis can identify running threads. _Why:_ threads reveal execution activity inside processes and may expose injected or suspicious execution paths. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **DLL association** — Memory analysis can associate running processes and threads with loaded DLLs. _Why:_ loaded modules can reveal malware components, injected libraries, and process behavior. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **File-handle association** — Memory analysis can associate runtime activity with file handles. _Why:_ open file handles can show which files a process is using even if other disk artifacts are incomplete. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Registry-key handle association** — Memory analysis can associate runtime activity with registry key handles. _Why:_ registry handles can expose configuration, persistence, or volatile state accessed by a process. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Behavior-first analysis** — Observing behavior in memory provides richer information than reconstructing many separate artifacts from disk. _Why:_ live runtime relationships can connect processes, modules, files, registry access, and activity in one investigative view. _[GCFA p.410]_

### Volatile Artifact Examples

- **Diskless advanced malware** — Some advanced malware attempts to avoid writing itself or its artifacts to disk. _Why:_ memory acquisition may be required to capture evidence of these threats. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Chat application default behavior** — Most chat programs are described as not saving communications to disk by default. _Why:_ investigators may need memory to recover conversation content or message context. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Privacy-aware user behavior** — Users increasingly use privacy-preserving features or habits. _Why:_ these behaviors reduce disk artifacts and increase the value of volatile evidence. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Private browsing artifacts** — Memory may contain artifacts from private browsing modes such as InPrivate sessions. _Why:_ private browsing is designed to reduce persistent local traces, so RAM may preserve otherwise unavailable evidence. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Incognito browsing artifacts** — Memory may contain artifacts from Incognito browsing sessions. _Why:_ browser privacy modes may still leave volatile traces while the system is running. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Registry volatility in memory** — The Windows registry has memory-resident behavior beyond its persistent on-disk form. _Why:_ registry evidence may exist only in volatile state during system operation. _[GCFA p.410]_
- **Volatile registry keys** — Some registry keys can be modified and exist only in memory. _Why:_ these keys may be lost after shutdown and therefore require memory capture to preserve them. _[GCFA p.410]_

### EDR Detection and Response

- **EDR expansion** — A newer generation of endpoint detection and response tools uses back-end analysis to identify suspicious activity. _Why:_ EDR combines collection and analytics rather than acting only as a static endpoint sensor. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Pattern analysis** — EDR products may use pattern analysis to evaluate endpoint activity. _Why:_ recurring behavior patterns can reveal malicious or suspicious operations. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Heuristic detection** — EDR products may use heuristic methods to detect suspicious behavior. _Why:_ heuristics can catch activity that does not match a fixed signature. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Machine learning** — EDR products may use machine-learning techniques on the back end. _Why:_ machine learning can assist with classifying suspicious behavior across large telemetry sets. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Automated blocking** — EDR analytics can enable automatic blocking of suspicious activity. _Why:_ blocking can interrupt attacker actions before a full manual investigation completes. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **EDR dual use** — EDR is characterized by usefulness for both detection and incident response. _Why:_ the same telemetry can identify threats and support post-detection investigation. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **EDR data store** — EDR platforms expose an interface into a stored collection of endpoint telemetry. _Why:_ searchable telemetry becomes a force multiplier for security operations. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Security-team force multiplier** — Access to EDR telemetry can significantly amplify a security team’s effectiveness. _Why:_ analysts can investigate many systems and past events without relying only on direct host access. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Hunting at scale** — EDR telemetry supports broad searches for malicious activity across many endpoints. _Why:_ scalable hunting helps find attacker behavior beyond a single known victim system. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Historical bad-activity searches** — EDR telemetry can be searched for previously known malicious activity. _Why:_ retrospective searching helps determine whether an indicator appeared elsewhere. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Intrusion scoping** — Historical EDR searches help define the extent of an intrusion. _Why:_ scoping determines which systems, accounts, or behaviors require response. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Remediation support** — EDR telemetry helps support remediation decisions after malicious activity is found. _Why:_ responders need evidence of affected systems and attacker actions to clean up effectively. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Indicator-driven lookback** — After an attack indicator is found, defenders can search backward in time for other occurrences. _Why:_ lookback capability helps identify related compromise activity that was not initially detected. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Reduced identification time** — Historical EDR searches can shorten the time needed to identify affected systems or activity. _Why:_ faster identification improves incident response efficiency. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Reduced containment time** — Historical EDR searches can shorten the time needed to contain an intrusion. _Why:_ quicker containment limits adversary dwell time and spread. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Adversary cost increase** — Discovering attacker tradecraft through EDR telemetry makes the operation more costly for the adversary. _Why:_ exposed methods may need to be abandoned, modified, or replaced. _[GCFA p.411]_

### Memory-Centric Attacks

- **Attacker move to memory** — Modern attackers increasingly place activity in memory to avoid disk-centered defenses. _Why:_ memory-resident execution can bypass tools focused on files and static disk artifacts. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Disk-based evasion** — Memory-focused attack techniques are used to evade security products that primarily inspect disk artifacts. _Why:_ defenders need memory visibility when malicious activity is not represented as a normal file. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Fileless malware emergence** — Fileless malware is identified as part of the shift toward memory-based attack techniques. _Why:_ fileless activity changes what evidence responders must collect and analyze. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Critical role of in-memory detection** — Memory-based detection is necessary for identifying newer attack methods. _Why:_ attacks that execute or hide in memory may not be visible through disk inspection alone. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **PowerShell memory detection** — In-memory detection is important for detecting attacks that use PowerShell. _Why:_ PowerShell activity can execute scripts and payloads without leaving conventional binaries on disk. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **WMI memory detection** — In-memory detection is important for detecting attacks that use WMI. _Why:_ WMI abuse can support stealthy execution, persistence, and lateral movement. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Code injection detection** — In-memory detection is important for identifying advanced code-injection techniques. _Why:_ injected code commonly lives inside another process’s memory space. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Obfuscation detection** — In-memory detection is important for identifying advanced obfuscation techniques. _Why:_ memory and runtime behavior can expose activity that is concealed in encoded or disguised source form. _[GCFA p.411]_

### EDR Memory Analysis Capabilities

- **Memory analysis in EDR** — EDR tools derive many advanced capabilities from analyzing memory. _Why:_ memory inspection reveals runtime evidence unavailable from static disk artifacts. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Event tracing in EDR** — EDR tools derive many advanced capabilities from tracing events. _Why:_ event sequences help reconstruct behavior over time. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Kernel-level endpoint access** — EDR tools often operate with kernel-level access on endpoints. _Why:_ high-privilege access enables deeper collection and inspection of system activity. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Memory-based analysis breadth** — Kernel-level access allows EDR tools to perform extensive memory-focused analysis. _Why:_ deeper endpoint visibility increases the chance of detecting stealthy runtime behavior. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Process information capability** — EDR tools commonly collect process information. _Why:_ process metadata is foundational for understanding what executed on a host. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Windows API usage capability** — EDR tools commonly observe Windows API usage. _Why:_ API calls can expose behavioral intent such as process manipulation, injection, or network use. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Command-line archival capability** — EDR tools commonly preserve command-line data for each process. _Why:_ saved command lines help investigators recover attacker commands and execution parameters. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Process-handle tracking capability** — EDR tools commonly track newly created process handles. _Why:_ handle activity can reveal relationships and access between processes. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Execution-tracing capability** — EDR tools commonly trace execution activity. _Why:_ execution traces help reconstruct what code ran and how activity unfolded. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Suspicious thread creation analysis** — EDR tools commonly analyze suspicious thread creation. _Why:_ unexpected thread creation can indicate code injection or malicious execution inside another process. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Suspicious memory allocation analysis** — EDR tools commonly analyze suspicious memory allocation. _Why:_ unusual allocations can indicate payload staging, unpacking, or injected code. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **DLL injection identification** — EDR tools commonly identify known DLL-injection techniques. _Why:_ DLL injection is a common way to run attacker-controlled code inside another process. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Rootkit hook identification** — EDR tools commonly identify known rootkit hooking techniques. _Why:_ hooks can hide activity or intercept system behavior for stealth and control. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **API-audit limitation** — Detection of DLL injection and rootkit hooks may be limited when a tool relies on system API calls to audit memory components. _Why:_ API-mediated inspection can miss activity hidden from or manipulated through those interfaces. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Memory-introspection distinction** — True memory introspection is presented as different from auditing memory through system API calls. _Why:_ direct memory inspection can provide deeper visibility than relying on operating-system APIs. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Host network recording** — EDR tools commonly record host-based network activity. _Why:_ host network evidence links processes and endpoints to communications. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Local DNS cache recording** — Host-based network recording may include local DNS cache data. _Why:_ cached DNS entries can reveal domains recently resolved by the endpoint. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **Socket recording** — Host-based network recording may include socket information. _Why:_ socket data can show active or recent network communication endpoints. _[GCFA p.411]_
- **ARP recording** — Host-based network recording may include ARP information. _Why:_ ARP data can help identify local network relationships and communication context. _[GCFA p.411]_

## Page 412

### EDR Versus Traditional Forensics

- **EDR scope limitation** — endpoint detection and response should be distinguished from classic enterprise forensic collection because it does not preserve every historical event from every endpoint. _Why:_ investigators must understand that EDR telemetry is selective, not complete evidence capture. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Historical event completeness** — retaining every past event from every enterprise system is described as impractical. _Why:_ this explains why EDR systems make collection tradeoffs and why gaps are expected. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Endpoint event volume** — one host can create millions of events in a single day. _Why:_ the volume explains why full endpoint telemetry is difficult to collect, store, and analyze continuously. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Sysinternals Process Monitor rate** — Microsoft Sysinternals Process Monitor can observe more than 5,000 events per second. _Why:_ this provides a concrete benchmark for how noisy raw endpoint activity can be. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **EDR collection rate example** — an EDR product may collect roughly 30 events per minute. _Why:_ the contrast with Process Monitor shows how aggressively EDR products reduce captured telemetry. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Host-impact tradeoff** — EDR products limit collected event volume partly to reduce performance impact on endpoints. _Why:_ collection limits are operational design choices, not necessarily investigative sufficiency choices. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **EDR data selection** — EDR tools choose a limited subset of endpoint data points to retain. _Why:_ analysts must treat EDR output as curated telemetry rather than a full system record. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **User control over EDR telemetry** — the user generally cannot define exactly which data points an EDR platform collects. _Why:_ investigators may be unable to recover missing event classes after the fact from EDR alone. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Traditional forensic collection goal** — conventional forensic tools are built to acquire complete disk images and memory images from systems. _Why:_ full images provide deeper evidence sources than selective EDR telemetry. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **EDR primary advantage** — EDR’s major benefit is the ability to operate at enterprise scale. _Why:_ broad deployment makes EDR useful for fleet-wide visibility and hunting. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Deep-dive forensic supplement** — EDR findings can be augmented with detailed forensic analysis when more complete reconstruction is needed. _Why:_ deeper examination can fill gaps left by selective endpoint telemetry. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Attacker activity reconstruction** — deep-dive forensics may be required to fully explain an attacker’s actions. _Why:_ EDR alerts and event records may not contain enough detail to reconstruct the complete intrusion narrative. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Root-cause investigation** — deep forensic work may be needed to determine the root cause of an incident. _Why:_ root-cause analysis often depends on artifacts outside the subset collected by EDR. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Network monitoring relationship** — EDR is a complement to network monitoring, not a substitute for it. _Why:_ endpoint telemetry and network telemetry answer different investigative questions. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **SIEM relationship** — EDR is also a complement to SIEM log collection, not a replacement. _Why:_ centralized log sources remain necessary for correlation and enterprise-wide evidence coverage. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Real-time activity visibility** — EDR is strong at detecting actions as they occur. _Why:_ this makes EDR valuable for live response, alerting, and active threat hunting. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Limited historical visibility** — EDR can identify some past activity, but its historical view is incomplete. _Why:_ analysts should avoid assuming that absence from EDR history means absence of activity. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Disk forensics depth** — disk forensics can often provide a richer account than EDR telemetry alone. _Why:_ persistent artifacts may reveal details that were never selected for EDR collection. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Memory forensics depth** — memory analysis can also provide a more detailed account than EDR telemetry alone. _Why:_ volatile artifacts may expose runtime behavior, injected code, credentials, or process state not captured by EDR. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Pre-EDR activity** — disk and memory forensics may reveal activity that occurred before EDR was installed. _Why:_ this is critical when investigating long-running compromises or deployments made after suspected intrusion. _[GCFA p.412]_

### Analyst Role

- **AI and machine-learning limitation** — marketing emphasis on artificial intelligence and machine learning does not remove the need for human analysts. _Why:_ automated tooling still requires human judgment to interpret evidence correctly. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Future analyst requirement** — human analysts are expected to remain necessary for effective use of EDR-like tools for the foreseeable future. _Why:_ complex investigations require reasoning, validation, and contextual understanding beyond automated outputs. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Attacker TTP knowledge** — analysts need to understand adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures. _Why:_ TTP knowledge helps analysts recognize malicious patterns and interpret telemetry accurately. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Use of multiple data sources** — analysts must know how to combine separate evidence sources to validate suspected malicious activity. _Why:_ corroboration reduces false positives and compensates for gaps in any one source. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Forensic skill requirement** — strong forensic analysis skills are necessary to fully benefit from endpoint and related data sources. _Why:_ forensic expertise enables analysts to move beyond alerts into evidence-based reconstruction. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Memory-analysis skill requirement** — memory forensics skills are specifically identified as important for taking full advantage of available data sources. _Why:_ memory artifacts can expose live or recently executed behavior that other logs may miss. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **Forensics and EDR complementarity** — forensic and memory-analysis skills work well alongside EDR use by analysts and threat hunters. _Why:_ EDR supplies scalable signals, while forensic methods provide depth and validation. _[GCFA p.412]_

- **FOR508 instructional goal** — the course section and the broader FOR508 material were designed to support these analyst capabilities. _Why:_ the curriculum frames EDR as one source within a larger forensic and hunting methodology. _[GCFA p.412]_

### Forensic Interpretation

- **Traditional forensic minimum finding** — conventional forensic review would likely establish that `rar.exe` executed on the system. _Why:_ execution evidence alone may be insufficient for confident incident assessment. _[GCFA p.413]_
- **Execution alone is incomplete** — simply knowing `rar.exe` ran may not answer whether an attack is underway. _Why:_ benign and malicious archive use can look similar without context. _[GCFA p.413]_
- **Command-line capture value** — captured command lines provide more investigative value than bare process-execution evidence. _Why:_ arguments reveal targets, options, archive names, and intent. _[GCFA p.413]_
- **Command-line context indicates unusual activity** — the shown command lines help an analyst recognize the behavior as unusual. _Why:_ document collection into passworded archives is stronger evidence than `rar.exe` execution by itself. _[GCFA p.413]_
- **Process tree value** — the process tree provides additional information for deciding whether activity is malicious. _Why:_ parent-child relationships expose abnormal execution paths. _[GCFA p.413]_
- **PowerShell-to-RAR interpretation** — PowerShell spawning `rar.exe` is noteworthy but not automatically proof of malicious activity. _Why:_ analysts should distinguish suspicious context from definitive conclusions. _[GCFA p.413]_
- **Service-originated PowerShell concern** — PowerShell reached through `services.exe` → `wrsa.exe` → `cmd.exe` is abnormal in the page’s assessment. _Why:_ unusual process ancestry makes the activity more suspicious. _[GCFA p.413]_
- **Memory-forensics relevance** — process-tree analysis is described as a critical component of memory forensics. _Why:_ memory analysis often reconstructs process relationships and runtime context. _[GCFA p.413]_
- **Experience effect** — analysts with more memory-forensics experience can use the EDR process tree more effectively. _Why:_ interpreting parentage and anomalies requires practiced forensic judgment. _[GCFA p.413]_
- **Traditional reconstruction burden** — conventional forensic methods could probably reconstruct much of the same story but would take significantly longer. _Why:_ EDR can accelerate triage by pre-correlating evidence. _[GCFA p.413]_
- **EDR correlation advantage** — EDR combines multiple data sources into one investigative view. _Why:_ unified context enables faster recognition of malicious behavior. _[GCFA p.413]_
- **Faster malicious-activity identification** — the page states that EDR enables quicker detection of malicious activity through consolidated visibility. _Why:_ speed matters during active incident response. _[GCFA p.413]_
- **Need for foundational knowledge** — analysts still need core forensic knowledge to use EDR tools effectively. _Why:_ tools surface evidence, but analysts must judge normal versus abnormal behavior. _[GCFA p.413]_
- **Normal-versus-abnormal judgment** — the page emphasizes analyst judgment when deciding whether behavior is expected or suspicious. _Why:_ EDR output requires interpretation rather than blind acceptance. _[GCFA p.413]_
- **Course learning objective** — the course aims to provide the foundational knowledge needed for effective EDR-supported investigations. _Why:_ the slide connects forensic fundamentals to modern endpoint detection workflows. _[GCFA p.413]_

## Page 416

### Volatile Memory Copies

- **Live acquisition dependency** — The memory acquisition tools discussed earlier require the target operating system to still be running. _Why:_ this limits collection options after shutdown or power-state changes. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **RAM volatility** — System memory is treated as volatile because its contents are normally lost when the machine powers off. _Why:_ responders must prioritize memory sources before they disappear or are overwritten. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Automatic RAM-derived artifacts** — Some operating systems automatically create disk-based files that contain memory-derived data. _Why:_ these files can preserve evidence even when live RAM is no longer available. _[GCFA p.~416]_

### Windows Hibernation Artifact

- **Windows hibernation support** — Many Windows systems, especially laptops, include a hibernation feature. _Why:_ hibernation can create a recoverable memory artifact without a forensic tool being run. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **`hiberfil.sys` creation trigger** — Windows creates `hiberfil.sys` when the system moves from sleep into a low-power hibernation state. _Why:_ the timing of this file reflects a power-state transition that may preserve memory from that moment. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **`hiberfil.sys` memory contents** — `hiberfil.sys` stores a copy of RAM from the time the power event occurred. _Why:_ it can contain process, network, credential, malware, or user-activity evidence present at hibernation. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **`hiberfil.sys` location** — The hibernation file can be collected from the root of the Windows system drive. _Why:_ knowing the expected location allows responders to preserve it during disk or triage collection. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **`hiberfil.sys` forensic use** — Copying `hiberfil.sys` can provide a preexisting memory image for later analysis. _Why:_ it may substitute for a live RAM acquisition when the original system state is no longer running. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **`hiberfil.sys` compression** — The hibernation file is compressed and requires processing before ordinary memory-analysis workflows can use it. _Why:_ analysts should not expect it to behave exactly like a raw memory dump. _[GCFA p.~416]_

### Windows Crash Dumps

- **Kernel-mode dump files** — Kernel-mode dumps are also referred to as crash dump files. _Why:_ both terms may appear in Windows settings, documentation, and forensic notes. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Crash dump forensic value** — Kernel-mode crash dumps can be useful sources for RAM analysis. _Why:_ crashes may preserve memory state from the time of failure. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **`MEMORY.DMP` filename** — Windows crash dumps may be stored as `MEMORY.DMP`. _Why:_ this is a key filename to search for during forensic collection. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **`MEMORY.DMP` folder** — `MEMORY.DMP` should be sought in `%SystemRoot%`. _Why:_ this environment-based path identifies the standard Windows crash dump location. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Typical `%SystemRoot%` value** — `%SystemRoot%` is commonly `C:\Windows`. _Why:_ this gives the practical default path for locating crash dump files. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Multiple dump categories** — Windows supports more than one kind of dump file. _Why:_ analysts must distinguish complete dumps from smaller or less useful dump types. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Complete memory dump size clue** — A complete memory dump is usually recognizable by its large size. _Why:_ file size can quickly indicate whether a dump may contain broad RAM coverage. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Complete memory dump contents** — A complete memory dump contains a large portion of RAM that existed when the crash occurred. _Why:_ this type of dump may support deeper memory forensics than limited crash dumps. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Complete memory dump rarity** — Complete memory dumps are uncommon in default real-world collections. _Why:_ responders should not assume this artifact will exist unless systems were configured for it. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Crash dump configuration option** — Windows systems can be configured to create complete memory dumps by default after crashes. _Why:_ proactive configuration can improve post-crash forensic evidence availability. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Crash dump registry key** — `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\CrashControl\` stores crash dump configuration information. _Why:_ this key helps determine dump behavior and expected artifact locations. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Crash dump path setting source** — `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\CrashControl\` contains information about dump file paths. _Why:_ analysts can use it to locate crash dump output. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Crash dump count setting source** — `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\CrashControl\` contains information about dump counts. _Why:_ this can explain retention behavior or the number of crash dumps expected. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **`CrashDumpEnabled` value** — The `CrashDumpEnabled` registry value indicates the default dump type. _Why:_ this value shows whether the system was set to create complete, partial, or other dump formats. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Microsoft kernel dump documentation** — Microsoft documentation covers varieties of kernel-mode dump files at `https://for508.com/b4d1f`. _Why:_ this is a cited reference for interpreting Windows dump types. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Microsoft memory dump options documentation** — Microsoft documentation covers Windows memory dump file options at `https://for508.com/9qc3l`. _Why:_ this supports validation of Windows dump configuration and behavior. _[GCFA p.~416]_

### Page And Swap Files

- **`pagefile.sys` memory scope** — `pagefile.sys` is not a full RAM image. _Why:_ analysts should treat it as a partial memory artifact rather than a complete acquisition. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **`swapfile.sys` memory scope** — `swapfile.sys` is not a full RAM image. _Why:_ it can supplement memory analysis but cannot replace a complete dump. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Paged-out memory evidence** — `pagefile.sys` and `swapfile.sys` can contain memory pages that Windows moved from RAM to disk. _Why:_ these files may preserve evidence no longer present in live physical memory. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **`swapfile.sys` introduction** — `swapfile.sys` first appeared with Windows 8 and Windows Server 2012. _Why:_ its presence or absence depends on operating system generation. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **`swapfile.sys` Modern application role** — `swapfile.sys` stores working-set memory for suspended Modern applications swapped to disk. _Why:_ it may contain application-state evidence from suspended Windows apps. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Microsoft swap file reference** — The cited reference for the Windows 8 and Windows Server 2012 swap file is `http://for508.com/mnzdt`. _Why:_ it provides supporting background on why `swapfile.sys` exists. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Page file relocation** — The Windows page file can be placed on different volumes or paths. _Why:_ responders must not assume `pagefile.sys` exists only at the default system-drive location. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **MemProcFS support** — Tools such as MemProcFS now support analysis involving page and swap files. _Why:_ broader tooling support increases the forensic value of collecting these files with memory. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Collection best practice** — `pagefile.sys` and `swapfile.sys` should be captured when memory is collected. _Why:_ they can provide additional memory-resident evidence that a RAM dump alone may miss. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Page file registry key** — Page file information is stored under `SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management`. _Why:_ this key can identify page file configuration and assist collection planning. _[GCFA p.~416]_

### Windows Server Collection

- **Server memory acquisition process** — Memory dumps from Windows Server systems use the same general process as Windows workstation memory dumps. _Why:_ existing collection procedures usually transfer to server-class Windows systems. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Virtualized server applicability** — The same server memory collection process applies to virtual machine and cloud-hosted Windows Server instances. _Why:_ responders can use familiar techniques in hosted and virtual environments. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Modern server driver requirement** — Modern Windows server products commonly require loaded drivers to be digitally signed. _Why:_ unsigned acquisition drivers may fail to load during collection. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **WHQL signing requirement** — Driver signing on modern Windows servers commonly depends on the Windows Hardware Quality Labs certification process. _Why:_ WHQL requirements can determine whether a memory acquisition tool works on the target. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **WHQL rigor** — WHQL is described as a stricter review and testing process than earlier driver oversight models. _Why:_ tool vendors may need additional validation before their drivers are accepted by Windows. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **WHQL expansion to clients** — WHQL-style driver requirements are also being extended to some Windows 10 and Windows 11 versions. _Why:_ driver-signing barriers are not limited to server operating systems. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Security benefit of signing** — Stronger driver-signing requirements improve security and system stability. _Why:_ they reduce risk from untrusted or unstable kernel drivers. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Collection-tool obstacle** — Driver-signing requirements can block memory tools whose drivers have not been submitted for WHQL release. _Why:_ a tool that works in one environment may fail during a live incident. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Pre-incident tool testing** — Memory acquisition tools should be tested on a similar Windows version before operational use. _Why:_ compatibility failures should be discovered before evidence collection depends on the tool. _[GCFA p.~416]_

### Virtual Machine Memory Collection

- **VM memory acquisition parity** — Virtual machine memory dumps can be collected with the same tools used for ordinary Windows memory acquisition. _Why:_ in-guest collection remains a viable method for virtual systems. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **In-guest VM collection method** — One straightforward VM approach is to run the chosen acquisition tool inside the guest operating system. _Why:_ this captures memory from the VM using normal endpoint procedures. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Mapped share output method** — A VM memory dump can be written from the guest to a mapped network share. _Why:_ this avoids storing the dump only inside the target VM’s local disk. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Hypervisor memory artifacts** — Some virtualization platforms maintain VM memory representations as files on disk. _Why:_ memory evidence may be obtainable from the hypervisor without running a tool inside the guest. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **VMware `.vmem` files** — VMware `.vmem` files are used to store virtual machine memory data. _Why:_ these files are important acquisition targets during VMware investigations. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **VMware `.vmss` files** — VMware `.vmss` files represent VMware saved state data and can store memory. _Why:_ saved-state files may contain memory from the point when the VM was suspended or saved. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **VMware `.vmsn` files** — VMware `.vmsn` files represent VMware snapshot data and can store memory. _Why:_ snapshot files may preserve memory from the snapshot time. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **VMware memory-file format caveat** — VMware memory-related files are not raw memory dumps. _Why:_ analysis tools must understand their container or address-space format. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **VMware full-memory potential** — VMware memory-related files can often contain a complete memory image. _Why:_ they may provide evidence comparable in scope to a full RAM acquisition. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Snapshot-specific memory files** — Each virtual machine snapshot commonly maintains its own associated memory files. _Why:_ multiple snapshots may preserve different historical memory states. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Volatility VMware support** — The Volatility project includes an address space capable of analyzing VMware memory-related files. _Why:_ analysts can process `.vmem`, `.vmss`, or `.vmsn`-style artifacts using supported memory-forensics tooling. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **VMware snapshot reference** — The cited VMware snapshot file reference is `http://for508.com/p5ae2`. _Why:_ it supports interpretation of VMware snapshot-related memory artifacts. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Suspend-and-copy VM collection** — A common collection method is to suspend the VM and copy the relevant memory files from the hypervisor. _Why:_ suspension can stabilize VM memory artifacts for acquisition. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **Snapshot-and-copy VM collection** — Another common method is to snapshot the VM and copy the memory files from the hypervisor. _Why:_ snapshots can preserve a point-in-time memory state for later analysis. _[GCFA p.~416]_
- **VM memory process validation** — Teams should test whether they can collect and analyze VM memory files before an actual incident. _Why:_ collection paths and tooling compatibility should be proven before time-sensitive response work. _[GCFA p.~416]_

## Page 417

### Hibernation File Nature

- **`hiberfil.sys`** — Windows stores hibernation data in a file named `hiberfil.sys`. _Why:_ this filename is the primary artifact to locate when looking for hibernation-derived memory evidence. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **System-drive root location** — `hiberfil.sys` resides at the root of the Windows system volume, commonly `C:\`. _Why:_ examiners should know the expected location when triaging a disk image or live system. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Hibernation memory capture** — the hibernation file contains a compressed representation of RAM from the moment the system entered hibernation. _Why:_ it can function as a historical memory image when live RAM is unavailable. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Creation trigger** — Windows creates a hibernation file when the machine is placed into hibernation or a power-saving state. _Why:_ user or power-management behavior can create memory artifacts without a forensic acquisition step. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Laptop lid behavior** — on laptops, closing the lid while the computer is still running commonly causes hibernation or a similar power-saving transition. _Why:_ ordinary user behavior may preserve memory evidence in `hiberfil.sys`. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Modern sleep/hibernate ambiguity** — recent Windows versions make the boundary between sleep and hibernation less clear. _Why:_ an examiner should not assume absence or presence of hibernation solely from the user’s description of “sleep.” _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Windows 10 and 11 prevalence** — power-management defaults and behavior in Windows 10 and Windows 11 make hibernation files more likely to be encountered. _Why:_ `hiberfil.sys` should be treated as a routine artifact in modern Windows examinations. _[GCFA p.~417]_

### Forensic Value

- **Routine existence check** — examiners should regularly check whether `hiberfil.sys` exists during Windows investigations. _Why:_ it may contain memory evidence missed by disk-only review. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Shutdown-system memory source** — even if responders arrive after a system has been powered down, the hibernation file may still provide access to prior RAM contents. _Why:_ it can preserve volatile evidence after live acquisition is no longer possible. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Additional memory timeline** — if the system is still running, investigators may have both current live RAM and older hibernation-derived memory to examine. _Why:_ comparing two memory points can reveal activity that existed earlier but is gone from current RAM. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Long-lived prior state** — the memory image derived from hibernation may date back days, weeks, or months. _Why:_ the artifact can extend memory analysis backward beyond the current boot state. _[GCFA p.~417]_

### Compression And Format Handling

- **Compressed format** — hibernation files use compression rather than storing a simple raw RAM dump. _Why:_ most memory tools need conversion or native support before analysis is practical. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Windows-version variation** — the hibernation file format has changed across Windows releases. _Why:_ tool compatibility depends on the Windows version that produced the file. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Decompression requirement** — a tool is needed to decompress a hibernation file before treating it as an alternative RAM dump. _Why:_ direct raw-memory workflows may fail until the file is converted. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **On-the-fly decompression** — some forensic tools decompress `hiberfil.sys` during analysis rather than requiring a separate conversion step. _Why:_ native support can simplify workflow and reduce preprocessing. _[GCFA p.~417]_

### Conversion Tools

- **Volatility 2 `imagecopy`** — Volatility 2 includes the `imagecopy` plugin for converting hibernation files. _Why:_ this is a named conversion capability analysts may encounter in legacy workflows. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Volatility address-space support** — Volatility has historically included address-space handling for reading Windows hibernation files. _Why:_ it allows the framework to interpret hibernation-backed memory sources. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Magnet Forensics `hibr2bin.exe`** — `hibr2bin.exe` is identified as a tool able to convert hibernation files into a raw form. _Why:_ it is a specific utility name relevant to hibernation-to-memory conversion. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Matthew Suiche memory suite** — Matthew Suiche created a respected memory-analysis suite that included `hibr2bin` for hibernation conversion. _Why:_ attribution helps identify the tool lineage and likely documentation/source references. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **`hibr2bin` source availability** — the source code for `hibr2bin` is available on GitHub. _Why:_ source availability can support validation, research, or historical tool recovery. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Legacy-tool maintenance concern** — Volatility 2-era conversion support and `hibr2bin` have not received updates for a long time. _Why:_ stale tools may fail against newer hibernation formats. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Windows 10/11 compatibility risk** — older hibernation conversion tools are likely to encounter problems with files produced by Windows 10 and Windows 11. _Why:_ investigators should validate tool output before relying on it. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Arsenal Hibernation Recon** — Arsenal Hibernation Recon is identified as a current tool focused specifically on hibernation-file analysis. _Why:_ it is presented as a notable modern option for this artifact class. _[GCFA p.~417]_

- **Hibernation Recon slack extraction** — Arsenal Hibernation Recon can extract residual slack space from hibernation files for analysis. _Why:_ slack may preserve data not present in the current logical hibernation content. _[GCFA p.~417]_

### Slack Space Evidence

- **Hibernation-file slack** — leftover slack can exist inside hibernation-file storage. _Why:_ slack can contain recoverable remnants beyond the main decompressed memory image. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Differently sized hibernation files** — varying hibernation-file sizes over time can create residual slack space. _Why:_ size changes may leave prior data behind for forensic recovery. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Recoverable slack data volume** — Arsenal Recon has shown that meaningful amounts of data may be recoverable from hibernation-file slack. _Why:_ investigators should not limit analysis to only the active decompressed memory stream. _[GCFA p.~417]_

- **Passware native analysis** — Passware is listed as a tool with native hibernation-file analysis capability. _Why:_ password-recovery and forensic workflows may use memory-derived material from `hiberfil.sys`. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **MemProcFS native analysis** — MemProcFS is listed as a tool that can analyze hibernation files natively. _Why:_ it may expose hibernation-derived memory through its filesystem-style analysis model. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Belkasoft Evidence Center native analysis** — Belkasoft Evidence Center is named as a forensic tool with native hibernation-file analysis capability. _Why:_ it is another suite that may decompress and process `hiberfil.sys` internally. _[GCFA p.~417]_

### Native Analysis Behaviors

- **String searching** — native hibernation-analysis tools commonly perform string searches after or during decompression. _Why:_ strings can reveal commands, URLs, credentials, process remnants, or other memory-resident indicators. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Data carving** — native hibernation-analysis tools commonly carve data from decompressed hibernation content. _Why:_ carving can recover files or structured artifacts embedded in memory. _[GCFA p.~417]_
- **Direct `hiberfil.sys` processing** — several forensic tools can process `hiberfil.sys` without requiring the examiner to manually create a raw image first. _Why:_ this affects workflow design, validation steps, and tool selection. _[GCFA p.~417]_
