### Windows Hibernation File Format

- **Windows 8 hibernation format change** — Windows 8 introduced a different hibernation file structure than earlier Windows releases. _Why:_ older parsing assumptions may not apply to Windows 8 and later hibernation evidence. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Windows 10 hibernation format inheritance** — Windows 10 uses the newer hibernation file format introduced with Windows 8. _Why:_ Windows 10 hibernation files may require newer tooling and may not convert like Windows 7 files. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Windows 11 hibernation format inheritance** — Windows 11 also uses the newer hibernation file format introduced with Windows 8. _Why:_ analysts should treat Windows 11 hibernation files as modern-format artifacts rather than legacy raw-convertible files. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Resume-from-hibernation behavior** — Research indicates that Windows 8+ systems may read portions of the hibernation file during resume and then overwrite some of that no-longer-needed data with zeros. _Why:_ the file may be altered after resume, reducing evidentiary completeness. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Live Windows 8+ hibernation collection limitation** — Acquiring `hiberfil.sys` from a running Windows 8 or later system may not produce a complete memory image. _Why:_ investigators cannot assume the live hibernation file still contains all suspended RAM contents. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Legacy hibernation completeness difference** — Earlier Windows versions were more likely to yield a full memory image from the hibernation file than Windows 8+ systems collected live. _Why:_ acquisition expectations must differ between older and modern Windows versions. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Hibernation Recon conversion risk** — Hibernation Recon may produce errors when converting modern Windows hibernation files. _Why:_ conversion failures can reflect file format or post-resume zeroing behavior rather than examiner error alone. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **MemProcFS parsing risk** — MemProcFS may report errors while parsing some Windows 8+ hibernation files. _Why:_ parser failures are a known issue for some modern hibernation artifacts and should be documented during analysis. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Arsenal Recon observation** — Arsenal Recon researchers observed that the post-resume zeroing behavior does not occur uniformly on every system. _Why:_ analysts should test and validate each artifact instead of assuming all Windows 8+ hibernation files are equally incomplete. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Storage-media influence** — Some observed differences in hibernation file behavior appear related to whether the system uses an SSD or a traditional hard drive. _Why:_ hardware context may help explain why two similar Windows systems preserve different hibernation evidence. _[GCFA p.~418]_

### Modern Windows Power Management

- **Modern power management changes** — Microsoft has made major changes to power management and power states in recent Windows versions. _Why:_ shutdown and sleep behavior can alter which forensic artifacts remain available. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Power-state visibility** — These power-management changes are mostly hidden from normal users. _Why:_ user testimony about “turning off” a system may not accurately describe the technical power state reached. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Artifact impact of power states** — Modern Windows power states can change what artifacts remain after a system is powered down. _Why:_ shutdown method and power state are part of evidence-preservation context. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Always-on Windows model** — Modern Windows is moving toward a persistent, responsive power model similar to mobile devices. _Why:_ systems may maintain or generate memory-related artifacts in scenarios where older desktops would not. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Modern Standby effect** — `Modern Standby` can influence whether a hibernation file is produced. _Why:_ this state may determine whether `hiberfil.sys` exists or contains useful evidence. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Hybrid Sleep effect** — `Hybrid Sleep` can influence creation of a hibernation file. _Why:_ systems using hybrid sleep may preserve disk-backed memory contents even when the user perceives the machine as asleep. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Fast Startup effect** — `Fast Startup` can affect whether Windows creates or uses a hibernation file. _Why:_ shutdown-like user actions may still involve hibernation artifacts. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Expanded hibernation-file prevalence** — Modern Windows power behavior is expected to increase the number of systems with hibernation files. _Why:_ investigators should check for `hiberfil.sys` more broadly than in older workflows. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **Desktop hibernation-file likelihood** — Desktops, which historically were less associated with hibernation files, may now contain them because of newer power features. _Why:_ examiners should not limit hibernation-file searches to laptops. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **`powercfg.exe` purpose** — The built-in Windows utility `powercfg.exe` can enumerate configured power-management schemes. _Why:_ it helps document how a system is configured to sleep, hibernate, or resume. _[GCFA p.~418]_
- **`powercfg.exe` device settings** — `powercfg.exe` can identify current device power settings. _Why:_ device-level configuration may explain whether hibernation artifacts should exist. _[GCFA p.~418]_

## Page 420

### Memory Analysis Definition

- **Memory analysis** — examination of data captured from a target system’s memory. _Why:_ defines the evidence source and scope of this analysis discipline. _[GCFA p.~420]_
- **Memory forensics** — another name for memory analysis. _Why:_ establishes that both terms refer to the same investigative practice. _[GCFA p.~420]_
- **Memory analysis data scope** — memory forensics works on information from system memory. _Why:_ frames memory as an evidentiary source distinct from disk media. _[GCFA p.~420]_
- **RAM as memory evidence** — physical memory from RAM is part of the ideal evidence set for memory analysis. _Why:_ RAM contains live system state that may not exist on disk. _[GCFA p.~420]_
- **Virtual memory storage as memory evidence** — page file or swap file data should be included when available. _Why:_ paged-out memory can preserve artifacts absent from captured RAM. _[GCFA p.~420]_
- **Ideal memory analysis input** — a complete analysis includes both physical RAM data and page file or swap file data. _Why:_ combining volatile and virtual-memory-backed artifacts improves recovery coverage. _[GCFA p.~420]_

### Acquisition Inputs

- **Parse Memory Structures · Process step 2** — After context is established, analysis proceeds by interpreting Windows memory structures. _Why:_ parsed structures expose processes, loaded modules, memory regions, and other forensic artifacts. _[GCFA p.421]_

- **PEB-loaded DLLs · Parsed artifact** — DLLs loaded by a process are specifically called out under PEB parsing. _Why:_ loaded libraries can reveal injected code, malicious dependencies, or suspicious runtime behavior. _[GCFA p.421]_

- **Process memory sections · Parsed artifact** — Analysts should parse the list of memory sections associated with a process. _Why:_ section mappings help connect process memory to files, DLLs, shared mappings, or anonymous memory. _[GCFA p.421]_

- **Unlinked threads · Outlier target** — Threads removed from expected structures are listed as outliers. _Why:_ hidden threads may execute malicious code while evading ordinary enumeration. _[GCFA p.421]_
- **Executable unmapped pages · Outlier target** — Memory pages that are not mapped but have execute permissions are listed as suspicious outliers. _Why:_ executable anonymous or unmapped memory can indicate injected shellcode or unpacked malware. _[GCFA p.421]_

### Virtual Address Descriptors

- **VAD tree** — Windows maintains a Virtual Address Descriptor tree for a process to track each memory region assigned to that process. _Why:_ memory analysts use this structure to understand a process’s actual mapped memory. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Memory section terminology** — The page treats a memory section and a memory page as equivalent terms in this context. _Why:_ recognizing the terminology prevents missing relevant process-memory references during analysis. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Process-specific VAD coverage** — The VAD tree records memory areas allocated to a particular process, not merely system-wide memory in general. _Why:_ per-process memory mapping is central to detecting hidden or injected process content. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **VAD tree as validation source** — Memory analysis tools use the VAD tree to compare process memory regions against what other memory lists report. _Why:_ cross-checking separate structures helps detect inconsistencies that a single list-based view might hide. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **VAD discrepancy significance** — A mismatch between VAD-tracked memory and list-reported memory can indicate suspicious activity. _Why:_ attackers may manipulate memory bookkeeping to conceal malicious changes. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **VAD discrepancy and code injection** — Code injection is one possible explanation when process memory regions do not align with expected memory lists. _Why:_ injected code often creates abnormal process-memory state that forensic tools can surface. _[GCFA p.422]_

### Kernel Modules

- **Kernel modules** — Kernel modules are code components that add functionality to the operating system. _Why:_ kernel-level code has privileged influence over system behavior and is important in memory investigations. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Device drivers as kernel modules** — Device drivers are identified as a common type of kernel module. _Why:_ analysts must distinguish ordinary driver presence from malicious kernel-resident code. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Driver function** — Device drivers expand the system’s ability to interact with hardware. _Why:_ legitimate hardware-support code can share the same broad category as malware-used kernel modules. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Kernel module location in memory** — Memory analysis tools must determine where kernel modules reside in memory. _Why:_ module location is necessary for inspection, validation, and detection of suspicious kernel activity. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Malware use of kernel modules** — Malware often abuses kernel modules to influence or control parts of the running system. _Why:_ kernel-resident malware can operate with high privilege and affect what investigators observe. _[GCFA p.422]_

### Outlier Detection

- **Component identification phase** — After a memory tool identifies the major memory-resident components, analysis shifts toward finding abnormal items. _Why:_ baseline enumeration is only the starting point; suspicious deviations must then be reviewed. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Windows memory structure complexity** — Windows memory structures are described as complex. _Why:_ analysts need tooling and careful interpretation because relevant state is distributed across intricate structures. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Windows memory structure evasion** — Despite their complexity, Windows memory structures can be bypassed or manipulated relatively easily. _Why:_ attackers can hide activity by changing bookkeeping structures rather than stopping the activity itself. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Process unlinking** — A running process can be hidden by removing it from the linked list that normally tracks processes. _Why:_ standard tools that depend on that list may fail to show the process. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Network socket unlinking** — A network socket can be concealed by unlinking it from its expected memory list. _Why:_ standard incident response views may miss active network communication if they trust only the list. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Hidden-but-running process behavior** — An unlinked process may disappear from ordinary incident response tools while continuing to execute. _Why:_ absence from normal tool output does not prove the process is gone. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Hidden-but-available socket behavior** — An unlinked network socket may remain available even though list-based tools no longer display it. _Why:_ network activity can persist behind a manipulated memory view. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Linked-list limitation** — Advanced memory tools should not depend only on linked lists to enumerate objects. _Why:_ list tampering is a common concealment technique. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Memory scanning for object types** — Advanced memory analysis suites scan memory directly for objects of a given type. _Why:_ pool or signature-style scanning can reveal artifacts that were removed from normal lists. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Outlier presentation** — Memory analysis tools attempt to identify abnormal memory artifacts and present them to the analyst. _Why:_ tooling narrows the review space, but human interpretation remains necessary. _[GCFA p.422]_

### Hooking

- **Hooking concept** — Hooking redirects execution or references away from the originally intended memory location to another location. _Why:_ redirection can be either legitimate system behavior or a malware control technique. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Hooking as kernel activity** — Hooking is described as a standard kernel-related activity. _Why:_ analysts must evaluate hooks in context rather than treating every hook as malicious. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Legitimate hooks** — Windows commonly contains legitimate hooks created by devices or antivirus software. _Why:_ normal security and hardware software can create noisy hook findings. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Malicious hooks obscured by legitimate hooks** — Normal hooks from devices and antivirus products can make malicious hooks harder to identify. _Why:_ attackers may blend into an environment where redirection mechanisms already exist. _[GCFA p.422]_

- **Hook outlier detection** — Memory tools attempt to find unusual hooks and present them for analyst review. _Why:_ suspicious redirection can reveal rootkits, malware control paths, or other stealth mechanisms. _[GCFA p.422]_

### Analyst Role

- **Volatility interface model** — Volatility is operated from the command line rather than through a graphical interface. _Why:_ memory-analysis workflows depend on precise CLI syntax and plugin arguments. _[GCFA p.~426]_

- **Volatility 3 executable** — The command used to launch Volatility 3 is `vol.py`. _Why:_ using the correct executable selects the newer Volatility framework and its plugin conventions. _[GCFA p.~426]_

### Profile Identification And Build Numbers

- **OS build dependency** — Windows memory layouts may change between operating system builds. _Why:_ memory parsers can fail or misread structures when they assume the wrong layout. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Volatility 2 profile requirement** — Volatility 2 needs an explicit operating-system profile for analysis, such as `Win10x64_16299`. _Why:_ the profile tells Volatility 2 which memory structure definitions to apply. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Volatility 3 symbol lookup behavior** — Volatility 3 can retrieve symbol-table information online instead of relying only on fixed profiles. _Why:_ dynamic symbols reduce the need to manually choose rigid profiles for each OS build. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Collection documentation requirement** — The Windows version and build should be recorded when acquiring memory. _Why:_ analysts need this information later to select or validate the correct parsing symbols/profile. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Volatility 2 `kdbgscan` purpose** — In Volatility 2, `kdbgscan` can help determine the Windows build string from a memory image. _Why:_ the build string guides profile selection for later plugins. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Profile-guessing fallback** — Analysts may initially estimate the correct Volatility 2 profile when exact build information is unavailable. _Why:_ profile testing can still proceed when acquisition notes are incomplete. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Bad-profile indicator · `pslist`** — If `pslist` returns nonsensical process names, the chosen profile may be wrong. _Why:_ corrupted-looking process output often reflects incorrect structure parsing. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Bad-profile indicator · `psscan`** — If `psscan` cannot locate any processes, the selected profile should be reconsidered. _Why:_ failure to recover expected process objects can indicate incompatible profile metadata. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Bad-profile indicator · `filescan`** — If `filescan` finds no files, the Volatility 2 profile may not match the image. _Why:_ file-object scanning depends on correct object signatures and structure interpretation. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Bad-profile indicator · `hivelist`** — If `hivelist` finds no registry hives, the analyst should try a different profile. _Why:_ registry hive discovery can fail when memory structures are parsed with the wrong assumptions. _[GCFA p.~428]_

### Windows 10 Build Cadence

- **Windows 10 update frequency** — Windows 10 introduced a faster major-update cadence, commonly about two major updates per year. _Why:_ frequent releases increase the number of memory layouts forensic tools must support. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Forensic-tool pressure** — Rapid Windows updates create maintenance pressure for memory forensics tools. _Why:_ tools must adapt as Microsoft changes internal memory structures. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Memory-structure drift** — New Windows versions usually include at least minor differences in in-memory data structures. _Why:_ even small structure changes can affect process, file, registry, and kernel-object parsing. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Microsoft build number tracking** — The Microsoft build number is the best identifier for following Windows version changes and related memory-structure changes. _Why:_ build numbers map more precisely to internal implementation details than broad product names. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Live-system build source** — On a live Windows system, the build can be viewed through the `About Your PC` interface. _Why:_ this gives the examiner a simple way to capture version/build metadata before or during acquisition. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Acquisition metadata value** — The Windows build should be documented at the time a memory image is collected. _Why:_ this reduces uncertainty during later profile or symbol selection. _[GCFA p.~428]_

### Symbol Tables And Volatility 3

- **Volatility 3 profile flexibility** — Build/profile mismatch is less problematic in Volatility 3 because it supports symbol-table lookups. _Why:_ symbol lookup lets Volatility adapt to the target build more dynamically. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Symbol table definition** — A symbol table describes object layouts and the locations of important fields, commonly using debugging information. _Why:_ forensic tools need this metadata to interpret raw memory correctly. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Symbol tables and source-code understanding** — Symbol information helps explain how objects are defined and where meaningful data is stored. _Why:_ this bridges raw memory bytes to analyzable operating-system objects. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Volatility-imported symbols** — Symbol tables used by Volatility enable discovery and parsing of important memory structures. _Why:_ without structure definitions, raw memory cannot reliably be turned into process and kernel artifacts. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Process-object parsing** — Process objects are an example of memory structures parsed with help from Volatility symbol tables. _Why:_ process enumeration is a core memory-forensics task. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Volatility 2 explicit profiles** — Volatility 2 profiles specify which symbol table or structure definitions should be used. _Why:_ the analyst must manually supply the correct parsing context. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Volatility 2 rigidity** — Volatility 2’s explicit profiles are less adaptable than Volatility 3’s dynamic symbol resolution. _Why:_ fixed profiles can fail when the target build differs from available profile definitions. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Volatility 3 Internet dependency** — Volatility 3 often needs Internet access to retrieve symbol tables from Microsoft. _Why:_ online lookup may be required before plugins can parse some Windows images. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Microsoft symbol source** — Volatility 3 can obtain needed symbol information from Microsoft’s website. _Why:_ Microsoft symbols provide authoritative layout data for Windows internals. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Offline symbol option** — Symbol tables can be downloaded and kept locally for offline use. _Why:_ this supports air-gapped labs or investigations where Internet access is unavailable. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Volatility symbol packs** — The Volatility project distributes large downloadable symbol-table/profile packs. _Why:_ prebuilt packs help analysts begin offline or semi-offline analysis without retrieving each symbol on demand. _[GCFA p.~428]_

### Volatility 2 `kdbgscan`

- **`kdbgscan` early-use pattern** — `kdbgscan` is commonly run first when analyzing a new memory image with Volatility 2. _Why:_ later Volatility 2 plugins require a correct profile value. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **`kdbgscan` profile-identification role** — The plugin helps determine which Volatility profile should be used for the image. _Why:_ choosing the right profile is a prerequisite for reliable downstream plugin output. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Volatility 2 `--profile=` option** — The chosen profile must be passed to later Volatility 2 plugins with the `--profile=` argument. _Why:_ each plugin needs the profile to interpret memory structures correctly. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Profile as required value** — In Volatility 2, the profile is an explicit parameter value rather than an automatically inferred setting. _Why:_ omission or mismatch can cause incorrect or empty forensic results. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **KDBGHeader signature scanning** — `kdbgscan` searches memory for known `KDBGHeader` signatures associated with multiple OS profiles. _Why:_ KDBG metadata can identify the kernel debugger block and guide profile selection. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Multiple-profile comparison** — `kdbgscan` checks for KDBG-related signatures across a range of operating-system profiles. _Why:_ this helps match an unknown memory image to a likely Windows build/profile. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Candidate-structure validation** — After finding a possible KDBG-related structure, `kdbgscan` performs sanity checks on it. _Why:_ validation reduces the chance of accepting a coincidental byte pattern as a real structure. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **KDBG false-positive risk** — Signature detection for KDBG data is especially susceptible to false positives and invalid candidate structures. _Why:_ analysts should not trust a raw signature hit without corroborating checks. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Windows 8 x64 KDBG encryption** — Beginning with Windows 8 x64, the KDBG structure is encrypted. _Why:_ encrypted KDBG data complicates profile identification and memory analysis. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **KDBG encryption motivation** — KDBG encryption was introduced as a measure to hinder some exploit techniques. _Why:_ defensive changes in the OS can also affect forensic parsing workflows. _[GCFA p.~428]_
- **Modern Windows `kdbgscan` implication** — For newer Windows versions, `kdbgscan` must account for encrypted KDBG handling rather than only plain structure signatures. _Why:_ relying solely on older KDBG discovery assumptions may fail on modern images. _[GCFA p.~428]_

### KDBG Scan Performance And Profile Selection

- **KdCopyDataBlock role** — Volatility’s `kdbgscan` may use the kernel function `KdCopyDataBlock` when deriving a decryption key. _Why:_ this explains why KDBG recovery can require extra computation instead of simple structure matching. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **`kdbgscan` runtime cost** — `kdbgscan` is among the slower Volatility plugins because its analysis can involve time-consuming key derivation and validation work. _Why:_ analysts should expect long runtimes and plan triage workflow accordingly. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **Profile trial strategy** — Instead of waiting for `kdbgscan`, an analyst can test several likely profiles until plugins begin returning coherent results. _Why:_ profile guessing can be faster during initial Volatility 2 triage. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **Image creation date as profile clue** — The date when a memory image was acquired can help narrow possible Windows profiles. _Why:_ operating system build timing can guide profile selection. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **Registry as profile clue** — If registry data is available, it may provide information useful for choosing the correct memory profile. _Why:_ registry artifacts can identify OS version/build information without relying only on memory scanning. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **Volatility profile verification guidance** — The Volatility project provides guidance for checking whether a selected profile is correct. _Why:_ profile validation should be evidence-based, not purely guessed. _[GCFA p.429]_

### Plugin-Based Profile Validation

- **`pslist` validation signal** — A sensible process listing from `pslist` suggests the profile can parse active process structures correctly. _Why:_ process enumeration depends on accurate interpretation of core kernel memory structures. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **`psscan` validation signal** — A sensible process listing from `psscan` supports the conclusion that the profile is compatible with the image. _Why:_ scan-based process recovery gives another check beyond linked-list traversal. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **`filescan` validation signal** — Good `filescan` output indicates that file object structures are being interpreted properly. _Why:_ coherent file-object results help confirm that memory object layouts match the selected profile. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **`hivelist` validation signal** — Good `hivelist` output indicates that registry hive structures are being parsed correctly. _Why:_ successful hive discovery strengthens confidence in the profile match. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **Multiple good plugin outputs** — Coherent results from `pslist`, `psscan`, `filescan`, and `hivelist` together indicate that major memory structures are being parsed correctly. _Why:_ cross-plugin agreement reduces the risk of a false profile match. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **No plugin data as bad-profile indicator** — If plugins return no meaningful data, the selected profile may not match the memory image. _Why:_ absence of expected structures is a practical warning sign during profile selection. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **Garbage plugin output as bad-profile indicator** — Nonsensical plugin results may indicate that the active profile is incorrect. _Why:_ wrong structure definitions can produce misleading artifact interpretation. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **Volatility 2 profile guessing use case** — The plugin-output validation technique is especially useful when estimating a profile for Volatility 2. _Why:_ Volatility 2 relies heavily on choosing the correct profile. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **Volatility 3 symbol-table testing use case** — The same validation idea can help evaluate whether Volatility 3 is using an appropriate symbol table. _Why:_ Volatility 3 uses symbol tables rather than the Volatility 2 profile model, but structure correctness still matters. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **Volatility 3 plugin conversion requirement** — When applying this validation approach in Volatility 3, the Volatility 2 plugin names must be replaced with their Volatility 3 equivalents. _Why:_ the command namespace and plugin names differ between versions. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **Volatility 3 `pslist` equivalent** — `windows.pslist.PsList` is cited as the Volatility 3 equivalent for process-list validation. _Why:_ analysts need the correct Volatility 3 plugin path when translating Volatility 2 workflows. _[GCFA p.429]_
- **Volatility 3 `windows.info.Info` plugin** — `windows.info.Info` displays information similar to what `kdbgscan` provides. _Why:_ this gives analysts a Volatility 3-oriented way to inspect comparable system metadata. _[GCFA p.429]_

- **Fallback candidate testing** — Analysts may need to choose the best candidate and then try alternatives if that choice does not work. _Why:_ KDBG/profile selection can require iterative validation. _[GCFA p.429]_

### Injection And Rootkits

- **Code-injection pivot** — if earlier process and object review does not reveal anomalies, the analyst should search for code-injection evidence. _Why:_ injected memory may reveal malware that does not appear as a standalone suspicious process. _[GCFA p.433]_
- **Legitimate process takeover** — injected code can indicate malware has occupied a legitimate process. _Why:_ this technique lets malicious code blend into trusted process context. _[GCFA p.433]_
- **Rootkit attention** — the analyst should watch for rootkit techniques during memory review. _Why:_ rootkits may manipulate normal system views and require memory-based validation. _[GCFA p.433]_
- **Live-system rootkit difficulty** — rootkits can be hard to identify while the system is running normally. _Why:_ stealth mechanisms may hide files, processes, drivers, or other indicators from ordinary tools. _[GCFA p.433]_
- **Memory-view rootkit exposure** — rootkit activity can become obvious when examined through memory artifacts. _Why:_ memory analysis may bypass or contradict the rootkit’s live-system deception. _[GCFA p.433]_

### Extraction And Follow-On Analysis

- **Suspicious process extraction** — suspect processes should be extracted from the memory image. _Why:_ dumped processes can be analyzed outside the original memory snapshot. _[GCFA p.433]_
- **Suspicious driver extraction** — suspect drivers should be extracted from the memory image. _Why:_ malicious kernel components may require separate static or dynamic analysis. _[GCFA p.433]_
- **Suspicious memory-page extraction** — suspicious memory pages should be extracted for separate review. _Why:_ injected or unpacked code may exist only in memory pages rather than in normal files. _[GCFA p.433]_
- **External analysis path** — extracted items should be examined outside the memory image. _Why:_ external tools can provide deeper inspection than triage plugins alone. _[GCFA p.433]_
- **Reverse-engineering follow-up** — malware reverse-engineering techniques are named as a follow-on method for extracted artifacts. _Why:_ reverse engineering can reveal functionality, configuration, and behavior. _[GCFA p.433]_
- **Antivirus follow-up** — simple antivirus scanning is named as another follow-on method for extracted artifacts. _Why:_ commodity scanning can quickly identify known malware or known tool families. _[GCFA p.433]_

### Layered Checklist Logic

- **Layered methodology** — the described process intentionally uses multiple investigative layers. _Why:_ different artifact categories can compensate for misses in earlier checks. _[GCFA p.433]_
- **Missed-process possibility** — an examiner may overlook a suspicious process among the many processes in a memory image. _Why:_ large memory images contain enough objects that visual or manual review can miss anomalies. _[GCFA p.433]_
- **Missed-DLL possibility** — an examiner may overlook a suspicious DLL among the many loaded libraries in memory. _Why:_ high object volume makes exhaustive manual recognition difficult. _[GCFA p.433]_
- **Checklist discipline** — rigorously following the checklist can surface a different clue even if an earlier item is missed. _Why:_ repeatable coverage improves the chance of finding at least one reliable lead. _[GCFA p.433]_
- **Injected-page lead** — an injected memory page can become the clue that identifies the malicious process. _Why:_ memory-only code can point back to the compromised process that contains it. _[GCFA p.433]_
- **Loaded-driver lead** — a loaded driver can become the clue that identifies the malicious process or activity. _Why:_ driver artifacts may expose stealth components connected to the broader compromise. _[GCFA p.433]_

## Page 434

### EPROCESS Overview

- **Processes in memory analysis** — Processes are a primary starting point because they are core objects in system memory. _Why:_ they reveal what was executing on the captured machine. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Process evidence in malware cases** — Process structures can contain some of the most important evidence for malware investigations. _Why:_ malicious activity often appears through process metadata, relationships, memory location, handles, or address-space links. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Process-to-file analogy** — In memory forensics, processes can be considered analogous to files in file-system forensics. _Why:_ this analogy helps analysts understand allocation state and recovery potential. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Allocated process blocks** — Some process structures represent processes that are still active. _Why:_ active process objects are normally easier to enumerate through operating-system-maintained lists. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Unallocated process blocks** — Some process structures may no longer be active and may remain in memory until reused. _Why:_ terminated processes can still be recoverable before their memory is overwritten. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **EPROCESS definition** — Windows tracks process information with an Executive Process Block, commonly shortened to EPROCESS. _Why:_ EPROCESS is the main kernel object analysts inspect to recover process metadata. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **EPROCESS metadata role** — An EPROCESS block stores most of the metadata associated with a process. _Why:_ process reconstruction depends heavily on fields contained in or referenced by this structure. _[GCFA p.434]_

### EPROCESS Metadata Fields

- **Image file name** — EPROCESS can identify the executable name associated with the process. _Why:_ the process image name is a first-pass indicator of legitimate, suspicious, or masqueraded execution. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Process Identifier** — EPROCESS contains the process ID. _Why:_ the PID lets analysts correlate process activity across memory artifacts, logs, handles, and parent-child relationships. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Parent Process Identifier** — EPROCESS contains the parent process ID. _Why:_ PPID analysis helps reconstruct process lineage and detect abnormal parent-child execution patterns. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Memory offset** — EPROCESS records or is associated with a location in memory. _Why:_ offsets allow tools and analysts to revisit the exact recovered process object. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Creation time** — EPROCESS can provide the time the process started. _Why:_ start times support event sequencing and timeline correlation during incident response. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Exit time** — EPROCESS can provide the time the process ended. _Why:_ termination timestamps help distinguish active processes from exited processes and establish activity windows. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Threads** — EPROCESS references the threads assigned to the process. _Why:_ thread information can expose execution activity, injected code paths, or suspicious runtime behavior. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Handles** — EPROCESS includes handles to other operating-system objects. _Why:_ handles can show files, registry keys, events, processes, tokens, or other resources the process interacted with. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Virtual Address Descriptor tree link** — EPROCESS links to the process’s VAD tree. _Why:_ the VAD tree is critical for analyzing a process’s virtual memory layout and injected or mapped regions. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Process Environment Block link** — EPROCESS links to the Process Environment Block. _Why:_ the PEB can provide user-mode process details such as loaded modules and execution context. _[GCFA p.434]_

### Doubly Linked Process List

- **Kernel process tracking** — When multiple processes run at the same time, the Windows kernel tracks them through a doubly linked list. _Why:_ this list is a major source for enumerating active process objects. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **EPROCESS list relationship** — Each EPROCESS block participates in the process list through link fields. _Why:_ these links are the mechanism that ties process objects together for kernel enumeration. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **flink field** — The `flink` field represents the forward link in the EPROCESS list. _Why:_ forward links allow traversal from one process object to the next. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **blink field** — The `blink` field represents the backward link in the EPROCESS list. _Why:_ backward links allow reverse traversal and support linked-list consistency checks. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Linked-list importance** — Understanding the doubly linked EPROCESS list is central to process analysis. _Why:_ process-hiding and process-recovery techniques often depend on whether this list is intact or manipulated. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Active-process bias** — The kernel-maintained EPROCESS list normally contains only allocated processes that are currently running. _Why:_ relying only on this list can miss terminated or deliberately hidden processes. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Process exit behavior** — After a process exits, its EPROCESS block is eventually removed from the linked list and discarded. _Why:_ exited process evidence may be transient and must be recovered before reuse or destruction. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Rootkit unlinking** — Malware with kernel-level access can remove its own EPROCESS object from the list. _Why:_ this is a process-hiding method that can defeat simple linked-list enumeration. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Direct Kernel Object Manipulation** — DKOM is identified as a rootkit technique that can unlink a process from kernel structures. _Why:_ DKOM can make a process invisible to tools that trust only standard kernel lists. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Tooling limitation** — Memory tools cannot stop after reading only the kernel’s doubly linked EPROCESS list. _Why:_ that approach misses exited, unlinked, or otherwise hidden process objects. _[GCFA p.434]_
- **Full-memory scanning requirement** — Thorough process discovery requires scanning the whole memory image for recoverable process blocks. _Why:_ scanning can identify process objects that are absent from the active kernel list. _[GCFA p.434]_

## Page 436

### Rogue Process Triage Criteria

- **Process metadata availability** — Memory forensic tools can enumerate running processes and expose related metadata for each process. _Why:_ the data collection step is usually straightforward; the investigative value comes from interpreting anomalies. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Process anomaly analysis** — The difficult part of process review is deciding which metadata values are abnormal or suspicious. _Why:_ attackers often rely on plausible-looking processes, so judgment matters more than simply listing processes. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Six process-review dimensions** — Process review in a memory image should focus on image name, full path, parent process, command line, start time, and security identifiers. _Why:_ these fields provide complementary ways to identify rogue or masquerading processes. _[GCFA p.~436]_

### Image Name

- **Image Name · Legitimacy check** — Determine whether the executable name corresponds to a process that should legitimately exist on the examined Windows system. _Why:_ unexpected process names can be quick indicators of malware or attacker tooling. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Image Name · Spelling check** — Inspect the executable name for subtle misspellings. _Why:_ attackers may use near-lookalike names to imitate normal Windows processes. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Image Name · System-context check** — Evaluate whether the process name fits the role and purpose of the host being analyzed. _Why:_ a process that is normal on one host type may be unusual on another. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Executable name as evidence** — The process executable’s image name can itself provide useful investigative information. _Why:_ experienced responders can often recognize process names that do not belong on a normal Windows installation. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Attacker naming strategy** — Attackers may choose process names that appear ordinary so their programs blend into the process list. _Why:_ Windows systems often run many processes, making name-based camouflage effective. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Windows process complexity** — The large number and complexity of Windows processes can help attacker-created process names avoid notice. _Why:_ analysts need to know normal process baselines rather than rely on casual visual review. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Subtle misspellings** — Process names should be checked for small spelling deviations from legitimate names. _Why:_ small naming changes can impersonate trusted executables while evading a quick glance. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Legitimate name in wrong context** — A real executable name can still be suspicious if that process should not normally run on the target system. _Why:_ context determines whether a familiar name is benign or anomalous. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Firefox executable value** — The Firefox browser executable name shown on the page is `firefox.exe`. _Why:_ this is an example of a legitimate process name that still requires host-context interpretation. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Firefox on workstation** — Seeing `firefox.exe` on a workstation may be unremarkable. _Why:_ browser activity is expected on many user endpoints. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Firefox on server** — Seeing `firefox.exe` on a server should be less common and more noteworthy. _Why:_ browser execution may not fit expected server behavior and can indicate suspicious activity. _[GCFA p.~436]_

### Full Path

- **Full Path · System-executable location check** — Confirm that a process using a system executable name is running from an appropriate directory. _Why:_ malware may borrow trusted names while executing from unusual locations. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Full Path · User-directory check** — Determine whether a process is running from a user-controlled directory. _Why:_ system-looking processes launched from user locations may indicate malware staging or execution. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Full Path · Temporary-directory check** — Determine whether a process is running from a temporary directory. _Why:_ temporary paths are common locations for dropped or transient malicious binaries. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Name-location mismatch** — Malware may disguise itself with a legitimate process name while executing from an abnormal path. _Why:_ image name alone is insufficient; the full path can expose masquerading. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Explorer expected location** — `Explorer.exe` is expected to run from the Windows directory. _Why:_ an `Explorer.exe` process outside its normal location can be a masquerading indicator. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Chrome expected location** — `chrome.exe` is expected to run from the Program Files directory. _Why:_ a Chrome-named process elsewhere may be abusing a trusted browser name. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **System32 path concern for named examples** — A process named like `Explorer.exe` or `chrome.exe` running from `\Windows\System32` should draw attention. _Why:_ the path does not match the expected location stated for those examples. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Temp execution location** — Malware may execute from a Temp directory. _Why:_ this can indicate dropped payload execution rather than normal installed software behavior. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Recycle Bin execution location** — Malware may execute from the Recycle Bin. _Why:_ this is an unusual execution location and should prompt deeper analysis. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Legitimate names from unusual locations** — Familiar process names launched from rare or inappropriate paths should be investigated. _Why:_ abnormal pathing is a strong clue for rogue process identification. _[GCFA p.~436]_

### Parent Process

- **Parent Process · Expected-parent check** — Determine whether the process parent is the expected creator for that process. _Why:_ abnormal parentage can reveal suspicious launch chains. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Parent Process · Orphan-process check** — Identify processes without a current parent. _Why:_ orphaned processes may be benign in some cases but can also indicate advanced execution behavior. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Parent-child relationship value** — Knowing which process launched another helps guide investigation. _Why:_ parentage provides context about how and when a process entered execution. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Explorer as user-shell parent** — Many user applications are parented by `Explorer.exe`, the Windows user shell. _Why:_ this parentage often indicates a process launched in an interactive user session. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **System-name process under Explorer** — A process using a system-like name such as `svchost.exe` with `Explorer.exe` as parent is suspicious. _Why:_ system services normally should not appear as user-shell-launched applications. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Parent process as boot-hierarchy evidence** — Parent process data helps infer where the process fits in the system startup or execution hierarchy. _Why:_ launch ancestry can distinguish boot-time services from post-logon activity. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Explorer-parented timing inference** — A process parented by `Explorer.exe` likely began after user logon. _Why:_ this helps separate interactive user activity from early system startup activity. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Services-parented timing inference** — A process parented by `Services.exe` may have started during boot. _Why:_ boot-time service ancestry can indicate persistence through a service mechanism. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Services.exe and persistence** — `Services.exe` parentage can suggest a process was launched through service-based persistence. _Why:_ services are a common way for programs to start automatically. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **No-parent process interest** — Processes without parents can be worth closer review. _Why:_ the missing parent may reflect terminated ancestry, normal system behavior, or suspicious execution. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **smss.exe orphan behavior** — Some system processes, including `smss.exe`, are commonly seen without a parent. _Why:_ analysts must avoid treating every orphan process as malicious. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Orphan process and code injection** — Lack of a parent process can indicate advanced techniques such as code injection. _Why:_ injected or manipulated execution can disrupt normal parent-child relationships. _[GCFA p.~436]_

### Command Line

- **Command Line · Image-name consistency check** — Confirm that the executable referenced in the command line matches the process image name. _Why:_ inconsistencies can expose masquerading, renamed binaries, or suspicious launch behavior. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Command Line · Argument-sanity check** — Evaluate whether the command-line arguments are reasonable for the process. _Why:_ odd switches or parameters may reveal malicious intent even when the process name appears normal. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Process Environment Block command line** — The Process Environment Block stores the complete command line used to launch a process. _Why:_ memory analysis can recover launch context beyond the image name alone. _[GCFA p.~436]_

### Start Time

- **Start Time · Boot-alignment check** — Determine whether the process began at boot alongside other system processes. _Why:_ boot-time execution can indicate normal system startup behavior or persistence. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Start Time · Attack-time proximity check** — Identify processes that started near the known or suspected attack time. _Why:_ temporal proximity can connect a process to intrusion activity. _[GCFA p.~436]_

### Security IDs

- **Security IDs · Plausibility check** — Evaluate whether the security identifiers associated with the process make sense. _Why:_ SID context can reveal whether the process is running under an expected account. _[GCFA p.~436]_
- **Security IDs · System-process user-SID check** — Question why a process that appears to be a system process is using a user account SID. _Why:_ a mismatch between process identity and account context can indicate masquerading or suspicious execution. _[GCFA p.~436]_

### Process Executable and Arguments

- **Executable-image-name consistency check** — Process analysis can compare the executable that actually ran against the image name reported for the process. _Why:_ a mismatch can reveal masquerading or suspicious process identity manipulation. _[GCFA p.~437]_

- **Command-line argument review** — Process command-line arguments should be examined for unusual or suspicious values. _Why:_ attacker activity may be visible in abnormal launch parameters even when the process name looks benign. _[GCFA p.~437]_

### Process Start Time

- **Start time as an analysis field** — A process start timestamp is often not used enough during investigations, despite being a valuable forensic clue. _Why:_ timing can connect a process to a known intrusion window. _[GCFA p.~437]_

- **Attack-time pivoting** — When there is evidence that malicious activity occurred around a known time, analysts should inspect processes that began after that point. _Why:_ processes launched immediately after an attack indicator may represent attacker tooling or follow-on execution. _[GCFA p.~437]_

- **svchost.exe timing anomaly example** — If six `svchost.exe` processes are present and five started within seconds of one another while one started at a different time, the differently timed instance deserves scrutiny. _Why:_ the outlier may indicate masquerading, delayed execution, or abnormal service-host behavior. _[GCFA p.~437]_

- **Suspicious-process time clustering** — After identifying one suspicious process, analysts should examine other processes that started around the same time. _Why:_ related attacker processes often appear in temporal clusters. _[GCFA p.~437]_

- **Boot-time versus later execution** — A process start time can often distinguish whether the process began during system startup or was launched later. _Why:_ later launch of a process expected at boot may indicate abnormal execution. _[GCFA p.~437]_

- **Known system-process timestamp comparison** — Process start times can be compared with timestamps from expected system processes such as `smss.exe` or `winlogon.exe`. _Why:_ these baseline processes help determine whether another process aligns with normal boot behavior. _[GCFA p.~437]_

- **`smss.exe` as timing baseline** — `smss.exe` is cited as a known system process whose start time can help evaluate whether another process started during boot. _Why:_ boot-sequence comparison helps separate normal startup activity from later suspicious launches. _[GCFA p.~437]_

- **`winlogon.exe` as timing baseline** — `winlogon.exe` is cited as a known system process whose timestamp can be used as a boot-time reference. _Why:_ comparison against expected system process timing can expose processes that started outside normal startup order. _[GCFA p.~437]_

### Security Identifiers

- **Security identifier process context** — A process security identifier can indicate the account privilege level under which the process was started. _Why:_ privilege context helps determine whether execution aligns with expected account behavior. _[GCFA p.~437]_

- **User SID length cue** — User SIDs are described as being much longer than typical built-in system account SIDs. _Why:_ SID length can provide a quick visual cue that a process was launched under a user account rather than a standard system account. _[GCFA p.~437]_

- **SID-to-account attribution** — Security identifiers can be used to determine the specific account that launched a process. _Why:_ account attribution is necessary for tying process execution to a user, service, or system context. _[GCFA p.~437]_

- **Expected-account validation** — Analysts should check whether a process ran under the account expected for that process. _Why:_ a process running under an unexpected account may indicate abuse, misconfiguration, or compromise. _[GCFA p.~437]_

- **System versus LocalService mismatch example** — The page gives the example of a process started by `System` when it should have been started by `LocalService`. _Why:_ this account-context mismatch can indicate suspicious or abnormal process execution. _[GCFA p.~437]_

### Rogue Process Review Criteria

- **Image name · Legitimacy check** — determine whether the process name corresponds to a legitimate executable. _Why:_ a fake or unexpected image name can indicate masquerading. _[GCFA p.438]_
- **Image name · Spelling check** — verify that the executable name is spelled correctly. _Why:_ attackers often use near-miss process names to imitate trusted Windows binaries. _[GCFA p.438]_
- **Image name · System-context match** — assess whether the process name fits the context in which it is running. _Why:_ a process name may be suspicious if it appears in a role or context where that executable should not normally operate. _[GCFA p.438]_

### Executable Path Review Criteria

- **Full path · System executable location** — verify whether the executable is running from a path appropriate for that system binary. _Why:_ legitimate Windows processes are expected to run from standard system directories, and path anomalies can reveal impostor binaries. _[GCFA p.438]_
- **Full path · User or temporary directory execution** — check whether the process is running from a user profile path or temporary directory. _Why:_ malware and attacker tools commonly execute from writable user or temp locations instead of protected system paths. _[GCFA p.438]_

### Parent Process Review Criteria

- **Parent process · Expected lineage** — evaluate whether the parent process is normal for the child process being examined. _Why:_ abnormal parent-child relationships can expose malicious launch chains. _[GCFA p.438]_
- **Parent process · Orphan status** — identify whether the process has become orphaned. _Why:_ orphaned processes may indicate unusual execution history, terminated launchers, or activity that needs additional timeline review. _[GCFA p.438]_

### Command-Line Review Criteria

- **Command line · Executable-name consistency** — confirm that the command-line executable corresponds to the recorded image name. _Why:_ mismatches can reveal process hollowing, masquerading, renamed binaries, or misleading process metadata. _[GCFA p.438]_
- **Command line · Argument reasonableness** — evaluate whether the supplied command-line arguments are logical for that process. _Why:_ suspicious flags, scripts, encoded content, or unusual parameters can expose attacker behavior. _[GCFA p.438]_

### Start-Time Review Criteria

- **Start time · Boot-time process correlation** — determine whether the process began during system startup alongside other expected system processes. _Why:_ core Windows processes usually start near boot, so late starts may be suspicious. _[GCFA p.438]_
- **Start time · Attack-time correlation** — identify processes that started near the known or suspected time of compromise. _Why:_ start times close to attacker activity can connect a process to the intrusion timeline. _[GCFA p.438]_

### Security Identifier Review Criteria

- **Security IDs · Plausibility check** — determine whether the process security identifiers are appropriate for that process. _Why:_ SID mismatches can reveal privilege misuse, impersonation, or execution under an unexpected account. _[GCFA p.438]_
- **Security IDs · System-process user SID anomaly** — question cases where a system process is associated with a user-account SID. _Why:_ system processes normally run under expected service or system identities, so a user SID may indicate masquerading or abnormal execution context. _[GCFA p.438]_

### Volatility Plugin Model

- **Plugin-per-task workflow** — A specialized Volatility plugin is used for each item or behavior the analyst wants to inspect or test. _Why:_ this encourages targeted, repeatable memory analysis instead of one monolithic scan. _[GCFA p.439]_

### Process Enumeration Tools

- **windows.pslist** — This Volatility plugin lists active processes found through the EPROCESS doubly linked list. _Why:_ it shows the normal kernel-maintained process view, which is useful for baseline process enumeration. _[GCFA p.439]_
- **windows.pslist · artifact source** — The plugin relies on the EPROCESS doubly linked list. _Why:_ malware that unlinks a process from this list may evade this view. _[GCFA p.439]_
- **windows.psscan** — This Volatility plugin searches physical memory for EPROCESS pool allocations. _Why:_ scanning memory can identify process objects that are not visible through the standard linked list. _[GCFA p.439]_
- **windows.psscan · artifact source** — The plugin looks for EPROCESS allocations in physical memory. _Why:_ pool scanning can reveal terminated, hidden, or unlinked process remnants depending on memory state. _[GCFA p.439]_
- **windows.pstree** — This Volatility plugin displays processes in a parent-child tree format. _Why:_ parent relationships help identify abnormal process ancestry. _[GCFA p.439]_
- **windows.pstree · relationship source** — The process tree is built using the EPROCESS doubly linked list. _Why:_ its view depends on the kernel process list and may differ from raw memory scanning results. _[GCFA p.439]_
- **Memory Baseliner** — This tool compares processes and loaded DLLs against a baseline memory image. _Why:_ baseline comparison helps flag deviations from known-good process and DLL patterns. _[GCFA p.439]_
- **Memory Baseliner · process comparison** — The tool checks process listings against a baseline image. _Why:_ unexpected processes can stand out when compared to a clean or representative system state. _[GCFA p.439]_
- **Memory Baseliner · DLL comparison** — The tool also compares loaded DLLs with the baseline image. _Why:_ suspicious module loading can reveal injection, persistence, or unusual process behavior. _[GCFA p.439]_

## Page 440

### Volatility Process Listing Purpose

- **windows.pslist.PsList** — Volatility 3 uses this plugin to enumerate active Windows processes from memory. _Why:_ running-process enumeration is a standard early triage step in memory forensics. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **PsList primary method** — the plugin identifies processes by traversing the Windows `EPROCESS` linked list. _Why:_ this explains both what the plugin sees and what it may miss. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **Kernel EPROCESS list** — `windows.pslist.PsList` locates the kernel’s process list before walking it. _Why:_ the plugin depends on kernel-maintained process structures rather than filesystem or event-log artifacts. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **Doubly linked list traversal** — the process list is followed through linked-list pointers connecting `EPROCESS` entries. _Why:_ attackers can target this linkage to hide processes from list-walking tools. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **Process-structure parsing** — after discovering each process entry, the plugin extracts fields from the associated process data structures. _Why:_ the reported process metadata comes directly from memory-resident Windows structures. _[GCFA p.~440]_

### Important Parameters

- **`--pid`** — this option limits output to one or more specified process IDs. _Why:_ focused PID filtering helps investigate a known suspicious process without reviewing the full process list. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **`-r pretty`** — this renderer formats plugin output into fixed-width, readable console columns. _Why:_ readable terminal output speeds analyst review during interactive triage. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **`-r` renderer option** — Volatility 3 uses the `-r` option with many plugins to select the output format. _Why:_ analysts can adapt the same plugin output for terminal viewing or downstream processing. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **`-r csv`** — this renderer exports plugin output as comma-separated values. _Why:_ CSV output is useful for spreadsheet review or importing into other analysis workflows. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **`-r json`** — this renderer exports plugin output as JSON. _Why:_ JSON output supports structured processing by databases, scripts, and review tools. _[GCFA p.~440]_

### Reported Process Fields

- **PID** — the plugin reports each process’s Process Identifier. _Why:_ PID is the core handle for correlating process activity across memory artifacts and other evidence. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **PPID** — the plugin reports the Parent Process Identifier for each process. _Why:_ parent-child relationships help identify abnormal launch chains. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **Image File Name** — the plugin reports the process’s executable image name. _Why:_ misspelled or unexpected process names are common rogue-process indicators. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **ImageFileName** — the investigative notes identify the binary-name field as `ImageFileName`. _Why:_ knowing the exact field name helps analysts interpret Volatility output and Windows process structures. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **Offset(V)** — the plugin reports the virtual memory offset of the process’s `EPROCESS` block. _Why:_ the offset lets analysts pivot to the exact process structure in memory. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **Threads** — the plugin reports the number of threads associated with each process. _Why:_ thread counts can be compared across similar processes to identify outliers. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **Handles** — the plugin reports the number of handles opened by each process. _Why:_ unusual handle counts may help distinguish anomalous instances from normal peers. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **SessionID** — the plugin reports the session identifier associated with each process. _Why:_ session context can sometimes help separate normal service activity from interactive or anomalous execution. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **Wow64** — Volatility 3 includes a `Wow64` column showing whether a process is running 32-bit code on a 64-bit Windows system. _Why:_ 32-bit execution context can be relevant when profiling process behavior or spotting unusual binaries. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **CreateTime** — the plugin reports when each process started. _Why:_ process start times can be correlated with intrusion timelines and suspicious activity windows. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **ExitTime** — the plugin reports when a process stopped, when that value is available. _Why:_ process termination timing can help reconstruct execution history from memory. _[GCFA p.~440]_

### Investigative Use

- **Early memory triage** — identifying running processes is described as one of the first recurring steps in memory analysis. _Why:_ process context anchors many later forensic pivots. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **Anomaly review** — every process attribute reported by `pslist` can be examined for abnormal values. _Why:_ rogue-process detection depends on comparing metadata against expected Windows behavior. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **Like-process comparison** — attributes from similar processes can be compared against each other to detect outliers. _Why:_ anomalies may become visible only when one instance differs from peer processes. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **Potentially excessive fields** — some output fields, such as `SessionID` and handle count, may not be needed for most memory-analysis tasks. _Why:_ analysts should avoid over-weighting low-value fields while still preserving them for comparison when useful. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **Volatility information extraction philosophy** — Volatility attempts to report as much recoverable structure-derived information as possible. _Why:_ broad output gives investigators more pivot points, even when some fields are not routinely used. _[GCFA p.~440]_

### Limitations And Evasion

- **Rootkit unlinking risk** — a rootkit can remove a malicious process from the linked list used by `pslist`. _Why:_ list unlinking can cause `windows.pslist.PsList` to miss hidden processes. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **Linked-list dependency** — because `pslist` relies on the active `EPROCESS` list, it is vulnerable to process-hiding techniques that manipulate that list. _Why:_ analysts should pair `pslist` with other process-discovery methods when rootkit activity is suspected. _[GCFA p.~440]_

### Volatility Version Mapping

- **Volatility 3 plugin name** — the page identifies the Volatility 3 plugin as `windows.pslist.PsList`. _Why:_ exact plugin naming is required to run the correct command in Volatility 3. _[GCFA p.~440]_

- **Volatility 2 equivalent** — the equivalent Volatility 2 plugin is `pslist`. _Why:_ analysts working across Volatility versions need the corresponding plugin name. _[GCFA p.~440]_

### Rogue Process Indicators

- **Malware hiding among normal processes** — the example demonstrates malicious code blending into an ordinary-looking process list. _Why:_ attackers may rely on analyst assumptions rather than advanced concealment. _[GCFA p.442]_
- **Misspelled process name** — the suspicious process name `scvhost.exe` is visually close to `svchost.exe`. _Why:_ small spelling differences can hide malware during quick triage. _[GCFA p.442]_
- **Initial analyst miss** — the sample was initially misread as containing another `svchost.exe` instance. _Why:_ the example shows why exact string review matters. _[GCFA p.442]_
- **Unexpected parent process** — the suspicious process is parented by `explorer.exe`, while a genuine `svchost.exe` process would be expected under `services.exe` in this context. _Why:_ abnormal parentage is a strong rogue-process clue. _[GCFA p.442]_
- **Expected svchost.exe parent** — normal `svchost.exe` instances are expected to have `services.exe` as their parent in this example. _Why:_ this gives analysts a concrete baseline for detecting the anomaly. _[GCFA p.442]_
- **Suspicious start-time mismatch** — the suspicious process did not start alongside the other `svchost.exe` processes. _Why:_ late execution can reveal malware masquerading as a startup service process. _[GCFA p.442]_
- **Name similarity explanation** — the suspicious process was not actually `svchost.exe`; it only used a nearly identical filename. _Why:_ the finding changes the interpretation from normal service hosting to deceptive naming. _[GCFA p.442]_
- **Misspelled name as an indicator** — once discovered, the filename `scvhost.exe` can be searched on the affected host and across other enterprise systems. _Why:_ a concrete lookalike name can become a practical detection indicator. _[GCFA p.442]_

### Tool Limitation

- **windows.pslist.PsList plugin** — `windows.pslist.PsList` is described as the most basic process-listing plugin. _Why:_ analysts should understand the visibility limits of the tool providing the process view. _[GCFA p.442]_
- **PsList hidden-process limitation** — `windows.pslist.PsList` may fail to show processes concealed by rootkits or other hiding techniques. _Why:_ a clean PsList result does not prove that no hidden processes exist. _[GCFA p.442]_

### svchost.exe Identity

- **svchost.exe role** — `svchost.exe` is a generic host process used by Windows services. _Why:_ it is not usually the service logic itself; it hosts service code, often DLL-based. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Service DLL hosting** — Windows uses `svchost.exe` to run service DLLs. _Why:_ malware can abuse this by loading a malicious DLL through service-host infrastructure. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Legitimate image path** — A normal `svchost.exe` should run from `%SystemRoot%\System32\svchost.exe`. _Why:_ the same filename outside System32 is a strong suspicious indicator. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Displayed image path variant** — The page also shows the path as `%SystemRoot%\system32\svchost.exe`. _Why:_ case differences in the directory spelling are not the key issue; the expected System32 location is. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Expected parent process** — A legitimate `svchost.exe` normally has `services.exe` as its parent. _Why:_ a different parent can indicate masquerading or abnormal launch behavior. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Parent process qualifier** — The screenshot notes `services.exe` as the parent “most often.” _Why:_ analysts should treat parentage as a high-value signal while still considering service-start edge cases. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Minimum service-host expectation** — A legitimate `svchost.exe` should host at least one service. _Why:_ a service-host process with no hosted service is inconsistent with its normal purpose. _[GCFA p.~444]_

### svchost.exe Instance Count

- **Many instances expected** — Windows commonly runs many `svchost.exe` processes. _Why:_ a high count is not automatically malicious. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **General instance-count floor** — The screenshot states that there are generally at least 10 `svchost.exe` instances. _Why:_ analysts should not flag normal multiplicity as suspicious without supporting anomalies. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **High instance counts** — The screenshot states that `svchost.exe` counts often exceed 50. _Why:_ modern Windows service isolation can produce large numbers of service-host processes. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Alternate minimum count note** — The text-layer summary states that five or more `svchost.exe` instances can be expected. _Why:_ even older or summarized baselines treat multiple instances as normal. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Windows 10 version 1703 change** — Starting with Windows 10 version 1703, Microsoft changed default service grouping behavior for certain systems. _Why:_ this OS-version detail explains why newer systems may show many more `svchost.exe` processes. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **RAM threshold for changed grouping** — The Windows 10 version 1703 grouping change applies by default to systems with more than 3.5 GB of RAM. _Why:_ hardware configuration affects the expected number of service-host processes. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Post-1703 service isolation effect** — On affected systems, most services run in separate `svchost.exe` instances. _Why:_ more than 50 service-host processes can be normal rather than inherently suspicious. _[GCFA p.~444]_

### svchost.exe User Context

- **Common service accounts** — `svchost.exe` commonly runs as Local System, Network Service, or Local Service. _Why:_ these accounts are normal service execution contexts. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Variable account context** — The account used by `svchost.exe` depends on the specific hosted service or instance. _Why:_ analysts must compare account context to the service being hosted instead of expecting one universal account. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Unexpected account warning** — `svchost.exe` instances running under accounts outside the common service-account set should be examined. _Why:_ unusual user context can indicate masquerading, abuse, or per-user service behavior requiring validation. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Windows 10+ per-user services** — Windows 10 and later can run per-user services under a user account. _Why:_ not every user-account `svchost.exe` is malicious on modern Windows. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Per-user service integrity level** — Windows 10+ per-user service-host processes can run with Medium integrity. _Why:_ integrity level helps distinguish modern legitimate per-user services from higher-privilege service-host behavior. _[GCFA p.~444]_

### svchost.exe Timing

- **Typical start time** — `svchost.exe` usually starts close to system boot. _Why:_ service-host processes are commonly launched as services initialize. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Boot-proximate timing** — The text-layer summary states that typical `svchost.exe` start time is within seconds of boot. _Why:_ start-time proximity is a useful baseline for identifying late-start anomalies. _[GCFA p.~444]_
