### Malware Abuse Patterns

- **svchost.exe ubiquity abuse** — Malware authors exploit the common presence of `svchost.exe` to hide malicious activity. _Why:_ common names reduce analyst attention unless baseline checks are applied. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Malicious DLL service hosting** — Attackers may configure a malicious DLL to run as a service inside `svchost.exe`. _Why:_ the process name may look normal while the hosted service code is malicious. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Direct svchost.exe abuse** — Malware can hide directly by installing itself as a service loaded into a legitimate `svchost.exe` instance. _Why:_ process-name review alone will miss this technique. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Indirect svchost.exe masquerading** — Malware can hide indirectly by creating a process that resembles legitimate `svchost.exe`. _Why:_ subtle visual similarity can mislead quick process-list review. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Correct-name wrong-location masquerade** — Attackers may name a malicious process `svchost.exe` but place it outside System32. _Why:_ image path is essential for detecting same-name masquerading. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Misspelled-name masquerade** — Attackers may use a near-match spelling to imitate `svchost.exe`. _Why:_ small spelling deviations are high-signal process anomalies. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **`scvhost.exe` example** — The page gives `scvhost.exe` as an example of a deceptive misspelling. _Why:_ transposed or similar-looking names can reveal masquerading malware. _[GCFA p.~444]_

### Windows 7 Signing Baseline

- **Windows 7 service executable signing** — On default Windows 7 installations, service executables are Microsoft-signed. _Why:_ unsigned service executables on such systems deserve scrutiny. _[GCFA p.~444]_
- **Windows 7 service DLL signing** — On default Windows 7 installations, service DLLs are Microsoft-signed. _Why:_ unsigned DLLs hosted by services can indicate tampering or malicious service installation. _[GCFA p.~444]_

## Page 445

### Volatility Plugin Identity

- **windows.psscan.PsScan plugin** — Volatility 3 provides `windows.psscan.PsScan` as a process-discovery plugin commonly referred to as `psscan`. _Why:_ it is part of the rogue-process identification workflow in memory forensics. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **psscan shorthand** — The shortened name `psscan` refers to the `windows.psscan.PsScan` plugin. _Why:_ analysts commonly use the short plugin name when comparing process-enumeration methods. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Rogue process identification use case** — The page presents `windows.psscan.PsScan` as a tool for finding suspicious or hidden processes. _Why:_ rogue processes may evade normal process listings. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **psscan versus pslist** — `psscan` collects process information differently from `windows.pslist.PsList`. _Why:_ contrasting the two plugins helps reveal processes that one method misses. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Scan naming convention** — The word `scan` in `psscan` signals that the plugin searches memory rather than relying on standard object links. _Why:_ Volatility plugin names often indicate how an artifact is discovered. _[GCFA p.445]_

### Purpose

- **EPROCESS pool allocation scanning** — `psscan` searches physical memory for pool allocations associated with EPROCESS structures. _Why:_ EPROCESS objects represent Windows processes in memory. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Physical memory target** — The plugin operates by scanning physical memory. _Why:_ scanning raw memory can find artifacts outside normal operating-system-maintained lists. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Process block discovery** — `psscan` looks for process-related memory blocks rather than only traversing active process links. _Why:_ this can reveal hidden or previously terminated processes. _[GCFA p.445]_

### Parameters

- **`--pid` parameter** — The `--pid` option limits displayed information to selected process identifiers. _Why:_ filtering by PID lets an analyst focus on a process of interest. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **`-r pretty` parameter** — The `-r pretty` option formats output using sized, readable columns. _Why:_ column-aligned output makes process triage easier to review. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Specific PID display** — `psscan` can show information for one or more specified process IDs. _Why:_ targeted review reduces noise in large memory images. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Readable-column rendering** — `psscan` output can be rendered in a visually structured table format. _Why:_ aligned fields help analysts compare process attributes quickly. _[GCFA p.445]_

### Scanning Method

- **Non-list-based enumeration** — Scanning plugins do not identify objects by following the usual operating-system-maintained structures. _Why:_ malware may tamper with those normal structures. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **EPROCESS linked-list avoidance** — `psscan` does not depend solely on the EPROCESS doubly linked list of processes. _Why:_ unlinking from this list is a known hiding technique. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Object-marker search** — Scanning plugins search memory for signatures or markers that identify specific object types. _Why:_ marker-based discovery can locate objects even when list metadata is manipulated. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Disk-carving analogy** — The page compares `psscan`-style memory scanning to carving data from disk. _Why:_ both approaches search raw storage for recognizable structures rather than relying on filesystem or OS indexes. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Analysis counterpoint** — Results from scanning plugins provide an alternate view from plugins that use normal enumeration paths. _Why:_ conflicting or additional results can expose evasion or stale artifacts. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Plugin comparison value** — `psscan` output can enrich analysis when compared with other Volatility plugin results. _Why:_ cross-plugin comparison helps validate process state and detect anomalies. _[GCFA p.445]_

### Hidden and Terminated Processes

- **Hidden process detection** — Scanning memory for process blocks can reveal processes hidden from the EPROCESS linked list. _Why:_ rootkits may hide processes by manipulating kernel process lists. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Kernel manipulation resistance** — `psscan` has a stronger chance than list-walking methods of finding processes hidden by rootkit-style kernel changes. _Why:_ it does not rely on the manipulated list as its only source. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Terminated process recovery** — `psscan` can identify processes that are no longer running. _Why:_ stopped processes may still be forensically important. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Unallocated memory process remnants** — `psscan` may locate terminated process objects in memory regions no longer actively allocated. _Why:_ process remnants can preserve evidence after execution ends. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Exited process anomaly pattern** — Processes that have exited often show zero threads and zero handles. _Why:_ this pattern helps identify dead process remnants even when exit metadata is incomplete. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Thread-count review** — Analysts should inspect thread counts for unusual values. _Why:_ thread counts can help distinguish active from terminated or anomalous process records. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Handle-count review** — Analysts should inspect handle counts for unusual values. _Why:_ handle counts provide another process-state indicator during triage. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Zero-thread implication** — A process with no threads has no code currently executing. _Why:_ this supports interpreting the process as inactive or terminated. _[GCFA p.445]_

### Performance Tradeoff

- **Slower execution** — `psscan` is significantly slower than `pslist` because it scans memory. _Why:_ full-memory scanning is more expensive than traversing an existing process list. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **pslist analog comparison** — The page treats `pslist` as the faster list-based counterpart to `psscan`. _Why:_ analysts must balance speed against artifact coverage. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Similar output fields** — Despite using a different discovery method, `psscan` returns process fields similar to `pslist`. _Why:_ comparable fields enable side-by-side analysis between plugins. _[GCFA p.445]_

### Output Fields

- **PID field** — `psscan` reports the Process Identifier as `PID`. _Why:_ the PID uniquely identifies a process instance within the captured system context. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **PPID field** — `psscan` reports the Parent Process Identifier as `PPID`. _Why:_ parent-child relationships help identify suspicious lineage. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Image File Name field** — `psscan` reports the process executable name as `Image File Name`. _Why:_ process names are a first-pass indicator for masquerading or unusual execution. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Offset(V) field** — `psscan` reports the virtual address of the EPROCESS block as `Offset(V)`. _Why:_ the EPROCESS offset anchors deeper memory inspection. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Threads field** — `psscan` reports the number of threads as `Threads`. _Why:_ thread count helps assess whether a process is active or suspiciously abnormal. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Handles field** — `psscan` reports the number of handles as `Handles`. _Why:_ handle count helps characterize process activity and state. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **SessionID field** — `psscan` reports the session identifier as `SessionID`. _Why:_ session context can help distinguish services, interactive logons, and user activity. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Wow64 field** — `psscan` reports whether the process is 32-bit or 64-bit using `Wow64`. _Why:_ process architecture may matter for malware behavior and plugin interpretation. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **CreateTime field** — `psscan` reports the process start timestamp as `CreateTime`. _Why:_ start time supports timeline reconstruction and process-duration analysis. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **ExitTime field** — `psscan` reports the process stop timestamp as `ExitTime`. _Why:_ stop time helps identify terminated processes and execution duration. _[GCFA p.445]_

### ExitTime Interpretation

- **Populated ExitTime meaning** — A filled `ExitTime` value indicates that the process being viewed has terminated. _Why:_ this is a direct state indicator in `psscan` output. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Execution-duration analysis** — Comparing `CreateTime` and `ExitTime` can show how long a process existed. _Why:_ process lifetime can reveal behavior patterns or staged execution. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Executable behavior insight** — A process’s lifetime may provide clues about how the executable operated internally. _Why:_ short-lived or repeated execution can be meaningful during malware analysis. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Incomplete ExitTime limitation** — Not every terminated process receives a populated `ExitTime`. _Why:_ analysts cannot rely on `ExitTime` alone to identify exited processes. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Zero threads and handles fallback** — Processes with zero threads and zero handles should be reviewed as possible terminated processes when `ExitTime` is absent. _Why:_ this compensates for incomplete termination metadata. _[GCFA p.445]_

### Cross-Plugin Comparison

- **psscan-to-pslist comparison** — Analysts can compare `psscan` results against `pslist` output. _Why:_ items present in `psscan` but absent from `pslist` may represent terminated or hidden processes. _[GCFA p.445]_
- **Missing-from-pslist indicator** — A process found by `psscan` but no longer present in `pslist` deserves attention. _Why:_ the difference can indicate either process exit or process hiding. _[GCFA p.445]_

## Page 446

### EPROCESS List Behavior

- **Exited processes in EPROCESS lists** — Processes that have already terminated can still appear in the EPROCESS process-list data structure. _Why:_ analysts should not assume every listed EPROCESS entry represents a currently running process. _[GCFA p.446]_

- **ExitTime marker** — An EPROCESS entry with an `ExitTime` timestamp indicates that the process has ended. _Why:_ this field helps distinguish terminated processes from active ones during memory analysis. _[GCFA p.446]_

- **Windows 10+ lingering behavior** — On Windows 10 and later systems, terminated processes commonly remain visible in the EPROCESS list for longer before being removed. _Why:_ lingering entries are normal on modern Windows and should not automatically be treated as suspicious. _[GCFA p.446]_

### Volatility Plugin Equivalence

- **Volatility 2 equivalent plugin** — The Volatility 2 plugin corresponding to this EPROCESS-list scanning context is `psscan`. _Why:_ analysts using Volatility 2 need the older plugin name to perform the equivalent process-discovery task. _[GCFA p.446]_

### Page-Displayed Values

- **Displayed numeric value `42`** — The page shows the standalone number `42`. _Why:_ terminal, slide, or screenshot-visible values are part of the forensic inventory and must be preserved when present. _[GCFA p.446]_

### Interpretation of a.exe

- **a.exe absence from pslist** — `a.exe` was found in `psscan` but was not present in the `pslist` results. _Why:_ a process missing from `pslist` but present in `psscan` may be exited, hidden, or unlinked. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **a.exe termination state** — the page states that `a.exe` had terminated. _Why:_ termination explains why it no longer appeared in normal active-process enumeration. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **a.exe list removal** — `a.exe` had been removed from the doubly linked process list. _Why:_ linked-list removal prevents `pslist` from seeing the process. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **a.exe memory residue** — even after removal from the process list, `a.exe` remained in unallocated memory. _Why:_ memory remnants let `psscan` recover process evidence after exit. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **ExitTime evidentiary value** — the presence of an exit timestamp strongly indicates that the process was not running when memory was acquired. _Why:_ this distinguishes historical execution from live execution. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **Zero-thread meaning** — `a.exe` had zero threads, indicating no executing code remained. _Why:_ thread absence corroborates that the process was no longer active. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **Wow64 meaning for a.exe** — `a.exe` had `Wow64 = True`, so it was a 32-bit process. _Why:_ architecture can affect plugin behavior, malware triage, and artifact interpretation. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **Loaded-DLL validation technique** — an analyst could test the exited-process conclusion by trying to enumerate loaded DLLs for `a.exe`. _Why:_ exited processes often no longer retain linked object lists needed for DLL enumeration. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **Handle-validation technique** — an analyst could also try to enumerate handles for `a.exe`. _Why:_ handles are commonly unlinked or absent after process termination. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **Exited-process object loss** — loaded DLLs and handles are typically unlinked when a process exits. _Why:_ missing subordinate objects can support an exited-process interpretation. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **a.exe runtime calculation** — comparing `CreateTime` `2022-06-27 20:17:06` to `ExitTime` `2022-06-27 22:01:27` shows roughly 104 minutes of execution. _Why:_ duration helps scope attacker activity and timeline windows. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **One-letter executable names** — malware can commonly use very short names such as `a.exe`, even though they look conspicuous. _Why:_ analysts should not dismiss simple filenames as too obvious to be malicious. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **Attacker laziness possibility** — a short name such as `a.exe` may result from careless attacker naming. _Why:_ simple naming choices can still be valid intrusion evidence. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **Stealth-workflow possibility** — the short name may also relate to malware or attacker steps intended to make the process less visible on the live system. _Why:_ process naming and hiding behavior should be interpreted together. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **Memory-image persistence** — the page emphasizes that hiding from a live running system is harder once a memory image is analyzed. _Why:_ memory forensics can preserve evidence that live enumeration misses. _[GCFA p.~447]_

### Offset-Based Follow-Up

- **Record suspicious-process offsets** — when a suspicious process appears in `psscan`, the analyst should document its listed offset. _Why:_ the offset may be needed for deeper plugin analysis. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **PID targeting flag** — many Volatility plugins can target a process with `--pid`. _Why:_ PID-based scoping narrows plugin output to a process of interest. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **Virtual-address targeting flag** — many Volatility plugins can target a process object with `--virtaddr`. _Why:_ virtual-address targeting can work when PID resolution does not. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **Offset advantage over PID** — `--virtaddr` may succeed in cases where the PID is not recognized. _Why:_ unlinked or exited process objects may be easier to reach by memory address than by active PID lookup. _[GCFA p.~447]_

### psscan Ordering and Duplicates

- **psscan sorting behavior** — `psscan` does not order output by process creation time the way `pslist` does. _Why:_ analysts must not infer chronological order from row order in `psscan`. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **psscan discovery order** — `psscan` rows are produced as process objects are found in memory. _Why:_ scan order reflects memory discovery rather than process timeline order. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **Moved-process duplicate possibility** — processes that moved within memory may appear more than once. _Why:_ duplicate rows can reflect memory movement rather than separate executions. _[GCFA p.~447]_
- **Duplicate-process signature** — such duplicates can have the same process name and PID while appearing at different memory offsets. _Why:_ offset comparison helps distinguish duplicate detections from distinct process instances. _[GCFA p.~447]_

## Page 449

### windows.pstree.PsTree Purpose

- **windows.pstree.PsTree** — Volatility 3 includes a `windows.pstree.PsTree` plugin, commonly referred to as `pstree`, for displaying Windows processes as a hierarchy. _Why:_ a tree view makes parent-child process relationships easier to inspect during rogue-process triage. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **Process-tree display** — The plugin presents the process list visually as a tree rather than as a flat table. _Why:_ process ancestry often exposes suspicious execution paths that are harder to see in a linear listing. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **Parent-process relationship visibility** — Viewing parent and child process relationships graphically is useful for spotting abnormal process lineage. _Why:_ malware often reveals itself through an unusual parent process. _[GCFA p.449]_

### Important Parameters

- **`-r pretty`** — The `-r pretty` option renders plugin output using sized, aligned columns. _Why:_ readable column formatting helps analysts compare process attributes quickly. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **`--pid`** — The `--pid` option limits output to a small process tree rooted at a selected parent process. _Why:_ focused output helps investigate one suspicious process family without scanning the full system tree. _[GCFA p.449]_

### Investigative Use

- **Wrong-parent anomaly detection** — `pstree` is especially useful for finding malicious processes launched by an unexpected parent. _Why:_ parentage mismatches are common indicators of masquerading or abnormal execution. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **`Explorer.exe` parent of `svchost.exe` example** — A process tree showing `Explorer.exe` as the parent of `svchost.exe` is given as an example of suspicious lineage. _Why:_ legitimate service-host processes normally do not originate from the interactive shell in that way. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **Visual anomaly hunting** — The tree format supports visual identification of suspicious process relationships. _Why:_ structural anomalies can stand out faster in a hierarchy than in raw process lists. _[GCFA p.449]_

### Data Source and Limits

- **EPROCESS linked-list dependency** — `pstree` depends on the kernel’s EPROCESS linked list. _Why:_ this determines which processes the plugin can and cannot enumerate. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **EPROCESS doubly linked list** — The plugin reads the kernel’s EPROCESS doubly linked list to build the process tree. _Why:_ this is the same class of process-enumeration source used by linked-list-based process plugins. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **Similarity to `pslist`** — `pstree` uses a linked-list approach similar to `pslist`. _Why:_ analysts should understand that both share similar blind spots against unlinked processes. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **Unlinked-process blind spot** — `pstree` will not show processes that have been removed from the EPROCESS linked list. _Why:_ rootkits or other hiding techniques may evade this view. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **Active-process bias** — Because it relies on the EPROCESS list, `pstree` generally visualizes active processes. _Why:_ the output should not be treated as a complete historical process record. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **Terminated-process exception** — Terminated processes can appear in `pstree` only if their entries still remain in the EPROCESS linked list. _Why:_ exited processes may sometimes remain visible, but their presence is conditional rather than guaranteed. _[GCFA p.449]_

### Output Fields

- **PID** — `pstree` reports the Process Identifier for each process. _Why:_ PID values support process correlation across Volatility plugins and other artifacts. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **PPID** — `pstree` reports the Parent Process Identifier for each process. _Why:_ PPID values are central to reconstructing process ancestry. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **Image File Name** — `pstree` reports the process name as the image file name. _Why:_ process names help identify masquerading, misspellings, and unexpected binaries. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **Offset(V)** — `pstree` reports the virtual offset of the EPROCESS block. _Why:_ the EPROCESS virtual address can be used to target or correlate a specific process object in memory analysis. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **Threads** — `pstree` reports the number of threads associated with each process. _Why:_ thread count helps distinguish active processes from suspicious or exited remnants. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **Handles** — `pstree` reports the number of handles associated with each process. _Why:_ handle count can provide context about process activity and lifecycle state. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **SessionID** — `pstree` reports the session identifier for each process. _Why:_ session context helps separate system, service, and interactive-user activity. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **Wow64** — `pstree` reports whether the process code is 64-bit or 32-bit. _Why:_ bitness can help identify compatibility-layer execution and guide follow-on analysis. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **CreateTime** — `pstree` reports the process start time. _Why:_ process creation timing supports event reconstruction and suspicious-sequence analysis. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **ExitTime** — `pstree` reports the process stop time. _Why:_ an exit time helps identify terminated processes and bound their period of activity. _[GCFA p.449]_
- **Output parity with other process plugins** — The process information produced by `pstree` mirrors the fields shown by other Volatility process plugins. _Why:_ consistent fields let analysts compare results across multiple process-enumeration methods. _[GCFA p.449]_

### Volatility Version Mapping

- **Volatility 2 equivalent** — The Volatility 2 plugin equivalent to `windows.pstree.PsTree` is `pstree`. _Why:_ analysts moving between Volatility versions can use the corresponding plugin name for the same investigative view. _[GCFA p.449]_

### Process-Lineage Interpretation

- **Same evidence set** — the example uses the same “hiding in plain sight” memory image discussed earlier in the courseware. _Why:_ the page demonstrates a different view of already analyzed evidence. _[GCFA p.450]_
- **PsTree organization** — `pstree` reorganizes the process list into parent-child relationships. _Why:_ lineage exposes anomalies that a flat process list can obscure. _[GCFA p.450]_
- **Visual anomaly detection** — the tree display can make unusual process relationships easier to identify. _Why:_ investigators can spot out-of-place descendants quickly. _[GCFA p.450]_
- **Lookalike process name** — `scvhost.exe` resembles `svchost.exe` but is not the normal spelling. _Why:_ close-name masquerading is a common rogue-process indicator. _[GCFA p.450]_
- **Expected svchost parent** — legitimate `svchost.exe` processes are expected to be launched by `services.exe`. _Why:_ deviation from expected parentage is a strong suspicious-process signal. _[GCFA p.450]_
- **Suspicious parentage** — `scvhost.exe` was spawned by `explorer.exe`, the Windows desktop shell. _Why:_ a service-host lookalike under the user shell is inconsistent with normal service-host lineage. _[GCFA p.450]_
- **Displayed normal contrast** — multiple correctly spelled `svchost.exe` rows have PPID `644`, the PID of `services.exe`. _Why:_ these rows provide the baseline used to identify `scvhost.exe` as abnormal. _[GCFA p.450]_

### Volatility PsTree Command

- **Volatility executable** — the command uses `vol.py` to run Volatility against a memory image. _Why:_ identifies the analysis framework used for process-tree extraction. _[GCFA p.451]_
- **Memory image input** — the target evidence file is `memory.img`. _Why:_ ties the displayed process hierarchy to the analyzed memory capture. _[GCFA p.451]_
- **Output renderer flag** — the command includes `-r pretty`. _Why:_ indicates the output was requested in a formatted, human-readable table style. _[GCFA p.451]_
- **PsTree plugin** — the plugin invoked is `windows.pstree.PsTree`. _Why:_ this plugin reconstructs parent-child process relationships from Windows memory. _[GCFA p.451]_
- **Full command line** — the shown command is `vol.py -f memory.img -r pretty windows.pstree.PsTree`. _Why:_ preserves the exact reproducible invocation used to generate the process tree. _[GCFA p.451]_

### PsTree Table Fields

- **Tree marker column** — leading asterisks show process nesting depth in the displayed hierarchy. _Why:_ the visual depth marker encodes parent-child process structure. _[GCFA p.451]_

- **Handles column** — each row reports the handle count for the process. _Why:_ handle counts provide context about process resource usage. _[GCFA p.451]_
- **Createtime column** — each row reports process creation time when available. _Why:_ start times support boot-sequence reconstruction and anomaly detection. _[GCFA p.451]_

## Page 452

### Webshell Parent-Process Analysis

- **Webshell hunting method** — Parent-child process relationships can reveal webshell activity when a web server process launches command-line utilities. _Why:_ abnormal ancestry is a strong memory-forensics lead for server compromise. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **Scenario system type** — The analyzed memory image came from a web server. _Why:_ webshell process behavior must be interpreted in the context of a server role. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **Compromise artifact** — The system contained an installed webshell. _Why:_ this explains why web-facing IIS activity produced local command execution. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **Threat attribution** — The webshell was attributed to Deep Panda. _Why:_ attribution context can guide intrusion scoping and intelligence correlation. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **Deep Panda aliases** — Deep Panda is also identified as Shell Crew and APT19. _Why:_ alias mapping prevents missed matches during threat-intelligence searches. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **Webshell definition** — A webshell is a small server-side script or code component placed on a web server to allow remote command execution. _Why:_ this defines the artifact class being hunted in memory. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **Common webshell format** — Webshells commonly appear as unauthorized PHP or ASP pages. _Why:_ responders should inspect server-side page files, not only binaries. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **Example webshell format** — The example used an ASP-based webshell. _Why:_ IIS environments commonly execute ASP content, making this format operationally relevant. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **Backdoor behavior** — A compromised web server with a webshell can function as a backdoor reachable over HTTP or HTTPS. _Why:_ normal web ports may carry attacker command traffic. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **IIS worker role** — `w3wp.exe` is the Microsoft IIS worker process involved in serving the webshell page. _Why:_ command execution beneath this process is suspicious when it spawns administrative utilities. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **Attacker interaction** — Attackers connected to the webshell page and executed multiple commands. _Why:_ child processes under IIS can preserve evidence of interactive remote activity. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **Anomalous process ancestry** — The attacker commands appeared as child processes of `w3wp.exe`. _Why:_ utilities such as `net.exe`, `ipconfig.exe`, and `whoami.exe` are unusual direct children of IIS. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **Expected command ancestry** — Similar command-line utilities would more normally descend from a shell such as `cmd.exe`. _Why:_ deviation from expected parentage is the detection signal. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **Process-pattern variability** — Different webshell implementations can produce different memory process patterns. _Why:_ analysts should use this pattern as a lead, not as the only possible webshell signature. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **Investigative implication** — The shown process tree pattern should prompt deeper examination of the system. _Why:_ IIS spawning administrative commands indicates likely unauthorized remote execution. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **External reference** — The slide points to “Analyzing and Detecting Webshells” at `https://for508.com/nqrab`. _Why:_ the linked material provides additional webshell detection background. _[GCFA p.452]_
- **Output truncation note** — Some columns were removed from the process-tree output so it would fit on the slide. _Why:_ analysts should know the displayed table is not the full plugin output schema. _[GCFA p.452]_

## Page 454

### Orphan Process Concepts

- **Orphan process** — a child process with no corresponding live parent is considered orphaned in Windows and Unix process analysis. _Why:_ missing parentage is uncommon and can expose suspicious execution chains. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Parent exits before child** — a parent process terminating before its child processes is generally abnormal. _Why:_ child processes usually exist to perform work on behalf of a parent. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Expected parent presence** — analysts normally expect a process’s parent to remain explainable in the process tree. _Why:_ absent parents are useful triage points for deeper review. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Legitimate orphan exceptions** — `System`, `explorer.exe`, `csrss.exe`, and `wininit.exe` can legitimately appear without active parents. _Why:_ these processes should not be treated as suspicious solely because parentage is missing. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **System process exception** — PID `4` for `System` is a normal parentless process. _Why:_ it can appear orphaned but is expected system behavior. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Explorer exception nuance** — `explorer.exe` may appear parentless in legitimate circumstances. _Why:_ parent absence alone needs process-specific interpretation. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **csrss exception** — `csrss.exe` is documented as a process that may lack an expected parent. _Why:_ this prevents false positives during orphan-process hunting. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **wininit exception** — `wininit.exe` is another known process that may appear without a live parent. _Why:_ it belongs on the analyst’s exception list. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **dllhost.exe role** — `dllhost.exe` commonly serves as a surrogate host for process extensions. _Why:_ its parent relationship should usually be explainable because it exists to support another process. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **dllhost.exe crash isolation** — code hosted through `dllhost.exe` can fail without taking down the original parent process. _Why:_ this explains why a parentless `dllhost.exe` would be suspicious. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Loader behavior** — malware loaders may start a payload and then terminate. _Why:_ this creates orphaned payload processes that can be hunted in memory. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Injection behavior** — some code-injection workflows create a process only to receive injected code, after which the creating process may no longer be needed. _Why:_ the injected process can remain as an orphaned execution artifact. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Meterpreter behavior** — many Metasploit Meterpreter payloads can show this parentless-child pattern. _Why:_ orphan processes can indicate post-exploitation activity. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Hunting technique source** — Hiroshi Suzuki and Hisao Nashiwa included orphan-process hunting among their highlighted techniques in “Super Easy Memory Forensics” at FIRST Conference Dublin in June 2022. _Why:_ the method is recognized by experienced memory-forensics practitioners. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Windows parent-child enforcement** — Windows commonly follows parent-child conventions but does not strictly enforce them. _Why:_ attackers can abuse this flexibility to mislead process-tree analysis. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **PID spoofing implication** — loose parent-child enforcement enables more advanced techniques such as parent process ID spoofing. _Why:_ analysts should not trust process lineage blindly. _[GCFA p.454]_

### Amadey Case Context

- **Case shown** — the page’s process tree depicts an early Amadey infection. _Why:_ the example ties orphan-process theory to real malware triage. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Bad process count** — three malicious processes are present in the shown process tree. _Why:_ the count defines the suspicious set in the example. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Shared bad-process trait** — all three malicious processes are orphan processes. _Why:_ orphan status is the detection clue tying them together. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **System PID 4 in display** — `System` PID `4` is shown but is legitimate. _Why:_ analysts must separate expected parentless processes from suspicious ones. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Suspicious name visibility** — `Sun07610e6b216` is visually unusual as a process name. _Why:_ odd naming can draw analyst attention even before lineage analysis. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Generic-looking malware name** — `setup_install.exe` could look ordinary enough to avoid immediate suspicion. _Why:_ generic names require behavioral context such as parentage. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Second generic-looking malware name** — `tkools.exe` could also appear unremarkable at first glance. _Why:_ orphan status helps surface malware with bland names. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **pstree branch marker** — a single `*` in `pstree` output marks the beginning of a branch. _Why:_ this marker helps identify processes whose parent is not present in the displayed tree. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Amadey components** — `Sun07610e6b216`, `setup_install.exe`, and `tkools.exe` were all Amadey components in this example. _Why:_ confirms that the orphan-process clue led to malware. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Explorer lineage nuance** — `explorer.exe` appears under its expected parent `userinit.exe` in the example. _Why:_ the tree can preserve expected lineage even when the parent has exited. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **userinit.exe termination** — `userinit.exe` has an exit time in the example and is no longer running. _Why:_ a displayed parent can still be terminated, changing how lineage should be interpreted. _[GCFA p.454]_

### Process Tree Table · Columns

- **Tree-depth column** — the leftmost marker column uses asterisks to show process-tree nesting. _Why:_ nesting indicates parent-child structure in the displayed process tree. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **PID column** — the `PID` column lists each process identifier. _Why:_ PIDs are needed to correlate process records and lineage. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **PPID column** — the `PPID` column lists each process’s parent process identifier. _Why:_ PPIDs are central to orphan-process detection. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **ImageFileName column** — the `ImageFileName` column lists the process executable name shown by the memory tool. _Why:_ names help spot masquerading, randomness, and known system processes. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Offset(V) column** — the `Offset(V)` column provides each process object’s virtual offset. _Why:_ offsets let analysts target specific process objects in memory tooling. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Threads column** — the `Threads` column shows each process’s thread count. _Why:_ zero threads can indicate a terminated process. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **Wow64 column** — the `Wow64` column records whether the process is running under WOW64. _Why:_ it distinguishes 32-bit processes on 64-bit Windows from native 64-bit processes. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **CreateTime column** — the `CreateTime` column shows process start time. _Why:_ timing helps reconstruct execution order. _[GCFA p.454]_
- **ExitTime column** — the `ExitTime` column shows process termination time or `N/A` if no exit time is recorded. _Why:_ exit times distinguish live processes from exited ones. _[GCFA p.454]_

### Process Tree Table Structure

- **Process hierarchy marker column** — the leading symbols show each process row’s depth in the displayed parent-child tree. _Why:_ tree depth helps identify normal lineage versus orphaned or suspicious ancestry. _[GCFA p.456]_
- **PID column** — the table records each process identifier. _Why:_ PIDs let analysts correlate processes across plugins, logs, handles, and memory structures. _[GCFA p.456]_
- **PPID column** — the table records each process’s parent process identifier. _Why:_ PPIDs expose process lineage and parent-child anomalies. _[GCFA p.456]_
- **ImageFileName column** — the table lists the executable image name associated with each process. _Why:_ image names reveal masquerading, suspicious binaries, and expected Windows processes. _[GCFA p.456]_
- **Offset(V) column** — the table gives each process’s virtual memory offset. _Why:_ offsets let analysts pivot directly to the process object in memory. _[GCFA p.456]_
- **Threads column** — the table reports the number of threads associated with each process. _Why:_ thread counts help distinguish active processes from exited or hollow remnants. _[GCFA p.456]_
- **Wow64 column** — the table indicates whether each process is running under WoW64. _Why:_ WoW64 status identifies 32-bit processes on 64-bit Windows, which can matter for malware tooling and plugin interpretation. _[GCFA p.456]_
- **CreateTime column** — the table shows when each process was created. _Why:_ creation timestamps establish execution sequence and infection timing. _[GCFA p.456]_
- **ExitTime column** — the table shows whether and when a process exited. _Why:_ exit times help identify short-lived launchers, droppers, and terminated parents. _[GCFA p.456]_

- **Service persistence tree · Legitimate child** — `svchost.exe` is shown beneath `services.exe` in the service example. _Why:_ normal service activity can create noisy process trees where malicious service children can hide. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Service persistence tree · Suspicious child** — `updater.exe` is shown beneath `services.exe` in the service example. _Why:_ the slide uses this process name as the malicious example to illustrate service-based persistence. _[GCFA p.457]_

- **Scheduled-task tree · Root process** — `services.exe` is shown as the top process in the scheduled-task example. _Why:_ scheduled-task execution ultimately traces back into the service execution infrastructure. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Scheduled-task tree · Schedule host** — `svchost.exe` is shown beneath `services.exe` in the scheduled-task example. _Why:_ triggered tasks execute under a service-hosting process rather than directly from Task Scheduler UI artifacts. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Scheduled-task tree · Task host indicator** — `taskhostw.exe` is shown beneath the scheduled-task `svchost.exe`. _Why:_ this child helps identify the particular `svchost.exe` instance responsible for scheduled tasks. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Scheduled-task tree · Suspicious child** — `updater.exe` is shown directly beneath the scheduled-task `svchost.exe`. _Why:_ task-launched binaries appear as children of this `svchost.exe`, which is the useful lineage point for detection. _[GCFA p.457]_

- **Registry Run key tree · User shell** — `explorer.exe` is shown as the parent process in the Registry Run key example. _Why:_ Run key programs commonly start during user logon under the interactive desktop shell. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Registry Run key tree · Security tray process** — `SecurityHealthSystray.exe` is shown as a child of `explorer.exe`. _Why:_ benign user-context children create baseline noise around the location where Run key malware may also appear. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Registry Run key tree · Suspicious child** — `updater.exe` is shown as a child of `explorer.exe` in the Run key example. _Why:_ this demonstrates how Run key persistence may surface in a user shell process tree. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Registry Run key tree · Browser process** — `msedge.exe` is shown as another child of `explorer.exe`. _Why:_ normal user applications also appear under `explorer.exe`, so analysts must distinguish routine user activity from persistence. _[GCFA p.457]_

### Windows Execution Model

- **Process-thread execution model** — Windows runs code inside process threads. _Why:_ persistence and lateral-movement methods often leave process artifacts that can be inspected in memory. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Persistence process artifacts** — Persistence techniques can create notable process-tree patterns on compromised systems. _Why:_ these patterns help analysts move from generic process lists to behavior-based detection. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Lateral-movement process artifacts** — Lateral-movement techniques can also create distinctive process relationships on victims. _Why:_ remote execution may be visible even when filesystem or log evidence is incomplete. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Common technique concentration** — Many real-world intrusions rely on a relatively small set of persistence and lateral-movement methods. _Why:_ learning recurring lineage patterns gives defenders practical detection leverage. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Slide-wide malicious placeholder** — The process name `updater.exe` is used in all four examples as the malicious process. _Why:_ the repeated name isolates the parent-child pattern as the teaching point rather than the filename itself. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Four demonstrated techniques** — The page illustrates Service, Task Scheduler, Registry Run Key, and PsExec process trees. _Why:_ these are common mechanisms whose process ancestry can expose attacker activity. _[GCFA p.457]_

### Services

- **Services as common execution method** — Windows services are a frequent mechanism for running code. _Why:_ malware using services may blend into a high-volume but analytically important part of the process tree. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **`services.exe` child volume** — Many child processes commonly appear beneath `services.exe`. _Why:_ analysts should expect noise but should still review this area because malicious services can appear there. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Service-child review priority** — Reviewing the child processes of `services.exe` is usually worthwhile during malware hunting. _Why:_ the location is long and noisy, but it is also a common execution point for attacks. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Technique overlap under `services.exe`** — Three of the four techniques shown on the page ultimately fall beneath `services.exe`. _Why:_ this makes `services.exe` ancestry a central triage focus for both persistence and lateral movement. _[GCFA p.457]_

### Scheduled Tasks

- **Scheduled-task population** — Modern Windows systems can contain hundreds of scheduled tasks. _Why:_ attackers can hide a single malicious task among many legitimate scheduled entries. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Scheduled-task trigger behavior** — When a scheduled task fires, it runs beneath a `svchost.exe` instance that handles task execution. _Why:_ the process parent is a key clue for identifying task-launched code in memory. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Scheduled-task `svchost.exe` discriminator** — The task-related `svchost.exe` can be recognized by the presence of a child process named `taskhostw.exe`. _Why:_ many processes are named `svchost.exe`, so child-process context helps identify the right instance. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Scheduled-task command line** — On Windows 10 and later, the task-hosting service process command line is `C:\Windows\system32\svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p -s Schedule`. _Why:_ this exact command line distinguishes the Schedule service host from other `svchost.exe` instances. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Windows version scope** — The scheduled-task command-line pattern is identified for Windows 10 and newer systems. _Why:_ version context prevents analysts from overapplying the process-command-line rule. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Scheduled-task payload parent** — Executables launched by scheduled tasks appear as direct children of the Schedule-related `svchost.exe`. _Why:_ analysts should inspect children of that `svchost.exe` for task-launched malware. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Scheduled-task non-parent** — Scheduled-task payloads do not appear beneath `taskhostw.exe` in the example described. _Why:_ looking under the wrong child can cause the malicious task payload to be missed. _[GCFA p.457]_

### Registry Run Keys

- **Run key timing** — Registry Run keys are intended to launch programs during user logon. _Why:_ execution timing explains why related processes often appear under the interactive shell. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Run key process parent** — Run key programs commonly appear as children of `explorer.exe`. _Why:_ `explorer.exe` lineage can reveal user-logon persistence. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **`explorer.exe` as desktop process** — The page identifies `explorer.exe` as the user desktop process. _Why:_ this clarifies why many user-context applications and persistence mechanisms branch from it. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **User-context process concentration** — Most applications running in a user context appear as children of `explorer.exe`. _Why:_ this makes `explorer.exe` a busy but valuable location for attack discovery. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Beyond Run key persistence** — The `explorer.exe` child list can reveal attacks beyond Registry Run key abuse. _Why:_ user-context malware and tools may surface in the same ancestry even when persistence is not Run-key based. _[GCFA p.457]_

### PsExec

- **PsExec remote execution model** — Code remotely executed with PsExec runs as a service on the target host. _Why:_ this service-based execution path leaves recognizable process ancestry in memory. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Default PsExec service name** — PsExec names its target-side service `PSEXESVC.exe` by default. _Why:_ this default process name is a high-signal clue for PsExec-style lateral movement. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **PsExec payload ancestry** — Binaries executed through PsExec appear as children of `PSEXESVC.exe`. _Why:_ child processes of this service can identify what was remotely launched. _[GCFA p.457]_
- **Default PsExec usage frequency** — The page notes that default PsExec usage is common. _Why:_ analysts should treat the default `PSEXESVC.exe` pattern as realistic, not merely theoretical. _[GCFA p.457]_

## Page 458

### PsExec Process Pattern Scope

- **Sysinternals PsExec `-r` option** — the service name or related execution pattern can be altered with PsExec’s `-r` parameter. _Why:_ analysts should not treat the default observed service/process naming as fixed when investigating PsExec activity. _[GCFA p.~458]_

- **Sysinternals-specific behavior** — the described parent/child process pattern applies to the Sysinternals PsExec implementation. _Why:_ attribution to PsExec activity must account for which implementation produced the artifact pattern. _[GCFA p.~458]_

- **Non-Sysinternals `psexec` tools** — other remote execution tools may use the `psexec` name while producing different runtime artifacts. _Why:_ relying only on the label “psexec” can mislead process-tree interpretation. _[GCFA p.~458]_

- **Cobalt Strike PsExec-style payloads** — Cobalt Strike’s payloads that use the `psexec` name are cited as common examples of PsExec-like tools that do not necessarily match Sysinternals PsExec behavior. _Why:_ red-team and malware frameworks may mimic PsExec terminology while leaving different forensic traces. _[GCFA p.~458]_

- **WMI-based PsExec copycats** — many PsExec-named alternatives execute through Windows Management Instrumentation rather than the Sysinternals PsExec mechanism. _Why:_ WMI execution changes the expected process lineage and artifact set. _[GCFA p.~458]_

- **PowerShell-based PsExec copycats** — many PsExec-named alternatives execute through PowerShell instead of following the Sysinternals PsExec process model. _Why:_ PowerShell-backed execution produces a different parent/child process relationship and should be analyzed separately. _[GCFA p.~458]_

- **Parent/child process variance** — WMI- or PowerShell-based PsExec-like tools can create process trees that differ substantially from Sysinternals PsExec. _Why:_ process ancestry is implementation-dependent, so analysts should avoid overgeneralizing one PsExec pattern to all similarly named tools. _[GCFA p.~458]_

- **High-investigation value of WMI-to-PowerShell** — even though it may be legitimate, the page states this relationship is usually worth examining. _Why:_ the pattern has enough attacker overlap to merit scrutiny. _[GCFA p.459]_

- **WMI Event Consumers for persistence** — WMI Event Consumers can be used to maintain persistence on a system. _Why:_ WMI persistence can survive reboots and may not appear as a typical startup artifact. _[GCFA p.459]_

### Data Reduction: Memory Baseliner

- **Memory Baseliner purpose** — Memory Baseliner is a standalone utility for comparing memory-resident objects in an investigated image against objects from a clean reference image. _Why:_ it reduces the analyst’s review set by highlighting items that do not appear in the known-good baseline. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Memory Baseliner implementation base** — The tool is built on Volatility 3. _Why:_ analysts must understand that it relies on Volatility 3 capabilities and object parsing. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Memory Baseliner library usage** — The current Memory Baseliner version uses Volatility 3 as a library rather than functioning only as a Volatility plugin. _Why:_ this affects deployment and how the tool is invoked in workflows. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Memory Baseliner author** — Csaba Barta created Memory Baseliner to bring baseline-comparison workflows into memory analysis. _Why:_ identifying the tool’s provenance helps analysts locate related documentation and methodology. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Baseline analysis definition** — Baseline analysis compares a suspicious dataset with a trusted clean dataset to identify deviations. _Why:_ the investigative value comes from focusing attention on outliers. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Baseline analysis scope** — Baseline comparison is useful across many DFIR artifact types, not only memory images. _Why:_ the same reduction principle can be applied broadly in forensic triage. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Known-good dataset role** — The clean baseline represents expected or normal artifacts for comparison. _Why:_ without a trusted baseline, the tool cannot reliably separate common objects from unusual ones. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Suspect dataset role** — The suspect memory image contains the objects under investigation. _Why:_ this is the dataset where unknown or uncommon artifacts may indicate malware or intrusion activity. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Outlier identification** — Objects present in the suspect image but absent from the baseline become candidate outliers. _Why:_ these differences can quickly surface attacker tooling or abnormal system components. _[GCFA p.~462]_

### Memory Analysis Challenge

- **Windows process volume** — A Windows memory image can contain more than one hundred processes. _Why:_ manual review at that scale is slow and error-prone. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Process object volume** — Each process can reference hundreds of process-related objects. _Why:_ the total artifact count expands far beyond the visible process list. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Driver volume** — Windows memory commonly includes hundreds of drivers. _Why:_ malicious drivers can hide among many legitimate kernel components. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Service volume** — Windows memory commonly includes hundreds of services. _Why:_ service-based malware or persistence can be difficult to spot manually. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Manual-review limitation** — Even experienced analysts can overlook malware when thousands of memory objects require review. _Why:_ data reduction is needed to prevent important anomalies from being buried in noise. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Similar-system baseline value** — A clean image from a comparable system allows many expected objects to be filtered out quickly. _Why:_ baselines work best when normal software, OS version, and role are close to the suspect system. _[GCFA p.~462]_

### Required Inputs

- **Baseline image flag `-b`** — The `-b` argument supplies the known-good memory image. _Why:_ this image defines what the tool treats as expected baseline content. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Suspect image flag `-i`** — The `-i` argument supplies the investigated memory image. _Why:_ this image is compared against the baseline to identify known and unknown objects. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Two-image comparison requirement** — A standard baseline comparison requires both a baseline image and a suspect image. _Why:_ Memory Baseliner needs both sides of the comparison to classify artifacts. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Volatility dual-image capability** — Csaba Barta’s approach gives Volatility-based analysis a way to process both the suspect image and the baseline image together. _Why:_ this enables automated known-versus-unknown memory object comparison. _[GCFA p.~462]_

### Object Types

- **Process and DLL baselining flag `-proc`** — The `-proc` option baselines processes and their associated DLLs. _Why:_ process and module differences are common places to find user-mode malware and injected components. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Driver baselining flag `-drv`** — The `-drv` option baselines drivers. _Why:_ uncommon drivers may reveal kernel-mode malware, rootkits, or suspicious software. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Service baselining flag `-svc`** — The `-svc` option baselines Windows services. _Why:_ services are a frequent persistence and execution mechanism. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Memory object category count** — The page describes Memory Baseliner as comparing four memory object categories: processes, associated DLLs, drivers, and services. _Why:_ analysts need to select the comparison mode that matches the artifact type under review. _[GCFA p.~462]_

### Output and Review

- **Output file flag `-o`** — The `-o` option saves Memory Baseliner results to a file. _Why:_ saved output can be reviewed, filtered, and shared outside the command-line session. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Spreadsheet review workflow** — Saved output can be analyzed in a spreadsheet or similar tabular viewer. _Why:_ filtering and sorting large comparison results is easier in a structured viewer. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Show-known flag `--showknown`** — The `--showknown` option includes both baseline-matched and baseline-missing items in the output. _Why:_ a complete table lets analysts filter, sort, and validate classifications without rerunning the tool. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Known-item output** — With `--showknown`, objects found in the baseline are included in the result set. _Why:_ retaining known objects supports comparison, context, and frequency analysis. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Unknown-item output** — With `--showknown`, objects absent from the baseline are also included in the result set. _Why:_ unknown objects are primary candidates for deeper investigation. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Large combined output** — Using `--showknown` can create one broad output containing both known and unknown data. _Why:_ one unified dataset supports flexible filtering strategies. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Column review importance** — Analysts should inspect the available output columns rather than focusing only on a single status field. _Why:_ supporting fields may explain whether an artifact is benign, suspicious, or worth escalation. _[GCFA p.~462]_

### Output Fields

- **Process name column** — Memory Baseliner output can include process names. _Why:_ names help identify expected system components and suspicious masquerading. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Command-line column** — Memory Baseliner output can include process command lines. _Why:_ command-line arguments often expose malicious execution intent or unusual launch context. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Parent process column** — Memory Baseliner output can include parent process information. _Why:_ abnormal parent-child relationships can reveal suspicious execution chains. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Loaded DLLs column** — Memory Baseliner output can include DLLs loaded by processes. _Why:_ unexpected modules can indicate injection, sideloading, or malicious dependencies. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Import hash column** — Memory Baseliner output can include import table hashes when those hashes are available. _Why:_ import hashes help cluster related binaries even when filenames differ. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Known/unknown status column** — Memory Baseliner output can label whether an item matched the baseline or did not. _Why:_ this status is the core triage indicator for baseline comparison. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **`KNOWN` status meaning** — A `KNOWN` label means the item was present in the baseline image. _Why:_ this indicates the artifact is not unique to the suspect image, though it may still require context-aware review. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Frequency-of-occurrence fields** — Memory Baseliner output can include per-process occurrence-frequency information. _Why:_ frequency helps distinguish common software from rare artifacts. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **`BASELINE Fo O` label** — `BASELINE Fo O` identifies frequency-of-occurrence information for the baseline side. _Why:_ baseline frequency helps show how common an artifact is among known-good data. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **`IMAGE Fo O` label** — `IMAGE Fo O` identifies frequency-of-occurrence information for the suspect image side. _Why:_ suspect-image frequency helps compare artifact prevalence during investigation. _[GCFA p.~462]_

### Refinement Options

- **JSON baseline saving** — Saving the initial baseline as JSON significantly accelerates later analysis runs. _Why:_ cached baseline data avoids repeating expensive baseline extraction. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Import-hash refinement `--imphash`** — The `--imphash` option tightens comparisons using import hash data. _Why:_ import hashes can distinguish binaries beyond filename or path-level matching. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Owner refinement `--owner`** — The `--owner` option tightens comparisons using ownership information. _Why:_ owner differences can expose unusual execution context or account misuse. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Command-line refinement `--cmdline`** — The `--cmdline` option tightens comparisons using process command-line data. _Why:_ the same executable may be benign or suspicious depending on launch arguments. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Service-state refinement `--state`** — The `--state` option tightens service comparisons using service state. _Why:_ service runtime state can separate expected installed services from active or suspicious ones. _[GCFA p.~462]_

### Stacking Analysis

- **Single-image baseline mode** — Memory Baseliner can baseline one memory image. _Why:_ this supports direct comparison between one clean reference and one suspect system. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Collection baseline mode** — Memory Baseliner can process a collection of images. _Why:_ multi-image analysis supports broader prevalence and rarity assessment. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Stacking definition** — Stacking compares artifacts across multiple memory images to find items with low occurrence frequency. _Why:_ rare artifacts are often more suspicious than widely present system components. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Stacking option example `--procstack`** — The page gives `--procstack` as an example option for process stacking. _Why:_ this flag supports least-frequency analysis across multiple suspect images. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Multiple suspect-image stacking** — Stacking can be performed across several suspect memory images at the same time. _Why:_ cross-host comparison helps identify artifacts that appear on only a small number of systems. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Least-frequency analysis principle** — Malware artifacts tend to appear less often than artifacts from normal system activity. _Why:_ rarity provides a useful prioritization signal during large-scale triage. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Executable collection for stacking** — Executables can be collected across many systems for frequency comparison. _Why:_ uncommon executables may indicate attacker tools or unusual software. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Driver collection for stacking** — Drivers can be collected across many systems for frequency comparison. _Why:_ rare drivers may expose kernel-level malicious components or unauthorized software. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **DLL collection for stacking** — DLLs can be collected across many systems for frequency comparison. _Why:_ low-prevalence DLLs can identify injected modules, sideloaded libraries, or malware dependencies. _[GCFA p.~462]_
- **Service collection for stacking** — Services can be collected across many systems for frequency comparison. _Why:_ uncommon services can reveal persistence, lateral movement tooling, or attacker-created service entries. _[GCFA p.~462]_

### External Reference

- **SANS DFIR blog reference** — The course page points to a SANS DFIR blog post that demonstrates analysis techniques for Memory Baseliner output. _Why:_ the blog provides practical methods for using the tool’s many fields during investigations. _[GCFA p.~462]_

## Page 463

### Memory Baseliner Stacking

- **Malware-associated item frequency** — artifacts tied to malware are expected to appear among the lowest-frequency entries when comparing many systems. _Why:_ rare items are better hunting candidates than artifacts common across the environment. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **DLL prevalence example · 73 systems** — a DLL observed on 73 systems is less suspicious than a DLL observed on only one system. _Why:_ broad occurrence suggests common software or shared configuration rather than a unique implant. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **DLL prevalence example · one system** — a DLL found on a single system is a stronger candidate for investigation than one found broadly. _Why:_ low prevalence helps surface outliers that may represent malware or unauthorized tooling. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Memory Baseliner `-d <image folder>` option** — the `-d <image folder>` argument points Memory Baseliner at a directory containing multiple memory images for comparison. _Why:_ this enables cross-image stacking rather than analyzing a single memory capture in isolation. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Memory image collection input** — Memory Baseliner can compare a folder of memory images as a set. _Why:_ enterprise-scale comparison makes uncommon processes, modules, drivers, or services easier to identify. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Process stacking** — processes can be stacked across multiple memory images. _Why:_ processes that appear rarely across comparable hosts may deserve closer forensic review. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **DLL stacking** — loaded DLLs can be stacked across memory images. _Why:_ uncommon DLLs may expose injected code, malicious libraries, or unusual application components. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Driver stacking** — drivers can be stacked across memory images. _Why:_ rare kernel components may indicate rootkits, custom tooling, or unauthorized software. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Service stacking** — services can be stacked across memory images. _Why:_ uncommon services may reveal persistence mechanisms or lateral movement tooling. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **`-drvstack` option example** — `-drvstack` is given as an example option for stacking drivers. _Why:_ driver comparison is a specific Memory Baseliner workflow for surfacing uncommon loaded drivers. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Least-frequent-first output behavior** — Memory Baseliner can place the least commonly occurring items near the top of the results. _Why:_ ranking by rarity reduces the analyst’s search space for outlier hunting. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Stacking is not instant malware detection** — the technique should not be treated as a guaranteed way to immediately identify malware. _Why:_ rarity is only a triage signal and still requires analyst validation. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Enterprise uniqueness problem** — enterprise systems contain many legitimate one-off or uncommon artifacts, even among similar builds. _Why:_ rare does not automatically mean malicious, so false positives are expected. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Similar-build targeting guidance** — stacking should be aimed at systems with similar builds. _Why:_ comparing unlike systems increases benign differences and weakens the value of rarity-based analysis. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **False-positive workload** — analysts should expect to review many rare-but-benign items before finding malicious activity. _Why:_ rarity filtering reduces volume but does not eliminate investigative judgment. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Dataset reduction value** — Memory Baseliner is useful for shrinking the volume of artifacts that need review. _Why:_ a smaller candidate set makes enterprise memory triage more practical. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Alternate outlier-hunting view** — stacking provides another way to look for unusual artifacts across memory captures. _Why:_ alternate analytical perspectives can reveal suspicious items missed by single-host review. _[GCFA p.~463]_

### Baseline Runtime and JSON Caching

- **Primary Memory Baseliner drawback** — the tool’s main practical limitation is long runtime. _Why:_ time cost affects whether the technique can be used during fast-moving incident response. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Current-version optimization** — the latest Memory Baseliner version has been optimized compared with earlier behavior. _Why:_ performance improvements make baseline workflows more usable, though not always fast. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Large-image runtime example** — producing baseline output for a large memory image can commonly take about 15 minutes. _Why:_ analysts should budget time for baseline generation. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **`--jsonbaseline` feature** — `--jsonbaseline` enables use of a JSON baseline file. _Why:_ JSON baselines avoid repeating expensive analysis of known-good memory images. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Known-good memory image JSON** — the JSON baseline represents analysis results from a known-good memory image. _Why:_ known-good baselines support future comparison without keeping or reprocessing the original memory image. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Future JSON reuse** — a saved JSON baseline can be loaded later. _Why:_ reuse removes the time needed to re-analyze the baseline memory image. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **`--savebaseline` argument** — `--savebaseline` creates the JSON baseline file. _Why:_ this is the option used to persist known-good baseline results for later runs. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **`--loadbaseline` argument** — `--loadbaseline` loads a previously generated baseline. _Why:_ this lets later analyses benefit from the saved baseline instead of regenerating it. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **`--savebaseline` dependency** — `--savebaseline` must be used together with `--jsonbaseline` naming the JSON file. _Why:_ the tool needs the JSON baseline filename when saving baseline output. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **`--loadbaseline` dependency** — `--loadbaseline` must be used together with `--jsonbaseline` naming the JSON file. _Why:_ the tool needs the JSON baseline filename when loading saved baseline data. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Analysis-type-specific JSON files** — baseline JSON files are tied to the specific analysis type being performed. _Why:_ one baseline file cannot be assumed to cover every artifact category. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Process-analysis JSON baseline** — process comparison requires its own JSON baseline file. _Why:_ process baseline data is distinct from driver or service baseline data. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Driver-analysis JSON baseline** — driver comparison requires its own JSON baseline file. _Why:_ loaded-driver baseline results are separate from process or service results. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Service-analysis JSON baseline** — service comparison requires its own JSON baseline file. _Why:_ service baseline results must be generated and stored separately for service-focused analysis. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Baseline image no longer required after JSON creation** — once a JSON baseline exists, the original baseline memory image does not need to be referenced or available. _Why:_ this reduces storage and handling requirements for future comparisons. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Baseline JSON size** — baseline JSON output is usually smaller than 1 MB. _Why:_ the small size makes baseline data much easier to store and move than full memory captures. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **JSON portability advantage** — baseline JSON files are more portable than complete memory images. _Why:_ analysts can carry or share baselines without transferring large forensic images. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Baseline repository concept** — analysts can maintain a collection of baseline JSON files for many system types and OS versions. _Why:_ reusable baselines improve readiness across varied environments. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **System-type coverage** — baseline repositories can cover different classes of systems. _Why:_ matching the baseline to the host type improves comparison quality. _[GCFA p.~463]_
- **Operating-system-version coverage** — baseline repositories can cover different OS versions. _Why:_ OS-version differences affect normal memory artifacts and should be reflected in baselines. _[GCFA p.~463]_

## Page 467

### Rogue Process Review Criteria

- **Process executable name** — Each discovered process should be checked to confirm that its image name or executable name is expected. _Why:_ Malware often uses misspelled, lookalike, or unusual process names to evade quick review. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Process file path** — Each discovered process should be checked to confirm that the executable resides in the expected filesystem location. _Why:_ A legitimate-looking process name is suspicious when it runs from an abnormal directory. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Process parent** — Each discovered process should be checked to confirm that its parent process is plausible. _Why:_ Abnormal parent-child relationships can reveal execution through web shells, WMI, PsExec, scripts, or other attacker launch paths. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Process command line** — Each discovered process should be checked to confirm that its command line is expected. _Why:_ Arguments often expose malicious behavior even when the executable name appears normal. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Process parameters** — Each discovered process should be checked to confirm that the parameters passed to the executable are expected. _Why:_ Suspicious flags, encoded commands, remote targets, or file paths can identify abuse of legitimate tools. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Process start time** — Each discovered process should be checked to determine whether its launch time makes sense. _Why:_ Process timing can correlate activity with intrusion events or expose processes started during suspicious windows. _[GCFA p.467]_

### Analyst Skill Development

- **Experience-based anomaly recognition** — Memory forensic expertise develops with practice rather than immediately. _Why:_ Repeated exposure helps analysts more quickly recognize abnormal process attributes. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Executable-name anomaly recognition** — Analysts learn to spot suspicious process image names through experience. _Why:_ Name-based anomalies can be an initial clue that a process deserves deeper examination. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Path anomaly recognition** — Analysts learn to identify process executable paths that do not match normal system behavior. _Why:_ Unexpected locations can indicate masquerading or attacker-staged binaries. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Parent-process anomaly recognition** — Analysts learn to recognize process parentage that does not fit normal Windows execution patterns. _Why:_ Parent-child mismatches often expose malicious execution chains. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Command-line anomaly recognition** — Analysts learn to identify suspicious command lines and parameters associated with processes. _Why:_ Command-line content can show intent, tooling, target files, and attacker tradecraft. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Start-time anomaly recognition** — Analysts learn to evaluate process start times for suspicious timing relationships. _Why:_ Launch times can help separate routine activity from activity tied to compromise. _[GCFA p.467]_

### Process Review in Memory Analysis

- **Running-process review** — Examining active processes is a foundational memory-analysis task. _Why:_ Process listings provide one of the first opportunities to identify suspicious execution. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Process attribute review** — Analysts inspect individual process attributes to decide whether a process appears abnormal. _Why:_ A single suspicious attribute can justify deeper investigation. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Suspicion-driven follow-up** — Anomalous process attributes can cause an analyst to suspect a process. _Why:_ Process triage directs attention toward artifacts that need confirmation. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Volatility follow-up analysis** — Volatility can be used to collect more information about a process after initial suspicion. _Why:_ Additional evidence helps validate or reject an initial hypothesis about malicious activity. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Confirming process suspicion** — Additional Volatility data can support an analyst’s suspicion about a process. _Why:_ Corroboration reduces reliance on a single weak indicator. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Dispelling process suspicion** — Additional Volatility data can also show that a suspicious-looking process is benign. _Why:_ Accurate triage requires eliminating false positives as well as finding threats. _[GCFA p.467]_

### Volatility Process-Review Methods

- **Volatility process visibility** — Volatility provides multiple mechanisms for reviewing process information. _Why:_ Different process-viewing methods expose different artifacts and evasion scenarios. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **windows.pslist** — The `windows.pslist` plugin provides a high-level view of processes in the EPROCESS linked list. _Why:_ It is useful for quick process enumeration using standard kernel-tracked process structures. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **EPROCESS linked list** — `windows.pslist` relies on the linked list of EPROCESS structures. _Why:_ This standard process list can be manipulated or bypassed by hidden-process techniques. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Pslist speed** — Pslist is described as quick and straightforward. _Why:_ It is well suited for initial triage when speed matters. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Pslist limitation** — Pslist can fail to show hidden processes. _Why:_ Malware may unlink a process from standard kernel lists to evade list-based enumeration. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **windows.psscan** — The `windows.psscan` plugin provides a lower-level process view by searching for process blocks that may not be linked. _Why:_ It can reveal processes that normal list traversal misses. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Psscan kernel-list independence** — Psscan does not rely on the normal kernel process-tracking mechanisms. _Why:_ Avoiding trusted list traversal helps detect process-hiding techniques. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Psscan full-memory scan** — Psscan scans across the memory image rather than only following the active process list. _Why:_ Broad scanning can locate process remnants outside the normal process list. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Psscan hidden-process detection** — Psscan can find hidden processes. _Why:_ Hidden-process discovery is essential when attackers unlink process structures. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Psscan terminated-process detection** — Psscan can identify processes that have exited but still leave recoverable traces in memory. _Why:_ Terminated process artifacts can preserve evidence of earlier attacker activity. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **windows.pstree** — The `windows.pstree` plugin displays process relationships in a tree format. _Why:_ Parent-child visualization helps analysts identify abnormal execution lineage. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Pstree parent-process visualization** — Pstree specifically emphasizes parent-process relationships. _Why:_ Process ancestry is a key signal for detecting suspicious launch chains. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Volatility process mechanisms count** — The page identifies three Volatility mechanisms for collecting and presenting process information: pslist, psscan, and pstree. _Why:_ Analysts should compare these complementary views during process triage. _[GCFA p.467]_

- **Memory Baseliner** — Memory Baseliner compares memory artifacts against a known-good baseline. _Why:_ Baseline comparison helps highlight deviations from expected system behavior. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Memory Baseliner anomaly detection** — Memory Baseliner can quickly direct an analyst toward anomalous items. _Why:_ It reduces the amount of process data that must be manually reviewed. _[GCFA p.467]_
- **Memory Baseliner data reduction** — Memory Baseliner performs data reduction during analysis. _Why:_ Reducing large memory-analysis output makes triage faster and more focused. _[GCFA p.467]_
