## Page 517

### Code Injection Detection

- **Code injection detection objective** — the detection task centers on finding code that does not belong inside a process. _Why:_ injected code is often hidden inside otherwise legitimate processes, so the analyst must identify the extra code rather than only the process. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Shared goal of injection techniques** — code injection methods all seek to make code run inside a chosen target process. _Why:_ this common outcome lets analysts use broad memory-analysis strategies across many different injection techniques. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Analyst mission** — the stated mission is to identify code added beyond what the process should normally contain. _Why:_ this frames the investigation around anomalous executable content rather than only malware family names or specific tools. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Memory analysis value** — memory analysis is useful because it can inspect code that is actually loaded and running. _Why:_ injected payloads may not be obvious from disk artifacts alone, but they must exist in memory to execute. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Primary detection paths** — the page groups code-injection detection into three broad approaches: auditing loader-introduced DLLs, finding unusual executable memory, and comparing kernel/userland inconsistencies. _Why:_ these approaches cover both conventional API-based loading and stealthier memory manipulation. _[GCFA p.517]_

### Windows Loader and DLL Artifacts

- **Windows-loader DLL detection** — one detection approach is to find DLLs that were added through normal Windows loader mechanisms. _Why:_ many injection and persistence methods still rely on legitimate loader behavior, leaving standard DLL artifacts. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Loaded DLL auditing** — analysts should review DLLs loaded into a process. _Why:_ unexpected DLLs can indicate injected code, side-loaded modules, or persistence through DLL hijacking. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **DLL persistence hijacks** — DLL persistence hijacking belongs in the loader-based detection category. _Why:_ even though the purpose is persistence, the malicious DLL is still loaded through Windows mechanisms and can appear in loaded-module evidence. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **DLL side-loading** — DLL side-loading is included in the loader-based detection category. _Why:_ side-loaded DLLs may look legitimate at execution time because the operating system loader brought them into the process. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Standard memory structures** — the first detection method audits normal in-memory process structures for entries that should not exist. _Why:_ API-loaded modules are typically registered in expected process bookkeeping structures. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Windows API usage** — many injection techniques use Windows API functions to load or register code. _Why:_ API use can make injected code visible in ordinary memory structures despite the malicious intent. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Loaded-code registration** — code loaded through Windows APIs is recorded in expected locations in memory. _Why:_ these records give analysts a place to look for suspicious loaded modules. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **PEB DLL lists** — the Process Environment Block keeps one or more lists of DLLs loaded in a process. _Why:_ the PEB’s loader data can expose DLLs introduced through legitimate loading paths. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **DLL load-order hijacking classification** — DLL load-order hijacking falls under the category of DLLs loaded through legitimate Windows functionality. _Why:_ the artifact may appear as a normal loaded DLL even when the selected DLL is malicious. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Side-loading classification** — side-loading also falls under legitimate-loader analysis because the DLL is ultimately brought in by Windows capabilities. _Why:_ the analyst should not dismiss loader-registered DLLs as benign solely because they were loaded normally. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Prior process-analysis overlap** — auditing unusual process objects such as loaded DLLs and file handles already covers much of the loader-based injection-detection work. _Why:_ earlier memory-analysis steps can contribute directly to code-injection detection. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Loaded DLL process objects** — loaded DLLs are an example of process-associated objects useful for identifying code injection. _Why:_ unexpected loaded modules can reveal injected or hijacked code. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **File handles as supporting artifacts** — file handles are another process object type relevant to this analysis workflow. _Why:_ handles may point to suspicious DLLs or other files associated with injected code. _[GCFA p.517]_

### Executable Memory Locations

- **Unusual executable memory detection** — a second detection approach is to identify executable memory regions where code should not normally reside. _Why:_ injected code must be executable somewhere in memory even when it avoids normal loader records. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Non-API-loaded code** — analysts should look for code that was not loaded through legitimate Windows API calls. _Why:_ stealthier injection methods may bypass normal loader bookkeeping. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Executable page searching** — memory should be searched for executable pages that contain code. _Why:_ execution requires memory pages with execute permissions, giving analysts a practical detection target. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Reflective injection behavior** — reflective injection is presented as a stealthier technique that avoids the Windows API. _Why:_ avoiding the API can keep the payload out of normal loaded-DLL lists. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Reflective injection residue** — even reflective injection leaves code in recognizable locations, such as pages marked executable. _Why:_ bypassing the loader does not eliminate the need for executable memory. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Executable-permission requirement** — every injection method must eventually place code on pages that allow execution. _Why:_ this is a universal constraint analysts can exploit across injection variants. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Out-of-place code** — this detection step focuses on executable pages and code located where they do not belong. _Why:_ anomalous placement can reveal stealthy injected payloads even without normal DLL artifacts. _[GCFA p.517]_

### Kernel and Userland Inconsistencies

- **Kernel/userland inconsistency detection** — a third detection approach compares process information from kernel-level and userland-level sources. _Why:_ advanced manipulation may hide in one view while leaving contradictions in another. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Permission-change artifacts** — permission changes are listed as a type of inconsistency or manipulation to examine. _Why:_ injected code may be allocated or written with one permission set and later changed to look less suspicious. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **File-mapping issues** — file mapping anomalies are listed as process inconsistencies relevant to injection detection. _Why:_ injected or hollowed code may not line up cleanly with the file-backed mappings expected for a normal process. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Pointer modifications** — pointer changes are listed as a manipulation category to investigate. _Why:_ modified pointers can redirect execution to malicious code while preserving parts of a normal-looking process. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Kernel view comparison** — kernel-tracked process information is characterized as harder for malware to change. _Why:_ kernel structures can provide a more resistant reference point during integrity comparisons. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Userland view comparison** — userland process information is characterized as easier for malware to alter. _Why:_ attackers may tamper with userland-visible structures to conceal injected code. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Advanced injection camouflage** — advanced techniques may use the same general ideas as DLL-based loading or executable-memory injection while also modifying memory to avoid looking abnormal. _Why:_ simple checks may miss injected code if attackers clean up or disguise obvious indicators. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Post-allocation permission changes** — advanced injection may change memory permissions after the original allocation. _Why:_ permission transitions can hide the earlier need to write or execute injected content. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Process hollowing pointer changes** — process hollowing is given as an example where pointers may be changed so execution reaches different code. _Why:_ the process may retain legitimate-looking characteristics while running substituted code. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Patching loaded code** — advanced techniques may patch code that was already loaded. _Why:_ modifying existing code can avoid introducing an obvious new module while still changing process behavior. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Multiple memory-tracking structures** — memory objects are recorded in several different memory structures. _Why:_ attackers may fail to alter every related structure consistently. _[GCFA p.517]_
- **Cross-source comparison** — inconsistencies can be found by comparing separate sources of memory-object information. _Why:_ mismatched views can expose manipulation that is hidden in only one structure. _[GCFA p.517]_

- **Multiple analytical views** — Memory-forensics workflows can examine the same available evidence from several different perspectives. _Why:_ viewing data in more than one way increases the chance of finding malicious activity that may be hidden in one representation but visible in another. _[GCFA p.~518]_

- **Detection across process stages** — The same principle used in earlier memory-forensics steps applies here: suspicious activity can be identified by reviewing available memory evidence from different angles. _Why:_ consistent methodology helps analysts avoid relying on a single artifact or tool output. _[GCFA p.~518]_

- **Attack residue principle** — Every intrusion or attack action leaves some trace behind. _Why:_ this is the basis for forensic detection: analysts search for remaining artifacts rather than assuming attacker activity is invisible. _[GCFA p.~518]_

- **Analyst objective** — The analyst’s task is to locate dependable ways to identify the traces left by attacker behavior. _Why:_ reliable detection markers are needed to distinguish meaningful evidence from noise or coincidence. _[GCFA p.~518]_

- **Detection-marker focus** — The page emphasizes finding indicators that can consistently reveal malicious behavior in memory data. _Why:_ dependable markers support repeatable investigation, validation, and threat hunting. _[GCFA p.~518]_

### Volatility Tools

- **Volatility ldrmodules** — identifies DLLs that have been removed from normal loader lists and files that are not backed by ordinary memory-mapped file structures. _Why:_ unlinked DLLs and abnormal mappings are common indicators of stealthy injected code. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **Volatility malfind** — searches for concealed or injected code and can extract the suspicious memory regions it finds. _Why:_ dumping affected regions lets analysts preserve and reverse-engineer injected payloads. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **Volatility hollowfind (Vol2)** — detects multiple artifact patterns associated with process hollowing. _Why:_ process hollowing can make a malicious process appear to be a legitimate executable unless memory artifacts are compared carefully. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **Volatility ptemalfind (Vol3)** — improves on malfind by using page-table information to detect injected code. _Why:_ page tables can reveal executable memory and permissions even when higher-level structures have been manipulated. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **Volatility framework capability** — Volatility has included code-injection detection plugins for a long time. _Why:_ these plugins form a standard baseline for memory-based injection triage. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **ldrmodules detection target** — ldrmodules is used to spot memory locations that appear unusual for loaded modules. _Why:_ advanced malware often places code where normal module-loading behavior would not put it. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **ldrmodules unlinked-DLL detection** — ldrmodules can identify DLLs that are present in memory but missing from expected loader-linked structures. _Why:_ unlinking a DLL is a stealth technique meant to hide code from ordinary module enumeration. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **Advanced-malware behavior** — unusual memory locations and unlinked DLLs are described as common in more sophisticated malware. _Why:_ these artifacts help separate benign process state from deliberate concealment. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **malfind purpose** — malfind is a dedicated scanner for artifacts left by multiple injection methods. _Why:_ one scanner can catch several families of injection behavior during memory triage. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **malfind reflective-injection coverage** — malfind can detect signs associated with reflective injection. _Why:_ reflective loaders avoid normal DLL-loading paths, so memory artifacts become especially important. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **malfind hollowing coverage** — malfind can detect signs associated with process hollowing. _Why:_ hollowed processes may look legitimate in process listings while containing replaced executable memory. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **Anti-plugin adaptation** — the popularity of ldrmodules and malfind has motivated evasion techniques aimed at defeating them. _Why:_ investigators should not treat one plugin’s clean output as conclusive. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **Third-party Volatility contributions** — additional plugins have been contributed to help Volatility keep up with evasion. _Why:_ injection detection evolves as attackers develop countermeasures. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **hollowfind specialization** — hollowfind is a focused plugin for finding advanced behaviors that suggest process hollowing. _Why:_ process hollowing often requires correlation across several process-memory artifacts. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **hollowfind PEB comparison** — hollowfind compares data in the process environment block with data that should correspond to the process VAD. _Why:_ mismatches between PEB and VAD information can expose hollowing or tampering. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **Process Environment Block (PEB)** — the PEB is one source of process metadata used by hollowfind for comparison. _Why:_ attackers may rely on inconsistencies between process metadata and actual memory layout. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **Virtual Address Descriptor (VAD)** — the VAD is the process memory-description source that hollowfind compares against PEB-derived information. _Why:_ VAD state helps reveal what memory regions actually exist in the process. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **hollowfind memory-permission checks** — hollowfind also searches for suspicious memory-section permissions in a way similar to malfind. _Why:_ executable or writable-executable regions can indicate injected code. _[GCFA p.~519]_

- **threadmap plugin** — threadmap is another Volatility 2-only plugin mentioned as similar in purpose. _Why:_ thread-based analysis can expose injection artifacts through execution context. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **threadmap information source** — threadmap primarily uses thread information. _Why:_ threads are described as harder for attackers to manipulate and hide than some other artifacts. _[GCFA p.~519]_
- **threadmap version limit** — threadmap is available only in Volatility 2. _Why:_ tool availability affects which memory-analysis workflow an investigator can use. _[GCFA p.~519]_

- **ptemalfind page-table method** — ptemalfind uses kernel page tables to determine executable locations and permissions. _Why:_ page-table state can provide a lower-level view than userland or loader metadata. _[GCFA p.~519]_

- **ptemalfind hollowing objective** — ptemalfind was designed to improve detection of process hollowing. _Why:_ hollowing detection benefits from checking actual executable mappings rather than trusting process metadata. _[GCFA p.~519]_

### Step 1: Attach To Victim Process

- **Attacker process attachment** — the attacker process must first obtain access to the victim process. _Why:_ without a handle or equivalent access, the attacker cannot manipulate the victim process memory. _[GCFA p.~521]_
- **OpenProcess()** — the example uses the Windows API call `OpenProcess()` for the attacker process to attach to the victim process. _Why:_ this API call is a concrete behavioral indicator for remote process access during injection. _[GCFA p.~521]_
- **Victim process target** — `OpenProcess()` is shown as operating against the victim process. _Why:_ this indicates cross-process access rather than activity limited to the attacker's own address space. _[GCFA p.~521]_
- **Token privilege requirement** — the attacker's process token must include `SeDebugPrivilege` to attach to another process in this example. _Why:_ privilege presence helps explain how the process obtained access and can guide token or SID-focused investigation. _[GCFA p.~521]_
- **SeDebugPrivilege** — `SeDebugPrivilege` is the named privilege required by the attacker token for this process attachment scenario. _Why:_ this privilege is commonly abused because it allows powerful inspection or manipulation of other processes. _[GCFA p.~521]_
- **Administrator default privilege** — Administrator accounts have `SeDebugPrivilege` by default. _Why:_ admin-context execution makes this injection prerequisite easier for malware or an attacker-operated process to satisfy. _[GCFA p.~521]_

### Step 2: Allocate And Write DLL Path

- **Remote allocation goal** — after attaching, the attacker process allocates a small memory region inside the victim process. _Why:_ injected workflows often need remote memory to stage parameters or payload-related data. _[GCFA p.~521]_
- **Allocated data purpose** — the allocated victim-process memory is used to hold the full path of the malicious DLL that will later be loaded. _Why:_ the DLL path is the handoff data needed for a later load operation. _[GCFA p.~521]_
- **VirtualAllocEx()** — the example uses `VirtualAllocEx()` to reserve or allocate memory inside the victim process. _Why:_ this API is a strong signal of remote memory preparation associated with injection. _[GCFA p.~521]_
- **WriteProcessMemory()** — the example uses `WriteProcessMemory()` to place data into the newly allocated memory in the victim process. _Why:_ writing into another process is a key behavioral artifact of injection. _[GCFA p.~521]_
- **API sequence in step 2** — `VirtualAllocEx()` is shown before `WriteProcessMemory()`. _Why:_ the attacker first creates usable space in the victim and then writes the DLL path into that space. _[GCFA p.~521]_
- **Written string value** — the diagram shows the DLL path string `C:\evil.dll`. _Why:_ this is the exact malicious DLL path value depicted as being staged inside the victim process. _[GCFA p.~521]_
- **Full DLL path staging** — the attacker writes the complete malicious DLL path rather than only a filename. _Why:_ a full path reduces ambiguity for the later DLL load operation and can appear as a recoverable memory artifact. _[GCFA p.~521]_
- **Newly allocated memory destination** — the malicious DLL path is written into the memory region that was just allocated inside the victim process. _Why:_ this links the allocation and write artifacts as parts of the same injection chain. _[GCFA p.~521]_
- **Ultimate loading intent** — the malicious DLL path is staged because the DLL is intended to be loaded afterward. _Why:_ the attach-and-allocate phase is preparatory, not the final execution step. _[GCFA p.~521]_

## Page 522

### Simple DLL Injection Execute Step

- **Injection phase 3** — the page describes the final simple DLL injection phase as the point where injected code is loaded and run. _Why:_ this distinguishes execution from earlier setup steps such as allocating memory or writing the DLL path. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **Attacker process role** — the attacker-controlled process initiates execution inside another process. _Why:_ identifying the source process helps trace the process responsible for causing injected code to run. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **Victim process role** — the victim process is the target process where the injected DLL code ultimately executes. _Why:_ defenders need to separate the process that initiated injection from the process now hosting malicious code. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **CreateRemoteThread() purpose** — `CreateRemoteThread()` is used by the attacker process to create a new thread inside the victim process. _Why:_ remote thread creation is a common execution primitive for process injection detection. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **Remote thread execution context** — the new thread runs within the address space of the victim process. _Why:_ this explains how malicious activity can appear to originate from an otherwise legitimate process. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **DLL path argument** — the injected execution step passes the previously written full DLL path as an argument. _Why:_ memory containing a suspicious path can be evidence of DLL injection preparation. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **Shown DLL path** — the diagram shows the malicious DLL path as `C:\evil.dll`. _Why:_ concrete path strings in process memory or telemetry can be high-value injection indicators. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **Shown DLL filename** — the diagram identifies the payload filename as `evil.dll`. _Why:_ the DLL name is an artifact defenders could search for on disk, in memory, or in logs. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **LoadLibraryA() argument** — `LoadLibraryA()` is supplied as the function to be executed by the remote thread. _Why:_ seeing `LoadLibraryA()` used with a foreign process is a classic simple DLL injection pattern. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **CreateRemoteThread() and LoadLibraryA() relationship** — `CreateRemoteThread()` causes execution of `LoadLibraryA()` in the victim process. _Why:_ this links the thread-creation API to the actual DLL-loading action. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **DLL retrieval from disk** — `LoadLibraryA()` causes Windows to retrieve the specified DLL from the filesystem. _Why:_ this creates disk-based artifacts that can be recovered or correlated with memory evidence. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **DLL loading into memory** — after retrieval from disk, the DLL is mapped and prepared in memory by the normal Windows loader path. _Why:_ properly loaded DLLs can appear in loader-maintained module lists, making them visible to module-enumeration techniques. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **Code execution start** — once the DLL is loaded, execution begins inside the newly created thread. _Why:_ this is the moment the victim process becomes an execution host for attacker-controlled code. _[GCFA p.~522]_

### Disk Requirement

- **LoadLibraryA() disk dependency** — Windows API loading through `LoadLibraryA()` requires the DLL to exist on disk. _Why:_ this limitation gives investigators a filesystem artifact to search for in simple DLL injection cases. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **No standard Windows memory-only loader API** — the page states there is no legitimate Windows function that loads code from a location other than disk. _Why:_ memory-only loading generally requires nonstandard techniques and is therefore more suspicious. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **Restriction bypass preview** — the page notes that some malware avoids the disk-loading restriction by using other methods discussed later. _Why:_ this frames reflective or manual loading as an evasion of normal Windows loader behavior. _[GCFA p.~522]_

### Payload Variants

- **DLL payload example** — the illustrated injection workflow uses a DLL as the malicious payload. _Why:_ DLL injection is the baseline technique from which related injection methods can be compared. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **Shellcode substitution** — shellcode can replace the DLL payload with only modest additional implementation work. _Why:_ investigators should not assume the same injection pattern always leaves a DLL file artifact. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **Arbitrary victim execution** — the described method can force a chosen victim process to execute attacker-controlled code. _Why:_ this is the central forensic significance of process injection. _[GCFA p.~522]_

### Windows Session Limitation

- **Windows Vista behavior change** — beginning with Windows Vista, `CreateRemoteThread()` is limited to processes in the same Windows session. _Why:_ OS version and session boundaries affect whether this injection method can work directly. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **Session isolation impact** — system processes run in a session isolated from user processes. _Why:_ this isolation prevents straightforward `CreateRemoteThread()` injection from a user session into many system-session targets. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **Same-session requirement** — `CreateRemoteThread()` only works across processes that share a Windows session under the stated Vista-and-newer behavior. _Why:_ failed or alternative injection attempts may be explained by session mismatch. _[GCFA p.~522]_

### Malware Evasion APIs

- **Mimikatz behavior** — Mimikatz is cited as modern malware/tooling that avoids the `CreateRemoteThread()` session restriction. _Why:_ known offensive tools may use alternative thread-creation APIs instead of the obvious API. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **Meterpreter behavior** — Meterpreter is cited as modern malware/tooling that avoids the `CreateRemoteThread()` session restriction. _Why:_ defenders should not rely only on `CreateRemoteThread()` telemetry to detect injection. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **NtCreateThreadEx alternative** — `NtCreateThreadEx` is named as a similar but undocumented API that can be used to bypass the `CreateRemoteThread()` limitation. _Why:_ monitoring lower-level or undocumented thread creation paths is important for detecting modern injection. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **RtlCreateUserThread alternative** — `RtlCreateUserThread` is named as another similar undocumented API used to evade the same restriction. _Why:_ API-based detection must include less common thread-creation functions. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **Injection workflow continuity** — aside from replacing the thread-creation API, the remaining injection steps are mostly unchanged. _Why:_ artifacts from allocation, path writing, DLL loading, and victim-process execution may still exist even when `CreateRemoteThread()` is absent. _[GCFA p.~522]_

- **Example victim process** — the shown injection target is `svchost.exe`. _Why:_ injected code must be tied back to the process that hosts it. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Example victim PID** — the target process ID in the example is `1000`. _Why:_ PID scoping lets the analyst focus plugin output on the affected process. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Injection API · CreateRemoteThread()** — the example used `CreateRemoteThread()` as part of the injection method. _Why:_ remote-thread creation is a common way to execute code inside another process. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Injection API · LoadLibraryA()** — the example used `LoadLibraryA()` to load the injected DLL into the target process. _Why:_ this API causes the injected DLL to be registered through normal loader mechanisms. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **API-loaded injected code visibility** — code loaded through API libraries is commonly visible in both PEB loader records and VAD-backed mappings. _Why:_ this makes API-based DLL injection easier to spot with tools that compare these data sources. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Malicious DLL appearance** — the injected DLL can resemble ordinary loaded DLLs in the listing. _Why:_ analysts cannot rely only on the presence of a DLL row; path and context matter. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Suspicious path principle** — a DLL loaded from a location unlike the other entries should be investigated. _Why:_ abnormal load locations can distinguish injected or attacker-controlled DLLs from standard system libraries. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Common legitimate DLL directory · System32** — many legitimate DLLs normally load from `\Windows\System32`. _Why:_ this path is a baseline for judging whether a mapped DLL location is expected. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Common legitimate DLL directory · Program Files** — legitimate application DLLs may load from `\Program Files`. _Why:_ this directory is another expected source location for normal modules. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Common legitimate DLL directory · WinSxS** — Windows side-by-side component DLLs may load from `\Windows\WinSxS`. _Why:_ this path helps separate normal Windows component loading from odd locations. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Suspicious directory · Temp** — the example contains a DLL loaded from a `Temp` directory. _Why:_ temporary directories are unusual sources for process modules and are often attacker-writable. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Suspicious DLL name · winsrv.dll** — the page flags `winsrv.dll` as a name not normally present in a default Windows installation. _Why:_ an unfamiliar DLL name in an unusual directory is a strong investigation lead. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Legitimacy caveat** — the unusual `winsrv.dll` entry could still be benign. _Why:_ forensic triage should treat the item as suspicious, not automatically malicious, until corroborated. _[GCFA p.523]_

### Volatility ldrmodules

- **Command shown** — the terminal command is `vol.py -f memory.img windows.ldrmodules.LdrModules --pid 1000`. _Why:_ it documents the exact Volatility invocation used to enumerate loaded modules for the process. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Memory image argument** — the command analyzes `memory.img`. _Why:_ the memory image is the evidence source for module enumeration. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Plugin namespace** — the command uses `windows.ldrmodules.LdrModules`. _Why:_ this identifies the Volatility 3 plugin used for PEB/VAD module correlation. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **PID filter flag** — the command uses `--pid 1000`. _Why:_ filtering limits output to the suspected `svchost.exe` process. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **ldrmodules plugin purpose** — `ldrmodules` combines loader information from multiple memory data sources. _Why:_ cross-source comparison helps reveal module hiding and inconsistent loader state. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **ldrmodules versus dlllist** — `dlllist` reports only PEB-derived module information, while `ldrmodules` adds VAD-derived context. _Why:_ `ldrmodules` provides more evidence for detecting injected or hidden modules. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **dlllist similarity** — `ldrmodules` output resembles `dlllist` output but contains additional columns and context. _Why:_ analysts familiar with `dlllist` can extend interpretation to richer `ldrmodules` output. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **PEB source fields** — `InLoad`, `InInit`, and `InMem` reflect PEB loader lists tracking loaded code. _Why:_ these booleans show whether a module appears in specific PEB loader lists. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **VAD source fields** — `MappedPath` and `Base` come from VAD tree-related mapping information. _Why:_ VAD data can expose mapped code even when loader lists are manipulated. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Extra data in this example** — the extra `ldrmodules` correlation is not strictly necessary here because the malicious code was loaded through normal Windows APIs. _Why:_ standard API loading leaves ordinary records, so the anomaly is visible without advanced hiding detection. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Future hiding relevance** — later hiding techniques require `ldrmodules`-style interpretation to identify inconsistencies. _Why:_ module hiding can remove or alter normal loader records while leaving other memory artifacts. _[GCFA p.523]_

### PEB, VAD, And InInit Behavior

- **PEB definition context** — the Process Environment Block is the source for loader-list module information. _Why:_ PEB lists are a key Windows user-mode structure for loaded module tracking. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **VAD tree definition context** — the Virtual Address Descriptor tree supplies memory mapping information such as mapped paths and base addresses. _Why:_ VAD records describe process memory regions independently of PEB loader lists. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Process executable InInit exception** — the process image binary normally does not appear in the PEB `InInit` list. _Why:_ a `False` value for the executable in `InInit` is expected and should not be treated as malicious by itself. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Example executable exception** — `svchost.exe` has `InInit` set to `False` in the shown output. _Why:_ this row illustrates the normal executable-specific exception. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Normal process pattern** — every normal process is expected to have a process-image entry with this same `InInit` absence pattern. _Why:_ analysts need this baseline to avoid false positives. _[GCFA p.523]_

### MemProcFS

- **MemProcFS module listing** — MemProcFS can list loaded DLLs for each process. _Why:_ it provides another way to inspect process module state from memory. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **MemProcFS findevil module** — MemProcFS `findevil` can identify anomalies across PEB and VAD data sources. _Why:_ automated PEB/VAD inconsistency checks help surface injected or hidden modules. _[GCFA p.523]_

### ldrmodules Output Columns

- **Output column · Pid** — `Pid` records the process ID associated with each module row. _Why:_ this ties each mapped module to the owning process. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Output column · Process** — `Process` records the process image name. _Why:_ this gives the analyst human-readable process context. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Output column · Base** — `Base` records the module base address. _Why:_ base addresses identify where the module is mapped in process virtual memory. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Output column · InLoad** — `InLoad` indicates whether the module appears in the PEB load-order list. _Why:_ missing loader-list membership can indicate tampering or unusual loading. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Output column · InInit** — `InInit` indicates whether the module appears in the PEB initialization-order list. _Why:_ this is one of the PEB list checks used for loader consistency. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Output column · InMem** — `InMem` indicates whether the module appears in the PEB memory-order list. _Why:_ this contributes to cross-checking loader visibility. _[GCFA p.523]_
- **Output column · MappedPath** — `MappedPath` records the mapped file path associated with the module. _Why:_ path anomalies often reveal attacker-controlled DLL locations. _[GCFA p.523]_

## Page 525

### Reflective Code Injection

- **Reflective code injection** — a code-injection method for running attacker-controlled code without directly invoking `LoadLibrary`. _Why:_ avoiding `LoadLibrary` changes the normal artifacts defenders expect from Windows module loading. _[GCFA p.525]_

- **Arbitrary execution goal** — the technique is used to execute arbitrary code inside a target context. _Why:_ arbitrary execution inside another process is a core behavior of post-exploitation implants and malware. _[GCFA p.525]_

- **Custom reflective loader** — reflective injection relies on its own loader logic rather than the standard Windows loader. _Why:_ custom loading bypasses normal operating-system bookkeeping for loaded modules. _[GCFA p.525]_

- **Windows loader avoidance** — the defining trait is self-loading code that does not explicitly use the Windows loader interface represented by `LoadLibrary`. _Why:_ this separates reflective loading from basic DLL injection workflows that depend on `LoadLibrary`. _[GCFA p.525]_

- **Broad reflective definition** — for the courseware’s purpose, any method where code loads itself without explicitly calling `LoadLibrary` is treated as reflective. _Why:_ this gives investigators a practical category even though many variants exist. _[GCFA p.525]_

- **Stephen Fewer** — Stephen Fewer developed reflective code injection to reduce the observable footprint of code-injection activity. _Why:_ the origin explains why the method emphasizes stealth and minimal host artifacts. _[GCFA p.525]_

- **Footprint reduction** — the technique was designed to leave fewer conventional signs than older injection approaches. _Why:_ fewer artifacts make host-based and audit-based detection harder. _[GCFA p.525]_

- **Remote-process execution** — the original concept focused on getting code to run inside another process without relying on the Windows loader. _Why:_ remote execution is what lets the injected component operate under another process’s identity and memory space. _[GCFA p.525]_

### Loader And Registration Artifacts

- **No standard module registration** — when `LoadLibrary` is avoided, the injected code is not added to the usual in-memory module tracking lists. _Why:_ tools that enumerate standard loader lists may miss the injected component. _[GCFA p.525]_

- **Host-system registration absence** — reflective code is not registered with the host system through normal loader mechanisms. _Why:_ the lack of registration makes the injected code difficult to discover with ordinary auditing or inventory methods. _[GCFA p.525]_

- **Hidden from many tools** — because the code is absent from standard in-memory lists, many security and auditing tools may not report it. _Why:_ defenders must look beyond ordinary module listings when investigating suspicious processes. _[GCFA p.525]_

- **Disk-loading requirement bypass** — avoiding `LoadLibrary` also avoids the normal requirement that the code be loaded from a disk-backed file. _Why:_ memory-only payloads reduce file-system evidence and shrink the detection surface. _[GCFA p.525]_

- **Memory-only code support** — reflective loading can execute code that exists only in memory. _Why:_ memory-resident payloads can evade file-based scanning and leave fewer persistent artifacts. _[GCFA p.525]_

- **Network-delivered code support** — reflective injection can use code obtained directly from a network source. _Why:_ network-to-memory loading can bypass the creation of a conventional malicious file on disk. _[GCFA p.525]_

- **Network or memory injection** — the page explicitly notes that code can be injected directly from network or memory sources. _Why:_ this highlights why disk-centric triage alone can miss reflective payloads. _[GCFA p.525]_

## Page 526

### Code Injection Detection

- **Code injection via DLL loading** — a basic injection approach makes a separate process load an additional DLL into its address space. _Why:_ injected DLLs can expose malware execution inside an otherwise legitimate process. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Injected DLL visibility in the PEB** — a newly loaded DLL may appear in the target process's Process Environment Block. _Why:_ the PEB can reveal module-loading activity associated with injection. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Volatility `dlllist`** — Volatility's `dlllist` plugin can be used to enumerate DLLs recorded for a process. _Why:_ it can identify straightforward DLL injection cases where the module is visible through normal loader structures. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Volatility `ldrmodules`** — Volatility's `ldrmodules` plugin can help identify loaded modules in a process. _Why:_ it supports detection of injected modules by examining loader-related module metadata. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Simple injection detectability** — DLL-loading injection methods are comparatively easy for defensive tools to notice. _Why:_ this detection pressure encourages malware authors to use less conventional injection techniques. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Evasion tradeoff** — malware that avoids normal Windows code-loading mechanisms may produce different forensic signatures. _Why:_ bypassing one detection surface often creates another artifact investigators can target. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Forensic artifact principle** — attempts to hide activity still tend to leave evidence elsewhere. _Why:_ this principle supports hunting for indirect traces of concealed execution. _[GCFA p. 526]_

### Three-Step Memory Detection Process

- **Detection step 1 · Executable memory** — the first suspicious condition is a memory region with execute permissions. _Why:_ executable permissions indicate the region may be able to run code. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Detection step 2 · No disk backing** — the second suspicious condition is a memory region that is not mapped to a file on disk. _Why:_ legitimate Windows code loading normally maps executable content back to an on-disk source. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Detection step 3 · Code present** — the third suspicious condition is a memory region that actually contains code, such as a PE file or shellcode. _Why:_ confirming code content reduces noise from unusual but harmless memory regions. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Advanced injection coverage** — the three-step process applies to many sophisticated injection styles, including reflective injection. _Why:_ reflective and similar techniques may evade simple DLL-listing checks but still create suspicious memory properties. _[GCFA p. 526]_

### VAD Tree Artifacts

- **VAD tree** — the Virtual Address Descriptor tree records memory sections associated with a process. _Why:_ it provides a process-level map of memory regions that can be inspected for injection indicators. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Per-process VAD traversal** — analysis tools can walk each process's VAD tree and review every memory location. _Why:_ systematic VAD inspection allows broad hunting across process memory rather than checking only loaded-module lists. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Memory section protection value** — each memory section has an assigned protection or permissions setting. _Why:_ permission values can identify regions capable of executing injected code. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Suspicious permission example** — `Page_Execute_ReadWrite` is presented as an unusual and notable memory protection value. _Why:_ pages that are writable and executable are strongly associated with injection techniques. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Writable executable memory risk** — memory that can both be modified and executed is dangerous. _Why:_ attackers can place or alter code in such regions and then run it. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Injection marker** — writable-and-executable permissions are described as a recurring artifact left by many injection methods. _Why:_ this makes the permission pattern a useful hunting signal. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Mapped file path in VAD** — the VAD tree stores the disk path mapped to a memory section when one exists. _Why:_ investigators can check whether executable memory corresponds to a legitimate file-backed mapping. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Auditable VAD path** — the mapped path recorded in the VAD can be reviewed during analysis. _Why:_ absence of a path on executable memory can indicate injected or manually mapped code. _[GCFA p. 526]_

### Legitimate Code Loading

- **Disk-backed code loading** — Windows legitimately loads code such as DLLs and EXEs from disk. _Why:_ executable memory without a disk-backed source is suspicious because it deviates from normal loading behavior. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **DLL disk mapping** — when a DLL is loaded normally, its code section maps back to the original disk path. _Why:_ the disk mapping gives investigators a reference point for validating loaded code. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **EXE disk mapping** — when an executable is loaded normally, its code section maps back to the original disk path. _Why:_ a missing backing file for executable code may indicate nonstandard loading. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Executable flag expectation** — a memory region should not be executable if it does not contain code. _Why:_ executable permissions on non-code memory can signal suspicious or abnormal memory handling. _[GCFA p. 526]_

### False Positives And Sanity Checks

- **False positives** — the executable-memory and disk-backing checks can detect many injection cases but also produce benign hits. _Why:_ analysts must validate suspicious regions before treating them as malicious. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Legitimate `.NET` activity** — normal software using `.NET` can create memory patterns that resemble suspicious executable memory. _Why:_ managed runtime behavior can cause false positives in injection hunting. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Just-in-time compiler activity** — legitimate just-in-time compilation can create memory regions with unusual permissions. _Why:_ JIT-generated code may look suspicious even when no malware is present. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Final code-content check** — analysts should verify whether suspicious memory actually contains executable code. _Why:_ this helps distinguish real injection candidates from benign unusual memory sections. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Portable Executable content** — a suspicious memory area may contain a PE file. _Why:_ PE content in an unusual memory region can indicate injected or manually loaded Windows code. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Shellcode content** — a suspicious memory area may contain shellcode. _Why:_ shellcode in executable memory is a strong indicator of malicious in-memory execution. _[GCFA p. 526]_

- **Unusual permissions without dangerous code** — some memory regions may have abnormal permissions but contain no harmful executable content. _Why:_ identifying these cases prevents analysts from over-counting benign artifacts as injection. _[GCFA p. 526]_

### Memory Analysis Tooling

- **Manual memory-check complexity** — detecting suspicious in-memory conditions can involve complicated checks, but dedicated forensic tools can automate much of that work. _Why:_ analysts can rely on purpose-built tooling to surface candidate findings instead of manually performing every low-level memory validation step. _[GCFA p.527]_

- **Volatility `malfind` plugin** — Volatility includes a `malfind` plugin intended to identify suspicious process memory regions for analyst review. _Why:_ `malfind` is a standard memory-forensics capability for triaging possible injected or malicious code in process memory. _[GCFA p.527]_

- **MemProcFS `findevil` capability** — MemProcFS includes a `findevil` feature designed to locate suspicious or malicious indicators in memory and present them for review. _Why:_ `findevil` provides another automated route for surfacing memory-resident attack artifacts. _[GCFA p.527]_

- **Automated review output** — both Volatility `malfind` and MemProcFS `findevil` are described as producing results that analysts must review rather than final conclusions. _Why:_ tool output should be treated as investigative leads requiring analyst validation. _[GCFA p.527]_

- **Purpose-built detection checks** — Volatility `malfind` and MemProcFS `findevil` were specifically created to perform the relevant memory-analysis checks discussed on the page. _Why:_ these tools encode specialized logic for detecting suspicious memory characteristics that would otherwise be tedious or error-prone to inspect manually. _[GCFA p.527]_

## Page 528

### Malfind Purpose

- **windows.malfind.Malfind** — Volatility’s Malfind plugin examines process memory regions for signs consistent with injected code. _Why:_ it helps locate suspicious in-memory code that may not appear as a normal on-disk module. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Code-injection scan target** — Malfind focuses on memory sections belonging to processes. _Why:_ process address spaces are where many injection techniques place malicious code. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Identified memory sections** — Memory regions flagged by Malfind can be exported from the memory image. _Why:_ dumped regions can be examined outside Volatility with reverse-engineering or malware-analysis tools. _[GCFA p.~528]_

### Important Parameters

- **`--dump`** — This option specifies a directory where Malfind should save extracted suspicious memory sections. _Why:_ preserving the bytes enables follow-on static analysis, disassembly, antivirus scanning, or reverse engineering. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **`--pid`** — This option restricts Malfind output to selected process IDs. _Why:_ narrowing analysis to known or suspected processes reduces noise in large memory images. _[GCFA p.~528]_

### Detection Logic

- **Executable memory indicator** — Malfind treats executable memory permissions as one sign that a region may contain injected code. _Why:_ injected payloads often require execute permissions to run from process memory. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **No mapped file indicator** — Malfind also looks for executable regions that lack an associated file mapping on disk. _Why:_ injected code commonly exists only in private process memory rather than as a normal loaded file-backed image. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Per-process scanning** — Malfind evaluates memory sections assigned to each process. _Why:_ injection is process-specific, so each process address space must be checked independently. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Hit reporting** — When Malfind identifies a suspicious section, it prints the finding to standard output. _Why:_ console output gives the analyst immediate triage details for each candidate injected region. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Conditional extraction** — Malfind writes a suspicious section to disk only when the analyst supplies `--dump`. _Why:_ extraction is optional because dumping every hit can create many files and requires analyst intent. _[GCFA p.~528]_

### Dumped Sections

- **Dump file granularity** — Malfind stores each dumped suspicious memory region as a separate file. _Why:_ separate files make it easier to track, analyze, and compare individual memory sections. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Dump file naming** — Dumped section filenames are based on the process ID and the section’s virtual-address offset. _Why:_ the filename preserves the process and location context needed to map the dump back to memory-analysis output. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Reverse engineering target** — Dumped Malfind sections can be analyzed with reverse-engineering tools. _Why:_ manual code analysis can confirm whether the bytes are shellcode, a PE image, or benign executable memory. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Antivirus scanning target** — Dumped Malfind sections can be submitted to antivirus scanners. _Why:_ signature or heuristic detections may help classify suspicious memory content. _[GCFA p.~528]_

### Analyst Validation

- **Executable-code confirmation** — A Malfind hit still requires confirmation that the region actually contains executable code. _Why:_ memory permissions alone do not prove malicious injection. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Analyst responsibility** — Malfind does not fully decide whether a flagged section is real injected code; the analyst performs the final validation. _Why:_ this prevents treating every heuristic match as confirmed malware. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Portable executable knowledge** — Understanding PE headers helps analysts judge Malfind output. _Why:_ injected DLLs or mapped images may expose PE structures that distinguish code from unrelated data. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Shellcode knowledge** — Familiarity with shellcode helps validate suspicious regions that do not look like normal PE files. _Why:_ raw injected payloads may be position-independent code without standard executable headers. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Disassembly sanity check** — Disassembling flagged bytes is useful for evaluating possible false positives. _Why:_ valid instructions, suspicious API usage, or nonsensical bytes can separate real code from benign regions. _[GCFA p.~528]_

### Investigative Notes

- **Modern malware limitation** — Newer malware can outperform or evade Malfind’s detection approach. _Why:_ current injection methods may deliberately alter the memory markers Malfind expects. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Educational value** — Malfind remains useful for learning why injection detection is difficult. _Why:_ its strengths and false positives demonstrate the practical limits of memory heuristics. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **False positives** — Malfind output can include benign memory regions. _Why:_ analysts must avoid treating every suspicious page as malicious without verification. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Multiple hits per process** — A single process can contain more than one Malfind-identified section. _Why:_ injected code may occupy multiple regions, and benign executable private pages may also appear more than once. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Unusual benign pages** — Some memory pages can look strange while still being legitimate. _Why:_ benign edge cases contribute to Malfind noise and require analyst review. _[GCFA p.~528]_

### Output Fields

- **`PID` field** — The PID column reports the process identifier. _Why:_ it links a suspicious memory section to the exact process instance. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **`Process` field** — The Process column reports the process name. _Why:_ process names provide quick context for whether a hit appears expected or suspicious. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **`Start VPN` field** — The Start VPN column reports the starting offset of the virtual page number for the memory region. _Why:_ it identifies where the suspicious section begins in the process address space. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **`End VPN` field** — The End VPN column reports the ending offset of the virtual page number for the memory region. _Why:_ it identifies the region boundary and supports size/location analysis. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **`Tag` field** — The Tag column reports the pool tag associated with the memory section type. _Why:_ pool tags help interpret what kind of memory allocation or object is being examined. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **`Protection` field** — The Protection column reports the permissions applied to the memory section. _Why:_ executable permissions are central to Malfind’s injection heuristic. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **`CommitCharge` field** — The CommitCharge column reports the number of committed pages assigned in RAM and the page file. _Why:_ committed-page counts help describe the memory resources backing the suspicious region. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **`PrivateMemory` field** — The PrivateMemory column reports whether the memory is mapped or private. _Why:_ private executable memory is more suspicious than ordinary file-mapped memory. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **`PrivateMemory` value `0`** — A value of `0` means the memory is mapped. _Why:_ mapped memory is associated with a backing object and may be less suspicious depending on context. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **`PrivateMemory` value `1`** — A value of `1` means the memory is private. _Why:_ private executable memory is a common characteristic of injected code. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Volatility 3 column caveat** — The listed Malfind columns describe Volatility 3 output and differ somewhat from Volatility 2. _Why:_ analysts must account for version-specific output when comparing notes, commands, or screenshots. _[GCFA p.~528]_

### Tool Background

- **Core Volatility plugin** — Malfind has historically been one of the main plugins in the Volatility framework. _Why:_ it is a standard first-pass memory-forensics tool for injection triage. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Plugin author** — Malfind was created by Michael Hale Ligh. _Why:_ attribution helps connect the plugin to established malware-analysis methodology and tooling history. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Malware Analyst’s Cookbook association** — Michael Hale Ligh is associated with *Malware Analyst’s Cookbook*. _Why:_ the plugin comes from a practitioner known for malware-analysis techniques. _[GCFA p.~528]_

### Effectiveness And Evasion

- **Traditional injection success** — Malfind works well against many traditional code-injection techniques. _Why:_ older injection methods often leave the executable-private-memory pattern Malfind checks for. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Reflective injection coverage** — Malfind can detect more advanced techniques such as reflective injection. _Why:_ reflective loaders often create suspicious executable memory without a normal disk-backed module. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Evasion by marker modification** — Newer injection techniques may alter memory indicators to avoid Malfind detection. _Why:_ attackers can target the exact heuristics defenders rely on. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **First-pass role** — Malfind remains useful as an initial detection pass. _Why:_ it can quickly surface candidate injected regions even though it is not sufficient by itself. _[GCFA p.~528]_
- **Need for added detection** — Additional code-injection detection methods are needed beyond Malfind. _Why:_ relying only on Malfind leaves gaps against evasive or modern injection tradecraft. _[GCFA p.~528]_

### Volatility Malfind Output

- **Malfind memory-section preview** — the output shows the beginning of each identified memory region as raw hexadecimal bytes. _Why:_ the byte preview helps an analyst quickly recognize file signatures or unusual injected content. _[GCFA p.529]_

- **Malfind disassembly preview** — the output also renders the start of the same memory region as assembly instructions. _Why:_ immediate disassembly helps distinguish executable code from non-code data during triage. _[GCFA p.529]_

- **Portable Executable header clue** — the displayed hex can reveal an `MZ` signature at the start of a memory section. _Why:_ `MZ` indicates a Windows Portable Executable image, which can support a DLL or PE-injection finding. _[GCFA p.529]_

- **Shellcode clue** — if the displayed bytes and disassembly do not resemble a PE header, the section may instead contain shellcode or other raw executable content. _Why:_ injected shellcode may not have normal PE structure, so analysts must inspect both bytes and instructions. _[GCFA p.529]_

### Dumping Suspicious Sections

- **Volatility 3 `--dump` option** — suspicious memory sections identified by malfind can be exported with `--dump`. _Why:_ dumping preserves the full region for deeper offline analysis instead of relying only on the preview. _[GCFA p.529]_

- **Dumped-section disassembly** — exported memory sections can be opened in a disassembler such as IDA Pro. _Why:_ full disassembly supports control-flow analysis, API review, and malware reverse engineering. _[GCFA p.529]_

- **Dumped-section malware scanning** — exported memory sections can be checked with anti-malware signatures. _Why:_ signature scanning may identify known malware families or injected payloads. _[GCFA p.529]_

- **Dumped-section string review** — exported memory sections can be searched manually for notable strings. _Why:_ strings may expose commands, URLs, file paths, registry keys, mutex names, or other indicators. _[GCFA p.529]_

- **Recommendation to dump findings** — memory sections located by malfind should be dumped for follow-up analysis. _Why:_ the preview is only a triage aid; the full content is needed for confident conclusions. _[GCFA p.529]_

### Volatility Version Differences

- **Volatility 2 equivalent plugin** — the Volatility 2 counterpart to the Volatility 3 malfind capability is also named `malfind`. _Why:_ analysts working with older workflows can map the same investigative task to the Volatility 2 plugin. _[GCFA p.529]_

- **Volatility 2 dump flag** — in Volatility 2, memory sections are dumped with `--dump-dir=<directory>`. _Why:_ the dumping syntax differs between framework versions, so using the correct flag matters operationally. _[GCFA p.529]_

- **Volatility 3 malfind port** — the Volatility 3 version of malfind was not implemented as a direct one-for-one copy of the Volatility 2 plugin. _Why:_ analysts should expect behavioral and output differences between the two framework generations. _[GCFA p.529]_

- **Volatility 3 disassembly improvement** — Volatility 3 provides stronger disassembly support than the older implementation. _Why:_ better instruction rendering improves rapid assessment of suspicious executable memory. _[GCFA p.529]_

- **Volatility 3 64-bit analysis advantage** — the improved Volatility 3 disassembly is especially useful for 64-bit samples. _Why:_ modern Windows malware and injected code are often 64-bit, making accurate disassembly important for analysis. _[GCFA p.529]_

### Code Injection Evasion Trends

- **Detection-driven injection evolution** — Modern injection methods are intentionally engineered to bypass common detection logic. _Why:_ defenders should expect injection tradecraft to change as analysis tools improve. _[GCFA p.~536]_
- **Header alteration** — Injected payloads may modify their in-memory headers after loading. _Why:_ header tampering can hide signatures that memory scanners often use to recognize executable content. _[GCFA p.~536]_
- **Header removal** — Injected payloads may erase header data from memory. _Why:_ removing headers can make executable regions appear less obviously malicious during memory inspection. _[GCFA p.~536]_
- **Header mirroring** — Injected code may copy or imitate benign-looking header structures. _Why:_ mirrored headers can mislead tools or analysts that rely on header-based identification. _[GCFA p.~536]_
- **Permission manipulation** — Malware may change memory permissions to avoid leaving regions marked as read-write-execute. _Why:_ RWX memory is a common suspicious indicator, so avoiding it reduces detection visibility. _[GCFA p.~536]_
- **PEB manipulation** — Malware may alter Process Environment Block data structures. _Why:_ the PEB is userland-accessible and can be abused to distort process and module evidence. _[GCFA p.~536]_
- **Process masquerading through PEB changes** — Malware may alter PEB fields so a process appears to have a different name or file path. _Why:_ manipulated identity fields can mislead triage and process lineage analysis. _[GCFA p.~536]_
- **Module overwriting** — Injected code may overwrite an existing module in memory. _Why:_ replacing legitimate module contents can hide malicious code behind expected module metadata. _[GCFA p.~536]_
- **Process hollowing** — Malware may hollow a process and place different code inside its address space. _Why:_ hollowing lets malicious code execute under the appearance of a legitimate process. _[GCFA p.~536]_
- **Module patching** — Attackers may patch loaded module contents. _Why:_ in-memory patches can alter execution while preserving enough normal structure to evade simple checks. _[GCFA p.~536]_

- **Orphan process detection** — Processes without expected parentage can still be useful simple indicators. _Why:_ process tree anomalies are commonly associated with malicious activity. _[GCFA p.~536]_
- **Unusual parent process detection** — Abnormal parent-child process relationships remain relevant detection clues. _Why:_ injected or malicious execution chains often produce process ancestry that does not match normal behavior. _[GCFA p.~536]_

### Injection Evasion Techniques

- **Injected-code camouflage** — Attackers may hide injected code by altering already-loaded code rather than placing an obvious new payload region in memory. _Why:_ this reduces the chance that basic injection checks will identify a separate malicious allocation. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Module stomping** — A malicious implant can overwrite the in-memory contents of a legitimate DLL while retaining the appearance of a normal loaded module. _Why:_ the memory region may look tied to a trusted DLL even though its contents have been replaced. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Patching into existing code** — More advanced injection can involve modifying code that already exists inside a process. _Why:_ this can avoid indicators that rely on newly allocated executable memory. _[GCFA p.~537]_

### Dumping Suspicious Memory

- **Deeper inspection requirement** — Stealthier injected code often requires analysts to examine suspicious memory contents directly. _Why:_ metadata alone may not reveal payloads that have been deliberately disguised. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Memory-section dumping** — Exporting suspicious memory regions can help defeat evasion based on altered headers, padding, or some forms of patching. _Why:_ analysts can inspect the real bytes present in memory instead of relying only on structural hints. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Volatility malfind dump option** — The `--dump` option for `malfind` writes the full contents of each suspicious memory section into separate output files. _Why:_ it creates standalone artifacts that can be searched, scanned, or reverse engineered. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Dumped file extension** — The example output uses `.dmp` files for dumped suspicious memory sections. _Why:_ these files are the extracted memory regions produced for follow-on analysis. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Volatility 2 dump naming basis** — In Volatility 2, dumped memory-section filenames include the injected process offset. _Why:_ the filename itself preserves the process object reference used by the framework. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Volatility 3 dump naming basis** — In Volatility 3, dumped memory-section filenames include the process PID. _Why:_ the filename identifies which process owned the suspicious memory range. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Suspicious page address in dump names** — Dump filenames include the suspicious memory page location from the target process address space. _Why:_ this lets analysts map a dump file back to the exact virtual memory region. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Second hexadecimal value in dump names** — The second hex value in the dump filename identifies the location of the suspicious page inside process memory. _Why:_ it is the memory address clue needed to correlate the dump with `malfind` output. _[GCFA p.~537]_

### Dump Analysis Methods

- **Strings analysis** — Dumped memory sections can be examined with simple string extraction. _Why:_ embedded paths, URLs, commands, or configuration values may be visible without full reversing. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Antivirus scanning** — Dump files can be submitted to antivirus tooling. _Why:_ known payloads or recognizable byte patterns may be detected after extraction from memory. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **IOC searching** — Dump files can be searched for known indicators of compromise. _Why:_ extracted memory may contain malware identifiers that are not obvious from process metadata. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **YARA signatures** — YARA rules are named as one capability for finding known indicators inside dumped memory. _Why:_ YARA can match byte patterns, strings, and structural traits associated with malware families or techniques. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Reverse engineering review** — The most thorough analysis path is a full code-level review of the dumped memory section. _Why:_ manual reverse engineering can explain payload behavior when automated checks are inconclusive. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Reverse engineering cost** — Complete reverse engineering of memory sections is expensive in analyst time and skill. _Why:_ attackers benefit when reliable confirmation requires costly manual work. _[GCFA p.~537]_

### Advanced Injection Detection Limits

- **Need for additional tooling** — The most advanced injection methods may require tools and methods beyond `malfind` memory dumping. _Why:_ some techniques do not expose themselves through the common suspicious-memory patterns shown on the page. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Advanced malware prevalence** — Only a minority of malware uses the most sophisticated injection techniques. _Why:_ analysts should prepare for advanced cases without assuming every incident uses them. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Privilege requirements** — Some advanced injection methods require elevated or additional privileges. _Why:_ privilege needs can limit how often a technique appears in real intrusions. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Stability risk** — Some advanced injection techniques can crash the target process or destabilize the system. _Why:_ unreliable techniques are less attractive to attackers who need persistence or operational continuity. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Proof-of-concept gap** — A working demonstration technique may be far from a dependable real-world exploit. _Why:_ analysts should distinguish research feasibility from common operational use. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Common injection simplicity** — Many injection attacks still use straightforward, detectable methods. _Why:_ simple methods remain useful to attackers because they are easy to implement and often still succeed. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Common injection stability** — Attackers continue using familiar injection approaches because they are stable and tested. _Why:_ reliability can matter more to adversaries than technical novelty. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Security-tool evasion by simple techniques** — Even easily detectable injection approaches may evade many security products. _Why:_ memory forensics can find artifacts that deployed defenses missed. _[GCFA p.~537]_

### Complementary Detection Ideas

- **Parent-child relationship anomalies** — Unusual process lineage can help detect injection activity, including some advanced cases. _Why:_ injection often occurs as part of a broader execution chain that leaves process-tree irregularities. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Orphan-file analysis** — Files without normal contextual relationships can be useful indicators when investigating injection. _Why:_ supporting payload files or staging artifacts may remain visible even when code is hidden in memory. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Behavioral context detection** — Non-memory artifacts can still reveal advanced injection activity. _Why:_ attackers may hide code placement while leaving suspicious process or file-system relationships behind. _[GCFA p.~537]_
- **Future-facing memory detection** — Memory detection methods are expected to improve before many advanced techniques become widely used. _Why:_ developing these skills now prepares analysts for techniques that may later become common. _[GCFA p.~537]_

## Page 538

### Process Memory Categories

- **Process memory · Three-category model** — process address space can be divided into private memory, shareable/mapped memory, and image-mapped memory. _Why:_ this classification helps analysts decide whether a memory region looks normal or suspicious during injection hunting. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Process memory understanding · Injection detection value** — deeper knowledge of normal process memory layout improves the ability to spot abnormalities introduced by advanced code-injection methods. _Why:_ injection often stands out because it places executable or PE-like content in memory categories where it normally should not appear. _[GCFA p.538]_

### Private Memory

- **Private memory · Process-local ownership** — private memory belongs only to the owning process and is not mapped into other processes. _Why:_ content found here should generally be process-specific data, so shared-file or executable artifacts can be anomalous. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Private memory · Typical allocation API** — private memory is commonly created through the Windows `VirtualAlloc` API. _Why:_ malware and injection tools frequently rely on this allocation path when creating memory for payloads. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Private memory · Application data** — application-specific data is a normal occupant of private memory. _Why:_ analysts should distinguish ordinary writable data from injected executable content. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Private memory · Heap** — the process heap is part of private memory. _Why:_ heap regions are expected to be writable and process-local, which affects how suspicious permissions should be interpreted. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Private memory · Stack** — the process stack is part of private memory. _Why:_ stack memory commonly needs read/write access, so executable permissions or PE-like data in this area deserve scrutiny. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Private memory · EXE files not expected** — full executable images such as `.exe` files are not expected to reside as normal content in private memory. _Why:_ an executable image in private memory may indicate injection or unpacked malware. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Private memory · DLL files not expected** — DLL images are not expected to appear as ordinary private-memory content. _Why:_ DLL-like content in private regions can suggest reflective loading or another nonstandard loading technique. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Private memory · Common protection** — most private-memory pages are created with `READWRITE` access. _Why:_ read/write permissions fit normal stack, heap, and data usage, while execute permissions in private memory are more suspicious. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Private memory diagram · Application data** — the slide labels application data as a private-memory use case. _Why:_ this reinforces that private memory normally contains process-specific data rather than mapped binaries. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Private memory diagram · Stack and heap** — the slide labels stack and heap as private-memory contents. _Why:_ these are baseline regions analysts expect when interpreting VADs and memory permissions. _[GCFA p.538]_

### Shareable / Mapped Memory

- **Shareable memory · Alternate name** — shareable memory is also described as mapped memory. _Why:_ tools and documentation may use either term when describing file-backed memory regions. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Shareable memory · File mapping purpose** — this memory category maps all or part of shared files for use inside a process. _Why:_ file-backed mappings are common and should be distinguished from private allocations. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Shareable memory · Sharing is optional** — data in this category can be shared with other processes, but sharing is not mandatory. _Why:_ the presence of mapped memory does not prove multiple processes are actively using it. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Shareable memory · Shared between processes** — the slide identifies shareable/mapped memory as memory that may be shared with other processes. _Why:_ shared mappings explain why the same backing data can appear across process address spaces. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Shareable memory · Shared with DLLs** — the slide notes that shareable/mapped memory can be shared with DLLs. _Why:_ DLL-related mappings are part of normal process memory behavior and should be separated from private injected code. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Shareable memory · Mapped data files** — the slide lists mapped data files as an example of shareable/mapped memory. _Why:_ mapped data files are expected artifacts in this memory class. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Shareable memory · `.dat` files** — `.dat` files are commonly found as mapped files in shareable memory. _Why:_ their presence can be normal and should not automatically be treated as executable injection. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Shareable memory · `.mui` files** — `.mui` files are also commonly mapped into shareable memory from disk. _Why:_ language/resource files may appear in process memory as ordinary file-backed mappings. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Shareable memory · Disk-backed mapping** — files in shareable memory are mapped or loaded from files present on disk. _Why:_ disk backing helps distinguish ordinary mapped files from memory-only payloads. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Shareable memory · Common protection** — most permissions in shareable/mapped memory are `READONLY`. _Why:_ writable or executable permissions in this category may be more notable depending on context. _[GCFA p.538]_

### Image-Mapped Memory

- **Image-mapped memory · Relationship to shareable memory** — image-mapped memory is technically a subset of shareable memory but is tagged separately. _Why:_ analysts should treat image mappings as a distinct VAD category even though they are file-backed. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Image-mapped memory · Disk-backed files** — files from disk are mapped into image memory. _Why:_ legitimate executable modules usually have a backing file rather than existing only in private memory. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Image-mapped memory · Intended executable content** — image memory is intended for legitimately loaded executable images. _Why:_ this is the expected location for normal executable code in a process. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Image-mapped memory · Image binaries** — image binaries are normal contents of image-mapped memory. _Why:_ executable images mapped by the loader should normally appear in this category. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Image-mapped memory · DLLs** — DLLs legitimately loaded by the image loader belong in image-mapped memory. _Why:_ a DLL outside this category may indicate reflective loading or another abnormal loading path. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Image-mapped memory · Drivers** — drivers are included among the legitimate image-backed objects associated with image-mapped memory. _Why:_ executable kernel or driver images are expected to use image-style mappings when properly loaded. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Image-mapped memory diagram · EXE or DLL loader mapping** — the slide states that EXE or DLL files loaded by the image loader are image-mapped. _Why:_ loader-created mappings provide a baseline for distinguishing normal modules from injected payloads. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Image-mapped memory diagram · VAD type** — the slide identifies the VAD type for image-mapped memory as `VadImageMap`. _Why:_ this VAD tag is a concrete artifact analysts can use when triaging memory regions. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Image-mapped memory · Execute permissions expected** — image-mapped memory is the process-memory area where execute permissions commonly appear during normal operation. _Why:_ executable permissions are less suspicious here than in private memory. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Image-mapped memory · Common protection `EXECUTE_WRITECOPY`** — most image mappings use `EXECUTE_WRITECOPY` rather than fully writable execute access. _Why:_ this permission pattern is typical for shared executable code and helps identify abnormal protections. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Image-mapped memory · Copy-on-write protection** — copy-on-write protects shared code by giving a process a private copy when modification is needed. _Why:_ this explains why writable-looking behavior can be handled without granting broad shared write access to code pages. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Image-mapped memory · Common protection `EXECUTE_READ`** — `EXECUTE_READ` is another common protection on image-mapped regions. _Why:_ executable code normally needs to be read and executed, not freely modified. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Image-mapped memory · Abused protection `EXECUTE_READWRITE`** — `EXECUTE_READWRITE` is called out as a commonly abused permission and is not the usual protection for most legitimate image mappings. _Why:_ executable and writable memory is a high-value indicator when investigating injection. _[GCFA p.538]_

### Process Memory Diagram Artifacts

- **Kernel memory · Present but restricted** — the diagram shows kernel memory as present and marked restricted. _Why:_ kernel memory is part of the broader memory picture but is not ordinary user-mode process content. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **PEB · Located in process memory** — the Process Environment Block resides in process memory. _Why:_ user-mode accessibility makes it a useful source of process metadata but also a target for manipulation. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **PEB · Malware manipulation risk** — because the PEB is in process memory, malware can alter it relatively easily. _Why:_ analysts should not blindly trust PEB-derived module or process metadata during malware investigations. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Diagram object · DLL** — the diagram depicts multiple DLL objects within process memory. _Why:_ DLL mappings are normal process-memory components and provide context for recognizing legitimate image-mapped regions. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Diagram object · EXE** — the diagram depicts an EXE object within process memory. _Why:_ the main executable image is a normal image-mapped component loaded into a process. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Diagram object · Heap** — the diagram labels heap memory inside the process layout. _Why:_ heap regions are expected private writable memory and should be interpreted differently from image mappings. _[GCFA p.538]_

- **Diagram object · Stack** — the diagram labels stack memory inside the process layout. _Why:_ stack regions are expected private writable memory and can be evaluated for abnormal executable permissions. _[GCFA p.538]_

### Detection Principles

- **FindEvil default state** — The `findevil` plugin is not enabled automatically during normal MemProcFS use. _Why:_ an examiner may miss these detections unless they explicitly activate forensic mode. _[GCFA p.~540]_
