- **Runtime activation file** — After MemProcFS is already running, `findevil` can be enabled by writing `1` into `M:\forensic\forensic_enable.txt`. _Why:_ this provides a post-launch method to turn on forensic processing. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Forensic-enable value** — The value used to enable forensic mode through the MemProcFS virtual filesystem is `1`. _Why:_ the exact value matters for activating the feature correctly. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Forensic-enable path** — The MemProcFS runtime control file for enabling forensic mode is `M:\forensic\forensic_enable.txt`. _Why:_ this is the precise virtual filesystem location an examiner must modify. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Windows version limitation** — The `findevil` feature is available only for Windows 10 and later systems. _Why:_ this limits when the detections can be used during memory analysis. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **False-positive reduction rationale** — The Windows 10+ restriction exists to reduce false-positive results. _Why:_ platform gating affects how confidently the detections can be interpreted. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **FindEvil report path** — When enabled, MemProcFS writes the FindEvil text report to `M:\forensic\findevil.txt`. _Why:_ this is the artifact an examiner reviews for flagged suspicious memory areas. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **FindEvil report format** — The generated `findevil.txt` report marks suspicious memory regions using the detection flags shown on the page. _Why:_ the flags are the vocabulary used to classify suspicious findings. _[GCFA p.~540]_

### Process Irregularity Flags

- **Process-irregularity category** — One group of FindEvil flags is intended to identify abnormal process characteristics. _Why:_ process metadata inconsistencies can reveal hiding, masquerading, or suspicious execution context. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Process-irregularity workflow relationship** — The process-irregularity checks correspond to process-analysis concepts covered earlier in the memory-analysis workflow. _Why:_ these detections should be interpreted alongside prior process-listing and process-context review. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PROC_NOLINK` table cell** — `PROC_NOLINK` indicates that a process is absent from the `EPROCESS` doubly linked process list. _Why:_ processes missing from this list may be hidden, terminated, or affected by acquisition/parsing issues. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PROC_NOLINK` definition** — A `PROC_NOLINK` finding means the process is not represented in the normal `EPROCESS` linked-list structure. _Why:_ malicious tools may unlink process objects to hide them from standard process enumeration. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PROC_NOLINK` benign cause: termination** — A process can be missing from the linked list because it was terminating. _Why:_ not every unlinked-looking process is necessarily malicious. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PROC_NOLINK` benign cause: memory-image issue** — Memory acquisition or image-quality problems can also produce a `PROC_NOLINK` condition. _Why:_ examiners must separate collection artifacts from attacker behavior. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PROC_NOLINK` malicious interpretation** — A `PROC_NOLINK` result may indicate that malware deliberately unlinked a process. _Why:_ process unlinking is a known stealth technique. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PROC_PARENT` table cell** — `PROC_PARENT` reports that a process has an unexpected parent, using limited checks for well-known process names. _Why:_ parent-process anomalies can expose process masquerading or suspicious launch chains. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PROC_PARENT` definition** — `PROC_PARENT` checks whether certain system processes deviate from commonly expected parent-process relationships. _Why:_ legitimate Windows system processes usually follow predictable ancestry patterns. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PROC_PARENT` limitation** — The parent-process validation is limited to some well-known processes. _Why:_ the flag should not be treated as a complete parent-child anomaly detector for every process. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PROC_USER` table cell** — `PROC_USER` indicates that a process token reflects an unexpected user-account context. _Why:_ a process running under the wrong identity may indicate impersonation, privilege abuse, or masquerading. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PROC_USER` definition** — `PROC_USER` checks for processes named like system components but running with an inappropriate account token. _Why:_ attackers may name malware after system binaries while failing to match the expected security context. _[GCFA p.~540]_

### Unusual Memory Page Flags

- **Unusual-memory-page category** — A second group of FindEvil flags focuses on suspicious memory-page properties. _Why:_ injected or manually mapped code often differs from normal process memory layout. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Process-memory knowledge requirement** — Understanding process memory layout is necessary for interpreting FindEvil memory-page findings. _Why:_ the meaning of private memory, image mappings, and page permissions determines whether a flag is suspicious. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PE_INJECT` table cell** — `PE_INJECT` identifies DLL or executable content that is present but not mapped as image memory. _Why:_ PE-format code outside normal image mappings is a strong indicator of manual mapping or injection. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PE_INJECT` definition** — `PE_INJECT` flags a memory location containing a PE header for an EXE or DLL when that location is not image-mapped memory. _Why:_ legitimate loaded PE files are normally represented through image mappings. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PE_INJECT` PE-header condition** — The `PE_INJECT` detection depends on finding a PE header in memory. _Why:_ PE headers can reveal injected executable images even when they are not loaded through standard mechanisms. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PE_INJECT` file types** — The PE content associated with `PE_INJECT` may correspond to an EXE or DLL. _Why:_ both executable programs and dynamic libraries can be injected into process memory. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PE_INJECT` mapping condition** — The suspicious condition for `PE_INJECT` is that the PE-bearing memory is not image mapped. _Why:_ this separates normal loader-backed modules from manually placed executable content. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PE_INJECT` Volatility analogy** — `PE_INJECT` is comparable to narrowing Volatility `malfind` output to entries containing `MZ` headers. _Why:_ both approaches highlight memory regions that look like PE files. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Volatility plugin reference** — The page references Volatility’s `malfind` plugin as an analogous memory-injection analysis tool. _Why:_ this helps map MemProcFS detections to a familiar memory-forensics workflow. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`MZ` header reference** — The page uses `MZ` headers as the PE-header signature relevant to injected executable images. _Why:_ `MZ` is a common marker for DOS/PE file headers in memory. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`NOIMAGE_RWX/RX` table cell** — `NOIMAGE_RWX/RX` indicates executable pages that are not mapped as image memory. _Why:_ executable memory outside image mappings can indicate injected or manually staged code. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`NOIMAGE_RWX` definition** — `NOIMAGE_RWX` flags memory sections with read, write, and execute permissions outside image-mapped memory. _Why:_ writable and executable non-image memory is especially suspicious for injected code. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`NOIMAGE_RX` definition** — `NOIMAGE_RX` flags memory sections with read and execute permissions outside image-mapped memory. _Why:_ attackers may remove write permission after injection, leaving executable non-image memory behind. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`NOIMAGE_RWX` permission set** — The `NOIMAGE_RWX` flag involves pages with RWX permissions. _Why:_ simultaneous write and execute access is a common memory-injection indicator. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`NOIMAGE_RX` permission set** — The `NOIMAGE_RX` flag involves pages with RX permissions. _Why:_ executable-only or read-executable non-image memory can still contain injected payloads after permissions are tightened. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`NOIMAGE_RWX/RX` mapping condition** — The `NOIMAGE_RWX/RX` family applies when executable pages are outside image-mapped memory. _Why:_ this distinguishes suspicious executable regions from normal loaded modules. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PRIVATE_RWX/RX` table cell** — `PRIVATE_RWX/RX` indicates executable pages located in private process memory such as data regions, stacks, or heaps. _Why:_ private executable memory is a common location for injected payloads or shellcode. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PRIVATE_RWX` definition** — `PRIVATE_RWX` flags private memory sections with read, write, and execute permissions. _Why:_ RWX private memory gives injected code both mutability and execution capability. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **`PRIVATE_RX` definition** — `PRIVATE_RX` flags private memory sections with read and execute permissions. _Why:_ RX private memory may represent injected code whose write permission was removed after staging. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Private-memory examples** — The page identifies data regions, stacks, and heaps as examples of private process memory covered by `PRIVATE_RWX/RX`. _Why:_ these are normal data-holding areas where executable permissions can be suspicious. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Private data memory** — Data areas are included in the private-memory category referenced by `PRIVATE_RWX/RX`. _Why:_ executable permissions in ordinary data memory can indicate code placement outside normal module loading. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Private stack memory** — Stack memory is included in the private-memory category referenced by `PRIVATE_RWX/RX`. _Why:_ executable stack pages may support injected code execution or exploitation artifacts. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Private heap memory** — Heap memory is included in the private-memory category referenced by `PRIVATE_RWX/RX`. _Why:_ heap-backed executable regions are common staging locations for payloads. _[GCFA p.~540]_

### Detection Interpretation

- **Injection ease** — The page states that placing code into another process is technically easy. _Why:_ defenders should expect code injection attempts to be common and practical for attackers. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Proper-memory-placement difficulty** — Making injected code appear to occupy the correct memory type and location is difficult. _Why:_ mismatches in mapping type or permissions create forensic detection opportunities. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Proper-dressing difficulty** — Making injected code look fully legitimate in memory is difficult. _Why:_ incomplete mimicry can leave detectable artifacts such as odd permissions or non-image PE headers. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Detection strength** — The FindEvil detections are described as highly effective because injected code often fails to match normal memory-layout expectations. _Why:_ memory-layout inconsistencies provide strong indicators of malicious activity. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Layered detection behavior** — FindEvil detections are layered, so more than one flag can apply to the same suspicious region. _Why:_ overlapping flags can strengthen confidence that a memory area deserves review. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Multiple flags per location** — A single malicious memory location may trigger several FindEvil detections. _Why:_ investigators should correlate flags rather than treat them as mutually exclusive findings. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **Example overlap condition** — The page begins an example where an `MZ` header appears in an RX memory section outside image-mapped memory. _Why:_ this scenario would combine PE-content evidence with suspicious mapping and permission evidence. _[GCFA p.~540]_
- **RX outside image mapping** — An RX section outside image-mapped memory is presented as suspicious in the overlapping-detection example. _Why:_ read-execute non-image memory can indicate injected code that no longer has write permission. _[GCFA p.~540]_

## Page 541

### MemProcFS FindEvil Injection Flags

- **Image-mapped executable memory detection** — executable code found in image-mapped memory can be reported with the `PE_INJECT` and `NOIMAGE_RX` indicators. _Why:_ these flags point to executable memory patterns that may reflect code injection rather than normal module loading. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **`PE_INJECT` flag** — `PE_INJECT` is one of the FindEvil-style indicators associated with suspicious executable memory content. _Why:_ it helps identify memory regions that may contain injected PE-like code. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **`NOIMAGE_RX` flag** — `NOIMAGE_RX` is a FindEvil-style indicator associated with executable read-only memory that is not backed by a normal image mapping. _Why:_ RX memory without a proper image relationship can indicate stealthy injected code. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **Private-memory flags** — indicators involving private memory are especially important because legitimate executable permissions are less expected in private process memory. _Why:_ private executable memory is rarer in normal processes, so it has stronger suspicious value. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **Private process memory** — private memory includes process-specific regions such as the stack and heap. _Why:_ attackers may place injected code in these areas to avoid normal image-backed module patterns. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **Stack as injection target** — some code-injection methods place executable content in stack memory. _Why:_ executable stack content is abnormal and can expose malicious runtime manipulation. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **Heap as injection target** — some code-injection methods place executable content in heap memory. _Why:_ executable heap regions are uncommon in benign activity and can reveal injected payloads. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **Legitimate executable private memory rarity** — valid executable flags are less commonly expected in private memory than in normal image-backed memory. _Why:_ this rarity makes private executable pages useful triage targets. _[GCFA p.541]_

### Malware Examples

- **NetTraveler private RX mapping** — NetTraveler is a real-world malware family known to map executable code into private memory regions with read-execute permissions. _Why:_ this provides a concrete example of the private-memory RX pattern being malicious in practice. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **NetTraveler prevalence** — NetTraveler is described as a widespread malware family. _Why:_ common malware using this pattern increases the practical value of detecting it. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **Cobalt Strike Beacon private RX pattern** — Cobalt Strike beacons often show the suspicious private-memory RX characteristic. _Why:_ this links the memory-permission pattern to a widely used adversary tool. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **Cobalt Strike Beacon detection implication** — the private RX memory behavior is a recognizable sign that may appear during Beacon detection. _Why:_ responders can use this memory trait as a hunting clue. _[GCFA p.541]_

### FindEvil Versus Malfind

- **FindEvil detection improvement** — these MemProcFS/FindEvil detections provide stronger coverage than Volatility `malfind` detections alone. _Why:_ they can surface suspicious memory conditions beyond the simpler `malfind` heuristics. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **Volatility `malfind` comparison** — Volatility `malfind` is presented as a baseline detection method that FindEvil improves upon. _Why:_ analysts should understand that tool choice affects which injected-memory patterns are surfaced. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **False-positive burden** — even with stronger detections, large volumes of false positives remain a challenge. _Why:_ analysts still need validation and triage instead of treating every flag as confirmed malware. _[GCFA p.541]_

### MemProcFS Page-State Flags

- **FindEvil page-origin flags** — FindEvil and other MemProcFS outputs may include flags describing what kind of memory page produced a result. _Why:_ page-state context helps interpret whether data came from live RAM, inactive memory, compressed memory, or paging artifacts. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **MemProcFS output context** — page-state flags can appear across multiple MemProcFS output files, not only FindEvil. _Why:_ analysts should recognize these flags when reviewing different MemProcFS artifacts. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **Page-state flags and evil detection** — the page-state flags are not always decisive for identifying malicious activity. _Why:_ they provide context but should not be treated as primary proof of compromise. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **Page-state flags and residency** — the flags can indicate whether a page was resident in memory or possibly associated with the page file. _Why:_ this helps analysts understand the availability and source of the observed data. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **`A` page flag** — `A` means the page is active. _Why:_ active pages are currently relevant in memory analysis and may represent live process state. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **`T` page flag** — `T` means the page is transient: not active, but still present in memory. _Why:_ transient pages may still contain useful evidence even though they are no longer active. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **`Z` page flag** — `Z` means the page is a zero page. _Why:_ zero pages may contain no meaningful payload content and can explain apparently empty memory regions. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **`C` page flag** — `C` means the page is compressed. _Why:_ compressed-page status affects interpretation because the data may or may not be backed by physical memory or paged storage. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **Compressed-page backing ambiguity** — a compressed page may be backed by memory, or it may have been paged out to the page file. _Why:_ analysts should avoid assuming a compressed page’s storage location without additional context. _[GCFA p.541]_
- **`Pf` page flag** — `Pf` means the page is associated with the pagefile. _Why:_ pagefile-backed data can preserve evidence that is no longer resident in active RAM. _[GCFA p.541]_

### Reference

- **MemProcFS FindEvil Wiki reference** — the page cites `FS_FindEvil - MemProcFS Wiki` at `https://for508.com/9roj0`. _Why:_ this reference identifies the supporting documentation for FindEvil behavior and flags. _[GCFA p.541]_

### Process-Inconsistency Detection

- **Kernel/userland inconsistency hunting** — the page frames this section as a method for exposing mismatches between process metadata stored in user-accessible memory and metadata stored in kernel-managed memory. _Why:_ injected code may look normal in one structure while remaining abnormal in another. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Advanced code-injection evasion** — modern injection methods may directly alter process memory structures to appear legitimate and bypass earlier detection approaches. _Why:_ responders cannot rely only on surface-level process or module listings. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Post-allocation permission changes** — attackers may allocate memory under one permission set and later change the protection flags. _Why:_ the original allocation state and the current execution state may diverge, creating a forensic inconsistency. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Pointer redirection** — attackers may alter pointers so execution reaches code other than the code originally loaded. _Why:_ apparent module identity may not match the actual code path being executed. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Process hollowing example** — process hollowing is cited as a technique where execution can be redirected away from the originally loaded code. _Why:_ it demonstrates how legitimate-looking process context can conceal substituted code. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Patching legitimate code** — attackers may directly modify code that was legitimately loaded into a process. _Why:_ malicious behavior can be hidden inside memory regions that appear to belong to trusted modules. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Detection remains possible** — even advanced memory-structure manipulation can still be detected. _Why:_ inconsistent metadata across independent memory-tracking structures can reveal tampering. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Need for deeper internals** — detecting these attacks requires examining lower-level process memory structures instead of only high-level artifacts. _Why:_ advanced injection may intentionally defeat common process and module enumeration methods. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Multiple memory-tracking sources** — memory objects are represented in several separate structures. _Why:_ comparing independent records lets analysts identify contradictions caused by injection or tampering. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Cross-structure comparison** — inconsistencies can be found by comparing metadata from different memory structures. _Why:_ attackers may successfully alter one structure while failing to alter all related sources consistently. _[GCFA p.~543]_

### Process Environment Block

- **Process Environment Block (PEB)** — the PEB is identified as a major process structure targeted by current injection techniques. _Why:_ it contains process identity and loader metadata that many userland tools depend on. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PEB memory location field** — the diagram lists memory location as a PEB-tracked item. _Why:_ mismatched or hidden memory locations can indicate process metadata manipulation. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PEB command-line field** — the diagram lists the process command line as PEB-associated information. _Why:_ attackers can alter it to misrepresent what was launched. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PEB loaded-DLL tracking** — the diagram states that the PEB maintains three lists for loaded DLLs. _Why:_ these lists are common sources for userland module enumeration and therefore attractive targets for hiding or spoofing modules. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PEB execution entry point** — the diagram identifies the code execution entry point as PEB-related information. _Why:_ entry-point metadata helps analysts compare expected execution flow with actual execution behavior. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PEB executable path field** — the diagram lists the on-disk executable path as PEB-associated data. _Why:_ attackers can change this path to make loaded code appear to come from a different location. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PEB is userland-accessible** — the PEB resides in the user-accessible portion of a process address space. _Why:_ its location makes it easier for attackers to alter than kernel-resident structures. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PEB modification prerequisite** — PEB tampering assumes the attacker already has sufficient privileges to inject or manipulate process memory. _Why:_ the page distinguishes accessibility from authorization; the structure is easy to modify only after the attacker has the needed access. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **DLL-list unlinking** — memory locations can be removed from the PEB’s three loaded-DLL lists. _Why:_ unlinking can hide modules from tools that trust those lists. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Task Manager visibility impact** — unlinking from loaded-DLL lists can hide memory locations from Task Manager-style views. _Why:_ common administrative tools may miss malicious modules if they depend on manipulated userland metadata. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PowerShell visibility impact** — unlinking from loaded-DLL lists can hide memory locations from PowerShell commands. _Why:_ script-based triage may be incomplete when it relies on PEB-backed enumeration. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Malware self-insertion into PEB lists** — some malware attempts to add itself to the loaded-DLL lists instead of removing entries. _Why:_ appearing in expected loader lists can make malicious code blend in with normal modules. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Legitimate DLL-list membership condition** — entries are legitimate in the loaded-DLL lists only when placed there by the Windows loader. _Why:_ a module appearing in the lists without normal loader involvement can be suspicious. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PEB masquerading** — PEB masquerading can alter process command-line and executable-path metadata. _Why:_ analysts may see a false process name or location if they trust the PEB alone. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Spoofed command line** — PEB masquerading can make loaded code appear to have been started with a different command line. _Why:_ command-line evidence may be intentionally falsified. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Spoofed executable path** — PEB masquerading can make loaded code appear to originate from a different filesystem path. _Why:_ path-based trust or reputation checks can be misled. _[GCFA p.~543]_

### Virtual Address Descriptors

- **Virtual Address Descriptors (VAD)** — the diagram identifies VADs as a kernel-side process memory structure. _Why:_ VAD metadata is harder for attackers to alter than userland PEB metadata. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **VAD memory location field** — the diagram lists memory location as VAD-tracked information. _Why:_ VAD ranges can be compared with PTEs and PEB module records to expose hidden memory. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **VAD type field** — the diagram lists VAD type as one of Private, Shareable, or Image. _Why:_ executable code in an unexpected VAD type can indicate injection. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **VAD Private type** — Private is one VAD type shown on the page. _Why:_ private memory that becomes executable is often more suspicious than image-backed executable memory. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **VAD Shareable type** — Shareable is one VAD type shown on the page. _Why:_ shareable mappings can be compared against expected file-backed or shared-memory behavior. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **VAD Image type** — Image is one VAD type shown on the page. _Why:_ legitimate executable modules are commonly expected to appear as image-backed mappings. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **VAD executable path field** — the diagram lists the path to the executable on disk as VAD-tracked information. _Why:_ VAD path metadata can be checked against PEB path metadata for masquerading or hiding. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **VAD original permissions** — the diagram labels VAD permissions as the original permissions. _Why:_ original permissions can differ from current PTE permissions after protection changes. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **VAD kernel location** — the process VAD tree is located in kernel memory. _Why:_ kernel residency makes VAD manipulation more difficult than PEB tampering. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **DKOM against VADs** — Direct Kernel Object Manipulation has been proposed to unlink and hide memory locations tracked by the VAD. _Why:_ attackers may try to remove kernel memory records to conceal injected regions. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **DKOM instability risk** — modifying kernel structures is dangerous and often causes system instability. _Why:_ instability risk makes kernel tampering harder to perform reliably and may itself create investigative clues. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **VAD gap detection** — PTEs can be used to identify missing coverage in the VAD tree. _Why:_ if memory exists in page tables but lacks corresponding VAD tracking, that mismatch can reveal tampering. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **VAD permission tracking** — the VAD tree also records page permissions. _Why:_ VAD permissions provide a comparison point against current PTE permissions. _[GCFA p.~543]_

### Page Table Entries

- **Page Table Entry (PTE)** — the diagram identifies PTEs as a kernel-side source of per-page memory metadata. _Why:_ PTEs provide low-level evidence of actual memory allocation and protection state. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PTE memory location field** — the diagram lists memory location as PTE-tracked information. _Why:_ PTE addresses can confirm whether memory exists even if higher-level structures are altered. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PTE modified-page indicator** — the diagram states that PTEs can show whether a page has been modified. _Why:_ modified pages may indicate runtime patching or injected code writes. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PTE paged-out indicator** — the diagram states that PTEs can show whether a memory location is paged out. _Why:_ analysts need to know whether the content is resident or must be recovered from paging artifacts. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PTE current permissions** — the diagram labels PTE permissions as current permissions. _Why:_ current page protections can reveal execution permissions that differ from the original VAD permissions. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PTE kernel location** — page table entries are located in kernel-managed memory. _Why:_ they are harder to manipulate than userland structures and provide a stronger validation source. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PTE ground truth** — PTEs are described as the authoritative source for memory allocations. _Why:_ they can verify whether memory is truly allocated regardless of what higher-level records claim. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PTE attacks observed in the wild** — attacks targeting page table entry behavior have been observed outside of theory. _Why:_ analysts must treat PTE-related manipulation as a real-world tactic, not only a research concern. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **NtProtectVirtualMemory abuse** — attackers have used the legitimate Windows API function `NtProtectVirtualMemory` to change page permissions. _Why:_ normal APIs can be abused to produce suspicious memory-protection transitions without needing direct kernel tampering. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **RW allocation stage** — the described PTE-based attack allocates memory with read/write permissions first. _Why:_ write access allows the attacker to place code into the allocated region. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Code-copy stage** — after RW allocation, attackers copy code into the allocated memory location. _Why:_ this step places executable payload content into process memory. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **RX transition stage** — after copying code, attackers switch the memory permissions to read/execute. _Why:_ the region becomes executable while avoiding an obvious long-lived RWX state. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Execution after permission switch** — the RW-to-RX change enables code execution from the injected location. _Why:_ this pattern can bypass detections that look only for memory simultaneously marked writable and executable. _[GCFA p.~543]_

### Userland And Kernel Boundary

- **Userland side of diagram** — the PEB is shown under the userland portion of the process memory model. _Why:_ userland placement explains why attackers commonly target it for metadata spoofing. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Kernel side of diagram** — VADs and PTEs are shown under the kernel portion of the process memory model. _Why:_ kernel placement makes these structures stronger comparison sources for detecting PEB deception. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **PEB versus VAD/PTE trust difference** — PEB data is easier to modify, while VAD and PTE data are harder to manipulate because they reside in the kernel. _Why:_ analysts should weigh evidence sources differently when investigating injected code. _[GCFA p.~543]_
- **Original versus current permissions** — VADs are associated with original permissions, while PTEs are associated with current permissions. _Why:_ a mismatch between original and current protection flags can expose stealthy permission changes used during injection. _[GCFA p.~543]_

## Page 545

### windows.ldrmodules Purpose

- **windows.ldrmodules** — Volatility plugin used to compare multiple process DLL-tracking sources for inconsistencies. _Why:_ mismatches can reveal suspiciously loaded code or injection artifacts. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **PEB DLL tracking** — each process has three linked lists in the Process Environment Block for tracking loaded DLLs. _Why:_ injected or manipulated modules may appear in memory while being absent from one or more normal loader lists. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Code injection and unlinked DLLs** — code injection can result in DLLs that are not linked into the expected PEB loader lists. _Why:_ absence from loader metadata is an indicator of stealthy module loading or post-load tampering. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **ldrmodules list comparison** — the plugin queries the PEB loader lists and displays their membership side by side. _Why:_ side-by-side comparison makes module-list anomalies easier to identify. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Volatility data-source correlation** — the plugin combines information from multiple memory structures rather than relying on a single artifact. _Why:_ cross-source comparison strengthens detection of process-memory irregularities. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Suspiciously loaded code objective** — the plugin is intended to help decide whether code inside a process was loaded in an unusual way. _Why:_ abnormal loading patterns are common in malware, injection, and evasion techniques. _[GCFA p.~545]_

### Important Parameter

- **--pid** — limits output to one or more specified process IDs. _Why:_ focused process selection reduces noise during targeted investigation. _[GCFA p.~545]_

### Process And Memory Structures

- **Process Environment Block (PEB)** — per-process user-mode structure that includes loader metadata, including three doubly linked DLL lists. _Why:_ PEB loader metadata is a key reference point for determining whether modules were normally loaded. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Three PEB loader lists** — the PEB stores loaded-module information in three separate doubly linked lists. _Why:_ attackers may fail to hide injected modules consistently across all loader structures. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Doubly linked loader lists** — the module lists in the PEB are doubly linked. _Why:_ list unlinking or inconsistent membership can expose concealment attempts. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Normal loader-list relationship** — in most ordinary cases, the three PEB module lists contain the same module set, but arranged in different orders. _Why:_ differing membership across the lists can indicate manipulation or nonstandard loading. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **VAD cross-reference** — ldrmodules compares PEB list data against image memory-mapped pages tracked in the Virtual Address Descriptor tree. _Why:_ code can exist in mapped process memory even when loader lists do not reflect it. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Image memory-mapped pages** — VAD-tracked image mappings are used as an additional source for module presence. _Why:_ image mappings can reveal executable content that PEB loader lists omit. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **VAD tree** — the plugin uses the process VAD tree to identify mapped image regions and their paths. _Why:_ VAD metadata provides an independent view of process memory mappings. _[GCFA p.~545]_

### Plugin Output Fields

- **PID field** — reports the process identifier. _Why:_ the PID ties each module finding to a specific process instance. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Process field** — reports the process name. _Why:_ process names provide immediate context for triaging module anomalies. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Base field** — reports the module base address inside the process as derived from the VAD tree. _Why:_ the base address identifies where the mapped object resides in process virtual memory. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **InLoad field** — reports whether the mapped object appears in the PEB InLoadOrderModule list. _Why:_ missing membership may indicate abnormal loading or unlinking. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **InInit field** — reports whether the mapped object appears in the PEB InInitializationOrderModule list. _Why:_ this list is one of the loader views used to detect inconsistencies. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **InMem field** — reports whether the mapped object appears in the PEB InMemoryOrderModule list. _Why:_ comparison against this list helps identify modules not consistently represented in loader metadata. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **MappedPath field** — reports the on-disk mapped path from the VAD tree. _Why:_ missing or unexpected path information can support an injection hypothesis. _[GCFA p.~545]_

### Expected Legitimate Pattern

- **Legitimate Windows API-loaded DLL** — a DLL loaded through normal Windows APIs should appear in all three PEB loader lists. _Why:_ complete list membership is the expected baseline for normally loaded DLLs. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **True loader-list values** — a normally loaded DLL is expected to be marked `True` in `InLoad`, `InInit`, and `InMem`. _Why:_ any `False` value can point to an inconsistency requiring review. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Mapped disk location** — a legitimately loaded DLL should have a mapped location on disk. _Why:_ absence of a mapped path can indicate injected or otherwise abnormal memory content. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Deviation triage rule** — any departure from the expected pattern of three `True` list entries plus a mapped disk path should be investigated. _Why:_ loader-list or path anomalies may represent malicious loading, unlinking, or injection. _[GCFA p.~545]_

### Injection Indicators

- **Unlinked module indicator** — a DLL present in process memory but missing from one or more PEB lists can indicate injected code. _Why:_ attackers may load or conceal code without preserving normal loader metadata. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Missing MappedPath** — absence of `MappedPath` information is identified as another possible sign of injection. _Why:_ injected code may not correspond cleanly to a normal file-backed image mapping. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **PEB/VAD inconsistency** — a module visible through VAD image mapping but absent from PEB loader lists is an inconsistency. _Why:_ it shows memory evidence and loader metadata disagree about loaded code. _[GCFA p.~545]_

### False Positives And Caveats

- **False positives are common** — ldrmodules anomalies should not be treated as automatically malicious. _Why:_ normal Windows behavior and tool limitations can create suspicious-looking entries. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Process executable InInit absence** — the main process executable is expected to be absent from the `InInit` list. _Why:_ executables are initialized differently from DLLs, so this absence is not inherently suspicious. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **lsass.exe example** — a process executable such as `lsass.exe` may be missing from the initialization-order list. _Why:_ this demonstrates a normal artifact that can resemble a loader-list anomaly. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Non-DLL image mappings** — image-mapped memory can contain files that are not real executable or DLL modules. _Why:_ such files may appear in VAD-derived output without appearing in PEB loader lists. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **.fon image-mapped files** — `.fon` files can be mapped as image memory without being actual DLL or EXE modules. _Why:_ they can produce benign ldrmodules discrepancies. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **.mui image-mapped files** — `.mui` files can appear in image-mapped memory while not being loaded DLLs. _Why:_ their absence from PEB lists may be normal. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **.winmd image-mapped files** — `.winmd` files can be image-mapped even though they are not loaded DLLs. _Why:_ they can create expected VAD-versus-PEB mismatches. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **.msstyles image-mapped files** — `.msstyles` files can be present in image-mapped memory but are not ordinary EXE or DLL modules. _Why:_ they should not be assumed malicious solely because PEB lists omit them. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Special mapped files not represented in PEB lists** — non-EXE/DLL image-mapped files are not represented in the PEB loader lists because they are not loaded DLLs. _Why:_ this explains a common benign source of `False` list values. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Unused legitimate DLLs** — legitimate DLLs can be mapped into process memory before they have actually been used or loaded. _Why:_ such DLLs may have a VAD `MappedPath` but be absent from PEB lists. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Unloaded legitimate DLLs** — legitimate DLLs may remain mapped or visible after being unloaded. _Why:_ this can leave VAD evidence without corresponding active PEB loader-list membership. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **MappedPath-only legitimate DLLs** — some benign DLLs may appear in VAD `MappedPath` output but not in the PEB loader lists. _Why:_ investigators must distinguish inactive or previously unloaded DLLs from injection. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Volatility 3 SysWOW64 behavior** — Volatility 3 often reports SysWOW64 DLLs as not loaded in the PEB lists. _Why:_ this tool behavior can create false positives during 32-bit-on-64-bit process analysis. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **SysWOW64 possible explanation** — SysWOW64 discrepancies may result from 32-bit loaded libraries being tracked differently. _Why:_ architecture-specific loader behavior can affect interpretation of ldrmodules output. _[GCFA p.~545]_
- **Volatility version cross-check** — running ldrmodules in both Volatility 2 and Volatility 3 is recommended as a validation step. _Why:_ comparing tool versions can help separate true anomalies from parser or version-specific artifacts. _[GCFA p.~545]_

## Page 546

### DLL Loading Artifacts

- **MappedPath column absence** — an empty `MappedPath` value indicates that the DLL does not have the expected full filesystem path associated with a normal disk-backed load. _Why:_ legitimate Windows API DLL loading should usually preserve path information, so missing path data is suspicious. _[GCFA p.546]_

- **DLL not loaded from disk** — when `MappedPath` has no value, the DLL was likely not loaded from disk in the ordinary manner used by legitimate Windows API loading behavior. _Why:_ memory-only or nonstandard loading is a common trait of injected code. _[GCFA p.546]_

- **Missing full path information** — lack of a full path is explained by the DLL not being mapped from a normal on-disk file source. _Why:_ path absence helps distinguish suspicious in-memory modules from standard DLL loads. _[GCFA p.546]_

- **DLL injection indicator** — an unnamed or pathless DLL entry is generally a sign of DLL injection. _Why:_ injected DLLs may appear in process module structures without the normal disk-backed metadata expected from benign modules. _[GCFA p.546]_

- **PEB list presence does not clear suspicion** — a DLL can still be suspicious even when it appears in the Process Environment Block module lists. _Why:_ injected DLLs may be linked into PEB-maintained lists, so list presence alone is not proof of legitimate loading. _[GCFA p.546]_

### Volatility Tooling

- **Volatility 2 equivalent plugin** — the Volatility 2 plugin corresponding to this analysis is `ldrmodules`. _Why:_ analysts using Volatility 2 can perform the comparable module-list and path-consistency check with this plugin. _[GCFA p.546]_

- **Volatility 2 `ldrmodules` verbose option** — the `-v` flag for `ldrmodules` displays full path information. _Why:_ full path output is needed to identify modules with missing or anomalous mapped path data. _[GCFA p.546]_

- **Plugin name rendering cross-check** — the Adobe text layer shows the Volatility 2 plugin as `l\drmodules`, but the OCR context indicates the intended plugin name is `ldrmodules`. _Why:_ the backslash is a text-layer artifact and should not be treated as part of the command or plugin name. _[GCFA p.546]_

### ldrmodules Data Sources

- **ldrmodules plugin context** — the page explains the data relationships used by Volatility's `ldrmodules` plugin when evaluating loaded DLL visibility across process structures. _Why:_ understanding the source comparison is necessary for detecting hidden or suspicious modules. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **EPROCESS as process representation** — each running process is represented in memory by an `EPROCESS` structure. _Why:_ `EPROCESS` is the starting point for locating process-specific structures used in memory forensics. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **EPROCESS to PEB relationship** — an `EPROCESS` structure contains a reference to the process's Process Environment Block. _Why:_ this link connects kernel process metadata to userland module-tracking data. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **Process Environment Block role** — the Process Environment Block stores, among other process metadata, linked lists used to track DLLs loaded into the process. _Why:_ malware can manipulate these userland lists to hide modules from common tools. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **PEB list count** — the PEB maintains three doubly linked lists related to loaded DLL tracking. _Why:_ `ldrmodules` checks all three lists for consistency when identifying suspicious modules. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **PEB list similarity** — in normal cases, the three PEB module lists contain the same DLL entries, but the entries are arranged according to different ordering rules. _Why:_ missing membership in only one or more lists can indicate tampering rather than a normal load state. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **InLoadOrderModule List** — one of the PEB's three DLL-tracking lists is the `InLoadOrderModule List`. _Why:_ absence from this list can be evidence that a module was unlinked to evade detection. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **InInitializationOrderModule List** — one of the PEB's three DLL-tracking lists is the `InInitializationOrderModule List`. _Why:_ comparing this list against other sources helps identify modules with inconsistent loader visibility. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **InMemoryOrderModule List** — one of the PEB's three DLL-tracking lists is the `InMemoryOrderModule List`. _Why:_ this list provides another independent PEB view of loaded DLL membership. _[GCFA p.~547]_

### Visual Diagram Elements

- **EPROCESS diagram node** — the slide diagram includes `EPROCESS` as a source structure. _Why:_ it identifies the process object as the root memory structure for this analysis path. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **Process Environment Block diagram node** — the diagram shows `Process Environment Block (PEB)` connected to the process representation. _Why:_ it highlights where the loader-maintained DLL lists reside. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **InInit diagram label** — the diagram labels one membership source as `InInit`. _Why:_ this corresponds to whether a module appears in the initialization-order PEB list. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **InMem diagram label** — the diagram labels one membership source as `InMem`. _Why:_ this corresponds to whether a module appears in the memory-order PEB list. _[GCFA p.~547]_

### DLL Unlinking and Injection Detection

- **DLL unlinking technique** — malware can hide an injected DLL by removing it from one or more of the PEB DLL linked lists. _Why:_ this is a straightforward anti-forensic method that creates inconsistencies between memory mappings and loader lists. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **Unlinking execution impact** — removing a DLL from PEB lists does not break the process's execution. _Why:_ the module can continue running while becoming invisible to tools that rely on those lists. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **dlllist visibility limitation** — Volatility's `dlllist` plugin may fail to show a DLL that has been unlinked from the PEB loader lists. _Why:_ analysts should not treat `dlllist` output as complete when investigating injection. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **Task Manager visibility limitation** — Windows Task Manager may not display a DLL that has been unlinked from PEB loader lists. _Why:_ GUI-based process inspection can miss intentionally hidden modules. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **Command-line tool visibility limitation** — standard Windows command-line tools may not show DLLs removed from the relevant PEB lists. _Why:_ common administrative tooling may be blind to userland list tampering. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **PEB privilege requirement** — because the PEB is a userland structure, changing its loader lists requires Administrator privileges rather than System or kernel-level access. _Why:_ attackers do not need kernel control to hide modules through PEB unlinking. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **Non-loader injection behavior** — injected code loaded without using the Windows loader may be absent from PEB module lists. _Why:_ loader bypasses naturally create evidence gaps in PEB-based module enumeration. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **VAD reporting of non-loader code** — code absent from PEB lists may still appear in VAD-based reporting. _Why:_ VAD analysis can expose memory regions that PEB-only methods miss. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **PEB/VAD mismatch value** — mismatches between PEB list membership and VAD-reported executable mappings are useful for detecting multiple injection methods. _Why:_ inconsistencies across redundant process-memory structures are strong investigative leads. _[GCFA p.~547]_

### ldrmodules Method

- **ldrmodules comparison model** — `ldrmodules` does not merely report DLLs listed in the process's PEB linked lists. _Why:_ it is designed to detect modules that are mapped but hidden from loader-list enumeration. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **VAD executable image discovery** — `ldrmodules` identifies executable memory areas in the VAD tree that are image-mapped. _Why:_ these regions provide an independent view of DLL-like mappings in process memory. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **PEB list comparison** — after identifying image-mapped executable VAD regions, `ldrmodules` compares those findings against the three PEB DLL lists. _Why:_ this comparison surfaces modules missing from one or more expected loader lists. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **True column meaning** — a `True` value in an `ldrmodules` list-membership column means the DLL was present in that corresponding PEB list. _Why:_ analysts use this value to confirm normal loader-list visibility. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **False column meaning** — a `False` value in an `ldrmodules` list-membership column means the DLL was absent from that corresponding PEB list. _Why:_ absence from expected lists can indicate unlinking or suspicious loading behavior. _[GCFA p.~547]_

- **Suspicious DLL identification** — comparing `InLoad`, `InInit`, and `InMem` values allows analysts to visually identify DLLs that may have been unlinked or loaded suspiciously. _Why:_ inconsistent membership patterns can point to malicious injected modules. _[GCFA p.~547]_

### ldrmodules Indicators

- **PEB loader lists** — the output compares whether a memory region appears in three PEB-tracked loader lists: `InLoad`, `InInit`, and `InMem`. _Why:_ disagreement across these lists can expose hidden or injected code. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **All-False suspicious pattern** — the row at base `0x8d0000` has `False` for `InLoad`, `InInit`, and `InMem`. _Why:_ absence from all three loader lists is a strong anomaly for executable code found in a process. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **Missing mapped file indicator** — the suspicious row has `MappedPath` set to `N/A`. _Why:_ lack of a backing file prevents normal attribution to an on-disk module. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **Suspicious memory region** — the page identifies one suspicious region inside `svchost.exe`. _Why:_ narrowing to one region gives analysts a concrete extraction and triage target. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **Suspicious base address** — the identified suspicious memory section begins at `0x8d0000`. _Why:_ the base address is needed to locate or dump the suspect memory. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **PEB-list absence** — memory section `0x8d0000` is absent from all three PEB module lists. _Why:_ legitimate loaded modules are usually represented in loader metadata. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **No disk mapping** — memory section `0x8d0000` is not associated with a file on disk. _Why:_ injected code often exists in memory without a normal file-backed VAD. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **VAD attribution failure** — `ldrmodules` can detect code at the suspicious location but cannot determine a disk origin because the VAD does not track a source file. _Why:_ missing VAD file association supports a memory-only injection hypothesis. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **Windows API loading implication** — memory sections without a normal file-backed origin may not have been loaded through standard Windows loader APIs. _Why:_ bypassing normal loading paths is consistent with process injection. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **Injection interpretation** — the page treats the all-False loader-list state plus missing mapped path as a clear code-injection sign. _Why:_ combining metadata absence with no file backing is more meaningful than either condition alone. _[GCFA p.~548]_

### Process Executable Row Behavior

- **Process image row** — the first table row represents the process executable itself. _Why:_ analysts must distinguish the main executable mapping from injected or DLL mappings. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **Process executable path** — the process image is located at `\WINDOWS\system32\svchost.exe`. _Why:_ this confirms the displayed process image path for PID `936`. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **Process code section handling** — `ldrmodules` also reports the process code section. _Why:_ the main executable appears in plugin output and should not be mistaken for a DLL anomaly. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **Expected InInit exception** — the row for the process executable is present in the loader-related results except for `InInit`. _Why:_ a `False` value in `InInit` for the executable row is expected behavior. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **Executable-row false value** — the `InInit` field always appears as `False` for the process executable row. _Why:_ this prevents analysts from treating the executable’s `InInit=False` as suspicious by itself. _[GCFA p.~548]_

### Table Header Fields

- **Pid column** — `Pid` records the process identifier for each listed memory region. _Why:_ it links each module or memory section to the owning process. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **Process column** — `Process` records the process name associated with each row. _Why:_ it identifies which executable owns the memory region. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **Base column** — `Base` records the starting virtual address for the listed region. _Why:_ base addresses are needed for memory inspection and extraction. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **InLoad column** — `InLoad` records whether the region appears in the PEB load-order list. _Why:_ absence can indicate loader metadata manipulation or nonstandard loading. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **InInit column** — `InInit` records whether the region appears in the PEB initialization-order list. _Why:_ this is one of the loader-list consistency checks used by `ldrmodules`. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **InMem column** — `InMem` records whether the region appears in the PEB memory-order list. _Why:_ discrepancies against other lists can reveal hidden modules. _[GCFA p.~548]_
- **MappedPath column** — `MappedPath` records the file path backing the memory region when available. _Why:_ file-backed mappings are easier to attribute than memory-only regions. _[GCFA p.~548]_

### Suspicious Regions

- **Suspicious-region count** — the page identifies two suspicious memory regions inside `lsass.exe`. _Why:_ this scopes the injection investigation to two anomalous base addresses. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Suspicious region · `0x80000`** — memory section `0x80000` is missing from all three checked PEB lists. _Why:_ complete absence from loader lists is consistent with injected code. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Suspicious region · `0x80000` disk mapping** — memory section `0x80000` has no mapped file on disk. _Why:_ an executable region without disk backing suggests code was placed directly in memory. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Suspicious region · `0x80000` interpretation** — the page treats `0x80000` as a sign of code injection. _Why:_ it combines no PEB-list presence with no disk mapping. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Suspicious region · `0x1000000` role** — memory section `0x1000000` is described as the expected process executable region. _Why:_ the main executable mapping is central to detecting hollowing. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Suspicious region · `0x1000000` disk mapping** — memory section `0x1000000` lacks a mapped disk path. _Why:_ an executable image region without its expected backing file is suspicious. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Suspicious region · `0x1000000` interpretation** — the page treats `0x1000000` as a process-hollowing indicator. _Why:_ the original executable appears to have been replaced in memory. _[GCFA p.~549]_

### Stuxnet Injection Behavior

- **Stuxnet injection variety** — Stuxnet uses more than one form of DLL injection. _Why:_ analysts should expect several injection patterns rather than a single artifact type. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Process hollowing as specialized injection** — the page describes process hollowing as a specialized form of injection. _Why:_ it explains why an executable image may appear present but no longer correspond to its disk file. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Potentially injected process selection** — ldrmodules was run against one process suspected of injection in the sample image. _Why:_ targeted plugin use helps validate suspicions from prior analysis. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **No MappedPath entries** — two ldrmodules rows for `lsass.exe` PID `868` have no mapped-path information. _Why:_ these are the key anomalies that drive the page’s analysis. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **No MappedPath meaning** — missing mapped-path data commonly indicates that the memory contents were not loaded through the normal Windows API path. _Why:_ normally loaded code should have disk-backed mapping evidence. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Windows API loading expectation** — code loaded through standard Windows APIs must originate from disk. _Why:_ this expectation makes memory-only code regions suspicious. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Memory-origin injection** — the unmapped sections may have been inserted into the process directly from memory. _Why:_ this explains how malicious code can exist in a process without a corresponding file path. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Disk avoidance motive** — malware may avoid writing code to disk to reduce exposure to antivirus and forensic collection. _Why:_ memory-only execution frustrates file-based detection and evidence gathering. _[GCFA p.~549]_

### PEB List Evidence

- **MappedPath as clue** — absence of MappedPath is itself a strong suspicious indicator. _Why:_ disk mapping is expected for normally loaded executable content. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **PEB linked-list absence** — the suspicious DLL-like entries are also missing from multiple linked lists in the Process Environment Block. _Why:_ inconsistencies in loader lists strengthen the injection assessment. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **PEB abbreviation** — PEB refers to the Process Environment Block. _Why:_ ldrmodules uses PEB list membership as part of its suspicious-module analysis. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Injected DLL pattern · `0x80000`** — section `0x80000` is not represented in any of the checked PEB lists. _Why:_ the page presents this as a clear example of injected DLL-style behavior. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Executable anomaly · `0x1000000`** — section `0x1000000` appears in all checked lists except InInit. _Why:_ this pattern must be interpreted differently from total list absence. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Process executable InInit behavior** — every process executable is absent from the InInit list by design. _Why:_ analysts should not treat the executable’s InInit `False` value alone as malicious. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **InInit value for process executable** — the InInit list will report `False` for a process executable. _Why:_ this avoids a false positive when reviewing ldrmodules output. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Expected LSASS mapped path** — the expected mapped path for the LSASS executable is `\WINDOWS\system32\lsass.exe`. _Why:_ the absence of this path at `0x1000000` is what makes the executable region suspicious. _[GCFA p.~549]_

### Process Hollowing Interpretation

- **Hollowing artifact** — the missing mapped path for the executable region is identified as an artifact of process hollowing. _Why:_ it indicates the original process image was displaced. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Unmapped legitimate executable** — the legitimate `lsass.exe` executable was unmapped from the process. _Why:_ unmapping the legitimate image creates space for replacement code. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Replacement code** — new code was placed where the legitimate `lsass.exe` image had been. _Why:_ this is the operational core of process hollowing. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Memory-only replacement** — the replacement of the executable occurred in memory. _Why:_ memory-only replacement leaves no corresponding file for the new executable contents. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **No disk file for hollowed contents** — there is no on-disk file representing the new contents of the process executable. _Why:_ this explains why MappedPath is absent for the hollowed executable region. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Host-tool evasion rationale** — keeping the replacement code off disk reduces the chance that host-based security tools will flag it. _Why:_ this explains why attackers use hollowing and memory-only injection. _[GCFA p.~549]_

### Cross-Tool Correlation

- **Malfind comparison** — ldrmodules findings can be compared with malfind results by matching base addresses. _Why:_ cross-plugin agreement increases confidence that a region is injected. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Base address as join key** — the Base address from ldrmodules is the value used to match suspicious regions against malfind output. _Why:_ it provides a concrete way to correlate tool findings. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Both tools flag same regions** — the page states that malfind and ldrmodules both identify the two suspicious memory sections. _Why:_ independent detection paths strengthen the forensic conclusion. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Ldrmodules analytical role** — ldrmodules provides another method for locating suspicious memory sections inside a process. _Why:_ it complements plugins that detect injection through other heuristics. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Dlllist comparison use case** — an advanced ldrmodules use is comparing its Base address for a suspicious executable or DLL with the offset reported by dlllist. _Why:_ mismatches between kernel-derived and userland-derived views can reveal manipulation. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Ldrmodules data source** — ldrmodules obtains its relevant data from the VAD tree in kernel memory. _Why:_ kernel-memory structures are harder for user-mode malware to alter. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Dlllist data source** — dlllist uses information from the PEB. _Why:_ PEB-based results can be easier for malware to tamper with. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **PEB trust limitation** — PEB data is userland information and is more easily manipulated. _Why:_ this explains why comparing PEB evidence against VAD evidence can expose hollowing. _[GCFA p.~549]_
- **Process hollowing detection by comparison** — several process-hollowing techniques can be found by comparing ldrmodules and dlllist views. _Why:_ disagreement between VAD-derived and PEB-derived module metadata can reveal hidden replacement of process code. _[GCFA p.~549]_

## Page 551

### MemProcFS FindEvil Scope

- **MemProcFS `findevil` plugin family** — this page describes `findevil` detections focused on identifying tampered or inconsistent memory structures. _Why:_ manipulated process and memory metadata are common signs of injection, hollowing, and masquerading. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **Manipulated memory structures** — the detections discussed are aimed less at ordinary file artifacts and more at altered in-memory process state. _Why:_ attackers often change memory-resident structures to hide code after execution. _[GCFA p.551]_

### Process Irregularities

- **Process Irregularities category** — one `findevil` grouping covers abnormal process metadata and process-list relationships. _Why:_ process anomalies can expose hidden, masqueraded, or suspiciously launched processes. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PROC_NOLINK`** — flags a process that is absent from the normal EPROCESS doubly linked process list. _Why:_ unlinking from EPROCESS lists is a classic process-hiding technique. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PROC_PARENT`** — flags a process whose parent process is unexpected, using limited checks against known process relationships. _Why:_ parent-child mismatches can reveal spoofed lineage or suspicious process creation. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PROC_USER`** — flags a process whose token shows an unexpected user-account context. _Why:_ an unusual security context may indicate privilege misuse, token theft, or process masquerading. _[GCFA p.551]_

### Unusual Memory Pages

- **Unusual Memory Pages category** — one `findevil` grouping covers executable content appearing in memory locations that do not match normal image-loading behavior. _Why:_ injected code often lives outside ordinary image-backed executable mappings. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PE_INJECT`** — detects DLL or EXE files located in memory pages that are not image-backed pages. _Why:_ PE content in non-image memory is a strong indicator of injected executable code. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`NOIMAGE_RWX/RX`** — detects executable pages that are not mapped to a DLL or EXE location. _Why:_ executable memory without an image mapping can indicate shellcode or unpacked injected code. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PRIVATE_RWX/RX`** — detects executable pages in private process memory such as data regions, stacks, or heaps. _Why:_ private executable memory is often used by injected payloads, stagers, and unpacked malware. _[GCFA p.551]_

### Kernel And PEB Inconsistencies

- **Kernel/PEB Inconsistencies category** — one `findevil` grouping compares memory-management data with process-environment metadata. _Why:_ mismatches between independent structures can reveal tampering that a single artifact view would miss. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PEB_MASQ` table entry** — detects a mismatch between an image binary path recorded in the PEB and the image path represented by the VAD. _Why:_ this discrepancy suggests the PEB may have been altered for masquerading. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PE_NOLINK` table entry** — detects a DLL present in the VAD but absent from the PEB module lists. _Why:_ unlinked modules can indicate stealthy DLL injection, though this detection has many false positives. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PE_PATCHED` table entry** — detects a DLL that has been modified after it was loaded. _Why:_ post-load modification can reveal hollowing, patching, or in-memory evasion, but 32-bit and JIT-generated code can cause many false positives. _[GCFA p.551]_

### `PEB_MASQ`

- **`PEB_MASQ` target behavior** — this detection looks for Process Environment Block masquerading. _Why:_ PEB masquerading lets malicious code present a misleading process name or path. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **PEB name alteration** — PEB masquerading may modify the name of the originally loaded code. _Why:_ a changed in-memory name can make a malicious or hollowed process appear legitimate. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **PEB file-path alteration** — PEB masquerading may modify the file path of the originally loaded code. _Why:_ path manipulation can mislead analysts and tools that trust PEB metadata. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PEB_MASQ` comparison method** — MemProcFS detects this condition by comparing PEB information with the VAD tree for the same image memory section. _Why:_ cross-checking two independent memory views exposes inconsistencies caused by tampering. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **PEB versus VAD same-image check** — the comparison is scoped to the same image memory section rather than unrelated memory regions. _Why:_ matching the same image section reduces ambiguity when identifying masqueraded image metadata. _[GCFA p.551]_

### `PE_NOLINK`

- **`PE_NOLINK` analytical model** — this detection uses information similar to the Volatility `ldrmodules` plugin. _Why:_ both approaches identify modules that exist in memory but are not properly represented in loader lists. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PE_NOLINK` hit condition** — a detection occurs when a DLL with a PE header is found in a VAD-tracked memory section but is missing from the PEB lists. _Why:_ this combination suggests a module exists in process memory without normal loader bookkeeping. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **DLL with PE header requirement** — `PE_NOLINK` specifically concerns DLL content that still contains a PE header. _Why:_ the PE header helps identify the memory region as a Windows executable module. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **VAD-tracked memory section requirement** — `PE_NOLINK` relies on the VAD tree showing the relevant memory section. _Why:_ the VAD tree provides a memory-manager perspective independent of PEB loader lists. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **PEB-list absence requirement** — `PE_NOLINK` treats absence from PEB lists as suspicious when the DLL is visible through the VAD. _Why:_ malware may unlink injected modules from PEB loader lists to evade module enumeration. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PE_NOLINK` injection coverage** — this detection can identify many forms of process injection. _Why:_ injected modules often appear in memory without normal loader-list representation. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PE_NOLINK` false positives** — the detection can produce false positives, consistent with caveats discussed for `ldrmodules`. _Why:_ analysts should not treat every unlinked module as malicious without corroboration. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **Paged-memory false positives** — MemProcFS reports that paged memory can cause many `PE_NOLINK` false positives. _Why:_ missing paged-out data can make legitimate structures appear incomplete or inconsistent. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **Corrupted-PEB false positives** — MemProcFS reports that damaged PEB structures can also cause many `PE_NOLINK` false positives. _Why:_ structural corruption can mimic deliberate unlinking. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **Page-file inclusion for `PE_NOLINK`** — including a page file in the analysis can reduce false positives. _Why:_ page-file data can restore memory content that would otherwise appear missing. _[GCFA p.551]_

### `PE_PATCHED`

- **`PE_PATCHED` purpose** — this detection looks for executable pages changed after executable code was loaded. _Why:_ post-load modification can reveal hidden tampering inside otherwise legitimate mapped code. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **Patched executable pages** — `PE_PATCHED` focuses on executable pages that have been altered after load time. _Why:_ modified executable pages can indicate hooks, patches, hollowing, or evasion logic. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **Advanced hollowing evolution** — some advanced process-hollowing techniques now modify already loaded executable code. _Why:_ altering legitimate loaded code can provide very strong concealment inside a real process image. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **Legitimately loaded process hiding** — patching loaded executable pages can hide malicious behavior within a process that was legitimately loaded. _Why:_ this reduces the obvious signs associated with replacing or mapping a separate malicious image. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **AMSI evasion patching** — in-memory code is often patched to evade Windows Defender AMSI. _Why:_ AMSI bypasses commonly rely on modifying code paths that inspect scripts or content. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **Page Table Entries** — PTEs track page-level state, including whether pages have been modified. _Why:_ PTE metadata provides low-level evidence of changes to executable memory. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **Prototype PTEs** — prototype PTE structures can indicate that a page was modified. _Why:_ these structures let MemProcFS identify image pages changed after loading. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PE_PATCHED` VAD inspection** — MemProcFS checks active image memory pages in the VAD against prototype PTE modification indicators. _Why:_ combining VAD image-page data with PTE modification state exposes post-load code changes. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PE_PATCHED` value** — this check is described as powerful and necessary. _Why:_ detecting modified executable image pages is important for advanced injection and hollowing investigations. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PE_PATCHED` noise risk** — this check can generate large numbers of false positives on some systems. _Why:_ legitimate runtime behavior can modify executable pages in ways that resemble malicious patching. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **SysWOW64 false-positive pattern** — many expected `PE_PATCHED` false positives occur with SysWOW64 32-bit code. _Why:_ 32-bit compatibility code can produce modification patterns that are not necessarily malicious. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **JIT false-positive pattern** — just-in-time compiled code, including .NET workloads, commonly causes `PE_PATCHED` noise. _Why:_ JIT execution naturally creates or modifies executable code at runtime. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **.NET prevalence in Windows** — many Windows components use .NET, including PowerShell. _Why:_ analysts should expect substantial `PE_PATCHED` noise on systems where .NET code runs. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **PowerShell as .NET example** — PowerShell is specifically identified as .NET-based Windows code. _Why:_ PowerShell activity can contribute to JIT-related detection noise. _[GCFA p.551]_

### Cross-Structure Analysis

- **Cross-referencing memory structures** — `PEB_MASQ`, `PE_NOLINK`, and `PE_PATCHED` rely heavily on comparing separate memory structures. _Why:_ attackers may manipulate one structure while leaving contradictory evidence in another. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`findevil` broader cross-checking** — the three highlighted detections are not the only `findevil` checks that compare different memory structures. _Why:_ the plugin family applies the same corroboration strategy beyond PEB/VAD inconsistency checks. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PE_INJECT` PTE usage** — `PE_INJECT` uses PTE information. _Why:_ PTE state can provide a lower-level view of memory behavior than higher-level process metadata. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`PRIVATE_RWX/RX` PTE usage** — `PRIVATE_RWX/RX` uses PTE information. _Why:_ page-table data helps identify executable private memory that may contain injected code. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **`NOIMAGE_RWX/RX` PTE usage** — `NOIMAGE_RWX/RX` uses PTE information. _Why:_ PTE evidence helps distinguish executable memory that lacks a normal image mapping. _[GCFA p.551]_

- **PTEs as near-ground-truth evidence** — the page describes PTE information as often being closest to ground truth. _Why:_ page-table state reflects actual memory mappings and permissions at a low level. _[GCFA p.551]_

### MemProcFS FindEvil Findings

- **Injection-count context** — the memory sample contains two separate injection patterns rather than one unified artifact. _Why:_ separating the techniques prevents misclassifying reflective injection as DLL hollowing or vice versa. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **Affected-process count** — MemProcFS `findevil` identifies two processes with suspicious memory conditions. _Why:_ multiple process hits suggest the analyst must triage each process independently. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **`sdev.exe` hollowing indicator** — `sdev.exe` is presented as having a DLL hollowing condition involving a DLL that is not linked through the PEB module lists. _Why:_ an unlinked DLL in a process can indicate loader metadata manipulation or replacement of expected code. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **`notepad.exe` reflective-injection indicator** — `notepad.exe` is described as showing signs consistent with reflective injection. _Why:_ reflective loading often leaves executable private memory and PE-header artifacts rather than normal file-backed DLL mappings. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **`notepad.exe` private RWX evidence** — `notepad.exe` has more than one `PRIVATE_RWX` finding. _Why:_ writable-and-executable private memory is unusual and is a common injection signal. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **`notepad.exe` PE-in-private-memory evidence** — `notepad.exe` has a `PE_INJECT` finding, meaning a PE header is present in private memory. _Why:_ a PE image in private memory can indicate code loaded without the normal Windows image-loader path. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **Reflective-loading inference** — the combination of private RWX pages and a private-memory PE header in `notepad.exe` likely points to reflectively loaded code. _Why:_ this combination links both executable permissions and PE structure to memory not backed like a normal module. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **Investigation priority for `notepad.exe`** — the `notepad.exe` indicators should be investigated further rather than treated as benign by default. _Why:_ the slide frames the combined evidence as suspicious enough for follow-up. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **Volatility malfind relevance** — a tool such as Volatility `malfind` should also be capable of detecting the same `notepad.exe` indicator combination. _Why:_ cross-tool confirmation strengthens confidence in suspected injection findings. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **`sdev.exe` PE_NOLINK meaning** — `PE_NOLINK` in `sdev.exe` indicates a PE-header-bearing section inside image memory that is absent from PEB tracking lists. _Why:_ memory that looks like an image but is missing from loader lists is a strong abnormality. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **`sdev.exe` attack class** — the `sdev.exe` condition represents a different attack style from the `notepad.exe` reflective-injection evidence. _Why:_ the analyst should distinguish image-space hollowing from private-memory reflective loading. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **Evidence to preserve for `sdev.exe`** — the virtual address and description fields for the `sdev.exe` finding should be recorded for later analysis. _Why:_ exact memory locations and labels allow targeted extraction, comparison, and reporting. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **Suspicion-driven triage** — the `sdev.exe` finding becomes especially important if the process was already considered suspicious. _Why:_ memory anomalies carry more weight when they reinforce prior process-level concern. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **DLL hollowing definition** — DLL hollowing targets a legitimately loaded DLL and replaces its code section with attacker-controlled code. _Why:_ the process can retain the appearance of a normal loaded DLL while executing different code. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **DLL hollowing sophistication** — the page characterizes DLL hollowing as an advanced hollowing variant. _Why:_ analysts should expect more subtle metadata and mapping behavior than in simpler injection cases. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **PEB-list limitation** — the Windows API behavior used in the DLL hollowing attack does not link the newly introduced DLL content into the three PEB module lists. _Why:_ this explains why the artifact appears as `PE_NOLINK`. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **`PE_NOLINK` cause** — the `PE_NOLINK` detection occurs because the replacement content is not represented in the PEB loader lists. _Why:_ the flag directly reflects a loader-list inconsistency. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **Modified location** — the altered memory location for the DLL hollowing example is `0x00007fff7b5e0000`. _Why:_ this address identifies the exact suspicious region for extraction and validation. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **Volatility attribution mismatch** — Volatility `ldrmodules` reports the suspicious memory section as associated with `aadauthhelper.dll`. _Why:_ the nominal DLL mapping can differ from the code that is actually running after hollowing. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **PEB-list absence for `aadauthhelper.dll` mapping** — the memory section attributed to `aadauthhelper.dll` is not present in any PEB module list. _Why:_ absence from all lists is the key inconsistency supporting the hollowing conclusion. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **Hollowed-DLL interpretation** — the page states that the region is no longer functioning as the original `aadauthhelper.dll` because it has been hollowed to execute replacement code. _Why:_ this explains why the mapped name alone is not reliable evidence of benign DLL content. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **DLL size as selection factor** — `aadauthhelper.dll` is described as relatively large, making it suitable for hollowing. _Why:_ the target DLL’s allocated memory must be large enough to hold the copied exploit code. _[GCFA p.553]_
- **Exploit-size constraint** — a DLL hollowing target must have allocated memory larger than the payload being copied into it. _Why:_ insufficient space would prevent the replacement code from fitting cleanly in the target region. _[GCFA p.553]_

- **YARA plus memory analysis** — Combining YARA rules with MemProcFS memory inspection helps expose malware variants that may otherwise be difficult to notice. _Why:_ signature hits can provide the first investigative lead into a stealthy process or memory region. _[GCFA p.~555]_
