## Page 601

### DLL Extraction

- **Shared DLL reuse** — DLLs can be mapped into many different processes at the same time. _Why:_ dumping DLLs process-by-process can produce repeated copies of the same library. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Duplicate DLL dumps** — extracting DLLs from several processes may yield many duplicate files. _Why:_ analysts should expect redundancy and avoid treating every dumped DLL as a unique artifact. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 3 DLL dump command** — `vol.py -f memory.img -o output-folder windows.dlllist --pid 1040 --dump` dumps DLLs associated with process ID `1040`. _Why:_ it shows the Volatility 3 syntax for targeted DLL extraction from one process. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 3 input image flag** — `-f memory.img` identifies `memory.img` as the memory image to analyze. _Why:_ the command must know which memory acquisition file to parse. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 3 output directory flag** — `-o output-folder` directs dumped output into `output-folder`. _Why:_ DLL dumping creates files that need a destination path. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 3 DLL listing plugin** — `windows.dlllist` is the plugin used in the shown Volatility 3 command. _Why:_ this plugin can enumerate process DLLs and, with dumping enabled, extract them. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 3 process selector** — `--pid 1040` limits the DLL operation to PID `1040`. _Why:_ targeting a single process reduces irrelevant dumped DLLs. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 3 DLL dump switch** — `--dump` instructs the DLL-listing operation to extract files rather than only list them. _Why:_ enumeration alone does not produce reviewable DLL files. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 2 DLL dump command** — `vol2.py -f memory.img profile=<profile> dlldump --dump-dir=output-folder -p 1040` dumps DLLs from process `1040` using Volatility 2. _Why:_ it provides the legacy equivalent for analysts using Volatility 2. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 2 profile parameter** — `profile=<profile>` specifies the operating-system profile required by Volatility 2. _Why:_ Volatility 2 commonly needs a correct profile to interpret memory structures. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 2 DLL extraction plugin** — `dlldump` is the Volatility 2 plugin shown for DLL extraction. _Why:_ it is the older plugin counterpart for dumping process DLLs. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 2 dump directory flag** — `--dump-dir=output-folder` sends extracted DLLs to `output-folder`. _Why:_ the extracted artifacts must be written to a chosen directory. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 2 process selector** — `-p 1040` targets process ID `1040` for DLL dumping. _Why:_ process scoping helps focus extraction on the process of interest. _[GCFA p.~601]_

### Driver Extraction

- **Malicious driver follow-up** — after a suspicious driver is found in memory, extracting it is a logical next analysis step. _Why:_ a dumped driver can be reviewed with static, dynamic, or malware-analysis tooling. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Driver extraction purpose** — drivers are extracted from memory to support deeper review and analysis. _Why:_ in-memory kernel components may contain evidence not available from disk. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 3 driver dump plugin** — `windows.modules --dump` is identified as the Volatility 3 method for dumping drivers. _Why:_ it provides a direct workflow for kernel-driver extraction. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Default `windows.modules --dump` behavior** — without narrowing options, `windows.modules --dump` dumps all kernel drivers present in the memory image. _Why:_ this can create many output files and makes output management important. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Output folder importance for driver dumps** — providing an output folder with `-o` is emphasized when dumping kernel drivers. _Why:_ dumping all drivers can generate substantial output that needs to be organized. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 3 modules dump command** — `vol.py -f memory.img -o output-folder windows.modules --dump` dumps kernel modules from `memory.img` into `output-folder`. _Why:_ it gives the exact Volatility 3 syntax for driver extraction. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 3 driver input image flag** — `-f memory.img` supplies the memory image for the `windows.modules --dump` command. _Why:_ driver extraction depends on parsing the correct acquisition file. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 3 driver output flag** — `-o output-folder` sets the destination directory for dumped driver files. _Why:_ kernel-driver dumping writes recovered artifacts to disk. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 3 kernel module plugin** — `windows.modules` is the plugin used for kernel driver/module enumeration and dumping. _Why:_ loaded kernel modules are the source objects for standard driver extraction. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 3 module dump switch** — `--dump` changes the module operation from listing to extraction. _Why:_ analysts need this switch to obtain driver files for later review. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Deeper driver recovery plugin** — `windows.modscan --dump` is recommended when deeper driver recovery is needed. _Why:_ scanning can locate driver-related objects beyond the ordinary loaded-driver list. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Unlinked driver recovery** — `windows.modscan --dump` can help recover drivers that are no longer linked into the normal driver list. _Why:_ malware or rootkits may hide by unlinking kernel structures. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Unloaded driver recovery** — `windows.modscan --dump` can be used to seek drivers that are not currently present in the active drivers list. _Why:_ previously loaded malicious drivers may still leave recoverable memory artifacts. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Driver list limitation** — the normal drivers list may omit unlinked or unloaded drivers. _Why:_ relying only on the active list can miss hidden or historical kernel artifacts. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 2 driver dump equivalent** — `moddump` is the Volatility 2 counterpart for driver extraction. _Why:_ analysts using older tooling need the equivalent plugin name. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 2 base-offset extraction** — `moddump` can extract a driver by base offset using `-b offset`. _Why:_ offset-based targeting supports precise extraction of a specific kernel module. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 2 regex extraction** — `moddump` can extract drivers matching a regular expression with `-r name_regex`. _Why:_ name-pattern targeting helps isolate drivers of interest without dumping everything. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 2 driver dump command** — `vol2.py -f memory.img profile=<profile> moddump --dump-dir=output-folder` dumps drivers with Volatility 2. _Why:_ it documents the legacy syntax for extracting kernel modules from memory. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 2 driver image flag** — `-f memory.img` identifies the memory image for the `moddump` command. _Why:_ the plugin must parse the intended evidence source. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 2 driver profile parameter** — `profile=<profile>` supplies the Volatility 2 operating-system profile for driver dumping. _Why:_ the correct profile is needed to interpret kernel memory structures. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Volatility 2 driver dump directory flag** — `--dump-dir=output-folder` writes dumped drivers into `output-folder`. _Why:_ extracted kernel artifacts need a defined storage location. _[GCFA p.~601]_

### Memory Residency and Paging

- **No guaranteed process-object availability** — a memory image may not contain every process object an analyst wants to extract. _Why:_ absence or incompleteness in RAM can limit artifact recovery. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Paged-out object risk** — all or part of an object may have been paged out of physical RAM. _Why:_ memory-only analysis may fail when relevant bytes reside outside the captured RAM image. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Extraction failure condition** — extraction can fail when needed object data is not resident in memory. _Why:_ failed dumps may reflect paging rather than proof that the object never existed. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Partial extraction condition** — extraction can produce incomplete data when only part of the object remains in RAM. _Why:_ analysts must treat dumped files as potentially incomplete unless validated. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Page file analysis value** — adding the page file to analysis can significantly improve recovery when memory objects were paged out. _Why:_ the page file may contain object content missing from the RAM acquisition. _[GCFA p.~601]_
- **Later page-file coverage** — page-file-assisted analysis is identified as a later topic in the same section. _Why:_ it signals that fuller recovery workflows may require evidence beyond the memory image alone. _[GCFA p.~601]_

## Page 602

### Process Memory Composition

- **Process memory scope** — A process address space contains both executable code regions and data regions owned by that process. _Why:_ separating code from data determines what evidence a dump is likely to expose. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **Code sections** — Process code regions are useful when building indicators of compromise and performing reverse engineering. _Why:_ code-oriented dumps approximate executable logic and can support malware identification. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **Data sections** — Process data regions are useful for recovering runtime content and reconstructing process behavior. _Why:_ data-oriented dumps can expose evidence that never existed as a standalone file on disk. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **Process-code interpretation** — Code memory can be treated as an approximate reconstruction of the process executable. _Why:_ this explains why some dump methods are suited to executable analysis rather than broad artifact recovery. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **PowerShell code dump expectation** — Dumping the executable-style PE for a PowerShell process would usually recover mostly Microsoft-authored code. _Why:_ analysts should not assume the executable image alone contains attacker scripts or commands. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **Mapped code variation** — Depending on the extraction tool, a code-focused dump may also include mapped code from DLLs or drivers. _Why:_ tool behavior affects what code artifacts appear in the output. _[GCFA p.602]_

### Code-Focused Dumping

- **Volatility 3 executable dump** — `windows.pslist --dump` attempts to recover a close copy of the process’s original executable image. _Why:_ this is the Volatility 3 path for executable-style process extraction. _[GCFA p.602]_

- **MemProcFS PE reconstruction name** — MemProcFS names the recreated executable `pefile.dll`. _Why:_ knowing the filename prevents analysts from overlooking the executable reconstruction. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **Code-focused use case** — Executable-style process dumps support IOC creation and reverse engineering. _Why:_ these outputs are best suited to examining code, not necessarily runtime data. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **Shown `pslist --dump` output file** — The slide lists `pid.8260.0x400000.dmp` as the `pslist --dump` executable-style dump. _Why:_ it identifies the code-focused dump artifact for PID 8260. _[GCFA p.602]_

### Runtime Data Evidence

- **Data-region volume** — Runtime data typically occupies many more process memory sections than code. _Why:_ analysts should expect the richest behavioral evidence outside executable-image dumps. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **Command-line buffers** — Full process memory may contain command-line buffers. _Why:_ recovered commands can reveal execution behavior and attacker intent. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **Typed-text buffers** — Full process memory may contain typed text. _Why:_ user or attacker input can survive in process memory. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **PowerShell scripts in memory** — A PowerShell process’s data memory may contain loaded scripts. _Why:_ script content may be recoverable even when not available from disk. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **PowerShell modules in memory** — A PowerShell process’s data memory may contain loaded modules. _Why:_ module recovery can help reconstruct in-memory PowerShell activity. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **DGA output in memory** — Malware domain generation algorithm output may appear in process data memory. _Why:_ generated domains can explain or predict network connections. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **Network insight from runtime data** — Process data can provide context about network activity. _Why:_ memory artifacts may expose connection targets or generated infrastructure. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **Heap inclusion differences** — Process-memory tools vary in whether they include heap data. _Why:_ heap coverage affects recovery of runtime artifacts. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **Stack inclusion differences** — Process-memory tools vary in whether they include stack data. _Why:_ stack coverage affects recovery of execution context and transient values. _[GCFA p.602]_
- **Private-memory inclusion differences** — Process-memory tools vary in how they include other private memory regions. _Why:_ private-memory handling changes what artifacts are available for analysis. _[GCFA p.602]_

## Page 603

### MemProcFS Process Memory Files

- **Full process-space representation** — MemProcFS can expose a file that models the entire possible virtual address space of a process. _Why:_ this representation is extremely large and awkward to process with ordinary forensic searching workflows. _[GCFA p.~603]_

- **Example full process-space file size** — the course example shows the full process-space representation as a 2 TB file. _Why:_ the size illustrates why this artifact is impractical for routine string searches or manual inspection. _[GCFA p.~603]_

- **Sparse content in full process-space file** — most of the 2 TB example file consists of zero-filled regions. _Why:_ zero-heavy content still creates a huge logical file that many tools cannot search efficiently. _[GCFA p.~603]_

- **Searchability limitation** — the full process-space file is not convenient for searching with many common tools. _Why:_ investigators need searchable artifacts for triage, string recovery, and malware hunting. _[GCFA p.~603]_

### minidump.dmp

- **MemProcFS minidump.dmp usability** — MemProcFS currently provides `minidump.dmp` as the most practical per-process file for tasks such as string searching. _Why:_ it offers a smaller and more usable artifact than the full virtual address space file. _[GCFA p.~603]_

- **minidump.dmp per-process scope** — each process has its own `minidump.dmp` file. _Why:_ per-process dumps let analysts target suspicious processes without searching the entire memory image. _[GCFA p.~603]_

- **minidump.dmp location** — the `minidump.dmp` file is located in the `minidump` folder. _Why:_ knowing the folder name helps analysts quickly find the searchable process dump artifact in MemProcFS output. _[GCFA p.~603]_

- **minidump.dmp stack content** — `minidump.dmp` includes stack memory. _Why:_ stacks may contain function arguments, strings, return addresses, and execution context useful for process analysis. _[GCFA p.~603]_

- **minidump.dmp heap content** — `minidump.dmp` includes heap memory. _Why:_ heaps commonly hold runtime strings, decoded configuration data, buffers, and malware-created objects. _[GCFA p.~603]_

- **minidump.dmp executable content** — `minidump.dmp` includes the process executable. _Why:_ the executable image can help connect recovered memory content to the running program. _[GCFA p.~603]_

- **minidump.dmp loaded DLL content** — `minidump.dmp` includes loaded DLLs. _Why:_ DLL contents can reveal imported code, injected modules, or libraries relevant to process behavior. _[GCFA p.~603]_

- **minidump.dmp private-memory limitation** — `minidump.dmp` omits many private memory regions. _Why:_ important artifacts may be absent, so analysts should not treat the minidump as a complete process-memory capture. _[GCFA p.~603]_

- **minidump.dmp triage role** — `minidump.dmp` is suitable for an initial review pass. _Why:_ it provides a practical first artifact before moving to more complete memory-mapping methods. _[GCFA p.~603]_

### Volatility Comparison

- **Volatility windows.memmap completeness** — the Volatility `windows.memmap` plugin is identified as the more complete option compared with MemProcFS `minidump.dmp`. _Why:_ analysts needing broader process-memory coverage should use `windows.memmap` when minidump coverage is insufficient. _[GCFA p.~603]_

## Page 605

### String Searching Scope

- **String searching** — locating readable text in raw data is a common forensic method. _Why:_ many investigative leads survive as text even when higher-level artifacts are unavailable. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Memory-analysis use case** — string searching is useful when examining memory. _Why:_ volatile data can contain network indicators, credentials, malware content, and process artifacts. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Malware reverse-engineering use case** — string searching supports malware analysis. _Why:_ embedded indicators such as domains, URLs, commands, and configuration fragments may be visible as strings. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Unallocated-space use case** — string searching can be applied to unallocated disk-image space. _Why:_ deleted or orphaned content may remain searchable even without filesystem metadata. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Evidence-as-strings concept** — common forensic evidence can appear as textual data. _Why:_ simple string extraction can expose leads before deeper parsing is performed. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **IP addresses as string evidence** — IP addresses are examples of artifacts that may be found through string searching. _Why:_ they can identify remote infrastructure or communications. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Domain names as string evidence** — domain names may be discoverable as strings. _Why:_ domains can reveal command-and-control, browsing, phishing, or malware configuration indicators. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Filenames as string evidence** — filenames may appear in extracted strings. _Why:_ filenames can identify tools, malware components, staged files, or user activity. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Internet communications as string evidence** — network-communication content may appear as text. _Why:_ communications can reveal services, destinations, protocols, or exchanged data. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Malware command-and-control packets as string evidence** — C2 packet content may be searchable as strings. _Why:_ C2 strings can expose malware infrastructure or protocol details. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Usernames as string evidence** — usernames may be recovered through string searching. _Why:_ account names can connect activity to users or systems. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Passwords as string evidence** — passwords may appear in searchable text. _Why:_ credential recovery can explain access paths and attacker capability. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Extracted process memory search target** — extracted process-memory data can be searched with string tools. _Why:_ process memory may contain runtime-only artifacts. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Memory-section search target** — individual memory sections can be searched. _Why:_ targeted section searches can reduce noise and preserve context. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Page-file search target** — page files can be searched for strings. _Why:_ paged-out memory may preserve evidence no longer resident in RAM. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Full-memory-image search target** — entire memory images can be searched. _Why:_ broad searches can discover leads across all captured physical memory. _[GCFA p.605]_

### `strings`

- **`strings` tool** — Linux includes a utility for extracting readable strings from a data stream. _Why:_ it provides a basic way to turn binary evidence into searchable text. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **`strings` ASCII capability** — the tool can extract English ASCII strings. _Why:_ ASCII strings commonly contain program text, paths, indicators, and user data. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **`strings` Unicode capability** — the tool can extract Unicode strings. _Why:_ Windows artifacts often store text in Unicode form. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **`strings -t d`** — this option prints string offsets in decimal. _Why:_ offsets let an examiner return to the exact location of an interesting hit in the original evidence. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Displayed `strings` option `-t d`** — the slide’s option summary lists `-t d` as the decimal-offset output mode. _Why:_ offset-aware string output preserves location context. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Byte offset output behavior** — when decimal offsets are enabled, the number appears before the extracted string. _Why:_ the leading number directly identifies where the string begins in the input stream. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Offset-driven context review** — after finding a relevant string, the examiner can inspect nearby bytes in the original stream. _Why:_ surrounding data can clarify whether a hit is meaningful or incidental. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **`strings -e l`** — this option extracts Unicode strings. _Why:_ a separate Unicode pass helps recover Windows-style wide-character text. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Displayed `strings` option `-e l`** — the slide’s option summary identifies `-e l` as the Unicode extraction option. _Why:_ missing Unicode extraction can cause important Windows artifacts to be overlooked. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **`strings -<num>`** — the option form using a number limits output to strings at least that length. _Why:_ minimum-length filtering can reduce noisy short fragments. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Two-pass `strings` workflow** — standard practice described on the page is to run `strings` separately for ASCII and Unicode. _Why:_ separate extraction modes increase coverage across common encodings. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Combined strings file** — ASCII and Unicode outputs can be merged into one strings file. _Why:_ a unified file simplifies later searching and sorting. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Command `strings -a -t d file > strings.txt`** — this example extracts strings from `file`, includes decimal offsets, and writes results to `strings.txt`. _Why:_ it creates an offset-preserving ASCII-oriented search corpus. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Command `strings -a -t d -e l file >> strings.txt`** — this example appends Unicode string extraction results with decimal offsets to `strings.txt`. _Why:_ it adds wide-character hits to the same search corpus without overwriting the first pass. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Command `sort strings.txt > sorted_strings.txt`** — this example sorts the combined strings output into `sorted_strings.txt`. _Why:_ sorting can make review and repeated searches more manageable. _[GCFA p.605]_

### `grep`

- **`grep` role** — after creating a strings file, the next step described is searching it with `grep`. _Why:_ extracted text must be queried to isolate investigative matches. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **`grep` availability** — `grep` is commonly present by default in Unix-like environments. _Why:_ investigators can often use it without adding specialized software. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **SIFT Workstation example** — Linux SIFT Workstation is named as an environment where `grep` is commonly available. _Why:_ SIFT is a forensic workstation environment used for analysis workflows. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **`grep` effectiveness** — the page characterizes `grep` as efficient and powerful for search. _Why:_ it is suitable for large extracted-string datasets. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Extract-before-grep workflow** — the usual process is to extract all strings from a dataset before running `grep`. _Why:_ searching pre-extracted text is simpler than repeatedly scanning raw binary data. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Pattern matching with `grep`** — `grep` is used to locate pattern matches in extracted strings. _Why:_ pattern matching turns broad string output into actionable hits. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Keyword-list importance** — effective searching depends heavily on choosing useful search terms. _Why:_ tool output quality depends on investigative hypotheses and indicator selection. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Keyword list as living document** — the page says the keyword list should evolve as the investigation develops. _Why:_ new facts can add search terms, while irrelevant terms can be removed. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Single-expression searching** — `grep` can search for one string or one regular expression at a time. _Why:_ targeted searches support focused hypothesis testing. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Multi-expression searching** — `grep` can search using a file containing multiple expressions. _Why:_ batch searching is useful when many indicators or keywords are known. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **`grep -i`** — this option ignores letter case. _Why:_ case-insensitive searches reduce missed hits caused by capitalization differences. _[GCFA p.605]_
- **Displayed `grep` option `-i`** — the slide’s option summary lists `-i` as case-insensitive matching. _Why:_ indicator casing may vary across artifacts. _[GCFA p.605]_

- **Displayed `grep` option `-B <num>`** — the slide’s option summary says `-B <num>` shows that many prior lines. _Why:_ context lines help interpret isolated string hits. _[GCFA p.605]_

- **Displayed `grep` option `-f <filename>`** — the slide’s option summary describes `-f <filename>` as using a file of strings. _Why:_ stored search lists reduce manual command repetition. _[GCFA p.605]_

- **Linux string searches** — when a string-search command runs in a case-sensitive Linux environment, letter case affects whether matches are found. _Why:_ investigators can miss relevant hits if they search for only one capitalization variant. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **`grep -i` option** — the `-i` flag makes `grep` perform matching without requiring exact capitalization. _Why:_ this reduces missed hits caused by case differences in extracted string sets. _[GCFA p.606]_

### Windows 10+ Memory Compression

- **Windows 10 memory compression** — memory compression became common starting with Windows 10. _Why:_ analysts must account for compressed memory when examining modern Windows systems. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Page file compression** — Windows 10 commonly uses compression for page file data. _Why:_ compressed page file content may not be directly readable by ordinary string extraction or scanning. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **RAM compression** — Windows 10 commonly compresses infrequently used regions of physical memory. _Why:_ inactive memory contents may be hidden from tools that cannot decompress them. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Performance purpose** — Windows memory compression is a performance optimization. _Why:_ understanding the operating-system behavior prevents analysts from treating compression itself as inherently suspicious. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Page-fault reduction** — memory compression reduces the number of page faults. _Why:_ this explains why Windows uses compression rather than immediately paging all inactive data to disk. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Multi-core CPU decompression** — modern multi-core CPUs can decompress memory transparently enough for Windows to use this feature efficiently. _Why:_ hardware capability is part of why compression is practical on modern systems. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Forensic visibility impact** — memory forensic tools may report less data when they cannot decompress compressed regions. _Why:_ tool output can underrepresent available evidence. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Scanning plugin limitation** — scanning plugins may locate fewer artifacts if they cannot reliably decompress data before signature matching. _Why:_ compressed bytes can prevent signatures from matching their original uncompressed form. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Volatility 3 compressed-memory capability** — Volatility 3 is described as having capability for handling compressed memory. _Why:_ analysts should consider whether their Volatility 3 workflow can access compressed regions. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **MemProcFS compressed-memory capability** — MemProcFS is described as having capability for handling compressed memory. _Why:_ MemProcFS may expose evidence that simpler scans of raw memory miss. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **MemProcFS relative strength** — at the time of the course writing, MemProcFS appeared to be well ahead of Volatility 3 for compressed-memory handling. _Why:_ tool choice affects how much data an analyst can recover from modern Windows memory. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Windows-native MemProcFS advantage** — MemProcFS may perform better with compressed memory because it runs natively on Windows. _Why:_ native Windows execution may give the tool better access to Windows memory-management behavior. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Windows version of MemProcFS** — the page identifies compressed-memory support as a reason to prefer the Windows version of MemProcFS. _Why:_ choosing the Windows build can improve recovery from compressed Windows memory artifacts. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **String extraction degradation** — memory compression reduces the ability to extract human-readable strings from memory files. _Why:_ compressed content does not appear as normal plaintext until decompressed. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **MemProcFS object extraction mitigation** — using MemProcFS to extract memory objects can reduce the string-recovery problem caused by compression. _Why:_ object-level extraction may expose decompressed or more usable content than raw image scanning. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Whole-image search problem** — compression can be a major issue when searching across an entire memory image. _Why:_ broad raw searches can skip meaningful data that remains compressed. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Page-file search problem** — compression can be a major issue when searching across a page file. _Why:_ pagefile evidence from Windows 10 and later may not be readable without decompression. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Required decompression workflow** — when scanning compressed memory or page files, analysts need a tool that detects compression and emits decompressed data. _Why:_ decompression creates a more complete search target for strings, carving, and signatures. _[GCFA p.606]_

### `winmem_decompress.py`

- **`winmem_decompress.py`** — Maxim Suhanov wrote `winmem_decompress.py` to scan memory for compressed regions and output decompressed data. _Why:_ it addresses the evidence-loss problem caused by Windows memory compression. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Maxim Suhanov** — Maxim Suhanov is identified as the author of `winmem_decompress.py`. _Why:_ attribution helps analysts locate and assess the tool. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Slow processing** — `winmem_decompress.py` is described as slow. _Why:_ analysts should expect decompression to add processing time to memory workflows. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Large output gain** — using `winmem_decompress.py` can commonly recover more than 150% additional data from a memory image. _Why:_ the size increase shows how much content may be hidden by compression. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Not for later memory-framework analysis** — output from `winmem_decompress.py` cannot be analyzed afterward by a memory forensic framework as though it were a normal memory image. _Why:_ the output is not a substitute for the original memory image in structured memory analysis. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **String-searching use case** — `winmem_decompress.py` output is intended for string searching. _Why:_ decompressed plaintext improves keyword and indicator discovery. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Carving use case** — `winmem_decompress.py` output is intended for file or artifact carving. _Why:_ decompressed data may reveal recoverable embedded objects that were not visible in compressed form. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **YARA scanning use case** — `winmem_decompress.py` output is intended for YARA scanning. _Why:_ signatures can match decompressed content that would fail to match compressed bytes. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **`page_brute.py` workflow** — some analysts commonly run the `page_brute.py` YARA scanner against `pagefile.sys`. _Why:_ page-file YARA scanning is a known workflow for finding suspicious memory-resident content. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **`pagefile.sys` target** — `pagefile.sys` is the page file named as the target for `page_brute.py` scanning. _Why:_ the page file can contain paged-out memory artifacts relevant to investigations. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Windows 10 compression impact on `page_brute.py`** — running `page_brute.py` directly against files from Windows 10 systems is less effective because of compression. _Why:_ compressed page-file contents reduce direct YARA hit rates. _[GCFA p.606]_
- **Preprocessing with `winmem_decompress.py`** — running `winmem_decompress.py` before searching provides more usable data for analysis. _Why:_ decompression improves the effectiveness of later strings, carving, and YARA workflows. _[GCFA p.606]_

### Console Memory Concept

- **Memory forensics limitation in practice** — despite powerful memory-analysis tools, analysts still frequently rely on many string searches across memory objects. _Why:_ manual string review remains a practical technique when structured plugins do not expose every artifact. _[GCFA p.607]_
- **Obvious string-search targets** — malicious processes and injected processes are natural candidates for deeper memory inspection. _Why:_ attacker-controlled or modified processes often contain payloads, commands, configuration, or indicators. _[GCFA p.607]_
- **Less obvious search target** — command history is presented as a less obvious but highly useful memory-search target. _Why:_ recovered console history can reveal attacker actions even when process execution alone is incomplete. _[GCFA p.607]_
- **Prior research source** — the command-history carving idea is tied to Stevens and Casey’s paper on extracting Windows command-line details from physical memory. _Why:_ this establishes that console-history recovery from memory is a known forensic technique. _[GCFA p.607]_
- **Windows XP console process** — on Windows XP, `csrss.exe` is identified as responsible for drawing and maintaining text consoles. _Why:_ knowing the responsible process tells analysts where console artifacts may reside on older systems. _[GCFA p.607]_
- **Windows 7 and later console process** — on Windows 7 and newer systems, `conhost.exe` is identified as responsible for drawing and maintaining text consoles. _Why:_ this makes `conhost.exe` a valuable memory target for modern Windows command-line investigations. _[GCFA p.607]_
- **Console examples** — `cmd.exe` and `powershell.exe` are named as examples of text-console applications. _Why:_ these shells often contain attacker commands and administrative activity. _[GCFA p.607]_

## Page 610

### Page Files and Memory Architecture

- **Virtual memory model** — Windows memory analysis must account for paged memory because portions of active memory can reside on disk rather than only in physical RAM. _Why:_ investigators may miss relevant artifacts if they analyze only the captured memory image. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Paged memory** — The courseware describes page-backed memory as a core part of modern memory architecture. _Why:_ forensic interpretation requires understanding that RAM-resident activity may have disk-backed components. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Active memory on disk** — Significant amounts of memory that were active during system operation may be stored in page files. _Why:_ page files can contain evidence from processes, modules, malware, and operating-system structures. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Page file use on high-RAM systems** — Windows may still use page files even when the system has more than enough physical RAM. _Why:_ analysts should not assume page files are unimportant just because the host had abundant memory. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **pagefile.sys without memory context** — By itself, `pagefile.sys` is mostly unstructured data that previously existed in RAM. _Why:_ standalone page-file review is harder than analysis that correlates the page file with a memory image. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Traditional page-file analysis** — Older workflows commonly examined page files with string extraction or file carving. _Why:_ this explains why modern page-file-aware memory tools represent a major improvement. _[GCFA p.~610]_

### Tool Support

- **Modern page-file integration** — Newer memory analysis tools can combine page files with a memory image during analysis. _Why:_ this gives tools more of the original virtual address space to reconstruct and search. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Rekal** — The Rekal project is identified as an early driver of integrating page files into memory analysis. _Why:_ it marks the historical origin of this capability in the Volatility ecosystem. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Rekal lineage** — Rekal is described as a fork of Volatility. _Why:_ this connects page-file support to the broader memory-forensics tooling family. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Volatility 3 support** — Volatility 3 supports using a page file alongside a memory image. _Why:_ analysts can include swap data in Volatility-based workflows. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **MemProcFS support** — MemProcFS supports ingesting page-file data with a memory image. _Why:_ it can expose additional recoverable memory-backed artifacts. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **MemProcFS current effectiveness** — Testing cited on the page indicates MemProcFS presently performs better than other tools for page-file-enhanced analysis. _Why:_ it guides tool choice when page-file artifacts matter. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Volatility 3 current testing result** — The page notes that Volatility 3 testing had not yet produced many page-file-related results. _Why:_ analysts should know the feature exists but may have uneven practical payoff. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Volatility 3 future expectation** — The page expects Volatility 3 page-file capability to improve over time. _Why:_ investigators should monitor tooling maturity rather than dismiss the feature. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **FindEvil benefit** — Adding `pagefile.sys` can improve detections in tools such as FindEvil. _Why:_ page-file data can surface malicious artifacts absent from the RAM image alone. _[GCFA p.~610]_

### Commands and Flags

- **MemProcFS page-file command** — `MemProcFS.exe -device memory.img -pagefile0 pagefile.sys` attaches `pagefile.sys` as the first page file while analyzing `memory.img`. _Why:_ this is the shown syntax for page-file-aware MemProcFS analysis. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **MemProcFS memory image flag** — `-device memory.img` identifies `memory.img` as the memory acquisition input for MemProcFS. _Why:_ the memory image provides the address-space context needed to use the page file meaningfully. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **MemProcFS first page-file flag** — `-pagefile0 pagefile.sys` supplies the primary Windows page file to MemProcFS. _Why:_ this expands the memory data available for reconstruction and scanning. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Volatility 3 page-file command** — `vol.py -f memory.img --single-swap-locations=pagefile.sys` runs Volatility 3 with `pagefile.sys` supplied as swap data. _Why:_ this is the shown Volatility 3 syntax for incorporating a page file. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Volatility 3 memory image flag** — `-f memory.img` points Volatility 3 at the memory image. _Why:_ the page file is useful when tied back to the captured memory context. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Volatility 3 swap-location flag** — `--single-swap-locations=pagefile.sys` tells Volatility 3 where the page-file data is located. _Why:_ this enables Volatility to consult paged-out memory during analysis. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **MemProcFS swapfile.sys flag** — `-pagefile1 swapfile.sys` lets MemProcFS ingest `swapfile.sys` as an additional paging source. _Why:_ modern Windows may store UWP-related memory data outside `pagefile.sys`. _[GCFA p.~610]_

### Investigative Advantages

- **File extraction advantage** — Page-file-aware analysis can improve file extraction from memory evidence. _Why:_ some file-backed content may only be recoverable when paged data is included. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Reduced extraction errors** — Including paging data should reduce failed extractions for processes, DLLs, and drivers. _Why:_ missing paged-out portions can cause incomplete or failed dumps. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Process extraction benefit** — Page-file inclusion may reduce process-dump failures. _Why:_ process memory can be partially paged to disk. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **DLL extraction benefit** — Page-file inclusion may reduce DLL extraction failures. _Why:_ module pages may be absent from RAM but present in paging data. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Driver extraction benefit** — Page-file inclusion may reduce driver extraction failures. _Why:_ driver-related memory may be more complete when paging data is available. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Injected code recovery** — Page files can improve recovery of injected code. _Why:_ injected malware may occupy memory regions that were paged out before acquisition. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Injected malware detection** — Adding page-file data increases the chance of detecting injected malware. _Why:_ scanning covers more memory locations than the RAM image alone. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Injected malware copy quality** — Page-file data can help obtain better copies of injected malicious content. _Why:_ more pages are available for reconstruction and recovery. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Memory-object scanning** — Page files increase the amount of data available to scan for memory objects. _Why:_ scanners can find artifacts that are not resident in physical memory at capture time. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Network connection scanning** — Page-file-supported scanning can help locate network connection artifacts. _Why:_ old or paged-out network structures may still exist in paging data. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Registry data scanning** — Page-file-supported scanning can help locate registry data. _Why:_ registry-related structures or hive content may be more complete with paging data. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Old data structure recovery** — Scanning page files can reveal older memory structures. _Why:_ remnants of prior activity may persist after the live structure is no longer active. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Exited data structure recovery** — Page-file scanning can help find structures from terminated activity. _Why:_ exited processes or stale objects may leave recoverable traces in paged memory. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Beacon traffic detection** — Including page-file data can improve detection of older beaconing network activity. _Why:_ past command-and-control communication artifacts may survive in paged memory. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **MFT artifact completeness** — Page files can help produce more complete copies of Master File Table entries. _Why:_ filesystem metadata may be partially recoverable from memory-backed paging data. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Registry hive completeness** — Page files can improve recovery of registry hive content. _Why:_ hive pages may be distributed across RAM and paging files. _[GCFA p.~610]_

### Malware Hiding and Evasion

- **Paged hiding techniques** — The page identifies paged hiding techniques as an analysis benefit area for page-file-aware tools. _Why:_ malware can exploit paging behavior to hide evidence from RAM-only analysis. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Malware paging for evasion** — Some real-world malware has intentionally paged malicious content out of RAM to evade detection. _Why:_ collecting and analyzing page files can expose content deliberately moved away from physical memory. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Extreme hiding example** — The page frames active paging-out of malicious material as a more extreme form of evasion. _Why:_ it shows that page-file collection is not merely completeness work but can be central to detecting stealthy malware. _[GCFA p.~610]_

### Windows Paging Files

- **pagefile.sys importance** — `pagefile.sys` is described as the most important Windows paging file for investigations. _Why:_ it should be prioritized during memory-related evidence collection. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **swapfile.sys existence** — Modern Windows versions also maintain `swapfile.sys`. _Why:_ relevant memory artifacts may exist outside the primary page file. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **swapfile.sys UWP use** — `swapfile.sys` is used by Universal Windows Platform applications. _Why:_ UWP application evidence may require collecting this file as well. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **MemProcFS swapfile ingestion** — MemProcFS can ingest `swapfile.sys` in addition to `pagefile.sys`. _Why:_ this lets analysts expand coverage to UWP-related paging artifacts. _[GCFA p.~610]_

### Collection Priority

- **Page-file collection priority** — Investigators should collect page files along with memory acquisitions. _Why:_ page files can materially improve detection, reconstruction, extraction, and artifact completeness. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Memory acquisition pairing** — Page files are most valuable when paired with the corresponding memory image. _Why:_ the memory image provides the context needed to interpret paged-out data correctly. _[GCFA p.~610]_
- **Investigation value judgment** — The page explicitly treats page-file inclusion as worthwhile for investigations. _Why:_ the added evidence can affect malware detection, object recovery, and forensic completeness. _[GCFA p.~610]_

### MemProcFS Cached Files

- **MemProcFS cached-file view** — the page shows MemProcFS mounted as `M:` from `\\MemProcFS`. _Why:_ the mounted filesystem exposes memory artifacts as browsable files. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Process-scoped cached files path** — cached-file artifacts are shown under `M:\name\msiexec.exe-6192\files`. _Why:_ this path ties cached-file recovery to a specific process, `msiexec.exe` PID `6192`. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Process name in MemProcFS path** — the relevant process directory is named `msiexec.exe-6192`. _Why:_ the folder name identifies both the executable and PID used for the cached-file investigation. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Files folder purpose** — MemProcFS places cached items for each process inside that process’s `files` directory. _Why:_ this is the analyst’s entry point for per-process cached-file recovery. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **MemProcFS object model** — MemProcFS represents memory objects as separate files. _Why:_ analysts can copy artifacts from the mounted drive or inspect them directly in place. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Mounted-object workflow** — MemProcFS artifacts can be copied out of the mounted filesystem. _Why:_ this enables straightforward extraction of recovered memory-resident files for later analysis. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **In-place analysis workflow** — MemProcFS artifacts can also be analyzed without first copying them out. _Why:_ this supports rapid triage directly from the mounted memory view. _[GCFA p.~611]_

### Cached File Sources

- **Windows file caching** — Windows keeps many files resident in memory. _Why:_ memory images may contain recoverable file content beyond active processes. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Frequently used files** — files used often may remain in memory to improve filesystem I/O performance. _Why:_ common system artifacts can be recoverable from RAM. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Registry hives as cached files** — registry hives are examples of files that may be cached in memory. _Why:_ registry evidence can sometimes be recovered from memory-resident file cache data. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Prefetch files as cached files** — Prefetch files are listed as examples of files Windows may cache. _Why:_ execution-history artifacts may be available from memory. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **`$MFT` as cached data** — the NTFS Master File Table is listed among files that may be cached. _Why:_ filesystem metadata may be recoverable from RAM. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Memory-mapped executables** — executables can appear in memory cache because they are memory-mapped. _Why:_ executable recovery may be possible even when disk access is unavailable or altered. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Memory-mapped DLLs** — DLLs can appear in memory cache as memory-mapped files. _Why:_ library files loaded by processes may be recoverable from RAM. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Recently loaded arbitrary files** — almost any recently opened file type can be cached in memory. _Why:_ memory may preserve user documents, logs, or other evidentiary content. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Word documents in cache** — Word files are examples of recently loaded files that may remain cached. _Why:_ user-created content may be recoverable from memory. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **PDF documents in cache** — PDF files are examples of recently loaded files that may remain cached. _Why:_ viewed or opened documents may leave recoverable traces in RAM. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Log files in cache** — log files are examples of recently loaded files that may be cached. _Why:_ event and application evidence may survive in memory. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **USB-origin cached files** — files opened from removable USB media may still be cached in memory. _Why:_ RAM may retain evidence from media that is no longer attached. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Encrypted-container cached files** — files opened from encrypted containers may also be cached. _Why:_ memory can expose content that was otherwise protected at rest. _[GCFA p.~611]_

### File Objects And Pointers

- **`File_Object` structures** — cached items are tracked through in-memory structures called `File_Object` objects. _Why:_ these structures are key targets for cached-file discovery and extraction. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Process handle references** — processes can point to `File_Object` structures through their handle tables. _Why:_ handles provide one route to identify files a process has opened or referenced. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **VAD tree references** — processes can also point to `File_Object` structures through the virtual address descriptor tree. _Why:_ VADs provide another route to memory-mapped or otherwise referenced files. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Memory tool enumeration** — memory analysis tools can enumerate these in-memory file-related structures. _Why:_ enumeration turns raw memory structures into recoverable forensic artifacts. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Cached-file extraction basis** — tools use information inside file-related memory structures to extract cached files. _Why:_ the metadata and pointers make reconstruction of cached files possible. _[GCFA p.~611]_

### MemProcFS Access Methods Table

- **`files\handles` method** — this method extracts files by using process handles that reference `File_Object` structures. _Why:_ handle-based recovery can reveal files opened or retained by a process. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **`files\modules` method** — this method extracts `.EXE`, `.DLL`, and `.SYS` files using the PEB. _Why:_ module metadata provides a structured way to recover loaded executable images and drivers. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **`files\vads` method** — this method extracts files through VAD tree pointers to `File_Object` structures. _Why:_ VAD-based recovery can reconstruct files mapped into a process address space. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **`handles` folder entry** — the `files` directory contains a `handles` subfolder. _Why:_ this exposes cached files found through process handle references. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **`modules` folder entry** — the `files` directory contains a `modules` subfolder. _Why:_ this exposes recoverable executable, DLL, and driver module artifacts. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **`vads` folder entry** — the `files` directory contains a `vads` subfolder. _Why:_ this exposes file recovery based on VAD information. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **`handles` capability** — `handles` gives access to cached files discovered from process handles pointing at `File_Object` structures. _Why:_ this can recover files tied to open or recently used process resources. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **`modules` capability** — `modules` recovers `.exe`, `.dll`, and `.sys` files through the Process Environment Block and PE headers. _Why:_ this targets loaded program images and drivers using known executable metadata. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **`vads` capability** — `vads` attempts file reconstruction from VAD tree information. _Why:_ this can recover files represented in process virtual memory mappings. _[GCFA p.~611]_
- **Three-method recovery coverage** — MemProcFS provides three separate cached-file access methods for each process. _Why:_ multiple discovery paths improve the chance of recovering memory-cached files. _[GCFA p.~611]_

## Page 613

### Volatility Cached File Recovery

- **Volatility cached-file support** — Volatility includes plugins that can locate and recover files cached in memory. _Why:_ cached files can preserve evidence even when disk access is unavailable or incomplete. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **`windows.dumpfiles` purpose** — The Volatility 3 `windows.dumpfiles` plugin extracts cached file content by using Windows `File_Object` structures. _Why:_ `File_Object` records provide the memory-level linkage needed to attempt file recovery. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **`windows.dumpfiles` default scope** — Without narrowing options, `windows.dumpfiles` attempts to recover every cached file it can find in the memory image. _Why:_ default extraction can produce a very large output set requiring triage. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Default recovered file categories** — A broad `windows.dumpfiles` run may recover executables, DLLs, registry hives, `.dat` databases, text files, PDFs, and Microsoft Office documents. _Why:_ investigators should expect both system artifacts and user data in the output. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Default extraction noise** — Most files recovered by a broad `windows.dumpfiles` run may have little or no relevance to the investigation. _Why:_ indiscriminate file dumping increases review burden. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **`--pid` targeting** — The `--pid` option can restrict `windows.dumpfiles` recovery to `File_Object` entries associated with a chosen process. _Why:_ process-scoped dumping reduces noise and focuses on suspect activity. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **`windows.filescan` purpose** — The Volatility 3 `windows.filescan` plugin scans memory for `File_Object` signatures. _Why:_ signature scanning can reveal file objects outside the structures normally walked by dump plugins. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **`windows.filescan` relationship to `dumpfiles`** — `windows.filescan` complements `windows.dumpfiles` by exposing file objects that `dumpfiles` may miss. _Why:_ pairing discovery with targeted dumping improves recovery coverage. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **`dumpfiles` VAD-tree dependency** — `windows.dumpfiles` identifies `File_Object` entries found through the VAD tree or process handle lists. _Why:_ this limits what the plugin can recover by default. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Closed `File_Object` limitation** — `windows.dumpfiles` may miss `File_Object` records that are closed. _Why:_ files no longer represented in active handles or VAD structures can still matter for evidence. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Manipulated `File_Object` limitation** — `windows.dumpfiles` may miss `File_Object` records altered by malicious activity. _Why:_ malware can interfere with normal object enumeration. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **NTFS special-file limitation** — NTFS metadata files such as `$MFT` and `$Logfile` are not in the VAD tree. _Why:_ they are unlikely to be recovered by default `dumpfiles` behavior. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **`windows.filescan` breadth** — `windows.filescan` generally provides a more complete memory search for file-related objects. _Why:_ it can locate objects not reachable through narrower process mappings. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Virtual offset workflow** — When `windows.filescan` finds a relevant `File_Object`, the investigator should record its virtual memory offset. _Why:_ that offset can be passed to `windows.dumpfiles` for a focused recovery attempt. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **`--virtaddr` recovery option** — `windows.dumpfiles --virtaddr` accepts a `File_Object` virtual address as a targeted extraction input. _Why:_ offset-driven dumping lets analysts recover a specific file object found by scanning. _[GCFA p.613]_

### Recovery Reliability

- **Memory-forensics uncertainty** — File recovery from memory is not guaranteed. _Why:_ analysts should treat failed extraction as normal rather than as proof that the file never existed. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Unmapped file data** — Some `File_Object` records do not have their contents currently mapped or cached in memory. _Why:_ a valid file object may not yield recoverable bytes. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Paged-out data** — File content may have been paged out. _Why:_ paging can leave the memory image without the data needed for a complete extraction. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Partial file availability** — Only fragments of a target file may be available in memory. _Why:_ partial recovery can produce incomplete or damaged files. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Zero padding behavior** — The dump plugin fills unavailable regions with zero bytes. _Why:_ padding can preserve offsets while still producing corrupted or unreadable output. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Common extraction failures** — Many memory-based file dumps fail, are corrupted, or cannot be opened. _Why:_ analysts must validate recovered files before relying on their content. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Registry hive recovery issue** — Registry hives are often present in memory, but extracted hive files may fail to open in registry viewers because data is missing. _Why:_ memory-resident registry data is frequently incomplete. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Partial registry parsing strategy** — MemProcFS and specialized Volatility plugins such as `windows.registry.printkey` parse available portions of registry data rather than requiring a complete hive file. _Why:_ partial parsing can still recover useful registry evidence from incomplete memory artifacts. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Existence as evidence** — A file’s presence on a system can be valuable even if its contents cannot be recovered. _Why:_ file-object evidence can support compromise assessment. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Malicious executable presence** — Demonstrating that a known malicious executable existed on a host can justify treating the system as compromised. _Why:_ existence alone can drive triage and response decisions. _[GCFA p.613]_

### Volatility 2 Equivalents

- **Volatility 2 `dumpfiles`** — The Volatility 2 equivalent of Volatility 3 `windows.dumpfiles` is `dumpfiles`. _Why:_ analysts working with older Volatility versions need the corresponding plugin name. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Volatility 2 `filescan`** — The Volatility 2 equivalent of Volatility 3 `windows.filescan` is `filescan`. _Why:_ this maps the file-object scanning workflow across major Volatility versions. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Volatility 2 offset extraction** — Volatility 2 `dumpfiles` can extract a file by offset using `-Q`. _Why:_ this is the older-version equivalent of targeting a discovered file object. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Volatility 2 regex extraction** — Volatility 2 `dumpfiles` can extract by filename regular expression using `-r`. _Why:_ name-pattern dumping provides a second targeted recovery method. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Volatility 2 case-insensitive regex** — Adding `-i` makes the Volatility 2 `dumpfiles -r` name match case-insensitive. _Why:_ case-insensitive matching reduces missed hits caused by filename casing. _[GCFA p.613]_
- **Volatility 2 output directory** — Volatility 2 uses `--dump-dir=` to specify the output folder for dumped files. _Why:_ analysts must set the correct destination option when using the older toolset. _[GCFA p.613]_

### MemProcFS Forensic Folders

- **MemProcFS `forensic\files`** — this folder exposes cached Windows `File_Object` entries recovered from memory. _Why:_ cached file objects can reveal files touched by processes even when full disk access is unavailable. _[GCFA p.~616]_
- **Cached File_Object scope** — files visible through `forensic\files` represent only part of the full on-disk file set. _Why:_ analysts should not treat cached memory file objects as a complete filesystem inventory. _[GCFA p.~616]_
- **MemProcFS `forensic\ntfs`** — this folder is the preferred MemProcFS location for examining the broader filesystem view. _Why:_ it gives a more complete NTFS-oriented view than cached file objects alone. _[GCFA p.~616]_
- **MemProcFS `$MFT` discovery** — MemProcFS locates the NTFS Master File Table in memory-backed data and builds a navigable virtual filesystem from it. _Why:_ this lets an analyst browse filesystem metadata similarly to browsing the original host. _[GCFA p.~616]_
- **Virtualized NTFS browsing** — MemProcFS presents `$MFT` contents as folders and files that can be explored in File Explorer. _Why:_ filesystem review becomes interactive and path-driven instead of requiring only raw record parsing. _[GCFA p.~616]_

### File Contents and Limitations

- **`forensic\ntfs` content limitation** — actual file content is rarely available from the `forensic\ntfs` folder. _Why:_ analysts should expect metadata-first results rather than full file recovery from this location. _[GCFA p.~616]_
- **`forensic\ntfs` data source** — the `forensic\ntfs` view is sourced only from the `$MFT`. _Why:_ this explains why the view usually exposes metadata and paths rather than full file bodies. _[GCFA p.~616]_
- **Resident MFT files** — if a file is resident inside the MFT, its contents may be visible through the NTFS view. _Why:_ resident files are an exception where MFT-backed browsing can include content. _[GCFA p.~616]_
- **Resident-file size expectation** — resident-file content availability typically applies only to very small files under about `600` bytes. _Why:_ this gives the analyst a practical threshold for when contents might appear. _[GCFA p.~616]_
- **Cached-file extraction fallback** — analysts can return to cached file extraction methods after identifying interesting paths in `forensic\ntfs`. _Why:_ metadata-derived leads may be recoverable through memory-cached file objects. _[GCFA p.~616]_
- **Suggested follow-up path** — the slide recommends reviewing locations such as `M:\forensic\files` after finding interesting NTFS paths. _Why:_ cached file objects may provide recoverable content that the MFT-derived view lacks. _[GCFA p.~616]_

## Page 617

### Folder Metadata Review

- **Same-folder output context** — The referenced output represents the same folder being examined, and includes timestamp information for both the folder itself and the files inside it. _Why:_ folder-level and file-level creation times can help reconstruct activity in a directory. _[GCFA p.~617]_

- **Folder creation time** — The output includes the creation time of the folder under review. _Why:_ the folder creation timestamp can indicate when a workspace, staging directory, tool directory, or artifact container first appeared. _[GCFA p.~617]_

- **File-content creation times** — The output includes creation times for files contained inside the folder. _Why:_ individual file creation times can show when contents were added to or materialized within the directory. _[GCFA p.~617]_

### Investigative Use Cases

- **Tool-folder review** — The feature can be used to inspect directories that contain tools. _Why:_ attacker or administrator tool folders may reveal when utilities were placed on disk and how their contents changed over time. _[GCFA p.~617]_

- **Exfiltration staging folders** — The feature can be applied to folders used to stage data before exfiltration. _Why:_ timestamps and folder contents can help identify when files were gathered, prepared, or organized for removal. _[GCFA p.~617]_

- **Cloud-storage folder review** — The feature can be used to examine synchronized or cloud-backed folders. _Why:_ cloud storage directories may contain files involved in collection, transfer, synchronization, or data theft workflows. _[GCFA p.~617]_

- **Prefetch folder review** — The feature can also be used against folders such as Windows Prefetch. _Why:_ Prefetch file timestamps can provide execution-timeline evidence for programs. _[GCFA p.~617]_

### Prefetch Timestamp Interpretation

- **Prefetch file creation time** — A Prefetch file’s creation timestamp can indicate the first time the associated executable ran. _Why:_ this supports first-execution timeline reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~617]_

- **Prefetch file modification time** — A Prefetch file’s modification timestamp can indicate the most recent time the associated executable ran. _Why:_ this supports last-execution timeline reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~617]_

- **Prefetch first-and-last execution inference** — Comparing Prefetch creation and modification timestamps can reveal both the first observed execution and the last observed execution of the related program. _Why:_ this gives investigators a compact execution window for a program without relying only on process logs. _[GCFA p.~617]_

### MemProcFS Registry Access

- **`M:\registry` purpose** — MemProcFS exposes registry data that still resides in memory through the `M:` virtual filesystem. _Why:_ this lets analysts inspect registry evidence without first carving or fully repairing hive files. _[GCFA p.619]_
- **Registry browsing method** — Investigators can traverse registry keys and values through Windows File Explorer when using the MemProcFS registry view. _Why:_ a familiar filesystem interface lowers friction during memory-based registry triage. _[GCFA p.619]_
- **Hive export capability** — MemProcFS can reconstruct registry hives for use in other analysis tools. _Why:_ exported hives may support deeper offline review when they are usable. _[GCFA p.619]_
- **Exported hive location** — Reconstructed registry hive files are stored under `M:\registry\hive_files`. _Why:_ this is the analyst’s collection point for attempting external hive parsing. _[GCFA p.619]_
- **Hive export limitation** — Exported hives from memory are frequently incomplete or damaged. _Why:_ many registry tools require structurally valid hives and may reject these exports. _[GCFA p.619]_
- **Fallback analysis approach** — When exported hives cannot be opened, analysts should browse directly to the relevant hive and key inside MemProcFS and check whether value data is exposed. _Why:_ direct virtual navigation can still reveal content even when hive reconstruction fails. _[GCFA p.619]_
- **Virtual registry usability** — MemProcFS presents registry data as a navigable virtual filesystem. _Why:_ this makes targeted registry inspection practical during incident response. _[GCFA p.619]_

### Attacker Abuse Patterns

- **Services as an execution mechanism** — Windows services are frequently misused by attackers to launch code. _Why:_ service review can reveal malicious execution paths. _[GCFA p.~621]_
- **Scheduled tasks as an execution mechanism** — scheduled tasks are frequently misused by attackers to launch code. _Why:_ task entries can preserve evidence of attacker-controlled execution. _[GCFA p.~621]_
- **Services for persistence** — attackers commonly use services to maintain access across reboots or logons. _Why:_ service startup configuration is a key persistence hunting target. _[GCFA p.~621]_
- **Scheduled tasks for persistence** — attackers commonly use scheduled tasks to keep malicious activity recurring or durable. _Why:_ scheduled-task review is central to persistence analysis. _[GCFA p.~621]_
- **Services for lateral movement** — adversaries may use services as part of movement between systems. _Why:_ service creation or modification can indicate remote execution activity. _[GCFA p.~621]_
- **Scheduled tasks for lateral movement** — adversaries may use scheduled tasks during movement across the network. _Why:_ remotely created or modified tasks can be evidence of compromise spread. _[GCFA p.~621]_
- **Prevalence of service and task abuse** — many intrusions include service or scheduled-task techniques. _Why:_ these artifacts deserve routine examination during incident response. _[GCFA p.~621]_
- **Memory value of service and task data** — extracting service and task information from memory can provide high investigative value. _Why:_ memory may expose registry-backed configuration even when disk access is limited or altered. _[GCFA p.~621]_

### Registry Basis

- **Windows services in registry** — Windows stores service configuration in the registry. _Why:_ memory-resident registry data can be parsed to recover service artifacts. _[GCFA p.~621]_
- **Scheduled tasks in registry** — Windows stores scheduled-task configuration in the registry. _Why:_ registry recovery from memory enables task analysis from a memory image. _[GCFA p.~621]_
- **Registry recovery prerequisite** — because registry information can be recovered from memory, service and task parsing depends on locating and interpreting those registry structures. _Why:_ the analyst needs tooling that can find and decode the relevant registry-backed data. _[GCFA p.~621]_

### Memory Extraction Workflow

- **Exporting suspicious memory content** — Analysts commonly carve out memory regions or file-like objects that look suspicious so they can inspect them outside the memory image. _Why:_ extraction enables deeper validation when in-memory triage is inconclusive. _[GCFA p.622]_
- **Process acquisition stage** — Collecting processes and drivers is described as the final phase of the memory-analysis workflow on this page. _Why:_ it marks the transition from triage and discovery to artifact-level follow-up analysis. _[GCFA p.622]_
- **Limits of memory analysis** — Memory examination can reveal many indicators, but it does not always provide enough information to fully resolve what an object is or does. _Why:_ analysts should expect to supplement memory findings with extracted-artifact analysis. _[GCFA p.622]_
- **Process extraction need** — Analysts may need to remove whole process objects from a memory image for closer examination. _Why:_ process-level extraction supports confirmation of suspicious runtime activity. _[GCFA p.622]_
- **Driver extraction need** — Analysts may need to extract drivers from memory for separate review. _Why:_ malicious or suspicious kernel components often require dedicated inspection beyond memory listings. _[GCFA p.622]_
- **Memory-section extraction need** — Analysts may need to export specific memory sections rather than whole processes or drivers. _Why:_ targeted sections can contain code, data, payloads, or injected regions relevant to an investigation. _[GCFA p.622]_
- **Suspicious process uncertainty** — Investigators may encounter several suspicious processes, such as three or four, without being fully confident which are malicious. _Why:_ uncertainty drives the need for corroborating analysis rather than relying only on process listings. _[GCFA p.622]_
- **Antivirus confirmation use** — Extracted process objects can be submitted to antivirus scanning to help confirm whether suspicious findings are meaningful. _Why:_ scan results can validate whether the analyst is pursuing the correct lead. _[GCFA p.622]_

## Page 623

### Six-Step Memory Analysis Process

- **Memory analysis workflow · Step 1** — The first step is to find unauthorized or suspicious processes. _Why:_ rogue processes are often the primary execution evidence for malware or attacker tooling in memory. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Rogue process identification · Process name** — Process names should be examined when identifying suspicious processes. _Why:_ unusual, masqueraded, misspelled, or context-inappropriate names can indicate malicious execution. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Rogue process identification · Executable path** — The on-disk path associated with a process should be reviewed. _Why:_ malware often runs from abnormal locations such as user-writable directories, temporary paths, or misleading folders. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Rogue process identification · Parent process** — The parent process relationship should be checked during rogue process triage. _Why:_ an abnormal parent-child chain can expose suspicious launch behavior or process spoofing. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Rogue process identification · Command line** — The command line used to start a process should be collected and analyzed. _Why:_ command-line arguments can reveal payload paths, execution flags, encoded content, or attacker intent. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Rogue process identification · Start time** — The process start timestamp should be part of rogue process analysis. _Why:_ start time helps correlate process execution with intrusion events, log entries, network activity, and user activity. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Memory analysis workflow · Step 2** — The second step is to inspect process objects. _Why:_ process object details expose runtime relationships and resources that may not be obvious from process listings alone. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Process object analysis · Loaded DLLs** — Loaded dynamic-link libraries should be reviewed for each process. _Why:_ unexpected DLLs can reveal malware modules, injected components, sideloading, or malicious dependencies. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Process object analysis · Handles** — Open handles associated with a process should be analyzed. _Why:_ handles can reveal files, registry keys, processes, tokens, or other objects the process is interacting with. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Process object analysis · SIDs** — Security identifiers tied to process objects should be examined. _Why:_ SIDs help determine the account or security context under which a process is running. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Memory analysis workflow · Step 3** — The third step is to review network-related artifacts. _Why:_ network state in memory can connect suspicious execution to command-and-control, lateral movement, or data transfer activity. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Network artifact review · Suspicious ports** — Unusual or suspicious listening or connected ports should be investigated. _Why:_ unexpected ports can identify backdoors, reverse shells, covert services, or malware communication channels. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Network artifact review · Connections** — Active or residual network connections should be reviewed. _Why:_ connection data can link processes to remote systems and establish communication timelines. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Network artifact review · Networked processes** — Processes associated with suspicious network activity should be identified. _Why:_ tying connections back to owning processes helps attribute network behavior to specific executables in memory. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Memory analysis workflow · Step 4** — The fourth step is to search for signs of code injection. _Why:_ injected code allows attackers to execute malicious logic inside another process and can evade simple process-name-based detection. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Code injection evidence · Injected memory sections** — Memory sections that appear injected should be examined. _Why:_ injected sections can contain malicious shellcode, payloads, or unpacked malware not present as a normal file-backed module. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Code injection evidence · Process hollowing** — Analysts should look for process hollowing indicators. _Why:_ process hollowing lets malware replace the legitimate contents of a process while retaining a benign-looking process wrapper. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Memory analysis workflow · Step 5** — The fifth step is to audit drivers and perform rootkit detection. _Why:_ kernel-level components can hide attacker activity and undermine the reliability of normal operating system views. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Driver audit · Drivers** — Loaded drivers should be audited as part of memory analysis. _Why:_ malicious or suspicious drivers can provide persistence, stealth, privilege, or kernel-level control. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Rootkit detection · Hook evidence** — Evidence of rootkit hooks should be checked. _Why:_ hooks can indicate that kernel or system behavior has been modified to hide files, processes, network activity, or other artifacts. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Memory analysis workflow · Step 6** — The sixth step is to dump suspicious processes and drivers. _Why:_ extracted memory-resident objects can be examined with static and dynamic techniques outside the memory image. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Suspicious object dumping · Processes** — Suspicious process memory should be dumped for further review. _Why:_ dumped process contents may contain payloads, configuration data, decoded strings, or unpacked code. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Suspicious object dumping · Drivers** — Suspicious drivers should be dumped for further analysis. _Why:_ driver extraction enables deeper inspection of possible kernel malware or rootkit components. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Dump analysis · Strings review** — Strings should be reviewed from dumped suspicious processes or drivers. _Why:_ strings can expose URLs, IP addresses, commands, registry paths, file paths, mutexes, and malware configuration clues. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Dump analysis · Antivirus scanning** — Dumped suspicious processes and drivers should be scanned with antivirus tools. _Why:_ AV results can provide quick triage, known-family identification, or corroborating detection evidence. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Dump analysis · Reverse engineering** — Dumped suspicious processes and drivers may require reverse engineering. _Why:_ reverse engineering can confirm functionality, persistence logic, evasion techniques, and attacker capabilities. _[GCFA p.~623]_

- **Process completion statement** — The page states that the six-step memory analysis process has been completed. _Why:_ this confirms the listed workflow is intended as a complete memory analysis sequence in the course context. _[GCFA p.~623]_
