### Pivot-Point Selection

- **Pivot point** — a pivot point is an investigation lead used to focus timeline review around a time, artifact, account, process, file, or activity pattern. _Why:_ timeline data is noisy, so pivots give the analyst a starting filter for finding relevant activity. _[GCFA p.~659]_

- **Pivot-point sources** — timeline pivots can come from many categories, and the page presents only a limited sample rather than a complete list. _Why:_ analysts should not treat the shown chart as exhaustive. _[GCFA p.~659]_

- **Investigation knowledge drives pivots** — the set of useful pivots depends on what the analyst already knows about the case. _Why:_ new evidence should change what the analyst searches for next. _[GCFA p.~659]_

- **Pivot expansion** — as the investigation develops, additional pivots can be identified from newly discovered facts. _Why:_ timeline analysis is iterative rather than a one-time search. _[GCFA p.~659]_

- **Review before and after each pivot** — for every chosen pivot, the analyst should inspect activity on both sides of that point in time. _Why:_ related artifacts usually appear before and after the obvious event. _[GCFA p.~659]_

- **Single-artifact rarity** — it is uncommon for a compromised system to contain only one artifact of investigative interest. _Why:_ surrounding events often reveal staging, execution, lateral movement, cleanup, or follow-on activity. _[GCFA p.~659]_

## Page 660

### Timeline Context Clues

- **Single Artifact Limitation** — Recovering one artifact by itself is comparable to finding one isolated word without its sentence. _Why:_ an isolated item can be misleading without surrounding evidence. _[GCFA p.660]_
- **Timeline Context Requirement** — Analysts need nearby timeline context to interpret an artifact accurately. _Why:_ surrounding events can change the meaning of the recovered item. _[GCFA p.660]_
- **Timeline Analysis vs. Data Extraction** — Timeline analysis differs from traditional artifact recovery because it focuses on relationships among events rather than only retrieving one data item. _Why:_ incident interpretation depends on sequence and context, not just presence. _[GCFA p.660]_
- **Single Artifact Insufficiency** — Identifying one artifact does not, by itself, explain its role in the broader investigation. _Why:_ the same artifact can support different conclusions depending on nearby activity. _[GCFA p.660]_
- **Artifact Temporal Proximity** — Artifact temporal proximity means evaluating an artifact in relation to events that occur near it in time. _Why:_ nearby events can reveal what the artifact likely represents. _[GCFA p.660]_
- **Context-Dependent Meaning** — An artifact that appears unclear when viewed alone may gain a different meaning when placed among other timeline entries. _Why:_ interpretation often emerges from event clustering. _[GCFA p.660]_

### Word Analogy

- **Recovered Word Analogy** — A recovered artifact can be treated like a single word whose meaning depends on the sentence around it. _Why:_ this illustrates why context is necessary for forensic interpretation. _[GCFA p.660]_
- **Ambiguous Example Term** — The example term is “sweet,” which can carry more than one meaning depending on usage. _Why:_ it models how one artifact can support multiple interpretations. _[GCFA p.660]_
- **Sweet · Personality Meaning** — In the example involving a girl caring for her brother, “sweet” means kind or friendly. _Why:_ the surrounding sentence determines the intended meaning. _[GCFA p.660]_
- **Sweet · Taste Meaning** — In the example involving tea and sugar, “sweet” means having a sugar-like taste. _Why:_ the same word has a different meaning when placed in a different context. _[GCFA p.660]_

### Timeline Interpretation

- **Artifact Ambiguity in Timelines** — A single timeline artifact can be ambiguous in the same way a single word can be ambiguous. _Why:_ analysts should avoid drawing conclusions from one event alone. _[GCFA p.660]_
- **Before-and-After Review** — Analysts should inspect timeline entries both before and after the artifact of interest. _Why:_ adjacent events can explain cause, user action, or investigative significance. _[GCFA p.660]_
- **Program Execution Context** — Nearby timeline entries may show that a program was run. _Why:_ execution evidence can explain why later artifacts appeared. _[GCFA p.660]_
- **File Opening Context** — Nearby timeline entries may show that a file was opened. _Why:_ file access evidence can distinguish user interaction from mere file presence. _[GCFA p.660]_
- **File Deletion Context** — Nearby timeline entries may show that files were deleted. _Why:_ deletion events can indicate cleanup, normal use, or malicious activity depending on context. _[GCFA p.660]_
- **Artifacts Require Interaction** — Artifacts generally do not appear or execute as programs without some related interaction. _Why:_ investigators should look for causal or supporting activity around the event. _[GCFA p.660]_
- **Connected Event Principle** — The page emphasizes that forensic events are interconnected rather than isolated. _Why:_ timeline analysis depends on tracing relationships among artifacts. _[GCFA p.660]_

## Page 662

### Timeline Scoping

- **Timeline scope question** — The first timeline step is to decide what investigative questions the timeline must answer. _Why:_ the question set controls which evidence sources and time ranges are relevant. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Case-type-driven scope** — Timeline boundaries should be based on both the important case questions and the type of incident being investigated. _Why:_ different case types require different artifact sources and levels of detail. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Date-range containment** — Investigators can often bound suspicious activity between an earlier date and a later date. _Why:_ a defined time window makes large forensic datasets manageable. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Scope narrowing** — Reducing the timeline scope is necessary to control the volume of data under review. _Why:_ broad timelines can overwhelm analysis with irrelevant events. _[GCFA p.662]_

### Pivot Points

- **Pivot-point narrowing** — After scoping, analysts should identify narrower anchors that are close to the suspected activity. _Why:_ pivots focus the timeline around evidence likely to explain the incident. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Time-based pivot** — One valid pivot type is a time near when the incident is believed to have occurred. _Why:_ nearby events can reveal activity immediately before and after the suspected action. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Artifact-based pivot** — Another valid pivot type is a relevant artifact connected to the suspected activity. _Why:_ artifacts can anchor the investigation when exact timing is uncertain. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Key-file pivot** — A file believed to have been involved in the activity can serve as an artifact-based pivot. _Why:_ file-centered review can expose execution, access, creation, or staging behavior. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **User-account pivot** — A user account suspected of involvement can be used as an artifact-based pivot. _Why:_ account-focused analysis helps connect activity to logons, access, and user actions. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Other-artifact pivot** — The page allows pivots based on artifacts beyond files and accounts. _Why:_ incident evidence may appear in many artifact classes, not just obvious file or user records. _[GCFA p.662]_

### Timeline Creation Process

- **Timeline-process selection** — Analysts should choose the timeline creation method based on the data sources needed for the case. _Why:_ the correct process depends on whether the investigation needs broad coverage or targeted evidence. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Filesystem timeline option** — A filesystem-based timeline is listed as one possible creation method. _Why:_ filesystem metadata can rapidly show file creation, modification, access, and metadata-change activity. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **FLS tool** — FLS is named as a tool for filesystem-based timeline generation. _Why:_ it supports fast triage-style timeline construction from filesystem metadata. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **MFTECmd tool** — MFTECmd is named as another filesystem-based timeline tool. _Why:_ it can process NTFS MFT data for rapid file activity review. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Filesystem timeline speed** — Filesystem-based creation is characterized as fast. _Why:_ speed makes it useful when quick triage is more important than collecting every possible event source. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Filesystem timeline triage mode** — Filesystem-based timeline creation is associated with triage-mode analysis. _Why:_ triage timelines support quick initial assessment and prioritization. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Super timeline option** — A super timeline is listed as another timeline creation method. _Why:_ it combines many artifact sources into a broader chronological view. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Automated super timeline** — Super timeline creation may be automated. _Why:_ automation helps gather broad event coverage when many sources may be relevant. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Targeted super timeline** — Super timeline creation may also be targeted. _Why:_ targeted collection reduces noise when the analyst already knows which data sources matter. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **LOG2TIMELINE tool** — LOG2TIMELINE is named as the tool associated with super timeline creation. _Why:_ it is used to build broad timelines from multiple forensic sources. _[GCFA p.662]_

### Choosing Timeline Breadth

- **Unknown-evidence scenario** — A super timeline is preferred when the analyst does not yet know what evidence they need. _Why:_ broad collection reduces the chance of missing relevant artifacts. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Need-everything scenario** — A super timeline is appropriate when the investigation may require inclusion of all available evidence sources. _Why:_ complete context can reveal relationships that narrow timelines may miss. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Predictable-data scenario** — If the necessary data sources can be anticipated, a narrower timeline process may be enough. _Why:_ predictable evidence needs allow faster, less noisy analysis. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Targeted super timeline sufficiency** — A targeted super timeline can be sufficient when the analyst knows which sources are needed. _Why:_ it balances artifact coverage with reduced data volume. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Filesystem timeline sufficiency** — A filesystem timeline can be sufficient when filesystem metadata answers the case questions. _Why:_ it avoids unnecessary ingestion of unrelated artifacts. _[GCFA p.662]_

### Timeline Filtering

- **Scope-based filtering** — Timeline filtering should use the previously defined investigative scope. _Why:_ scope filters remove events outside the relevant case window or question set. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Deduplication** — The timeline should be deduplicated during filtering. _Why:_ duplicate records can waste analyst time and distort event interpretation. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Irrelevant-data removal** — Analysts should eliminate data that does not need examination. _Why:_ reducing noise improves speed and clarity during timeline review. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Keyword filtering** — Keywords can be used to locate relevant timeline records. _Why:_ terms tied to files, users, hosts, tools, or paths can expose useful pivot points. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Keywords as pivots** — Keyword hits may identify new pivot points for analysis. _Why:_ searchable terms can reveal evidence anchors not known at the start. _[GCFA p.662]_

### Timeline Analysis

- **Evidence-context focus** — Timeline analysis should emphasize the surrounding context of discovered evidence. _Why:_ nearby events often explain the meaning of an isolated artifact. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Before-pivot review** — Analysts should examine events preceding each pivot. _Why:_ earlier events can show preparation, access, execution, or initial compromise activity. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **After-pivot review** — Analysts should examine events following each pivot. _Why:_ later events can show follow-on actions, persistence, cleanup, or data access. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **User-activity reconstruction** — Reviewing events around pivots helps determine what the user did. _Why:_ temporal context links artifacts into an activity narrative. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Windows Forensic Analysis Poster** — The Windows Forensic Analysis Poster is recommended as an analysis aid. _Why:_ it helps map evidence categories to Windows forensic artifacts. _[GCFA p.662]_
- **Evidence of reference items** — The poster’s “Evidence of” categories are specifically recommended for timeline interpretation. _Why:_ those categories help analysts connect artifacts to user and system behaviors. _[GCFA p.662]_

## Page 664

### Filesystem Timeline Role

- **Filesystem timeline** — this timeline type is presented as the earliest and most commonly used timeline category. _Why:_ it is a baseline DFIR method for reconstructing file and directory activity. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Filesystem timeline scope** — a filesystem timeline gathers information from files and directories across a volume. _Why:_ volume-wide collection helps analysts see activity beyond a single suspicious file. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Allocated metadata coverage** — filesystem timelines include metadata structures that are still allocated by the filesystem. _Why:_ allocated metadata describes currently existing filesystem objects. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Unallocated metadata coverage** — filesystem timelines also include metadata structures no longer allocated. _Why:_ unallocated metadata can preserve evidence of objects that are no longer active in the filesystem namespace. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Deleted-file visibility** — unallocated metadata can reveal information about deleted files. _Why:_ deleted files may still be relevant to intrusion activity, staging, cleanup, or anti-forensic behavior. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Orphan-file visibility** — unallocated metadata can expose orphaned files within the filesystem. _Why:_ orphaned records may identify files disconnected from normal directory references but still forensically useful. _[GCFA p.664]_

### Parsed Metadata Sources

- **Tools Will Parse · Filesystem metadata** — the listed timeline tools parse filesystem metadata. _Why:_ metadata is the source of filesystem timeline entries. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Tools Will Parse · Directories** — the listed tools parse directory metadata. _Why:_ directory records help reconstruct folder-level activity and file organization. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Tools Will Parse · Files** — the listed tools parse file metadata. _Why:_ file records provide timestamps and object-level context for timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Tools Will Parse · Deleted files** — the listed tools parse metadata associated with deleted files. _Why:_ deleted-file records may preserve evidence after user or attacker cleanup. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Tools Will Parse · Unallocated metadata** — the listed tools parse metadata found in unallocated filesystem structures. _Why:_ unallocated structures can contain historical records for deleted or orphaned filesystem objects. _[GCFA p.664]_

### Timestamp Types

- **Filesystem timestamp variation** — different filesystems maintain different timestamp types. _Why:_ analysts must interpret timeline fields according to the filesystem being examined. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Data Modified timestamp** — the data-modification timestamp records when file content was modified and is abbreviated as `M`. _Why:_ content modification time helps identify when data inside a file changed. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Data Access timestamp** — the data-access timestamp records file access activity and is abbreviated as `A`. _Why:_ access time can help identify when a file may have been read or interacted with. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Metadata Change timestamp** — the metadata-change timestamp records changes to filesystem metadata and is abbreviated as `C`. _Why:_ metadata change time can reveal renames, permission changes, moves, or other non-content updates depending on filesystem behavior. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **File Creation timestamp** — the file-creation timestamp records file birth or creation time and is abbreviated as `B`. _Why:_ creation time helps determine when an object first appeared on a volume or in a location. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **`m` abbreviation** — lowercase `m` is associated with modification. _Why:_ knowing timestamp shorthand prevents misreading compact timeline output. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **`a` abbreviation** — lowercase `a` is associated with access. _Why:_ knowing timestamp shorthand supports correct interpretation of MACB-style timeline entries. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **`c` abbreviation** — lowercase `c` is associated with change. _Why:_ this distinguishes metadata changes from content modifications. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **`b` abbreviation** — lowercase `b` is associated with birth. _Why:_ birth time represents creation semantics in timeline notation. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Combined timestamp interpretation** — the meaning of a filesystem event often comes from evaluating multiple timestamp fields together. _Why:_ timestamp combinations can reveal behavior that one timestamp alone would not explain. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Created-on-volume inference** — timestamp combinations may help determine when a file was created on a volume. _Why:_ creation timing is central to intrusion scoping and file provenance. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Copied-to-location inference** — timestamp combinations may help determine whether a file was copied into a location. _Why:_ copy behavior can explain mismatches between creation and modification times. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Deleted-file inference** — timestamp combinations may help determine whether or when a file was deleted. _Why:_ deletion timing can identify cleanup activity and attacker dwell-time boundaries. _[GCFA p.664]_

### Timestamp Collection Table Cells

- **Collect Times From · Data Modified `(M)`** — timeline tools collect data-modification time. _Why:_ this field anchors content-change events in a filesystem timeline. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Collect Times From · Data Access `(A)`** — timeline tools collect data-access time. _Why:_ this field can show when a file was accessed, subject to filesystem and OS behavior. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Collect Times From · Metadata Change `(C)`** — timeline tools collect metadata-change time. _Why:_ this field can identify filesystem record updates separate from file content writes. _[GCFA p.664]_
- **Collect Times From · File Creation `(B)`** — timeline tools collect file-creation time. _Why:_ this field helps establish when a file object first appeared. _[GCFA p.664]_

### NTFS Timestamp Labels

- **M timestamp** — M denotes the file data modification time. _Why:_ it identifies when file contents last changed. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **M timestamp meaning** — M records the most recent change to a file’s data content. _Why:_ content edits are central to reconstructing file activity. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **A timestamp** — A denotes the file data access time. _Why:_ it can indicate possible file interaction, though interpretation is limited. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **A timestamp meaning** — A records an approximate time when file data was last accessed. _Why:_ its approximate nature makes it weaker evidence than more deterministic timestamps. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **C timestamp** — C denotes metadata change time. _Why:_ it tracks changes to the NTFS FILE record rather than file content. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **C timestamp meaning** — C records when the NTFS FILE record was last modified. _Why:_ it can expose filesystem-level changes that may not alter file contents. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **B timestamp** — B denotes file birth or creation time. _Why:_ it helps establish when an object first appeared on the volume. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **B timestamp meaning** — B records when the file was created within the volume. _Why:_ creation time is a core anchor for timeline reconstruction. _[GCFA p.665]_

### NTFS Timestamp Table Cells

- **File System · NTFS** — the listed filesystem is NTFS. _Why:_ the timestamp rules on this page apply to NTFS evidence. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **Time Stored · NTFS** — NTFS stores its listed times in UTC. _Why:_ UTC storage avoids direct dependence on local timezone or daylight-saving settings. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **Time Resolution · NTFS** — NTFS timestamp precision is 100 nanoseconds counted from January 1, 1601. _Why:_ this granularity can separate events that occur within the same second. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **M · NTFS** — the NTFS M field corresponds to Modified. _Why:_ analysts use it for content modification timing. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **A · NTFS** — the NTFS A field corresponds to Accessed. _Why:_ analysts may use it as a possible access indicator with caveats. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **C · NTFS** — the NTFS C field corresponds to FILE record modification. _Why:_ it reflects metadata-record activity rather than ordinary content editing alone. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **B · NTFS** — the NTFS B field corresponds to Created. _Why:_ it marks file creation on the NTFS volume. _[GCFA p.665]_

### Stored NTFS Times

- **Four NTFS filesystem times** — NTFS maintains four important timestamps for files and directories. _Why:_ timeline analysis must account for all four fields instead of treating “file time” as a single value. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **NTFS object coverage** — the four timestamp fields apply to both files and directories. _Why:_ directory timestamps can also provide investigative timeline evidence. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **Last modification time** — NTFS stores a last modification time as one of its major timestamps. _Why:_ this is the primary indicator for content changes. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **Last access time** — NTFS stores a last access time as one of its major timestamps. _Why:_ it may support access analysis, but only with careful interpretation. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **FILE record modification time** — NTFS stores a timestamp for the last modification of the FILE record. _Why:_ this can reveal metadata activity such as renames or permission changes. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **Creation time** — NTFS stores a creation timestamp for filesystem objects. _Why:_ it helps identify when a file or directory was introduced to the volume. _[GCFA p.665]_

### Metadata Change Time

- **C timestamp difficulty** — metadata change time is often the most difficult NTFS timestamp for students to understand. _Why:_ misreading C can lead to incorrect conclusions about what kind of file activity occurred. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **Rename effect on C** — renaming a file can update the metadata change timestamp. _Why:_ a changed C value may indicate a name change even when content did not change. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **File-size effect on C** — a change in file size can update the metadata change timestamp. _Why:_ size changes can leave evidence in C in addition to content-related timestamps. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **Permission effect on C** — updates to security permissions can update the metadata change timestamp. _Why:_ access-control changes may be visible through FILE record modification timing. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **Ownership effect on C** — changing file ownership can update the metadata change timestamp. _Why:_ ownership changes may be detectable even if file data remains unchanged. _[GCFA p.665]_

### Access Time Caveats

- **A timestamp interpretation difficulty** — access times have historically been hard to interpret. _Why:_ many different actions can cause access-time changes, reducing specificity. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **Multiple causes for A updates** — numerous actions may update the last access timestamp. _Why:_ an A timestamp alone usually cannot prove a specific user action. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **Windows treatment of A timestamps** — Windows has historically treated last access time as a lower-priority timestamp. _Why:_ operating-system behavior can make A less reliable than other NTFS times. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **Delayed A updates** — some Windows versions may delay last access timestamp updates by as much as one hour. _Why:_ timeline ordering based on A can be misleading at sub-hour precision. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **Disabled A updates** — some Windows versions do not update last access timestamps. _Why:_ absence of A movement does not necessarily prove absence of access. _[GCFA p.665]_

### Investigative Priority

- **Preferred timestamp focus** — absent a specific reason otherwise, investigators should focus mainly on M and B timestamps. _Why:_ modification and creation times are generally more useful for time-based forensic questions. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **M and B interpretability** — modified and created timestamps are described as well understood. _Why:_ they are less ambiguous than access time and metadata change time in many investigations. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **M and B suitability** — modified and created timestamps are well suited to time-focused forensic queries. _Why:_ they provide clearer anchors for timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.665]_

### UTC And Timezone Behavior

- **NTFS UTC storage** — NTFS stores timestamp values in UTC. _Why:_ UTC storage helps normalize evidence across systems and time zones. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **NTFS daylight-saving independence** — NTFS timestamp storage is not directly altered by daylight-saving time changes. _Why:_ analysts can avoid treating daylight-saving shifts as filesystem timestamp changes. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **Filesystem contrast** — not all filesystems store timestamps the same way as NTFS. _Why:_ analysts must know the source filesystem before interpreting times. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **FAT local-time storage** — FAT stores dates and times using the computer’s local time. _Why:_ FAT timestamps can shift meaning when interpreted across time zones. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **NTFS timezone example** — a file saved at 3:00 PM Pacific time in California would appear as 6:00 PM Eastern time in New York on an NTFS volume. _Why:_ UTC-based storage supports correct timezone conversion. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **FAT timezone example** — the same 3:00 PM Pacific event may appear incorrectly as 3:00 PM Eastern time in New York on a FAT volume. _Why:_ local-time storage can create misleading cross-timezone interpretations. _[GCFA p.665]_

### FILETIME Format

- **NTFS timestamp structure** — NTFS uses the Windows FILETIME data structure for timestamp values. _Why:_ forensic tools must decode FILETIME correctly to produce valid timelines. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **FILETIME width** — FILETIME is a 64-bit structure. _Why:_ the field size defines how timestamp values are stored and parsed. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **FILETIME unit** — FILETIME counts time in 100-nanosecond intervals. _Why:_ this explains the high precision shown in NTFS timestamps. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **FILETIME epoch** — FILETIME counts from 12:00 AM on January 1, 1601, UTC. _Why:_ timestamp conversion requires the correct epoch. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **High timestamp resolution** — NTFS timestamp resolution is especially useful for Windows forensic work. _Why:_ fine granularity can distinguish closely spaced actions. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **UNIX timestamp contrast** — UNIX dates are stored as seconds since January 1, 1970. _Why:_ comparing NTFS and UNIX timelines requires awareness of different epochs and resolutions. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **Subsecond event ordering** — many system events can occur within a single second. _Why:_ NTFS’s finer resolution can provide important ordering context that second-level timestamps may lose. _[GCFA p.665]_

### Cited References

- **Windows File Times reference** — the page cites Microsoft Windows file-time documentation at `http://for508.com/nep4l`. _Why:_ it provides supporting authority for Windows timestamp behavior. _[GCFA p.665]_
- **Windows FILETIME reference** — the page cites Microsoft FILETIME structure documentation at `http://for508.com/sucit`. _Why:_ it supports the technical description of the 64-bit FILETIME format. _[GCFA p.665]_

## Page 666

### Courseware Context

- **Course identifier** — The page belongs to SANS FOR508, “Advanced Incident Response, Threat Hunting, and Digital Forensics.” _Why:_ this identifies the DFIR training context for the timestamp rules. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Slide section** — The page discusses Windows timestamp behavior rules. _Why:_ this frames the page as guidance for interpreting NTFS time evidence. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Artifact scope** — The matrix applies to `$Standard_Information` on Windows 10 version 1903. _Why:_ timestamp behavior can vary by artifact and OS version, so scope is critical. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Timestamp family** — The page focuses on the four NTFS MACB timestamps. _Why:_ Modified, Accessed, Metadata Changed, and Birth/Created times are core file-system chronology evidence. _[GCFA p.~666]_

### $Standard_Information Timestamp Matrix

- **Modified timestamp · File Creation** — set to the file creation time. _Why:_ a newly created file initializes its Modified value at birth. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Modified timestamp · File Access** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ simple access should not be treated as evidence of content modification. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Modified timestamp · File Modification** — set to the time the file data changed. _Why:_ this is the primary timestamp for content alteration. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Modified timestamp · File Rename** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ renaming affects naming metadata rather than file contents. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Modified timestamp · File Copy (new file)** — copied from the source file’s Modified value. _Why:_ this can make the copied file’s Modified time older than its Creation time, indicating movement from another source. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Modified timestamp · Local File Move** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ moving within the same local context does not imply content modification. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Modified timestamp · Volume File Move via CLI** — copied from the original file. _Why:_ command-line volume moves can preserve old Modified times and create a movement signature. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Modified timestamp · Volume File Move via Explorer cut/paste** — copied from the original file. _Why:_ GUI cut/paste volume moves can also preserve source Modified time. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Modified timestamp · Shift-delete File Deletion** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ deletion does not create a file Modified-time update. _[GCFA p.~666]_

- **Access timestamp · File Creation** — set to the file creation time. _Why:_ a new file receives an initial Access value when it is created. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Access timestamp · File Access** — set to the access time, except it may remain unchanged on system volumes larger than 128 GiB. _Why:_ Access timestamps have conditional behavior and are therefore weak standalone evidence. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Access timestamp · File Modification** — set to the time the data changed. _Why:_ modifying a file can involve reading or touching file data, which can update Access time. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Access timestamp · File Rename** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ a rename does not necessarily represent file-content access. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Access timestamp · File Copy (new file)** — set to the copy time. _Why:_ copy operations can update Access evidence even though the source content may be older. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Access timestamp · Local File Move** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ same-volume movement does not necessarily touch file data. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Access timestamp · Volume File Move via CLI** — set to the command-line move time. _Why:_ CLI movement across volumes can leave an Access-time trace of the transfer. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Access timestamp · Volume File Move via Explorer cut/paste** — set to the cut/paste time. _Why:_ Explorer-mediated movement can produce a GUI-specific Access-time value. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Access timestamp · Shift-delete File Deletion** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ deleting a file does not record a new Access time. _[GCFA p.~666]_

- **Metadata timestamp · File Creation** — set to the file creation time. _Why:_ file creation establishes the initial metadata-change time. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Metadata timestamp · File Access** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ reading or opening a file does not necessarily alter its file-record metadata. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Metadata timestamp · File Modification** — set to the data modification time. _Why:_ changing contents or file size also changes file metadata. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Metadata timestamp · File Rename** — set to the rename time. _Why:_ changing the name is a metadata event. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Metadata timestamp · File Copy (new file)** — set to the copy time. _Why:_ the copied file receives new metadata when it is created at the destination. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Metadata timestamp · Local File Move** — set to the local move time. _Why:_ moving locally changes parent-folder metadata for the file record. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Metadata timestamp · Volume File Move via CLI** — inherited. _Why:_ CLI volume movement can preserve metadata timing in a way that differs from local moves. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Metadata timestamp · Volume File Move via Explorer cut/paste** — copied from the original file. _Why:_ Explorer cut/paste can preserve the source metadata timestamp during a volume move. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Metadata timestamp · Shift-delete File Deletion** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ NTFS does not store a deletion timestamp in this timestamp set. _[GCFA p.~666]_

- **Creation timestamp · File Creation** — set to the file creation time. _Why:_ the Birth/Created value records when the file object was made. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Creation timestamp · File Access** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ access alone should not alter the file’s birth time. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Creation timestamp · File Modification** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ content edits do not reset the original creation timestamp. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Creation timestamp · File Rename** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ renaming does not create a new file object. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Creation timestamp · File Copy (new file)** — set to the copy time. _Why:_ a copy creates a new destination file, so its Creation time marks the copy event. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Creation timestamp · Local File Move** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ a local move preserves the same file object rather than creating a new one. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Creation timestamp · Volume File Move via CLI** — set to the command-line move time. _Why:_ this value can indicate when the cross-volume CLI move occurred. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Creation timestamp · Volume File Move via Explorer cut/paste** — copied from the original file. _Why:_ Explorer cut/paste across volumes can preserve the original Creation value rather than recording the move time. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Creation timestamp · Shift-delete File Deletion** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ deletion does not update the file’s Creation timestamp. _[GCFA p.~666]_

### Interpretation Rules

- **Guidance reliability** — The timestamp matrix is intended as a reasonable baseline, not an absolute rule set. _Why:_ Windows has many ways to perform similar actions, and not every variation has been validated. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Long-running research note** — The slide has been refined over many years. _Why:_ timestamp behavior is complex enough that documented rules evolve with testing and OS behavior. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Version sensitivity** — Different Windows versions can change timestamp outcomes for the same user action. _Why:_ investigators must avoid assuming one OS version’s behavior applies universally. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Action-method sensitivity** — Different ways of performing the same apparent operation can lead to different timestamp results. _Why:_ forensic conclusions must account for the exact mechanism used, such as CLI versus Explorer. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Hypothesis testing requirement** — When a timestamp’s origin is important, the recommended practice is repeated testing on a system close to the original environment. _Why:_ controlled reproduction reduces the risk of overclaiming from ambiguous timestamp evidence. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Creation behavior** — when a file is first made, all four MACB timestamps need initial values and are set to the creation moment. _Why:_ this explains why new files begin with synchronized timestamps. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Access-time history** — Windows Vista disabled routine Access-time updating, while later Windows 10 and Windows 11 versions brought it back. _Why:_ Access-time interpretation depends strongly on OS generation and configuration. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Access-time exceptions** — even when routine Access-time updates were disabled, operations such as copying and moving could still affect Access values. _Why:_ disabled Access updating does not mean Access timestamps are forensically irrelevant in every scenario. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Access-time caution** — Access timestamps are usually poor evidence because their behavior is inconsistent and difficult to constrain. _Why:_ relying on Access time can create fragile timelines. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Modification effects** — changing file contents requires interacting with data and file size, which affects Modified, Access, and Metadata timestamps. _Why:_ a content edit can produce a multi-timestamp pattern rather than a single Modified-time change. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Rename effect** — a rename primarily changes file metadata, especially the filename, so the Metadata timestamp is the one expected to change. _Why:_ this helps distinguish name changes from content edits. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Local move effect** — moving a file locally primarily changes metadata, especially the parent folder reference. _Why:_ this can explain a Metadata timestamp update without a content modification. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Deletion timestamp absence** — Windows does not maintain a dedicated deletion time in these NTFS timestamps. _Why:_ lack of MACB timestamp change does not prove deletion did not occur. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Shift-delete behavior** — a shift-delete operation is shown as producing no change across the four listed timestamps. _Why:_ investigators must look outside MACB timestamps for deletion timing evidence. _[GCFA p.~666]_

### Copy And Move Indicators

- **Inherited Modified-time pattern** — copied files and command-line volume moves can retain the original file’s Modified timestamp. _Why:_ this is a key sign that a file originated elsewhere. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Modified-before-Creation anomaly** — a copied file or CLI volume-moved file may show a Modified time earlier than its Creation time. _Why:_ this impossible-looking sequence is a strong copy or transfer indicator. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Creation time as transfer time** — when Modified time is inherited but Creation time is new, Creation time can identify when the copy or move occurred. _Why:_ it provides timing for file movement even without a dedicated copy artifact. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Filesystem copy-artifact limitation** — file systems commonly lack explicit artifacts that say a copy occurred. _Why:_ timestamp patterns may be one of the best available indicators of copied material. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **GUI versus CLI movement** — cross-volume moves performed by Explorer cut/paste can update timestamps differently from command-line moves. _Why:_ investigators must avoid treating all “moves” as equivalent. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **Explorer cut/paste distinction** — the matrix explicitly separates volume moves by Explorer cut/paste from volume moves by CLI. _Why:_ the user interface used for the move affects forensic timestamp interpretation. _[GCFA p.~666]_
- **CLI move distinction** — the matrix explicitly treats command-line volume movement as its own case. _Why:_ command-line behavior can produce the Modified-before-Creation signature. _[GCFA p.~666]_

### $Standard_Information Timestamp Matrix

- **$Standard_Information · File Modification → Modified** — the Modified timestamp is set to the time file data was changed. _Why:_ this timestamp marks content-level writes. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · File Rename → Modified** — the Modified timestamp does not change when the file is renamed. _Why:_ a rename affects metadata rather than file contents. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · File Copy, New File → Modified** — the Modified timestamp is carried over from the original file. _Why:_ inherited Modified time can make a copied file appear older than its filesystem creation event. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · Local File Move → Modified** — the Modified timestamp does not change for a move within the same local context. _Why:_ local moves preserve content-change timing. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · Volume File Move via CLI → Modified** — the Modified timestamp is inherited from the source file. _Why:_ command-line moves across volumes can preserve original content-modification timing. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · Volume File Move via Explorer Cut/Paste → Modified** — the Modified timestamp is inherited from the original file. _Why:_ Explorer cut/paste across volumes can retain original content-modification timing. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · Shift+Delete File Deletion → Modified** — the Modified timestamp does not change during Shift+Delete deletion. _Why:_ deletion should not be interpreted as a file-content modification. _[GCFA p.667]_

- **$Standard_Information · File Creation → Access** — the Access timestamp is set to the file creation time. _Why:_ the file’s first access state begins at creation. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · File Access → Access** — the Access timestamp is set to the time of access, with a note that it may not change on system volumes larger than 128 GiB. _Why:_ access-time behavior can vary by volume characteristics, affecting timeline interpretation. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · File Modification → Access** — the Access timestamp is set to the time file data was changed. _Why:_ writes can update the access-related timestamp as part of the file activity footprint. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · File Rename → Access** — the Access timestamp does not change when the file is renamed. _Why:_ rename activity is not reflected as an access-time update. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · File Copy, New File → Access** — the Access timestamp is set to the time the copy was made. _Why:_ this helps distinguish the new copy event from the source file’s older timestamps. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · Local File Move → Access** — the Access timestamp does not change during a local file move. _Why:_ same-location moves preserve the prior access timestamp. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · Volume File Move via CLI → Access** — the Access timestamp is set to the time the command-line volume move occurred. _Why:_ this timestamp can reveal when the move operation happened. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · Volume File Move via Explorer Cut/Paste → Access** — the Access timestamp is set to the time of the Explorer cut/paste action. _Why:_ this provides a timeline marker for GUI-based cross-volume movement. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · Shift+Delete File Deletion → Access** — the Access timestamp does not change during Shift+Delete deletion. _Why:_ deletion alone does not provide a new access-time marker. _[GCFA p.667]_

- **$Standard_Information · File Creation → Metadata** — the Metadata timestamp is set to the file creation time. _Why:_ creation initializes the file’s metadata-change time. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · File Access → Metadata** — the Metadata timestamp does not change when the file is only accessed. _Why:_ simple reads do not alter file metadata. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · File Modification → Metadata** — the Metadata timestamp is set to the time file data was changed. _Why:_ content changes also cause metadata-state changes. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · File Rename → Metadata** — the Metadata timestamp is set to the time of the file rename. _Why:_ renaming is a metadata operation and leaves a metadata-time trace. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · File Copy, New File → Metadata** — the Metadata timestamp is set to the time the copy was made. _Why:_ a copied file receives fresh metadata timing for the new filesystem object. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · Local File Move → Metadata** — the Metadata timestamp is set to the time of the local file move. _Why:_ moving a file locally changes metadata even when content timestamps remain stable. _[GCFA p.667]_

- **$Standard_Information · Shift+Delete File Deletion → Metadata** — the Metadata timestamp does not change during Shift+Delete deletion. _Why:_ deletion does not itself create a metadata timestamp update in this matrix. _[GCFA p.667]_

- **$Standard_Information · File Creation → Creation** — the Creation timestamp is set to the file creation time. _Why:_ this is the baseline creation-time behavior for a new file. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · File Access → Creation** — the Creation timestamp does not change when the file is accessed. _Why:_ access activity should not be treated as evidence of file creation. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · File Modification → Creation** — the Creation timestamp does not change when file data is modified. _Why:_ edits preserve the original creation time. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · File Rename → Creation** — the Creation timestamp does not change when the file is renamed. _Why:_ renaming does not create a new file object in this context. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · File Copy, New File → Creation** — the Creation timestamp is set to the time the copy was made. _Why:_ a copied file is a newly created filesystem object even when other timestamps are inherited. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · Local File Move → Creation** — the Creation timestamp does not change during a local file move. _Why:_ same-volume movement preserves the file’s creation timestamp. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · Volume File Move via CLI → Creation** — the Creation timestamp is set to the time the command-line volume move occurred. _Why:_ this can expose when a cross-volume CLI move created the destination object. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · Volume File Move via Explorer Cut/Paste → Creation** — the Creation timestamp is inherited from the original file. _Why:_ Explorer cut/paste across volumes can preserve the original Creation time, which may differ from CLI behavior. _[GCFA p.667]_
- **$Standard_Information · Shift+Delete File Deletion → Creation** — the Creation timestamp does not change during Shift+Delete deletion. _Why:_ deletion does not alter the file’s original creation timestamp in this matrix. _[GCFA p.667]_

### $Standard_Information Win11 v22H2 Matrix

- **$SI Modified · File Creation** — A newly created file receives a Modified timestamp equal to the file-creation event time. _Why:_ this establishes the baseline Modified value for a new file. _[GCFA p.668]_
- **$SI Modified · File Access** — Accessing a file does not alter the Modified timestamp. _Why:_ a later access should not be mistaken for content modification. _[GCFA p.668]_
- **$SI Modified · File Modification** — Modifying file data sets the Modified timestamp to the data-change time. _Why:_ this is the primary timestamp for detecting content updates. _[GCFA p.668]_
- **$SI Modified · File Rename** — Renaming a file does not change the Modified timestamp. _Why:_ unchanged Modified time can distinguish a rename from a content edit. _[GCFA p.668]_
- **$SI Modified · File Copy New File** — A copied file inherits its Modified timestamp from the original file. _Why:_ a copy may show a Modified time earlier than its Creation time, which is an important copy indicator. _[GCFA p.668]_

### Time Rule Exceptions

- **Timestamp rule exceptions** — Some file activity can alter timestamps in ways that do not follow the usual Windows timestamp-update patterns. _Why:_ investigators should avoid treating timestamp rules as absolute when reconstructing activity. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Complex OS behavior** — Current operating systems contain many interacting components that can affect file timestamps. _Why:_ timestamp changes may be caused by ordinary platform behavior rather than direct user intent or attacker action. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Application-layer effects** — Programs running on top of the operating system can independently trigger timestamp changes. _Why:_ forensic timestamp interpretation must consider application behavior, not only filesystem rules. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Nonstandard timestamp updates** — Numerous actions may modify times in ways that break expected timestamp-update models. _Why:_ unexpected timestamp patterns are not automatically evidence of tampering. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Common exception categories** — The page identifies applications, anti-forensic tools, archives, and scanning as frequent causes of timestamp anomalies. _Why:_ these categories provide likely hypotheses when timestamps appear inconsistent. _[GCFA p.670]_

### Applications

- **Applications · Office products** — Microsoft Office products are listed as applications that can create timestamp-rule exceptions. _Why:_ Office activity can explain access-time changes that otherwise look suspicious. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Microsoft Office access-time behavior** — Microsoft Office has historically updated file access times. _Why:_ Office document interaction may leave access-time evidence even when normal access-time updates are expected to be disabled. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Office vs. registry access-time setting** — Microsoft Office may update access timestamps even when registry configuration disables access-time updates. _Why:_ registry settings alone do not guarantee that access times remain unchanged. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Applications · WinZip** — WinZip is listed as an application associated with timestamp-rule exceptions. _Why:_ archive-handling applications can produce timestamp patterns that resemble copy or manipulation activity. _[GCFA p.670]_

### Anti-Forensics

- **Anti-forensics category** — Anti-forensic activity is identified as a timestamp-rule exception source. _Why:_ attackers or cleanup tools may intentionally alter time evidence. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Anti-forensics · Timestomp** — Timestamp-tampering tools such as Timestomp are listed as anti-forensic timestamp offenders. _Why:_ timestomping can make files appear older, newer, or better aligned with surrounding files. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Anti-forensics · Touch** — Touch-style utilities are listed as tools that can alter timestamps. _Why:_ legitimate timestamp-editing utilities may be used benignly or for evidence manipulation. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Anti-forensics · Privacy cleaners** — Privacy-cleaning tools are listed as anti-forensic software that can affect timestamps. _Why:_ cleanup utilities may destroy or distort temporal evidence during deletion or sanitization. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Malware timestamp manipulation** — Malware can use filesystem APIs to modify file timestamps. _Why:_ malicious files may be time-aligned with existing files to reduce suspicion. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Anti-forensic filesystem API use** — Anti-forensic utilities can call filesystem APIs to change timestamps. _Why:_ timestamp values may be deliberately edited through normal OS-supported mechanisms. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Timestamp blending** — Timestamp modification can be used to make suspicious files appear consistent with nearby or preexisting files. _Why:_ matching timestamps can hide attacker-created files during triage. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Timestamp evidence destruction** — Timestamp manipulation can be used to damage or erase useful temporal evidence. _Why:_ altered times can weaken timeline reconstruction and event ordering. _[GCFA p.670]_

### Archives

- **Archives category** — Archive extraction is identified as a timestamp-rule exception source. _Why:_ unpacked files may not receive timestamps that reflect extraction time. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Archives · ZIP** — ZIP archives are listed as archive formats relevant to timestamp exceptions. _Why:_ files extracted from ZIP containers may preserve prior timestamp values. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Archives · RAR** — RAR archives are listed as archive formats relevant to timestamp exceptions. _Why:_ RAR extraction can produce timestamp patterns that require archive-aware interpretation. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Archives · TGZ** — TGZ archives are listed as archive formats relevant to timestamp exceptions. _Why:_ Unix-style compressed tar archives may retain original file time metadata when extracted. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Archive timestamp retention** — Archives may preserve the original file dates and timestamps. _Why:_ extracted files can appear to predate the extraction event. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Archive modified-time effect** — Archive extraction usually affects only the modified timestamp. _Why:_ this can create a timestamp pattern similar to a copied file. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Archive backdating behavior** — Many archive tools set extracted files’ modification times back to the values stored when the archive was created. _Why:_ extracted files may look temporally older than their actual placement on disk. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Archive extraction copy-like artifact** — Backdated modification times from archive extraction can make the result resemble a file-copy event. _Why:_ investigators may misclassify extraction as copying unless archive context is considered. _[GCFA p.670]_

### Scanning

- **Scanning category** — File scanning is identified as a possible timestamp-rule exception source. _Why:_ security tools can touch files during routine inspection. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Scanning variability** — Whether scanning changes timestamps depends on the quality and behavior of the antivirus implementation. _Why:_ different endpoint products may leave different timestamp artifacts. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Security software interaction** — Locally installed security software may scan or otherwise interact with files. _Why:_ investigator-owned or enterprise security tooling can create timestamp noise. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Security software timestamp updates** — Security software interaction with files may cause timestamp changes. _Why:_ timestamp updates are not always caused by a user opening or modifying the file. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Antivirus daily access-time updates** — Many antivirus products historically updated file access timestamps during daily scans. _Why:_ repeated access-time changes may reflect scheduled scanning rather than file use. _[GCFA p.670]_

### Analysis Guidance

- **Contextual timestamp interpretation** — Timestamp evidence should be interpreted alongside other actions that could explain the observed changes. _Why:_ a single timestamp anomaly is weak evidence without corroborating context. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Alternative explanations** — Analysts should consider applications, archives, anti-forensic utilities, and security scanning before concluding that a timestamp is maliciously altered. _Why:_ multiple benign or administrative activities can produce similar timestamp artifacts. _[GCFA p.670]_
- **Hypothesis testing** — When timestamp behavior is uncertain, analysts should test the proposed explanation. _Why:_ controlled testing can distinguish normal tool behavior from suspicious manipulation. _[GCFA p.670]_

### Lateral Movement Timestamp Pattern

- **Remote-copy timestamp rules** — NTFS timestamp behavior remains consistent when files are transferred through a network share, assuming the source and destination filesystems are both NTFS. _Why:_ local NTFS copy rules can be applied to SMB-based lateral movement analysis. _[GCFA p.671]_
- **Filesystem prerequisite** — The described timestamp behavior depends on both communicating filesystems being NTFS. _Why:_ analysts should avoid overgeneralizing the rule to non-NTFS transfers. _[GCFA p.671]_
- **Remote filesystem handling** — The operating system treats a remotely mounted filesystem similarly to a locally mounted filesystem. _Why:_ this explains why normal copy timestamp mechanics still apply over SMB shares. _[GCFA p.671]_
- **SMB copy behavior** — When a file is copied to a target host through an SMB file share, the destination file receives a fresh creation timestamp. _Why:_ the creation time can identify when the file arrived on the target. _[GCFA p.671]_
- **SMB copy behavior · Modified timestamp** — During an SMB file-share copy, the destination file keeps the original file’s modification timestamp. _Why:_ inherited modification time lets analysts distinguish copied files from newly authored files. _[GCFA p.671]_
- **Copy indicator** — A destination file whose modification time is earlier than its creation time is consistent with a copied file. _Why:_ this timestamp inversion is a practical file-movement indicator. _[GCFA p.671]_
- **Lateral movement timing** — For a copied payload, the destination creation timestamp represents the time the file was copied to the target system. _Why:_ this gives a concrete timestamp for possible lateral movement. _[GCFA p.671]_
- **Pivot-point selection** — The destination file creation time can be used as a timeline pivot point on the target host. _Why:_ nearby artifacts may reveal the account, execution method, or related malware activity. _[GCFA p.671]_
- **Executable-copy suspicion** — An `.exe` file showing copied-file timestamp characteristics is noteworthy. _Why:_ executables normally warrant scrutiny when their timestamps suggest transfer onto a host. _[GCFA p.671]_

- **macb column** — the `macb` field identifies which filesystem timestamp type or types correspond to the displayed time. _Why:_ this column explains what the timestamp actually represents. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **File Size column** — the timeline can include the file’s size as a separate column. _Why:_ size helps distinguish files and supports correlation across repeated entries. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Permissions column** — Unix timelines may include permissions information. _Why:_ permissions can provide access-control context on Unix-derived systems. _[GCFA p.672]_

- **Group column** — Unix timelines may include the owning group. _Why:_ group ownership can clarify Unix access context. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Meta column** — the `Meta` field records the metadata address; for NTFS this is the `$MFT` record number. _Why:_ metadata addresses let analysts tie timeline rows back to filesystem metadata records. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **File Name column** — the timeline includes the file path or name associated with the timestamped object. _Why:_ the filename is the primary artifact identifier in timeline review. _[GCFA p.672]_

- **Table header · Meta** — the fourth displayed table column is labeled `Meta`. _Why:_ it links the row to the metadata address, such as an NTFS `$MFT` record number. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Table header · File Name** — the fifth displayed table column is labeled `File Name`. _Why:_ it identifies the object represented by the row. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Example row 1 · Timestamp** — the first row’s timestamp is `2023-10-03 16:20:37`. _Why:_ this is the time shared by the row’s indicated timestamp types. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Example row 1 · macb** — the first row’s `macb` value is `m.c.`. _Why:_ it shows that modification and metadata-change times equal the displayed timestamp. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Example row 1 · File Size** — the first row’s file size is `20452`. _Why:_ the same size appears across both sample entries for the same file. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Example row 1 · Meta** — the first row’s metadata value is `80932`. _Why:_ this identifies the same metadata record referenced by both sample rows. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Example row 1 · File Name** — the first row’s filename is `C:\calc.exe`. _Why:_ it shows the timeline object whose modification and metadata-change timestamps are being represented. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Example row 2 · Timestamp** — the second row’s timestamp is `2023-11-04 18:46:51`. _Why:_ this is the time shared by the row’s indicated timestamp types. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Example row 2 · macb** — the second row’s `macb` value is `.a.b`. _Why:_ it shows that access and birth times equal the displayed timestamp. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Example row 2 · File Size** — the second row’s file size is `20452`. _Why:_ matching size helps show both rows describe the same file object. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Example row 2 · Meta** — the second row’s metadata value is `80932`. _Why:_ the repeated metadata value ties the second row to the same filesystem metadata record as the first row. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Example row 2 · File Name** — the second row’s filename is `C:\calc.exe`. _Why:_ the same path demonstrates that one file can appear multiple times in a timeline. _[GCFA p.672]_

### Timestamp Granularity

- **Timestamp precision** — the first timeline column records time to the nearest second. _Why:_ subsecond ordering is not represented in this timeline format. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Same-second activity** — many system events may occur within a single second. _Why:_ rows close together in time may not be perfectly ordered. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Ordering limitation** — events occurring within the same one-second granularity can appear out of sequence. _Why:_ analysts should avoid overclaiming exact order when timestamps are equal or very close. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Practical impact of second granularity** — slight same-second ordering ambiguity is often either unimportant or resolvable by analyst judgment. _Why:_ the limitation should be considered but does not usually invalidate the timeline. _[GCFA p.672]_

### macb Semantics

- **macb difficulty** — the `macb` column is presented as the most challenging timeline field to understand. _Why:_ it encodes multiple timestamp meanings compactly. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **macb importance** — the `macb` column is also presented as the most important field to understand. _Why:_ it determines the forensic meaning of the displayed time. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **macb timestamp mapping** — `macb` specifies which timestamp value or values are represented by the first column. _Why:_ the same displayed time may correspond to one or several timestamp classes. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Multiple timestamp classes per row** — a single timeline row can represent more than one timestamp type. _Why:_ matching timestamp values are consolidated into one row. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **M meaning** — `M` in `macb` denotes file modification time. _Why:_ modification time is central to determining when file content last changed. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **A meaning** — `A` in `macb` denotes file access time. _Why:_ access time may indicate when a file was last opened or otherwise accessed. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **C meaning** — `C` in `macb` denotes metadata-change time. _Why:_ metadata-change time can reveal changes to filesystem metadata rather than content. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **B meaning** — `B` in `macb` denotes birth or creation time. _Why:_ birth time helps establish when the filesystem object was created. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Fixed macb order** — the `macb` characters always appear in the same positional order. _Why:_ analysts can interpret each position consistently across rows. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Period placeholder** — a period character, `.`, is used where a timestamp type is absent from the row. _Why:_ the placeholder preserves positional meaning in the `macb` field. _[GCFA p.672]_

### C:\calc.exe Example Interpretation

- **Same file with multiple timeline rows** — the example shows two timeline entries for `C:\calc.exe`. _Why:_ one filesystem object can generate multiple rows when its timestamp values differ. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **First row timestamp pairing** — `m.c.` means the file’s modification time and metadata-change time are both `2023-10-03 16:20:37`. _Why:_ this explains why two timestamp classes are combined into one row. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **First row absent access time** — the `.` in the access position of `m.c.` means access time is not represented by `2023-10-03 16:20:37`. _Why:_ the row should not be interpreted as evidence of access at that time. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **First row absent birth time** — the trailing `.` in `m.c.` means birth time is not represented by `2023-10-03 16:20:37`. _Why:_ the row should not be treated as the file’s creation time. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Second row timestamp pairing** — `.a.b` means the file’s access time and birth time are both `2023-11-04 18:46:51`. _Why:_ this explains the second row’s forensic meaning. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Second row absent modification time** — the leading `.` in `.a.b` means modification time is not represented by `2023-11-04 18:46:51`. _Why:_ the row should not be read as a content-modification event. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Second row absent metadata-change time** — the third-position `.` in `.a.b` means metadata-change time is not represented by `2023-11-04 18:46:51`. _Why:_ the row should not be read as a metadata-change event. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Four timestamps per file** — each file can have four relevant timestamp values in this timeline model. _Why:_ one file may contribute multiple timeline entries. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Maximum rows per file from timestamps** — a file may appear up to four separate times in a timeline if all four timestamp values differ. _Why:_ repeated filenames are not automatically duplicates or separate files. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Two-row example reason** — `C:\calc.exe` appears twice because modification and metadata-change times match each other, while access and birth times match each other at a different time. _Why:_ grouped equal timestamps reduce four possible entries to two. _[GCFA p.672]_

### Additional macb Examples

- **macb example · `m.cb`** — `m.cb` indicates modification, metadata-change, and birth timestamps share the row’s displayed time. _Why:_ three timestamp classes can be combined when their values match. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **macb example · `m.cb` absent access** — the period in `m.cb` means access time is not represented by that row. _Why:_ absence must be interpreted positionally. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **macb example · `.a..`** — `.a..` indicates only the access timestamp matches the row’s displayed time. _Why:_ a row can represent a single timestamp class. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **macb example · `.a..` absent modification** — the leading period in `.a..` means modification time is not represented. _Why:_ this prevents confusing an access-only row with a content-change event. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **macb example · `.a..` absent metadata change** — the third-position period in `.a..` means metadata-change time is not represented. _Why:_ the row does not indicate metadata alteration. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **macb example · `.a..` absent birth** — the trailing period in `.a..` means birth time is not represented. _Why:_ the row does not indicate file creation. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **macb example · `mac.`** — `mac.` indicates modification, access, and metadata-change timestamps share the row’s displayed time. _Why:_ multiple timestamp meanings may be packed into one compact string. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **macb example · `mac.` absent birth** — the trailing period in `mac.` means birth time is not represented. _Why:_ the row should not be interpreted as creation-time evidence. _[GCFA p.672]_

### Evidence Aging

- **Only latest timestamp retained** — the timeline reflects only the last value for each timestamp class. _Why:_ older timestamp states are not preserved in the normal filesystem timestamp fields. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Word document modification example** — for a Word document, the available `M` value is only the most recent modification time, not a list of every prior edit time. _Why:_ filesystem timelines do not provide full edit history. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **No historical timestamp series** — the page explicitly distinguishes current timestamp values from historical timestamp information. _Why:_ analysts must not infer every past activity from a single current timestamp. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Evidence aging concept** — timestamp evidence can be overwritten as later activity updates the same timestamp field. _Why:_ filesystem evidence can lose earlier state as normal use continues. _[GCFA p.672]_
- **Modification-time overwrite** — when the Word document is updated again, its `M` timestamp changes to the new modification time. _Why:_ the previous modification timestamp is erased from the active filesystem metadata. _[GCFA p.672]_

## Page 673

### Filesystem Timeline Columns

- **Modification time** — the page is continuing a discussion of the file modification timestamp as one of the timeline fields. _Why:_ modification time is a core pivot for determining when file content likely changed. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **File size** — a file’s byte size can support matching between files that share the same size. _Why:_ size-based correlation can help identify related or duplicate files during timeline review. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **File size · Large-file hunting** — unusually large file sizes can help surface archives or encrypted container files. _Why:_ large archives and encrypted volumes may hold staged, exfiltrated, or concealed data. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **Meta column** — the `Meta` field records the metadata address of the filesystem structure that supplied the timeline data. _Why:_ this value links a timeline entry back to the underlying filesystem record for deeper examination. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **Meta column · NTFS meaning** — on Windows NTFS, the `Meta` value corresponds to the relevant `$MFT` record number. _Why:_ the `$MFT` record number lets an examiner pivot from a timeline row into the specific NTFS file record. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **Meta column · Linux meaning** — on a Linux filesystem, the `Meta` value corresponds to the inode number. _Why:_ the inode number identifies the filesystem metadata object behind the file entry. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **Meta column · Later MFT use** — the course notes that `Meta` values will be used later for deeper analysis of `$MFT` records. _Why:_ retaining the metadata address preserves a path from high-level timeline triage to low-level NTFS record inspection. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **File Name column** — the `File Name` field stores the complete path for the file. _Why:_ full paths provide both filename and directory context for filtering and investigative pivots. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **File Name column · Deleted marker** — entries for files that are currently unallocated have `(deleted)` appended to the `File Name` value. _Why:_ this marker helps distinguish deleted/unallocated filesystem entries from active allocated files. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **File Name column · Filtering use** — the `File Name` column is one of the timeline fields most frequently used for filtering. _Why:_ filenames and paths are high-signal selectors when narrowing large filesystem timelines. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **Permissions column** — the `Permissions` field can contain file security and ownership-related information. _Why:_ permission data may help interpret access control context on filesystems that expose this model. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **UID column** — the `UID` field can contain ownership information for the file. _Why:_ user ownership can help associate filesystem activity with local accounts on Unix-like systems. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **GID column** — the `GID` field can contain group ownership information for the file. _Why:_ group ownership can help interpret access scope and account grouping on Unix-like systems. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **Permissions/UID/GID · Unix relevance** — `Permissions`, `UID`, and `GID` are meaningful for Unix-based filesystems. _Why:_ Unix-like systems represent ownership and permission data using these fields. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **Permissions/UID/GID · Windows limitation** — Windows does not represent permissions and ownership through `Permissions`, `UID`, and `GID` in the same way. _Why:_ these fields should not be treated as normal Windows security descriptors during Windows timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **Permissions/UID/GID · Windows analysis practice** — these Unix-oriented columns are commonly hidden when analyzing Windows systems. _Why:_ hiding irrelevant columns reduces visual noise and keeps attention on fields that matter for Windows forensic review. _[GCFA p.673]_

- **`-f` supported input: `$J`** — `$J` is listed as a valid input file for `-f`. _Why:_ the USN journal can provide filesystem change activity useful for timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.674]_

- **`-f` supported input: `$SDS`** — `$SDS` is listed as a valid input file for `-f`. _Why:_ the NTFS security descriptor stream can be processed for security metadata context. _[GCFA p.674]_
- **`-f` supported input: `$I30`** — `$I30` is listed as a valid input file for `-f`. _Why:_ directory index records can preserve directory-entry metadata relevant to forensic reconstruction. _[GCFA p.674]_

## Page 675

### MFTECmd Input Selection

- **`-f <f>`** — selects the file that MFTECmd will parse; the accepted targets shown are `$MFT`, `$J`, `$Boot`, `$SDS`, and `$I30`, and this argument is mandatory. _Why:_ choosing the correct NTFS artifact controls which forensic parser path and output fields are produced. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`$MFT` as `-f` target** — MFTECmd can process the NTFS Master File Table when supplied through `-f`. _Why:_ `$MFT` parsing exposes file records, timestamps, names, attributes, and directory relationships. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`$J` as `-f` target** — MFTECmd can process the NTFS USN change journal when supplied through `-f`. _Why:_ `$J` records file-system change activity that can support timeline and activity reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`$Boot` as `-f` target** — MFTECmd can process the NTFS boot file when supplied through `-f`. _Why:_ `$Boot` contains filesystem metadata needed for low-level NTFS interpretation. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`$SDS` as `-f` target** — MFTECmd can process the NTFS security descriptor stream when supplied through `-f`. _Why:_ `$SDS` analysis helps map security IDs to stored security descriptors. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`$I30` as `-f` target** — MFTECmd can process NTFS directory index data when supplied through `-f`. _Why:_ `$I30` artifacts can preserve directory listing evidence, including entries relevant to deleted or historical file activity. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`-m <m>`** — provides an `$MFT` file when the primary `-f` input is a `$J` file. _Why:_ the `$MFT` lets MFTECmd resolve parent paths in `$J` CSV output. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`-m <m>` parent-path resolution** — when parsing `$J`, the supplied `$MFT` is used to resolve parent directory paths in CSV results. _Why:_ resolved paths make change-journal records far more useful for investigation and timeline review. _[GCFA p.~675]_

### JSON Output

- **`--json <json>`** — specifies the directory where MFTECmd writes JSON-formatted results. _Why:_ JSON output supports structured downstream processing and repeatable analysis pipelines. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`--json <json>` output requirement** — either `--json` or `--csv` is required unless `--de` or `--body` is used. _Why:_ MFTECmd normally needs an explicit structured-output destination unless the user is dumping details or creating bodyfile output. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`--jsonf <jsonf>`** — specifies the JSON output filename. _Why:_ naming the result file explicitly helps preserve predictable evidence-processing outputs. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`--jsonf <jsonf>` default override** — when `--jsonf` is present, it replaces MFTECmd’s default JSON filename. _Why:_ this prevents automated or default naming from obscuring which run produced which artifact. _[GCFA p.~675]_

### CSV Output

- **`--csv <csv>`** — specifies the directory where MFTECmd writes CSV-formatted results. _Why:_ CSV output is suitable for spreadsheet review, filtering, sorting, and timeline ingestion. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`--csv <csv>` output requirement** — either `--csv` or `--json` is required unless `--de` or `--body` is specified. _Why:_ the tool requires an output mode for normal parsing workflows. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`--csvf <csvf>`** — specifies the CSV output filename. _Why:_ investigator-controlled filenames make exported evidence easier to track. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`--csvf <csvf>` default override** — when `--csvf` is used, it replaces the default CSV filename. _Why:_ this supports reproducible naming in scripted forensic processing. _[GCFA p.~675]_

### Bodyfile Output

- **`--body <body>`** — specifies the directory where MFTECmd writes bodyfile-formatted results. _Why:_ bodyfile output can be consumed by timeline tools. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`--body <body>` dependency** — using `--body` also requires `--bdl`. _Why:_ bodyfile output needs a drive-letter context to form usable timeline records. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`--bodyf <bodyf>`** — specifies the bodyfile output filename. _Why:_ explicit bodyfile naming helps distinguish timeline exports from different sources or runs. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`--bodyf <bodyf>` default override** — when `--bodyf` is supplied, it overrides MFTECmd’s default bodyfile name. _Why:_ analyst-defined naming improves evidence organization. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`--bdl <bdl>`** — supplies the drive letter to use in bodyfile output, such as `C` or `D`. _Why:_ bodyfile entries require a volume identifier for timeline paths. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`--bdl <bdl>` value format** — the option expects only the drive letter itself. _Why:_ including extra path syntax could produce incorrect bodyfile paths. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`C` bodyfile drive-letter example** — `C` is shown as an acceptable drive-letter value for `--bdl`. _Why:_ it demonstrates the expected single-letter format. _[GCFA p.~675]_

### Line Endings

### Resident File Extraction

- **`--dr`** — when enabled, dumps resident `$MFT` files. _Why:_ resident files may store their full content inside the MFT record, making direct recovery possible. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`--dr` destination source** — resident files are dumped into the directory specified by `--csv` or `--json`. _Why:_ MFTECmd reuses the selected output directory for recovered resident content. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`<AttributeNumber>` in resident filename** — the resident dump filename includes the attribute number. _Why:_ this identifies which resident attribute produced the dumped data. _[GCFA p.~675]_

### Timestamp Formatting

- **`--dt <dt>`** — sets a custom date and time display format for timestamps. _Why:_ timestamp formatting affects readability and downstream comparison. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`yyyy` in default timestamp format** — the default format uses a four-digit year component. _Why:_ full-year display avoids ambiguity in forensic timelines. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`MM` in default timestamp format** — the default format uses a two-digit month component. _Why:_ fixed-width dates sort and compare cleanly. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`dd` in default timestamp format** — the default format uses a two-digit day component. _Why:_ fixed-width day values support consistent timeline output. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`HH` in default timestamp format** — the default format uses a two-digit hour component. _Why:_ hour precision is necessary for event sequencing. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`mm` in default timestamp format** — the default format uses a two-digit minute component. _Why:_ minute precision supports tighter activity reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`ss` in default timestamp format** — the default format uses a two-digit second component. _Why:_ second precision is often needed for correlating filesystem and log events. _[GCFA p.~675]_
