- **`--sn`** — includes DOS filename types in `$MFT` output when enabled. _Why:_ short-name artifacts may reveal legacy names, alternate naming evidence, or additional file-name metadata. _[GCFA p.~675]_

### Timestamp Attribute Controls

- **`0x10` comparison attribute** — by default, `0x30` timestamps are included only when they differ from `0x10` timestamps in the `$MFT`. _Why:_ differences between these timestamp sets can indicate file operations or metadata inconsistencies worth investigating. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`--at` default behavior** — without `--at`, MFTECmd limits `0x30` timestamp reporting to cases where those timestamps differ from `0x10`. _Why:_ this reduces output volume while preserving timestamp discrepancies. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **`--rs`** — when enabled, recovers slack space from FILE records while processing `$MFT` files. _Why:_ FILE record slack can contain remnants of prior metadata useful for forensic recovery. _[GCFA p.~675]_

- **Example command recursion flag** — the example command includes `-r`, meaning directory traversal is recursive. _Why:_ recursive processing is required to collect filenames beneath nested directories instead of only one directory level. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Example command bodyfile flag** — the example command includes `-m C:`, meaning output is generated in bodyfile format with `C:` as the mount-point prefix. _Why:_ the bodyfile prefix controls how paths appear in downstream timeline records. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Example evidence image path** — the source image in the example is `/cases/cdrive/cdrive.E01`. _Why:_ this is the forensic image being parsed for filename-layer timeline data. _[GCFA p.~676]_

### fls Options

- **`fls -d` option** — `-d` restricts output to deleted entries. _Why:_ this supports focused recovery and timeline review of removed filename records. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **`fls -r` option** — `-r` makes `fls` descend through directories recursively. _Why:_ this allows broad collection of filename records across directory trees. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **`fls -p` option** — `-p` displays complete paths during recursive listing. _Why:_ full paths improve artifact context and reduce ambiguity when similar filenames exist in different folders. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **`fls -m` option** — `-m` emits results in timeline bodyfile format. _Why:_ bodyfile format is the common intermediate format used to create forensic timelines. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **`fls -s <sec>` option** — `-s <sec>` applies a system time-skew adjustment measured in seconds. _Why:_ time-skew correction helps align filesystem timestamps with real-world time during timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Time-skew wording variant** — the page describes `-s <sec>` both as “timeskew of system in seconds” and as “timeskew correction for system in seconds.” _Why:_ both descriptions refer to the same adjustment capability and confirm that the unit is seconds. _[GCFA p.~676]_

### fls Functionality

- **Filesystem-like image interaction** — `fls` lets an examiner browse or process a forensic image in a way that resembles working with a normal filesystem. _Why:_ this enables file listing and metadata extraction without mounting or altering the evidence. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Filename-layer timeline source** — The Sleuth Kit’s `fls` can gather timeline information from the filename layer. _Why:_ filename-layer records can preserve directory-entry evidence relevant to file existence, deletion, and path context. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Directory inode processing** — `fls` can take a directory inode, examine that directory’s contents, and output the filenames contained there. _Why:_ inode-targeted processing lets analysts enumerate specific filesystem directories from metadata structures. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Deleted item listing** — `fls` directory output can include deleted entries. _Why:_ deleted filename records may remain useful even after the active file is removed. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Filename information extraction** — `fls` is designed to extract filename information for files. _Why:_ filenames and path records are core inputs for reconstruction of user and attacker activity. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Metadata information extraction** — `fls` is also designed to extract file metadata information. _Why:_ metadata fields provide timestamps, permissions, and other attributes needed for timeline construction. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Bodyfile output purpose** — using `-m` directs `fls` to write data in the common bodyfile timeline format. _Why:_ this format is the initial artifact used to build later forensic timelines. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Timeline creation stage** — producing the bodyfile is described as the first step in timeline creation. _Why:_ this places `fls -m` at the beginning of the timeline workflow. _[GCFA p.~676]_

### The Sleuth Kit Context

- **The Sleuth Kit identity** — The Sleuth Kit, abbreviated TSK, is described as an early open-source forensic toolkit. _Why:_ this establishes `fls` as part of a long-standing forensic tool suite. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **TSK ecosystem use** — TSK is used by many other forensic suites, including both free and commercial tools, for filesystem parsing. _Why:_ widespread dependency makes TSK behavior important beyond direct command-line use. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Filesystem parsing role** — TSK is used to parse filesystems. _Why:_ filesystem parsing is required to interpret evidence images and recover file records. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **`fls` suite membership** — `fls` is part of The Sleuth Kit suite. _Why:_ knowing the suite helps analysts locate documentation, installation packages, and related tools. _[GCFA p.~676]_

### Data Types Collected

- **Three collection categories** — page 676 identifies three types of data to collect: allocated files, deleted files, and orphan files. _Why:_ these categories define the scope of filename-layer timeline evidence. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Allocated file definition** — allocated files are active files normally visible in a directory listing. _Why:_ these represent current filesystem contents and baseline user-visible artifacts. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Deleted file definition** — deleted files are unallocated files whose filename structures still remain. _Why:_ these records can reveal removed items that no longer appear as active files. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Deleted file path retention** — depending on the filesystem, deleted file metadata may still preserve full path information. _Why:_ retained paths help place deleted evidence in its original directory context. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Deleted file timestamp retention** — depending on the filesystem, deleted file metadata may still include time values. _Why:_ retained timestamps help position deleted activity in a timeline. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Deleted file permission retention** — depending on the filesystem, deleted file metadata may still include permissions. _Why:_ permissions can help interpret ownership, access, and execution context for deleted artifacts. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Orphan file definition** — orphan files are data from unallocated metadata structures where parent directory information is no longer available. _Why:_ orphan records preserve evidence of file existence even after directory linkage is lost. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Orphan filename knowledge** — an orphan record can still show that a file with a particular name once existed. _Why:_ the filename remains an investigative lead even without a known parent folder. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Orphan timestamp knowledge** — an orphan record can still provide a set of timestamps for the former file. _Why:_ those timestamps can be added to investigative timelines despite missing path context. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Orphan folder limitation** — for orphan files, the original containing folder is unknown. _Why:_ analysts must avoid overclaiming path context when the parent relationship has been lost. _[GCFA p.~676]_

### fls Versus MFTECmd

- **Primary input difference** — `fls` extracts metadata using an image of a filesystem volume, while MFTECmd uses the `$MFT` file from the C: drive. _Why:_ tool choice depends on whether the examiner has a full volume image or only MFT data. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **`fls` volume-image input** — `fls` is designed to work from a filesystem volume image, such as an image of the entire C: drive. _Why:_ this makes it suitable when full disk or volume evidence is available. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **MFTECmd `$MFT` input** — MFTECmd can build timeline data from only the C: drive’s `$MFT` file. _Why:_ this is useful when imaging the whole disk is unavailable or impractical. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **MFTECmd acquisition advantage** — MFTECmd provides timeline capability when a disk image cannot be obtained or is not feasible to acquire. _Why:_ it supports lighter-weight triage and constrained collection scenarios. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Filesystem support difference** — `fls` can parse many filesystems beyond NTFS. _Why:_ this makes `fls` broader than NTFS-specific tooling. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **MFTECmd filesystem limitation** — MFTECmd supports only NTFS. _Why:_ this limits MFTECmd use to NTFS evidence sources. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Live filesystem capability** — `fls` can also run against live filesystems. _Why:_ this makes it potentially useful during live triage acquisition, not only post-acquisition image analysis. _[GCFA p.~676]_
- **Live triage relevance** — because `fls` can operate on live filesystems, it may be useful in multiple live collection scenarios. _Why:_ investigators can gather filename-layer timeline data when full forensic imaging is delayed or impractical. _[GCFA p.~676]_

- **Filesystem metadata source · MFTECmd** — a bodyfile can also be created from filesystem metadata exported by `MFTECmd`. _Why:_ this identifies a Windows-focused upstream source for bodyfile generation. _[GCFA p.~677]_
- **mactime role in triage timelines** — mactime converts bodyfile data into a format that is easier for an investigator to read and analyze. _Why:_ raw bodyfile records are less useful until sorted and rendered for review. _[GCFA p.~677]_
- **Chronological sorting** — mactime organizes bodyfile-derived records by time order. _Why:_ chronological ordering lets investigators reconstruct activity sequences. _[GCFA p.~677]_
- **The Sleuth Kit association** — mactime is part of The Sleuth Kit, abbreviated `TSK`. _Why:_ tool provenance matters when selecting, documenting, and validating forensic tooling. _[GCFA p.~677]_
- **Filesystem timeline process** — creating a filesystem timeline is described as a two-step workflow: first obtain a bodyfile, then use a tool such as mactime to render and sort it. _Why:_ separating extraction from timeline rendering clarifies where each tool fits. _[GCFA p.~677]_

### Time Zone Handling

- **NTFS timestamp storage** — Windows NTFS stores timestamps natively in UTC. _Why:_ analysts should preserve this baseline when correlating NTFS data with other artifacts. _[GCFA p.~677]_
- **UTC recommendation** — the course recommends standardizing mactime output on UTC. _Why:_ UTC avoids confusion from local time zones and daylight saving time changes. _[GCFA p.~677]_
- **Cross-artifact correlation** — using UTC helps align filesystem timeline records with other forensic artifacts. _Why:_ consistent time bases are necessary for accurate event sequencing. _[GCFA p.~677]_
- **Daylight saving risk** — daylight saving changes can complicate timeline interpretation if output is converted into local time. _Why:_ DST shifts can make event order and correlation harder to validate. _[GCFA p.~677]_
- **Local workstation default behavior** — mactime may convert timestamps to the forensic workstation’s local time zone by default. _Why:_ an analyst can unintentionally alter the displayed time basis if the time zone is not explicitly set. _[GCFA p.~677]_
- **UTC preservation command** — using `-z UTC` prevents local-time conversion and keeps output in UTC. _Why:_ this preserves the native NTFS timestamp basis and improves consistency across evidence sources. _[GCFA p.~677]_
- **`-z` meaning in slide bullets** — the slide identifies `-z` as the option controlling the output time zone. _Why:_ this is the specific switch analysts use to standardize timeline time handling. _[GCFA p.~677]_

### Output And Analysis Use

- **CSV use in class** — the course uses CSV output for mactime timelines. _Why:_ CSV can be imported into many tools and supports scalable analysis workflows. _[GCFA p.~677]_
- **Spreadsheet import** — comma-delimited mactime output can be loaded into spreadsheet software. _Why:_ spreadsheets support sorting, filtering, and manual review of timeline records. _[GCFA p.~677]_
- **Database import** — comma-delimited mactime output can be inserted into a database. _Why:_ databases support larger-scale querying and analysis than manual-only formats. _[GCFA p.~677]_
- **Result-set flexibility** — mactime options let the investigator control how the resulting data is formatted and scoped. _Why:_ output choices affect downstream analysis, scalability, and correlation. _[GCFA p.~677]_
- **Human-readable timeline goal** — the second step of filesystem timeline creation is to make metadata readable and chronologically usable. _Why:_ investigators need accessible timelines to interpret file activity efficiently. _[GCFA p.~677]_

### Plaso Overview

- **Plaso purpose** — Plaso is used to gather time-based events from macOS, Linux, and Windows sources. _Why:_ cross-platform event collection lets an investigator build one timeline from multiple operating systems. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Super timeline creation** — Plaso is presented as the backend engine used to create super timelines. _Why:_ it is the processing foundation for combining many artifact-derived timestamps into one investigative timeline. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Python implementation** — Plaso is described as Python-based. _Why:_ implementation language affects deployment, dependencies, troubleshooting, and extensibility. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Name meaning** — The phrase associated with Plaso is “plaso langar að safna öllu,” indicating the idea of collecting everything. _Why:_ the name reflects the tool’s role as a broad forensic event collector. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Plaso/log2timeline terminology** — The course states that Plaso and log2timeline are used interchangeably in this section. _Why:_ students should treat references to either name as referring to the same timeline-generation ecosystem in this context. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Single reference point** — The tool’s value is framed around giving investigators one place to review many parsed time artifacts. _Why:_ consolidating artifacts reduces context switching and supports faster timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Artifact parser coverage** — The page states that log2timeline/Plaso helps parse many forensic artifacts. _Why:_ parser breadth determines how much system activity can be represented in a super timeline. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Forensic community importance** — The page describes Kristinn Guðjónsson’s project as highly significant to forensic practitioners. _Why:_ widely relied-upon tooling influences common DFIR workflows and training practices. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Ongoing maintenance** — The project is described as being continuously updated by Kristinn Guðjónsson. _Why:_ active maintenance matters because artifacts, applications, and operating systems change over time. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Community contribution request** — The page encourages users with suggestions or comments to contribute to the project. _Why:_ open feedback can improve parser support and forensic usefulness. _[GCFA p.685]_

### Origin And Motivation

- **Creator** — log2timeline was created by Kristinn Guðjónsson. _Why:_ knowing the author helps identify tool provenance and historical context. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Certification context** — log2timeline originated from work connected to Kristinn Guðjónsson’s GCFA Gold Certification discussion at SANS. _Why:_ this ties the tool’s development to forensic education and applied incident response needs. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Prompting need** — SANS Faculty Fellow Rob Lee identified the need to combine many sources of time information into one file. _Why:_ this is the core investigative problem super timelines are meant to solve. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Initial design idea** — Kristinn Guðjónsson concluded that one tool with many options was likely the best approach. _Why:_ this explains why the tool is built as a flexible collector rather than a narrow parser. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Unexpected impact** — The page says the resulting project became more valuable to the forensic community than initially expected. _Why:_ this highlights Plaso/log2timeline as a foundational DFIR timeline tool rather than a minor utility. _[GCFA p.685]_

### Component Flow

- **log2timeline component role** — In the diagram, `log2timeline` is associated with extracting timelines. _Why:_ it identifies the collection stage of the Plaso workflow. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **pinfo component role** — In the diagram, `pinfo` is associated with displaying storage metadata. _Why:_ it identifies the inspection stage for Plaso storage-file metadata. _[GCFA p.685]_

- **Workflow sequence** — The diagram presents `log2timeline`, `pinfo`, and `psort` as distinct Plaso-related utilities with separate responsibilities. _Why:_ separating collection, metadata inspection, and output processing helps analysts choose the right tool for each task. _[GCFA p.685]_

### log2timeline

- **Main frontend** — `log2timeline` is the primary single-machine frontend for the Plaso backend. _Why:_ it is the main command an examiner uses to feed evidence into Plaso on a standalone system. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Event extraction** — `log2timeline` extracts events from input evidence. _Why:_ event extraction is the first step in building a usable forensic timeline. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **File-group input** — `log2timeline` can process a group of files as input. _Why:_ targeted file collections can be parsed without requiring a full disk image. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Mount-point input** — `log2timeline` can process a mounted filesystem location. _Why:_ mounted evidence can be parsed directly as a filesystem source. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Forensic-image input** — `log2timeline` can process a forensic image. _Why:_ full evidence images can be converted into timeline data while preserving a forensic workflow. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Storage-file output** — `log2timeline` saves extracted results into a Plaso storage file. _Why:_ the storage file preserves parsed timeline data for later filtering, sorting, and analysis. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Deferred analysis support** — The Plaso storage file created by `log2timeline` is intended for later processing and examination. _Why:_ collection and analysis can be separated, which helps with repeatability and large evidence sets. _[GCFA p.685]_

### pinfo

- **Storage metadata tool** — `pinfo` prints information from a Plaso storage database file. _Why:_ it lets an analyst inspect how a timeline collection was generated. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Collection timing metadata** — A Plaso storage file records information about when collection occurred. _Why:_ collection timing supports auditability and helps interpret timeline-generation context. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Collection process metadata** — A Plaso storage file records information about how collection occurred. _Why:_ knowing collection parameters helps assess completeness and reliability. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Preprocessing metadata** — A Plaso storage file may include information from preprocessing stages. _Why:_ preprocessing can affect what artifacts were available or how they were interpreted. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Simple reporting function** — `pinfo` is described as a straightforward utility for displaying storage-file information. _Why:_ quick metadata review helps validate a Plaso file before deeper analysis. _[GCFA p.685]_

### psort

- **Post-processing tool** — `psort` is the Plaso utility used after collection to process storage-file contents. _Why:_ collected timeline data generally needs transformation before it is useful to an analyst. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Filtering function** — `psort` can filter events from a Plaso storage file. _Why:_ filtering narrows a large timeline to relevant times, sources, users, or activities. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Sorting function** — `psort` can sort events from a Plaso storage file. _Why:_ chronological ordering is central to reconstructing activity. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Processing function** — `psort` can process Plaso storage-file data. _Why:_ processing converts stored event records into forms suited for investigation. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Tagging function** — `psort` supports tagging of storage-file events. _Why:_ tags help mark, categorize, and track relevant events during analysis. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Output generation** — `psort` is used to produce usable output from a Plaso storage file. _Why:_ the native storage format is not meant for direct human review. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Non-human-readable storage** — The Plaso storage format is described as not human-readable. _Why:_ analysts usually need `psort` or another compatible processor to review results meaningfully. _[GCFA p.685]_
- **Need for post-processing** — Because the storage file is not directly readable by people, running `psort` is typically necessary. _Why:_ this step turns raw Plaso storage into analyst-consumable timeline output. _[GCFA p.685]_

### Windows Parser Definitions

- **`bencode` parser** — parses files encoded with the bencode format. _Why:_ bencoded data appears in some application artifacts and must be decoded before timeline use. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`bencode_transmission` parser** — parses bencoded files associated with Transmission. _Why:_ Transmission artifacts can reveal torrent-related user activity or downloaded content. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`bencode_utorrent` parser** — parses bencoded files associated with uTorrent. _Why:_ uTorrent artifacts can expose peer-to-peer download activity and related file acquisition. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`custom_destinations` parser** — parses files matching `*.customDestinations-ms`. _Why:_ custom destination Jump List files can record application-specific recent destinations and user activity. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`esedb` parser** — parses Extensible Storage Engine database files. _Why:_ ESE databases back multiple Windows artifacts, so ESE parsing broadens timeline coverage. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`filestat` parser** — parses filesystem stat metadata. _Why:_ file metadata supplies timestamp and attribute facts for filesystem timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`hachoir` parser** — uses Hachoir as the underlying parsing wrapper. _Why:_ wrapper parsers allow Plaso to incorporate parsing capabilities from external libraries. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`lnk` parser** — parses Windows Shortcut files. _Why:_ LNK files can show targets, file interaction, and paths relevant to user or attacker activity. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`mcafee_protection` parser** — parses McAfee AV Access Protection log files. _Why:_ antivirus protection logs may identify blocked, detected, or suspicious activity. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`olecf_document_summary` parser** — parses the `DocumentSummaryInformation` stream inside OLE Compound File data. _Why:_ this stream can contain document metadata useful for attribution, document handling, and timeline context. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`olecf_summary` parser** — parses the `SummaryInformation` stream inside OLE Compound File data. _Why:_ summary metadata can expose document properties and timestamps relevant to file provenance. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`onedrive_log` parser** — parses OneDrive log files. _Why:_ OneDrive logs can reveal cloud synchronization and account-linked file activity. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`openxml` parser** — parses OpenXML/OXML files. _Why:_ OpenXML parsing helps extract metadata from modern Office-style document containers. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`pe` parser** — parses Portable Executable files. _Why:_ PE parsing helps collect executable metadata that may support malware triage or execution analysis. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`powershell_transcript` parser** — parses PowerShell transcript events. _Why:_ transcript records can preserve command activity directly relevant to attacker actions. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`prefetch` parser** — parses Windows Prefetch files. _Why:_ Prefetch artifacts help establish whether and when executables ran. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`recycle_bin` parser** — parses Windows `$Recycle.Bin` `$I` metadata files. _Why:_ `$I` files preserve deletion-related metadata such as original path and deletion information. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`skydrive_log` parser** — parses OneDrive or SkyDrive log files. _Why:_ these logs can expose cloud-storage synchronization events on Windows systems. _[GCFA p.686]_
- **`skydrive_log_error` parser** — parses OneDrive or SkyDrive error log files. _Why:_ sync errors can still document attempted cloud activity and operational context. _[GCFA p.686]_

## Page 687

### Plaso Parser Modules

- **sqlite parser** — Plaso includes a parser named `sqlite` for reading SQLite database files. _Why:_ SQLite databases commonly store application history and user activity artifacts. _[GCFA p.687]_

- **symantec_scanlog parser** — Plaso includes a parser named `symantec_scanlog` for Symantec Anti-Virus log files. _Why:_ Antivirus logs can record malware detections, scan activity, quarantines, and security-relevant timestamps. _[GCFA p.687]_

- **winevt parser** — Plaso includes a parser named `winevt` for legacy Windows Event Log files with the `EVT` format. _Why:_ EVT files preserve event records on older Windows systems and can support timeline reconstruction. _[GCFA p.687]_

- **winevtx parser** — Plaso includes a parser named `winevtx` for Windows XML Event Log files with the `EVTX` format. _Why:_ EVTX logs are a major Windows evidence source for logons, process activity, service changes, PowerShell activity, and many other events. _[GCFA p.687]_

- **windefender_history parser** — Plaso includes a parser named `windefender_history` for Windows Defender scan `DetectionHistory` data. _Why:_ Defender history can show detected threats, remediation events, and timestamps tied to malware investigation. _[GCFA p.687]_

- **winfirewall parser** — Plaso includes a parser named `winfirewall` for Windows Firewall log files. _Why:_ Firewall logs can reveal allowed or blocked network connections useful for intrusion scoping. _[GCFA p.687]_

- **winiis parser** — Plaso includes a parser named `winiis` for Microsoft IIS log files. _Why:_ IIS logs can document web requests, client IPs, response codes, user agents, and activity relevant to web compromise investigations. _[GCFA p.687]_

- **winjob parser** — Plaso includes a parser named `winjob` for Windows Scheduled Task job files, including At-job files. _Why:_ Scheduled tasks are a common persistence and execution mechanism, so job files can expose attacker-created automation. _[GCFA p.687]_

- **winreg parser** — Plaso includes a parser named `winreg` for Windows NT Registry hive files in `REGF` format. _Why:_ Registry data contains configuration, execution traces, persistence keys, user activity, and system state evidence. _[GCFA p.687]_

- **google_drive parser** — Plaso includes a parser named `google_drive` for Google Drive SQLite database files. _Why:_ Google Drive databases can preserve cloud-sync activity, file metadata, and user interaction evidence. _[GCFA p.687]_

- **Plaso Registry parsing focus** — Log2timeline/Plaso is specifically strong at extracting timeline evidence from Windows Registry hive files. _Why:_ Registry hives contain many high-value user and system activity artifacts for Windows investigations. _[GCFA p.688]_
- **Windows Registry evidentiary value** — Windows Registry files are described as especially rich sources of forensic evidence. _Why:_ Registry data can preserve user actions, execution traces, device use, and configuration history. _[GCFA p.688]_
- **NTUSER.DAT evidentiary value** — The NTUSER.DAT hive is singled out as a particularly important Registry hive for forensic evidence. _Why:_ NTUSER.DAT stores user-specific activity artifacts, making it central to attributing actions to an account. _[GCFA p.688]_
- **Shellbag folder history** — Shellbag data records evidence related to folders a user opened or browsed. _Why:_ Folder interaction history can prove user awareness of locations, mounted media, or suspicious directories. _[GCFA p.688]_
- **RecentDocs** — RecentDocs is identified as evidence of files opened by a user. _Why:_ Recently accessed document artifacts help reconstruct user activity and file interaction. _[GCFA p.688]_
- **Open/SaveMRU lists** — Open/SaveMRU artifacts record file or folder selections made through open/save dialogs. _Why:_ These MRU lists can show paths and files a user interacted with even when the original files are gone. _[GCFA p.688]_

- **Execution-evidence category** — AppCompatCache, UserAssist, RunMRU, and related artifacts are presented as execution-evidence additions. _Why:_ These Registry artifacts help identify programs that likely ran or were invoked. _[GCFA p.688]_
- **Combined Registry parsers** — The large number of Registry parsers/plugins makes Log2timeline/Plaso a strong tool for Windows forensic collection. _Why:_ Broad parser coverage reduces missed Registry-based timeline evidence. _[GCFA p.688]_
- **Windows operating system target** — The page frames these Plaso Registry parsers as useful when run against Windows operating systems. _Why:_ The listed parsers target Windows-specific Registry artifacts. _[GCFA p.688]_

## Page 689

### Plaso Windows Registry Parsers

- **mstsc_rdp_mru parser** — `mstsc_rdp_mru` extracts Terminal Server Client most-recently-used Registry entries. _Why:_ RDP MRU data can identify remote systems a user connected to or attempted to access. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **network_drives parser** — `network_drives` processes Windows Registry data describing mapped or remembered network drives. _Why:_ Network drive artifacts can show access to shared resources and lateral movement paths. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **networks parser** — `networks` parses Windows NetworkList Registry information. _Why:_ NetworkList data can associate a host with previously connected networks and connection context. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **userassist parser** — `userassist` extracts UserAssist Registry artifacts. _Why:_ UserAssist entries can help reconstruct GUI-launched program execution by user profile. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **windows_boot_execute parser** — `windows_boot_execute` parses Registry values related to boot-time execution. _Why:_ Boot execution locations can reveal persistence or startup behavior before normal user activity. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **windows_boot_verify parser** — `windows_boot_verify` processes Windows boot-verification Registry data. _Why:_ Boot verification artifacts can support analysis of system startup state and boot-related configuration. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **windows_run parser** — `windows_run` extracts Run and RunOnce Registry entries. _Why:_ Run and RunOnce keys are common locations for legitimate startup items and malware persistence. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **windows_sam_users parser** — `windows_sam_users` parses Security Accounts Manager user Registry data. _Why:_ SAM user artifacts can identify local accounts relevant to authentication, privilege use, and compromise scope. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **windows_services parser** — `windows_services` extracts Registry data for Windows services and drivers. _Why:_ Services and drivers are frequent persistence and privilege mechanisms, including for malicious code. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **windows_shutdown parser** — `windows_shutdown` parses Registry data recording the most recent Windows shutdown. _Why:_ Last-shutdown data helps anchor timelines and identify system power-state transitions. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **windows_task_cache parser** — `windows_task_cache` processes Task Scheduler cache Registry data. _Why:_ Scheduled task cache entries can expose task-based persistence and execution history. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **windows_timezone parser** — `windows_timezone` extracts Windows time zone Registry configuration. _Why:_ Time zone context is required to normalize event times accurately during timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **windows_typed_urls parser** — `windows_typed_urls` parses Windows Explorer typed URL Registry data. _Why:_ Typed URL artifacts can show user-entered locations or web destinations. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **windows_usb_devices parser** — `windows_usb_devices` extracts Windows USB device Registry artifacts. _Why:_ USB device records help identify removable or attached hardware used on the system. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **windows_usbstor_devices parser** — `windows_usbstor_devices` parses USBStor Registry data from the Windows USB Plug and Play Manager. _Why:_ USBStor entries can identify USB storage devices connected to the host. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **windows_version parser** — `windows_version` extracts Windows product/version Registry data. _Why:_ OS version context affects artifact interpretation, parser expectations, and incident scope. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **winlogon parser** — `winlogon` parses Windows logon Registry data. _Why:_ Winlogon configuration can reveal authentication-related settings and possible logon persistence mechanisms. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **winrar_mru parser** — `winrar_mru` extracts WinRAR history Registry artifacts. _Why:_ WinRAR MRU entries can identify archives recently opened or handled by a user. _[GCFA p.689]_
- **winreg_default parser** — `winreg_default` provides generic parsing for Windows Registry data. _Why:_ A default Registry parser preserves broader Registry-derived timeline coverage beyond specialized parser categories. _[GCFA p.689]_

### Linux, Android, And Other Parser Definitions

- **android_app_usage** — parses Android `usage-history.xml` application-use history files. _Why:_ this artifact can show when Android apps were used. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **android_calls** — parses Android call-log SQLite databases. _Why:_ call records can identify communication events and contacts over time. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **android_sms** — parses Android SMS SQLite databases. _Why:_ text-message records can provide message timing and communication context. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **bencode** — parses files encoded with the bencode format. _Why:_ bencoded artifacts may hold application state or transfer metadata. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **bencode_transmission** — parses Transmission BitTorrent bencoded files. _Why:_ Transmission artifacts can reveal torrent-related activity. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **bencode_utorrent** — parses uTorrent bencoded files. _Why:_ uTorrent artifacts can expose peer-to-peer transfer history. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **filestat** — parses filesystem stat metadata. _Why:_ stat information supplies core file timestamps and attributes for timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **google_drive** — parses Google Drive SQLite databases. _Why:_ these databases can show cloud-drive synchronization and file activity. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **openxml** — parses OpenXML/OXML document files. _Why:_ OpenXML files can contain document metadata useful for attribution and timing. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **pls_recall** — parses PL-SQL Recall files. _Why:_ database interaction artifacts may help reconstruct developer or administrator activity. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **popularity_contest** — parses popularity-contest log files. _Why:_ these logs can help infer package usage on Linux systems. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **selinux** — parses SELinux audit logs. _Why:_ SELinux events can show policy enforcement, denials, and access attempts. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **syslog** — parses syslog records. _Why:_ syslog is a central event source for Linux/Unix host activity. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **skype** — parses Skype SQLite databases. _Why:_ Skype databases can preserve chat, call, and account activity. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **utmp** — parses Linux/Unix UTMP records. _Why:_ UTMP data supports logon, logoff, and session reconstruction. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **utmpx** — parses UTMPX records. _Why:_ UTMPX provides login-session evidence in systems using the extended format. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **xchatlog** — parses XChat log files. _Why:_ chat logs can provide communication content and timestamps. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **xchatscrollback** — parses XChat scrollback files. _Why:_ scrollback can preserve conversational history even when separate logs are absent. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **zeitgeist** — parses Zeitgeist activity SQLite databases. _Why:_ Zeitgeist records can reveal user activity and application interaction on Linux desktops. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **mactime** — parses SleuthKit mactime bodyfile data. _Why:_ this allows existing bodyfile timelines to be consumed in Plaso processing. _[GCFA p.691]_
- **pcap** — parses packet-capture files. _Why:_ PCAP support lets network traffic evidence contribute to timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.691]_

- **Timezone difficulty** — timezone handling is identified as a difficult but necessary part of forensic work. _Why:_ incorrect timezone treatment can misplace events and distort investigative conclusions. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **Timezone importance for reporting** — forensic reporting requires understanding how tools handle timezone values. _Why:_ reported event times must be explainable and defensible. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **Plaso timezone stages** — Plaso has timezone handling considerations during both input and output stages. _Why:_ collection-time normalization and final display-time choices are separate concerns. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **log2timeline as input stage** — log2timeline is the Plaso input-stage tool. _Why:_ timezone settings given to log2timeline affect how source artifacts are interpreted during ingestion. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **`--timezone <TZ>` input-stage relevance** — the `--timezone <TZ>` option matters specifically during input processing. _Why:_ local-time artifacts may need conversion before being merged with UTC-based artifacts. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **Investigated-system timezone** — `--timezone <TZ>` should represent the timezone configured on the examined computer. _Why:_ this value is used to interpret source timestamps correctly. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **Not output timezone** — `--timezone <TZ>` is not meant to specify the desired display or reporting timezone. _Why:_ confusing input timezone with output timezone can shift events incorrectly. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **Local-time artifacts** — some forensic artifacts store timestamps using local time rather than UTC. _Why:_ these artifacts require timezone context before they can be correlated accurately. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **UTC artifacts** — other artifacts collected by log2timeline store timestamps in UTC. _Why:_ mixed timestamp storage formats require normalization into a consistent timeline. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **Local-time adjustment need** — log2timeline must know the local timezone offset to adjust certain local-time artifacts. _Why:_ otherwise local-time events may not align with UTC-stored events. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **Artifact-aware conversion** — log2timeline knows that some artifacts need timezone adjustment. _Why:_ parser-level awareness reduces manual timestamp correction work. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **Manual timezone value use** — when supplied, the timezone value guides adjustment for applicable artifacts. _Why:_ this supports consistent event comparison across artifact sources. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **Forensic image preprocessing** — when a forensic image is used as the source, log2timeline usually runs preprocessing. _Why:_ preprocessing can collect system metadata before artifact parsing. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **Mounted-device preprocessing** — when a mounted device is used as the source, log2timeline also typically runs preprocessing. _Why:_ mounted evidence may expose configuration data needed for accurate parsing. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **Automatic timezone collection** — the preprocessor attempts to collect timezone information automatically. _Why:_ automatic discovery can remove the need for a manually supplied `--timezone` value. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **Discovered timezone application** — if preprocessing finds a timezone, log2timeline uses that value where relevant. _Why:_ applicable local-time artifacts can then be normalized using the discovered system setting. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **Operating system detection** — preprocessing also attempts to identify the operating system type. _Why:_ knowing the OS helps Plaso select appropriate parsing behavior for the evidence. _[GCFA p.~693]_
- **OS-dependent selection** — if the operating system type can be determined, log2timeline will choose processing behavior based on that result. _Why:_ OS-specific parsing improves artifact interpretation accuracy. _[GCFA p.~693]_

## Page 696

### Disk Image Processing

- **Direct image parsing preference** — When a full disk image is available, the recommended workflow is to have `log2timeline` process the image file itself instead of analyzing the image through a mounted directory. _Why:_ direct parsing reduces evidence-access differences introduced by the analyst system’s mount mechanism. _[GCFA p.~696]_

- **Mount-point processing drawback** — Mounting an image can change which files or metadata objects are visible to tools, depending on the driver or method used to mount the image. _Why:_ incomplete exposure of evidence can cause timeline generation to miss important artifacts. _[GCFA p.~696]_

- **Driver-dependent file visibility** — The set of files presented from a mounted image is not guaranteed to be identical across mounting drivers. _Why:_ forensic results may vary based on tooling rather than evidence content. _[GCFA p.~696]_

- **NTFS mounted-image limitation** — In an NTFS image mounted to a filesystem path, the `$MFT` may not be visible to `log2timeline`. _Why:_ if the Master File Table is hidden from the parser, filesystem metadata timeline coverage can be incomplete. _[GCFA p.~696]_

- **`$MFT` artifact role** — `$MFT` refers to the NTFS Master File Table. _Why:_ it is a central NTFS metadata source used for file timeline reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~696]_

- **`log2timeline` image target recommendation** — The preferred `log2timeline` target is the complete disk image rather than a mounted mount point when the image file is available. _Why:_ the full image gives the parser access to evidence through forensic image-handling layers instead of relying on mounted filesystem presentation. _[GCFA p.~696]_

### dfVFS

- **dfVFS image parsing support** — Disk image parsing for this workflow is supplied through the Digital Forensics Virtual File System toolset, abbreviated `dfVFS`. _Why:_ `dfVFS` is the component that enables forensic tools to read storage media formats directly. _[GCFA p.~696]_

- **Digital Forensics Virtual File System name** — `dfVFS` expands to Digital Forensics Virtual File System. _Why:_ knowing the full name identifies the underlying framework responsible for virtualized evidence access. _[GCFA p.~696]_

- **dfVFS supported media formats** — The current list of storage media file types supported by `dfVFS` should be checked in the dfVFS documentation. _Why:_ supported image formats can change, so tool capability should be verified against the maintained documentation. _[GCFA p.~696]_

- **dfVFS documentation URL** — The courseware points to `https://for508.com/8vhmg` for dfVFS documentation. _Why:_ this link is the cited reference for checking current supported storage media file types. _[GCFA p.~696]_

### Targeted Timeline Strategy

- **Timeline-analysis approaches** — analysts commonly choose between building a broad super timeline and building narrower mini-timelines. _Why:_ the chosen approach affects collection scope, processing time, and risk of missing artifacts. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **All-inclusive super timeline** — the broad approach runs `log2timeline` across an entire disk image. _Why:_ this captures the widest set of supported timeline evidence before filtering. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **All-inclusive artifact extraction** — a full `log2timeline` run attempts to extract every supported timestamp and artifact from the disk image. _Why:_ this maximizes artifact coverage for later analysis. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **Post-collection filtering** — in the all-inclusive workflow, analysts filter and investigate after the complete dataset has already been collected. _Why:_ this separates evidence acquisition from later analytical narrowing. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **Common meaning of super timeline** — many practitioners use “super timeline” to mean the complete dataset produced by broad `log2timeline` collection. _Why:_ the term can imply a full-image, all-supported-artifact workflow. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **Deriving smaller timelines** — a larger all-inclusive timeline can be subsetted later into narrower timelines. _Why:_ broad collection preserves flexibility for later pivots. _[GCFA p.~698]_

### Targeted Collection

- **Targeted timeline approach** — the narrower workflow collects only files or artifacts relevant to the analyst’s immediate needs. _Why:_ this reduces scope and speeds up initial analysis. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **Targeted acquisition focus** — targeted collection is file-selective rather than whole-disk exhaustive. _Why:_ the analyst intentionally limits evidence ingestion to likely-relevant sources. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **Advanced log2timeline usage** — targeted-timeline practitioners often rely on more advanced `log2timeline` capabilities. _Why:_ selective collection requires more precise control over parsing behavior. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **Use with external tools** — targeted workflows may combine `log2timeline` with other utilities. _Why:_ specialized tools can gather or parse focused evidence more quickly. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **One-off scripts** — ad hoc scripts are identified as tools that may support targeted collection. _Why:_ custom scripting helps collect or prepare case-specific artifacts. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **Dedicated parsing tools** — specialized parsers are identified as another companion tool category for targeted timelines. _Why:_ purpose-built parsers can extract focused artifacts without a full super-timeline run. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **Targeted collection advantage** — speed is the main benefit of collecting only selected evidence. _Why:_ faster processing lets investigators begin analysis earlier. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **Full-image runtime estimate** — running `log2timeline` broadly against a large disk can take about `12-24 hours`. _Why:_ this time cost may delay investigative triage and response. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **Targeted runtime estimate** — a targeted timeline commonly takes about `5-30 minutes`. _Why:_ this makes targeted timelines useful for rapid early-case analysis. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **Targeted collection disadvantage** — narrow timelines can omit an important artifact. _Why:_ reduced scope creates evidentiary blind spots. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **Early-analysis tradeoff** — the page frames early analytical progress as usually worth the limited risk of missing something in targeted collection. _Why:_ rapid initial understanding can guide later evidence expansion. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **Adding artifacts later** — analysts can often return and add more artifacts after learning more about the case and available data. _Why:_ targeted timelines can be expanded iteratively instead of remaining fixed. _[GCFA p.~698]_
- **log2timeline targeted support** — `log2timeline.py` includes multiple capabilities intended to help create targeted timelines. _Why:_ targeted collection is directly supported by the tool rather than requiring only external workarounds. _[GCFA p.~698]_

- **Filter-file speed benefit** — using a filter file is described as a fast way to process targeted artifacts. _Why:_ speed matters when full-disk parsing would be unnecessarily broad or time-consuming. _[GCFA p.~699]_

- **Full-disk use case for filter files** — file filtering is especially useful when the source is a complete disk but the examiner only wants selected files parsed. _Why:_ this avoids processing the whole disk when only known high-value artifacts are needed. _[GCFA p.~699]_

- **Filter files avoid pre-collection** — a filter file can remove the need to first build a separate triage file collection before timeline generation. _Why:_ this can simplify workflow by letting log2timeline target files directly from the full disk source. _[GCFA p.~699]_

- **Parser limiting for performance** — Selecting a defined parser set is an older log2timeline method for reducing processing time by avoiding unnecessary parsers. _Why:_ parser scope directly affects timeline creation speed and evidence coverage. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Built-in parser presets** — log2timeline distributions include predefined parser groups that can be selected instead of manually naming every parser. _Why:_ presets make common evidence-processing profiles easier to invoke consistently. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Mixed parser syntax** — The command line can combine preset names and individual parser names in one comma-separated parser specification. _Why:_ this allows targeted customization without creating a new preset file. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Parser inclusion behavior** — Individual parsers can be added alongside preset parser groups in the parser list. _Why:_ investigators can expand a preset when a specific artifact type is needed. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Parser exclusion behavior** — A parser name prefixed with `!` is removed from the selected parser set. _Why:_ exclusions let analysts avoid slow, irrelevant, or problematic parsers while still using a broad preset. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Example command** — `log2timeline.py --parsers "win7,!filestat" --storage-file out.plaso <target>` runs log2timeline with a Windows preset while writing results to `out.plaso`. _Why:_ the example shows the exact parser-selection and output-database syntax. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Example parser preset** — The command uses the `win7` parser preset. _Why:_ this determines the baseline set of artifact parsers applied to the target. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Example parser exclusion** — The command removes `filestat` from the selected `win7` parser set. _Why:_ this demonstrates the practical effect of the `!` exclusion operator. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Storage-file option** — `--storage-file out.plaso` specifies `out.plaso` as the Plaso storage file. _Why:_ this identifies where parsed timeline data will be saved. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Target placeholder** — `<target>` represents the evidence source supplied to log2timeline. _Why:_ parser choices apply to whatever image, directory, or artifact source is passed as the target. _[GCFA p.700]_

### Preset Discovery and Documentation

- **Parser listing command** — `--parsers list` displays the parsers and presets available in the installed log2timeline environment. _Why:_ available parser names can vary by Plaso version and installation. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Plaso parser documentation link** — `https://for508.com/i9k8v` is provided as a reference for Plaso parser-related documentation. _Why:_ it gives analysts a source for details beyond the slide. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Plaso plugin and preset documentation link** — `https://for508.com/s0zj1` is provided as another Plaso developer-documentation reference. _Why:_ parser behavior, plugin details, and preset structure may require external documentation. _[GCFA p.700]_

### Windows Preset Behavior

- **`win7` naming caveat** — The `win7` preset applies to Windows Vista and later systems, not only Windows 7. _Why:_ using the name literally could cause analysts to avoid the correct preset for newer Windows versions. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Windows artifact format shift** — Many Windows artifact formats changed between Windows XP and Windows Vista. _Why:_ this explains why XP-era and Vista-or-newer parser groupings differ. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **`win7` includes `win_gen`** — The `win7` preset references the `win_gen` preset. _Why:_ selecting `win7` also brings in broadly applicable Windows parsers. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **`winxp` includes `win_gen`** — The `winxp` preset references the `win_gen` preset. _Why:_ XP-focused parsing still includes parsers common across Windows versions. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **`win_gen` purpose** — `win_gen` contains parsers for Windows artifacts that are generally stable across Windows versions. _Why:_ shared parsers reduce duplication between Windows preset definitions. _[GCFA p.700]_

### Automatic Preset Selection

- **No explicit parser list behavior** — If no parser or preset is specified, log2timeline may infer the operating system of the evidence source. _Why:_ the tool can silently narrow parser coverage based on its OS estimate. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Automatic preset application** — After estimating the OS, log2timeline may apply an appropriate preset automatically. _Why:_ analysts need to know when parser selection is being handled implicitly. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Windows 10 image example** — A Windows 10 full disk image may be processed with only the `win7` preset. _Why:_ this illustrates that the `win7` preset is used for modern Windows evidence. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Efficiency benefit** — Automatic use of a matching preset can be desirable because it avoids running irrelevant parsers. _Why:_ focused parsing can reduce processing time. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **All-parser limitation** — At the time described, log2timeline has no built-in option to force every file through every available parser when it can infer the OS type. _Why:_ analysts seeking maximum parser coverage must use another method. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Custom all-parser workaround** — A custom preset can be created that enumerates all parsers. _Why:_ this provides a way to override OS-based parser narrowing. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Preset file name** — Parser preset definitions are stored in `presets.yaml`. _Why:_ editing or replacing this file changes available preset definitions. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **Typical preset file path** — On a typical Linux or Docker installation, `presets.yaml` is located under `/usr/share/plaso`. _Why:_ this is the expected place to inspect or modify preset definitions. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **FOR508 custom preset file** — The FOR508 cloud share contains a modified `presets.yaml` in the `Tooling` directory. _Why:_ course users have access to a prepared preset configuration. _[GCFA p.700]_
- **FOR508 `all_parsers` preset** — The FOR508 custom preset file includes an `all_parsers` preset. _Why:_ it supports broad parser coverage when default log2timeline behavior would otherwise be selective. _[GCFA p.700]_

## Page 701

### log2timeline.py Filter-File Purpose

- **`log2timeline.py` filter files** — filter files restrict parsing to selected files or directories instead of processing everything in the source. _Why:_ this enables targeted timeline creation from large evidence sets. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Targeted input selection** — a filter file identifies which paths should be parsed and causes other paths to be ignored. _Why:_ this reduces noise and avoids spending time on irrelevant filesystem content. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Fast extraction workflow** — filtering lets an analyst pull only artifacts of interest from a data source. _Why:_ this supports rapid investigative triage when specific questions must be answered quickly. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Disk image suitability** — filter files are especially useful when processing full disk images. _Why:_ disk images contain many unrelated files, and filtering can greatly reduce processing time. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Filesystem skipping behavior** — log2timeline can bypass most unrelated files and folders when a filter is supplied. _Why:_ skipping irrelevant content can accelerate processing by orders of magnitude. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Incident-response use case** — filter files should be considered when an analyst needs a quick answer about a system. _Why:_ speed may matter more than exhaustive collection during early response or triage. _[GCFA p.~701]_

### Filter-File Formats

- **Legacy text filter format** — log2timeline supports an older plain-text filter-file syntax. _Why:_ existing workflows and examples may still use this format. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **YAML filter format** — log2timeline also supports a newer YAML-based filter-file syntax. _Why:_ YAML enables richer filter definitions than the legacy text format. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Text filter line structure** — the text format uses one path expression per line. _Why:_ each line independently defines a file or path target for parsing. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Text filter path separator** — text-format paths separate path components with forward slashes. _Why:_ analysts must format paths correctly for the filter to match intended files. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Regular-expression support** — both supported filter formats can use basic regular expressions. _Why:_ regex matching allows one filter entry to cover multiple matching paths. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Wildcard support** — both supported filter formats can use wildcards. _Why:_ wildcard matching supports broader artifact targeting without listing every exact path. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Path recursion support** — both supported filter formats can express recursive path matching. _Why:_ recursive matching helps collect artifacts from variable-depth directory structures. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Path-variable support** — both supported filter formats can use path variables. _Why:_ variables allow filters to adapt to system-specific locations. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Plaso preprocessing variables** — path expansion variables can come from Plaso preprocessing modules. _Why:_ preprocessing-derived values such as system root paths make filters portable across hosts. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **`{systemroot}` variable** — `{systemroot}` is shown as an example of a path expansion variable. _Why:_ this variable lets a filter refer to the Windows installation directory without hardcoding a drive path. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **YAML-only exclusion filters** — exclusion filters are supported only in YAML filter files. _Why:_ analysts needing explicit include and exclude logic must use YAML rather than the legacy text format. _[GCFA p.~701]_

### Command Examples

- **Text filter invocation** — `log2timeline.py -f filter_windows.txt` runs log2timeline with a legacy text filter file. _Why:_ the `-f` option supplies the path filter used to limit parsing. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **YAML filter invocation** — `log2timeline.py -f filter_windows.yaml` runs log2timeline with a YAML filter file. _Why:_ this demonstrates that the same `-f` option is used for YAML-based filtering. _[GCFA p.~701]_

### Legacy Text Filter: Windows Registry Entries

- **Registry section comment** — `# Windows Registry files.` labels a group of registry-related filter paths. _Why:_ comments document the artifact category targeted by the following entries. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **User hive path pattern** — `/(Users|Documents And Settings)/.+/NTUSER[.]DAT` targets `NTUSER.DAT` files under either `Users` or `Documents And Settings`. _Why:_ this collects per-user registry hives across modern and older Windows profile layouts. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Modern UsrClass.dat pattern** — `/Users/.+/AppData/Local/Microsoft/Windows/UsrClass[.]dat` targets `UsrClass.dat` under each user profile’s local AppData path. _Why:_ this collects per-user shell and COM-related registry data. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Legacy UsrClass.dat pattern** — `/Documents And Settings/.+/Local Settings/Application Data/Microsoft/Windows/UsrClass[.]dat` targets `UsrClass.dat` in the older Windows profile layout. _Why:_ this keeps the filter compatible with legacy Windows systems. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **System registry hive pattern** — `{systemroot}/System32/config/(SAM|SOFTWARE|SECURITY|SYSTEM)` targets the `SAM`, `SOFTWARE`, `SECURITY`, and `SYSTEM` hives under the Windows config directory. _Why:_ these hives contain core system, account, security, and configuration evidence. _[GCFA p.~701]_

### Legacy Text Filter: Recent File Activity

- **Recent activity section comment** — `# Recent file activity.` labels shortcut artifacts associated with recently accessed files. _Why:_ recent-file artifacts help reconstruct user activity. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Modern Windows Recent LNK pattern** — `/Users/.+/AppData/Roaming/Microsoft/Windows/Recent/.+[.]lnk` targets Recent-folder shortcut files for user profiles under `Users`. _Why:_ these shortcuts can show files a user opened or interacted with. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Microsoft Office Recent LNK pattern** — `/Users/.+/AppData/Roaming/Microsoft/Office/Recent/.+[.]lnk` targets Office recent-document shortcut files. _Why:_ Office Recent artifacts can identify documents accessed through Microsoft Office applications. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Legacy Recent LNK pattern** — `/Documents And Settings/.+/Recent/.+[.]lnk` targets Recent-folder shortcuts in older Windows profile paths. _Why:_ this preserves artifact coverage for pre-`Users` profile layouts. _[GCFA p.~701]_

### Legacy Text Filter: Jump Lists

- **Jump List section comment** — `# Jump List files.` labels filter entries for Windows Jump List artifacts. _Why:_ Jump Lists can record application usage and file access. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **AutomaticDestinations pattern** — `/Users/.+/AppData/Roaming/Microsoft/Windows/Recent/Automaticdestinations/.+[.]automaticDestinations-ms` targets automatic Jump List files. _Why:_ automatic Jump Lists can expose files and destinations associated with application activity. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **CustomDestinations pattern** — `/Users/.+/AppData/Roaming/Microsoft/Windows/Recent/Customdestinations/.+[.]customDestinations-ms` targets custom Jump List files. _Why:_ custom Jump Lists can preserve user- or application-defined destination records. _[GCFA p.~701]_

### Legacy Text Filter: Windows Event Logs

- **Event log section comment** — `# Windows Event Logs.` labels filter entries for Windows log files. _Why:_ event logs are key sources for system, security, and application activity timelines. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **EVTX pattern** — `{systemroot}/System32/winevt/Logs/.+[.]evtx` targets modern Windows Event Log files. _Why:_ `.evtx` logs commonly contain high-value incident-response events. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **EVT pattern** — `{systemroot}/System32/config/.+[.]evt` targets legacy Windows event log files. _Why:_ `.evt` support keeps filtering useful for older Windows systems. _[GCFA p.~701]_

### Legacy Text Filter: Setup and Miscellaneous Logs

- **Log file section comment** — `# Various log files.` labels setup-related log artifacts. _Why:_ setup logs can reveal driver, device, and installation activity. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **SetupAPI INF log pattern** — `{systemroot}/inf/setupapi[.].+[.]log` targets SetupAPI logs under the Windows `inf` directory. _Why:_ these logs can document hardware and driver installation events. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Root SetupAPI log pattern** — `{systemroot}/setupapi.log` targets the SetupAPI log at the Windows root. _Why:_ this captures setup activity from systems that use the older log location. _[GCFA p.~701]_

### Text Filter Regex Explanation

- **Example NTUSER.DAT expression** — `/(Users|Documents And Settings)/.+/NTUSER.DAT` is presented as a sample text-filter entry. _Why:_ it illustrates how one regex can match user hives across multiple profile-root names. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Alternation in profile root** — `(Users|Documents And Settings)` means the path may contain either `Users` or `Documents And Settings` at that position. _Why:_ this allows one filter line to cover both newer and older Windows profile structures. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Arbitrary subfolder match** — `.+` in the NTUSER.DAT example represents one or more characters for the user-profile subdirectory. _Why:_ this lets the filter match every user account name without listing them individually. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Specific hive filename match** — the NTUSER.DAT example is intended to match files named `NTUSER.DAT`. _Why:_ this ensures Plaso parses each user’s primary registry hive. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Per-user hive collection outcome** — the NTUSER.DAT example causes Plaso to parse `NTUSER.DAT` for all user profiles on the system. _Why:_ user hives are central to reconstructing user-specific activity and configuration. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Second example event-log expression** — `{systemroot}/winevt/Logs/.+evtx` is shown as another filter-entry example. _Why:_ it demonstrates combining a path variable with a regex-style event-log filename match. _[GCFA p.~701]_

### YAML Filter Structure

- **YAML document separator** — `---` separates YAML filter entries. _Why:_ each YAML document can describe a distinct filter rule group. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Registry YAML description** — `description: Windows Registry files.` names the YAML rule group for registry artifacts. _Why:_ descriptions make filter intent clear during review and maintenance. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Registry YAML type** — `type: include` marks the registry YAML rule as an inclusion filter. _Why:_ this tells log2timeline to include matching registry paths. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Registry YAML separator** — `path_separator: '\'` specifies backslash as the path separator for the registry YAML rule. _Why:_ Windows artifact paths conventionally use backslashes. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Registry YAML paths key** — `paths:` introduces the registry paths listed in the YAML rule. _Why:_ this is where the actual target patterns are enumerated. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Recent activity YAML description** — `description: Recent activity files.` names the YAML rule group for recent-file artifacts. _Why:_ this separates recent-activity targeting from registry targeting. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Recent activity YAML type** — `type: include` marks the recent-activity YAML rule as an inclusion filter. _Why:_ matching Recent and Office shortcut files are selected for parsing. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Recent activity YAML separator** — `path_separator: '\'` specifies backslash as the path separator for recent-activity paths. _Why:_ correct separator handling is required for matching Windows-style paths. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **Recent activity YAML paths key** — `paths:` introduces the recent-activity path list. _Why:_ this defines the artifact locations to include for Recent-file analysis. _[GCFA p.~701]_

### YAML Registry Path Entries

- **YAML NTUSER.DAT path** — `*\\Users\\Documents And Settings\\.+\\NTUSER[.]DAT` is listed as a registry include path. _Why:_ it targets user registry hive material according to the shown YAML filter. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **YAML modern UsrClass.dat path** — `*\\Users\\.+\\AppData\\Local\\Microsoft\\Windows\\UsrClass[.]dat` is listed as a registry include path. _Why:_ it targets per-user `UsrClass.dat` hives in modern profile paths. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **YAML legacy UsrClass.dat path** — `*\\Documents And Settings\\.+\\Local Settings\\Application Data\\Microsoft\\Windows\\UsrClass[.]dat` is listed as a registry include path. _Why:_ it targets `UsrClass.dat` in legacy Windows profile layouts. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **YAML system hive path** — `*$SystemRoot\\System32\\config\\(SAM|SOFTWARE|SECURITY|SYSTEM)` is listed as a registry include path. _Why:_ it targets the principal Windows system registry hives. _[GCFA p.~701]_

### YAML Recent Activity Path Entries

- **YAML Windows Recent LNK path** — `*\\Users\\.+\\AppData\\Roaming\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Recent\\.+[.]lnk` is listed as a recent-activity include path. _Why:_ it targets user Recent-folder shortcut artifacts. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **YAML Office Recent LNK path** — `*\\Users\\.+\\AppData\\Roaming\\Microsoft\\Office\\Recent\\.+[.]lnk` is listed as a recent-activity include path. _Why:_ it targets Microsoft Office recent-document shortcuts. _[GCFA p.~701]_
- **YAML legacy Recent LNK path** — `*\\Documents And Settings\\.+\\Recent\\.+[.]lnk` is listed as a recent-activity include path. _Why:_ it targets Recent-folder shortcuts on older Windows profile layouts. _[GCFA p.~701]_

### Text-Based Plaso Filters

- **EVTX include rule behavior** — the referenced filter rule directs Plaso to process EVTX files located below the Windows system-root `winevt\Logs` directory. _Why:_ this defines the event-log collection scope for log2timeline processing. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **`winevt\Logs` target path** — the event-log path shown on the page is `winevt\Logs` under the system root. _Why:_ this is the Windows Event Log directory being selected by the filter. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **`{systemroot}` expansion variable** — `{systemroot}` is a path placeholder used in the filter line. _Why:_ log2timeline can substitute discovered image-specific paths during preprocessing. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **Curly-brace variable syntax** — text-filter path expansion variables are enclosed in `{` and `}`. _Why:_ analysts must use the correct syntax when authoring text-based Plaso filters. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **Disk-image preprocessing substitution** — Plaso replaces expansion variables with path values learned while preprocessing a disk image. _Why:_ preprocessing determines whether symbolic paths resolve to real filesystem locations. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **Expansion mapping reliability warning** — the page states that variable-to-path mapping is not perfectly reliable in practice. _Why:_ missed or incorrect expansion can cause expected artifacts to be skipped. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **Full-path preference** — specifying the complete path is often more dependable than relying on automatic variable discovery. _Why:_ explicit paths reduce filter ambiguity during forensic processing. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **Case-insensitive filter expressions** — expressions in the filter file are evaluated without regard to case. _Why:_ path matching is not broken by Windows capitalization differences. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **Literal special-character syntax** — special characters that should be matched literally are wrapped in square brackets. _Why:_ this prevents regex metacharacters from being interpreted as pattern operators. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **Literal dollar-sign example** — `[$]` is the shown syntax for matching a dollar sign as a literal character. _Why:_ this matters for Windows forensic paths containing `$`, such as NTFS metadata names. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **Text-filter inclusion-only model** — text-based filters define only what log2timeline should include. _Why:_ they are allowlists rather than mixed include/exclude rule sets. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **Implicit exclusion in text filters** — any file or path absent from the text filter is ignored by log2timeline. _Why:_ incomplete filter lists can silently omit important artifacts. _[GCFA p.~702]_

### YAML-Based Filter Files

- **YAML filter purpose** — YAML filter files were added to give analysts more flexible filtering rules. _Why:_ YAML supports richer scoping than the older text format. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **YAML exclusion capability** — YAML-based filters can define exclusion rules. _Why:_ analysts can explicitly suppress unwanted artifacts during parsing. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **YAML include-and-exclude capability** — YAML rules can describe both data to process and data to skip. _Why:_ this enables more precise control over log2timeline workload. _[GCFA p.~702]_

- **YAML `paths` field** — `paths` contains the rule’s path-matching pattern list. _Why:_ this is where the actual filesystem selection criteria are defined. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **YAML event-log exclusion pattern** — the listed path pattern is `%SystemRoot%\\System32\\config\\.+[.]evt`. _Why:_ files matching this expression are excluded from log2timeline processing. _[GCFA p.~702]_

- **YAML regex similarity** — the YAML path expression uses a regex-style pattern similar to the earlier text-filter example. _Why:_ analysts can reuse regex concepts across filter formats. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **`[.]` literal-dot syntax** — the YAML path uses `[.]` to match a period before `evt`. _Why:_ this prevents the dot from acting as a regex wildcard. _[GCFA p.~702]_
- **`.evt` extension target** — the exclusion pattern targets files ending in `.evt`. _Why:_ the example is focused on Windows event-log artifacts. _[GCFA p.~702]_

- **Filter file metadata** — If a filter file was used, the Plaso storage container can include information about it. _Why:_ filters affect scope, so knowing whether one was applied is essential when interpreting missing or present artifacts. _[GCFA p.~706]_
- **Preprocessing information** — The Plaso database can store information collected during preprocessing. _Why:_ preprocessing data can identify system context that influenced parser behavior and event interpretation. _[GCFA p.~706]_
- **Artifact count data** — The Plaso storage container tracks counts for parsed artifact categories. _Why:_ artifact counts help assess coverage and identify whether expected sources were processed. _[GCFA p.~706]_
- **Error information** — The Plaso storage container includes errors generated during processing. _Why:_ parsing errors can explain missing events or incomplete extraction from specific sources. _[GCFA p.~706]_
- **Storage container metadata** — The Plaso storage container includes metadata about the container itself. _Why:_ container metadata supports integrity checks and confirms database format details. _[GCFA p.~706]_
- **Parsed-content validation** — `pinfo.py` reports what was parsed into the database. _Why:_ this helps determine whether the timeline includes the intended forensic sources. _[GCFA p.~706]_
- **Parsing-time validation** — `pinfo.py` reports when parsing occurred. _Why:_ parsing timestamps support chain-of-analysis documentation and later review of workflow timing. _[GCFA p.~706]_
- **Plugin validation** — `pinfo.py` reports which plugins extracted data. _Why:_ knowing the extraction plugins clarifies how specific events entered the timeline. _[GCFA p.~706]_
- **Verbose preprocessing output** — Verbose `pinfo.py` output includes preprocessor data. _Why:_ preprocessor results can affect parser configuration and interpretation of host-specific artifacts. _[GCFA p.~706]_
- **Verbose error output** — Verbose `pinfo.py` output includes extensive error messaging. _Why:_ detailed errors help troubleshoot parser failures or incomplete database creation. _[GCFA p.~706]_
