### NTFS System File MFT Records

- **MFT record 0 · Filename** — record 0 is named `$MFT`. _Why:_ this identifies the primary NTFS metadata file that describes the filesystem’s file records. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 0 · Description** — `$MFT` is the Master File Table, a volume-wide metadata database that accounts for every file on the NTFS volume. _Why:_ the MFT is the central index for locating and interpreting NTFS file and directory metadata. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 1 · Filename** — record 1 is named `$MFTMIRR`. _Why:_ this identifies the special NTFS metadata file used for MFT recovery. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 1 · Description** — `$MFTMIRR` stores a backup of the first four MFT records. _Why:_ these mirrored records can help recover critical filesystem metadata if the primary MFT beginning is damaged. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 2 · Filename** — record 2 is named `$LOGFILE`. _Why:_ this identifies the NTFS transactional log file. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 2 · Description** — `$LOGFILE` contains NTFS transaction log data. _Why:_ transaction records can explain filesystem consistency operations after crashes or unclean shutdowns. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 3 · Filename** — record 3 is named `$VOLUME`. _Why:_ this record stores volume-level NTFS metadata. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 3 · Description** — `$VOLUME` contains the volume label, the NTFS version, and the dirty-status flag. _Why:_ these fields help determine volume identity, filesystem format level, and whether the volume was cleanly closed. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 4 · Filename** — record 4 is named `$ATTRDEF`. _Why:_ this record defines the attribute vocabulary used by the NTFS volume. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 4 · Description** — `$ATTRDEF` stores NTFS attribute definitions. _Why:_ attribute interpretation depends on the definitions present for the NTFS version in use. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 5 · Filename** — record 5 is named `.`. _Why:_ the single-dot name marks the NTFS root directory entry. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 5 · Description** — record 5 represents the root directory of the disk. _Why:_ this is the fixed starting directory for the volume namespace. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 6 · Filename** — record 6 is named `$BITMAP`. _Why:_ this record identifies the NTFS allocation bitmap file. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 6 · Description** — `$BITMAP` records whether each cluster on the volume is allocated or free. _Why:_ cluster allocation state is essential for carving, recovery, and filesystem consistency analysis. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 7 · Filename** — record 7 is named `$BOOT`. _Why:_ this record identifies the NTFS volume boot record file. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 7 · Description** — `$BOOT` contains the volume boot record. _Why:_ boot-record data includes filesystem startup parameters and the pointer needed to locate the MFT. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 8 · Filename** — record 8 is named `$BADCLUS`. _Why:_ this record tracks unusable disk clusters. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 8 · Description** — `$BADCLUS` marks defective clusters so NTFS avoids allocating them. _Why:_ bad-cluster tracking affects whether missing data reflects damage, allocation behavior, or normal filesystem avoidance. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 9 · Filename** — record 9 is named `$SECURE`. _Why:_ this record identifies the NTFS security metadata file. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 9 · Description** — `$SECURE` stores security information associated with files on the volume. _Why:_ centralized security metadata supports permission and access-control reconstruction. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 10 · Filename** — record 10 is named `$UPCASE`. _Why:_ this record identifies the case-mapping table used by NTFS. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 10 · Description** — `$UPCASE` contains Unicode uppercase character mappings used when sorting filenames. _Why:_ filename comparison and ordering depend on NTFS’s Unicode case-handling rules. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 11 · Filename** — record 11 is named `$EXTEND`. _Why:_ this record identifies the directory that contains several extended NTFS metadata files. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record 11 · Description** — `$EXTEND` is a directory containing `$ObjId`, `$Quota`, `$Reparse`, and `$UsnJrnl`. _Why:_ these child metadata files support object identifiers, quotas, reparse behavior, and change journaling. _[GCFA p.756]_

### `$MFT`

- **`$MFT` record number** — `$MFT` is stored in MFT record 0. _Why:_ record 0 is the fixed metadata entry that describes the Master File Table itself. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **`$MFT` self-description** — MFT record 0 describes the MFT file. _Why:_ the filesystem uses this record to locate and interpret the rest of the MFT. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **`$MFT` name storage** — record 0 provides the name `$MFT`. _Why:_ the record identifies the primary metadata file by its NTFS system filename. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **`$MFT` cluster-location metadata** — record 0 contains information needed to locate the additional clusters that hold the rest of the MFT. _Why:_ forensic parsing of NTFS depends on following these references to reconstruct the full MFT file. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **VBR pointer to `$MFT` record** — the Volume Boot Record points to the cluster where the `$MFT` record is located. _Why:_ this pointer is the starting point for finding the MFT on disk. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record pointers** — MFT records contain pointers to the clusters used by every other filesystem object. _Why:_ NTFS object recovery relies on interpreting these cluster references. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **NTFS fixed-location exception** — in NTFS, the Volume Boot Record is the only object fixed to a specific disk sector. _Why:_ this distinguishes the VBR from other NTFS structures that can be relocated. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **NTFS VBR immobility** — the NTFS Volume Boot Record cannot be moved to another disk location. _Why:_ investigators can use the VBR’s fixed placement as an anchor for locating filesystem metadata. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **NTFS versus FAT placement behavior** — NTFS differs from FAT because only the NTFS VBR is tied to a particular sector. _Why:_ this affects expectations when comparing FAT and NTFS metadata layout during forensic examination. _[GCFA p.756]_

### `$MFTMIRR`

- **`$MFTMIRR` record number** — `$MFTMIRR` is the second MFT record. _Why:_ its fixed early placement makes it a known recovery target. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **`$MFTMIRR` recovery purpose** — `$MFTMIRR` backs up the primary `$MFT` information. _Why:_ it can be used when the primary MFT record cannot be read. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **Physical-damage use case** — `$MFTMIRR` is intended for cases where disk damage prevents reading the primary MFT record. _Why:_ this makes it relevant when diagnosing filesystem corruption from media failure. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **Minimum necessary backup content** — the crucial backup need is the record 0 information required to find and read the rest of `$MFT`. _Why:_ recovering the MFT’s location metadata can restore access to the wider filesystem catalog. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **Cluster-sized mirror allocation** — because disk space is allocated by cluster, the mirror stores a full cluster worth of MFT records. _Why:_ allocation granularity explains why more than just record 0 is normally mirrored. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **Default cluster size** — the page states the default NTFS cluster size as 4 KB. _Why:_ this value explains the usual number of mirrored MFT records. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **MFT record size** — the page states an MFT record size of 1 KB. _Why:_ this size determines how many records fit into the mirrored cluster. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **Typical mirror count** — with 4 KB clusters and 1 KB records, `$MFTMIRR` usually backs up the first four MFT records. _Why:_ this explains why records 0 through 3 are commonly available in the mirror. _[GCFA p.756]_

### `$LOGFILE`

- **`$LOGFILE` content** — `$LOGFILE` stores NTFS transactional logging information. _Why:_ this data supports analysis of filesystem operations and recovery behavior. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **`$LOGFILE` integrity role** — NTFS uses `$LOGFILE` to preserve filesystem integrity after a crash. _Why:_ log records can indicate how NTFS repaired or completed metadata updates. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **Transactional logging terminology** — comparable filesystems usually call this crash-consistency process journaling. _Why:_ recognizing the terminology helps map NTFS behavior to broader filesystem concepts. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **Later course dependency** — the page notes that `$LOGFILE` will be discussed further later. _Why:_ this flags `$LOGFILE` as an artifact with deeper forensic treatment beyond this page. _[GCFA p.756]_

### `$VOLUME`

- **`$VOLUME` volume label** — `$VOLUME` stores the user-friendly volume name. _Why:_ this can identify the logical volume as shown to users and applications. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **`$VOLUME` display context** — the friendly volume name is used in My Computer and similar display locations. _Why:_ this links forensic metadata to what a user would have seen in the Windows interface. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **`$VOLUME` NTFS version** — `$VOLUME` records the NTFS version number for the volume. _Why:_ version information affects expected metadata structures and feature support. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **`$VOLUME` flags** — `$VOLUME` contains flags about the volume’s last-use state. _Why:_ these flags help determine whether shutdown or unmount behavior may have left pending recovery work. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **Clean-unmount indication** — `$VOLUME` flags indicate whether the volume was cleanly unmounted during its previous use. _Why:_ an unclean state can explain log replay, dirty volumes, or filesystem inconsistency. _[GCFA p.756]_

### `$ATTRDEF`

- **`$ATTRDEF` version-specific definitions** — `$ATTRDEF` defines NTFS attributes for the NTFS version used on the volume. _Why:_ the correct attribute definitions are required to interpret MFT record contents accurately. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **`$ATTRDEF` naming source** — the attribute names used when discussing NTFS come from `$ATTRDEF`. _Why:_ this file anchors attribute terminology in the volume’s own metadata rather than external labels. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **`$ATTRDEF` later course dependency** — the page notes that some NTFS attributes will be covered later. _Why:_ `$ATTRDEF` is introduced here as background for later attribute-level forensic analysis. _[GCFA p.756]_

### Root Directory `.`

- **Root directory record number** — MFT record 5 is the NTFS root directory. _Why:_ the fixed record number gives investigators a known starting point for walking the directory tree. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **Root directory filename** — the root directory’s name is a single dot, `.`. _Why:_ this distinguishes the root directory entry from ordinary named directories. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **Root directory functional behavior** — the root directory behaves like other NTFS directories. _Why:_ standard directory-parsing methods apply to the root once its fixed record is located. _[GCFA p.756]_
- **Root directory fixed placement** — the root directory differs from ordinary directories because it is always MFT record 5. _Why:_ this fixed location provides a reliable forensic reference point. _[GCFA p.756]_

### $BITMAP

- **$BITMAP** — NTFS represents volume cluster allocation as a binary sequence with one bit corresponding to each cluster. _Why:_ this metadata identifies which clusters are occupied versus potentially available for allocation. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$BITMAP · Per-cluster bit mapping** — every cluster on the volume has a matching bit in `$BITMAP`. _Why:_ forensic interpretation of free and allocated space depends on this one-to-one cluster-to-bit relationship. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$BITMAP · Bit value meaning** — each cluster’s bit is set to either `1` or `0` based on whether that cluster is assigned to a file. _Why:_ the bit state is the filesystem’s allocation record for that cluster. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$BITMAP · Allocation tracking role** — `$BITMAP` records whether clusters are currently used or free. _Why:_ this affects file recovery, carving expectations, and interpretation of unallocated space. _[GCFA p.757]_

### $BOOT

- **$BOOT** — NTFS exposes the Volume Boot Record through this metadata file so it can be read using ordinary file input/output mechanisms. _Why:_ investigators can access VBR-related data through the filesystem abstraction rather than only by raw-sector access. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$BOOT · VBR access** — the Volume Boot Record is made available via normal file operations through `$BOOT`. _Why:_ this explains why boot-sector information can appear as a named NTFS metadata file. _[GCFA p.757]_

### $BADCLUS

- **$BADCLUS** — NTFS uses `$BadClus` to mark physically damaged clusters so the filesystem avoids storing data in them. _Why:_ damaged-cluster handling changes allocation behavior and can explain clusters that are intentionally unavailable. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$BADCLUS · Physical damage purpose** — clusters recorded through `$BadClus` are treated as unreliable storage locations. _Why:_ this prevents normal files from being placed on storage areas the filesystem considers unsafe. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$BADCLUS · Sparse file type** — `$BadClus` is implemented as a sparse file. _Why:_ sparse behavior lets NTFS represent a volume-sized logical file without consuming equivalent disk space. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$BADCLUS · Logical file size** — `$BadClus` has a file size equal to the entire volume size. _Why:_ this lets offsets inside the file correspond directly to locations across the volume. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$BADCLUS · Initial contents** — `$BadClus` begins as logically filled with zeros. _Why:_ an all-zero sparse representation means the file initially requires no physical allocation. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **Sparse file** — a sparse file does not physically write disk clusters for regions that contain only zeros. _Why:_ this explains how NTFS can represent very large logical files efficiently. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$BADCLUS · Initial disk usage** — because `$BadClus` initially consists entirely of zero-filled sparse regions, it does not allocate disk space at first. _Why:_ investigators should distinguish logical file size from actual allocated storage. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$BADCLUS · Bad-cluster offset mapping** — when NTFS identifies a bad cluster, it records data in `$BadClus` at the file offset matching that cluster’s location. _Why:_ the offset placement ties the metadata entry to the affected physical cluster location. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$BADCLUS · Placeholder data behavior** — the data associated with a bad cluster in `$BadClus` is not actually written to the damaged disk location. _Why:_ the metadata effect matters more than physical content placement. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$BADCLUS · Interaction with $BITMAP** — the presence of the placeholder data causes `$Bitmap` to mark the bad cluster as allocated. _Why:_ this prevents the cluster from being reused by ordinary files. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$BADCLUS · Future allocation prevention** — once a bad cluster is represented through `$BadClus`, other files should not attempt to use that cluster later. _Why:_ this is the filesystem-level protection mechanism for unreliable clusters. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$BADCLUS · Modern disk behavior** — in practical use, hard drive controllers typically remap failing sectors themselves. _Why:_ this means `$BadClus` is rarely exercised on real systems. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$BADCLUS · Fail-safe role** — `$BadClus` functions mainly as a fallback mechanism because hardware-level sector remapping usually handles failures first. _Why:_ this contextualizes why investigators may seldom encounter meaningful `$BadClus` usage. _[GCFA p.757]_

### $SECURE

- **$SECURE** — NTFS stores an index in `$Secure` for filesystem security metadata. _Why:_ this centralizes security-related information used across files. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$SECURE · File security tracking** — the `$Secure` index tracks security information associated with files on the system. _Why:_ file ownership and access controls are part of forensic metadata interpretation. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **File security information** — individual files contain security details describing the file owner. _Why:_ ownership metadata can help attribute activity or explain access rights. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **File access permissions** — individual files contain information about who is permitted to open them. _Why:_ access-control metadata can support privilege and authorization analysis. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$SECURE · Centralized owner lookup** — `$Secure` provides a central location for owner-related security information. _Why:_ this avoids redundant security lookups for every file. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$SECURE · Lookup efficiency** — NTFS uses the `$Secure` index so security information does not need to be repeatedly resolved separately for each file. _Why:_ this explains the performance and normalization purpose of the metadata file. _[GCFA p.757]_

### $UPCASE

- **$UPCASE** — NTFS stores uppercase/lowercase Unicode mapping information in `$UpCase`. _Why:_ filename comparison and sorting depend on case-mapping rules. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$UPCASE · Unicode code pages** — `$UpCase` contains case-mapping entries for each Unicode code page used by filenames on the system. _Why:_ Unicode-aware filename handling must account for locale and character set behavior. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$UPCASE · Filename sorting** — NTFS uses the `$UpCase` table when sorting files by name. _Why:_ filename ordering in directories relies on this metadata. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$UPCASE · Case-insensitive adjacency** — the table helps ensure uppercase and lowercase forms of the same letter, such as `A` and `a`, sort near each other alphabetically. _Why:_ this explains case-insensitive ordering behavior in NTFS directory listings. _[GCFA p.757]_

### $EXTEND

- **$EXTEND** — NTFS uses `$Extend` as a directory for newer system metadata files rather than placing those files directly into the reserved system record set. _Why:_ this explains where later NTFS system files are organized. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **Reserved system records** — NTFS reserves 24 records for system use. _Why:_ reserved MFT record ranges affect expectations about where system metadata may reside. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$EXTEND · New system-file design choice** — when new system files were added, NTFS did not store them directly in the reserved 24 records. _Why:_ investigators should not assume all system files occupy only the original reserved records. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$EXTEND · Directory entry location** — NTFS placed a directory entry in record number `11` to hold newer system files. _Why:_ record `11` is significant as the container reference for `$Extend`. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$EXTEND · New system-file records** — newer system files under `$Extend` are stored in records that are otherwise normal-use records. _Why:_ these files can appear outside the fixed early metadata-record positions. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$EXTEND · Format-time creation order** — the format command writes the listed `$Extend` files before user files are written. _Why:_ creation order explains why these records tend to appear early in the MFT. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$EXTEND · Typical record placement** — the listed `$Extend` files are usually found in the first four non-reserved records. _Why:_ this gives a practical expectation for locating them during MFT analysis. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$EXTEND · Typical record range** — those first non-reserved records are identified as record numbers `24-28` on the page. _Why:_ these numeric MFT record references are concrete locator facts for NTFS metadata review. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$EXTEND · Non-static placement** — `$Extend` child files do not have fixed record numbers in the same way the first 12 NTFS records do. _Why:_ forensic tooling and manual analysis should not rely on immutable MFT record IDs for these files. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **First 12 NTFS records** — the first 12 records always use their indicated record numbers. _Why:_ this contrasts fixed early metadata records with the more variable `$Extend` child-file placement. _[GCFA p.757]_

### $EXTEND\$ObjId

- **$EXTEND\$ObjId** — NTFS stores an index of object IDs used on the volume in `$Extend\$ObjId`. _Why:_ object IDs support durable file identification beyond ordinary pathnames. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **Object IDs** — object IDs allow NTFS to continue tracking a file even after changes that would otherwise break path-based references. _Why:_ this matters when reconstructing file movement or rename history. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **Object IDs · Move resilience** — a file can still be tracked by object ID after it has been moved. _Why:_ movement may change paths without destroying object-based continuity. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **Object IDs · Rename resilience** — a file can still be tracked by object ID after it has been renamed. _Why:_ rename events can defeat simple pathname tracking but not necessarily object-ID tracking. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **Object IDs · Link-file contrast** — object IDs help in situations where a pointer such as a shortcut/link file might fail to locate the target after changes. _Why:_ this distinguishes object-ID tracking from weaker path-dependent references. _[GCFA p.757]_

### $EXTEND\$Quota

- **$EXTEND\$Quota** — NTFS stores volume disk-quota information in `$Extend\$Quota`. _Why:_ quota metadata can explain user storage limits and allocation accounting. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$EXTEND\$Quota · Allowed space** — the file records how much allocated disk space each user is permitted to consume on the volume. _Why:_ per-user limits can affect file creation and allocation behavior. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **$EXTEND\$Quota · Current usage** — the file records how much allocated volume space each user is currently using. _Why:_ usage accounting may support attribution and resource-consumption analysis. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **Disk quotas · Administrative control** — when quotas are enabled, administrators can restrict users from consuming excessive disk space. _Why:_ quota enforcement is a system policy mechanism visible through NTFS metadata. _[GCFA p.757]_

### $EXTEND\$Reparse

- **$EXTEND\$Reparse** — NTFS stores an index of all volume reparse points in `$Extend\$Reparse`. _Why:_ this metadata helps locate path redirection and special filesystem behaviors. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **Reparse points** — reparse points support many filesystem functions. _Why:_ they are a broad NTFS mechanism, not limited to one feature. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **Reparse points · Common symbolic-link use** — the page identifies symbolic links as the most common use of reparse points. _Why:_ symbolic links can redirect file access and complicate path interpretation. _[GCFA p.757]_
- **Symbolic links** — in this context, a symbolic link is a file-like entry that points to another file. _Why:_ link targets may differ from the visible path an investigator first inspects. _[GCFA p.757]_

## Page 758

### Reparse Points

- **Reparse points · Volume mounting** — NTFS reparse points can make another volume appear as a directory within an existing volume. _Why:_ mounted volumes may hide additional filesystem content behind an ordinary-looking directory path during forensic review. _[GCFA p.758]_

### USN Journal

- **`$Extend\$UsnJrnl`** — the NTFS USN Journal resides under the `$Extend` metadata directory with the name `$UsnJrnl`. _Why:_ this path identifies the filesystem artifact to examine when reconstructing file change activity. _[GCFA p.758]_

- **Update Sequence Number Journal** — the USN Journal is also referred to as the Change Journal. _Why:_ analysts and tools may use either name for the same NTFS change-tracking artifact. _[GCFA p.758]_

- **USN Journal · Change index** — the USN Journal functions as an index of files that have changed on the system. _Why:_ it can help identify file activity even when other evidence is incomplete or unavailable. _[GCFA p.758]_

- **USN Journal · Reason tracking** — the USN Journal records why a listed file change occurred. _Why:_ change reasons provide investigative context beyond the mere fact that a file was touched. _[GCFA p.758]_

- **USN Journal · Later coverage** — the courseware indicates that the USN Journal is introduced here and discussed in greater detail later. _Why:_ this page establishes the artifact’s role before deeper forensic interpretation is presented elsewhere. _[GCFA p.758]_

## Page 759

### MFT Entry Allocation State

- **Metadata entries have allocation state** — NTFS metadata records can be either active or inactive, similar to how file-content clusters can be allocated or unallocated at the data layer. _Why:_ investigators must evaluate both metadata records and data clusters when determining whether file evidence is live, deleted, or recoverable. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Allocated MFT entry** — an allocated Master File Table entry is currently assigned to an existing file or directory. _Why:_ this identifies records that describe live filesystem objects rather than deleted remnants. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Unallocated MFT entry** — an unallocated Master File Table entry is not currently assigned to a live file or directory. _Why:_ unallocated entries may still preserve evidence from deleted filesystem objects. _[GCFA p.759]_

### Allocated MFT Entry Contents

- **Allocated MFT entry · metadata presence** — an active MFT record contains populated metadata fields for the file or directory it represents. _Why:_ live MFT records provide direct filesystem metadata for current objects. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Allocated MFT entry · filename metadata** — an active MFT record includes name information for the referenced object. _Why:_ names help identify the file or directory represented by the record. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Allocated MFT entry · timestamp metadata** — an active MFT record includes timestamp values. _Why:_ timestamps support timeline reconstruction and activity analysis. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Allocated MFT entry · permissions metadata** — an active MFT record includes permission-related metadata. _Why:_ permissions can help explain access, ownership, and security context. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Allocated MFT entry · content pointers** — an active MFT record can store references to the disk clusters that hold the file’s content. _Why:_ cluster pointers allow investigators and tools to locate the file’s data on disk. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Allocated MFT entry · resident data exception** — when a file’s data is resident, the file content itself is stored inside the MFT record rather than only being referenced by cluster pointers. _Why:_ small resident files may be recoverable directly from the MFT without reading external data clusters. _[GCFA p.759]_

### Unallocated MFT Entry Contents

- **Unallocated MFT entry · metadata may be absent** — an inactive MFT record may contain no meaningful metadata if it has never been used. _Why:_ an empty unused record provides little or no historical file evidence. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Unallocated MFT entry · metadata may remain** — an inactive MFT record may still contain metadata from a prior filesystem object. _Why:_ stale MFT metadata can reveal deleted files or directories. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Unallocated MFT entry · deleted object indicator** — if an inactive MFT record still contains populated metadata, that metadata belongs to a deleted file or folder that previously used the record. _Why:_ this creates a forensic opportunity to identify deleted objects even when they are no longer visible in directory listings. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Unallocated MFT entry · deleted-file cluster references** — an inactive MFT record may still point to clusters formerly used by the deleted file or folder. _Why:_ those references can guide recovery attempts for deleted content. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Unallocated MFT entry · deleted data may remain** — clusters referenced by an inactive MFT record may still contain the deleted object’s data. _Why:_ this means full or partial file recovery may still be possible. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Unallocated MFT entry · deleted data may be gone** — clusters referenced by an inactive MFT record may no longer contain the deleted object’s data. _Why:_ recovery depends on whether later filesystem activity overwrote the original clusters. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Unallocated MFT entry · cluster reuse risk** — clusters formerly associated with a deleted object may have been reassigned to newer data. _Why:_ reused clusters can destroy or contaminate recoverable file content. _[GCFA p.759]_

### Unallocated Entry States

- **Never-used MFT entry** — one possible state for an unallocated metadata entry is that it was never written to and remains empty. _Why:_ this distinguishes records with no historical evidentiary value from records containing deleted-object remnants. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Previously-used MFT entry** — another possible state for an unallocated metadata entry is that it was used earlier and still contains information about the most recent deleted file or directory assigned to it. _Why:_ these records can preserve deleted-object metadata after filesystem deletion. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Last deleted object metadata** — a previously used unallocated MFT entry reflects the last deleted file or directory that occupied that record. _Why:_ investigators should interpret stale metadata as belonging to the prior occupant, not a current file. _[GCFA p.759]_

### Forensic Value

- **Deleted-object name recovery** — a reused-but-now-unallocated MFT entry may reveal the name of the deleted file or folder. _Why:_ filenames can identify user activity, malware components, staging locations, or exfiltration artifacts. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Deleted-object timestamp recovery** — a reused-but-now-unallocated MFT entry may preserve timestamps for the deleted object. _Why:_ these timestamps can place deleted activity on a forensic timeline. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Deleted-object ownership recovery** — a reused-but-now-unallocated MFT entry may retain ownership-related metadata. _Why:_ ownership can help attribute filesystem activity to users or security principals. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Deleted-object metadata analysis** — when stale metadata remains in an unallocated MFT entry, investigators can analyze information about the deleted file or folder even if the object is no longer allocated. _Why:_ metadata remnants can survive deletion and provide evidence independent of successful content recovery. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Full deleted-file recovery condition** — a deleted file may be recoverable in full if the clusters it previously occupied have not been reused after deletion. _Why:_ intact clusters allow content reconstruction from stale MFT references. _[GCFA p.759]_
- **Overwrite condition for failed recovery** — if newer files have overwritten the clusters formerly used by a deleted file, full recovery may no longer be possible. _Why:_ overwrite activity can permanently replace deleted content while leaving some metadata behind. _[GCFA p.759]ぺ

## Page 760

### Sequential MFT Allocation Pattern

- **MFT allocation order** — NTFS file creation commonly consumes MFT records in increasing, near-contiguous order rather than distributing new records randomly. _Why:_ adjacent MFT record numbers can reveal files created around the same time. _[GCFA p.760]_
- **Directory independence** — Sequential MFT allocation can occur even when the created files are located in different directories. _Why:_ investigators should compare metadata record proximity across the whole filesystem, not only inside one folder. _[GCFA p.760]_
- **Next available MFT record behavior** — When NTFS needs a metadata record for a newly created file, it typically assigns the next available MFT entry. _Why:_ this behavior explains why rapid file creation often leaves clustered record numbers. _[GCFA p.760]_
- **Rapid creation clustering** — Multiple files written close together in time often receive neighboring MFT record numbers. _Why:_ clusters of metadata addresses can identify related file drops or execution byproducts. _[GCFA p.760]_
- **Contiguous metadata analysis technique** — Analysts can inspect neighboring metadata values to locate files probably created in the same short interval. _Why:_ this can connect related artifacts even when they reside in separate paths. _[GCFA p.760]_
- **MFT proximity as creation-time evidence** — MFT records near a known file of interest may indicate other files created at roughly the same time. _Why:_ this provides an independent lead when file timestamps are incomplete or manipulated. _[GCFA p.760]_
- **MFT clustering as alternate creation signal** — When clustering appears, MFT record order can act like a secondary creation-time indicator. _Why:_ this can expose relationships hidden by timestomping. _[GCFA p.760]_
- **Pattern reliability limitation** — Sequential MFT clustering is not guaranteed in every case. _Why:_ investigators should treat it as a useful lead, not definitive proof by itself. _[GCFA p.760]_
- **Pattern frequency** — Although not universal, sequential clustering is common enough to be operationally useful. _Why:_ it justifies routinely checking nearby MFT entries during file-system analysis. _[GCFA p.760]_
- **Investigation value** — Viewing filesystem activity through MFT allocation order can reveal additional investigative paths. _Why:_ metadata order can uncover relationships missed by timeline sorting alone. _[GCFA p.760]_

- **Spinlock scenario** — The upper example represents first execution of a malicious program named `spinlock.exe`. _Why:_ first-run activity often creates support files and execution artifacts together. _[GCFA p.760]_
- **Embedded resource extraction** — During execution, `spinlock.exe` extracted multiple bundled resource files. _Why:_ dropped resources can identify malware packaging and execution behavior. _[GCFA p.760]_

## Page 761

### NTFS MFT Structure

- **Master File Table (MFT)** — NTFS uses the MFT as the central file-system metadata store. _Why:_ many file, directory, and volume artifacts are interpreted through MFT records. _[GCFA p.761]_
- **MFT as structured data** — the MFT is organized like a highly structured database rather than an unstructured byte store. _Why:_ predictable structure enables forensic parsing and record-level interpretation. _[GCFA p.761]_
- **MFT metadata coverage** — the MFT stores metadata entries for files and folders on the NTFS volume. _Why:_ investigators can use it as a primary source for filesystem object metadata. _[GCFA p.761]_
- **Object-to-record model** — each NTFS object receives an MFT entry. _Why:_ individual filesystem objects can be tracked through their own record. _[GCFA p.761]_
- **MFT entry attributes** — MFT records contain attributes that describe the object represented by the entry. _Why:_ attributes are the units that hold names, timestamps, data, indexes, and other forensic evidence. _[GCFA p.761]_
- **Typical MFT record size** — MFT entries are usually 1024 bytes. _Why:_ record size affects parsing, carving, and record-boundary validation. _[GCFA p.761]_
- **Predefined entry size** — each MFT entry has a fixed size determined by the filesystem. _Why:_ fixed-size records support systematic parsing and record-number addressing. _[GCFA p.761]_
- **Larger MFT records** — in uncommon cases, NTFS may use MFT entries larger than 1024 bytes. _Why:_ parsers and analysts should not assume every NTFS volume uses 1024-byte records. _[GCFA p.761]_
- **4096-byte MFT records** — when MFT records are larger than usual, 4096 bytes is identified as the typical larger size. _Why:_ this gives a concrete alternate size to check during filesystem analysis. _[GCFA p.761]_
- **File MFT entry** — a file receives its own MFT entry. _Why:_ file metadata and content references are record-based in NTFS. _[GCFA p.761]_
- **Directory MFT entry** — a directory receives its own MFT entry. _Why:_ directories have their own attributes and index structures that can preserve evidence of contained names. _[GCFA p.761]_
- **Volume-name MFT entry** — the volume name also has an MFT entry. _Why:_ even volume-level metadata is represented inside the MFT. _[GCFA p.761]_
- **$VOLUME reserved record** — the volume name is associated with the `$VOLUME` system file at reserved MFT entry number 3. _Why:_ reserved entry numbers help identify NTFS metadata files reliably. _[GCFA p.761]_
- **Slide deck page marker** — the visible courseware slide footer shows page `29`. _Why:_ screenshot/footer values can help reconcile extracted page images with courseware pagination. _[GCFA p.761]_

- **File attribute · $DATA alternate data stream** — common file MFT entries sometimes include `$DATA` as an alternate data stream. _Why:_ ADS evidence is relevant to malware staging, downloaded-file metadata, and hidden content analysis. _[GCFA p.761]_

- **Directory attribute · $INDEX_ROOT** — common directory MFT entries include `$INDEX_ROOT`. _Why:_ this attribute stores the root of a directory index. _[GCFA p.761]_

- **Directory attribute · $INDEX_ALLOCATION** — common directory MFT entries sometimes include `$INDEX_ALLOCATION`. _Why:_ this attribute can contain directory index entries beyond the resident index root. _[GCFA p.761]_

## Page 762

### MFT Entry Overview

- **MFT entry purpose** — An MFT `FILE` record is the core NTFS structure used to describe a filesystem object such as a file. _Why:_ investigators parse this record to recover metadata, names, timestamps, allocation state, and sometimes file contents. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Example object type** — The illustrated MFT record describes a file, not a directory. _Why:_ file records and directory records can contain different practical evidence, especially around data storage and indexing. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Example filename** — The example record is for `winclient.reg`. _Why:_ the filename anchors the parsed structure to a concrete artifact visible in the record. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **MFT entry size** — The shown record is a single 1024-byte MFT entry. _Why:_ record size determines where attributes, slack, and the next record boundary should be expected. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Next-entry boundary** — The bottom of the screenshot shows the beginning of the following MFT entry. _Why:_ recognizing the next record prevents misinterpreting unused space or the next object’s header as part of the current file. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Repeated MFT structure** — A normal NTFS volume contains many thousands of MFT records with this general structure. _Why:_ large-scale filesystem analysis depends on repeatedly parsing these records consistently. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Record organization** — The MFT record begins with a header and is followed by attributes that describe the referenced object. _Why:_ this ordering guides manual parsing and validation of automated parser output. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Attribute role** — Attributes inside the MFT entry provide detailed metadata and, in some cases, content for the object. _Why:_ evidence may reside in multiple attributes rather than in a single monolithic record field. _[GCFA p.~762]_

### MFT Header

- **MFT header signature** — The MFT header starts with the ASCII signature `FILE`. _Why:_ this signature confirms the parser is aligned at the start of an NTFS file record. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **MFT header hex signature** — The record start is shown as `0x46494C45`, which corresponds to `FILE` in ASCII. _Why:_ this byte pattern is a direct validation marker when reviewing raw hex. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **MFT header allocation state** — The header includes the record’s allocation status. _Why:_ allocation state helps distinguish active entries from deleted or reusable records. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **MFT header entry number** — The header includes the MFT entry number. _Why:_ the entry number uniquely identifies the record within the MFT and supports parent-child reference resolution. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Allocation status value** — The called-out allocation status is `0x01`. _Why:_ this value identifies the example record as actively in use. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Allocation status meaning** — `0x01` means the record represents a file currently marked in use. _Why:_ this separates live files from records that may contain deleted-file remnants. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **MFT record number value** — The record number is shown as `0x0000EDF7`. _Why:_ this is the raw identifier investigators can use to correlate references. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **MFT record number decimal** — `0x0000EDF7` equals decimal `60,919`. _Why:_ forensic tools may display either hexadecimal or decimal record identifiers. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **MFT record number endian format** — The record number is stored in little-endian byte order. _Why:_ endian interpretation is required to convert the raw bytes to the correct record number. _[GCFA p.~762]_

### $STANDARD_INFORMATION Attribute

- **$STANDARD_INFORMATION marker** — `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` begins with attribute type value `0x10`. _Why:_ this value identifies the start of the standard metadata attribute in raw MFT data. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **$SI screenshot label** — The screenshot marks the start of `$SI`. _Why:_ this callout shows where the standard information attribute begins in the record layout. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **$STANDARD_INFORMATION timestamp set** — `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` contains four timestamps. _Why:_ these timestamps are primary NTFS temporal evidence for file activity. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **$STANDARD_INFORMATION timestamp format** — The four `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` timestamps are Windows 64-bit timestamps. _Why:_ correct timestamp decoding requires using the Windows FILETIME-style representation. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **$STANDARD_INFORMATION called-out timestamps** — The screenshot specifically highlights the four Windows 64-bit timestamps inside `$STANDARD_INFORMATION`. _Why:_ this identifies the exact region where these times are stored in the record. _[GCFA p.~762]_

### $FILE_NAME Attributes

- **$FILE_NAME marker** — `$FILE_NAME` begins with attribute type value `0x30`. _Why:_ this value identifies filename attributes during raw MFT parsing. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **$FILE_NAME timestamp set** — `$FILE_NAME` contains four timestamps. _Why:_ `$FILE_NAME` timestamps can preserve metadata that differs from `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` and can support timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.~762]_

- **Second $FILE_NAME screenshot label** — The screenshot labels the start of the second `$FN`. _Why:_ this identifies the long-name attribute’s location in the record. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Parent directory reference** — The `$FILE_NAME` attribute contains a parent directory reference. _Why:_ this links the file to its containing directory for path reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Parent MFT entry number raw value** — The parent directory reference includes parent MFT entry number `0x017C`. _Why:_ this raw reference can be used to locate the parent directory record. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Parent MFT entry number decimal** — Parent MFT entry number `0x017C` equals decimal `380`. _Why:_ tools and notes may represent the same parent directory reference in decimal form. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **$FILE_NAME timestamp format** — The timestamps in `$FILE_NAME` are Windows 64-bit timestamps. _Why:_ they require the same timestamp decoding logic used for other NTFS FILETIME values. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **$FILE_NAME called-out timestamps** — The screenshot highlights four Windows 64-bit timestamps in the `$FILE_NAME` attribute. _Why:_ these fields provide additional temporal evidence tied to the filename metadata. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Short filename value** — The first `$FILE_NAME` attribute contains short name `WINCLI~1.REG`. _Why:_ this is the DOS 8.3 alias for the file and may appear in artifacts that do not record the long filename. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Long filename value** — The second `$FILE_NAME` attribute contains long name `winclient.reg`. _Why:_ this is the normal filename used for file identification and correlation. _[GCFA p.~762]_

### $DATA Attribute

- **$DATA marker** — `$DATA` begins with attribute type value `0x80`. _Why:_ this value identifies where the file-content attribute begins. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **$DATA screenshot label** — The screenshot labels the start of `$DATA`. _Why:_ this shows where file content metadata or content begins in the MFT record. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **$DATA storage alternatives** — `$DATA` contains either the file’s resident data or cluster-run information pointing to nonresident content. _Why:_ this determines whether data is inside the MFT record or stored elsewhere on disk. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Resident data in example** — The example file’s `$DATA` is resident. _Why:_ the file content can be recovered directly from the MFT entry without following external cluster runs. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Residence status field** — The `$DATA` attribute includes a residence status value. _Why:_ this field tells the examiner whether the data is embedded in the record or stored outside it. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Resident status value** — Residence status `0x00` means the data is resident. _Why:_ this indicates that file content is stored within the MFT entry itself. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Nonresident status value** — Residence status `0x01` means the data is nonresident. _Why:_ this indicates that the attribute points to clusters outside the MFT entry. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Small-file behavior** — The example file is small enough for its data to fit inside the MFT entry. _Why:_ small resident files may be fully recoverable from MFT records alone. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **File data callout** — The screenshot calls out the actual file data inside the MFT entry. _Why:_ this demonstrates that MFT records can contain user file content, not only metadata. _[GCFA p.~762]_

### Entry Terminator And Slack

- **End-of-entry marker** — `0xFFFFFFFF` marks the end of the current MFT entry’s used structure. _Why:_ this sentinel helps distinguish valid attributes from remaining unused bytes. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Unused slack space** — Bytes after the end marker are unused slack space within the MFT entry. _Why:_ this area may contain residual data and must not be confused with active attributes. _[GCFA p.~762]_
- **Next MFT entry start** — The screenshot marks the start of the next MFT entry after the current record. _Why:_ this confirms the boundary between adjacent 1024-byte MFT records. _[GCFA p.~762]_

### NTFS MFT Entry Boundary Markers

- **MFT entry terminator value** — the value `0xFFFFFFFF` marks the end of an MFT entry. _Why:_ this boundary marker helps an examiner recognize where one NTFS file record stops during raw MFT parsing. _[GCFA p.763]_

- **Next MFT record start offset pattern** — after the prior MFT entry ends, the following MFT entry begins on the next `1024-byte` record boundary. _Why:_ NTFS MFT records are commonly parsed in fixed-size units, so this size helps validate record alignment. _[GCFA p.763]_

- **MFT record signature value** — the next MFT entry begins with hexadecimal `0x46494C45`. _Why:_ this signature is a recognizable indicator that the parser or examiner has reached the start of another NTFS file record. _[GCFA p.763]_

- **MFT record signature ASCII rendering** — hexadecimal `0x46494C45` corresponds to ASCII text `FILE`. _Why:_ the human-readable signature provides a quick validation point when inspecting raw hex or forensic tool output. _[GCFA p.763]_

### The Sleuth Kit and `istat`

- **The Sleuth Kit** — The Sleuth Kit is an open-source toolkit used for forensic examination of disk images and file systems. _Why:_ it provides trusted command-line utilities for filesystem-level evidence analysis. _[GCFA p.~764]_
- **The Sleuth Kit as a learning aid** — The toolkit is useful not only for casework but also for studying how different file systems store and expose metadata. _Why:_ understanding filesystem internals helps analysts interpret artifacts correctly. _[GCFA p.~764]_
- **`istat` purpose** — `istat` reports details about a selected filesystem metadata record, also described generically as an inode. _Why:_ metadata records contain timestamps, allocation state, flags, and structural evidence about files or directories. _[GCFA p.~764]_
- **`istat` and NTFS MFT entries** — `istat` can parse NTFS Master File Table entries. _Why:_ MFT records are the primary NTFS metadata source for files and directories. _[GCFA p.~764]_
- **Generic `istat` syntax** — The command format shown is `istat [options] image inode`. _Why:_ analysts must provide both the evidence source and the metadata record number to inspect. _[GCFA p.~764]_

- **`inode` argument** — The `inode` parameter identifies the metadata structure to parse; for NTFS this corresponds to an MFT record number. _Why:_ selecting the correct metadata number determines which file or directory is examined. _[GCFA p.~764]_
- **“i” in `istat`** — The tool name reflects its focus on inode-style metadata records. _Why:_ this explains why NTFS MFT records are addressed through an inode-oriented interface. _[GCFA p.~764]_

### MFT Entry Header

- **MFT entry header purpose** — The header exposes whether the MFT record is currently in use and what kind of filesystem object it represents. _Why:_ allocation state and object type help determine whether a record describes an active file, directory, or recoverable prior object. _[GCFA p.766]_
- **Allocation status** — The example record is marked as an allocated file. _Why:_ this indicates the entry was active at the time represented by the parsed MFT data. _[GCFA p.766]_
- **MFT entry number** — The header stores the record identifier for the MFT entry. _Why:_ the entry number lets investigators reference and correlate a specific filesystem object across tools and artifacts. _[GCFA p.766]_
- **$LogFile sequence number** — The header includes a sequence value associated with NTFS transaction logging. _Why:_ this value can help correlate filesystem metadata activity with NTFS journaling evidence. _[GCFA p.766]_

### $STANDARD_INFORMATION Attribute

- **$STANDARD_INFORMATION role** — This attribute stores core metadata about a file or folder. _Why:_ it is one of the primary NTFS metadata sources examined during file timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.766]_
- **File and folder flags** — The attribute can record flags such as read-only, hidden, and archive. _Why:_ these flags may reveal normal user activity, staging behavior, or attempts to conceal files. _[GCFA p.766]_
- **Security metadata** — The attribute includes security-related identifiers. _Why:_ security identifiers help link a file object to ownership and access-control context. _[GCFA p.766]_
- **USN journal sequence number** — The attribute records a sequence value tied to the NTFS USN journal. _Why:_ the value can support correlation with filesystem change journal entries. _[GCFA p.766]_
- **Creation timestamp** — $STANDARD_INFORMATION contains the object creation time. _Why:_ creation time is part of MACB-style timeline reconstruction. _[GCFA p.766]_
- **Data modified timestamp** — $STANDARD_INFORMATION contains the time when file content was last changed. _Why:_ this timestamp can identify when payloads, documents, or other file contents were altered. _[GCFA p.766]_
- **MFT metadata modified timestamp** — $STANDARD_INFORMATION contains the time when filesystem metadata for the record last changed. _Why:_ metadata updates can expose renames, moves, permission changes, or timestamp manipulation. _[GCFA p.766]_
- **Last accessed timestamp** — $STANDARD_INFORMATION contains the time when the file data was last accessed. _Why:_ access time can support usage analysis, subject to filesystem update behavior and policy. _[GCFA p.766]_
- **MACB timestamp set** — The page identifies the $STANDARD_INFORMATION timestamps as MACB-style times. _Why:_ MACB timelines are a core method for sequencing activity in Windows filesystem investigations. _[GCFA p.766]_

### MFT Entry Signatures

- **Valid MFT entry signature** — a normal NTFS MFT record begins with the ASCII signature `FILE`, represented by bytes `0x46 0x49 0x4C 0x45`. _Why:_ this marker identifies valid MFT records during parsing and carving. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Corrupt MFT entry signature** — an MFT record may begin with `BAAD`, represented by bytes `0x42 0x41 0x44`, when NTFS has detected an error in that entry. _Why:_ this distinguishes damaged metadata records from ordinary valid records. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **MFT fragment carving marker** — searching for `FILE` at the beginning of a sector can help locate MFT fragments in unallocated space. _Why:_ this provides a practical carving technique for recovering filesystem metadata remnants. _[GCFA p.767]_

### Fixup Array Fields

- **Fixup Array offset field** — immediately after the MFT entry signature is a 2-byte field that stores the Fixup Array offset relative to the start of the MFT entry. _Why:_ this tells a parser where the sector-fixup metadata begins. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Fixup Array entry-count field** — the next 2-byte field after the Fixup Array offset stores the number of entries in the Fixup Array. _Why:_ this tells a parser how many fixup values must be processed. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Fixup Array purpose** — the Fixup Array validates MFT-related data structures that cross sector boundaries. _Why:_ this helps detect corruption in NTFS metadata spanning multiple sectors. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Fixup Array scope exclusion** — Fixup Array checking applies to metadata structures spanning sectors, but not to sectors containing file content data. _Why:_ this clarifies that the mechanism protects filesystem structures rather than ordinary file payload sectors. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Fixup Array write behavior** — when protected structures are written to disk, NTFS copies the final 2 bytes from each sector into a special array. _Why:_ these original bytes must be preserved so they can be restored after validation. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Fixup signature write behavior** — after copying each sector’s final 2 bytes, NTFS writes a signature value into the final 2 bytes of each sector. _Why:_ the repeated signature provides a consistency check for multi-sector metadata records. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Fixup Array read comparison** — when the structures are read back, NTFS compares each sector’s final 2 bytes against the expected signature value. _Why:_ mismatches indicate that the metadata record may be corrupt or incomplete. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Fixup Array restoration behavior** — if the signature checks succeed, NTFS replaces the signature values with the original 2-byte values saved in the array. _Why:_ this restores the metadata record to its usable in-memory form. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Corrupt FILE entry detection** — the Fixup Array process allows NTFS to identify damaged `FILE` records. _Why:_ forensic tools must account for fixup validation when interpreting MFT records. _[GCFA p.767]_

### $LogFile Sequence Number

- **LSN field offset** — the `$LogFile` Sequence Number is stored at offset `0x08` in the MFT record. _Why:_ this fixed location lets examiners identify the journaling reference for a record. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **LSN journaling role** — the LSN belongs to the journaling filesystem mechanism. _Why:_ it links an MFT record to NTFS recovery and consistency operations. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **LSN consistency function** — the LSN helps determine whether filesystem actions must be redone or undone to return the filesystem to a consistent state. _Why:_ it explains how NTFS uses journal state during recovery. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **LSN as `$LogFile` offset** — the value in the LSN field points to the offset inside `$LogFile` where the relevant record for this MFT entry is located. _Why:_ this gives investigators a way to correlate an MFT record with journal entries. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Example LSN value** — the example resolves to `$LogFile` offset `0x021F7EA9E6`. _Why:_ this is a concrete value shown for interpreting the field. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **LSN endian interpretation** — the example value is interpreted as `0x021F7EA9E6` because the bytes are stored in little-endian order. _Why:_ incorrect endian handling would produce the wrong journal offset. _[GCFA p.767]_

### Sequence Number

- **Sequence Number field offset** — the Sequence Number is located at offset `0x10` in the MFT record. _Why:_ this fixed field helps identify reuse history for an MFT entry. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Sequence Number meaning** — the Sequence Number acts as a counter for how many times the MFT record has been reused. _Why:_ it provides evidence about prior allocation and deletion activity. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Initial Sequence Number value** — when an MFT record is first allocated, its Sequence Number is set to `1`. _Why:_ this establishes the baseline value for a newly used record. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Sequence Number deletion behavior** — when a file is deleted and the MFT record becomes unallocated, the Sequence Number is incremented. _Why:_ the increment can indicate that a prior object was removed from that record. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Sequence Number subsequent behavior** — after the initial allocation, the Sequence Number increments only during later deallocations. _Why:_ this prevents misreading reuse as the event that directly increases the counter. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Sequence Number non-increment on creation** — the Sequence Number does not increase when a new `FILE` record is created or reused. _Why:_ this matters when reconstructing whether a value changed because of deletion rather than allocation. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Sequence Number deletion indicator** — the Sequence Number rises when a file is deleted, not when a new record is created. _Why:_ this makes the field useful for interpreting record lifecycle events. _[GCFA p.767]_

### Hard Link Count

- **Hard Link count field offset** — the Hard Link count is stored at offset `0x12` in the MFT record. _Why:_ this field helps determine how many filename attributes point to the record. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Hard Link count meaning** — the Hard Link count represents the number of `$FILE_NAME` attributes associated with the file. _Why:_ this count can reveal multiple names or namespace entries for the same file record. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Long and short filename tracking** — multiple `$FILE_NAME` attributes may represent long and short names for the same file. _Why:_ an examiner may need to account for both naming forms even if only one is displayed by a tool. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Displayed filename limitation** — when long and short filenames exist, a user may see only one of the two displayed. _Why:_ visible output may hide additional `$FILE_NAME` metadata in the record. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **True hard link representation** — multiple `$FILE_NAME` attributes may also indicate real hard links using different names or different directories. _Why:_ this distinguishes alternate namespace entries from true multi-link file references. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Shared MFT record reference** — whether the names are long/short variants or true hard links, the `$FILE_NAME` attributes refer to the same MFT record. _Why:_ this prevents treating multiple names as separate file objects when they share one record. _[GCFA p.767]_

- **Flags meaning for `0x03`** — flag value `0x03` means the record is an in-use directory. _Why:_ this identifies an allocated directory record. _[GCFA p.767]_

### Deleted Record Recovery

- **Deleted file flag change** — deleting a file changes the in-use bit in the flags field to `0`. _Why:_ this is the direct metadata state change that marks the MFT record unallocated. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Deleted file data persistence** — deleting a file does not erase the other data in the MFT record. _Why:_ record contents can remain available after deletion. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Recoverable deleted metadata** — much of a deleted file’s metadata can remain recoverable if the MFT record has not been reused. _Why:_ this supports metadata recovery from unallocated MFT entries. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **MFT reuse overwrite risk** — once the MFT record is reused for another file, prior deleted-file metadata may be overwritten. _Why:_ reuse limits the evidentiary value of stale MFT record contents. _[GCFA p.767]_

### FILE Record Size Fields

- **Used FILE record size offset** — offset `0x18` stores the current number of bytes being used by the `FILE` record. _Why:_ this identifies how much of the record is occupied by active record content. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Allocated FILE record size offset** — offset `0x1C` stores the total number of bytes allocated to the `FILE` record. _Why:_ this identifies the full record capacity available for metadata. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Standard FILE record allocation example** — the allocated size value `0x0400` corresponds to `1024` bytes. _Why:_ this confirms the typical MFT record size represented by the field. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **FILE record slack calculation** — the difference between the used size at `0x18` and the allocated size at `0x1C` is slack space inside the `FILE` record. _Why:_ MFT record slack may preserve residual metadata bytes. _[GCFA p.767]_

### Base Record Reference

- **File Reference to Base Record offset** — the File Reference to Base Record field is located at offset `0x20`. _Why:_ this field links extension records back to their primary MFT record. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Base Record field usage** — the File Reference to Base Record is used only for extended records. _Why:_ ordinary records do not need a pointer to another base record. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Extended Record purpose** — extended records are used when an MFT record has too many attributes to fit within `1024` bytes. _Why:_ this explains why a file may require metadata spread across more than one MFT record. _[GCFA p.767]_
- **Typical Base Record field value** — for most MFT records, the File Reference to Base Record field contains all zero values. _Why:_ zeros indicate the entry is usually not an extension record. _[GCFA p.767]_

### Attribute ID Tracking

### NTFS MFT Record Header Version Differences

- **Older NTFS header layout** — On pre-Windows XP NTFS versions, the byte immediately following the Attribute Count field began the fixup area. _Why:_ parser behavior and carving signatures depend on which NTFS header layout is present. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Windows XP and later NTFS layout** — Beginning with Windows XP and NTFS 3.1, the MFT record number, also called the inode number, is stored at offset `0x2C`. _Why:_ this field helps identify and place MFT fragments during recovery. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **MFT Record Number field** — The value at offset `0x2C` records the MFT entry number for that record. _Why:_ recovered fragments can be tied back to their logical MFT record identity. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Header-length change** — Adding the MFT Record Number field changed the MFT record header size. _Why:_ tools that assume the older header structure can misread newer records. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Offset-to-fixup location** — The header field at offset `0x04` indicates where the fixup data begins. _Why:_ this value distinguishes older and newer MFT record layouts. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Older Offset-to-Fixup value** — Older NTFS records commonly show `0x2A` as the offset-to-fixup value. _Why:_ `0x2A` corresponds to the older header layout and may appear in carving signatures. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Newer Offset-to-Fixup value** — Newer NTFS records commonly show `0x30` as the offset-to-fixup value. _Why:_ `0x30` corresponds to the expanded header used with NTFS 3.1 and later. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **ASCII representation of `0x2A`** — The older offset value `0x2A` renders as `*` in ASCII. _Why:_ some older carving signatures may include this byte as a literal character. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **ASCII representation of `0x30`** — The newer offset value `0x30` renders as `0` in ASCII. _Why:_ a signature expecting the older byte can fail against newer records. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Legacy carving signature risk** — A carving tool that searches for `FILE*` may miss records whose header pattern is effectively `FILE0`. _Why:_ MFT recovery can be incomplete when signatures are tied to the older fixup offset byte. _[GCFA p.768]_

### MFT Fixup Mechanism

- **Fixup data location** — Fixup information begins at offset `0x30` in the described newer MFT record layout. _Why:_ this is where integrity-check replacement values are stored. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Fixup code composition** — The first three 2-byte fixup-related entries consist of the Update Sequence Number and the Update Sequence Array. _Why:_ these values protect sector-ending bytes inside the MFT record. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Update Sequence Number abbreviation** — `USN` refers here to the Update Sequence Number used in MFT fixups. _Why:_ this USN is part of the record-integrity mechanism, not the separate USN Journal concept. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Update Sequence Array abbreviation** — `USA` refers to the Update Sequence Array used with MFT fixups. _Why:_ the USA stores the original bytes displaced by the USN. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Fixup Length field** — The field at offset `0x06` gives the count of 2-byte entries that make up the combined USN and USA data. _Why:_ the parser uses this count to know how many fixup entries to process. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **MFT sector size in example** — Each MFT record described is split into 512-byte sectors. _Why:_ fixup checks occur at the end of each sector. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **MFT record size in example** — The described MFT record is 1,024 bytes long. _Why:_ a 1,024-byte record contains two 512-byte sectors, so two sector endings are protected. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **USN placement** — NTFS writes the USN into the final 2 bytes of each 512-byte sector within the MFT record. _Why:_ mismatches reveal torn or inconsistent sector reads. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Fixup entry count for 1,024-byte MFT records** — With the normal 1,024-byte MFT record length, the fixup structure contains three 2-byte entries. _Why:_ one entry is the USN and two entries are USA replacements for the two sectors. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Sector-read validation** — When NTFS reads the sectors, it compares the sector-ending values against the USN stored in the record header. _Why:_ the comparison detects corruption or incomplete writes. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Successful fixup validation** — If all three relevant fixup values match as expected, the record passes the integrity check. _Why:_ matching values indicate the protected sector endings are consistent. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Failed fixup validation** — If the fixup comparison fails, the `FILE` record signature is replaced with `BAAD`. _Why:_ `BAAD` marks the record as damaged or invalid for forensic interpretation. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Fixup error handling** — A failed fixup check also causes an error message to be returned. _Why:_ tools and analysts may see both a modified signature and an error condition. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **USA purpose** — Each USA entry stores the original 2 bytes that were replaced at the end of a sector. _Why:_ NTFS can restore the in-memory view of the original record contents after validation. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **First-sector restoration** — For the first sector, NTFS checks the final 2 bytes against the USN and then replaces those bytes in memory with the first USA entry. _Why:_ the original sector-ending data is reconstructed only after validation. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Second-sector restoration** — For the second sector, NTFS repeats the check and uses the second USA entry for the replacement. _Why:_ each sector has its own saved original ending bytes. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Directory index fixups** — Directory indexes use the same general fixup concept. _Why:_ fixup validation is not limited to MFT records. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Directory index fixup volume** — Directory entries usually contain more fixup values than the MFT record example. _Why:_ larger directory index structures may span more protected sectors. _[GCFA p.768]_
