### `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` Decoded Table Fields

- **Attribute signature bytes** — Bytes `10 00 00 00` at offset `0000000` identify the attribute type. _Why:_ decoded little-endian, this is `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` type `0x10`. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Length-of-attribute bytes** — Bytes `60 00 00 00` at offset `0000000:4` are labeled as the attribute length including the signature. _Why:_ the field defines the full size of this attribute record. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Attribute content length bytes** — Bytes `48 00 00 00` at offset `0000010:0` are labeled as the attribute content length. _Why:_ this gives the length of the resident content portion. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Content offset bytes** — Bytes `18 00 00 00` at offset `0000010:4` are labeled as the content offset. _Why:_ this points to where the attribute’s content begins. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Creation-time bytes** — Bytes `BE 2A CD E6 D1 1F D2 01` at offset `0000010:8` are labeled as creation time. _Why:_ this is the raw FILETIME value for created time. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Content-modified-time bytes** — Bytes `BE 2A CD E6 D1 1F D2 01` at offset `0000020:0` are labeled as content modified time. _Why:_ this is the raw FILETIME value for file-content modification. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Metadata-modified-time bytes** — Bytes `BE 2A CD E6 D1 1F D2 01` at offset `0000020:8` are labeled as metadata modified time. _Why:_ this is the raw FILETIME value for MFT-entry metadata modification. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Last-accessed-time bytes** — Bytes `BE 2A CD E6 D1 1F D2 01` at offset `0000030:0` are labeled as last accessed time. _Why:_ this is the raw FILETIME value for access time. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Flags bytes** — Bytes `20 00 00 00` at offset `0000030:8` are labeled as flags. _Why:_ this stores file attribute flags within `$STANDARD_INFORMATION`. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Max-versions bytes** — Bytes `00 00 00 00` at offset `0000030:C` are labeled as max versions. _Why:_ this field is part of the standard information structure. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Version-number bytes** — Bytes `00 00 00 00` at offset `0000040:0` are labeled as version number. _Why:_ this field is present in the shown `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` layout. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Class-ID bytes** — Bytes `00 00 00 00` at offset `0000040:4` are labeled as class ID. _Why:_ this field is part of the displayed metadata structure. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Owner-ID bytes** — Bytes `00 00 00 00` at offset `0000040:8` are labeled as owner ID. _Why:_ this field can connect file metadata to ownership-related identifiers. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Security-ID bytes** — Bytes `8E 0A 00 00` at offset `0000040:C` are labeled as security ID. _Why:_ this identifier links the file to security descriptor metadata. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Quota-charged bytes** — Bytes `00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` at offset `0000050:0` are labeled as quota charged. _Why:_ this field records quota accounting data in the attribute structure. _[GCFA p.768]_
- **Update-sequence-number bytes** — Bytes `68 FB F6 4F 00 00 00 00` at offset `0000050:8` are labeled as update sequence number. _Why:_ this field records a sequence value associated with file metadata changes. _[GCFA p.768]_

## Page 769

### NTFS Timestamp Presentation

- **End-user timestamp set** — the timestamps discussed on this page are the authoritative NTFS times shown to users, even though related time values may exist elsewhere. _Why:_ investigators should distinguish user-facing timestamps from other internal filesystem time artifacts. _[GCFA p.~769]_

### `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` Flags Offset

- **Flags field offset** — the file-attribute flags are stored at offset `0x38`. _Why:_ this offset tells an examiner where to locate the attribute bitmask inside the structure. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Flags field purpose** — the flags record filesystem attributes for the file, such as whether it is hidden or read-only. _Why:_ these bits can explain file visibility, indexing behavior, compression, encryption, and other forensic characteristics. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Flag encoding model** — each listed flag value represents one individual bit set to `1`. _Why:_ multiple file attributes are interpreted by decoding the bitmask rather than reading a single enumerated value. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Example flag value `0x20`** — a flags value of `0x20` indicates that the Archive bit is set. _Why:_ this demonstrates how a single attribute is decoded from the bitmask. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Example combined flag value `0x2608`** — a flags value of `0x2608` indicates Archive, Hidden, System, and Compressed are all set. _Why:_ combined values reveal multiple simultaneous file attributes and must be decomposed bit by bit. _[GCFA p.~769]_

### File Attribute Flag Table

- **Directory flag** — value `10 00 00 00` maps to the Directory attribute. _Why:_ this identifies an MFT record as representing a directory rather than an ordinary file. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Read Only flag** — value `01 00 00 00` maps to the Read Only attribute. _Why:_ this attribute can affect file modification behavior and user expectations. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Offline flag** — value `00 10 00 00` maps to the Offline attribute. _Why:_ this can indicate data may not be immediately resident or locally available. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Temporary flag** — value `00 01 00 00` maps to the Temporary attribute. _Why:_ this can help classify files intended for short-lived use. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Archive flag** — value `20 00 00 00` maps to the Archive attribute. _Why:_ this is a common file state bit and appears in the page’s example decoding. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Hidden flag** — value `02 00 00 00` maps to the Hidden attribute. _Why:_ hidden files may be missed during casual review but remain visible in filesystem metadata. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Not Indexed flag** — value `00 20 00 00` maps to the Not Indexed attribute. _Why:_ this can affect whether file content or metadata is discoverable through indexing artifacts. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Sparse File flag** — value `00 02 00 00` maps to the Sparse File attribute. _Why:_ sparse allocation affects how logical file size relates to physical disk usage. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Device flag** — value `40 00 00 00` maps to the Device attribute. _Why:_ this identifies a special file attribute value that differs from normal user data files. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **System flag** — value `04 00 00 00` maps to the System attribute. _Why:_ system files often require special handling during triage and interpretation. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Encrypted flag** — value `00 40 00 00` maps to the Encrypted attribute. _Why:_ this can indicate NTFS encryption and potential access constraints for forensic collection. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Reparse Point flag** — value `00 04 00 00` maps to the Reparse Point attribute. _Why:_ reparse points can redirect path interpretation and affect filesystem traversal. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Normal flag** — value `80 00 00 00` maps to the Normal attribute. _Why:_ this identifies the baseline file attribute state when special attributes are not present. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Compressed flag** — value `00 08 00 00` maps to the Compressed attribute. _Why:_ compression changes storage behavior and may affect acquisition or parsing workflows. _[GCFA p.~769]_

### Tracking Numbers And NTFS System Files

- **Remaining property fields** — the remaining properties store tracking numbers used for the file by NTFS metadata indexes. _Why:_ these values link the file record to entries elsewhere in the filesystem metadata. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **`$Secure` tracking use** — one set of tracking numbers is used by the `$Secure` system file. _Why:_ `$Secure` parsing may require these identifiers to connect security metadata back to a file. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **`$Quota` tracking use** — one set of tracking numbers is used by the `$Quota` system file. _Why:_ quota metadata may refer to files using internal NTFS identifiers rather than paths. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **`$UsnJrnl` tracking use** — one set of tracking numbers is used by the `$UsnJrnl` system file. _Why:_ USN journal entries can reference files by these tracking values, making them important for activity reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Filesystem-local uniqueness** — the tracking numbers are unique identifiers for this file within the relevant filesystem indexes. _Why:_ they should be interpreted only in the context of the filesystem that assigned them. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **No meaning outside the filesystem** — these tracking identifiers do not carry useful meaning beyond the filesystem where they were assigned. _Why:_ investigators should not treat them as portable identifiers across volumes or systems. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Security ID distinction** — the Security ID in this NTFS context is not the same as the Windows SID used to identify a user. _Why:_ confusing these two identifiers can lead to incorrect attribution or security interpretation. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Importance for `$Secure` parsing** — the tracking fields are critical when analyzing `$Secure`. _Why:_ some `$Secure` entries may point back to a file only by the tracking number stored here. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Importance for `$UsnJrnl` parsing** — the tracking fields are critical when analyzing `$UsnJrnl`. _Why:_ some USN journal entries may identify the file only through the tracking number rather than a filename or path. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Version dependence** — most of these tracking fields exist only in NTFS versions `3.0` and `3.1`. _Why:_ parser expectations must account for NTFS version differences when these fields are absent or present. _[GCFA p.~769]_

### Reference Material

- **Windows `MFT_SEGMENT_REFERENCE` structure** — the page points to Microsoft documentation for the Windows `MFT_SEGMENT_REFERENCE` structure at `http://for508.com/n0k-4`. _Why:_ this structure helps explain how NTFS references MFT records. _[GCFA p.~769]_
- **Brian Carrier reference** — the page cites Brian Carrier’s *File System Forensic Analysis*, pages `353-355` and `360-362`. _Why:_ these sections provide supporting filesystem-forensics detail for the NTFS metadata concepts discussed. _[GCFA p.~769]_

## Page 770

### $FILE_NAME Attribute Purpose

- **$FILE_NAME attribute role** — The `$FILE_NAME` attribute stores metadata for a file-system object, including file or directory properties, its name, its parent directory reference, and an additional timestamp set. _Why:_ `$FILE_NAME` is a second metadata source inside an MFT record that can corroborate or conflict with `$STANDARD_INFORMATION`. _[GCFA p.770]_

- **$FILE_NAME object-type coverage** — `$FILE_NAME` applies to both files and directories. _Why:_ investigators should check this attribute for directory records as well as ordinary file records. _[GCFA p.770]_

- **$FILE_NAME attribute flags** — `$FILE_NAME` can record file or directory attributes such as ReadOnly, Hidden, and Archive. _Why:_ these flags can reveal object properties that affect visibility, handling, or user interpretation. _[GCFA p.770]_

- **$FILE_NAME name storage** — `$FILE_NAME` stores the file or directory name associated with the MFT entry. _Why:_ the filename in `$FILE_NAME` is a direct naming artifact for the object being examined. _[GCFA p.770]_

- **Example filename** — The example `$FILE_NAME` value names the object `winclient.reg`. _Why:_ this shown value identifies the file represented by the example MFT entry. _[GCFA p.770]_

- **Parent directory reference** — `$FILE_NAME` contains the MFT entry number for the object's parent directory. _Why:_ this links the file or directory to its containing folder and supports path reconstruction. _[GCFA p.770]_

- **Additional timestamp set** — `$FILE_NAME` contains four timestamps separate from the commonly displayed Windows timestamps. _Why:_ alternate timestamp sets are useful for detecting inconsistencies, movement, or timestamp manipulation. _[GCFA p.770]_

- **Windows display limitation** — The four timestamps in `$FILE_NAME` are not normally surfaced by Windows user-facing views. _Why:_ analysts must use forensic tooling rather than relying only on Windows Explorer or standard Windows displays. _[GCFA p.770]_

- **Namespace Type offset** — Offset `0x59` in the `$FILE_NAME` attribute stores the Namespace Type value, which identifies the naming convention used for the file name. _Why:_ this byte explains whether the name is POSIX, Win32, DOS 8.3, or shared Win32/DOS format. _[GCFA p.772]_
- **Namespace Type `0x00` · POSIX** — Value `0x00` indicates a POSIX-style name where letter case is retained and case differences make names distinct. _Why:_ this affects name comparison and can explain multiple names that differ only by capitalization. _[GCFA p.772]_
- **Namespace Type `0x01` · Win32** — Value `0x01` identifies a Win32 long-name entry. _Why:_ this marks a long file name stored in `$FILE_NAME`. _[GCFA p.772]_
- **Namespace Type `0x02` · DOS** — Value `0x02` identifies a DOS-compatible short-name entry. _Why:_ this distinguishes an 8.3 alias from the longer Win32 name. _[GCFA p.772]_
- **Namespace Type `0x03` · Win32/DOS** — Value `0x03` means the name is short enough that one `$FILE_NAME` attribute can satisfy both Win32 and DOS naming requirements. _Why:_ this explains why some files have only one `$FILE_NAME` attribute instead of separate long and short names. _[GCFA p.772]_

### Multiple `$FILE_NAME` Attributes

- **Long file name behavior** — A file with a longer name such as `This is a Really Long Name.txt` receives two `$FILE_NAME` attributes. _Why:_ NTFS preserves both the long name and a DOS-compatible alias. _[GCFA p.772]_
- **Long-name `$FILE_NAME` purpose** — One `$FILE_NAME` attribute stores the long name while preserving capitalization. _Why:_ this preserves the user-facing Win32 name for forensic interpretation. _[GCFA p.772]_
- **DOS 8.3 `$FILE_NAME` purpose** — A second `$FILE_NAME` attribute stores a DOS-compatible 8.3 short name. _Why:_ the short alias can reveal additional filename metadata and timestamps. _[GCFA p.772]_

- **Three timestamp sets per file** — A file can have three timestamp groups: one `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` set and two `$FILE_NAME` sets. _Why:_ investigators must compare all available timestamp sources, not only the values shown by common user tools. _[GCFA p.772]_
- **Directory index timestamp source** — Directory index entries use the same layout as the `$FILE_NAME` attribute. _Why:_ directory indexes can provide another timestamp set for the same file. _[GCFA p.772]_
- **Additional timestamp opportunity** — Because directory indexes mirror `$FILE_NAME` structure, they can add yet another timestamp group for a file. _Why:_ this can provide corroborating or conflicting time evidence. _[GCFA p.772]_

### NTFS Timestamp Scope

- **NTFS timestamp sets** — NTFS stores two separate timestamp groups, and those groups do not update identically. _Why:_ analysts must compare timestamp families rather than assuming one universal MACB behavior. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **$STANDARD_INFORMATION focus** — the page documents file timestamp behavior for the `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` attribute. _Why:_ this attribute is one of the core NTFS sources for file time interpretation. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **$FILE_NAME contrast** — `$FILE_NAME` timestamp rules are identified as separate from `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` and deferred to the following slide. _Why:_ differences between these two NTFS attributes can reveal file activity and inconsistencies. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **File-only applicability** — the listed rules apply to files, not directories. _Why:_ applying file rules to folders can lead to incorrect timeline conclusions. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Tested interfaces** — the rules are based on testing with Windows File Explorer and the `cmd.exe` shell. _Why:_ timestamp behavior may depend on the interface or subsystem used to perform an action. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Windows version context** — the table is labeled for `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` on Windows 11 version 22H2. _Why:_ timestamp behavior can vary across Windows releases. _[GCFA p.773]_

### General Caveats

- **Rules are generalizations** — the page frames the timestamp behaviors as usually correct but not absolute. _Why:_ investigators should treat them as strong heuristics, not immutable laws. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Windows 10+ variability** — frequent Windows 10 and later changes can alter timestamp behavior. _Why:_ OS build context matters when validating timeline interpretations. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Last-access exception** — beginning with Windows 10 version 1803, last-access updates may be re-enabled in some circumstances. _Why:_ analysts cannot always assume last-access suppression on modern Windows systems. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **`NTFSDisableLastAccessUpdate` reference** — the page cites changes involving the `NTFSDisableLastAccessUpdate` key and links to `https://for508.com/4hzc-`. _Why:_ this setting directly affects whether access times are useful in a case. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **WSL exception** — Windows Subsystem for Linux updates timestamps differently from the displayed Windows shell rules. _Why:_ file activity through WSL can produce timeline artifacts that do not match Explorer or `cmd.exe` expectations. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **13Cubed reference** — Richard Davis’s “13Cubed” Windows MACB timestamp video is cited as testing many timestamp behaviors. _Why:_ external testing helps validate edge cases beyond the course table. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **WSL timing in video** — around 23 minutes into the cited video, WSL Bash is shown not following normal Windows shell timestamp behavior. _Why:_ investigators should consider WSL as a distinct execution context when interpreting file times. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **13Cubed short link** — the cited Windows MACB timestamp video link is `https://for508.com/qp3tb`. _Why:_ the link identifies the supporting timestamp-behavior demonstration. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Imperfect-rule utility** — the page states that rules that are usually correct can still help infer likely system activity. _Why:_ forensic conclusions often rely on weighted interpretation rather than perfect determinism. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Edge-case warning** — analysts are warned that abnormal timestamp behavior can occur. _Why:_ unexpected timestamp patterns should prompt validation instead of automatic dismissal or overconfidence. _[GCFA p.773]_

### $STANDARD_INFORMATION · Modified Timestamp Rules

- **Modified timestamp · File Creation** — set to the time the file was created. _Why:_ this establishes the initial modified value for a newly created file. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Modified timestamp · File Access** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ a simple access event should not be inferred from the modified timestamp. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Modified timestamp · File Modification** — set to the time the file data changed. _Why:_ this timestamp is a primary indicator of content modification. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Modified timestamp · File Rename** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ renaming alone should not be mistaken for content modification. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Modified timestamp · File Copy (new file)** — inherited from the source file. _Why:_ a copied file may have a modified time older than its creation time, which can indicate copying. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Modified timestamp · Local File Move** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ moving a file within the same local context does not necessarily alter its content-modified time. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Modified timestamp · Volume File Move via CLI** — inherited from the original file. _Why:_ command-line movement across volumes can preserve the content-modified value from the source. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Modified timestamp · Volume File Move via Explorer cut/paste** — inherited from the original file. _Why:_ Explorer cut/paste across volumes can preserve the source modified time, affecting copy-versus-move interpretation. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Modified timestamp · Shift-delete File Deletion** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ deletion does not itself update the file’s modified timestamp in this rule set. _[GCFA p.773]_

### $STANDARD_INFORMATION · Access Timestamp Rules

- **Access timestamp · File Creation** — set to the time the file was created. _Why:_ new files begin with access time aligned to creation under this rule. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Access timestamp · File Access** — set to the time the file was accessed. _Why:_ when enabled and applicable, this timestamp can record read/access activity. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Access timestamp · File Modification** — set to the time file data was modified. _Why:_ data modification can also refresh access time, affecting MACB interpretation. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Access timestamp · File Rename** — set to the time the file was renamed. _Why:_ rename activity may be visible through access time in this rule set. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Access timestamp · File Copy (new file)** — set to the time the copy was made. _Why:_ access time can help distinguish the copied object from the original. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Access timestamp · Local File Move** — set to the time of the local move. _Why:_ same-volume or local movement can leave an access-time trace. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Access timestamp · Volume File Move via CLI** — set to the time of the command-line file move. _Why:_ CLI-driven volume moves can be reflected in access time. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Access timestamp · Volume File Move via Explorer cut/paste** — set to the time of the cut/paste operation. _Why:_ Explorer-based cross-volume movement can be visible through access time. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Access timestamp · Shift-delete File Deletion** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ deletion should not be inferred solely from a changed access timestamp under this rule. _[GCFA p.773]_

### $STANDARD_INFORMATION · Metadata Timestamp Rules

- **Metadata timestamp · File Creation** — set to the time the file was created. _Why:_ the MFT metadata-change time initializes when the file record is created. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Metadata timestamp · File Access** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ access alone does not necessarily modify file-record metadata. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Metadata timestamp · File Modification** — set to the time file data was modified. _Why:_ content changes also alter NTFS metadata state. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Metadata timestamp · File Rename** — set to the time the file was renamed. _Why:_ rename activity changes metadata even when file contents are unchanged. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Metadata timestamp · File Copy (new file)** — inherited from the original file. _Why:_ this inherited value can complicate interpretation of when the copied file’s metadata record was created. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Metadata timestamp · Local File Move** — set to the time of the local move. _Why:_ moving a file locally can update NTFS metadata even if content is untouched. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Metadata timestamp · Volume File Move via CLI** — set to the time of the command-line move. _Why:_ CLI volume movement leaves a metadata-change timing artifact. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Metadata timestamp · Volume File Move via Explorer cut/paste** — set to the time of the cut/paste operation. _Why:_ Explorer cross-volume movement updates metadata timing in this rule set. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Metadata timestamp · Shift-delete File Deletion** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ permanent deletion does not necessarily alter the retained metadata timestamp value. _[GCFA p.773]_

### $STANDARD_INFORMATION · Creation Timestamp Rules

- **Creation timestamp · File Creation** — set to the time the file was created. _Why:_ this is the baseline birth time for the file object. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Creation timestamp · File Access** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ reading or opening a file should not be treated as evidence of new file creation. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Creation timestamp · File Modification** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ content edits do not change the original creation time in this rule set. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Creation timestamp · File Rename** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ renaming does not reset the file’s creation time. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Creation timestamp · File Copy (new file)** — set to the time the copy was made. _Why:_ a new copied file receives a new creation time even while other timestamps may be inherited. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Creation timestamp · Local File Move** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ moving a file locally does not create a new file object for timestamp purposes. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Creation timestamp · Volume File Move via CLI** — set to the time of the command-line move. _Why:_ a CLI move across volumes can create a new destination object with a new creation time. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Creation timestamp · Volume File Move via Explorer cut/paste** — inherited from the original file. _Why:_ Explorer cut/paste across volumes can preserve creation time, making it differ from CLI behavior. _[GCFA p.773]_
- **Creation timestamp · Shift-delete File Deletion** — remains unchanged. _Why:_ deletion does not rewrite the original creation timestamp under these rules. _[GCFA p.773]_

- **$FILE_NAME timestamp testing scope** — The page reports Windows 11 version 22H2 timestamp behavior for the NTFS `$FILE_NAME` attribute. _Why:_ `$FILE_NAME` timestamps can differ from `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` timestamps and provide independent forensic evidence. _[GCFA p.~774]_
- **$FILE_NAME rules differ from $STANDARD_INFORMATION rules** — The same file-operation tests produce different timestamp outcomes when examining `$FILE_NAME` values. _Why:_ investigators should not assume both NTFS timestamp attribute sets follow identical update logic. _[GCFA p.~774]_
- **$FILE_NAME timestamp discrepancies as evidence** — Differences between `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` and `$FILE_NAME` creation times may point to timestomping. _Why:_ mismatched creation times can expose timestamp manipulation attempts. _[GCFA p.~774]_
- **$FILE_NAME creation-time similarity to $STANDARD_INFORMATION** — The `$FILE_NAME` creation timestamp updates under rules that are nearly the same as the `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` creation timestamp rules. _Why:_ this similarity makes creation-time disagreement between the two attributes especially suspicious. _[GCFA p.~774]_

## Page 776

### Timestomping Overview

- **Timestomping** — Attackers and malware developers often alter file timestamps so malicious files appear ordinary among legitimate system files. _Why:_ timestamp camouflage can reduce the chance that analysts notice newly introduced malware during timeline review. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Tool-dependent timestomping artifacts** — The forensic traces left by timestamp manipulation differ depending on which utility or method performed the change. _Why:_ detection logic must account for tool behavior instead of assuming every timestomped file will show the same anomaly. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Legitimate timestamp modification** — Timestamp changes are not always malicious; some normal applications intentionally adjust file times. _Why:_ analysts must separate expected application behavior from attacker-driven anti-forensics. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Illegitimate timestamp modification** — Attackers modify timestamps to make malicious files blend into surrounding operating-system or application files. _Why:_ this is a common anti-forensic tactic intended to mislead timeline-based triage. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Timestomp tool origin** — The term “timestomping” is associated with an early NTFS timestamp-changing utility named `timestomp`. _Why:_ knowing the origin clarifies that the term usually refers to malicious timestamp alteration, not all timestamp changes generally. _[GCFA p.~776]_

### Timestamp Anomaly Checks

- **$STANDARD_INFORMATION birth time before $FILE_NAME birth time** — A file whose `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` creation value is earlier than its `$FILE_NAME` creation value is listed as a detection anomaly. _Why:_ inconsistency between NTFS timestamp sources can indicate that only one metadata location was altered. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Zeroed fractional seconds** — Timestamp values with all fractional-second fields set to zero are listed as suspicious. _Why:_ naturally generated Windows file times normally have subsecond precision, while older manual timestamp tools often lacked that granularity. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **$STANDARD_INFORMATION modified time before ShimCache or Amcache evidence** — A `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` modified timestamp earlier than related ShimCache or Amcache evidence is listed as an anomaly. _Why:_ execution or program-inventory artifacts may contradict a backdated file timestamp. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **$STANDARD_INFORMATION time before executable compile time** — A file timestamp in `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` that predates the executable’s compile timestamp is listed as suspicious. _Why:_ a binary cannot normally exist on disk before it was compiled, so this mismatch can expose backdating. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **$STANDARD_INFORMATION time before $I30 slack evidence** — `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` timestamps earlier than related `$I30` slack entries are listed as an anomaly. _Why:_ directory-index remnants can preserve historical timing evidence that conflicts with the file’s current metadata. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **USN Journal contradiction** — USN Journal records that conflict with the file’s current creation timestamp are listed as suspicious. _Why:_ the journal can retain filesystem activity history that reveals a different creation sequence than the current MFT timestamps show. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Unexpected MFT entry sequence** — An MFT record number outside the expected allocation range is listed as an anomaly. _Why:_ MFT numbering can provide context about when a file record was allocated relative to neighboring filesystem activity. _[GCFA p.~776]_

### Cloud Sync Timestamp Behavior

- **Cloud sync as a legitimate timestamp-change scenario** — Modern cloud synchronization software is given as a normal reason file timestamps may be changed. _Why:_ not every backdated file is attacker-created; sync clients may intentionally preserve metadata across devices. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Dropbox example** — Dropbox is used as an example of a cloud provider whose client may alter timestamps during synchronization. _Why:_ investigators may encounter Dropbox-created timestamp patterns during endpoint analysis. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Cross-device modification-time consistency** — Cloud-synced files are expected to show the same last-modified time across multiple devices. _Why:_ consistent modification times help represent when the user last edited the content rather than when each local copy appeared. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **User-change time as preferred modified time** — For synchronized files, the desired last-modified timestamp corresponds to the user’s actual last content change. _Why:_ this explains why cloud tools may overwrite the host-created modification timestamp. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **New host perspective** — When a cloud client downloads files onto a newly configured system, the local host initially treats those files as newly created local objects. _Why:_ the filesystem’s native view can differ from the cloud provider’s historical metadata. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Windows new-file timestamp initialization** — Windows assigns all timestamps on a newly created file to the creation moment. _Why:_ this default behavior creates a mismatch when cloud files are newly materialized but historically older. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Cloud metadata mismatch** — The Windows creation-time default for a newly synced local file may not match the modification time tracked by the cloud provider. _Why:_ this mismatch is why cloud clients may rewrite timestamps after synchronization. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Cloud clients sync data and metadata** — Cloud storage applications can synchronize both file contents and selected timestamp metadata. _Why:_ analysts must consider application-level metadata restoration when interpreting NTFS times. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Provider-specific timestamp syncing** — The exact set of timestamps preserved during synchronization varies by cloud provider. _Why:_ investigators should avoid assuming all sync products update the same NTFS fields. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Minimum common sync behavior** — Most cloud synchronization tools preserve at least the last-modified timestamp. _Why:_ modified time is the most likely timestamp to be intentionally backdated by legitimate sync software. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Dropbox backdating behavior** — In the Dropbox example, the client changes newly synced local files to the modification time stored by Dropbox. _Why:_ this can create older-looking timestamps on files that were just downloaded to the endpoint. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Windows API timestamp setting** — The Dropbox example states that the client performs the timestamp backdating through Windows API calls. _Why:_ legitimate timestamp alteration can use normal operating-system interfaces rather than raw disk modification. _[GCFA p.~776]_

### Attacker Timestamp Camouflage

- **Malware blending objective** — Attackers modify timestamps so malware resembles nearby files on the target system. _Why:_ similar timestamps make malicious files less obvious during directory sorting or timeline review. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **System32 placement example** — A classic attacker tactic is placing malware in `C:\Windows\System32`. _Why:_ that directory contains many legitimate Windows components, so malicious files may be harder to notice there. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Impersonating standard Windows processes** — Malware placed in `C:\Windows\System32` may be intended to look like a normal Windows process. _Why:_ location-based trust can bias manual inspection and triage. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Filename camouflage** — Attackers can rename malware to appear legitimate. _Why:_ plausible naming reduces suspicion when analysts or users inspect filesystem listings. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Timestamp camouflage in target directory** — Attackers improve the deception by changing malware timestamps to resemble other files in the same directory. _Why:_ matching surrounding timestamps helps the malicious file avoid standing out as recently added. _[GCFA p.~776]_

### Historical Detection Limitations

- **Older offensive-tool weakness** — Earlier attacker tools had limitations that made some backdated timestamps easier to identify. _Why:_ historical artifacts explain why certain timestomping checks work well against older tooling but may be weaker against newer utilities. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Manual timestamp setting limitation** — Many older tools used for manual timestamp changes did not support fractional-second precision. _Why:_ lack of subsecond data creates unnatural timestamp patterns. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Windows timestamp resolution** — Windows timestamps can represent time at 100-nanosecond precision. _Why:_ this precision makes all-zero fractional seconds unusual for normally generated file timestamps. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Exact-second timestamp anomaly** — A timestamp landing exactly on a whole second, with zero decimal-place values, is described as unlikely to be naturally generated. _Why:_ exact-second values can expose manually assigned or tool-generated timestamps. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **$STANDARD_INFORMATION versus $FILE_NAME creation mismatch** — Analysts historically checked for differences between `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` and `$FILE_NAME` creation timestamps. _Why:_ mismatched NTFS creation values can show that a tool altered one timestamp source but missed another. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Older tools often missed $FILE_NAME timestamps** — Many earlier timestamp-changing tools could not update `$FILE_NAME` timestamp values. _Why:_ unmodified `$FILE_NAME` metadata could preserve evidence of the file’s true creation timing. _[GCFA p.~776]_
- **Newer tool development** — The page notes that newer timestamp manipulation tools have since been created. _Why:_ analysts should not rely only on older detection assumptions, because modern tools may alter more timestamp sources or preserve subsecond precision. _[GCFA p.~776]_

## Page 777

### Timestomping Detection Limits

- **Reference-file timestamp copying** — some timestomping utilities can copy every timestamp from a benign reference file onto a malicious file. _Why:_ this can bypass simple checks that look only for obvious timestamp inconsistencies. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Copied-good-file timestamps defeat prior checks** — when a malicious file receives the same timestamps as a trusted-looking file, the two earlier detection approaches discussed before this page may no longer reveal the manipulation. _Why:_ analysts should not rely on a single timestomp-detection heuristic. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Multiple timestamp checks** — the recommended approach is to combine several independent checks when looking for suspicious timestamp behavior. _Why:_ no single timestamp anomaly test is reliable enough by itself. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Timestamp checks are not definitive** — every timestamp-anomaly method on the page has exceptions or failure cases. _Why:_ findings should be treated as leads that require corroboration, not automatic proof. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Scope timestamp hunting to already-suspicious files** — intensive timestamp anomaly review should focus on files already identified as suspicious by other evidence. _Why:_ broad timestamp hunting can create too many false positives to be useful. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **False positives in timestamp analysis** — legitimate system and user activity can produce timestamp patterns that look unusual. _Why:_ abnormal timestamps alone can mislead an investigation. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Cloud sync as legitimate timestamp alteration** — cloud storage synchronization is one legitimate reason file timestamps may change. _Why:_ timestamp changes are not automatically malicious. _[GCFA p.~777]_

### $FILE_NAME Versus $STANDARD_INFORMATION

- **$FILE_NAME to $STANDARD_INFORMATION comparison** — compare timestamps stored in `$FILE_NAME` attributes against timestamps stored in `$STANDARD_INFORMATION`. _Why:_ mismatches can expose timestomping by tools that do not update every NTFS timestamp source consistently. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Manual timestamp input risk** — timestomping tools are more likely to leave detectable `$FILE_NAME` versus `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` differences when an operator manually supplies timestamp values. _Why:_ manually chosen values may be applied incompletely or inconsistently. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **mftecmd for timestamp comparison** — `mftecmd` can be used to compare `$FILE_NAME` timestamps with `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` timestamps. _Why:_ it can expose timestomp artifacts in MFT metadata. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **fls for timestamp comparison** — `fls` can assist with comparing `$FILE_NAME` and `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` timestamp data. _Why:_ Sleuth Kit filesystem output can support NTFS timestamp anomaly review. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **istat for timestamp comparison** — `istat` can be used to inspect timestamp data needed for `$FILE_NAME` versus `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` comparison. _Why:_ it exposes file metadata useful for validating timestamp consistency. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **FTK Imager for timestamp comparison** — FTK Imager can assist in checking `$FILE_NAME` timestamps against `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` timestamps. _Why:_ GUI forensic tooling can still reveal NTFS timestamp discrepancies. _[GCFA p.~777]_

### Fractional-Second Checks

- **Zeroed fractional seconds** — check whether timestamp decimal places are all zero. _Why:_ some timestomping tools create timestamps with missing or zeroed sub-second precision. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Sub-second timestamp anomaly** — timestamps with all-zero fractional seconds may indicate artificial timestamp assignment. _Why:_ normal filesystem activity often preserves sub-second resolution, while manual timestomping may not. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Manual timestamp values and zeroed decimals** — zeroed fractional seconds are especially relevant when a perpetrator manually specifies a timestamp. _Why:_ human-supplied timestamps often lack realistic sub-second granularity. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Tool limitation for sub-second review** — fewer forensic tools support this check because not every tool displays sub-second timestamp precision. _Why:_ an analyst may miss the artifact if the chosen tool truncates timestamp detail. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **mftecmd sub-second support caveat** — `mftecmd` is useful for fractional-second review, but not when using body file format output. _Why:_ body file format output does not preserve the needed sub-second detail for this check. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **istat for fractional-second review** — `istat` can support checking timestamps for zeroed fractional seconds. _Why:_ it can expose timestamp precision needed to spot this timestomp artifact. _[GCFA p.~777]_

### ShimCache Comparison

- **ShimCache alternate name** — ShimCache is also known as AppCompatCache. _Why:_ tools and references may use either term for the same Windows artifact. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **ShimCache comparison target** — when available, compare the ShimCache timestamp for an executable with that executable’s `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` modification time. _Why:_ disagreement can reveal that the executable’s current modification time was changed. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Application Compatibility subsystem activity** — when Windows detects an executable, the Application Compatibility subsystem examines it. _Why:_ that examination can create a cache record useful for forensic comparison. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **ShimCache hive location** — ShimCache data is stored in the `SYSTEM` registry hive. _Why:_ the analyst must know which hive contains the artifact for collection and parsing. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **ShimCache records executable observation** — Windows adds detected executables to ShimCache. _Why:_ this can prove that Windows observed the executable at some point. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **ShimCache stores first-observed `$SI` modification time** — ShimCache includes the executable’s `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` last modification time as it existed when Windows first observed the file. _Why:_ this creates an older reference value that can be compared against current file metadata. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Executable modification expectation** — executables usually are not modified after creation during normal use. _Why:_ unexpected executable modification-time changes are more suspicious than similar changes on many document types. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Modification time should not move backward** — an executable’s modification time is not expected to change to an earlier value after Windows has observed it. _Why:_ a backward-moving timestamp is consistent with backdating. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Expected ShimCache match** — ShimCache’s stored timestamp and the executable’s current `$SI` modification time should normally match. _Why:_ matching values support the idea that the on-disk modification time was not later backdated. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Backdated executable indicator** — if a suspicious executable’s current `$SI` modification time is much earlier than the ShimCache date, that strongly indicates modification-time alteration. _Why:_ ShimCache preserves a prior view of the file that can contradict the current MFT timestamp. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Filesystem tools for `$SI` M-time** — the previously listed filesystem tools can be used to check the current `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` last modification time. _Why:_ the current on-disk timestamp is one side of the ShimCache comparison. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **AppCompatCacheParser.exe** — `AppCompatCacheParser.exe` can parse ShimCache data for comparison against file timestamps. _Why:_ it extracts the cache timestamp needed to identify backdating. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **ShimCacheParser.py** — `ShimCacheParser.py` can parse ShimCache data for timestamp comparison. _Why:_ it provides another way to obtain the ShimCache timestamp used in timestomp analysis. _[GCFA p.~777]_

### Executable Compile-Time Comparison

- **Embedded compile-time check** — for executables, compare the embedded compile timestamp against the file’s timestamps on disk. _Why:_ impossible or illogical ordering can reveal timestamp manipulation. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Compile time should precede disk creation** — an executable should not have a compile time later than the time it was written to disk. _Why:_ compilation creates the executable, so a file cannot normally exist before it is compiled. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Filesystem tools for executable disk timestamps** — the same filesystem tools referenced earlier can be used to check executable `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` timestamps. _Why:_ disk metadata provides the comparison point for embedded compile time. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Windows PE parsers for compile time** — most Windows PE parsers can be used to inspect executable compile timestamps. _Why:_ the compile timestamp is stored in PE metadata rather than NTFS metadata. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Sysinternals sigcheck** — Sysinternals `sigcheck` can be used to examine executable compile-time information. _Why:_ it is a practical tool for comparing PE metadata against filesystem timestamps. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **ExifTool for compile time** — Phil Harvey’s ExifTool can inspect executable compile-time metadata. _Why:_ it is versatile enough to support PE timestamp review during timestomp analysis. _[GCFA p.~777]_

### Parent Directory Index Evidence

- **Parent directory index as historical source** — for any file type, older information about a file may remain in the file’s parent directory index. _Why:_ directory index remnants can preserve metadata that differs from the current file record. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **`$I30` directory indexes** — `$I30` directory indexes are NTFS directory structures that will be discussed later in the course. _Why:_ they can contain file metadata useful for reconstructing past states. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Directory index stores file name** — `$I30` directory index entries contain the file name. _Why:_ the name ties stale metadata to a specific file artifact. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Directory index stores full `$SI` timestamp set** — `$I30` directory index entries include a complete set of `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` timestamps. _Why:_ these timestamps may show values before later timestomping. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Directory index stores MFT entry number** — `$I30` directory index entries contain the file’s MFT entry number. _Why:_ this helps associate the index entry with the correct file record. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Directory index stores sequence number** — `$I30` directory index entries include the MFT sequence number. _Why:_ the sequence number helps conclusively track the file and distinguish reused MFT records. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Stale directory index entries** — old entries may remain in the parent directory index after file activity. _Why:_ stale entries can preserve a prior timestamp set. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Previous timestamps from `$I30`** — stale `$I30` entries may reveal timestamps that existed before the current metadata values. _Why:_ prior values can expose later timestamp changes. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Backdating indicator from `$I30`** — if older directory-index metadata shows timestamps more recent than the file’s current timestamps, that indicates possible timestamp backdating. _Why:_ current timestamps should not normally be earlier than preserved prior values for the same file. _[GCFA p.~777]_

### USN Journal Evidence

- **USN Journal filesystem visibility** — the USN Journal provides strong visibility into file changes on an NTFS filesystem. _Why:_ it can independently record activity that file timestamps may later try to hide. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **USN Journal creation-time relevance** — USN Journal data can include file creation-time-related evidence. _Why:_ this can help reconstruct when a file was actually created. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Original creation time recovery** — the USN Journal may allow an analyst to find the original creation time of a backdated file. _Why:_ original creation evidence can contradict a manipulated current creation timestamp. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **USN comparison method** — compare the file’s current creation time with the creation time recorded by the USN Journal. _Why:_ discrepancies can reveal that the current creation timestamp was altered. _[GCFA p.~777]_

### MFT Allocation Pattern

- **NTFS efficiency behavior** — the Windows NTFS driver attempts to minimize unnecessary work during filesystem operations. _Why:_ this implementation behavior creates predictable artifact patterns. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Next-available MFT record allocation** — when creating new files, NTFS writes them into the next available MFT records. _Why:_ file creation order can sometimes be inferred from nearby MFT record allocation. _[GCFA p.~777]_
- **Many files created together** — if many new files are created at about the same time, they are likely to receive nearby MFT records. _Why:_ clustered MFT entry numbers can corroborate a batch creation event or expose timestamps inconsistent with allocation order. _[GCFA p.~777]_

## Page 778

### MFT Record Number Sequencing

- **Sequential MFT record numbers** — NTFS file records may appear in roughly increasing order when many files are created during the same installation or creation event. _Why:_ record-number ordering can provide a second timeline signal beyond timestamps. _[GCFA p.778]_

- **Non-perfect MFT sequencing** — MFT record numbers used for comparison do not have to be exactly consecutive to be useful; close clustering can still be meaningful. _Why:_ investigators should look for relative record-number proximity rather than requiring a perfectly continuous sequence. _[GCFA p.778]_

- **System32 install-time clustering** — Files under `C:\Windows\System32` commonly have MFT records near one another because many are created sequentially during operating system installation. _Why:_ this directory can provide a baseline cluster for detecting later-created outliers. _[GCFA p.778]_

- **Install-created files in `C:\Windows\System32`** — Most files placed in `C:\Windows\System32` during OS installation are created around the same creation event. _Why:_ their timestamps and MFT record numbers can form an expected population for comparison. _[GCFA p.778]_

### Backdated Malware Detection

- **Malware staged in `C:\Windows\System32`** — An attacker may place a malicious file in `C:\Windows\System32` after the operating system has already been installed. _Why:_ this location is commonly trusted and crowded, making malicious files easier to hide visually. _[GCFA p.778]_

- **Backdating to blend in** — An attacker may alter the malware’s timestamps so they appear similar to legitimate `C:\Windows\System32` files. _Why:_ timestomping can defeat simple timestamp-based file review. _[GCFA p.778]_

- **Standard file listing weakness** — A normal directory listing sorted or reviewed by timestamps may show the malicious file within the same apparent time range as legitimate files. _Why:_ timestamp-only triage can miss files whose times were intentionally manipulated. _[GCFA p.778]_

- **Timestamp proximity as concealment** — When malicious file timestamps are close to surrounding legitimate files, the malicious file becomes harder to distinguish in ordinary listings. _Why:_ attackers exploit the investigator’s reliance on visible timestamp similarity. _[GCFA p.778]_

- **MFT record number as outlier signal** — A backdated malicious file created much later will probably have an MFT record number outside the nearby range of legitimate install-time files. _Why:_ MFT allocation order may expose creation chronology even when timestamps were modified. _[GCFA p.778]_

- **Late-created file record behavior** — Because the attacker’s file is created after the original install-time files, its MFT record is unlikely to be close to the legitimate files’ MFT records. _Why:_ this mismatch can reveal timestomping or late file introduction. _[GCFA p.778]_

### Tooling And Workflow

- **Filesystem timelining tools** — Tools that enumerate filesystem records are recommended for checking timestamp and MFT-record consistency. _Why:_ complete filesystem output allows investigators to compare multiple ordering dimensions. _[GCFA p.778]_

- **Output-all-records requirement** — The preferred tools are those that output all file records rather than only selected files. _Why:_ full-record output supports sorting and outlier detection across the whole directory or volume. _[GCFA p.778]_

- **Sort by timestamp** — Investigators should sort filesystem timeline output by file times during this check. _Why:_ timestamp sorting shows which files appear to belong to the same time cluster. _[GCFA p.778]_

- **Sort by MFT record number** — Investigators should also sort filesystem timeline output by MFT record number. _Why:_ record-number sorting can reveal files whose allocation order conflicts with their apparent timestamps. _[GCFA p.778]_

- **`mftecmd`** — `mftecmd` is named as an example tool suitable for producing filesystem timeline data for this analysis. _Why:_ it can help compare file timestamps against MFT record ordering. _[GCFA p.778]_

- **`fls`** — `fls` is named as another example tool suitable for filesystem record enumeration. _Why:_ it can list filesystem metadata useful for timeline and MFT-order analysis. _[GCFA p.778]_

### Referenced Resources

- **ForensicsWiki timestomp.exe article** — The page references an archived ForensicsWiki article about `timestomp.exe` at `https://for508.com/zdyx9`. _Why:_ `timestomp.exe` is relevant background for understanding timestamp manipulation tools. _[GCFA p.778]_

- **ExifTool reference** — The page references Phil Harvey’s ExifTool at `https://for508.com/clize`. _Why:_ ExifTool is relevant to metadata inspection or modification in forensic workflows. _[GCFA p.778]_

- **Expected Windows 11 task host filename** — the legitimate Windows 11 filename referenced on the page is `taskhostw.exe`. _Why:_ distinguishing `taskhost.exe` from `taskhostw.exe` helps detect impostor binaries. _[GCFA p.779]_

- **Four-check timestomp approach** — the page demonstrates four separate timestamp checks against the suspicious executable. _Why:_ multiple independent checks reduce reliance on any single noisy indicator. _[GCFA p.779]_

- **MFTECmd sub-second precision** — CSV output includes fractional-second timestamp precision. _Why:_ fractional seconds can reveal artificial timestamp values such as zeroed sub-second fields. _[GCFA p.779]_
- **MFTECmd built-in anomaly checks** — MFTECmd CSV output includes automated anomaly fields. _Why:_ built-in checks help triage large MFT datasets for suspicious timestamp relationships. _[GCFA p.779]_

### `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` Versus `$FILE_NAME`

- **`$SI Creation time < $FN Creation time` check** — the page highlights the condition where `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` creation precedes `$FILE_NAME` creation. _Why:_ that ordering can reveal that only one timestamp source was backdated. _[GCFA p.779]_
- **False-positive caution for `$SI < $FN`** — the `$SI` earlier-than-`$FN` condition can produce many false positives if used alone. _Why:_ analysts should not treat this relationship as conclusive without corroborating artifacts. _[GCFA p.779]_
- **True-positive context for `taskhost.exe`** — in this case, the `$SI < $FN` condition supported a true timestomping finding when combined with other evidence. _Why:_ corroboration converted a noisy anomaly into a meaningful detection. _[GCFA p.779]_
- **MFTECmd `SI<FN` anomaly name** — MFTECmd labels the `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` earlier-than-`$FILE_NAME` check as `SI<FN`. _Why:_ knowing the exact column name helps analysts locate the check in CSV output. _[GCFA p.779]_

### Zeroed Fractional Seconds

- **All-zero fractional seconds check** — the page highlights `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` creation timestamps whose fractional-second portion is entirely zeros. _Why:_ natural filesystem timestamps often contain nonzero fractional values, so zeroed sub-seconds can suggest manipulation. _[GCFA p.779]_
- **MFTECmd `u Sec Zeros` anomaly name** — MFTECmd labels the all-zero fractional-second anomaly as `u Sec Zeros`. _Why:_ this column provides an automated way to locate suspicious timestamp precision artifacts. _[GCFA p.779]_
- **MFTECmd output limitation for `u Sec Zeros`** — `u Sec Zeros` is available when MFTECmd is not producing bodyfile output. _Why:_ analysts must choose an output mode that preserves this anomaly check. _[GCFA p.779]_

- **ShimCache comparison heading** — the page compares ShimCache time against filesystem modification time. _Why:_ disagreement between execution-evaluation artifacts and file metadata can expose backdating. _[GCFA p.779]_

## Page 780

### NTFS $DATA Attribute Basics

- **$DATA attribute** — NTFS stores file content through the `$DATA` attribute. _Why:_ this is the core NTFS attribute to inspect when determining where a file’s bytes are stored. _[GCFA p.~780]_
- **Non-resident $DATA** — when file content is non-resident, the `$DATA` attribute records the disk clusters that contain the file’s bytes. _Why:_ cluster listings let an examiner locate and recover file content outside the MFT record. _[GCFA p.~780]_
- **Resident $DATA** — when file content is roughly 700 bytes or smaller, NTFS may store the content inside the `$DATA` attribute itself. _Why:_ small files may be recoverable directly from MFT records without reading external clusters. _[GCFA p.~780]_
- **Resident-file extraction with MFTECmd** — `MFTECmd` can extract resident files from an `$MFT` when run with the `--dr` option. _Why:_ this provides a direct way to recover small resident file contents from MFT evidence. _[GCFA p.~780]_
- **Multiple $DATA streams** — a single NTFS file can have more than one `$DATA` stream. _Why:_ examiners must check beyond the primary stream or they may miss hidden or secondary content. _[GCFA p.~780]_
- **Alternate Data Streams (ADS)** — additional `$DATA` streams are alternate data streams and must have names. _Why:_ named streams can hold secondary content such as metadata or concealed payloads. _[GCFA p.~780]_
- **Primary $DATA stream** — the main file content stream is the unnamed `$DATA` attribute. _Why:_ distinguishing unnamed primary data from named ADS content prevents misinterpreting metadata streams as the main file. _[GCFA p.~780]_
- **$DATA type signature** — the `$DATA` attribute uses signature value `0x80`, which is decimal `128`. _Why:_ this type value identifies file-content attributes in MFT parsing output and raw NTFS structures. _[GCFA p.~780]_

### $DATA Attribute Header Fields

- **Attribute signature field** — the header diagram labels the first displayed bytes as the attribute signature. _Why:_ the signature identifies which NTFS attribute type is being parsed. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Attribute signature value** — the displayed signature bytes are `80 00 00 00`. _Why:_ this exact byte sequence identifies the shown attribute as a `$DATA` attribute. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Attribute length field** — the diagram labels the next displayed bytes as the total attribute length. _Why:_ the parser needs this size to know how far the attribute record extends. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Attribute length value** — the displayed length bytes are `48 00 00 00`. _Why:_ this records the shown attribute’s length in the MFT attribute entry. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Resident-status field** — the byte at offset `0x08` controls whether the attribute content is stored inside the MFT record or elsewhere on disk. _Why:_ this determines whether an examiner reads content directly from the attribute or follows cluster-mapping information. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Resident-status value in example** — offset `0x08` contains `01`. _Why:_ the shown `$DATA` attribute is non-resident, so the data runs must be interpreted to locate file content. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Resident encoding** — a resident attribute is indicated by value `0x00`. _Why:_ this tells an examiner the attribute’s payload is contained within the MFT entry. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Non-resident encoding** — a non-resident attribute is indicated by value `0x01`. _Why:_ this tells an examiner the attribute contains mapping information rather than the file bytes themselves. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Starting virtual cluster number field** — the diagram labels one header area as the first VCN covered by the attribute extent. _Why:_ this anchors the logical cluster range represented by the data runs. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Starting VCN value in example** — the displayed starting VCN bytes are all `00`. _Why:_ this shows the run list begins at logical cluster zero for the file content. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Ending virtual cluster number field** — the diagram labels one header area as the last VCN covered by the attribute extent. _Why:_ this bounds the logical cluster range represented by the non-resident attribute. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Ending VCN value in example** — the displayed ending VCN bytes are all `00`. _Why:_ the example’s logical cluster range covers only the initial cluster. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Offset-to-data-run field** — the diagram labels the header value that points from the attribute start to the data-run list. _Why:_ this offset tells a parser where the cluster mapping entries begin. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Offset-to-data-run value** — the displayed bytes for the data-run offset begin with `40 00 00 00`. _Why:_ this indicates the run list starts at offset `0x40` in the shown attribute. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Allocated-size field** — the diagram labels a header field for the disk space assigned to the file data. _Why:_ this separates reserved cluster space from the file’s logical content size. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Allocated-size bytes in example** — the displayed allocated-size bytes are `00 10 00 00 00 00 00 00`. _Why:_ these bytes record the storage allocated to the non-resident content. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **True-size field** — the diagram labels a header field for the actual content length. _Why:_ this value is the file’s meaningful byte count, excluding slack. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **True-size bytes in example** — the displayed true-size bytes are `94 07 00 00 00 00 00 00`. _Why:_ these bytes record the actual data size for the example file content. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Initialized-size field** — the diagram labels a header field for the amount of allocated space initialized for the file. _Why:_ this distinguishes usable initialized data from merely reserved future growth space. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Initialized-size bytes in example** — the displayed initialized-size bytes are `94 07 00 00 00 00 00 00`. _Why:_ these bytes show the initialized amount matches the true size in the example. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Data-runs field** — the diagram labels the bytes beginning at the run-list area as data runs. _Why:_ these entries map logical file content to physical cluster locations. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Padding field** — the diagram labels the bytes after the run list as padding. _Why:_ padding fills unused bytes after the meaningful data-run entries. _[GCFA p.781]_

### Resident Versus Non-Resident $DATA Content

- **Post-header `$DATA` content behavior** — after the `$DATA` attribute header, the remaining attribute content either stores the actual file bytes or stores metadata for locating those bytes in clusters. _Why:_ this is the basic distinction an examiner must resolve before recovering file content. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Resident `$DATA` content** — when the resident flag indicates residence, the attribute body contains the file content itself. _Why:_ a parser can extract the content from the MFT record without reading external clusters. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Non-resident `$DATA` content** — when the resident flag indicates non-residence, the attribute body provides the information needed to determine which clusters contain the file data. _Why:_ file recovery requires translating the run list into disk locations. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Offset `0x08` role** — byte offset `0x08` in the attribute header is the resident/non-resident indicator. _Why:_ this single byte changes the interpretation of the attribute payload. _[GCFA p.781]_

### Virtual Cluster Numbers

- **Virtual Cluster Numbers (VCNs)** — VCNs describe the file’s logical clusters in continuous order. _Why:_ they let NTFS track the ordered logical content independently of physical disk placement. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **VCN ordering purpose** — VCNs represent the ordered sequence of clusters that compose file content. _Why:_ forensic reconstruction depends on placing clusters in the correct file order. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Typical starting VCN** — VCN sequences normally begin at zero, except for unusual cases. _Why:_ a zero starting point is the normal baseline when validating a run list. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Typical ending VCN meaning** — the ending VCN normally reflects the count of clusters consumed by the file content. _Why:_ it helps verify whether the run list accounts for the expected amount of data. _[GCFA p.781]_

### Size Fields

- **Allocated Size** — allocated size is the cluster space consumed by the file, including both content and slack space. _Why:_ this value shows how much disk space is tied up by the file, not just how much data the file logically contains. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **File slack inclusion** — allocated size includes slack beyond the file’s true content. _Why:_ slack can contain residual data and matters in forensic examination. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **True Size** — true size is the actual length of the file’s meaningful content. _Why:_ this is the value used to distinguish file bytes from padding or slack. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Initialized Size** — initialized size is the amount of space set aside for the file to grow into. _Why:_ it records preallocated capacity that is not necessarily part of current file content. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Initialized-size semantics** — Windows may reserve growth space for a file without treating that reserved area as current file content. _Why:_ examiners should not confuse reserved capacity with actual file bytes. _[GCFA p.781]_

### Data Run Structure

- **Data runs** — a data run is a sequence of entries describing where each file segment starts and how long it is. _Why:_ non-resident file content is recovered by interpreting these segment mappings. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Data-run segmentation** — each data-run entry maps one segment of the file. _Why:_ multiple entries are how NTFS represents fragmented file data. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Data-run entry header** — every data-run entry begins with a one-byte header. _Why:_ this header tells the parser how many following bytes belong to the length and offset fields. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Data-run header nibbles** — the one-byte data-run header is split into two four-bit fields. _Why:_ each nibble encodes the size of a different part of the run entry. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Example data-run bytes** — the displayed run-list bytes are `41 01 9B 5B D4 00 00 00`. _Why:_ these are the exact bytes used to demonstrate run-list decoding. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Example data-run header byte** — the first byte of the run entry is `0x41`. _Why:_ this byte controls how the rest of the run entry is parsed. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Run-length size encoded by `0x41`** — header `0x41` indicates that one following byte stores the run length. _Why:_ the parser must consume exactly one byte for the length field. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Run-length value in example** — the one-byte length field is `0x01`. _Why:_ this means the run covers one cluster. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Run-offset size encoded by `0x41`** — header `0x41` indicates that four following bytes store the run’s starting-cluster offset. _Why:_ the parser must consume four bytes for the location field. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Run-offset bytes in example** — the starting-cluster offset bytes are `9B 5B D4 00`. _Why:_ these bytes provide the physical starting cluster information for the run. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Little-endian run-offset interpretation** — bytes `9B 5B D4 00` decode to cluster `0x00D45B9B`. _Why:_ NTFS stores the value little-endian, so byte order must be reversed for interpretation. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Displayed alternate offset notation** — the text also presents the four offset bytes as `0x9B5BD400` before explaining the little-endian result. _Why:_ this shows the raw byte order before conversion to the cluster value. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **End-of-runs marker** — the byte after the example run fields is `0x00`. _Why:_ this marks the end of the data-run list. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Cluster-run length statement** — the example’s cluster run length is `0x01` clusters. _Why:_ this confirms that the file content occupies one cluster in the demonstrated run. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Starting cluster statement** — the example’s run starts at cluster `0x00D45B9B`. _Why:_ this is the physical cluster location needed to read the file data. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Little-endian storage statement** — the starting cluster value is stored in little-endian byte order. _Why:_ failing to reverse the byte order would point to the wrong cluster. _[GCFA p.781]_

### Fragmentation Interpretation

- **Non-fragmented example** — the example file is not fragmented because it has only one data run. _Why:_ a single run means the relevant content is stored contiguously for this example. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Single-cluster example** — the demonstrated file uses only one cluster. _Why:_ this reinforces why only one data run is needed in the example. _[GCFA p.781]_
- **Fragmented-file indicator** — a fragmented file has at least two data runs. _Why:_ multiple run entries show that the file content is split across more than one disk extent. _[GCFA p.781]_

## Page 782

### Alternate Data Streams Concept

- **Alternate Data Stream (ADS)** — an ADS exists when an NTFS file record contains an additional `$DATA` attribute beyond the unnamed primary data stream. _Why:_ investigators can identify ADS by inspecting file-record attributes rather than relying on ordinary file listings. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Primary `$DATA` stream** — the main stream is the `$DATA` attribute whose name length is `0x00`, meaning it has no stored stream name. _Why:_ distinguishing unnamed primary data from named ADS data is required when parsing NTFS records. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Primary stream naming rule** — the unnamed primary data stream effectively takes its user-visible filename from the file’s `$FILE_NAME` attribute. _Why:_ the primary stream is addressable by the normal filename even though the `$DATA` attribute itself has no name. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Named subsequent `$DATA` attributes** — every `$DATA` attribute after the primary one must have a name so that the stream can be individually referenced. _Why:_ named streams are how ADS content can be addressed separately from the primary file content. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **ADS compared to multiple `$FILE_NAME` attributes** — multiple `$DATA` attributes are conceptually similar to NTFS files having more than one `$FILE_NAME` attribute. _Why:_ this frames ADS as normal NTFS attribute multiplicity rather than a separate filesystem object. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Resident ADS name placement** — for resident ADS attributes, the stream name is stored as a Unicode string immediately before the stream content. _Why:_ parsers must account for the name occupying space before resident stream bytes begin. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Nonresident ADS name placement** — for nonresident ADS attributes, the Unicode stream name is stored immediately before the data-run information. _Why:_ nonresident ADS parsing requires locating the name before interpreting cluster run mappings. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Nonresident ADS content representation** — if an ADS is nonresident, the `$DATA` attribute stores data runs rather than inline file content. _Why:_ analysts must switch from reading resident bytes to resolving cluster runs when stream data is nonresident. _[GCFA p.~782]_

### Resident `$DATA` Attribute Parsing

- **Resident indicator offset** — offset `0x8` in the `$DATA` attribute stores the resident/nonresident indicator. _Why:_ this byte determines whether content is inline in the MFT record or referenced by runs elsewhere on disk. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Resident indicator value** — value `0x00` at offset `0x8` means the `$DATA` attribute is resident. _Why:_ resident data can be recovered directly from the attribute body. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Name-length offset** — offset `0x9` stores the length of the attribute name. _Why:_ the name-length byte determines whether the stream is unnamed primary data or a named ADS. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Primary stream name length** — a name length of `0x00` means the stream has no stored name. _Why:_ this identifies the primary data stream. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Name-offset field** — after the name-length byte, the attribute records the relative offset where a name would begin. _Why:_ stream-name extraction depends on this offset when a name exists. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **No name at offset `0x18` for primary stream** — when the name length is `0x00`, no name bytes are stored at the listed name offset `0x18`. _Why:_ a parser should not treat bytes at that location as a stream name for the primary attribute. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Resident content-length offset** — offset `0x10` stores the resident content length. _Why:_ this value tells the examiner how many bytes of inline content to read. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Resident content-offset field** — offset `0x14` stores the relative offset to the beginning of resident content. _Why:_ content recovery starts at this attribute-relative location. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Unnamed resident offset equality** — when a resident `$DATA` attribute has a zero-length name, the name offset and content offset are the same. _Why:_ this explains why the primary stream’s content begins where a name would otherwise have started. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Resident content extraction method** — to recover resident content, jump to the content offset and read the number of bytes specified by the content length. _Why:_ this is the direct recovery procedure for resident primary streams and resident ADS. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **ADS name extraction method** — for the named ADS example, jump to relative offset `0x18` and read `name length * 2` bytes. _Why:_ NTFS stores the name in double-byte Unicode, so character count must be converted to byte count. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Unicode stream-name storage** — the ADS name uses two bytes per character. _Why:_ reading only one byte per character would truncate or misparse the stream name. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Named ADS offset separation** — the named ADS has different name and content offsets because the stream name occupies space before the content. _Why:_ parsers must not assume name offset and content offset match once a stream name exists. _[GCFA p.~782]_

### Windows and Macintosh Context

- **Windows NT origin** — ADS support was introduced in Windows NT as part of Services for Macintosh. _Why:_ ADS exists partly because NTFS needed to interoperate with Macintosh file concepts. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Resource Fork compatibility goal** — ADS was intended to let a Windows file server represent the Macintosh Resource Fork concept. _Why:_ this explains why NTFS can store multiple data streams for one file. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Mac client behavior** — Macintosh clients did not rely on NTFS ADS for that purpose and instead used a second hidden file to hold the extra data. _Why:_ the feature’s historical reason differs from how Mac clients actually behaved. _[GCFA p.~782]_

### Forensic Visibility and Metadata Limits

- **Primary-stream bias in Windows tooling** — much of Windows is built around the assumption that files have only the primary data stream. _Why:_ alternate streams may be absent from normal user and tool views. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **Tool-reporting limitation** — many tools cannot show that an alternate stream exists. _Why:_ ADS can hide data from tools that enumerate only normal file content. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **ADS size-reporting limitation** — many tools cannot report the size of an alternate stream. _Why:_ stream size can be missed unless ADS-aware tooling or direct NTFS parsing is used. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **ADS content-reporting limitation** — many tools cannot display or extract alternate-stream contents. _Why:_ hidden content can remain unexamined during incomplete forensic collection. _[GCFA p.~782]_
- **ADS metadata limitation** — no additional metadata for an alternate stream is maintained beyond the attribute information shown in the file-record layout. _Why:_ analysts should not expect a separate rich metadata record for each ADS. _[GCFA p.~782]_

## Page 783

### Alternate Data Streams

- **ADS hiding value** — NTFS alternate data streams can provide a useful location for concealing unauthorized tools or data. _Why:_ hidden stream content may not appear in ordinary file listings and can preserve attacker artifacts. _[GCFA p.783]_

- **Microsoft ADS restrictions** — Microsoft has previously limited some uses of alternate data streams to reduce abuse. _Why:_ platform controls may affect which ADS techniques work on a given Windows system. _[GCFA p.783]_

- **ADS restriction bypasses** — Attackers have continued to identify ways around Microsoft’s ADS-related restrictions. _Why:_ analysts should not assume ADS abuse is obsolete merely because mitigations exist. _[GCFA p.783]_

- **Unexpected ADS monitoring** — Forensic review should include checks for alternate data streams that are unusual or unexplained. _Why:_ unexpected streams can indicate hidden malware, staged data, or other anti-forensic activity. _[GCFA p.783]_
