## Page 801

### $UsnJrnl Purpose And Storage

- **$UsnJrnl** — NTFS stores the Update Sequence Number change journal in a hidden system file named `$UsnJrnl`. _Why:_ this is a core NTFS artifact for reconstructing file-system activity. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Change-tracking role** — `$UsnJrnl` records summary-level changes involving files and directories. _Why:_ it provides a compact activity timeline without requiring full file-system scans. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Reason codes** — `$UsnJrnl` entries include codes that identify the type of change that occurred. _Why:_ reason codes help classify activity such as creation, data growth, and close events. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Application use case** — applications use `$UsnJrnl` to identify which files require processing. _Why:_ this lets software react only to changed objects instead of inspecting the whole volume. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Windows Backup usage** — Windows Backup uses the change journal to find recently modified files that need backup. _Why:_ this explains why the artifact exists for normal operating-system workflows. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Efficiency advantage** — using `$UsnJrnl` is more efficient than periodically checking every file or backing up all files whether changed or not. _Why:_ the artifact exists because it avoids high-cost full-volume enumeration. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Other consumers** — antivirus tools can use `$UsnJrnl` change tracking. _Why:_ security software may leave indirect evidence of journal-dependent scanning behavior. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Windows Search Index** — Windows Search Index can use `$UsnJrnl` to detect file changes. _Why:_ search indexing activity depends on the same change-monitoring mechanism. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Windows File Replication Service** — Windows FRS can use `$UsnJrnl` change notifications. _Why:_ replication workflows may depend on these journal records. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Recovery support** — `$UsnJrnl` has some failure-recovery utility, including helping quickly re-index a volume. _Why:_ this distinguishes operational recovery use from forensic timeline use. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Primary purpose** — the main function of `$UsnJrnl` is efficient detection of file changes across a volume. _Why:_ investigators should treat it as a change-summary journal, not a full transaction log. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Default enablement** — Microsoft enabled `$UsnJrnl` by default starting with Windows Vista. _Why:_ default availability affects how often the artifact should be expected in cases. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Windows XP behavior** — on Windows XP, `$UsnJrnl` existed but was usually not enabled. _Why:_ absence on older systems may be normal rather than suspicious. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Windows 2000 behavior** — on Windows 2000, `$UsnJrnl` existed but was usually not enabled. _Why:_ version context matters when assessing artifact availability. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **$J alternate data stream** — the main journal data is stored in a large `$J` ADS. _Why:_ examiners must know where the high-volume journal content resides. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **$Max alternate data stream** — `$UsnJrnl` also has a `$Max` stream shown in the filesystem listing. _Why:_ the stream is part of the `$UsnJrnl` file’s metadata layout. _[GCFA p.801]_

### Comparison With $LogFile

- **$UsnJrnl concision** — compared with `$LogFile`, `$UsnJrnl` logging is more compact and consistent. _Why:_ it is easier to interpret during timeline reconstruction. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Same creation, fewer records** — the page shows 3 USN records for a file creation that produced more than two dozen `$LogFile` events on the previous slide. _Why:_ this demonstrates the summary nature of `$UsnJrnl` versus the transaction detail in `$LogFile`. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Interpretability** — `$UsnJrnl` events are easier to read because the journal summarizes changes. _Why:_ responders can quickly identify meaningful file activity. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Retention advantage** — active `$UsnJrnl` entries usually persist much longer than `$LogFile` entries. _Why:_ the change journal often gives investigators a broader lookback window. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Typical active-system retention** — active systems commonly retain several days to a week or more of `$UsnJrnl` records. _Why:_ this frames realistic expectations for timeline coverage. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Slide retention summary** — the slide states that `$UsnJrnl` tends to last a few days on active systems. _Why:_ active-volume churn limits how far back records remain available. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Secondary-drive retention** — secondary drives often retain `$UsnJrnl` records much longer, including week-scale retention. _Why:_ lower activity can preserve older evidence. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Less-active-system retention** — less active systems store `$UsnJrnl` records for longer durations than busy systems. _Why:_ usage level affects artifact survival. _[GCFA p.801]_

### USN Record Fields

- **Changed object name** — each USN record tracks the name of the changed file or folder. _Why:_ the object name ties the journal event to a visible filesystem item. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Changed object MFT number** — each USN record includes the MFT number of the changed object. _Why:_ MFT references help correlate journal entries with metadata records. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Parent directory MFT number** — each USN record includes the MFT number of the parent directory. _Why:_ this supports path reconstruction and parent-child correlation. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Change timestamp** — each USN record stores the time when the change was recorded. _Why:_ timestamps allow event ordering in a forensic timeline. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Reason code field** — each USN record includes a reason code describing what changed. _Why:_ the code distinguishes creation, data changes, closure, and other activity types. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **File size field** — each USN record tracks the changed file’s size. _Why:_ size can help identify growth, content creation, or correlation with other artifacts. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Attribute field** — each USN record tracks file attributes such as hidden, archived, and read-only. _Why:_ attribute states can indicate concealment, normal archival marking, or permission-related context. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Screenshot field limitation** — the page notes that not all USN fields fit in the displayed screenshot. _Why:_ the visible table is only a partial representation of the record structure. _[GCFA p.801]_

### Meaning Of “File” In Journals

- **Journal “File” terminology** — in the journals, “File” events refer to actions on MFT `FILE` entries. _Why:_ the label can apply to both files and directories, preventing misinterpretation. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **MFT FILE entries** — MFT `FILE` entries store metadata for files. _Why:_ journal events referencing `FILE` records can represent ordinary file objects. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Directory metadata in FILE entries** — MFT `FILE` entries also store metadata for directories. _Why:_ a `FileCreate` reason can indicate directory creation as well as file creation. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **FileCreate interpretation** — a `FileCreate` reason code indicates creation of a new file or directory. _Why:_ this reason code is a marker for new filesystem object creation. _[GCFA p.801]_
- **Creation marker** — the slide explicitly identifies the shown creation events as markers for file and directory creation. _Why:_ responders can use these records to identify object birth events. _[GCFA p.801]_

## Page 802

### Volume Shadow Copies And Retention

- **Change journal data in VSS** — NTFS change journal content can be preserved inside Volume Shadow Copies. _Why:_ shadow copies may extend the available history beyond the live journal. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Historical journal span** — When change journal data is present in shadow copies, investigators may find more than one month of journal history. _Why:_ this can substantially widen the reconstruction window for file activity. _[GCFA p.802]_

### $UsnJrnl Storage Layout

- **$UsnJrnl system file** — The NTFS change journal is associated with the hidden system file named `$UsnJrnl`. _Why:_ analysts must know the container file before extracting the artifact. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **$J alternate data stream** — Change journal records are stored in the `$J` alternate data stream of `$UsnJrnl`. _Why:_ `$UsnJrnl:$J` is the primary data stream that contains the change records used for analysis. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Record tracking method** — USN records are not assigned simple sequential record numbers. _Why:_ parsers and analysts should not expect a conventional row-number style record identifier. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Record offset tracking** — Each USN record is located by its byte offset within the `$J` stream. _Why:_ offsets function as the practical locator for individual journal entries. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **MFT-resident USN value** — Each file and directory has an Update Sequence Number stored in its MFT record. _Why:_ the MFT keeps a pointer-like value tied to the file system object’s latest journal activity. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **USN update trigger** — A file or directory’s Update Sequence Number is refreshed after each change to that object. _Why:_ the value can indicate where the most recent recorded change for that object is represented in the journal. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **USN points into `$J`** — The Update Sequence Number stored in the MFT identifies the location in `$J` where the corresponding change information is recorded. _Why:_ this links object metadata to the journal entry describing the change. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Variable-length USN records** — USN record size varies because filenames are not all the same length. _Why:_ offset-based tracking is efficient when records do not have a fixed byte size. _[GCFA p.802]_

### Extraction And Access

- **Primary extraction target** — For analysis, the `$J` alternate data stream is the part of `$UsnJrnl` that must be exported. _Why:_ exporting the wrong stream can miss the actual change records. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Locked artifact** — `$UsnJrnl` is locked by the operating system. _Why:_ ordinary file access may fail or provide incomplete access during live collection. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Hidden artifact** — `$UsnJrnl` is hidden as a system file. _Why:_ investigators usually need forensic-aware tooling rather than normal file browsing. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Forensic extraction tools** — Specialized forensic tools are generally required to collect `$UsnJrnl` data. _Why:_ the file’s locked and hidden status makes standard acquisition unreliable. _[GCFA p.802]_

### Sparse `$J` Stream Behavior

- **Large `$J` stream** — `$J` is commonly a very large sparse data stream. _Why:_ its apparent size affects collection planning and storage requirements. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Typical workstation `$J` size** — A typical workstation screenshot on the slide shows `$J` exceeding 3 GB. _Why:_ this gives a practical scale estimate for the artifact during acquisition. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Sparse file definition** — A sparse file contains large regions that logically exist but are filled with null bytes rather than meaningful data. _Why:_ sparse allocation explains why apparent size and disk usage can differ dramatically. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Null byte value** — Empty regions in the sparse file are represented as `0x00` null bytes. _Why:_ null-filled ranges matter when interpreting exported stream contents or carved data. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Sparse storage optimization** — Modern file systems can record where null-filled ranges should exist without physically writing all those null bytes. _Why:_ this saves disk capacity and reduces write activity. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Disk-space benefit** — Sparse file handling avoids storing long runs of null data on disk. _Why:_ the live artifact may occupy less physical storage than its logical size suggests. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **I/O benefit** — Sparse file handling reduces unnecessary input/output operations for null-filled ranges. _Why:_ the file system can manage a huge logical stream more efficiently. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Copy-out expansion** — When a sparse file is copied out normally, the file system may reinsert the null bytes into the copied file. _Why:_ an exported copy can become much larger than the live on-disk allocation. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Large exported sparse stream** — Extracting `$UsnJrnl:$J` commonly produces a large output file because null ranges are materialized during collection. _Why:_ acquisition storage and transfer sizing must account for the expanded copy. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Compression behavior** — Exported `$UsnJrnl:$J` data compresses effectively. _Why:_ null-heavy sparse data can often be reduced significantly after collection. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Remote collection challenge** — The large logical size of `$UsnJrnl:$J` can create problems when collecting it over a network. _Why:_ bandwidth, time, and remote triage constraints may become limiting factors. _[GCFA p.802]_

### Journal Size Management And Deleted Records

- **Sparse-file side effect** — The sparse design of `$UsnJrnl` creates a useful forensic side effect: recoverable unallocated records. _Why:_ deleted journal entries may remain available outside the active stream allocation. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Windows journal cap** — Windows typically caps `$UsnJrnl` at about 32 MB. _Why:_ the active journal is limited even though older records may still be recoverable elsewhere. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Journal size command** — The command `fsutil usn queryJournal` can be used to check the journal configuration. _Why:_ this provides a native way to inspect journal size-related metadata. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Sparse size illusion** — NTFS treats the sparse journal as though it is a much larger file than its allocated disk usage suggests. _Why:_ this behavior explains how allocation and deallocation can rotate through a logically huge stream. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Cluster allocation continuation** — The file system can keep allocating clusters to the existing sparse `$J` stream because it views the file as large and mostly null-filled. _Why:_ new journal records can be appended without creating a new file. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Initially unallocated null regions** — Large null-filled portions of `$J` may not have clusters allocated at first. _Why:_ this is the core sparse-file behavior that conserves disk usage. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **New record writes** — As new records are appended to the end of `$J`, NTFS detects that those ranges now contain non-null data. _Why:_ non-null data requires real storage allocation. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **New cluster allocation** — NTFS allocates additional clusters when newly appended journal data replaces previously sparse/null ranges. _Why:_ this is how current journal records become physically stored. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Old beginning marked sparse** — At the same time new records are added, Windows marks data at the beginning of `$J` as sparse/null. _Why:_ this ages out older active journal content while maintaining the stream structure. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Old cluster deallocation** — Marking the beginning of `$J` as sparse deallocates the clusters that previously held older journal data. _Why:_ those clusters may still contain recoverable USN record bytes until overwritten. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Stable on-disk footprint** — This allocation/deallocation process keeps `$J`’s physical disk usage relatively steady. _Why:_ the journal can behave like a rolling artifact without continuous growth. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **USN records in unallocated space** — Deallocated clusters can still contain old USN records in unallocated space. _Why:_ investigators may recover journal entries no longer present in the active `$J` stream. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Deleted USN record recovery** — A substantial number of deleted USN records can often be recovered. _Why:_ carved USN records can extend activity reconstruction beyond the active journal. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Record carving topic** — The course indicates that carving these records is covered later. _Why:_ recovery of deallocated USN entries is a distinct analysis technique. _[GCFA p.802]_

### `$Max` Stream

- **Second alternate data stream** — `$UsnJrnl` also has an alternate data stream named `$Max`. _Why:_ `$J` is not the only stream associated with the change journal file. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **`$Max` size** — `$Max` is typically about 32 bytes. _Why:_ its small size distinguishes it from the much larger `$J` data stream. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **`$Max` contents** — `$Max` stores metadata about the change journal. _Why:_ it contains configuration-oriented information rather than the journal record body. _[GCFA p.802]_
- **Maximum-size metadata** — `$Max` includes the journal’s maximum size value. _Why:_ this helps explain how the change journal is configured and bounded. _[GCFA p.802]_

## Page 803

### Journal Interpretation

- **NTFS journal analysis** — NTFS journal records can be difficult to interpret without recognizing repeated activity patterns. _Why:_ pattern knowledge helps convert low-level codes into investigator-meaningful actions. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **$LogFile interpretation difficulty** — $LogFile records are especially opaque compared with other NTFS journal data. _Why:_ analysts should avoid treating isolated $LogFile entries as self-explanatory evidence. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **Pattern-based detection** — The page provides common file-system actions with journal code combinations that can indicate those actions. _Why:_ combinations reduce the chance of false positives from individual codes. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **Code-combination requirement** — Analysts are advised to look for groups of related journal codes instead of relying on a single code. _Why:_ a lone journal operation may occur in multiple contexts. _[GCFA p.~803]_

### Common Activity Pattern Table

- **File/Directory Creation · $LogFile code 1** — creation activity is associated with `AddIndexEntryAllocation`. _Why:_ this code indicates a directory index entry being added for the new object. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **File/Directory Creation · $LogFile code 2** — creation activity is associated with `InitializeFileRecordSegment`. _Why:_ this code indicates preparation of an MFT record for the new file or directory. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **File/Directory Creation · $UsnJrnl code** — creation activity is associated with `FileCreate`. _Why:_ this USN reason code directly records a new file-system object being created. _[GCFA p.~803]_

- **File/Directory Deletion · $LogFile code 1** — deletion activity is associated with `DeleteIndexEntryAllocation`. _Why:_ this code indicates removal of the object's directory index entry. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **File/Directory Deletion · $LogFile code 2** — deletion activity is associated with `DeallocateFileRecordSegment`. _Why:_ this code indicates the MFT record segment was released from active use. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **File/Directory Deletion · $UsnJrnl code** — deletion activity is associated with `FileDelete`. _Why:_ this USN reason code directly records file or directory deletion. _[GCFA p.~803]_

- **File/Directory Rename or Move · $LogFile code 1** — rename or move activity is associated with `DeleteIndexEntryAllocation`. _Why:_ a rename or move removes the prior directory-index entry. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **File/Directory Rename or Move · $LogFile code 2** — rename or move activity is associated with `AddIndexEntryAllocation`. _Why:_ the renamed or moved object receives a new directory-index entry. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **File/Directory Rename or Move · $UsnJrnl code 1** — rename or move activity is associated with `RenameOldName`. _Why:_ this USN reason records the previous name side of the rename event. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **File/Directory Rename or Move · $UsnJrnl code 2** — rename or move activity is associated with `RenameNewName`. _Why:_ this USN reason records the new name side of the rename event. _[GCFA p.~803]_

- **ADS Creation · $LogFile code** — alternate data stream creation is associated with `CreateAttribute` where the created attribute name ends with `:ADS`. _Why:_ the stream name suffix marks the new named data stream rather than the unnamed default data stream. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **ADS Creation · $UsnJrnl code 1** — alternate data stream creation is associated with `StreamChange`. _Why:_ this USN reason indicates a named stream changed on the file. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **ADS Creation · $UsnJrnl code 2** — alternate data stream creation is associated with `NamedDataExtend`. _Why:_ this USN reason indicates growth of a named data stream. _[GCFA p.~803]_

- **File Data Modification · $LogFile limitation** — $LogFile operation codes are often inadequate by themselves for confirming file-content modification. _Why:_ analysts may need additional context before concluding that file data changed. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **File Data Modification · $UsnJrnl code 1** — file data modification is associated with `DataOverwrite`. _Why:_ this USN reason indicates existing file data was overwritten. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **File Data Modification · $UsnJrnl code 2** — file data modification is associated with `DataExtend`. _Why:_ this USN reason indicates file data grew. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **File Data Modification · $UsnJrnl code 3** — file data modification is associated with `DataTruncation`. _Why:_ this USN reason indicates file data was shortened. _[GCFA p.~803]_

### $UsnJrnl Analysis

- **$UsnJrnl readability** — $UsnJrnl reason codes are presented as easier to understand than $LogFile operations. _Why:_ USN records are generally quicker to triage during filesystem timeline analysis. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **$UsnJrnl documentation** — $UsnJrnl codes are described as better documented than $LogFile events. _Why:_ stronger documentation supports more confident interpretation. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **Microsoft USN explanations** — The course notes use Microsoft’s own explanations for USN codes. _Why:_ primary vendor definitions reduce ambiguity in reason-code interpretation. _[GCFA p.~803]_

### $LogFile Analysis

- **$LogFile documentation gap** — $LogFile events are described as less clear and less documented than $UsnJrnl reason codes. _Why:_ investigators must apply more interpretation and validation when using this artifact. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **Single action, many $LogFile events** — One file-system action can generate many $LogFile records. _Why:_ high event volume complicates reconstruction of user or system activity. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **$LogFile value despite complexity** — $LogFile analysis can still provide useful context when interpreted with NTFS structural knowledge. _Why:_ it may preserve evidence not available from other artifacts. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **$LogFile dependency on available data** — The usefulness of $LogFile analysis depends on the condition and availability of the files under examination. _Why:_ overwritten or absent records limit what can be reconstructed. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **$LogFile contains richer file details** — $LogFile can store more file-related information than $UsnJrnl. _Why:_ it can support deeper reconstruction than USN reason codes alone. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **$LogFile MFT attribute content** — $LogFile may include MFT attributes. _Why:_ MFT attribute details can reveal metadata that is no longer visible in the live file-system state. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **$LogFile $I30 content** — $LogFile may include `$I30` directory index records. _Why:_ directory index data can help reconstruct filenames, parent directories, and directory membership changes. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **$LogFile object-of-interest rule** — If $LogFile contains records for a relevant file or directory, the page recommends analyzing that data. _Why:_ the artifact may hold unique context about the object’s history. _[GCFA p.~803]_

### External Reference

- **Forensic Insight reference** — The page recommends the Forensic Insight presentation titled `NTFS Log Tracker` for more detail. _Why:_ it is identified as a useful secondary source for journal-pattern analysis. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **$LogFile event-analysis reference** — Within `NTFS Log Tracker`, the page specifically points to the section `The Event Analysis of $LogFile`. _Why:_ that section is described as helpful for breaking down complex $LogFile events. _[GCFA p.~803]_

### $I30 Index Operation Variants

- **AddIndexEntryAllocation equivalence** — When the page mentions `AddIndexEntryAllocation`, the corresponding operation may instead be `AddIndexEntryRoot`. _Why:_ the exact operation depends on where the directory index entry was stored. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **DeleteIndexEntryAllocation equivalence** — When the page mentions `DeleteIndexEntryAllocation`, the corresponding operation may instead be `DeleteIndexEntryRoot`. _Why:_ deletion from the index root and deletion from index allocation represent the same logical class of activity in different storage locations. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **$I30 storage-location dependency** — The distinction between root and allocation operations depends on the part of the `$I30` index tree that held the entry. _Why:_ analysts should map operation names to index structure before over-interpreting them. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **Index root location** — `$I30` root entries are stored inside the MFT record. _Why:_ small directory indexes may not require external allocated clusters. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **Index allocation location** — `$I30` allocation entries are stored in allocated clusters outside the MFT record. _Why:_ larger directories need additional storage beyond the resident root index. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **Large-directory requirement** — Allocated `$I30` clusters are only needed when directories grow large enough to exceed root-index storage. _Why:_ directory size affects which journal operation names appear. _[GCFA p.~803]_
- **Terminology simplification** — The page generally uses `AddIndexEntryAllocation` and `DeleteIndexEntryAllocation` as shorthand for the more common cases. _Why:_ analysts must remember that root variants may represent the same activity pattern. _[GCFA p.~803]_

## Page 804

### $LogFile Creation Markers

- **File or Directory Creation · $LogFile Activity Volume** — creating a file or directory causes NTFS to perform multiple underlying operations, so the `$LogFile` may contain several related records for one creation action. _Why:_ investigators should expect a cluster of low-level log entries rather than a single creation record. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Creation Marker · InitializeFileRecordSegment + AddIndexEntryAllocation** — the paired `$LogFile` operation codes `InitializeFileRecordSegment` and `AddIndexEntryAllocation` commonly indicate that a file or directory was created. _Why:_ the combination ties together MFT record allocation and parent-directory index insertion, making it a strong creation signature. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **InitializeFileRecordSegment** — this `$LogFile` operation records that NTFS initialized a new MFT `FILE` record for the newly created object. _Why:_ a new file or directory needs an MFT record to hold its metadata and attributes. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **New MFT FILE Record Requirement** — creating either a file or a directory requires NTFS to allocate a new `FILE` record in the Master File Table. _Why:_ the MFT record is the primary metadata container for the object. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **MFT Attribute Storage** — the newly allocated MFT `FILE` record stores attribute information for the created file or directory. _Why:_ attribute metadata is central to reconstructing the object's filesystem state. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **InitializeFileRecordSegment Payload** — the `$LogFile` entry for `InitializeFileRecordSegment` includes a copy of the data that NTFS intends to write into the MFT. _Why:_ the log can preserve recoverable MFT-record content relevant to the created object. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **InitializeFileRecordSegment Parsing Analogy** — parsing `InitializeFileRecordSegment` data is comparable to using `istat` to interpret MFT records. _Why:_ the event payload can expose MFT-style metadata without parsing the live MFT directly. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Tool Name · istat** — `istat` is referenced as a tool used earlier for parsing MFT records. _Why:_ it provides the conceptual comparison for interpreting logged MFT record payloads. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **AddIndexEntryAllocation** — this `$LogFile` operation records that NTFS created an index entry for the new file or directory in its parent directory. _Why:_ parent-directory index insertion is required for the object to appear in the directory namespace. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Parent Directory Index Requirement** — a newly created file or directory requires an index entry under its parent directory. _Why:_ the parent index links the object into the visible directory structure. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **AddIndexEntryAllocation Payload** — the `$LogFile` record for `AddIndexEntryAllocation` includes the data that will be inserted into the parent directory index. _Why:_ the log may contain directory-index evidence even if later filesystem state changes. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **$I30 Parsing Analogy** — parsing the `AddIndexEntryAllocation` payload is similar to parsing a `$I30` directory index entry. _Why:_ both expose directory-entry metadata useful for reconstructing file or directory presence. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Index Entry Field · Object Name** — the index-entry data can include the name of the file or directory. _Why:_ the name identifies what object was created. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Index Entry Field · MFT Record Number** — the index-entry data can include the created object's MFT record number. _Why:_ this links the directory entry to its MFT metadata record. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Index Entry Field · Parent MFT Record Number** — the index-entry data can include the MFT record number of the parent directory. _Why:_ this identifies where the object was placed in the directory hierarchy. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Index Entry Field · $STANDARD_INFORMATION Timestamps** — the index-entry data can include a complete set of `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` timestamps. _Why:_ these timestamps help reconstruct object timing and detect timeline inconsistencies. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Creation Evidence in $LogFile** — both MFT-record data and parent-directory index-entry data can be recorded in `$LogFile` during creation. _Why:_ `$LogFile` may provide multiple independent metadata views of the same created object. _[GCFA p.804]_

### $UsnJrnl Creation Markers

- **$UsnJrnl Abstraction Level** — `$UsnJrnl` reason codes describe filesystem activity at a higher level than `$LogFile` operation codes. _Why:_ they can summarize many lower-level NTFS changes into a simpler event trail. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **FileCreate** — the `$UsnJrnl` event code `FileCreate` is a clear indicator that a file or directory was created. _Why:_ it provides a direct high-level creation marker. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **USN Term · File** — in this context, `File` refers to an MFT `FILE` record, not only to ordinary user files. _Why:_ the same USN terminology can apply to both files and directories. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **FileCreate Scope** — `FileCreate` can indicate creation of either a file or a directory. _Why:_ analysts should not assume the event applies only to non-directory files. _[GCFA p.804]_

### $LogFile Deletion Markers

- **Deletion Is Creation-Like but Not Exact Reverse** — deleting files and directories resembles creation in reverse but is not described as a perfect inverse operation. _Why:_ investigators should use deletion-specific evidence rather than assuming every creation step simply reverses. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Deletion Component · MFT FILE Record Removal** — deletion involves removal or deallocation of the object's MFT `FILE` record. _Why:_ MFT record removal is one necessary component of deleting a file or directory. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Deletion Component · Parent Index Entry Removal** — deletion involves removing the object's index entry from its parent directory. _Why:_ directory-index removal disconnects the object from the parent namespace. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Deletion Marker · DeleteIndexEntryAllocation + DeallocateFileRecordSegment** — the paired `$LogFile` operation codes `DeleteIndexEntryAllocation` and `DeallocateFileRecordSegment` are a strong marker for deletion. _Why:_ together they represent removal from the parent index and deallocation of the MFT record. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **DeleteIndexEntryAllocation** — this `$LogFile` operation is associated with removing an index entry. _Why:_ it helps identify deletion, rename, or move activity depending on its paired events and metadata changes. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **DeallocateFileRecordSegment** — this `$LogFile` operation is associated with deallocating an MFT file record. _Why:_ it is a key low-level sign that the object itself was deleted. _[GCFA p.804]_

### $UsnJrnl Deletion Markers

- **FileDelete** — the `$UsnJrnl` event code `FileDelete` indicates deletion of a file or directory. _Why:_ it provides a direct high-level deletion marker. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **FileDelete Scope** — `FileDelete` can apply to either files or directories. _Why:_ analysts should treat it as an object-deletion indicator, not solely as ordinary-file deletion. _[GCFA p.804]_

### $LogFile Rename Markers

- **Rename Behavior · Old Name Index Removal** — when Windows renames a file or directory, it deletes the parent directory's index entry for the old name. _Why:_ the old name disappears from the directory index as part of the rename process. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Rename Behavior · New Name Index Creation** — when Windows renames a file or directory, it creates a new index entry using the new name. _Why:_ the new name is represented as a fresh directory-index entry. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Rename Marker · DeleteIndexEntryAllocation + AddIndexEntryAllocation** — the simultaneous occurrence of `DeleteIndexEntryAllocation` and `AddIndexEntryAllocation` in `$LogFile` is a strong rename indicator. _Why:_ it shows removal of one directory entry and creation of another for the renamed object. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Rename Timing Relationship** — the rename-signature `$LogFile` events are described as occurring at the same time. _Why:_ close temporal proximity helps distinguish a single rename operation from unrelated delete and add activity. _[GCFA p.804]_

### $UsnJrnl Rename Markers

- **RenameOldName** — during a rename, `$UsnJrnl` records a `RenameOldName` event containing the prior file or directory name. _Why:_ it preserves the object's name before the rename. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **RenameNewName** — during a rename, `$UsnJrnl` records a `RenameNewName` event containing the new file or directory name. _Why:_ it preserves the object's name after the rename. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Rename Event Order** — `$UsnJrnl` records `RenameOldName` immediately before `RenameNewName` for a rename. _Why:_ the sequence links the before-and-after names into one rename action. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Rename Documentation Value** — the `$UsnJrnl` rename pair both proves that a rename occurred and records the old and new names. _Why:_ this supports reconstruction of filename history. _[GCFA p.804]_

### $LogFile Move Markers

- **Move Behavior · Old Parent Index Removal** — moving a file or directory causes Windows to delete the object's index entry from the old parent directory. _Why:_ the object is removed from its previous directory location. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Move Behavior · New Parent Index Creation** — moving a file or directory causes Windows to create an index entry for the object in the new parent directory. _Why:_ the object is inserted into its new directory location. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Move Marker · DeleteIndexEntryAllocation + AddIndexEntryAllocation** — `$LogFile` records moves using the same event pair as renames: `DeleteIndexEntryAllocation` and `AddIndexEntryAllocation`. _Why:_ analysts must use metadata differences to distinguish movement from renaming. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Move vs Rename · Name Stability** — a move can be distinguished from a rename because the object's name does not change. _Why:_ unchanged filename with changed parent implies relocation rather than renaming. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Move vs Rename · Parent Directory Change** — a move can be distinguished from a rename because the parent directory changes. _Why:_ changed parent MFT record or directory context identifies movement across directories. _[GCFA p.804]_

### $UsnJrnl Move Markers

- **Move Event Pair · RenameOldName + RenameNewName** — `$UsnJrnl` records a move using the same event pair used for renames: `RenameOldName` followed by `RenameNewName`. _Why:_ this can be confusing unless the analyst compares names and parent locations. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Move Event Order** — for a move, `$UsnJrnl` records `RenameOldName` before the move and `RenameNewName` after the move. _Why:_ the before-and-after records bracket the relocation event. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Move vs Rename in $UsnJrnl · Name Stability** — a move can be separated from a rename in `$UsnJrnl` because the name remains unchanged. _Why:_ unchanged name suggests the action was not a pure rename. _[GCFA p.804]_

- **Move vs Rename in $UsnJrnl · Parent Directory Change** — a move can be separated from a rename in `$UsnJrnl` because the parent directory changes. _Why:_ parent change is the evidence of relocation. _[GCFA p.804]_

## Page 805

### Alternate Data Streams in $LogFile

- **ADS creation frequency** — Alternate data streams are not normally created in large numbers during routine activity. _Why:_ a small population of ADS-related events makes unusual stream creation easier to triage. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **ADS creation as anomaly signal** — Searching for newly created alternate data streams can reveal suspicious behavior. _Why:_ attackers may create streams for concealment or staging. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **ADS malware hiding technique** — Attackers can place malware in alternate data streams to make it less visible through ordinary file inspection. _Why:_ ADS can hide payload content behind a visible host filename. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Zone.Identifier ADS creation by downloads** — Downloaded executables or scripts may receive a `Zone.Identifier` alternate data stream. _Why:_ this stream records web-origin context and can affect execution behavior. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Mark of the Web relationship** — The `Zone.Identifier` ADS is the stream associated with Windows “Mark of the Web” handling. _Why:_ it can trigger Windows protections for downloaded content. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Executable blocking behavior** — Windows commonly blocks or restricts execution of downloaded executables when the `Zone.Identifier` ADS is present. _Why:_ this makes the stream relevant to both user protection and attacker cleanup. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **PowerShell script blocking behavior** — Windows commonly blocks or restricts PowerShell scripts when the `Zone.Identifier` ADS is present. _Why:_ script execution failures or bypasses may be tied to this ADS. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Attacker ADS deletion motive** — Attackers may remove the `Zone.Identifier` ADS to avoid Mark-of-the-Web execution restrictions. _Why:_ deletion of this stream can be an evasion step after download. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **$LogFile ADS deletion limitation** — Testing did not identify a clear $LogFile marker for alternate data stream deletion. _Why:_ absence of a simple deletion signature limits direct detection from $LogFile alone. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **$LogFile ADS creation visibility** — Testing did identify a clear $LogFile indicator for alternate data stream creation. _Why:_ creation events are more directly detectable than deletion events in this artifact. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **ADS name suffix in $LogFile records** — When $LogFile records refer to alternate data streams, the stream name is followed by `:ADS`. _Why:_ this suffix provides a practical search term for stream-related journal records. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Example ADS field value** — The example record value is `"name":"Zone.Identifier:ADS"`. _Why:_ it shows the exact style of stream-name representation to look for in parsed output. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **$LogFile CreateAttribute marker** — ADS creation produces a `CreateAttribute` record. _Why:_ this record type is a concrete indicator of a newly created NTFS attribute. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **CreateAttribute payload stream reference** — The `CreateAttribute` record includes payload data that names the stream with the `:ADS` suffix. _Why:_ payload review can identify which stream was created. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Low expected ADS event volume** — $LogFile output is unlikely to contain many alternate-data-stream references in ordinary conditions. _Why:_ reviewing all `:ADS` hits is likely manageable and high value. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Simple ADS triage query** — Reviewing all $LogFile events containing `:ADS` can surface notable stream activity. _Why:_ this is a direct hunting method for ADS-related behavior. _[GCFA p.805]_

### Alternate Data Streams in $UsnJrnl

- **$UsnJrnl ADS change coverage** — The $UsnJrnl records ADS creation, deletion, and rename activity. _Why:_ it captures stream lifecycle changes that may not be clear in $LogFile. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **StreamChange code** — The USN reason code `StreamChange` is used when an ADS is created, deleted, or renamed. _Why:_ this is the main USN marker for significant alternate-stream changes. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **StreamChange ambiguity** — `StreamChange` does not by itself specify whether the stream was created, deleted, or renamed. _Why:_ analysts need surrounding records to interpret the exact action. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **NamedDataExtend follow-on marker** — `NamedDataExtend` following `StreamChange` helps identify ADS creation. _Why:_ it indicates data was added to a named stream. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Named stream creation interpretation** — In the described ADS creation pattern, `NamedDataExtend` means the newly created named stream received data. _Why:_ this distinguishes creation-with-content from a generic stream change. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **USN ADS event timing gap** — Testing showed a possible delay of a few seconds between `StreamChange` and `NamedDataExtend`. _Why:_ correlation logic should allow a short time gap instead of requiring immediate adjacency. _[GCFA p.805]_

### File Data Modification in $LogFile

- **$LogFile metadata focus** — $LogFile records low-level changes to NTFS metadata structures. _Why:_ it is primarily a filesystem consistency log, not a high-level file content audit trail. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **$LogFile data-content limitation** — $LogFile does not directly monitor changes to file data content. _Why:_ analysts cannot simply search it for a definitive “file content modified” event. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **File data changes affect metadata** — Modifying file content still causes related NTFS metadata changes. _Why:_ indirect modification evidence may exist even when content changes are not directly logged. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **$Bitmap allocation metadata** — File content changes can alter `$Bitmap` allocation state. _Why:_ cluster allocation changes may be one indirect sign of file growth, shrinkage, or relocation. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **$DATA attribute metadata** — File content changes can modify the `$DATA` attribute. _Why:_ changes to data size, residency, or runs may reflect content updates. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **$STANDARD_INFORMATION timestamp metadata** — File content changes can update timestamps stored in `$STANDARD_INFORMATION`. _Why:_ timestamp updates can provide indirect evidence of modification. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **$FILE_NAME timestamp metadata** — File content changes can update timestamps stored in `$FILE_NAME`. _Why:_ comparison with other timestamp sources can support timeline interpretation. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Resident data variable** — Metadata changes differ depending on whether the file data is resident. _Why:_ resident content updates affect NTFS structures differently than non-resident data. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Non-resident data variable** — Metadata changes differ when file data is non-resident. _Why:_ cluster runs and allocation metadata may become relevant. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Resident-to-non-resident transition** — Metadata patterns vary when data changes from resident to non-resident storage. _Why:_ growth across this threshold can create metadata activity beyond a simple content update. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Non-resident-to-resident transition** — Metadata patterns vary when data changes from non-resident back to resident storage. _Why:_ analysts must account for storage-form changes when interpreting journal records. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Defragmentation complication** — Defragmentation can move file data to different clusters without changing the file’s content. _Why:_ $LogFile may show cluster movement that is not a true content modification. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Defrag cluster movement visibility** — $LogFile tracks the metadata effects of moving data to new clusters during defragmentation. _Why:_ location changes can be logged even when the user data is unchanged. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Metadata interpretation variability** — Multiple variables determine which metadata changes and how those changes should be interpreted. _Why:_ a single $LogFile pattern is not reliable for all file modifications. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Attribute update payload idea** — Because $LogFile records attribute updates, analysts might consider searching embedded payloads for timestamp updates. _Why:_ this appears promising for discovering file modification evidence. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **$STANDARD_INFORMATION timestamp payload** — $LogFile may include writes to `$STANDARD_INFORMATION`, including its timestamp set. _Why:_ those payloads can contain modification-time values. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Previous-value limitation** — $LogFile does not report the prior contents of an attribute. _Why:_ analysts cannot directly see what changed by comparing old and new values inside one record. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Pending-write semantics** — $LogFile records the data that is about to be written to an attribute. _Why:_ the logged payload is the incoming state, not a before-and-after diff. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Changed-field ambiguity** — A $LogFile attribute update does not directly identify which field inside the attribute changed. _Why:_ timestamp changes cannot be isolated automatically from the record alone. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Manual timestamp comparison** — An analyst can compare the transaction’s Last Modification timestamp with the file’s current Last Modification timestamp. _Why:_ differences may reveal a formerly held modification time. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Previously unknown modification time** — If the transaction timestamp differs from the current timestamp, it may expose a modification time no longer visible in current metadata. _Why:_ this can recover timeline evidence lost from the live file record. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **$LogFile modification detection difficulty** — $LogFile can support file modification analysis, but the process is not straightforward. _Why:_ reliable detection requires careful manual interpretation or more advanced tooling. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **$LogFile research status** — $LogFile analysis for accurate file-modification detection remains an active research area. _Why:_ current tooling may not yet combine all relevant evidence reliably. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Future tooling possibility** — Later tools may be able to combine multiple $LogFile clues to flag file modification more accurately. _Why:_ present limitations may be reduced as parser and correlation methods improve. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Current reliability warning** — Reliably identifying file modification from $LogFile is currently challenging. _Why:_ analysts should avoid overclaiming based on incomplete $LogFile indicators. _[GCFA p.805]_

### File and Directory Modification in $UsnJrnl

- **$UsnJrnl modification advantage** — $UsnJrnl makes file modification much easier to identify than $LogFile. _Why:_ USN reason codes directly describe data modification activity. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Primary data stream focus** — Three USN reason codes are specifically tied to modification of the primary data stream. _Why:_ these codes distinguish ordinary file content changes from ADS changes. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **DATA_EXTEND code** — `DATA_EXTEND` is one of the USN reason codes for primary-stream data modification. _Why:_ it indicates file data was extended. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **DATA_OVERWRITE code** — `DATA_OVERWRITE` is one of the USN reason codes for primary-stream data modification. _Why:_ it indicates existing file data was overwritten. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **DATA_TRUNCATION code** — `DATA_TRUNCATION` is one of the USN reason codes for primary-stream data modification. _Why:_ it indicates file data was reduced or truncated. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Microsoft code descriptions reference** — The page points to a chart containing Microsoft’s descriptions of the USN change codes. _Why:_ Microsoft’s definitions are the authoritative reference for interpreting these reason codes. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Journal pattern reference purpose** — The described patterns are intended as starting points for journal analysis. _Why:_ they provide practical entry points before deeper USN and $LogFile interpretation. _[GCFA p.805]_
- **Additional code list reference** — The page introduces a following list of codes as a reference for deeper journal analysis. _Why:_ broader code knowledge supports more complete interpretation of journal records. _[GCFA p.805]_

### USN Journal Reason Codes

- **USN journal reason-code table** — page 806 lists Windows USN journal reason constants, their hexadecimal bit values, and the file-system activity each reason represents. _Why:_ these reason fields let investigators interpret what kind of NTFS change a USN record is reporting. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_BASIC_INFO_CHANGE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_BASIC_INFO_CHANGE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies metadata-only changes in USN records. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_BASIC_INFO_CHANGE · Value** — the hexadecimal value is `0x00008000`. _Why:_ parsers and analysts can match this bit value to basic information changes. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_BASIC_INFO_CHANGE · Description** — this reason indicates that one or more attributes or timestamps for a file or directory were changed by a user. _Why:_ it can point to timestamp manipulation or attribute modification activity. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_CLOSE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_CLOSE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies closure events in USN records. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_CLOSE · Value** — the hexadecimal value is `0x80000000`. _Why:_ this bit value marks that the object handle was closed. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_CLOSE · Description** — this reason records that a file or directory was closed. _Why:_ close events often finalize a set of earlier USN reason flags for the same object. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_COMPRESSION_CHANGE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_COMPRESSION_CHANGE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies compression-state changes. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_COMPRESSION_CHANGE · Value** — the hexadecimal value is `0x00020000`. _Why:_ this bit value maps a USN record to compression-related metadata activity. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_COMPRESSION_CHANGE · Description** — this reason means a file or directory changed between compressed and uncompressed states. _Why:_ compression changes can explain metadata updates without ordinary content edits. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_DATA_EXTEND · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_DATA_EXTEND`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies growth of unnamed file data. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_DATA_EXTEND · Description** — this reason means data was appended or otherwise added to a file or directory. _Why:_ it helps distinguish growth from overwrites or truncation. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_DATA_OVERWRITE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_DATA_OVERWRITE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies overwrite activity on primary data. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_DATA_OVERWRITE · Description** — this reason means existing data in a file or directory was overwritten. _Why:_ it separates modification-in-place from append or shrink operations. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_DATA_TRUNCATION · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_DATA_TRUNCATION`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies reductions in unnamed data. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_DATA_TRUNCATION · Description** — this reason means a file or directory was shortened. _Why:_ truncation can indicate wiping, log rotation, or content replacement behavior. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_EA_CHANGE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_EA_CHANGE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies extended-attribute changes. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_EA_CHANGE · Description** — this reason means a user modified extended attributes on a file or directory. _Why:_ extended attributes may contain metadata relevant to provenance or application behavior. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_ENCRYPTION_CHANGE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_ENCRYPTION_CHANGE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies encryption-state changes. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_ENCRYPTION_CHANGE · Description** — this reason means a file or directory was encrypted or decrypted. _Why:_ encryption transitions may explain access issues or anti-forensic activity. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_FILE_CREATE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_FILE_CREATE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies object creation. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_FILE_CREATE · Value** — the hexadecimal value is `0x00000100`. _Why:_ this bit value marks creation of a file-system object. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_FILE_CREATE · Description** — this reason means a file or directory was newly created. _Why:_ creation events help establish first-seen timelines. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_FILE_DELETE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_FILE_DELETE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies deletion activity. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_FILE_DELETE · Value** — the hexadecimal value is `0x00000200`. _Why:_ this bit value maps a USN record to file or directory deletion. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_FILE_DELETE · Description** — this reason means a file or directory was deleted. _Why:_ deletion events are central to recovery and anti-forensic timelines. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_HARD_LINK_CHANGE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_HARD_LINK_CHANGE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies hard-link count or association changes. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_HARD_LINK_CHANGE · Value** — the hexadecimal value is `0x00010000`. _Why:_ this bit value marks addition or removal of an NTFS hard link. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_HARD_LINK_CHANGE · Description** — this reason means an NTFS hard link was added to or removed from a file or directory. _Why:_ hard-link changes can alter path-based interpretation of file access and deletion. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_INDEXABLE_CHANGE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_INDEXABLE_CHANGE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies changes to indexing eligibility. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_INTEGRITY_CHANGE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_INTEGRITY_CHANGE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies integrity-stream attribute changes. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_INTEGRITY_CHANGE · Description** — this reason means a user changed the `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_INTEGRITY_STREAM` state for the relevant stream. _Why:_ integrity-stream changes matter when interpreting resilient or integrity-protected NTFS data. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_NAMED_DATA_EXTEND · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_NAMED_DATA_EXTEND`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies growth of named streams. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_NAMED_DATA_OVERWRITE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_NAMED_DATA_OVERWRITE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies overwrites inside named streams. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_NAMED_DATA_OVERWRITE · Description** — this reason means data in one or more named streams for a file was overwritten. _Why:_ it can expose alternate data stream modification even when the default stream is not the focus. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_NAMED_DATA_TRUNCATION · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_NAMED_DATA_TRUNCATION`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies shortening of named streams. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_NAMED_DATA_TRUNCATION · Value** — the hexadecimal value is `0x00000040`. _Why:_ this bit value marks truncation of one or more named streams. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_NAMED_DATA_TRUNCATION · Description** — this reason means one or more named data streams for a file were shortened. _Why:_ truncation of alternate streams can indicate cleanup, staging, or concealment behavior. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_OBJECT_ID_CHANGE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_OBJECT_ID_CHANGE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies object identifier changes. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_OBJECT_ID_CHANGE · Description** — this reason means the object identifier for a file or directory was changed. _Why:_ object IDs can support tracking across renames and path changes. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_RENAME_NEW_NAME · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_RENAME_NEW_NAME`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies the post-rename name record. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_RENAME_NEW_NAME · Value** — the hexadecimal value is `0x00002000`. _Why:_ this bit value indicates that the USN record carries the new name after a rename. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_RENAME_NEW_NAME · Description** — this reason means a file or directory was renamed and the name stored in the `USN_RECORD_V2` structure is the new filename. _Why:_ it provides the destination name for rename reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_RENAME_OLD_NAME · Description** — this reason means a file or directory was renamed and the name stored in the `USN_RECORD_V2` structure is the former filename. _Why:_ it provides the source name for rename reconstruction. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_REPARSE_POINT_CHANGE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_REPARSE_POINT_CHANGE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies reparse point modifications. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_REPARSE_POINT_CHANGE · Description** — this reason means a reparse point in a file or directory was changed, created, or removed. _Why:_ reparse points affect path resolution and may indicate junction, symlink, or special filesystem behavior. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_SECURITY_CHANGE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_SECURITY_CHANGE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies permission-related changes. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_SECURITY_CHANGE · Description** — this reason means access rights for a file or directory were changed. _Why:_ permission changes can show privilege adjustments, concealment, or access enablement. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_STREAM_CHANGE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_STREAM_CHANGE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies named-stream lifecycle or rename changes. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_STREAM_CHANGE · Description** — this reason means a named stream was added to a file, removed from a file, or renamed. _Why:_ named-stream activity is important for detecting alternate data stream use. _[GCFA p.~806]_

- **USN_REASON_TRANSACTED_CHANGE · Code** — the reason constant is `USN_REASON_TRANSACTED_CHANGE`. _Why:_ this symbolic name identifies TxF-mediated stream modification. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_TRANSACTED_CHANGE · Value** — the hexadecimal value is `0x00400000`. _Why:_ this bit value marks a change made through a transactional NTFS operation. _[GCFA p.~806]_
- **USN_REASON_TRANSACTED_CHANGE · Description** — this reason means the stream was modified through a TxF transaction. _Why:_ transactional changes may affect how file activity is interpreted and correlated. _[GCFA p.~806]_

## Page 808

### Journal Filtering

- **Parent directory filtering** — Journal logs can be filtered by parent directory to focus file-system activity on locations that matter to an investigation. _Why:_ parent-directory scope turns high-volume journal data into targeted evidence. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Journal parent-directory metadata** — Both `$UsnJrnl` and `$LogFile` record the parent directory MFT entry associated with files. _Why:_ this enables filtering activity by directory even when looking across many file events. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Directory-of-interest filtering** — Filtering for file changes inside selected directories can reveal activity that would otherwise be buried in large journal datasets. _Why:_ adversary activity often clusters in predictable or attacker-controlled paths. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Creative journal searches** — Journal visibility supports flexible searches and filters that can surface notable findings. _Why:_ journals preserve activity history beyond the current file-system state. _[GCFA p.~808]_

### Parent Directory Filter Table

- **Parent directory filter · `C:\Windows` and `C:\Windows\System32`** — These paths are listed as directories attackers value. _Why:_ malware placed there can appear similar to legitimate Windows executables. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Investigative relevance · `C:\Windows` and `C:\Windows\System32`** — Activity in these directories is important because attackers seek them out. _Why:_ file or directory creation/deletion there is uncommon enough that it should be checked. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Parent directory filter · `C:\Windows\Prefetch`** — The Prefetch directory is a recommended journal-filter target. _Why:_ attackers may delete Prefetch artifacts while cleaning up after execution. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Investigative relevance · `C:\Windows\Prefetch`** — Prefetch files are often removed by attackers. _Why:_ deletions here can indicate an attempt to hide program execution evidence. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Parent directory filter · attacker working directories** — Known or suspected attacker work locations are recommended filter targets. _Why:_ these directories may expose previously unknown attacker utilities or staged data. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Investigative relevance · attacker working directories** — Filtering attacker workspaces can reveal unknown tools and exfiltration-related material. _Why:_ attacker-controlled folders often contain payloads, scripts, archives, or collected data. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Parent directory filter · temp directories** — Temporary directories are recommended filter targets. _Why:_ adversaries commonly stage or execute files from temporary locations. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Investigative relevance · temp directories** — Executables are the main focus when filtering temporary directories. _Why:_ executable creation or deletion in temp paths can identify malware staging or execution. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Parent directory filter · `C:\Users\*\Downloads`** — User Downloads folders are recommended journal-filter targets. _Why:_ downloaded files may show recent acquisition of tools, payloads, or documents. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Investigative relevance · `C:\Users\*\Downloads`** — Filtering Downloads paths helps identify recently downloaded files. _Why:_ this can connect browser or user activity to files later used in an intrusion. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Parent directory filter · `C:\Users\*\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Recent`** — The Windows Recent folder is a recommended journal-filter target. _Why:_ Recent artifacts can add file-open evidence and timing context. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Investigative relevance · `C:\Users\*\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Recent`** — Filtering this path can identify additional timestamps and files opened by users. _Why:_ Recent entries can corroborate user interaction with files. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Parent directory filter · `C:\$Recycle.Bin\<SID>`** — Per-user Recycle Bin paths are recommended journal-filter targets. _Why:_ they can show deleted files before the Recycle Bin was emptied. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Investigative relevance · `C:\$Recycle.Bin\<SID>`** — Filtering this path helps check for files deleted before Recycle Bin cleanup. _Why:_ it may preserve evidence of deletion activity that is no longer visible in the live Recycle Bin. _[GCFA p.~808]_

### MFT Timeline Limits

- **MFT timeline scope** — A file-system timeline built from `$MFT` reflects files and directories as they existed when `$MFT` was acquired. _Why:_ it is a point-in-time view, not a complete historical record. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **MFT acquisition-time state** — `$MFT` analysis shows the file-system state at the exact collection time of the `$MFT` file. _Why:_ this limits what can be inferred about prior file names, paths, moves, and deletions. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **MFT usefulness** — `$MFT` state can provide substantial investigative value and may satisfy some investigative needs. _Why:_ current and residual metadata can still identify files, paths, and timestamps. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **MFT deletion timestamp limitation** — `$MFT` timestamps are not updated merely because a file is deleted. _Why:_ `$MFT` alone may not reveal the deletion time for a removed file. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Deleted file in unreused MFT record** — If a deleted file’s unallocated MFT record has not been reused, MFT analysis may recover the file name and location as of deletion. _Why:_ unreused records can preserve metadata for deleted entries. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Deleted file in reused MFT record** — If the deleted file’s MFT record has been reused, the old name and location may no longer be available from that record. _Why:_ record reuse can overwrite evidence of the deleted object. _[GCFA p.~808]_

### Journal History Value

- **Journal analysis advantage** — Adding journal analysis provides a rolling record of file-system activity. _Why:_ journals can show historical events that are not visible in the current `$MFT` state. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Renamed-file visibility** — Journal analysis can show that a file was renamed. _Why:_ rename events explain why a known file may have appeared under multiple names. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Rename timing** — Journal analysis can identify when a rename occurred. _Why:_ timing supports event reconstruction and correlation with attacker activity. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Prior name recovery** — Journal analysis can reveal the file name that existed before a rename. _Why:_ earlier names may match known indicators or user-recognizable artifacts. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Moved-file visibility** — Journal analysis can show that a file was moved. _Why:_ movement history can connect staging, execution, and cleanup locations. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Move timing** — Journal analysis can identify when a file move occurred. _Why:_ timing helps reconstruct the order of attacker actions. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Previous location recovery** — Journal analysis can reveal where a moved file was located before the move. _Why:_ prior paths may identify attacker working directories or original download locations. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Deletion confirmation** — Journal analysis can confirm that a file was deleted. _Why:_ deletion evidence may remain even when the file and current metadata are gone. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Deletion timing** — Journal analysis can identify when a file deletion occurred. _Why:_ deletion time is often unavailable from `$MFT` timestamps alone. _[GCFA p.~808]_

### Journal Analysis Order

- **First-pass journal source · `$UsnJrnl`** — The `$UsnJrnl` is generally recommended as the first journal to analyze. _Why:_ it usually covers a longer time span and is simpler to interpret. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **`$UsnJrnl` time coverage** — `$UsnJrnl` is described as having a longer time horizon than `$LogFile`. _Why:_ longer retention increases the chance of finding older attacker actions. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **`$UsnJrnl` readability** — `$UsnJrnl` is described as easier to read than `$LogFile`. _Why:_ easier interpretation speeds triage and reduces analytical complexity. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Second-pass journal source · `$LogFile`** — `$LogFile` analysis can follow `$UsnJrnl` analysis. _Why:_ it can provide additional context after the broader, easier journal review. _[GCFA p.~808]_

### Specific Directory Guidance

- **`C:\Windows` attacker appeal** — Attackers value `C:\Windows` because files there can blend with normal Windows content. _Why:_ suspicious additions or removals in this path deserve validation. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **`C:\Windows\System32` attacker appeal** — Attackers value `C:\Windows\System32` because malware stored there can resemble legitimate Windows executables. _Why:_ the directory’s legitimacy can help malicious binaries avoid casual notice. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Windows directory activity frequency** — File and directory creation or deletion in `C:\Windows` and `C:\Windows\System32` occurs only occasionally. _Why:_ low normal churn makes observed changes more meaningful. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Windows directory validation** — Activity in `C:\Windows` and `C:\Windows\System32` should always be validated. _Why:_ rare changes in attacker-favored system directories can indicate compromise. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Prefetch cleanup targeting** — Attackers may target Prefetch files during cleanup. _Why:_ Prefetch can reveal execution evidence, making deletion behavior suspicious. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Prefetch deletion pattern** — During an intrusion, all `.pf` files or only selected `.pf` files may be deleted. _Why:_ broad or selective Prefetch deletion can indicate anti-forensic cleanup. _[GCFA p.~808]_

- **Prefetch extension · `.pf`** — Prefetch files are identified by the `.pf` extension on this page. _Why:_ `.pf` deletions in journal data can be searched directly. _[GCFA p.~808]_

### Prefetch Execution Evidence

- **Prefetch-file changes** — Modifications to `.pf` prefetch files can provide another execution-time signal even when the prefetch files still exist. _Why:_ journal activity can supplement normal prefetch parsing when reconstructing program execution. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Windows 7 prefetch limitation** — Windows 7 prefetch records only the latest execution time for a program. _Why:_ journal-observed `.pf` updates may reveal execution timing context that the prefetch file itself no longer preserves. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Prefetch and attacker TTPs** — Prefetch-related activity can help infer attacker tools, techniques, and procedures. _Why:_ execution artifacts connect observed files to attacker behavior. _[GCFA p.809]_

### Attacker Working Directories

- **Attacker working-directory discovery** — Finding directories used by an attacker to stage or store files is highly valuable during an investigation. _Why:_ those paths become leads for scoping similar activity across other systems. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Directory contents as IOCs** — Files found within an attacker working directory can become additional indicators of compromise. _Why:_ filenames, tools, and staged content can be searched elsewhere in the environment. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Journal filtering by attacker directory** — Filtering NTFS journals for records whose parent directory matches an attacker-controlled directory can reveal prior contents. _Why:_ this can expose files the attacker deleted or moved before collection. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Deleted-or-moved working-directory files** — Journal records may identify items that once existed in an attacker directory but are absent from the live file system. _Why:_ journal history can provide visibility that a current `$MFT` review alone would miss. _[GCFA p.809]_

- **Perfmon directory MFT entry** — MFT entry number `111311` corresponds to the attacker’s `Perfmon` directory in the case example. _Why:_ this gives the analyst a concrete directory identifier for journal scoping. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Perfmon live-file-system absence** — The three named items shown in the example were not present in the active `Perfmon` directory. _Why:_ this demonstrates the added historical visibility provided by journal data compared with live file-system review. _[GCFA p.809]_

### Directory Paths Of Interest

- **Temp directories** — Temporary directories are common first-stage locations for exploit-delivered content on victim systems. _Why:_ suspicious executables or scripts may appear there briefly and later be removed. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Historical temp-directory review** — Looking backward through journal data for temp-directory activity can reveal suspicious executables or scripts. _Why:_ temporary storage behavior makes live-only review incomplete. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **`C:\Users\*\Downloads`** — User Downloads directories are useful to review for downloaded files. _Why:_ download activity can matter especially in end-user-focused investigations. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **`C:\Users\*\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Recent`** — User Recent folders contain LNK artifacts that can show files opened by a user or attacker. _Why:_ LNK evidence helps identify documents or files accessed during intrusion activity. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Recent-folder LNK analysis** — Analyzing LNK files in Recent folders can reveal opened files. _Why:_ opened-file evidence helps infer what data the attacker viewed or targeted. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Interactive desktop attacker behavior** — Attackers in intrusion cases may obtain interactive desktop access to support data discovery. _Why:_ this behavior creates user-shell artifacts such as Recent-folder LNK files. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Attacker file review before exfiltration** — Attackers may open files for inspection before stealing them. _Why:_ LNK artifacts can show the attacker’s selection and discovery process. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Deleted Recent LNK files** — Deleted LNK files in Recent folders are useful targets for journal-based review. _Why:_ they may preserve evidence of files opened even after cleanup. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Existing LNK modification times** — Additional modification times for existing LNK files can indicate further file-opening activity. _Why:_ those changes help reconstruct when files were accessed. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **LNK findings and attacker objectives** — Deleted LNKs and LNK modification activity can clarify what the attacker sought or accomplished. _Why:_ opened-file evidence connects intrusion behavior to objectives and possible exfiltration. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **`C:\$Recycle.Bin\<SID>`** — A user-specific Recycle Bin path can be reviewed for files added to that user’s Recycle Bin. _Why:_ this artifact may be useful in end-user investigations and some intrusions. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Recycle Bin in desktop compromise** — Interactive desktop access can make the Recycle Bin relevant during attacker activity. _Why:_ files deleted through the shell may leave Recycle Bin evidence. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Recycle Bin versus Shift-Delete** — A capable attacker is less likely to use the Recycle Bin and more likely to permanently delete with Shift-Delete. _Why:_ Recycle Bin evidence may still exist but should be interpreted with attacker tradecraft in mind. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **User Recycle Bin scoping** — Focusing on files added to the Recycle Bin for a specific user can produce important findings. _Why:_ it links deleted content to a user context and deletion mechanism. _[GCFA p.809]_

### File Types And Names To Search Globally

- **Location-independent filename searches** — Some file types and names should be searched regardless of their directory path. _Why:_ attacker tools and IOCs may appear outside the initially interesting parent directories. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Executable extension `.exe`** — `.exe` files are useful search targets. _Why:_ executable artifacts may represent attacker tools or payloads. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Executable extension `.dll`** — `.dll` files are useful search targets. _Why:_ dynamic libraries may be malicious payloads, loaders, or support files. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Executable extension `.sys`** — `.sys` files are useful search targets. _Why:_ driver files can be relevant to malware or privileged tooling. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Executable extension `.pyd`** — `.pyd` files are useful search targets. _Why:_ Python extension modules may appear in attacker toolsets. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Script extension `.ps1`** — `.ps1` files are useful search targets. _Why:_ PowerShell scripts are common in intrusion activity. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Script extension `.vbs`** — `.vbs` files are useful search targets. _Why:_ VBScript files may contain attacker automation or execution logic. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Script extension `.bat`** — `.bat` files are useful search targets. _Why:_ batch files can automate attacker commands and staging actions. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Archive extension `.rar`** — `.rar` files are useful search targets. _Why:_ archives may contain staged tools or compressed stolen data. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Archive extension `.7z`** — `.7z` files are useful search targets. _Why:_ 7-Zip archives are commonly used for packaging or staging data. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Archive extension `.zip`** — `.zip` files are useful search targets. _Why:_ ZIP archives may indicate collection, transfer preparation, or tool staging. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Archive extension `.cab`** — `.cab` files are useful search targets. _Why:_ cabinet archives may be used to package files or tools. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Known IOC file names** — Any file names already identified as IOCs should be searched. _Why:_ known indicators help scope compromise across file-system history. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Known IOC folder names** — Any folder names already identified as IOCs should be searched. _Why:_ directory-name indicators can reveal repeated attacker staging patterns. _[GCFA p.809]_

### Search Volume And Filtering

- **Common executable-extension noise** — Searches for frequent executable extensions such as `.exe` and `.dll` can return many results. _Why:_ high-volume results can obscure the suspicious records an analyst needs. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Windows updates as noise source** — Windows updates and similar system activity can produce many executable-extension hits. _Why:_ benign operating-system activity can inflate search results for `.exe` and `.dll`. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **Directory-focused executable searches** — Common executable extensions may be better searched within selected directories of interest. _Why:_ path filtering reduces noise and improves investigative focus. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **`C:\Windows\System32` as filtered search path** — `C:\Windows\System32` is listed as a directory of interest for focused executable-extension searches. _Why:_ system-directory activity can matter but should be scoped carefully because of result volume. _[GCFA p.809]_
- **User temp directories as filtered search paths** — Users’ temp directories are listed as directories of interest for focused executable-extension searches. _Why:_ temp paths are common malware and exploit staging locations while still narrowing search volume. _[GCFA p.809]_
