### Tool Context

- **Limited historical tooling** — NTFS `$LogFile` has traditionally had relatively few parsers available. _Why:_ explains why this artifact is less commonly analyzed than simpler sources. _[GCFA p.810]_
- **Parsing difficulty cause** — `$LogFile` parsing is difficult because the structure is complex. _Why:_ complexity affects tool reliability and analyst expectations. _[GCFA p.810]_
- **Documentation limitation** — `$LogFile` has not been thoroughly documented. _Why:_ sparse documentation increases reverse-engineering burden. _[GCFA p.810]_
- **Shorter retention window** — `$LogFile` usually covers a shorter time span than `$UsnJrnl`. _Why:_ limits historical reconstruction compared with longer-lived journals. _[GCFA p.810]_
- **Relative relevance** — Because of its shorter time horizon, `$LogFile` may be less useful than `$UsnJrnl` in some investigations. _Why:_ helps prioritize artifact triage. _[GCFA p.810]_
- **Payload richness** — `$LogFile` stores complete payload data destined for important NTFS structures. _Why:_ makes it valuable even when the time window is short. _[GCFA p.810]_

### Log Sequence Numbers

- **LSN meaning** — LSN stands for Log Sequence Number. _Why:_ defines the ordering field used by `$LogFile`. _[GCFA p.810]_
- **LSN ordering role** — Log Sequence Numbers order `$LogFile` entries. _Why:_ they provide sequence when timestamps are absent. _[GCFA p.810]_
- **Chronology importance** — LSN values are critical for interpreting `$LogFile` event order. _Why:_ event sequence is central to forensic timelines. _[GCFA p.810]_
- **No per-event timestamps** — `$LogFile` does not directly store a timestamp for every event. _Why:_ analysts cannot build `$LogFile` timelines from native event times alone. _[GCFA p.810]_
- **Increasing sequence** — `$LogFile` assigns events an LSN that rises as newer events are recorded. _Why:_ higher LSNs indicate later log entries. _[GCFA p.810]_
- **Filename pivot workflow** — A filename hit in `LogFile_FileNames.csv` can be paired with its LSN for further analysis. _Why:_ the LSN connects a name hit to the surrounding chronological log activity. _[GCFA p.810]_

### Operation Fields

- **Redo operation meaning** — The `Redo` operation describes the change the file system is preparing to apply. _Why:_ indicates the forward action represented by a log record. _[GCFA p.810]_
- **Undo operation meaning** — The `Undo` operation describes how the logged change could be reversed. _Why:_ helps interpret rollback semantics and the inverse of the action. _[GCFA p.810]_

### $LogFile Timestamp Inference

- **$LogFile contextual lookup** — An event identified in a smaller extract can be located inside the larger `LogFile.csv` to review nearby activity in the same time window. _Why:_ surrounding transaction activity can explain what happened before and after a target event. _[GCFA p.811]_
- **$LogFile timing limitation** — Exact event times are not always available directly from the main parsed `$LogFile` transaction context. _Why:_ investigators must know when a timestamp must be inferred from embedded payload records instead of the outer log entry. _[GCFA p.811]_
- **Payload-based timestamp recovery** — Actual times can be derived from payload structures stored inside `$LogFile`, including `$UsnJrnl` records and `$I30` index entries. _Why:_ embedded artifact payloads may preserve timestamps even when the surrounding transaction view is insufficient. _[GCFA p.811]_
- **$UsnJrnl timestamp behavior** — Each `$UsnJrnl` update contains its own timestamp. _Why:_ this makes `$UsnJrnl` records especially useful for assigning times to `$LogFile` activity. _[GCFA p.811]_
- **$UsnJrnl payloads inside $LogFile** — Complete `$UsnJrnl` update payloads can be present within `$LogFile`. _Why:_ the log may preserve journal record details that support event reconstruction. _[GCFA p.811]_
- **$UsnJrnl-derived inference** — Because `$LogFile` can contain full `$UsnJrnl` update payloads, analysts can infer timestamps from those embedded updates. _Why:_ this provides a method for dating transaction activity when the parser output lacks direct timing. _[GCFA p.811]_

### $LogFile Data-Run Recovery

- **Beyond metadata recovery** — `$LogFile` analysis can assist with more than recovering metadata for files under investigation. _Why:_ the artifact can support broader reconstruction tasks. _[GCFA p.811]_
- **Potential file-data reconstruction support** — `$LogFile` can sometimes help recover information needed to retrieve file content. _Why:_ it may preserve storage-location data even after active filesystem metadata changes. _[GCFA p.811]_
- **No direct file-content storage** — `$LogFile` does not contain the actual contents of the file as normal file data. _Why:_ analysts should not expect `$LogFile` itself to hold a full deleted file payload. _[GCFA p.811]_
- **Cluster-run preservation** — `$LogFile` can store cluster run information associated with file data. _Why:_ cluster runs identify where file content resided on disk. _[GCFA p.811]_
- **Deleted-file recovery scenario** — If a significant file was recently deleted, `$LogFile` may still contain its former cluster locations. _Why:_ this can preserve recovery leads after the file disappears from active filesystem views. _[GCFA p.811]_
- **Reused MFT record scenario** — `$LogFile` can be useful when the deleted file’s MFT record has already been reused and overwritten by a new file. _Why:_ normal MFT-based recovery may fail once the original record is replaced. _[GCFA p.811]_
- **Original cluster locations** — The original disk cluster locations for a deleted file may be discoverable in `$LogFile`. _Why:_ those locations can guide targeted recovery of the deleted content. _[GCFA p.811]_
- **LogFileParser `/ReconstructDataruns` option** — LogFileParser includes `/ReconstructDataruns` to recover or rebuild data-run information from `$LogFile`. _Why:_ this option directly supports reconstruction of deleted-file storage mappings. _[GCFA p.811]_
- **Fragmented-file advantage** — Data-run reconstruction from `$LogFile` is especially useful for fragmented files. _Why:_ fragmented files are difficult to recover completely through ordinary carving. _[GCFA p.811]_
- **Standard carving limitation** — Typical file carving often cannot fully recover fragmented files. _Why:_ carving depends on contiguous or recognizable content and may miss scattered file fragments. _[GCFA p.811]_

### $UsnJrnl Analysis Purpose

- **$UsnJrnl volume-change overview** — The NTFS `$UsnJrnl` gives a summarized record of changes made on an NTFS volume. _Why:_ it lets investigators quickly reconstruct file-system activity at volume scale. _[GCFA p.813]_
- **$UsnJrnl as an early analysis target** — Investigators commonly examine `$UsnJrnl` early when reviewing a volume’s change history. _Why:_ it is compact, comparatively simple to interpret, and useful for triage. _[GCFA p.813]_
- **$UsnJrnl compactness** — The `$UsnJrnl` format is relatively small and direct compared with more detailed NTFS logs. _Why:_ this makes it efficient to parse and review during incident response. _[GCFA p.813]_
- **$UsnJrnl retention advantage** — The `$UsnJrnl` usually spans a longer period than `$LogFile`. _Why:_ it can preserve change-history evidence after `$LogFile` no longer covers the relevant time window. _[GCFA p.813]_
- **Multiple parser availability** — Several tools can parse `$UsnJrnl` data. _Why:_ investigators are not limited to one parser or workflow. _[GCFA p.813]_
- **MFTECmd parser option** — Eric Zimmerman’s MFTECmd is identified as a strong tool choice for `$UsnJrnl` parsing. _Why:_ it provides a practical way to convert journal records into analyst-friendly output. _[GCFA p.813]_

### MFTECmd Command Usage

- **MFTECmd `$UsnJrnl` workflow** — Running MFTECmd against `$UsnJrnl` is similar to running it against `$MFT`. _Why:_ analysts can reuse familiar MFTECmd syntax with only journal-specific inputs added. _[GCFA p.813]_
- **`$J` ADS requirement** — The `$J` alternate data stream is supplied when parsing the `$UsnJrnl`. _Why:_ `$J` contains the USN journal records that MFTECmd needs to parse. _[GCFA p.813]_
- **`$MFT` companion input** — The `$MFT` file is also supplied alongside `$J`. _Why:_ MFTECmd can use MFT records to resolve entry references into file paths. _[GCFA p.813]_

- **MFT Entry Number correlation** — MFTECmd uses the journal’s MFT Entry Number references for `$MFT` lookup. _Why:_ this links a USN event to the affected file or directory record. _[GCFA p.813]_
- **Parent Entry Number correlation** — MFTECmd uses the journal’s Parent Entry Number references for `$MFT` lookup. _Why:_ this helps determine where the affected object resided in the directory tree. _[GCFA p.813]_

- **CSV output filename value** — The demonstrated output filename is `usnjrnl.csv`. _Why:_ this is the analyst-facing CSV produced by the example command. _[GCFA p.813]_

### MFTECmd Deduplication

- **MFTECmd dedupe option** — MFTECmd supports a `--dedupe` option. _Why:_ this flag can reduce redundant parsing when duplicate inputs are supplied. _[GCFA p.~814]_
- **Deduplication method** — `--dedupe` computes or checks hashes for each input file. _Why:_ hash comparison is used to identify identical input content. _[GCFA p.~814]_
- **Duplicate handling** — If multiple input files have the same hash, MFTECmd parses only the first matching file it finds. _Why:_ this avoids processing identical data more than once. _[GCFA p.~814]_
- **Snapshot journal uniqueness** — `$J` streams are unlikely to hash-match across different snapshots. _Why:_ USN Journal contents normally change over time, so deduplication is not expected to eliminate many VSS journal inputs. _[GCFA p.~814]_

## Page 815

### NTFS Deletion Overview

- **NTFS deletion · forensic importance** — File deletion is a core NTFS behavior that strongly affects forensic recovery and artifact interpretation. _Why:_ deletion leaves evidence across multiple NTFS layers rather than simply erasing all traces. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **NTFS deletion · incomplete sequence** — The listed deletion effects are illustrative and are not guaranteed to occur in the displayed order. _Why:_ analysts should avoid assuming a strict chronological sequence from the slide alone. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **NTFS deletion · partial process description** — The page explicitly notes that the listed effects are not the full set of NTFS deletion operations. _Why:_ absence from the list does not mean an NTFS structure was unaffected. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **NTFS deletion · resilient filesystem design** — NTFS deletion behavior reflects multiple mechanisms intended to preserve filesystem consistency and resilience. _Why:_ those mechanisms create recoverable forensic traces after deletion. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **NTFS deletion · forensic artifact sources** — Deleted-file evidence can be mined from several NTFS resources, including allocation metadata, file records, directory indexes, and journals. _Why:_ recovery and timeline analysis should examine more than active directory listings. _[GCFA p.815]_

### Data Layer

- **Deleted file clusters · $Bitmap state** — When a file is deleted, the file’s clusters are marked available in `$Bitmap`. _Why:_ allocation status changes even when content remains recoverable. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file clusters · content preservation** — Deletion does not immediately erase the bytes stored in the file’s clusters. _Why:_ the original file content may remain recoverable until another file reuses those clusters. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file clusters · reuse condition** — Deleted-file cluster contents persist only until the clusters are allocated again and overwritten. _Why:_ recovery potential depends on whether later filesystem activity reused the space. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file data · continued existence** — File content can still exist on disk after deletion. _Why:_ data carving or metadata-guided recovery may still succeed. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file slack · continued existence** — Slack space associated with a deleted file can remain present after deletion. _Why:_ slack may contain residual data useful for forensic recovery. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file clusters · not touched directly** — NTFS marks the related clusters as available but does not modify the cluster contents as part of the basic deletion action described. _Why:_ allocation metadata and stored bytes diverge after deletion. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file clusters · possible later overwrite** — Deleted-file clusters may eventually be reused and overwritten. _Why:_ delayed overwrite explains why deleted data is sometimes recoverable and sometimes lost. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file clusters · possible non-reuse** — Deleted-file clusters may remain unreused for an unspecified period. _Why:_ old deleted content can persist longer than expected on quiet volumes. _[GCFA p.815]_

### Metadata Layer

- **Deleted file · `$MFT` record status bit** — NTFS flips a bit in the file’s `$MFT` record to mark the record available. _Why:_ the metadata record can indicate deletion without being physically erased. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file · `$MFT` metadata persistence** — File metadata in the `$MFT` record remains until that record is reused. _Why:_ deleted files can often be reconstructed from inactive MFT entries. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file · `$MFT` record availability** — The MFT record is marked available after deletion. _Why:_ this makes the record eligible for reuse by a future file. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file · `$MFT` not immediately overwritten** — Marking the MFT record available does not mean NTFS overwrites it immediately. _Why:_ metadata may remain intact after deletion. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file · intact `$MFT` record window** — A deleted file’s MFT record can remain completely intact for some time. _Why:_ this creates a recovery window for filename, timestamps, attributes, and other metadata. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file · `$LogFile` reference** — `$LogFile` can continue to contain references to the deleted file. _Why:_ transactional records may preserve evidence of file activity after active metadata changes. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file · `$USNJrnl` reference** — `$USNJrnl` can continue to reference a deleted file. _Why:_ the USN journal can provide deletion evidence and timeline context. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file · other system log references** — Other NTFS or system logs may still refer to the deleted file. _Why:_ deletion does not eliminate all secondary records of the file. _[GCFA p.815]_

### Filename Layer

- **Deleted file · `$FILE_NAME` preservation** — The `$FILE_NAME` attribute remains preserved until the MFT record is reused. _Why:_ deleted-file names can survive even after the file disappears from normal directory views. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file · parent `$I30` index entry** — The parent directory’s `$I30` index entry may remain after deletion. _Why:_ directory indexes can preserve evidence of filenames no longer present in the live filesystem. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file · parent directory index availability** — During deletion, the parent directory’s index marks the file’s entry available. _Why:_ directory metadata changes independently from file content and MFT metadata. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file · directory index rebalancing trigger** — Marking the directory index entry available may cause the index to rebalance. _Why:_ rebalancing can alter or destroy residual directory-entry evidence. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file · possible index-entry overwrite** — Directory index rebalancing may overwrite the deleted file’s index entry. _Why:_ absence of a residual `$I30` entry does not prove the file never existed. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deleted file · possible index-entry survival** — Directory index rebalancing may leave the deleted file’s index entry unoverwritten. _Why:_ `$I30` analysis may recover deleted filenames and metadata. _[GCFA p.815]_

### NTFS System Files and Journals

- **Deletion · `$LogFile` update** — NTFS updates `$LogFile` to record that a filesystem transaction occurred. _Why:_ `$LogFile` can provide transaction-level evidence around deletion. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deletion · `$USNJrnl` update** — NTFS updates `$USNJrnl` to reflect the file deletion when the journal is enabled. _Why:_ the USN journal can directly show that deletion activity occurred. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deletion · `$UsnJrnl` Windows version caveat** — `$UsnJrnl` is not enabled on Windows XP and earlier systems. _Why:_ analysts should not expect USN deletion records on those older systems. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deletion · `$Secure` update** — `$Secure` is updated during deletion when applicable to the file. _Why:_ security-descriptor metadata may be affected by deletion workflows. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deletion · `$ObjID` update** — `$ObjID` is updated during deletion when applicable to the file. _Why:_ object identifier metadata may provide additional deletion-related traces. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deletion · `$Quota` update** — `$Quota` is updated during deletion when applicable to the file. _Why:_ quota accounting may change as part of file deletion. _[GCFA p.815]_
- **Deletion · conditional metadata updates** — `$Secure`, `$ObjID`, and `$Quota` are not necessarily updated for every deleted file; applicability depends on the file. _Why:_ analysts should treat these artifacts as conditional evidence sources. _[GCFA p.815]_

## Page 818

### Anti-Forensics Detection Framing

- **Missing expected evidence** — An expected artifact being absent can mean the system is innocent of the suspected activity. _Why:_ absence of evidence must be interpreted cautiously during forensic conclusions. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Missing expected evidence as suspicious** — An expected artifact being absent can also indicate that wiping, privacy-cleaning, or other anti-forensic activity occurred. _Why:_ investigators should treat unexplained gaps as potential evidence of concealment, not only as exculpatory. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Anti-forensic destruction indicators** — Investigators can search for traces that data-destruction tools or techniques were used. _Why:_ the destruction process may leave its own artifacts even when target evidence is removed. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Advanced recovery techniques** — Deeper recovery methods may retrieve evidence after ordinary artifacts are unavailable. _Why:_ forensic work should not stop when standard locations no longer contain the expected data. _[GCFA p.818]_

### Threat Context

- **Rising intrusion frequency** — Computer crimes and intrusions are described as continuing to become more common. _Why:_ increased attacker activity raises the likelihood of encountering anti-forensics in investigations. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Increasing concealment attempts** — Perpetrators increasingly try to hide their actions as part of criminal or intrusion activity. _Why:_ investigators should expect deliberate artifact removal or manipulation. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Anti-forensics trend persistence** — The courseware characterizes attacker concealment as a trend that is unlikely to disappear soon. _Why:_ anti-forensics should be treated as an ongoing investigative concern, not an edge case. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Network-intrusion concealment pressure** — Attackers involved in network intrusions are pushed to work harder to hide activity. _Why:_ better defensive visibility can drive adversaries toward more deliberate cleanup. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Improved organizational security effect** — Stronger security programs can indirectly cause attackers to use more anti-forensic methods. _Why:_ defensive maturity changes adversary behavior and post-compromise cleanup patterns. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Trace-removal motivation** — Anti-forensic actions are used to remove, or at least attempt to remove, evidence of attacker activity. _Why:_ failed or partial cleanup attempts may still reveal intent and tool usage. _[GCFA p.818]_

### File Wipers

- **File wipers as intrusion anti-forensics** — File-wiping utilities are a commonly observed anti-forensic method in intrusion cases. _Why:_ finding evidence of wiping can support an inference that an attacker attempted cleanup. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **File-wiper behavior** — File wipers overwrite deleted file contents promptly instead of leaving deleted data temporarily recoverable. _Why:_ overwriting reduces the chance of recovering the deleted file from unallocated space. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Overwritten file version loss** — Once a file’s contents have been overwritten, that specific prior version is effectively unavailable from that location. _Why:_ investigators must shift to alternate sources when the primary bytes are destroyed. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Deleted-data vulnerability window** — Deleted files may otherwise remain on disk for some time before being overwritten naturally. _Why:_ file wipers target this ordinary recovery window. _[GCFA p.818]_

### Recovery Opportunities

- **Pre-overwrite recovery possibility** — Some techniques may recover a file as it existed before later overwrite activity. _Why:_ overwriting one location does not always eliminate every historical copy. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Volume shadow copies as workaround** — Volume shadow copies can bypass file wiping or deletion when relevant snapshots are available. _Why:_ snapshots may preserve earlier file states outside the active filesystem view. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Volume shadow copy availability limitation** — Volume shadow copy recovery depends on whether usable shadow copies exist. _Why:_ investigators must verify snapshot availability before relying on this path. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Multiple-location file data principle** — File contents often exist in more than one place on a drive. _Why:_ wiping a primary file does not necessarily remove all copies or fragments. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Windows duplicate-data behavior** — Windows features and normal system behavior can cause copies of files or file data to appear elsewhere. _Why:_ operating-system artifacts may preserve data outside the attacker’s cleanup target. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Application duplicate-data behavior** — Applications can create additional copies or representations of file data in separate locations. _Why:_ application artifacts may retain evidence after original files are deleted or wiped. _[GCFA p.818]_
- **Alternate recovery strategy** — When shadow copies are not available, investigators should look for other filesystem or application locations containing the same data. _Why:_ distributed copies can provide a recovery path after targeted destruction. _[GCFA p.818]_

## Page 819

### SDelete Overview

- **SDelete provenance** — SDelete is part of Microsoft's Sysinternals utilities. _Why:_ a signed Microsoft utility can appear legitimate while being used for destructive activity. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **SDelete wipe targets** — SDelete can wipe individual files. _Why:_ wiped file content may be intentionally destroyed while metadata survives. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **SDelete directory wiping** — SDelete can operate on directories. _Why:_ directory-scoped use can affect many files while leaving directory-level artifacts. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **SDelete free-space wiping** — SDelete can wipe unallocated space. _Why:_ free-space wiping targets recoverable deleted data rather than only live files. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **Residual artifacts after SDelete** — SDelete activity still leaves multiple forensic traces. _Why:_ file wiping does not erase every timeline, index, journal, or execution artifact. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **Attacker appeal of SDelete** — SDelete is attractive to intruders because it is Microsoft-signed. _Why:_ signed tooling may bypass some allow-listing, antivirus, or trust-based controls. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **Living-off-the-land use** — SDelete can blend into environments where Sysinternals tools are already used by administrators. _Why:_ legitimate administrative presence can reduce the suspiciousness of the binary alone. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **File-wiper identification** — The shown artifacts can indicate both that wiping occurred and that SDelete was the likely tool. _Why:_ tool-specific behavior supports attribution of the wiping method. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **SDelete rename strategy** — SDelete overwrites deleted filenames by repeatedly renaming the file 26 times using successive alphabetic replacement characters. _Why:_ alphabetic rename sequences are a distinctive SDelete indicator. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **SDelete rename example behavior** — A short filename such as `foo.txt` would first be transformed into an all-`A` style name such as `AAA.AAA`. _Why:_ this explains why repeated `A`, `B`, `C`, and later-letter filenames appear in artifacts. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **SDelete overwrite method for ordinary files** — For files that are not compressed, encrypted, or sparse, SDelete wipes by overwriting content with a secure-delete pattern. _Why:_ this explains why overwrite-related journal reasons accompany rename artifacts. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **Special attribute exclusions** — Compressed files are excluded from the simple overwrite description. _Why:_ NTFS special attributes can change wiping mechanics and expected artifacts. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **Encrypted file exclusion** — Encrypted files are excluded from the simple overwrite description. _Why:_ encrypted-file handling may differ from ordinary resident or nonresident data overwrites. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **Sparse file exclusion** — Sparse files are excluded from the simple overwrite description. _Why:_ sparse allocation behavior can alter overwrite evidence. _[GCFA p.819]_

### $UsnJrnl Behavior

- **$UsnJrnl forensic role** — The $UsnJrnl provides a rolling record of file-system changes. _Why:_ it can preserve evidence of file renames and overwrites even after file content is wiped. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **$UsnJrnl parsed artifact** — The upper-right artifact is parsed $UsnJrnl output. _Why:_ it shows the file-system operation history behind the wipe. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **MFT entry continuity** — The repeated events point to MFT entry `47736`. _Why:_ the same record number links the original filename to later wipe-generated names. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **Original filename in journal** — The file began as `Nokia Strategy.docx`. _Why:_ this preserves the target file identity despite later obfuscating renames. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **Alphabetical rename pattern** — The journal shows sequential alphabetic renames after the original name. _Why:_ this pattern is consistent with SDelete filename scrubbing. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **DataOverwrite reason meaning** — The `DataOverwrite` reason indicates file content was altered. _Why:_ overwrite reasons are direct evidence of wiping behavior, not just renaming. _[GCFA p.819]_
- **DataOverwrite in first two journal entries** — The first two concrete journal events include `DataOverwrite`. _Why:_ the journal records both content overwrite and later metadata/name operations. _[GCFA p.819]_

## Page 820

### Windows Search Gather Logs

- **USN change journal dependency** — Windows Search uses the USN change journal to identify file-system changes efficiently. _Why:_ this creates a secondary artifact trail derived from file-system change activity. _[GCFA p.~820]_
- **Indexed-location requirement** — A changed file must reside in a location configured for indexing before Windows Search will add its path to the gather queue. _Why:_ gather logs are useful only for files inside indexed scope. _[GCFA p.~820]_
- **FANCI exclusion condition** — Files with the `FANCI` attribute bit set are excluded from content indexing. _Why:_ this attribute can explain why an expected file path may be absent from Windows Search artifacts. _[GCFA p.~820]_
- **FANCI meaning** — `FANCI` stands for `File Attribute Not Content Indexed`. _Why:_ the attribute name identifies files intentionally marked to avoid content indexing. _[GCFA p.~820]_
- **URI path queuing** — For eligible changed files, Windows Search adds their URI paths to the gather queue. _Why:_ queued URI paths can preserve evidence of file names and locations after other artifacts are deleted. _[GCFA p.~820]_
- **Gather logs as USN backup** — Windows Search gather logs can function as a partial backup source for USN journal activity. _Why:_ investigators may still recover file-change evidence when USN records are unavailable or incomplete. _[GCFA p.~820]_
- **Gather-log scope limitation** — Gather logs mainly help for files in indexed directories, especially user profile folders. _Why:_ this limits where investigators should expect useful gather-log coverage. _[GCFA p.~820]_

### Eraser Overview

- **Eraser · Tool category** — Eraser is identified as a common open-source data-wiping utility. _Why:_ tool family helps frame expected wiping behavior and likely forensic traces. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Eraser · Longevity** — Eraser has existed since 2003. _Why:_ long-lived tools may appear in older and newer investigations alike. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Eraser · Recommendations** — Eraser has been recommended by multiple organizations, including US-CERT. _Why:_ legitimate endorsement can explain benign presence while still requiring forensic scrutiny. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Eraser · NTFS journal exposure** — Eraser activity was visible in NTFS journals during testing. _Why:_ journal records can preserve evidence even when file content is wiped. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Eraser vs. BCWipe · Journal exposure similarity** — Eraser, like BCWipe, left observable traces in NTFS journals. _Why:_ investigators can use NTFS journals against multiple wiping tools, not only one product. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Eraser vs. BCWipe · $I30 slack difference** — Eraser did not clear deleted entries from $I30 directory-index slack in the tested scenario, unlike BCWipe. _Why:_ $I30 slack can retain deleted-name evidence after an attempted wipe. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Eraser · Parent directory index remnant** — Testing found at least one deleted-file entry remaining in the parent directory index. _Why:_ parent indexes can preserve traces of erased files. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Eraser · Random-name index remnant** — The deleted entry found in the parent index reflected the file after it had been renamed to a random name. _Why:_ even when the original name is gone, rename behavior can still indicate wiping. _[GCFA p.824]_

### Eraser MFT Effects

- **Eraser · Unallocated MFT persistence** — Unallocated MFT records remained after files were deleted with Eraser. _Why:_ remaining MFT records may still reveal wiping behavior or final filenames. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Eraser · Real-name final rename option** — Eraser includes an option to use a legitimate-looking filename for the final rename before deletion. _Why:_ this can make residual unallocated MFT records appear less suspicious. _[GCFA p.824]_

### Eraser Timestamp Effects

- **Eraser · Pre-deletion rename** — Eraser renamed files before deleting them. _Why:_ rename-before-delete behavior is a common wiper signature. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Wipers · General rename behavior** — The page states that virtually all wiping tools rename files before deletion. _Why:_ repeated rename events are a broad anti-forensic indicator. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Eraser · Timestamp modification** — Eraser changed file timestamps during wiping. _Why:_ timestamp anomalies can identify tool use even when content is gone. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Date Modified · `January 1, 1601`** — The screenshot’s Date Modified value is January 1, 1601. _Why:_ this date is the Windows FILETIME zero point. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Windows 64-bit timestamp zero · Meaning** — January 1, 1601 indicates a zeroed Windows 64-bit timestamp. _Why:_ null timestamps are a strong sign of metadata manipulation. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Eraser · $SI timestamp nulling** — Eraser overwrote all `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` timestamps with null values. _Why:_ $SI timestamp nulling removes normal timeline values but leaves a recognizable pattern. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Eraser · $FN timestamp nulling** — Eraser overwrote all `$FILE_NAME` timestamps with null values. _Why:_ $FN timestamp nulling shows the wiping affected both major NTFS timestamp sources. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Eraser · MFT entry-change side effect** — The metadata changes caused the MFT entry change time to update for the `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` attribute. _Why:_ the C-time can remain trustworthy when other timestamps are wiped. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Eraser · Valid C-time** — In testing, the `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` MFT entry change time was consistently valid. _Why:_ this timestamp may anchor the wiping event in the timeline. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Eraser · Other timestamp values** — All tested timestamps other than the valid C-time were set to January 1, 1601. _Why:_ a single valid C-time among zeroed timestamps is a distinctive artifact pattern. _[GCFA p.824]_

### Eraser Rename Count and Wipe Passes

- **Eraser · Default rename count** — By default, Eraser renames a file seven times before deletion. _Why:_ multiple rename events can be counted in NTFS journal evidence. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Seven renames · Historical origin** — The seven-renaming behavior reflects an older U.S. Department of Defense seven-pass wiping standard. _Why:_ legacy sanitization defaults can explain excessive rename activity. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Modern hard drives · Single-pass sufficiency** — Most experts consider one overwrite pass enough for modern magnetic hard drives because of storage density. _Why:_ multiple passes may be unnecessary yet still create additional forensic traces. _[GCFA p.824]_
- **Seven-pass behavior · Suspicious journal profile** — The seven-pass behavior makes NTFS journal records look more suspicious than a single rename would. _Why:_ excess rename churn can flag anti-forensic activity. _[GCFA p.824]_

### Cipher.exe Free-Space Wiping Artifacts

- **EFSTMPWP directory creation** — `EFSTMPWP` is created at the root of a volume the first time `cipher.exe` is run against that volume. _Why:_ this directory can mark prior cipher activity on a specific volume. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Volume-specific EFSTMPWP behavior** — the `EFSTMPWP` artifact is tied to the particular volume that was processed. _Why:_ investigators can associate the artifact with wiping activity on that volume rather than assuming system-wide execution. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Cipher cleansing process** — during its wiping operation, `cipher.exe` creates temporary files to consume free space with overwrite data. _Why:_ these temporary files explain how cipher attempts to remove recoverable deleted data from unallocated space. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Temporary file purpose** — the temporary files are used to fill the volume so free space is overwritten. _Why:_ this behavior can affect disk capacity, timeline artifacts, and recovery prospects. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Temporary file naming pattern `fil<xxxx>.tmp`** — test systems showed temporary files using the pattern `fil<xxxx>.tmp`. _Why:_ this filename pattern can be searched in file system artifacts, journals, and timelines. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **`<xxxx>` value format** — in the `fil<xxxx>.tmp` pattern, `<xxxx>` represents four pseudorandom alphanumeric characters. _Why:_ the variable component helps distinguish cipher-generated names from fixed indicators. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Temporary file naming pattern `<x>.E`** — tests also showed temporary files using the pattern `<x>.E`. _Why:_ this is another concrete filename pattern linked to cipher free-space wiping. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **`<x>` value sequence** — in the `<x>.E` pattern, `<x>` is an incrementing number. _Why:_ numeric sequencing can help reconstruct the tool’s temporary-file creation behavior. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **`<x>` initial value** — the `<x>.E` numbering begins at `0`. _Why:_ the starting value can help validate whether observed files match the documented cipher pattern. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Temporary file deletion** — after cipher completes, the temporary files created during wiping are deleted. _Why:_ investigators may need journals, metadata remnants, or timelines rather than live directory listings to find them. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **EFSTMPWP persistence after completion** — the `EFSTMPWP` directory remained after the temporary files were deleted. _Why:_ the leftover directory is a durable indicator even when the transient wipe files are gone. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Windows 10 test coverage** — cipher’s `EFSTMPWP` behavior was tested on Windows 10. _Why:_ the artifact was observed on a common workstation operating system. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Windows Server 2016 test coverage** — cipher’s `EFSTMPWP` behavior was tested on Windows Server 2016. _Why:_ the artifact was observed on a server operating system relevant to enterprise investigations. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Windows Server 2012 R2 test coverage** — cipher’s `EFSTMPWP` behavior was tested on Windows Server 2012 R2. _Why:_ the artifact was observed on an older server platform still encountered in investigations. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Post-test reboot validation** — each test system was rebooted after cipher execution. _Why:_ this checked whether `EFSTMPWP` survived beyond a single running session. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **EFSTMPWP persistence after reboot** — the `EFSTMPWP` directory remained present after reboot in the described testing. _Why:_ persistence across reboot increases its value as a forensic indicator. _[GCFA p.825]_

### Contradiction With Common Online Claims

- **Reported online claim** — some online articles describe `EFSTMPWP` as a temporary folder removed when `cipher.exe` finishes. _Why:_ investigators should not rely on that claim when evaluating real systems. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Courseware test finding** — across the described tests, `EFSTMPWP` was not removed when cipher completed. _Why:_ this finding makes the directory a possible persistent artifact of wiping activity. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Number of tests** — the observed persistence finding came from five tests. _Why:_ the behavior was not based on a single run. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Operating-system diversity** — the five tests covered multiple Windows operating systems. _Why:_ persistence was not limited to one Windows version in the reported testing. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Installation-type diversity** — the tests included both virtual and physical installations. _Why:_ the behavior was observed across different deployment environments. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Indicator-of-compromise value** — unexpected `EFSTMPWP` evidence may be useful as an indicator of compromise. _Why:_ attackers may use cipher as an anti-forensic cleanup step. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Unexpected EFSTMPWP condition** — `EFSTMPWP` is suspicious when its presence is not expected. _Why:_ context determines whether the artifact is benign or potentially tied to wiping. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **EFS context check** — `EFSTMPWP` is especially suspicious when Encrypting File System usage is not expected on the system. _Why:_ absent legitimate EFS context, cipher activity becomes a stronger investigative lead. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Cipher execution inference** — unexplained `EFSTMPWP` evidence should be treated as a possible sign that `cipher.exe` ran. _Why:_ it may indicate free-space wiping even when direct file targets are unavailable. _[GCFA p.825]_

### Evidence of Execution

- **Execution artifacts beyond the file system** — core evidence-of-execution artifacts are strong indicators of cipher use. _Why:_ file system artifacts alone may not fully prove execution. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Cipher populates both execution-artifact locations** — when cipher is used, both referenced evidence-of-execution locations are populated. _Why:_ investigators should check both locations for corroboration. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Execution-artifact reliability** — the page characterizes these execution artifacts as excellent indicators for cipher. _Why:_ they can support attribution of observed wiping artifacts to `cipher.exe`. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Cipher does not target individual files directly** — cipher’s wiping behavior is not run directly against specific files. _Why:_ investigators should not expect cipher artifacts to identify exact overwritten filenames by direct targeting. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Overwritten data ambiguity** — because cipher operates on free space rather than direct file targets, it is not obvious which deleted data was overwritten. _Why:_ this limits the precision of conclusions from cipher artifacts alone. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Cipher prefetch file-list limitation** — the parsed file list from cipher’s prefetch file is described as uninformative. _Why:_ prefetch may prove execution but may not reveal meaningful wipe targets. _[GCFA p.825]_

### Attacker Workflow and Investigative Approach

- **Common attacker workflow** — attackers commonly delete important files through ordinary deletion methods before running `cipher.exe`. _Why:_ normal deletion artifacts may identify targets that cipher later made harder to recover. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Cipher as final cleanup** — attackers often use `cipher.exe` as a final cleanup step after deleting files. _Why:_ cipher activity should be interpreted in the broader sequence of deletion and anti-forensic behavior. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Need for journal analysis** — journal analysis is recommended to determine what files and directories were deleted before being wiped. _Why:_ journals may preserve activity that cipher’s prefetch does not reveal. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Need for timeline analysis** — timeline analysis over a broader time range is recommended. _Why:_ a longer view can connect earlier deletions with later cipher free-space wiping. _[GCFA p.825]_
- **Deleted-file reconstruction goal** — the recommended analysis aims to identify files and directories that were deleted and eventually affected by cipher wiping. _Why:_ this is necessary because cipher does not directly disclose what data it overwrote. _[GCFA p.825]_

## Page 826

### Registry Structure And Deletion

- **Windows Registry** — Windows registry evidence is important enough in investigations that it should be treated as a core forensic source. _Why:_ registry artifacts often show user activity, application execution, and attempts to hide behavior. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Registry as database** — The registry functions like a database made up of stored records. _Why:_ deleted registry content can be reasoned about like deleted database records rather than ordinary text. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Registry records** — Registry records are represented primarily as keys and values. _Why:_ analysts recover and interpret these record types when examining hive slack or deleted registry material. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Registry hives and unused space** — Registry hive files can contain unallocated areas, comparable to unused space in a filesystem. _Why:_ deleted registry evidence may remain inside hive slack after deletion. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Deleted registry key state** — When a registry key is deleted, the hive marks that key’s storage as available rather than immediately erasing the content. _Why:_ the prior key data may remain recoverable until overwritten or compacted. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Deleted database-record behavior** — Deleted registry records are generally flagged as deleted first, not instantly destroyed. _Why:_ this delayed destruction creates an opportunity for forensic recovery. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Deleted data persistence** — Deleted registry data commonly remains present for some period after deletion. _Why:_ timing of acquisition can determine whether deleted keys and values are still available. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Space reuse limit** — Deleted registry material may disappear once the same hive space is reused for new records. _Why:_ later registry activity can overwrite evidence. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Hive compaction limit** — Registry compaction can remove deleted record remnants. _Why:_ compaction reduces or eliminates recoverable deleted registry artifacts. _[GCFA p.~826]_

### Recoverable Registry Content

- **Deleted key recovery** — Deleted hive keys may be recoverable from unallocated hive space. _Why:_ recovered keys can reveal prior configuration, activity, or cleanup attempts. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Deleted value recovery** — Registry values associated with deleted records may be recoverable. _Why:_ values often contain the actual evidence, such as command names, search terms, paths, or execution counts. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Timestamp recovery** — Deleted registry records can retain timestamp information. _Why:_ timestamps help place deleted activity on a timeline. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Associated-data recovery** — If a deleted key can be recovered, its related data often has a strong chance of recovery as well. _Why:_ this increases the evidentiary value of a recoverable deleted key beyond the key name alone. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Deleted keys retain case value** — Deleted keys commonly still contain information useful to an investigation, including values and time data. _Why:_ deleted registry material should not be dismissed as merely structural residue. _[GCFA p.~826]_

### Anti-Forensics And Privacy Cleaners

- **Deleted registry recovery use case** — Recovering deleted registry data can show that a user ran privacy-cleaning software. _Why:_ privacy-cleaner execution can indicate an effort to remove traces of activity. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Uninstall-coverup use case** — Deleted registry data can help show that programs were uninstalled to conceal prior activity. _Why:_ uninstall traces may remain even when the installed application is gone. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **BleachBit artifact context** — The screenshot shows deleted records from a user NTUSER.DAT hive after BleachBit was run. _Why:_ it demonstrates that privacy cleaning can leave recoverable registry evidence. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **BleachBit behavior** — BleachBit targets registry areas that are especially useful for forensic review. _Why:_ artifacts selected by privacy cleaners often identify high-value evidence categories. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **CCleaner comparison** — Testing with CCleaner showed similar registry-deletion effects. _Why:_ the recovery issue is not limited to BleachBit and applies to other privacy cleaners. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Other privacy cleaners** — Privacy-cleaning tools beyond BleachBit and CCleaner can produce comparable recoverable registry remnants. _Why:_ investigators should examine hive slack after any suspected privacy-cleaner use. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Registry wiping rarity** — Direct wiping of registry data is possible but is not commonly encountered. _Why:_ most cases may involve deletion or cleaner activity rather than full registry overwriting. _[GCFA p.~826]_

### Registry Explorer Tooling

- **Eric Zimmerman’s Registry Explorer** — Registry Explorer can present deleted registry keys and values for review. _Why:_ it reduces the difficulty of locating deleted hive records. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Registry Explorer ease of recovery** — The slide characterizes Registry Explorer as making deleted registry recovery straightforward. _Why:_ analysts can quickly inspect deleted records without manually carving all hive structures. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Deleted-entry presentation** — Registry Explorer provides a review-friendly view of deleted registry entries. _Why:_ usable presentation helps analysts validate deleted keys and values efficiently. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Multiple-tool availability** — More than one tool can display deleted registry keys and values. _Why:_ Registry Explorer is not the only possible analysis path, though it is highlighted. _[GCFA p.~826]_

### Targeted Registry Artifact Areas

- **WordWheelQuery** — WordWheelQuery is identified as a registry area containing keyword-search activity. _Why:_ recovered entries may reveal user searches that a cleaner attempted to remove. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **UserAssist** — UserAssist is identified as a registry area tracking GUI-launched applications. _Why:_ it can show program execution even after cleanup. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **ComDlg32** — ComDlg32 is identified as a registry area tied to Open/Save dialog usage. _Why:_ it can expose files and locations accessed through common Windows file dialogs. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **RecentDocs** — RecentDocs is identified as a registry area storing recently opened file information. _Why:_ it can reveal documents accessed before deletion or privacy cleaning. _[GCFA p.~826]_

### Transaction Logs And Shadow Copies

- **Registry transactional logs** — Prior registry data can sometimes be recovered from registry transaction logs after an overwrite. _Why:_ overwriting a hive record does not always eliminate older registry evidence. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Transactional-log persistence** — Registry transaction-log data may remain for days or weeks. _Why:_ older registry states can remain available well after the relevant registry change. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Activity-level dependency** — How long transaction-log remnants persist depends partly on system activity volume. _Why:_ busier systems may cycle or overwrite log evidence sooner. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Major-change dependency** — Large system changes, including Windows updates, can affect survival of transaction-log evidence. _Why:_ major updates may reduce the retention window for older registry information. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Volume Shadow Copy registry storage** — Volume shadow copies can contain copies of registry hive files. _Why:_ shadow copies may preserve earlier registry states even when live hives have changed. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Volume Shadow Copy transaction-log storage** — Volume shadow copies can also contain copies of registry transaction logs. _Why:_ analysts may recover deleted or overwritten registry evidence from historical log copies. _[GCFA p.~826]_
- **Shadow-copy recovery value** — Shadow copies expand the chance of recovering deleted or overwritten registry data. _Why:_ historical snapshots provide additional evidence sources beyond the active hive. _[GCFA p.~826]_

### Registry-Hidden Malware

- **Registry noise as concealment** — Attackers can bury malicious registry content among very large numbers of legitimate registry items. _Why:_ the artifact may remain present but be hard to notice during review. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Data recovery challenge** — Registry evidence may be difficult to find because it is hidden in volume, not because it has been removed. _Why:_ investigators should search for anomalous content, not only deleted records. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Registry-stored payloads** — Adversaries may place malicious payload material in obscure registry locations. _Why:_ registry persistence or staging can avoid obvious file-system artifacts. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Fileless malware pattern** — A common registry-abuse technique stores malicious scripts in the registry rather than as normal script files. _Why:_ this can reduce the number of conventional file artifacts available to investigators. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **PowerShell script storage** — PowerShell scripts are specifically highlighted as payloads commonly hidden in registry values. _Why:_ PowerShell can execute attacker logic and support command-and-control activity. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Command-and-control role** — Registry-hidden scripts may provide the logic used for controlling the compromised host. _Why:_ the registry value may contain operational malware code, not merely configuration. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Script bundled with launcher** — The malicious script can be embedded directly inside the PowerShell execution command. _Why:_ investigators may need to inspect command strings, not only separate payload locations. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Script stored separately** — The malicious script can also be stored in a different registry value from the launching command. _Why:_ separating launcher and payload increases obfuscation and requires cross-reference analysis. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Screenshot sample behavior** — The displayed sample shows a Base64-encoded script stored apart from the code that launches it. _Why:_ the payload and persistence trigger may appear in different registry locations. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Different registry caller** — The Base64 script in the screenshot is invoked from another registry location. _Why:_ finding the payload alone may not identify the persistence mechanism. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Run key launcher** — The example’s launch mechanism was stored in a Run key. _Why:_ Run keys are common persistence locations and should be checked when registry payloads are discovered. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **COMSPEC obfuscation** — The example adds another layer by invoking `%COMSPEC%` before PowerShell starts. _Why:_ command indirection can hide the true interpreter from quick inspection. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **COMSPEC meaning** — `%COMSPEC%` resolves to `cmd.exe`. _Why:_ investigators should treat `%COMSPEC%` as a command-shell execution indicator. _[GCFA p.827]_

### Registry Explorer Capabilities

- **Tool name** — Eric Zimmerman’s Registry Explorer is the tool shown and discussed. _Why:_ it provides targeted features for finding suspicious registry payloads. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Anomaly detection** — Registry Explorer can help surface unusual registry content. _Why:_ anomaly-oriented searching is useful when malicious data is hidden in normal registry volume. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Large value detection** — Registry Explorer can search for unusually large registry values. _Why:_ embedded scripts or payloads often require more data than ordinary configuration values. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Base64 value detection** — Registry Explorer can search for Base64-looking registry value data. _Why:_ encoded script content may be stored this way to hide readable commands. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Find feature** — The screenshot shows Registry Explorer’s `Find` function. _Why:_ this is the interface used to search targeted registry fields. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Searchable key names** — The Find feature can search registry key names. _Why:_ suspicious naming patterns may identify attacker-created keys. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Searchable value names** — The Find feature can search registry value names. _Why:_ attacker value names may be random, anomalous, or reused across systems. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Searchable value data** — The Find feature can search registry value contents. _Why:_ payload strings, commands, encodings, and URLs may be inside value data. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Searchable value slack** — The Find feature can search registry value slack space. _Why:_ remnants outside the active value data may retain useful evidence. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Value slack definition** — Value slack is the unused region between the end of registry value data and the end of that registry cell. _Why:_ slack may preserve prior or residual data. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Simple search mode** — Registry Explorer supports simple string searches. _Why:_ direct keyword searches can quickly locate obvious suspicious content. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Regex search mode** — Registry Explorer supports regular-expression searches. _Why:_ pattern searches help find encoded strings or families of related artifacts. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Time filtering** — Registry Explorer can filter by time ranges, though that control is not shown in the screenshot. _Why:_ date filtering narrows review to activity near the incident window. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Minimum-size filtering** — Registry Explorer can filter search results by a minimum registry value size. _Why:_ payload-like registry values can be prioritized over small normal settings. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Base64-size filtering** — Registry Explorer can search for Base64 data above a configured length. _Why:_ this helps distinguish meaningful encoded payloads from short benign strings. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Default thresholds** — The course notes say the default sizes are usually reasonable starting points for finding hidden scripts. _Why:_ investigators can begin with defaults before tuning thresholds. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **False positives** — Searches for large or encoded values are expected to produce some benign hits. _Why:_ analysts must validate results instead of treating every match as malicious. _[GCFA p.827]_
- **Time sorting** — Results can be sorted by timestamp. _Why:_ recent changes can be reviewed first during triage. _[GCFA p.827]_

### Deleted File Recovery Overview
- **Deleted data recovery interest** — Investigators usually want at least some deleted-data recovery regardless of whether a wiping tool was used. _Why:_ deleted content can preserve evidence even when anti-forensics is suspected. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Recovery complexity range** — Deleted-data recovery methods span from straightforward approaches to more specialized techniques. _Why:_ sets expectations that recovery work may require escalating from simple file recovery to advanced methods. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Whole-file recovery first** — The page presents whole deleted-file recovery before discussing more specialized recovery choices. _Why:_ whole-file recovery is the first practical recovery layer to evaluate. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Two main whole-file recovery methods** — Whole deleted files are primarily recovered either through filesystem metadata or through file carving. _Why:_ separates recovery strategy into metadata-driven and signature-driven approaches. _[GCFA p.828]_

### Metadata Method
- **Metadata method premise** — After deletion, a file’s metadata may be flagged as unused while the metadata record itself still exists. _Why:_ deleted metadata can still describe where the file content resides. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Metadata method action** — The examiner reads metadata records marked as deleted and retrieves data from the clusters referenced by those records. _Why:_ cluster pointers can allow precise reconstruction of the deleted file. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Metadata method preferred status** — Metadata-based recovery is the best whole-file recovery option when the relevant metadata remains available. _Why:_ it can recover the file using the filesystem’s own record of the file layout. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Metadata marked deleted** — The filesystem metadata may show the file as deleted even though its descriptive record and data pointers remain present. _Why:_ deleted status does not necessarily mean evidentiary metadata is gone. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Cluster reuse dependency** — Metadata recovery can restore the original whole file if the file’s clusters have not been reused. _Why:_ reused clusters can overwrite the original file content. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Exact prior-state recovery** — If metadata and clusters are intact, metadata recovery can reproduce the deleted file as it existed before deletion. _Why:_ this is stronger evidence than a partial or inferred reconstruction. _[GCFA p.828]_

### Carving Method
- **Carving method trigger** — File carving becomes necessary when the file’s metadata entry has been reused or overwritten. _Why:_ without usable metadata, the examiner must locate content by other means. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Residual data after metadata reuse** — Even after a metadata record is reused, the file’s data may still remain somewhere on disk. _Why:_ data content can outlive the filesystem record that previously described it. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Carving search requirement** — When metadata no longer points to the file, investigators must search storage content directly. _Why:_ recovery shifts from record-based extraction to content discovery. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Carving signature use** — File carving relies on known file signatures to identify the beginning of candidate files. _Why:_ signatures provide type-specific byte patterns for locating deleted files. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Carving extraction endpoint by footer** — A carved file may be extracted until a known file footer is reached. _Why:_ footers can identify where a recovered file should end. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Carving extraction endpoint by size limit** — A carved file may instead be extracted up to a reasonable configured size boundary. _Why:_ size limits prevent uncontrolled extraction when no reliable footer is available. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Carving target area** — File carving uses signatures of known file types to search unallocated clusters for deleted files. _Why:_ unallocated space may still contain deleted file content. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Cluster-start scanning** — Carving tools are commonly configured to look for known signatures at the beginning of clusters. _Why:_ file content often starts on cluster boundaries in filesystem storage. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Carving extraction action** — When a configured signature is found, the tool extracts the associated bytes as a candidate file. _Why:_ carving converts raw unallocated data into reviewable recovered files. _[GCFA p.828]_

### File Signatures
- **File signature definition** — A file signature, also called a magic number, is a byte sequence near the start of a file that identifies a file type. _Why:_ signatures allow type-based recovery without filesystem metadata. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Signature uniqueness by type** — File signatures are treated as distinctive byte patterns for particular file types. _Why:_ type-specific signatures reduce ambiguity during carving. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Windows executable signature value** — Windows executable files are described as beginning with the value `0x4d5a9000`. _Why:_ this byte pattern is a concrete carving target for executable recovery. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Windows executable ASCII marker** — The first two bytes of the Windows executable signature correspond to ASCII `MZ`. _Why:_ `MZ` is a recognizable indicator of a PE-style executable. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Executable carving match** — A carver configured for executable recovery searches unused clusters for the exact executable signature sequence. _Why:_ exact signature matching is how the tool identifies candidate deleted executables. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Executable carving size rule** — For executable recovery, extraction may use a configured maximum length for that file type. _Why:_ max-length rules bound recovery when file termination is uncertain. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Executable carving footer rule** — For executable recovery, extraction may stop when the tool finds a known footer for that file type. _Why:_ footer recognition can produce a cleaner recovered file boundary. _[GCFA p.828]_

### Reliability and Limitations
- **Carving false positives** — File carving can produce many false positives depending on the target data and search location. _Why:_ recovered candidates may not all be valid evidence-bearing files. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Search target affects accuracy** — The type of file being searched for influences the false-positive rate. _Why:_ some signatures or formats are more prone to accidental matches. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Search location affects accuracy** — The storage source being carved influences the false-positive rate. _Why:_ different sources have different fragmentation and data-layout characteristics. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **SSD fragmentation issue** — Solid-state drives are described as highly fragmented for carving purposes. _Why:_ fragmentation can prevent whole-file reconstruction from contiguous data assumptions. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **SSD unallocated carving result** — Carving full files from SSD unallocated space often produces many partial-file recoveries. _Why:_ partial results require careful review and may not prove complete file content. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Memory image carving result** — Carving files from memory images also commonly produces partial-file recoveries. _Why:_ memory does not preserve files in clean filesystem order. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Memory carving reliability comparison** — Partial-file recovery is even more pronounced in memory-image carving than in SSD unallocated-space carving. _Why:_ memory carving is especially likely to yield incomplete artifacts. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Mechanical drive reliability** — Carving results from mechanical drives are generally more dependable than from SSDs or memory images. _Why:_ less problematic fragmentation can improve whole-file carving outcomes. _[GCFA p.828]_

### Investigative Workflow Guidance
- **Carving not first step** — File carving should not be treated as the initial investigative move. _Why:_ it is expensive and should be driven by case needs. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Carving time cost** — The carving process itself can consume significant time. _Why:_ investigators must budget analysis time and avoid broad unnecessary carving. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Review time cost** — Reviewing carved output can also consume significant time. _Why:_ large numbers of recovered candidates and false positives can slow analysis. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Case understanding requirement** — Effective carving requires understanding the facts and needs of the case. _Why:_ case context determines which recovered data would be probative. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Targeted file-type selection** — Investigators should carve only file types that are especially relevant to the matter under investigation. _Why:_ targeted recovery reduces noise and analyst workload. _[GCFA p.828]_

### Files to Target
- **Target selection principle** — The file types worth targeting are generally dependent on the case. _Why:_ relevant evidence varies by intrusion, user activity, and investigative question. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Link files as targets** — Windows shortcut/link files are listed as possible recovery targets. _Why:_ link files can reveal file access, paths, and user interaction. _[GCFA p.828]_

- **Web history as target** — Browser history is listed as a possible recovery target. _Why:_ web activity can explain downloads, staging, research, and exfiltration behavior. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Prefetch as target** — Prefetch files are listed as possible recovery targets. _Why:_ they can show program execution evidence. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Binaries as targets** — Executable binaries are listed as possible recovery targets. _Why:_ recovered binaries can identify malware, tools, or unauthorized programs. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Scripts as targets** — Scripts are listed as possible recovery targets. _Why:_ scripts can reveal attacker automation, commands, and logic. _[GCFA p.828]_
- **Archives as targets** — Archive files are listed as possible recovery targets. _Why:_ archives can contain staged tools, compressed evidence, or packaged exfiltration data. _[GCFA p.828]_

- **CAD drawings as targets** — CAD drawing files are listed as possible recovery targets. _Why:_ CAD files can represent sensitive intellectual property or engineering data. _[GCFA p.828]_

## Page 829

### Baseline Windows Investigation File Targets

- **Shortcut files (.lnk)** — Windows shortcut files are commonly relevant in many Windows forensic investigations. _Why:_ they can preserve evidence of user interaction with files, folders, applications, and paths. _[GCFA p.829]_
- **Prefetch files (.pf)** — Windows Prefetch files are a routinely useful operating-system artifact type in Windows investigations. _Why:_ they can help identify program execution activity, including execution that may no longer be visible through the original executable. _[GCFA p.829]_
- **Recycle Bin metadata files ($I)** — Recycle Bin `$I` metadata files are a standard file type to consider in Windows investigations. _Why:_ they can retain metadata about deleted files, supporting recovery of deletion context. _[GCFA p.829]_
- **Executables** — Executable files are often relevant evidence, particularly in intrusion investigations. _Why:_ malware, attacker tools, and legitimate binaries used during compromise may all appear as executable artifacts. _[GCFA p.829]_

### Case-Driven File Selection

- **Additional target files by case type** — After collecting generally useful Windows artifacts, investigators usually choose extra file types based on the investigation scenario. _Why:_ case context determines which deleted or retained files are most probative. _[GCFA p.829]_
- **Deleted processes** — Many investigations, including network intrusion cases, should look for evidence of processes that were deleted. _Why:_ attackers may remove tools after execution, leaving secondary artifacts behind. _[GCFA p.829]_
- **Scripts** — Scripts are a file category of interest in many investigations, including network intrusions. _Why:_ scripts may show automation, attacker commands, staging activity, or post-exploitation behavior. _[GCFA p.829]_
- **Archives** — Archive files are often worth targeting during forensic review. _Why:_ archives may contain bundled tools, staged data, or collected victim files. _[GCFA p.829]_
- **Encrypted archives** — Encrypted archive files are specifically called out as relevant. _Why:_ they are commonly used to package data for exfiltration or to hide downloaded tools. _[GCFA p.829]_
- **Archives for exfiltration** — Encrypted archives may be used to prepare data for removal from a victim environment. _Why:_ their presence can indicate collection and staging before data theft. _[GCFA p.829]_
- **Archives for covert tool transfer** — Encrypted archives may also be used to bring tools onto a system discreetly. _Why:_ encryption can conceal contents from casual inspection and some security controls. _[GCFA p.829]_

### Exfiltration-Oriented File Targets

- **Collected exfiltration files** — Investigators may search for signs that files were gathered and later deleted for exfiltration. _Why:_ deleted staging artifacts can reveal what data an attacker intended to steal. _[GCFA p.829]_
- **Office documents** — Office document files are examples of possible exfiltration targets. _Why:_ they may contain business records, sensitive communications, or other valuable data. _[GCFA p.829]_
- **Spreadsheets** — Spreadsheet files are another possible target category when looking for collected and deleted exfiltration data. _Why:_ spreadsheets often contain structured business, financial, operational, or credential-adjacent information. _[GCFA p.829]_
- **Engineering design files** — Engineering design files are identified as possible exfiltration targets. _Why:_ they may contain intellectual property or sensitive technical designs. _[GCFA p.829]_

### Content-Investigation File Targets

- **Images in child exploitation cases** — Image files are likely targets in child exploitation investigations. _Why:_ they may constitute direct evidence of illegal content possession, access, or distribution. _[GCFA p.829]_
- **Videos in child exploitation cases** — Video files are likely targets in child exploitation investigations. _Why:_ they may contain direct evidence relevant to the alleged activity. _[GCFA p.829]_
- **Images in inappropriate Internet usage cases** — Image files are likely targets in corporate inappropriate Internet usage investigations. _Why:_ they may document policy violations or user activity relevant to the allegation. _[GCFA p.829]_
- **Videos in inappropriate Internet usage cases** — Video files are likely targets in corporate inappropriate Internet usage investigations. _Why:_ they may preserve content evidence tied to policy or misconduct review. _[GCFA p.829]_

## Page 830

### Metadata-Based Deleted File Recovery

- **Metadata recovery method** — Deleted files may be recovered by using surviving filesystem metadata that still points to their data clusters. _Why:_ intact metadata can allow exact file extraction without file carving. _[GCFA p.830]_
- **Metadata entry requirement** — A deleted file’s metadata record must remain unused for metadata-based recovery to work cleanly. _Why:_ if the record has been reused, the original file references may no longer be reliable. _[GCFA p.830]_
- **Cluster availability requirement** — The data clusters referenced by the deleted file’s metadata must also remain unused. _Why:_ overwritten clusters can corrupt or prevent recovery even when metadata still exists. _[GCFA p.830]_
- **Disk forensic tool behavior** — Many disk forensic suites can search for unallocated metadata entries and export data from the clusters those entries reference. _Why:_ this is a common workflow for recovering deleted files from filesystem metadata. _[GCFA p.830]_
- **MFT unallocated-entry search** — Forensic tools can identify Master File Table records marked unallocated. _Why:_ unallocated MFT records may still describe deleted files. _[GCFA p.830]_
- **Deleted-file export from MFT entries** — Tools may export deleted files by following the cluster references stored in unallocated MFT entries. _Why:_ this allows recovery without scanning the entire disk for signatures. _[GCFA p.830]_
- **Cluster cross-validation** — Forensic tools can check whether another file has claimed clusters formerly associated with a deleted file. _Why:_ this helps determine whether recovered data is still trustworthy. _[GCFA p.830]_
- **Reallocation warning** — Tools may report wording such as “realloc” or “reallocated” when a deleted file’s clusters have been reused. _Why:_ this warns the examiner that the recovered file may be incomplete or contaminated. _[GCFA p.830]_
- **Partial-cluster reuse** — Only some clusters of a deleted file may have been reused. _Why:_ remaining clusters can still preserve useful fragments. _[GCFA p.830]_
- **Fragmentary recovery value** — Even an incomplete recovered file fragment can have investigative value. _Why:_ partial content may still reveal filenames, payloads, configuration, commands, or other evidence. _[GCFA p.830]_

- **The Sleuth Kit** — The page identifies The Sleuth Kit as providing straightforward deleted-file recovery using metadata. _Why:_ it names a standard forensic toolkit for this recovery method. _[GCFA p.830]_
- **icat** — `icat` can recover a deleted file when the examiner supplies the image and a specific inode or MFT entry number. _Why:_ it supports targeted recovery of one file at a time. _[GCFA p.830]_
